choices: Distant supernovae appeared dimmer than expected, implying the cosmic expansion is speeding up
Galaxies were found rotating faster at their edges than their visible mass allows
The Sun's neutrino output was measured to be lower than predicted
Light from distant stars was seen bending around the Sun during an eclipse

quiz.q: What is the name for the simplest candidate explanation of dark energy, a constant vacuum energy term Einstein originally introduced into his field equations?

media.caption: The energy budget of the universe: dark energy about 68%, dark matter 27%, ordinary matter only 5%.

cards.title: Gutenberg's printing press (~1440)
cards.fact: Cheap printed books in the 1400s helped trigger the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.
cards.detail: Movable-type printing in Europe (~1440) collapsed the cost of copying text. Literacy spread, ideas travelled faster than authorities could suppress them, and standardised knowledge accumulated. A scribe copying a book by hand took a year or more and had to be paid for that whole time; a print shop could spread that labour across a run of hundreds of copies, cutting the cost per book by one to two orders of magnitude. Luther's 95 Theses spread across Germany in about two weeks in 1517 because printers reprinted them faster than the Church could respond.
cards.deploy: Information technology reshapes who holds power — a historical anchor for arguments about the printing press / internet / AI.
cards.counter: Printing predates Gutenberg in East Asia (Bi Sheng's movable type ~1040, Korean metal type earlier). His contribution was the European system and its economics, not the raw idea.

quiz.q: Whose movable-type printing in East Asia, around 1040, predates the European press by roughly four centuries?
Which historical development is most directly credited to the spread of cheap printed books in 1400s Europe?
choices: The Protestant Reformation, as dissenting ideas spread faster than authorities could suppress them
The fall of the Western Roman Empire to invading tribes
The construction of the first Gothic cathedrals across France
The establishment of the first transatlantic trade routes to the Americas

quiz.q: If the European movable-type press dates to about 1440 and Bi Sheng's movable type in China to about 1040, how many years earlier was the Chinese invention?

cards.title: The Black Death (1347–1351)
cards.fact: A plague that killed a third or more of Europe also raised the wages of those who survived.
cards.detail: With labour suddenly scarce, surviving workers could demand more, accelerating the decline of serfdom in parts of Western Europe. Catastrophe restructured the economy. The mechanism is supply and demand for labour: when a third of workers die but the land and tools remain, each surviving worker is scarcer and can hold out for higher pay. English real farm wages roughly doubled over the century from 1350 to 1450, even after landlords pushed laws like the Statute of Labourers (1351) to cap them at pre-plague rates; that the cap failed shows how far bargaining power had shifted.
cards.deploy: Shocks can shift the balance of power between labour and capital — scarcity changes bargaining position.
cards.counter: The 'wages rose' story varies sharply by region and institutions; in places elites tightened controls instead. Single mechanisms oversimplify.

quiz.q: Why did wages rise for surviving workers in parts of Western Europe after the Black Death?
choices: Labour became scarce, so survivors could demand more for their work
Governments passed laws mandating higher minimum pay for peasants
A flood of New World silver inflated all prices and wages together
Surviving workers were better educated and thus more productive

quiz.q: If a region had 6 million people before the Black Death and the plague killed one third of them, roughly how many people survived?
The bargaining power of surviving labourers helped accelerate the decline of which medieval system that bound peasants to a lord's land?

cards.title: The Peace of Westphalia (1648)
cards.fact: The 1648 treaties ending the Thirty Years' War are often called the birth of the sovereign state.
cards.detail: They're cited as the origin of 'Westphalian sovereignty' — the principle that states are supreme within their own borders and don't answer to outside authority. The two treaties were signed in 1648 at Munster and Osnabruck, and confirmed that rulers within the Holy Roman Empire could set their territory's religion, the principle cuius regio, eius religio carried over from the 1555 Peace of Augsburg and now extended to Calvinism. The leap from that religious settlement to a general theory of state sovereignty is what Osiander disputes.
cards.deploy: A foundational reference for debates about national sovereignty vs international intervention.
cards.counter: Historians (e.g. Andreas Osiander) argue the 'Westphalian myth' is a 19th-century back-projection; the treaties didn't actually establish modern sovereignty as commonly claimed.

quiz.q: What principle, named after the 1648 treaties, holds that a state is the supreme authority within its own borders and answers to no outside power?
The Thirty Years' War ended with the 1648 treaties. In what year did that war begin?
What is the central claim of historians like Andreas Osiander who speak of a 'Westphalian myth'?
choices: The treaties did not actually establish modern sovereignty; that reading is a later back-projection
The treaties were never signed and the war continued for decades afterward
The treaties created a single European empire rather than separate states
The treaties applied only to maritime law and not to land borders

cards.title: The Thucydides Trap
cards.fact: When a rising power threatens a ruling one, the result is often war.
cards.detail: Graham Allison studied 16 cases over 500 years and found war in 12. Named after Thucydides' line that it was the rise of Athens, and the fear it caused in Sparta, that made war inevitable. Applied today to the US and China.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for great-power-rivalry arguments — names the mechanism (fear of a shifting balance).
cards.counter: Beyond the contested case selection (4 of 16 avoided war, and 'often' is not 'inevitable'), the frame itself is disputed: Xi Jinping flatly rejects it — 'there is no Thucydides Trap' — and liberal and constructivist scholars argue deep economic interdependence and nuclear deterrence make structural war far from fated. Reaching for the 'trap' already takes the anxious US vantage point as the neutral one.

quiz.q: A historian replicates the Thucydides Trap method on a new dataset of 25 rising-power-vs-ruling-power cases and finds the same war rate Graham Allison reported (war in 12 of 16). To the nearest whole number, how many of the 25 cases would end in war?
In the original ancient analogy, which rising power's growth and the fear it provoked was said to make war with Sparta unavoidable?
Which objection to the Thucydides Trap rests on conditions specific to the modern era rather than on disputing how the 16 historical cases were counted?
choices: Deep economic interdependence and nuclear deterrence make a structural war between great powers far from fated
Only 12 of the 16 cases actually ended in war, so the pattern is weaker than claimed
The set of 16 cases was chosen in a way that biases the result
The word 'often' was overstated into 'inevitable'

cards.title: Chokepoint: the Strait of Hormuz
cards.fact: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through one narrow strait.
cards.detail: About 20–21 million barrels a day move through the Strait of Hormuz between the Persian Gulf and open ocean — a single point of geographic leverage. At its narrowest the strait is about 54 km (29 nautical miles) wide, but ships are funnelled into two traffic lanes only about 3 km across, one inbound and one outbound, so there is little room to route around trouble. Qatar's gas and most Gulf crude have no full pipeline alternative to this sea route, which is why a closure scare moves oil prices within hours.
cards.deploy: Physical geography concentrates strategic power — concrete grounding for arguments about energy security.
cards.counter: Shares and volumes shift; new pipelines and changing demand steadily reduce any one chokepoint's leverage.

quiz.q: If about 20 million barrels of oil pass through the Strait of Hormuz each day and global oil consumption is roughly 100 million barrels per day, what percentage of world oil consumption transits the strait?
The Strait of Hormuz connects the open ocean to which body of water bordered by major oil exporters?
Why does the strategic leverage of a maritime chokepoint like Hormuz tend to weaken over time?
choices: New pipelines and shifting demand reroute flows around the single point
Narrow straits gradually widen through erosion, easing congestion
International law eventually bans any state from interdicting shipping there
Oil tankers are steadily replaced by smaller vessels that need no strait

cards.title: Mackinder's Heartland theory (1904)
cards.fact: Whoever controls the Eurasian 'Heartland' could dominate the world — a classic land-power doctrine.
cards.detail: Halford Mackinder argued that control of inner Eurasia (the 'World-Island') was the key to global power, because it was beyond the reach of sea power. His slogan put it in three steps: who rules East Europe commands the Heartland, who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island (Eurasia plus Africa), and who rules the World-Island commands the world. The Heartland he meant is the inner Eurasian zone, roughly east of the Volga and north of the Himalayas, whose rivers drain to the frozen Arctic or to landlocked seas and so cannot be reached by a navy.
cards.deploy: The founding lens of geopolitical 'land power vs sea power' thinking — still echoed in analyses of Russia and Central Asia.
cards.counter: Airpower, nuclear weapons, and globalised trade undercut pure land-centric determinism; geography constrains but doesn't dictate.

quiz.q: Who formulated the 1904 theory that whoever controls inner Eurasia controls the world?
What was Mackinder's core reasoning for why the Eurasian Heartland was the pivot of world power?
choices: It lay beyond the reach of sea power, making it a secure base for land power
It held the largest share of the world's oil and gas reserves
Its coastlines gave the easiest access to global maritime trade routes
Its dense population could field the world's largest navy

quiz.q: Mackinder gave the great Eurasian landmass a name to capture its size and centrality. What did he call it?

cards.title: Rimland: the reply to Heartland
cards.fact: The rival to Heartland theory: control the coastal 'rim' of Eurasia, not its core.
cards.detail: Nicholas Spykman (1940s) inverted Mackinder: power lies not in the inaccessible Eurasian Heartland but in the 'Rimland' — the densely populated coastal fringe (Europe, the Middle East, South and East Asia). 'Who controls the Rimland rules Eurasia.' It shaped US Cold War containment, which ringed the Soviet and Chinese landmass with alliances and bases.
cards.deploy: Decodes US grand strategy: containment and the alliance network around Eurasia's rim are Rimland thinking in action.
cards.counter: It's a doctrine, not a law — air power, nuclear weapons and economics complicate any neat 'geography decides power' story. It also has a target's-eye flip side: what Washington calls 'containment', Moscow and Beijing read as hostile encirclement, and revisionist historians (the Wisconsin School around William Appleman Williams) cast US Cold War strategy as expansionist, not merely defensive.

quiz.q: Spykman's Rimland theory says power lies in…
choices: The Eurasian interior
Eurasia's populated coastal fringe
The polar regions
Outer space

quiz.q: Which strategist argued in the 1940s that power lay in Eurasia's coastal fringe rather than its core?
Which US Cold War policy is best understood as Rimland theory put into practice?
choices: Containment, ringing the Soviet and Chinese landmass with alliances and bases
Massive retaliation, threatening nuclear strikes against any aggression
Detente, easing tensions through arms-control treaties
Non-alignment, avoiding commitments to either bloc

quiz.q: A revisionist (Wisconsin School) reading of US Cold War strategy reframes the same alliance network around Eurasia's rim as what, rather than as defensive containment?
choices: An expansionist project, read from Moscow and Beijing as hostile encirclement
A purely economic free-trade arrangement with no military purpose
An accidental byproduct of decolonization with no grand design
A short-lived experiment quickly abandoned after 1950

cards.title: The security dilemma
cards.fact: Arming to feel safer can make everyone less safe — the 'security dilemma'.
cards.detail: Even with no aggressive intent, one state's defensive build-up looks threatening to others, who arm in response, leaving all less secure — a spiral driven by fear and uncertainty about intentions (Herz, 1950; Jervis). It's a core reason rising-power tensions (the Thucydides Trap) can escalate without anyone actually wanting war.
cards.deploy: Explains how war can come from fear, not aggression — and why signalling restraint and intentions matters so much.
cards.counter: It's not inevitable: arms control, transparency, and clearly non-threatening 'defensive' postures can defuse the spiral; not every build-up is misread.

quiz.q: The 'security dilemma' is when…
choices: A state is invaded
Defensive arming makes others feel threatened, spiralling insecurity
Two states form an alliance
A war ends

quiz.q: Country A doubles its missile-defence and naval forces purely to feel safer, with no plans to attack anyone. Country B sees this and races to build up its own forces, and now both feel more threatened than before. This outcome is the central mechanism of which concept?
choices: The security dilemma
Mutually assured destruction
Comparative advantage
The democratic peace

quiz.q: What single emotion, combined with uncertainty about others' true intentions, does the card identify as the main driver that turns one state's defensive build-up into an escalating arms spiral?
Which measure is LEAST likely to defuse a security-dilemma spiral between two states?
choices: Secretly accelerating a weapons programme while denying it
Signing a verifiable arms-control treaty
Increasing transparency about military deployments
Adopting a visibly defensive, non-threatening posture

cards.title: The Malacca dilemma
cards.fact: Most of East Asia's oil squeezes through one narrow strait — the 'Malacca dilemma'.
cards.detail: The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, is the world's busiest — around 80% of China's imported crude passes through it, plus much of Japan's and Korea's trade. China's reliance on a single chokepoint a rival navy could blockade is its 'Malacca dilemma' (Hu Jintao's term, 2003), and a driver of overland pipelines, a bigger navy and the Belt and Road.
cards.deploy: A concrete lens on China's strategy: much of its energy security hangs on a strait it doesn't control.
cards.counter: A blockade would be an act of war with huge costs to all sides, so the vulnerability is more strategic anxiety than likely event — and alternatives (pipelines, reserves) are being built.

quiz.q: The 'Malacca dilemma' refers to…
choices: A border war
East Asia's reliance on one strait for oil and trade
A trade treaty
An oil price cap

quiz.q: A country imports 12 million barrels of crude oil per day, and 80% of it passes through a single strait. How many million barrels per day flow through that strait?
Which two countries border the Strait of Malacca, through which roughly 80% of China's imported crude oil passes?
Building overland pipelines, expanding the navy, and pursuing the Belt and Road Initiative are best understood as China's attempts to do what?
choices: Reduce dependence on a single maritime chokepoint a rival navy could blockade
Increase the share of oil shipped through the Strait of Malacca
Lower its total demand for imported energy
Avoid building strategic petroleum reserves

cards.title: When populations shrink
cards.fact: The demographic transition's final twist: much of the world is now ageing and shrinking.
cards.detail: Past the transition, fertility in many countries has fallen below replacement (~2.1). Japan, South Korea, much of Europe and now China face ageing and then shrinking populations — fewer workers supporting more retirees, strained pensions and slower growth. South Korea's fertility (~0.7) is the world's lowest. Migration can offset it but is politically fraught.
cards.deploy: Reframes the population debate: for a growing share of the world the worry is too few people, not too many.
cards.counter: It's uneven — much of sub-Saharan Africa is still growing fast — and forecasts are uncertain. The 'crisis' framing is also contested: degrowth and ecological economists (Jason Hickel) argue a smaller population eases planetary limits and isn't inherently catastrophic, and feminist demographers warn that 'too few babies' rhetoric instrumentalises women's fertility and fuels coercive pronatalism. Whether decline is a problem depends on whether endless growth is the goal.

quiz.q: Below-replacement fertility leads to…
choices: Endless growth
Ageing and eventually shrinking populations
No change
More children per family

quiz.q: If each woman has on average 0.7 children over her lifetime, then for every 1000 women in one generation, roughly how many daughters are born in the next (assuming about half of births are girls)?
A country's total fertility rate sits steadily at 1.4 children per woman, with little migration. What is the most likely long-run demographic outcome?
choices: The population ages and then shrinks
The population grows steadily
The population stays exactly constant
Child mortality rises sharply

quiz.q: Which region does the card cite as the main exception to global population decline because its population is still growing fast?

cards.title: The demographic transition
cards.fact: As countries develop, they shift from high birth-and-death rates to low — then they age.
cards.detail: Falling child mortality and development first cause a population boom, then birth rates fall and the population stabilises and greys, raising the ratio of retirees to workers. A country can swing from around 6 workers per retiree to nearer 2 within a few decades, which is why pension and healthcare costs rise even when the total population is flat. Japan dropped below 2 working-age people per person over 65 around 2021, and China is moving the same way after its sharp fall in birth rates.
cards.deploy: Explains why growth slows and why ageing (China, Japan, Europe) reshapes economies and pensions.
cards.counter: Trajectories vary widely; immigration, policy, and culture can speed up, slow down, or reverse parts of the transition.

quiz.q: In the demographic transition, why does a population typically boom BEFORE birth rates fall?
choices: Death rates (especially child mortality) drop first, while birth rates stay high for a while
Birth rates rise sharply before death rates change
Immigration always surges at the start of development
Retirees suddenly outnumber workers early on

quiz.q: In a small town there are 600 working-age adults and 150 retirees. What is the ratio of retirees to workers, expressed as retirees per worker?
What word describes the late stage of the demographic transition in which the share of older people rises and the population 'greys'?

cards.title: Natural selection
cards.fact: Heritable variation plus differential survival produces design without a designer.
cards.detail: Darwin (1859): organisms vary, some variations are inherited, and those that aid survival and reproduction become more common over generations — yielding apparent design. A worked case: in a population of bacteria, a few cells carry a mutation that resists an antibiotic. Add the drug and the non-resistant cells die while the resistant ones reproduce, so within a few generations the whole population is resistant. No cell tried to adapt; the drug just sorted the variation that was already there.
cards.deploy: Complexity can arise from blind, cumulative processes — the canonical answer to 'it looks designed, so it was designed'.
cards.counter: Selection is one mechanism among several. Genetic drift, gene flow, and sheer contingency also shape evolution; not every trait is an adaptation.

quiz.q: Natural selection requires variation that is…
choices: Acquired in a lifetime
Heritable
Always beneficial
Identical in all individuals

quiz.q: A population of cave fish lives in total darkness for thousands of generations and gradually loses its eyes. Which option best explains how natural selection could drive this loss?
choices: Eyes are costly to build, so individuals born with reduced eyes left more offspring in the dark
The fish consciously stopped using their eyes, so the trait faded
Living in darkness directly damaged the eye genes of each individual fish
An external designer optimized the fish for cave life

quiz.q: Name the 19th-century naturalist whose 1859 book set out the theory that heritable variation plus differential survival produces apparent design.
Why is 'this trait helps the organism, so it must be an adaptation built by selection' an unreliable inference?
choices: Traits can also spread by drift, gene flow, or contingency, so not every helpful-looking trait was shaped by selection
Selection never produces helpful traits, only harmful ones
Adaptations always reduce an organism's survival
Heritable variation plays no role in evolution

cards.title: You're about half bacteria (by cell count)
cards.fact: Your body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — about 1:1, not the old '10:1'.
cards.detail: A 2016 re-estimate put it near 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells. The widely-repeated '10 times more bacteria than your own cells' was never well-founded. Most of those bacteria sit in the large intestine, so a single bowel movement can drop the count by a noticeable fraction, which is part of why any 1:1 figure is a rough average rather than a fixed number. The 2016 estimate by Sender, Fuchs, and Milo also found that bacterial cells are far smaller than human cells, so by mass your microbes add up to only about 200 grams, not half of you.
cards.deploy: Doubles as a fact and a myth-correction — a clean way to show how a 'known' figure can be wrong.
cards.counter: These are estimates with wide ranges and they vary person to person; function matters more than raw counts.

quiz.q: If a person has about 36 trillion bacterial cells and 30 trillion human cells, what is the ratio of bacterial to human cells, rounded to one decimal place?
The popular claim that the human body holds '10 times more bacteria than its own cells' was overturned by a 2016 re-estimate. What did the corrected figure show?
choices: The numbers of bacterial and human cells are roughly equal, about 1 to 1
Human cells outnumber bacteria by about 10 to 1
There are essentially no bacterial cells in a healthy body
Bacteria outnumber human cells by about 100 to 1

quiz.q: Beyond raw cell counts, what do scientists say matters more for the body's bacteria, given that counts vary widely between people?

cards.title: CRISPR: programmable gene editing
cards.fact: Since 2012 we've been able to cut and edit DNA at a chosen spot, cheaply and precisely.
cards.detail: Doudna and Charpentier showed the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 system can be guided by a custom RNA to cut DNA wherever you point it (Nobel Prize 2020). It transformed biotech almost overnight. The guide RNA works by base-pairing: you write a roughly 20-letter RNA sequence that matches the DNA target, Cas9 carries it along, and the enzyme cuts only where the RNA finds its complementary stretch. So editing a new gene means swapping in a new 20-letter guide instead of engineering a whole new protein, which is why it got cheap fast.
cards.deploy: Cheap, precise editing changes every debate about medicine, agriculture, and 'designer' organisms.
cards.counter: Off-target edits and the ethics of heritable (germline) changes remain serious, unresolved caveats.

quiz.q: In the CRISPR-Cas9 system, what type of guide molecule is customized to direct the Cas9 protein to cut DNA at a chosen location?
CRISPR gene editing was demonstrated in 2012 and its developers won the Nobel Prize in 2020. How many years passed between the demonstration and the Nobel award?
Which concern is the most serious unresolved caveat specifically tied to making CRISPR edits that would be passed on to a person's children?
choices: Heritable germline edits raise unresolved ethical questions because the changes affect future generations who cannot consent
The edits are far too expensive to ever attempt in humans
Cas9 can only cut RNA, never DNA, so the edits do not last
Germline edits are guaranteed to be perfectly accurate, removing all risk

cards.title: Evolution by pure chance
cards.fact: Evolution isn't only survival of the fittest — pure chance ('genetic drift') also shapes which genes survive.
cards.detail: Beyond selection, gene frequencies wander randomly across generations through sheer sampling luck — who happens to reproduce. This 'genetic drift' is strongest in small populations, where it can fix or erase a gene regardless of fitness, and (per Kimura's neutral theory) it drives much molecular evolution. Selection and drift act together, not in opposition.
cards.deploy: Corrects the 'everything is an adaptation' reflex — much genetic change is just noise, not design.
cards.counter: Drift and selection are partners, not rivals; their relative weight depends on population size, and teasing them apart is genuinely hard.

quiz.q: Genetic drift changes gene frequencies through…
choices: Natural selection
Random chance, especially in small populations
Mutation alone
Migration alone

quiz.q: Two isolated populations of a beetle carry a neutral color gene at 50% frequency. One population has 20 beetles, the other has 20,000. In which is the gene's frequency more likely to swing dramatically by chance alone over a few generations, and why?
choices: The 20-beetle population, because sampling luck has a bigger effect when fewer individuals reproduce
The 20,000-beetle population, because more individuals means more random change
Both equally, because drift ignores population size
Neither, because a neutral gene cannot change frequency

quiz.q: Whose neutral theory holds that genetic drift, rather than selection, drives much of molecular evolution?
How should genetic drift and natural selection be understood in relation to each other?
choices: As partners acting together, with their relative weight depending on population size
As strict opposites, where one being active means the other is switched off
As the same process described with two different names
As forces that only operate in different species, never the same one

cards.title: What your microbes do for you
cards.fact: Your resident microbes earn their keep — digesting fibre, making vitamins and training your immune system.
cards.detail: Gut microbes ferment dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids, help synthesise vitamins (K and several B's), and help calibrate the immune system, while crowding out invaders. Disruption ('dysbiosis') — e.g. from broad-spectrum antibiotics — is associated with conditions from inflammatory bowel disease to metabolic problems, though much of the 'gut–brain' story is still emerging.
cards.deploy: Reframes microbes as partners, not passengers — and explains why broad antibiotics have side effects.
cards.counter: The field is hot and over-hyped: many microbiome–disease links are correlations, and popular 'gut–brain axis' claims often run ahead of the evidence.

quiz.q: A well-supported role of the gut microbiome is…
choices: Producing all your DNA
Digesting fibre and training the immune system
Replacing the liver
Setting eye colour

quiz.q: A patient on a two-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics develops diarrhoea and a yeast infection. Which microbiome mechanism best explains why wiping out resident gut bacteria can cause this?
choices: Losing the resident bacteria removes their crowding-out of potential invaders, letting opportunistic organisms overgrow
Antibiotics directly damage the lining of the gut wall, exposing nerves
The body compensates by producing excess stomach acid
Antibiotics block the synthesis of dietary fibre in the colon

quiz.q: Gut microbes ferment dietary fibre into a class of molecules that nourish colon cells. What is the general name (the abbreviation SCFA is fine) for these molecules?

A study reports that people with inflammatory bowel disease tend to have lower gut bacterial diversity, but cannot show the low diversity came first. In one word, what kind of relationship has the study actually demonstrated, as opposed to causation?

cards.title: The gene-edited babies line
cards.fact: In 2018 a scientist edited the genes of babies — crossing a line the field had agreed not to.
cards.detail: CRISPR can edit body cells (somatic) to treat one patient, or the germline (eggs, sperm, embryos), whose changes pass to all descendants. In 2018 He Jiankui announced gene-edited twins in China; the work drew near-universal condemnation and a prison sentence — it was unsafe, the consent forged, the ethics indefensible. Most countries ban heritable germline editing while allowing somatic gene therapies.
cards.deploy: Marks the bright line in gene editing: treating a patient vs. permanently altering the human lineage.
cards.counter: The line is contested at the edges — a 2017 US National Academies report cautiously allowed heritable editing in principle for serious disease, so 'never' isn't a settled consensus.

quiz.q: The 2018 He Jiankui case involved editing…
choices: Adult body cells only
The germline (heritable embryo edits)
Plants
Bacteria

quiz.q: A clinic uses CRISPR to edit blood stem cells removed from an adult with sickle-cell disease, then returns them to that same patient. Why is this widely permitted while editing an embryo is mostly banned?
choices: The edits affect only that patient's body cells and are not passed to any children
Blood stem cells cannot be permanently altered, so the change is temporary
Sickle-cell disease is the only condition for which gene editing is legal
Editing adults requires no consent, simplifying the ethics

quiz.q: What is the term for the reproductive-cell lineage (eggs, sperm, embryos) whose edits are inherited by all of a person's descendants?

He Jiankui announced the gene-edited twins in 2018. A US National Academies report had cautiously discussed allowing heritable editing the year before. How many years before the announcement was that report published?

cards.title: Wolves reshaped Yellowstone
cards.fact: Reintroducing wolves in 1995 rippled all the way down to the rivers.
cards.detail: With wolves back, elk grazed differently, letting willow and aspen recover, which helped beavers and stabilised some streambanks — a 'trophic cascade' from a top predator. Concretely, the northern Yellowstone elk herd fell from about 17,000 in the mid-1990s to roughly 6,000 to 7,000 by the late 2000s, after which young willows along some creeks grew taller again. Ecologists Matthew Kauffman and David Mech argue the willow and beaver recovery also tracked wetter years, fewer elk from hunting, and the return of grizzlies, so wolves were one driver among several.
cards.deploy: Top predators have outsized, system-wide effects — a memorable case that removing one species isn't a local change.
cards.counter: The popular 'wolves changed the rivers' story is partly overstated; recovery had multiple drivers and the magnitude is debated.

quiz.q: A top predator's return alters the behaviour of its prey, which changes the vegetation, which in turn affects other species and even streambanks. What two-word ecological term names this top-down chain of effects?
After wolves returned to Yellowstone, willow and aspen along streams recovered. What was the most direct mechanism linking the wolves to that plant recovery?
choices: Elk changed how and where they grazed, reducing browsing pressure on young trees
Wolves fertilised the soil with carcasses, directly feeding the trees
Wolves ate the beavers that had been eating the saplings
Wolf urine raised water tables along the streams

quiz.q: If wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, how many full years had passed by the year 2025?

cards.title: Planetary boundaries
cards.fact: Scientists have mapped nine limits for a stable planet — and we've crossed several.
cards.detail: The framework defines a 'safe operating space' across climate, biodiversity, the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, freshwater, land use, and more. A 2023 update found six of nine boundaries transgressed. Concretely, the climate boundary is set at 350 parts per million of atmospheric CO2; we are already past 420 ppm, which is why climate counts as transgressed. The framework comes from a team led by Johan Rockstrom and Will Steffen, who picked each threshold as the point beyond which they judged the risk of abrupt, large-scale change rises sharply.
cards.deploy: Moves environmental debate from 'climate only' to a systems view of multiple, interacting limits.
cards.counter: The specific boundary values carry real uncertainty, and some boundaries are global while others are really regional — the numbers are estimates, not constants.

quiz.q: The planetary-boundaries framework defines nine limits for a stable planet, and a 2023 update found six of them already transgressed. How many of those nine limits were still within the safe operating space?
Which statement best captures why the planetary-boundaries framework is more than a restatement of climate change?
choices: It treats climate as one of several interacting limits, alongside things like biodiversity loss and the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles
It replaces climate targets with a single combined pollution index
It argues climate change is not actually a planetary boundary
It applies only to freshwater and land-use change, not the atmosphere

quiz.q: Some planetary boundaries are genuinely global while others are really driven by local conditions, and the threshold values themselves carry uncertainty. In one word, what does this make the published boundary numbers, rather than fixed constants?

cards.title: Half the nitrogen in you came from one factory process
cards.fact: The Haber-Bosch process (1909) pulls nitrogen from the air to make fertiliser — and now feeds roughly half the world.
cards.detail: Before it, crop yields were capped by natural nitrogen. Synthetic ammonia broke that ceiling; a large share of the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through this industrial reaction. The reaction forces nitrogen gas and hydrogen together over an iron catalyst at roughly 400-500 degrees C and 150-300 atmospheres of pressure, conditions needed because the triple bond in N2 is very hard to break. Running it at industrial scale consumes around 1-2 percent of all the energy humans use each year, most of it from natural gas that supplies the hydrogen.
cards.deploy: One chemical process underpins modern food security — a striking dependency to put on the table.
cards.counter: It's double-edged: the same nitrogen runoff drives algal blooms, dead zones, and potent nitrous-oxide emissions.

quiz.q: Before synthetic ammonia, what was the main ceiling on crop yields?
choices: The amount of nitrogen available from natural sources
The lack of mechanical harvesting equipment
Insufficient sunlight reaching cultivated fields
A shortage of suitable seed varieties

quiz.q: Which gas, a far stronger greenhouse gas than CO2, is released as a side effect of heavy nitrogen fertiliser use?

A region grows enough food for 8 million people. If the same fraction of people sustained by synthetic-nitrogen fertiliser holds as for the world overall (roughly half), how many of those people depend on it?

cards.title: Reinforcing vs balancing feedback
cards.fact: Two loop types explain most system behaviour: one amplifies, one stabilises.
cards.detail: Reinforcing (positive) loops compound — interest, viral spread, arms races. Balancing (negative) loops push back toward a target — a thermostat, hunger, market correction. Trace each loop and the difference is plain. A savings account compounds: a bigger balance earns more interest, the interest adds to the balance, and that larger balance earns still more, so the loop reinforces itself. A thermostat runs the loop in reverse: the further the room drops below your setting, the harder the heater works to close the gap, which pulls the room back to one temperature and shuts the heater off.
cards.deploy: Lets you name why something grows explosively or stays stubbornly stable instead of hand-waving.
cards.counter: Real systems chain many loops with delays; reading off a single loop usually misleads.

quiz.q: A thermostat that switches the heater off as room temperature approaches the set point is an example of which loop?
choices: A balancing (negative) loop
A reinforcing (positive) loop
A delay-free open loop with no feedback
Two reinforcing loops cancelling out

quiz.q: What single word describes a feedback loop that compounds its own output, like compound interest or viral spread?
Why does reading off a single feedback loop usually mislead when analysing a real-world system?
choices: Real systems chain many loops together with time delays
Feedback loops only exist in engineered, not natural, systems
A single loop always switches sign over time
Balancing loops cancel reinforcing loops exactly

cards.title: The tragedy of the commons — and its rebuttal
cards.fact: Shared resources get overused when each user pockets the gain but shares the cost — yet communities often solve this without the state or markets.
cards.detail: Hardin (1968) argued a shared pasture is doomed to overgrazing. Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) then documented many real communities that govern shared fisheries, forests and irrigation sustainably through their own rules. Ostrom's fieldwork on Swiss alpine pastures, Spanish irrigation networks and Japanese village forests led her to eight design principles that make self-governance hold, among them clear boundaries on who may draw from the resource, monitoring carried out by the users themselves, and graduated penalties for cheating. The pasture fails in Hardin's telling because each herder acts in isolation; Ostrom's communities communicate, watch each other, and escalate penalties on over-use.
cards.deploy: Carries its own counter-argument: useful whether you're arguing for regulation OR for local self-governance.
cards.counter: Hardin overgeneralised from a model; Ostrom showed the 'tragedy' is not inevitable when users can communicate and make binding rules.

quiz.q: Which economist won a Nobel for documenting communities that sustainably govern shared resources through their own rules?
What incentive structure drives overuse of a shared resource in the tragedy-of-the-commons argument?
choices: Each user keeps the full gain but spreads the cost across everyone
Each user pays the full cost but shares the gain equally
Users gain and lose in exactly equal proportion
The resource regenerates faster than anyone can extract it

quiz.q: According to Ostrom's findings, what key ability lets users avoid the 'tragedy' and govern a shared resource without the state or markets?

cards.title: Heavy tails: when the average lies
cards.fact: Wealth, city sizes, and word frequencies follow heavy-tailed distributions where a few cases dominate.
cards.detail: In a power-law-like distribution, the 'typical' value and the average can be wildly different — think the 80/20 rule. A handful of extreme cases carry most of the total. Picture a bar with 10 people each earning 40,000 a year: the mean is 40,000 and describes everyone in the room. Now Jeff Bezos walks in with roughly 200 billion in wealth; the mean across the eleven jumps to about 18 billion, so the 'average' patron is a near-billionaire while ten of the eleven still earn 40,000. The median, the middle person, stays at 40,000, which is why heavy-tailed data is usually reported with medians and percentiles rather than the mean.
cards.deploy: Warns against reasoning from the mean in unequal systems — 'average income' or 'average user' can be meaningless.
cards.counter: True power laws are statistically hard to distinguish from lognormal distributions, and the label is often slapped on data that doesn't fit it.

quiz.q: Suppose 1000 customers spend a total of $2,000,000, but following an 80/20 pattern, 20% of customers account for 80% of spending. How many dollars do that top 20% of customers spend in total?
In a heavy-tailed distribution like wealth or city sizes, why can the average be a misleading summary?
choices: A few extreme cases dominate the total, so the mean sits far from the typical value
The distribution has no defined total, so any average is invalid
Every value is identical, making the mean equal to the median
The values are negative, so the average is meaningless

quiz.q: Which other distribution is statistically hard to distinguish from a true power law, making the 'power law' label often unreliable?

cards.title: Why the rich get richer
cards.fact: Why do a few get so much? Often because 'the rich get richer' — preferential attachment.
cards.detail: Power-law distributions frequently arise from one simple rule: the more you already have, the more you attract. New web pages link to already-popular pages; citations flow to already-cited papers; wealth begets wealth. Barabási and Albert (1999) showed this 'preferential attachment' generates the heavy-tailed, 'scale-free' patterns seen across many networks.
cards.deploy: A mechanism behind heavy tails: unequal outcomes can emerge from a neutral 'rich-get-richer' process, not just from differences in merit.
cards.counter: It's one route to power laws, not the only one; real systems mix it with chance, fitness and resets, so pure preferential attachment rarely fits perfectly.

quiz.q: Preferential attachment ('rich get richer') tends to produce…
choices: A bell curve
A power-law / heavy-tailed distribution
A flat distribution
A single value

quiz.q: What family of statistical distributions, marked by heavy tails and 'scale-free' structure, does a rich-get-richer growth process typically generate?
A new node joins a growing network and attaches to existing nodes with probability proportional to how many connections each already has. Which node is MOST likely to gain the new connection?
choices: The node that already has the most connections
The node that joined the network most recently
Every existing node, with exactly equal probability
The node with the fewest connections, to balance the network

quiz.q: Under preferential attachment, attachment probability is proportional to a node's current connection count. In a network, node A has 30 links and node B has 6 links. How many times more likely is a new node to attach to A than to B?

cards.title: Where to push a system
cards.fact: There are places to push a system for big change — and the obvious ones are usually the weakest.
cards.detail: Donella Meadows ranked twelve 'leverage points' for intervening in a system. Tweaking numbers (taxes, subsidies) is low leverage; changing feedback loops and rules is stronger; the highest leverage is shifting the system's goals and the underlying paradigm. People sense these points but often push them the wrong way.
cards.deploy: A change toolkit: stop fiddling with parameters and aim at goals and mindsets, where leverage is greatest.
cards.counter: High-leverage points (paradigms) are exactly the hardest to move and easiest to get catastrophically wrong; the ranking is a heuristic, not a formula.

quiz.q: In Meadows' framework, the highest-leverage intervention is…
choices: Adjusting a tax rate
Changing the system's goals or paradigm
Adding a buffer
Changing a constant

quiz.q: Which researcher ranked twelve 'leverage points' for intervening in a system, from adjusting numbers up to shifting paradigms?
A city wants to durably reduce car dependence. Ordered from lowest to highest leverage in Meadows' framework, which sequence is correct?
choices: Raise the fuel tax; rewrite zoning rules; redefine the city's goal from car throughput to people's access
Redefine the city's goal; rewrite zoning rules; raise the fuel tax
Rewrite zoning rules; raise the fuel tax; redefine the city's goal
Raise the fuel tax; redefine the city's goal; rewrite zoning rules

quiz.q: Meadows numbered her leverage points so that lower numbers mean higher leverage, running from 12 (weakest) down to 1 (strongest, shifting the underlying paradigm). What number corresponds to the highest-leverage intervention?

cards.title: Governing the commons
cards.fact: Elinor Ostrom showed communities can govern shared resources themselves — and found the rules that make it work.
cards.detail: Against the idea that commons inevitably collapse, Ostrom's fieldwork on fisheries, forests and irrigation found communities sustainably self-governing for generations. Her eight design principles include clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, participation in rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions, cheap conflict resolution and nested governance. She won the 2009 Nobel in economics.
cards.deploy: The empirical rebuttal to 'tragedy of the commons': self-organised governance is a real third option beyond the state and the market.
cards.counter: Her principles aren't a guarantee — they work best for bounded, local resources; scaling them to global commons like the climate is far harder.

quiz.q: Ostrom showed commons can be sustained by…
choices: Only privatisation
Only state control
Community self-governance with the right rules
Doing nothing

quiz.q: Whose fieldwork on fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems demonstrated that communities can sustainably self-govern shared resources, earning a 2009 Nobel in economics?
A village irrigation cooperative wants to follow Ostrom's design principles. Which practice best fits her principle of 'graduated sanctions'?
choices: First-time over-users get a small warning, while repeat offenders face steadily harsher penalties
Anyone who breaks a rule even once is permanently banned from the system
Rule-breakers are reported to a distant national authority for prosecution
All members pay the same flat fee regardless of how much water they take

quiz.q: Ostrom distilled her findings into a well-known set of numbered design principles for enduring commons institutions. How many such principles are in this set?

cards.title: Climate tipping points
cards.fact: Push a natural system too far and it can flip — abruptly, and sometimes for good.
cards.detail: Some Earth systems have thresholds where change becomes self-reinforcing: melting ice exposes dark water that absorbs more heat; a drying Amazon can flip toward savanna; the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) could slow sharply. Past a tipping point the shift can be fast and effectively irreversible, and crossing one can nudge others — a cascade.
cards.deploy: Why climate risk isn't smoothly proportional: some changes don't ease back once you stop pushing.
cards.counter: Exact thresholds are uncertain and hotly debated — some 'tipping' claims outrun the evidence, and timescales range from years to centuries.

quiz.q: A climate 'tipping point' is…
choices: A gradual, reversible change
A threshold past which change is self-reinforcing and often irreversible
A daily temperature swing
A measurement error

quiz.q: What is the name of the large-scale Atlantic ocean current system, abbreviated AMOC, whose sharp slowing is treated as a potential climate tipping point?
Sea ice melts, exposing dark open water that absorbs more sunlight, which warms the region and melts still more ice. What kind of process makes this a candidate tipping mechanism?
choices: A self-reinforcing positive feedback loop
A stabilizing negative feedback that restores equilibrium
A purely linear response proportional to forcing
A one-off shock with no further consequences

quiz.q: Which statement best captures why crossing a climate tipping point is more worrying than ordinary warming?
choices: The shift can be rapid and effectively irreversible even if the original push is removed
It always reverses fully within a single year once emissions stop
It only changes one isolated system and never affects any other
Its threshold and timing are precisely known well in advance

cards.title: Keystone species
cards.fact: Some species hold a whole ecosystem together — far out of proportion to their numbers.
cards.detail: A 'keystone species' has an outsized effect relative to its abundance (Robert Paine, 1969). Remove sea otters and urchins strip the kelp forests; remove the ochre sea star and mussels crowd everyone out; remove wolves and herbivores reshape the land. Like the keystone of an arch, pull it and the structure can collapse.
cards.deploy: Explains why protecting one species can matter for a whole ecosystem — and why Yellowstone's wolves rippled so far.
cards.counter: The label is overused (200+ claimed keystones) and context-dependent; real food webs are messier than a single linchpin.

quiz.q: A keystone species is one that…
choices: Is the most abundant
Has an outsized effect relative to its abundance
Lives the longest
Eats only plants

quiz.q: A small predatory snail makes up under 1% of the biomass on a rocky shore, yet removing it lets one mussel species blanket the rock and cut the number of resident species from 15 to 8. What does this most strongly suggest about the snail?
choices: It is a keystone species, since its effect on the community far exceeds its abundance
It is a dominant species, since it controls the most biomass
It is an invasive species, since it suppresses native mussels
It is a generalist, since its loss has little measurable effect

quiz.q: Which ecologist introduced the keystone species concept, based on experiments removing the ochre sea star (Pisaster) from rocky tidepools?

If a tidepool holds 18 species while a keystone predator is present, but collapses to a stable 7 species after the predator is removed, how many species are lost as a direct consequence of the removal?

cards.title: Fertiliser's dead zones
cards.fact: The fertiliser that feeds the world also chokes its waters — creating ocean 'dead zones'.
cards.detail: Nitrogen and phosphorus runoff from farms (and sewage) over-fertilise rivers, lakes and coasts. The nutrients trigger algal blooms; when the algae die and decompose they strip oxygen from the water, creating hypoxic 'dead zones' (like the Gulf of Mexico's) where fish can't survive. It's the downstream cost of Haber–Bosch abundance.
cards.deploy: The other half of the fertiliser story: the reactive nitrogen that feeds billions also pollutes the water that receives the runoff.
cards.counter: It's manageable, not inevitable — better nutrient timing, buffer strips and treatment cut runoff; the obstacle is mostly cost and governance, not chemistry.

quiz.q: Eutrophication creates 'dead zones' by…
choices: Adding oxygen
Nutrient runoff → algal blooms → oxygen depletion
Cooling the water
Removing all nutrients

quiz.q: In a coastal bay receiving heavy farm runoff, what is the correct ordering of events that produces a hypoxic dead zone?
choices: Nutrient influx, then algal bloom, then algae die and decompose, then oxygen is depleted
Oxygen depletion, then algal bloom, then nutrient influx, then fish die
Algae die, then nutrient influx, then oxygen rises, then bloom forms
Fish die first, releasing nutrients that fuel a bloom that adds oxygen

quiz.q: Besides nitrogen, which other plant nutrient running off from farms and sewage is the main driver of eutrophication?

Water with dissolved oxygen below 2 mg/L is considered hypoxic. If a river measures 9 mg/L upstream of farmland but only 1.5 mg/L in the bloom-affected estuary, by how many mg/L has the dissolved oxygen dropped?

cards.title: Comparative advantage
cards.fact: Two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.
cards.detail: Ricardo (1817): what matters is opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Each side specialises where it gives up the least, and total output rises. It's the core case for trade. Concretely, Portugal makes a unit of wine in 80 hours and cloth in 90, while England needs 120 for wine and 100 for cloth (Ricardo's own four numbers). Portugal uses fewer hours for both, yet making a unit of cloth costs it 90/80 of a unit of wine, while England forgoes only 100/120. England gives up less wine per cloth, so it makes cloth, Portugal makes wine, and they trade.
cards.deploy: The standard answer to 'they can make it cheaper, so trade hurts us' — gains come from specialisation, not from winning at everything.
cards.counter: Named critics — Friedrich List in the 1840s, Ha-Joon Chang today — argue infant industries need protection to ever become competitive; and the clean result assumes full employment and mobile resources while ignoring distribution: trade can raise the total yet leave specific workers and regions worse off.

quiz.q: Comparative advantage says gains from trade come from differences in…
choices: Absolute skill
Opportunity cost
Population size
Currency strength

quiz.q: A country should specialise where it has the lowest…
choices: Absolute cost
Opportunity cost
Tax rate
Wage bill

quiz.q: In one hour, Country A can make 6 shirts or 3 computers. For Country A, what is the opportunity cost of producing one computer, measured in shirts?
Country A can make 6 shirts or 3 computers per hour; Country B can make 2 shirts or 4 computers per hour. According to comparative advantage, who should specialise in computers?
choices: Country B, because it gives up only 0.5 shirts per computer versus A's 2 shirts
Country A, because it can also make more shirts overall
Neither, because A is not absolutely better at everything
Country B, because it has the higher absolute computer output regardless of opportunity cost

quiz.q: Which classical economist set out the theory of comparative advantage in 1817, arguing that opportunity cost rather than absolute skill drives the gains from trade?

cards.title: Externalities
cards.fact: When a cost or benefit lands on third parties, the market price gets it wrong.
cards.detail: Pollution is the classic case: a factory's price doesn't include the harm downstream. Pigou (1920) proposed taxing the activity to make the price tell the truth. The Pigouvian tax is set equal to the harm at the efficient quantity: if each tonne of emissions does about 50 dollars of downstream damage, a 50-dollar-per-tonne tax makes the factory feel that cost and cut output to the point where its private gain from one more tonne just matches the 50 dollars of harm.
cards.deploy: Justifies carbon taxes, congestion charges, and the like: prices need correcting when costs spill over.
cards.counter: Coase (1960) showed that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, private parties can fix externalities without taxes — the right remedy depends on the situation.

quiz.q: A chemical plant's production imposes pollution costs on a downstream town that the plant never pays. Why does the unregulated market price of the chemical end up too low?
choices: It reflects only the plant's private costs, leaving out the external cost borne by third parties
It includes the town's cleanup costs, which inflate the apparent supply
It overstates demand because buyers value pollution
It double-counts the social cost, pushing the price below marginal benefit

quiz.q: Which economist argued in 1960 that, with clearly defined property rights and low bargaining costs, private parties can resolve an externality without government taxes?

A factory's private cost of making a tonne of product is 80 dollars, but its pollution imposes an external cost of 35 dollars per tonne on others. What Pigouvian tax per tonne makes the price reflect the full social cost?

media.caption: Demand (downward) meets private supply at the marked point; the parallel social-cost supply sits higher by the external harm, the gap a Pigouvian tax would add to the price.

cards.title: Loss aversion
cards.fact: Losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good.
cards.detail: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) showed people don't weigh outcomes by final wealth but by gains and losses from a reference point — and losses loom larger. It helped found behavioural economics. You can feel it in a coin-flip test: most people refuse a 50/50 bet to win 100 dollars or lose 100, and take it only when the possible win rises to roughly 200 — the upside has to be about twice the possible loss before the gamble feels worth it.
cards.deploy: Undercuts the assumption that people are cool rational maximisers — framing a choice as a loss vs a gain changes behaviour.
cards.counter: The exact 2:1 ratio varies by context and there's ongoing replication debate; it's a robust tendency, not a fixed constant.

quiz.q: Losing a dollar hurts about twice as much as gaining a dollar feels good. For a 50/50 gamble with a possible $60 loss, what is the smallest win amount at which a typical loss-averse person breaks even and would accept the bet?
A gym advertises the same offer two ways. Which framing best exploits loss aversion to maximise sign-ups?
choices: 'Pay $30/month and keep your fitness'
'Don't lose the $30/month you'd waste staying unfit'
'Members report feeling 30% happier'
'Join the average member who works out twice a week'

quiz.q: In prospect theory, outcomes are judged as gains and losses relative to a baseline rather than as final wealth. What is the name for that baseline?

cards.title: Hume's is–ought gap
cards.fact: You can't logically derive what ought to be purely from what is.
cards.detail: Hume (1739) noticed writers slide from describing facts ('is') to prescribing duties ('ought') without justifying the jump. Facts alone don't entail values. An example of the slide: 'Eating meat is natural, so it's permissible.' The first clause only describes how things are; the conclusion adds a value the premise never supplied. To make it valid you need a hidden 'ought' premise, such as 'whatever is natural is permissible,' and stating that premise out loud is usually where the argument falls apart.
cards.deploy: A precision tool for spotting when an opponent smuggles a value claim in under cover of 'the science says'.
cards.counter: Some philosophers (ethical naturalists) argue the gap can be bridged; it's a powerful warning, not a settled proof that values float free of facts.

quiz.q: Which argument commits the is-ought fallacy by deriving a value claim from facts alone?
choices: Eating meat causes suffering, so if suffering matters morally we ought to reduce meat consumption
Humans have always eaten meat, therefore eating meat is morally permissible
If we ought to minimise suffering, and factory farming maximises it, we ought to oppose factory farming
Lying erodes trust, and since we value trust, we should avoid lying

quiz.q: Hume's gap warns against illegitimately concluding what kind of claim from purely factual premises: a claim about what is the case, or a claim about what should be done?
Which group of philosophers most directly challenges the is-ought gap by arguing values can be derived from facts?
choices: Ethical naturalists
Logical positivists
Existentialists
Stoics

cards.title: Falsifiability
cards.fact: A claim that nothing could ever disprove isn't really scientific.
cards.detail: Popper argued the mark of a scientific theory is that it sticks its neck out — it forbids certain observations, so it could be proven wrong. 'What would change your mind?' is the key question. Compare two claims. 'All swans are white' forbids a black swan, so the first black swan European explorers recorded in Australia killed it. 'Everything happens for a reason' rules out nothing, because any outcome can be read as the reason, so no observation could ever count against it. The first claim takes a risk; the second is safe precisely because it predicts nothing.
cards.deploy: A sharp test against unfalsifiable claims ('it's true, you just can't see the evidence').
cards.counter: Kuhn and Lakatos showed real science doesn't work by naive falsification — a failed prediction is often blamed on auxiliary assumptions, not the core theory.

quiz.q: For Popper, a scientific theory must be…
choices: Proven true
Falsifiable
Popular
Mathematical

quiz.q: By Popper's criterion, which claim is LEAST scientific (unfalsifiable)?
choices: Heavy objects fall at g in a vacuum
Light bends near the Sun
Whatever happens was meant to be
Water boils at 100°C at sea level

quiz.q: By Popper's falsifiability criterion, which of these is the most scientific statement?
choices: All swans are white
Everything happens for a reason we can't always understand
Some events are influenced by unmeasurable forces
History unfolds according to a hidden purpose

quiz.q: Which two philosophers are most associated with the objection that scientists rescue a failing theory by blaming auxiliary assumptions rather than abandoning the core?
A fortune teller predicts 'something significant will affect your life this year.' Why does this fail Popper's test?
choices: No possible outcome could count as the prediction failing
It was not published in a peer-reviewed journal
It relies on statistics rather than observation
It has not yet been repeated by other fortune tellers

cards.title: Rawls's veil of ignorance
cards.fact: To find fair rules, choose them not knowing who you'll be in the society.
cards.detail: Rawls (1971): behind a 'veil' that hides your wealth, talents, race and class, you'd pick principles that protect everyone — because you might end up at the bottom. Another way to see it: you cut a cake for a group, but you won't learn which slice is yours until everyone else has taken theirs. You cut the slices as evenly as you can, because any slice you shortchange might end up being yours. The veil works the same way, forcing the rule-maker to treat being the worst-off person as a live possibility for themselves.
cards.deploy: A portable fairness test for any institution or policy: would you accept it not knowing your place in it?
cards.counter: Nozick and others reject the setup: why assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse (favouring the worst-off) rather than gambling on the average?

quiz.q: In Rawls's thought experiment, what is the name of the device that hides your wealth, talents, race and class while you choose principles of justice?
Using the veil-of-ignorance test, which tax policy would a chooser most likely endorse if they knew nothing about their future income?
choices: One that funds a strong safety net in case they end up poor
One that abolishes all taxes to maximise top earners' wealth
One that taxes only the bottom income bracket
One designed by sampling current voters' preferences

quiz.q: Which philosopher most prominently objected that there is no good reason to assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse rather than gambling on the average outcome?

cards.title: The median voter theorem
cards.fact: In a simple two-way majority vote, the middle voter decides — so parties drift to the centre.
cards.detail: If opinion lines up on one axis and the winner needs a majority, the option preferred by the median voter beats all others. Candidates converge toward that voter to win. Put five voters on a left-right line at positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; the median is the voter at 3. Any platform to the left of 3 loses, because voters 3, 4 and 5 (a majority) prefer something further right, and the same logic holds on the other side. Only the position at 3 cannot be beaten, so a candidate who wants a majority moves there.
cards.deploy: Explains why rival parties can end up sounding alike — a clean model for centrist convergence.
cards.counter: It assumes one dimension, two options, and full turnout. Primaries, multidimensional issues, and abstention routinely break it.

quiz.q: A new candidate is choosing where to stand on a single left-right policy line. Their opponent has already locked in a position slightly right of the electorate's midpoint. To maximize their chance of winning a two-way majority vote, where should the new candidate position themselves?
choices: Just to the left of the opponent, capturing the median and everyone to the left
Far left, to lock in the most committed base voters
Far right, to outflank the opponent on their own side
Exactly mirroring the opponent's position to look consistent

quiz.q: Seven voters have ideal points on a 0-to-10 line at positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, and 10. In a one-dimensional majority vote, what is the position of the voter whose preference is decisive (the median)?
Name one of the core assumptions of the simple median voter model whose violation (for example by multi-issue politics or low participation) typically causes the result to break down.

cards.title: Duverger's law
cards.fact: Winner-take-all elections tend to produce two big parties; proportional systems produce many.
cards.detail: Under first-past-the-post, votes for small parties are 'wasted', so voters and donors consolidate around two contenders. Proportional representation rewards smaller parties, so more survive. The squeeze is strategic as well as mechanical. A voter who most prefers a third party but fears their least-favourite winning will vote for the larger of the two front-runners instead, so the third party's support drains away even where it has genuine backing. Maurice Duverger framed this as the joint effect of the rule mechanically discarding small-party votes and voters anticipating that waste.
cards.deploy: Shows that party systems are shaped by the voting rules, not just by the electorate's views — institutions matter.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not an iron law: the UK and India sustain strong regional/third parties under the same rules.

quiz.q: A country switches from first-past-the-post to proportional representation. Based on the institutional logic of how electoral rules shape party systems, what is the most likely change to its party landscape?
choices: More small parties survive and win seats
The two largest parties consolidate into one
Voter turnout automatically falls to near zero
Regional parties immediately disappear

quiz.q: Under first-past-the-post, what term describes a vote cast for a small party that wins no seat and so effectively counts for nothing — the mechanism that pushes voters to consolidate around two contenders?

Strong regional and third parties persist in countries like the UK and India despite their use of winner-take-all elections. What does this best illustrate about the relationship between electoral rules and party numbers?
choices: The two-party outcome is a strong tendency rather than a guaranteed law
Proportional representation must secretly be in use there
Electoral rules have no effect on party systems at all
Winner-take-all rules reliably produce many parties

cards.title: The collective action problem
cards.fact: Even when everyone would benefit, large groups often fail to act — because each person can free-ride.
cards.detail: Olson (1965): if you'll get the benefit whether or not you contribute, the rational move is to let others do the work. So big diffuse groups under-organise while small concentrated interests punch above their weight. Concretely: a few thousand US sugar producers each gain a lot from import quotas that keep domestic sugar prices high, so they organise and lobby hard. The 300-plus million consumers each lose only a few dollars a year on pricier sugar, too little to bother fighting, so almost nobody shows up on their side.
cards.deploy: Explains why concentrated lobbies beat diffuse majorities, and why obvious public goods get under-provided.
cards.counter: Selective incentives, social pressure, leadership, and repeated interaction (Ostrom) routinely overcome free-riding — it's a hurdle, not a wall.

quiz.q: A policy would give each of 30 million consumers about 4 dollars a year in lower prices, while costing 200 firms roughly 600,000 dollars each. Which side is more likely to organize effectively to influence the outcome, and why?
choices: The firms, because their stake is large and concentrated while each consumer's is tiny and diffuse
The consumers, because they vastly outnumber the firms
Neither, because both groups face identical incentives
The consumers, because each one alone has more at stake than any single firm

quiz.q: In Olson's account, what is the term for a benefit (such as a member-only service or perk) offered specifically to those who contribute, used to overcome free-riding by rewarding participation rather than the whole group?

Which scholar's work on how communities self-organize to manage shared resources — through monitoring and repeated interaction — is the standard counterpoint to the claim that diffuse groups inevitably fail to act?

cards.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
cards.fact: No voting system can be perfectly fair — Arrow proved it's mathematically impossible.
cards.detail: Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951): with three or more options, no ranked voting method can satisfy a short list of reasonable conditions at once — no dictator, respect unanimity, and 'independence of irrelevant alternatives'. Every ranked system trades something off (and has a spoiler effect). It's a foundational result in social choice.
cards.deploy: Ends the hunt for a 'perfect' voting system — the real question is which trade-offs you accept, not whether you can avoid them.
cards.counter: It applies to ranked orderings; rated systems (approval, score voting) that use grades rather than rankings sidestep the exact theorem, so it's not a counsel of despair.

quiz.q: Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that…
choices: One party always wins
No ranked voting rule can meet all fairness criteria at once
Voting is pointless
The median voter always wins

quiz.q: Arrow's impossibility theorem proves that no ranked voting method can simultaneously satisfy its short list of fairness conditions. Which design choice lets approval and score voting sidestep the exact theorem?
choices: They use independent grades or ratings rather than a single ranked ordering of all options
They require a dictator to break every tie
They restrict every election to exactly two candidates
They forbid voters from expressing any preference at all

quiz.q: Arrow's theorem bites once the number of distinct options or candidates on the ballot is at least what value?
Arrow's condition that says adding or removing a losing, non-competitive option should not flip the group's ranking of the others — the one closely tied to the spoiler effect — is known by what name?

cards.title: Proportional representation's trade-off
cards.fact: Proportional representation trades the stability of two big parties for fuller representation.
cards.detail: Where winner-take-all tends toward two parties (Duverger), proportional representation allocates seats in line with vote share, so smaller parties win seats and parliaments hold many. That mirrors diverse views more faithfully and wastes fewer votes, but usually means coalition governments — more inclusive, sometimes less decisive. It's the central trade-off in electoral-system design.
cards.deploy: Frames the electoral-system choice: representativeness (PR) versus governability and clear accountability (FPTP) — no free lunch.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not a law: PR systems vary hugely (thresholds, district size) and many are perfectly stable; 'PR equals chaos' is a caricature.

quiz.q: Compared with winner-take-all, proportional representation tends to produce…
choices: Two big parties
Many parties and coalition governments
No parties
One-party rule

quiz.q: A country switches from a winner-take-all system to proportional representation. Which outcome is the most likely consequence?
choices: Single-party majority governments become more frequent
Coalition governments become more common as more parties win seats
Voter turnout is guaranteed to fall sharply
The total number of legislative seats must shrink

quiz.q: In a 200-seat parliament elected by pure proportional representation, a party wins 23% of the national vote. Ignoring any threshold and rounding to the nearest whole seat, how many seats does it receive?
Which political scientist's name is attached to the principle that single-member winner-take-all districts tend to produce a two-party system?

cards.title: You never test one idea alone
cards.fact: A failed experiment never cleanly refutes a single hypothesis — you always test a whole bundle.
cards.detail: The Duhem–Quine thesis: any prediction leans on a web of auxiliary assumptions (the instrument works, no other forces, the background theory holds). When a test fails, logic alone can't say which link broke — you can always save the core idea by blaming an auxiliary. This complicates Popper's clean falsification and feeds Kuhn's picture of theories defended within a 'paradigm' until anomalies pile up.
cards.deploy: A check on naive falsification: 'the experiment disproved it' is rarely as clean as it sounds.
cards.counter: It can be overstated into 'anything goes' — in practice scientists do reach justified verdicts; the holism is real but not paralysing.

quiz.q: The Duhem–Quine thesis says a failed test…
choices: Cleanly refutes one hypothesis
Can't pinpoint which assumption failed — you test a whole web
Proves the theory
Is impossible

quiz.q: An astronomer predicts a planet's position using Newtonian mechanics, but the telescope reading disagrees with the prediction. Per the Duhem-Quine thesis, what can logic alone NOT determine?
choices: Whether the disagreement actually occurred
Which specific assumption (the theory, the instrument, or a background condition) is the one at fault
Whether the telescope produced a reading at all
Whether the astronomer recorded the number correctly

quiz.q: Whose model of science describes theories being defended within a 'paradigm' until anomalies accumulate, a view the Duhem-Quine holism is often said to support?
The Duhem-Quine thesis most directly complicates which philosopher's idea?
choices: Popper's clean falsification
Bacon's inductive method by simple enumeration
Descartes' method of radical doubt
Mill's harm principle

cards.title: The naturalistic fallacy
cards.fact: Calling something 'natural' doesn't make it good — and defining 'good' as any natural property is a trap.
cards.detail: G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy (1903): you can't define 'good' as identical to a natural property (pleasure, survival, what evolution favours), because his 'open question' always remains — 'this is pleasant, but is it good?' still makes sense, so the two aren't the same. It's cousin to Hume's is–ought gap and to the everyday 'appeal to nature' (natural = better).
cards.deploy: Disarms 'it's natural, therefore good/right' arguments — and warns against reading ethics straight off biology.
cards.counter: Ethical naturalists reject Moore's argument and hold that moral facts can be natural facts; the 'fallacy' label is itself contested (Frankena).

quiz.q: The 'naturalistic fallacy' warns against…
choices: Studying nature
Equating 'good' with a natural property (e.g. 'natural = good')
Using logic
Believing in ethics

quiz.q: Which philosopher introduced the naturalistic fallacy, in his 1903 work Principia Ethica?
Someone argues, 'Refined sugar is bad for you because it isn't natural, while honey is natural and therefore healthy.' Which reasoning error is this?
choices: Appeal to nature
Affirming the consequent
Circular reasoning
Equivocation on 'sweet'

quiz.q: Moore's 'open question argument' shows that 'good' cannot just mean 'pleasant' because which question still makes genuine sense?
choices: 'This act is pleasant, but is it good?'
'Is pleasure ever experienced?'
'Does anything feel pleasant?'
'Can good things exist?'

cards.title: Nozick's reply to Rawls
cards.fact: Nozick's reply to Rawls: a just outcome is whatever free exchanges produce — even if unequal.
cards.detail: In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Robert Nozick countered Rawls with an 'entitlement theory': holdings are just if they were acquired and transferred justly, whatever pattern results. His 'Wilt Chamberlain' example: if fans freely pay to watch a star, the resulting inequality is just, and forcibly redistributing it violates liberty. He defends only a 'minimal state'.
cards.deploy: The libertarian counterweight to Rawls: justice as fair process and liberty, not as a fair distribution pattern.
cards.counter: Egalitarians like G.A. Cohen argue that 'just steps' ignore tainted starting points (conquest, slavery) and that pure process can entrench injustice; Nozick's initial-acquisition principle is the weak link.

quiz.q: Nozick's entitlement theory judges a distribution by…
choices: How equal it is
Whether it arose through just acquisition and free transfer
A central plan
Majority vote

quiz.q: What is the name of Nozick's celebrated thought experiment in which fans freely pay a basketball star to watch him play, producing a just inequality?
On Nozick's entitlement theory, which feature makes a distribution of holdings just?
choices: Each holding was acquired and transferred through just steps, regardless of the final pattern
The final pattern leaves no one below a guaranteed minimum
The distribution maximizes total happiness across society
The least advantaged are made as well off as possible

quiz.q: Nozick argues that only what kind of state is justified, one limited to protecting against force, theft and fraud and enforcing contracts?

cards.title: What economics is about
cards.fact: Economics starts from one awkward fact: we have unlimited wants and limited means.
cards.detail: Because you can't have everything, every choice means giving something up. Economics studies how people and societies handle those trade-offs — and the cost of any choice is the best alternative you gave up (its opportunity cost). Concretely: if you spend a free Saturday studying instead of taking a 120-dollar shift at work, the opportunity cost of studying is that 120 dollars, the single best thing you gave up. You count the best forgone option, not the sum of every option.
cards.deploy: Reframes almost any policy fight as 'what are we giving up?' rather than just 'is this nice?'.
cards.counter: The scarcity frame can hide questions of power and distribution — who decides what's scarce, and for whom.

quiz.q: The opportunity cost of a choice is…
choices: Its money price
The best alternative you gave up
Always zero
The sales tax on it

quiz.q: Economics begins from the problem of…
choices: Inflation
Scarcity — unlimited wants, limited means
Taxation
The money supply

quiz.q: A student has a free evening and chooses to study instead of either going to a concert (which she values most among the alternatives) or sleeping early. What is the opportunity cost of studying?
choices: Going to the concert
Both the concert and sleeping early combined
Sleeping early
Nothing, since the evening was free
