quiz.q: Economics exists as a discipline because human wants are unlimited but the means to satisfy them are limited. What single word names this fundamental condition?
Which objection best captures a limitation of framing every social problem purely as 'scarcity and trade-offs'?
choices: It can obscure questions of power and distribution — who decides what counts as scarce, and for whom
It assumes resources are unlimited rather than limited
It only applies to money and ignores time
It makes opportunity cost impossible to define

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.fact: In the basic model, price isn't set by cost or fairness — it's where supply meets demand.
cards.detail: When price rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more; the price settles where the two meet. It's a powerful starting model — but it assumes competition, good information and flexible prices that real markets often lack. Concretely: if at 3 dollars buyers want 80 coffees a day but sellers offer only 50, the shortage pushes the price up; at 5 dollars sellers offer 90 but buyers want 40, so the surplus pushes it back down. The price settles near the point where both sides want about 65, which is where supply meets demand.
cards.deploy: Explains how a price emerges from supply and demand — and why interventions like caps or subsidies ripple into quantity (shortages or surpluses), not just price.
cards.counter: Perfect competition is rare; with market power, information gaps or sticky prices the simple model can mislead.

quiz.q: In the basic model, the market price settles where…
choices: Costs are lowest
Supply equals demand
The government sets it
Profit is zero

quiz.q: In a market, demand is Qd = 100 - 2P and supply is Qs = 10 + P, where P is price. At the equilibrium price, what quantity is traded (in units)?
A government sets a price ceiling well below the equilibrium price for a good. According to the basic supply-and-demand model, what is the most likely result?
choices: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
A surplus, because sellers offer more than buyers want
No change, because price caps only affect fairness, not quantity
Higher quality, because sellers compete harder

quiz.q: The basic supply-and-demand model can mislead when one buyer or seller is large enough to influence the price on their own. What two-word term describes such an actor's ability to move the price?

media.caption: Upward supply (m>0) and downward demand (m<0) cross at the equilibrium price and quantity.

cards.title: What GDP measures
cards.fact: GDP measures the money value of what a country produces — and quietly leaves a lot out.
cards.detail: GDP totals the market value of a country's output. It misses unpaid work, ignores distribution, and treats some harms as gains — which is why 'growth' is one of economics' biggest arguments. Concretely on counting harms as gains: a car crash raises GDP through the repair work, hospital bills, and a replacement car, even though everyone involved is worse off. The spending is recorded; the lost health and wrecked vehicle are not. Economists call missing the destruction the broken-window fallacy, after Bastiat.
cards.deploy: Cuts through 'the economy grew, so we're better off' — ask what the number counts and what it omits.
cards.counter: For all its flaws, GDP tracks real things — jobs, output, tax revenue — and no rival measure has cleanly replaced it.

quiz.q: GDP does NOT directly count…
choices: Factory output
Unpaid care work
Restaurant meals
Government spending

quiz.q: A country's GDP rises sharply in a year when a major oil spill triggers a costly cleanup paid for with new contracts. Why might this rise be misleading as a sign of improved wellbeing?
choices: GDP can count spending to repair harm as added output, treating some damage as a gain
GDP excludes all government spending, so the cleanup would not appear
GDP only counts exports, so domestic cleanup is irrelevant
GDP automatically subtracts environmental damage from output

quiz.q: GDP totals the market value of output but assigns no value to a parent caring for their own children at home. What category of activity does GDP systematically miss for this reason?

Two countries each produce a total output worth 600 billion dollars. In Country A, one household captures 500 billion and the rest share 100 billion; in Country B output is shared evenly. By how many billion dollars do their GDP figures differ?

cards.title: Why 'political economy'?
cards.fact: Before it was 'economics', it was 'political economy' — and the politics never really left.
cards.detail: The classical writers studied 'political economy' — wealth and its distribution between classes. Around 1900 the field rebranded as 'economics' on the model of physics, pushing power to the margins; 'political economy' names the traditions that keep it central. The rebrand has names and a year. William Stanley Jevons pressed for the single word 'economics', and Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics (1890) made it stick. The physics model meant treating prices and quantities like forces settling into equilibrium, with who owns what taken as a given rather than a question to ask.
cards.deploy: Reminds an opponent that 'just the economics' is rarely just the economics.
cards.counter: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be studied with evidence.

quiz.q: Classical thinkers like Smith and Ricardo studied a field whose name combined the words for the state and for household/wealth management, keeping power and class central. What two-word name did they use for it?
Around 1900 the field rebranded from 'political economy' to 'economics', modelling itself on a particular natural science. Which science was the model, and what was a consequence?
choices: Physics — and questions of power and class were pushed to the margins
Biology — and the field became focused on evolution of firms
Chemistry — and it emphasised the mixing of inputs
Astronomy — and it focused on long-run cycles

quiz.q: Which statement best reflects a fair counterpoint to the claim that 'just the economics' always hides politics?
choices: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be examined with evidence
Economics has no political content whatsoever, so the worry is baseless
Only political economy uses evidence; mainstream economics does not
Because politics is everywhere, no economic claim can ever be tested

cards.title: The rival schools
cards.fact: There is no single 'economics' — there are rival schools that disagree about how the economy works.
cards.detail: Economics is plural: classical, Marxian, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, Austrian, behavioural and ecological schools give different answers to the same questions. The mainstream is one paradigm among several, not the last word. One question splits them sharply: why does a recession happen? Austrians (Hayek) blame central banks holding interest rates too low, so capital pours into projects that cannot pay off. Keynesians blame a collapse in total spending that the government should offset. Marxians blame a falling rate of profit squeezing investment. Same slump, three diagnoses.
cards.deploy: Whenever someone says 'economists agree', ask which economists — the field is plural.
cards.counter: Pluralism can tip into 'anything goes'; some claims really are better supported by the evidence than others.

quiz.q: A friend says 'all economists agree that the central bank should cut interest rates.' Which response best reflects the pluralist view of economics?
choices: Ask which school they mean — Keynesians, monetarists and Austrians often draw opposite conclusions from the same situation
Agree, since monetary policy is the one area where every school converges
Point out that economics is a settled science, so dissent is just error
Reply that only behavioural economists are qualified to judge interest rates

quiz.q: Name the school of economic thought, named after the writer who built on the labour theory of value, that analyses the economy through class conflict and the dynamics of capital.
Which statement captures the 'counter' caution about economic pluralism?
choices: Treating every school as equally valid risks 'anything goes' — some claims are still better supported by evidence than others
Pluralism proves that no economic claim can ever be tested against evidence
Once you accept many schools exist, the mainstream school must be discarded
Disagreement among schools means economic data is always fabricated

cards.title: Adam Smith and the invisible hand
cards.fact: Smith argued a butcher feeds you not from kindness but from self-interest — and somehow it works.
cards.detail: Smith (1776) argued self-interested exchange, coordinated 'as if by an invisible hand', can benefit all, powered by the division of labour. But he also rooted society in sympathy and distrusted merchants — he's far more nuanced than the caricature. The 'invisible hand' line appears exactly once in The Wealth of Nations, in Book IV, and there it is narrow: a merchant who prefers to invest at home rather than abroad ends up supporting domestic industry without intending to. Smith's earlier book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), opens by saying people are interested in the fortune of others and want their happiness even when they get nothing from it but the pleasure of seeing it, which is why reading him as a prophet of pure selfishness misses half his work.
cards.deploy: Useful against caricatures of 'capitalism = greed is good' — even Smith didn't say that.
cards.counter: Smith still defended self-interest and markets as broadly benign — he isn't the proto-socialist some make him either.

quiz.q: Smith's 'invisible hand' is the idea that…
choices: Government must guide markets
Self-interested action can benefit all
Greed is morally good
Prices are always fair

quiz.q: Smith's butcher example is meant to show that:
choices: Self-interested exchange, not benevolence, is what reliably gets your dinner on the table
Butchers are uniquely generous and supply meat out of kindness
Markets fail whenever participants act in their own interest
Central planners must direct the butcher to supply the right amount of meat

quiz.q: Besides self-interest, Smith grounded human society in a moral sentiment he wrote a whole book about. What is that sentiment?
In which year did Smith publish 'The Wealth of Nations', where the invisible-hand argument appears?

cards.title: The division of labour
cards.fact: Smith watched a pin factory and saw the secret of modern wealth: split the job up.
cards.detail: Splitting work into specialised steps multiplies output — Smith's pin factory is the classic example. But he and later Marx warned it can also deskill and alienate the worker. Smith's own figures: a worker doing every step alone could make perhaps twenty pins a day, but ten workers splitting the job into about eighteen distinct operations made upwards of forty-eight thousand, or 4,800 each. Marx's worry, in Capital, was the flip side of that arithmetic: a worker who repeats one motion all day loses the wider skill of the trade and becomes easy to replace.
cards.deploy: Explains assembly lines, supply chains and outsourcing — and their human downside.
cards.counter: Specialisation also lifted billions out of subsistence; the gains are real, not just the costs.

quiz.q: Suppose one worker doing every step of pin-making alone produces 20 pins a day. If splitting the work into specialised steps raises output to 4,800 pins per worker per day, by what factor did per-worker output increase?
Modern global supply chains, where a single product is assembled from components made in many specialised factories worldwide, are a large-scale application of which idea?
choices: The division of labour
The labour theory of value
The invisible hand of price signals only
The theory of rent

quiz.q: What one-word term did Smith and later Marx use for the worker's sense of disconnection that repetitive, fragmented work can cause?

cards.title: Ricardo and the logic machine
cards.fact: David Ricardo turned economics into a machine of pure logic — and reached unsettling conclusions.
cards.detail: Ricardo built ruthless logical models: comparative advantage, the theory of rent (landlords gain as population grows), and a labour theory of value later taken up by Marx and dropped by the mainstream. Comparative advantage is the counterintuitive part: even if Portugal makes both cloth and wine more cheaply than England in absolute terms, both gain if each specialises where its own cost ratio is lowest and they trade. Say at home England gives up 1 wine to make a cloth while Portugal gives up 2; England should make cloth and swap it for Portuguese wine, and both end up with more of each.
cards.deploy: Shows distribution-as-class-conflict has deep roots inside classical economics, not just in Marx.
cards.counter: The labour theory of value faces hard problems (capital, time, skill) that marginalism was designed to solve.

quiz.q: Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage implies that a country should specialise in and export the goods in which it:
choices: Has the lowest relative (opportunity) cost, even if a trading partner is better at making everything
Has an absolute productivity lead over every other country
Faces the highest land rents
Employs the most workers per unit of output

quiz.q: According to Ricardo's theory of rent, which class captures a growing share of income as population rises?
The labour theory of value, which Ricardo developed and Marx later adopted, was largely abandoned by the mainstream because it struggled to account for the role of:
choices: Capital, time and differences in skill in determining prices
International borders in restricting trade
Population growth in raising land rents
Self-interest in motivating exchange

cards.title: Where does value come from?
cards.fact: Is a thing valuable because of the work in it, or because of how much you want it?
cards.detail: Classical economists and Marx located value in labour; marginalists from the 1870s relocated it in usefulness at the margin. The mainstream took the second path — but the first still frames profit as extraction rather than reward. Take the old puzzle of why a diamond fetches more than a bucket of water though water keeps you alive. The labour answer points to the days of mining and cutting behind the diamond; the marginal answer points to the next unit, since one more bucket is worth little where water is plentiful while one more diamond is still scarce.
cards.deploy: Lets you locate an argument: profit-as-reward (marginalist) vs profit-as-extraction (Marxian).
cards.counter: Marginalism resolved real puzzles — like why water is cheap and diamonds dear — that the labour theory struggled with.

quiz.q: A factory owner sells goods for far more than the wages and materials cost. A labour-theory-of-value advocate and a marginalist describe the gap differently. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Labour view: extraction of unpaid worker effort; marginalist view: reward for supplying a scarce, useful factor
Labour view: reward for risk-taking; marginalist view: theft from consumers
Labour view: a market accident; marginalist view: surplus value created by labour
Both views: the gap is purely a measurement error in accounting

quiz.q: Marginalists located the value of a good not in the labour embodied in it but in its usefulness at the margin. Give the two-word concept (the usefulness of one more unit).
Water is essential to life yet cheap, while diamonds are inessential yet dear. Why does this 'paradox of value' favour the marginalist account over the labour theory?
choices: Value tracks the usefulness of the last available unit, so an extra unit of abundant water is worth little while a scarce diamond is worth much
Value tracks the total hours of labour, so water took longer to produce
Value tracks how essential a good is overall, which predicts water should be priciest
Value tracks the raw materials consumed, which are higher for water

cards.title: The marginal revolution (1870s)
cards.fact: In the 1870s economics quietly changed its mind about what value even is.
cards.detail: Around 1871–1874, Jevons, Menger and Walras relocated value in marginal utility, founding neoclassical economics and shifting the field from class and distribution toward individual optimisation and equilibrium. Marginal utility means the worth of one more unit, not the total: your tenth glass of water on an ordinary day adds almost nothing, so price tracks that last glass rather than water's life-or-death usefulness. This is why the new economics could explain prices by individual choices about the next purchase instead of by how much labour a good contained.
cards.deploy: Explains why mainstream economics talks about utility and equilibrium rather than class.
cards.counter: The marginalist tools genuinely unified price theory and remain the workhorse of applied economics.

quiz.q: Name any one of the three economists credited with independently founding the marginalist (neoclassical) approach to value in the early 1870s.
The marginal revolution is dated to roughly 1871-1874, with a midpoint of about 1872. How many years separate 1872 and the year 2026?
After the marginal revolution, the central questions of mainstream economics shifted away from one focus and toward another. Which shift describes it?
choices: From class and the distribution of output toward individual optimisation and equilibrium
From individual choice toward the labour embodied in commodities
From equilibrium analysis toward the historical study of class conflict
From price theory toward the moral philosophy of just wages

cards.title: Marx's Capital
cards.fact: Marx didn't just dislike capitalism — he tried to reverse-engineer its hidden machinery.
cards.detail: Marx (1867) argued workers produce more value than their wage ('surplus value'), the source of profit and capital; competition drives accumulation, crises and concentration. His critique outlived his failed predictions. The surplus-value claim works like this: if a worker's day produces goods worth 8 hours of value but the wage only covers the 4 hours needed to keep the worker living, the other 4 hours are unpaid and become the owner's profit. Marx called that 4-hours-on-4 ratio the rate of exploitation, and argued competition forces owners to plough the surplus back into more machinery, which sets off the cycles he tracked.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for arguments about exploitation, inequality and recurring financial crises.
cards.counter: How to read this is itself contested. Cold-War liberals point to the shortages and repression of Soviet-style central planning. Western Marxists (David Harvey) and market socialists (Oskar Lange) reply that Marx analysed capitalism, not a blueprint for command economies, and that his crisis theory is distinct from Stalinist planning; dependency theorists add that capitalism exports its crises to the periphery. Whether the USSR refutes Marx, or only one statist version of socialism, is disputed.

quiz.q: For Marx, profit ('surplus value') comes from…
choices: Clever investment
Value workers produce above their wage
Government subsidy
Lucky trades

quiz.q: Under Marx's account, suppose a worker's daily wage covers the value they create in the first 5 hours of a 9-hour shift. How many hours of surplus value does the capitalist appropriate that day?
Which 20th-century geographer and Marxist scholar argued that Marx analysed capitalism itself rather than offering a blueprint for Soviet-style command economies?
A debater claims 'the collapse of the USSR proves Marx was wrong.' Which response best reflects the contested reading of Marx's Capital?
choices: Marx critiqued capitalism's dynamics, so a failed statist planning system may refute one version of socialism without refuting his analysis of capitalism
Marx wrote Capital as a detailed operating manual for central planning, so the USSR is a direct test of it
Marx predicted the USSR specifically, so its fall confirms his crisis theory
Marx denied that crises occur, so the USSR is irrelevant to his work

cards.title: Historical materialism
cards.fact: Marx's big bet: to understand history, follow how people make their living.
cards.detail: Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes a society's politics and ideas, and that history advances as productive forces outgrow old ownership arrangements. Powerful as a habit of analysis, contested as a law of history. Marx's own example is the hand-mill versus the steam-mill: the hand-mill, he wrote, gives you society with the feudal lord, the steam-mill society with the industrial capitalist. Concretely, the heavy plough and water mills of medieval Europe made large manorial estates workable and tied peasants into serfdom under lords; once merchant trade and early factories grew, feudal labour duties became a drag on owners who wanted wage labour they could hire and fire, and the legal and political order broke to fit the new way of producing.
cards.deploy: Prompts the sharp question: 'whose material interests does this idea serve?'.
cards.counter: Culture, religion and ideas have driven huge changes no economic base predicted.

quiz.q: Historical materialism claims history advances through a particular tension. Which best states it?
choices: Growing productive forces strain against the existing ownership and property arrangements
Competing religious doctrines strain against scientific discovery
National identities strain against international institutions
Individual preferences strain against market prices in equilibrium

quiz.q: In historical materialism, what term names the economic foundation of production that is said to shape a society's politics and ideas (as opposed to the 'superstructure')?
A historian shows the Protestant Reformation reshaped European economies in ways no prior change in production foretold. How does this bear on historical materialism?
choices: It is a standard objection: religion and ideas drove major change the economic base did not predict
It confirms the theory, since religion is part of the economic base
It is irrelevant, because historical materialism only concerns the 20th century
It proves the superstructure always determines the base

cards.title: Keynes and the stuck economy
cards.fact: Keynes argued a market economy can get stuck in a slump — and just sit there.
cards.detail: Keynes (1936) argued economies can settle below full employment when demand collapses, so government should boost demand in slumps. Dominant until 1970s stagflation, revived after 2008. The mechanism is a spending chain: one person's spending is another's income, so a fall in spending cuts incomes, which cuts spending again, and the economy settles at a lower level with idle workers and idle factories. Government spending in a slump is meant to restart that chain when households and firms will not.
cards.deploy: The canonical case for stimulus in a recession — private demand can fail to recover by itself.
cards.counter: Sustained deficit spending can stoke inflation and debt; the 1970s showed demand management has limits.

quiz.q: Keynes argued that in a slump, the economy…
choices: Always self-corrects fast
Can stay stuck below full employment
Needs higher interest rates
Should cut all spending

quiz.q: Keynes's prescription for a demand-deficient slump was…
choices: Cut public spending to balance the budget
Government spending to lift aggregate demand
Raise interest rates sharply
Wait for wages to fall on their own

quiz.q: A country's private firms and households cut spending sharply after a financial crisis, and output stays well below capacity for years with no automatic rebound. Whose framework best explains why the economy fails to self-correct?
choices: Keynes, who argued an economy can settle at an equilibrium below full employment
Hayek, who argued dispersed prices coordinate the economy automatically
Friedman, who argued inflation is always a monetary phenomenon
Smith, who argued an invisible hand always restores full output

quiz.q: Keynes laid out his theory of demand-deficient slumps in his 1936 book. What is the one-word concept (starting with 'd') that, when it collapses, his theory says traps the economy below full employment?

Keynesian thinking dominated policy from the publication of his General Theory until stagflation discredited it, then was revived after the global financial crisis. Using 1936 and the 1973 onset of 1970s stagflation, for how many years did Keynesian demand management dominate before that setback?

cards.title: The paradox of thrift
cards.fact: If everyone saves more at once, the country can end up saving less.
cards.detail: Saving is prudent for one household but, if everyone does it at once in a slump, spending and incomes fall and total saving can drop — a 'fallacy of composition' Keynes used to justify stimulus. Concretely, suppose ten shops in a town each try to save by cutting their wage bills. Each shop's customers are partly the other shops' laid-off workers, so sales drop across the town, profits shrink, and the shops end up with less cash to set aside than before they tried to save.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'everyone should just budget like a household' fails for a whole economy at once.
cards.counter: In normal times saving does finance investment; the paradox is a slump phenomenon, not a general law.

quiz.q: During a recession, a politician argues 'every family tightens its belt when times are hard, so the whole nation should too.' Why does the paradox of thrift say this reasoning can backfire?
choices: When all households cut spending at once, others' incomes fall, so total saving can drop
Higher saving by everyone permanently raises the inflation rate
Banks are legally barred from lending out additional household deposits
Individual budgeting always increases a single household's debt

quiz.q: The paradox of thrift is a classic example of a reasoning error where what is true for one part is wrongly assumed true for the whole. What is the name of this logical fallacy?

Suppose in normal times an economy's households together save 600 billion per year. A panic hits and everyone tries to save more, but spending and incomes fall so much that actual total saving drops to 480 billion. By what percent did total saving fall, illustrating the paradox of thrift?

cards.title: Friedman and monetarism
cards.fact: Milton Friedman's counter-revolution: inflation is always, everywhere, about money.
cards.detail: Friedman argued inflation is fundamentally monetary and government meddling does more harm than good. Strict monetarism failed in practice, but his free-market politics shaped the neoliberal era. His reasoning runs through the quantity equation MV = PY: money supply times how often each unit is spent equals the price level times real output. Friedman held that spending frequency (velocity) and output are fairly steady over the long run, so pushing more money in mainly raises prices. He concluded central banks should grow the money supply at a slow fixed rate tied to expected output growth, roughly three to five percent a year, instead of reacting to each downturn.
cards.deploy: The standard hawkish case that loose money, not greedy sellers, drives inflation.
cards.counter: Keynesian economists like James Tobin disputed the tight money–inflation link; in practice supply shocks and expectations matter, and central banks abandoned strict monetary targets when they failed to hold. Critics also point to the 'Chicago Boys' in Pinochet's Chile — the view, associated with Naomi Klein's 'shock doctrine', that free-market reforms were imposed under dictatorship rather than chosen democratically.

quiz.q: Two economists debate a country's rising prices. One insists the inflation must trace back to excessive growth in the money supply, not to supply shocks or seller behaviour. Which thinker's position is this?
choices: Milton Friedman's monetarist view
John Maynard Keynes's demand-management view
James Tobin's Keynesian view
Friedrich Hayek's knowledge-problem view

quiz.q: Naomi Klein popularised a phrase for the idea that free-market reforms were imposed during crises or under dictatorship rather than chosen democratically, citing the U.S.-trained economists who advised Pinochet's Chile. What two-word phrase is associated with her?
Critics of Friedman point to the group of free-market economists, trained at one U.S. university, who advised Pinochet's regime in Chile. By what nickname is this group known?

cards.title: Hayek and the knowledge problem
cards.fact: Hayek's argument against central planning: nobody knows enough — but prices do.
cards.detail: Hayek (1945) argued that dispersed knowledge makes central planning impossible, while prices coordinate it automatically — a deep case for markets that information economists like Joseph Stiglitz later qualified, citing externalities, monopoly and imperfect information. Another way to see it: no single person knows that a tin mine has collapsed somewhere, yet the tin price rises worldwide within days and thousands of users cut back or switch to other metals without ever learning why. The price carries the news that no planner could have gathered in time. This is close to Hayek's own tin example in the 1945 paper.
cards.deploy: The strongest principled argument against detailed central planning — it's a knowledge problem, not just a motivation one.
cards.counter: Information economists like Joseph Stiglitz showed markets with imperfect information aren't efficient either, and prices routinely misprice externalities and public goods — which is why even market economies regulate. The socialist-calculation debate also had another side: Oskar Lange argued planners could simulate prices, and modern computational-planning advocates (and Chile's 1970s Cybersyn experiment) claim better data narrows Hayek's knowledge gap.

quiz.q: Hayek's core objection to detailed central planning is best summarised as which of the following?
choices: The knowledge needed is dispersed among millions of people, so no central body can gather it, while prices convey it automatically
Central planners lack the motivation to act in the public interest
Planning is impossible because money has no intrinsic value
Markets fail whenever there are externalities, so planning is required

quiz.q: In the socialist-calculation debate, one economist argued against Hayek that planners could mimic markets by adjusting administered prices through trial and error. Name this economist.

Information economists argued markets with imperfect information are not efficient, qualifying Hayek's case. Which economist does the card name as most associated with this critique of the price mechanism?

cards.title: The hockey stick
cards.fact: For most of history, ordinary living standards barely moved. Then, around 1800, they exploded.
cards.detail: After millennia of near-flat living standards, sustained growth began with Britain's Industrial Revolution (~1800), lifting output per person many-fold — at an immense early human and environmental cost. To picture the scale: Broadberry and colleagues' figures have English output per person taking roughly 400 years to double before 1800, then doubling again in about a century during the nineteenth century and faster after that. A person in 1700 lived much as their great-great-grandparents had; a person in 1900 had railways, gaslight and Atlantic steamships their grandparents never knew.
cards.deploy: Anchors any argument about technology and growth — the modern world is a recent, fragile exception.
cards.counter: Why Britain, and why then, is fiercely contested. The Eurocentric 'European genius' story is challenged by Kenneth Pomeranz and the California School (cheap coal and New World land broke the deadlock, not innate superiority) and by Eric Williams and Sven Beckert, who root the take-off in Atlantic slavery and colonial extraction ('war capitalism'). The early human and ecological costs were also immense and unevenly borne.

quiz.q: The 'hockey stick' of economic history refers to…
choices: Steadily falling prices
Living standards flat for millennia then rising sharply
The economics of sport
A series of stock crashes

quiz.q: The 'California School' explanation (Kenneth Pomeranz) for why Britain industrialised first emphasises which factor?
choices: A unique European cultural genius for invention
Access to cheap coal and New World land that broke an ecological deadlock
A superior work ethic relative to Asia
Earlier adoption of parliamentary democracy

quiz.q: Which historian rooted Britain's industrial take-off in Atlantic slavery and colonial extraction, a thesis later developed by Sven Beckert as 'war capitalism'?
Sustained modern growth began around 1800. Counting from that take-off to the year 2050, how many years is that?

cards.title: Enclosure and the making of workers
cards.fact: Before there were factory workers, common land had to be fenced off — and people pushed into wage labour.
cards.detail: English enclosure (1500s–1800s) privatised common land, creating a wage-dependent workforce — Marx's 'primitive accumulation'. Read either as an efficiency gain or as mass dispossession. Concretely, a villager who had grazed a cow, cut firewood and gleaned grain on the common lost all of it once the field was hedged and deeded to a single owner. With no land to fall back on, selling a day's labour for a wage became the only way to eat, which is the workforce the new factories needed.
cards.deploy: Reminds us markets in land and labour were created — often by force — not simply 'natural'.
cards.counter: Enclosure also raised food output sharply at a time of rising population; it wasn't pure loss.

quiz.q: What two-word term did Marx use for the process by which enclosure stripped people of common land and pushed them into wage labour?
Which outcome is the strongest counter-argument to viewing English enclosure as pure dispossession?
choices: It restored common grazing rights to villagers
It sharply raised agricultural food output during a period of rising population
It reduced the supply of wage labourers for early factories
It returned privatised land to communal ownership by 1800

quiz.q: If English enclosure is dated roughly from 1500 to 1850, over how many centuries did the process unfold?

cards.title: Bretton Woods and the end of gold
cards.fact: For 27 years the world's money was anchored to gold through the dollar — until one night in 1971 it wasn't.
cards.detail: Bretton Woods (1944) pegged currencies to a gold-backed dollar; Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971 and money became pure fiat. Whether money needs a hard anchor is still argued.
cards.deploy: Background for any argument about fiat money, inflation, gold standards or cryptocurrencies.
cards.counter: Whether money needs a hard anchor is genuinely split. Austrian-school 'sound money' advocates (Mises, Rothbard, and today Ron Paul's 'End the Fed' current) argue fiat invites inflation and debt; Keynesians reply gold's discipline deepened the Great Depression. Robert Triffin warned a dollar anchor builds in instability, while Modern Monetary Theory takes the opposite pole — a sovereign fiat issuer faces inflation, not solvency, limits. No camp has won.

quiz.q: Bretton Woods pegged currencies to a gold-backed dollar from its 1944 founding until the US ended gold convertibility. If the arrangement lasted 27 years, in what year did it end?
Which economist warned that anchoring the world's money to one nation's currency builds in instability, an idea now known by his name as a 'dilemma'?
How does Modern Monetary Theory characterise the binding constraint on a government that issues its own sovereign fiat currency?
choices: Solvency: it can run out of money and default
Inflation: real resource limits, not insolvency, are the true constraint
Gold reserves: spending is capped by the metal it holds
Foreign approval: it must match the discipline of a gold standard

cards.title: The Great Depression
cards.fact: The 1930s slump was so deep it rewrote economics — and economists still argue about why.
cards.detail: The 1930s Depression — mass unemployment after the 1929 crash — birthed Keynesianism and the activist state. Its causes (demand collapse, monetary contraction, the gold standard) remain contested. Concretely, more than 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933 and US unemployment reached about 25 percent in 1933. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Federal Reserve for letting the money supply shrink by about a third; Keynes blamed collapsing demand; Barry Eichengreen pointed to the gold standard, which forced countries to defend their exchange rate instead of their economy, and the ones that left it earliest recovered first.
cards.deploy: Every modern crisis response (2008, 2020) is haunted by 'don't repeat the 1930s'.
cards.counter: There's no settled single cause — demand, money, banking and the gold standard all played a part.

quiz.q: The Great Depression gave rise to which school of macroeconomic thought, named after the economist who argued for an activist state managing demand?
The stock market crash that preceded the slump occurred in 1929. How many years separate the 1929 crash from the year 1939?
Why is there no single agreed cause of the Great Depression among economists?
choices: Records from the 1930s were almost entirely destroyed
Demand collapse, monetary contraction, banking failures and the gold standard each plausibly contributed
Economists agree it was caused solely by the 1929 stock crash
It only affected the United States, so global data is missing

cards.title: The 1970s stagflation
cards.fact: In the 1970s, prices and unemployment rose together — which the textbooks said couldn't happen.
cards.detail: 1970s stagflation — high inflation and unemployment together — broke the simple Phillips curve and was widely used to discredit Keynesian demand management and usher in monetarism and the free-market turn.
cards.deploy: The go-to counter to naive Keynesianism — and the origin story of modern central banking.
cards.counter: That 'Keynes failed, markets won' lesson is itself contested. Heavy oil shocks drove much of the inflation, and post-Keynesians in Hyman Minsky's tradition read stagflation as distributional conflict — a wage–price spiral — not proof demand management is futile. The turn to monetarism and deregulation was a political choice as much as a technical verdict; Friedman's own strict money targets were abandoned soon after.

quiz.q: The combination of high inflation and high unemployment occurring at the same time is known by what one-word term?
1970s stagflation was widely taken to break which relationship, normally drawn as a downward-sloping trade-off between inflation and unemployment?
choices: The Phillips curve
The Laffer curve
The Lorenz curve
The yield curve

quiz.q: Which reading of 1970s stagflation comes from the post-Keynesian tradition associated with Hyman Minsky?
choices: It proved demand management is always futile
It was caused purely by central banks printing too much money
It reflected a distributional wage-price spiral rather than disproving demand management
It showed unemployment and inflation can never move together

cards.title: The neoliberal turn
cards.fact: Around 1980, the rich world swung from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'.
cards.detail: From ~1980, Thatcher and Reagan drove privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation and weaker unions, drawing on Friedman and Hayek. Credited with taming inflation, blamed for inequality and the 2008 crisis. Concretely, the US top marginal income-tax rate fell from 70 percent in 1980 to 28 percent by 1988, and British trade-union membership dropped from over 13 million in 1979 to around 7 million by 1997. David Harvey reads the turn as a project to restore the income and wealth share of the top few percent rather than to free growth as such; the intellectual source it drew on, Hayek's 1944 The Road to Serfdom, had argued specifically against central economic planning, and Hayek himself allowed for a welfare-state safety net within general rules.
cards.deploy: Names the framework most current economic arguments are still reacting for or against.
cards.counter: It's a loose, contested label: its architects (Friedman, Hayek, Thatcher, Reagan) sold it as freeing growth, while critics like Joseph Stiglitz and Naomi Klein blame it for inequality and financial crises — and results varied enormously by country.

quiz.q: Name one of the two economists most often cited as the intellectual sources of the post-1980 free-market turn led by Thatcher and Reagan.
Which set of policies best characterises the post-1980 shift from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'?
choices: Nationalisation, higher tariffs, and stronger union power
Privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation, and weaker unions
Fixed exchange rates, capital controls, and price ceilings
Universal basic income, wage floors, and central planning

quiz.q: Which economist is named as a critic blaming the neoliberal turn for rising inequality and financial crises?
choices: Friedrich Hayek
Milton Friedman
Margaret Thatcher
Joseph Stiglitz

cards.title: The 2008 financial crisis
cards.fact: In 2008 the financial system nearly stopped — and the faith that markets police themselves took a beating.
cards.detail: A 2008 mortgage bubble froze global finance and triggered the worst slump since the 1930s. The bailout-and-stimulus response revived Keynes and dented 'efficient markets' faith; its causes and the later austerity remain contested. Concretely, US house prices roughly doubled from 2000 to 2006 then fell about a third, and when Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008 banks stopped lending to each other because nobody could tell who held the bad mortgage-backed securities. Raghuram Rajan had warned at Jackson Hole in 2005 that risk was building up in the financial system; the Austrian-school camp, such as Lawrence White at the Cato Institute, instead blamed the Fed's low interest rates and government programmes (the Community Reinvestment Act, FHA loans) that pushed banks to expand home lending.
cards.deploy: The modern reference point for financial regulation, bailouts and 'too big to fail'.
cards.counter: Causes are contested — reckless private finance, or government distortions and easy money, or both.

quiz.q: The 2008 crisis was triggered by the collapse of a bubble in which type of lending?
Which idea about financial markets lost the most credibility as a result of the 2008 crisis?
choices: The belief that markets efficiently price assets and police themselves
The belief that governments should run balanced budgets
The belief that inflation is always a monetary phenomenon
The belief that free trade raises total output

quiz.q: The bailout-and-stimulus response to the 2008 crisis is most associated with reviving the ideas of which economist?
choices: Friedrich Hayek
Milton Friedman
John Maynard Keynes
Adam Smith

cards.title: A letter is a number you don't know yet
cards.fact: A variable like x is just a placeholder standing in for a number.
cards.detail: A variable is a name for a number. Writing \(2x\) means 'two times x', whatever x turns out to be. An expression like \(3x + 5\) is a recipe: feed in a number for \(x\) and it gives one out — if \(x = 4\), then \(3x + 5 = 17\). The point of a letter is generality: \(A = \pi r^2\) gives the area of every circle in one line, instead of a separate sum for each radius.

media.caption: An expression is a recipe; plug in a value.

cards.deploy: Lets one statement cover every case at once — the move from arithmetic to algebra.
cards.counter: A symbol only helps if you track what it stands for and its units; the same letter meaning two different things inside one argument is a classic error.

quiz.q: If x = 4, what is 3x + 5?
Using the rule 3x + 5, what value comes out when you feed in x = 10?
The area of a circle is A = pi times r^2. For a circle of radius r = 3, what is its area? Use pi = 3.14.
In the expression 7y, what single operation is implied between the 7 and the y?

cards.title: An equation is a balance scale
cards.fact: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other — and it stays true.
cards.detail: An equation says two things are equal. \(x + 3 = 7\) reads 'some number plus 3 equals 7'. Think of \(=\) as the pivot of a balance: the two sides weigh the same. To find \(x\), undo what surrounds it by doing the same thing to both sides. Subtract 3 from each: \(x + 3 - 3 = 7 - 3\), so \(x = 4\). The scale never tips because you changed both sides equally. That single habit — do the same to both sides — solves most of school algebra.

media.caption: Subtract 3 from both sides to isolate x.

cards.deploy: Turns 'solving for x' into a mechanical routine: isolate the unknown by undoing operations symmetrically.
cards.counter: Balance holds only for reversible operations applied equally. Multiplying both sides by zero, or by an unknown that might be zero, can erase real solutions or invent fake ones.

quiz.q: To solve x + 3 = 7, you…
choices: Add 3 to the left only
Subtract 3 from both sides
Multiply both sides by 0
Swap x and 7

quiz.q: Keeping both sides equal, solve for x in: x - 5 = 12. What is x?
Which operation applied to both sides of an equation can destroy a real solution or invent a false one, breaking the balance-scale guarantee?
choices: Multiplying both sides by an expression that could equal zero
Adding the same constant to both sides
Subtracting the same constant from both sides
Dividing both sides by 2

quiz.q: To isolate x in 4x = 20 you divide both sides by the same number to keep them balanced. What value of x results?

cards.title: A function is a machine
cards.fact: Put a number in, get exactly one number out — that's a function.
cards.detail: Write \(f(x)\) — read 'f of x' — for the output when the input is \(x\). The rule \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) doubles the input and adds one, so \(f(3) = 7\). 'Exactly one output' is the whole idea: a function never returns two answers for the same input. Lay the input along the bottom and the output up the side and you get a graph — a picture of the rule. Functions are the things calculus and machine learning act on.

media.caption: f(x) = 2x + 1 — one output for every input.

cards.deploy: Names the basic object of all higher maths: a dependable input→output rule you can graph, combine and analyse.
cards.counter: A relation that gives two outputs for one input (like 'a number's square roots', ±) is not a function — distinguishing the two avoids real mistakes.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 2x + 1, what is f(3)?
For the rule g(x) = 3x - 2, what is g(5)?
A rule pairs one input with two different outputs (for example, mapping 9 to both +3 and -3). Why is this not a function?
choices: A function must give exactly one output for each input
A function cannot use negative numbers
A function must always increase as the input grows
A function can only take whole numbers as inputs

quiz.q: When you plot a function with inputs along the horizontal axis and outputs up the vertical axis, what is the resulting picture of the rule called?

cards.title: Powers and roots
cards.fact: A power is repeated multiplication; a root undoes it.
cards.detail: \(a^n\) means multiply \(a\) by itself \(n\) times: \(2^3 = 2\times2\times2 = 8\), and \(2^{10} = 1024\). The square root undoes squaring: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) because \(3^2 = 9\). Powers of the same base add when you multiply: \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\). This is what lets us write the huge and the tiny compactly — scientific notation: \(6.02\times10^{23}\) particles, or \(10^{-9}\) for a billionth.

media.say: a-to-the-m times a-to-the-n equals a-to-the-(m plus n).
media.caption: Multiplying powers adds the exponents.
2ˣ explodes — each step doubles the last.

cards.deploy: Compresses repeated multiplication and gives a clean way to handle very large or very small numbers.
cards.counter: Sign and fraction rules trip people up: \(a^0 = 1\), a negative exponent means a reciprocal (\(a^{-1} = 1/a\)), and a fractional one means a root (\(a^{1/2} = \sqrt a\)).

quiz.q: What is 2¹⁰?
Using the rule that powers of the same base add when multiplied, what is 3^2 times 3^3? Give the final value.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal. What is the value of 5^-1 as a decimal?
Which statement correctly applies the exponent rules?

cards.title: Logarithms: the inverse of powers
cards.fact: A logarithm answers one question: what power produces this number?
cards.detail: \(\log_{10} 1000 = 3\) because \(10^3 = 1000\). The log is the exponent. Its key trick is turning multiplication into addition: \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\). A log scale (decibels, the Richter scale, pH) spaces powers of ten evenly, so 10 and 1000 sit the same distance apart, which tames quantities that span many orders of magnitude. In machine learning logs are everywhere — they turn long products of probabilities into manageable sums.

media.say: log-base-b of x-times-y equals log of x plus log of y.
media.caption: Logs convert products into sums.
The logarithm: quick to rise, then a slow crawl.

cards.deploy: Lets you read quantities that span orders of magnitude, and replace awkward products with sums.
cards.counter: Logs are only defined for positive numbers, and the base matters: base 10, base 2 and the natural base \(e\) differ by a constant factor, so always say which you mean.

quiz.q: What is log₁₀(1000)?
Since a logarithm asks 'what power produces this number?', what is log base 2 of 32?
Using log(ab) = log(a) + log(b): if log(a) = 0.7 and log(b) = 1.3, what is log(a times b)?
Why must you always state the base when working with logarithms?
choices: Base 10, base 2, and the natural base e give values that differ by a constant factor
Logs of the same number are identical in every base
Only base 10 is mathematically valid
The base determines whether negative inputs are allowed

cards.title: The straight line: y = mx + b
cards.fact: Every straight line is y = mx + b: m is the slope, b is where it crosses the axis.
cards.detail: The slope \(m\) is rise over run — how much \(y\) climbs for each step right. The intercept \(b\) is the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\), where the line meets the vertical axis. So \(y = 2x + 1\) starts at 1 and climbs 2 for every 1 across. A bigger \(m\) tilts the line steeper; a negative \(m\) sends it downhill. This is the simplest model in all of statistics and machine learning — a prediction that changes at a constant rate.

media.caption: Drag m and b: the line tilts and shifts.

cards.deploy: The default first model whenever one quantity changes steadily with another.
cards.counter: Most real relationships aren't straight; a line is a deliberately simple approximation, useful precisely because it has just two numbers to find.

quiz.q: In y = mx + b, what does b represent?
choices: The slope
Where the line crosses the y-axis
The steepness
The x-value

quiz.q: For the line y = -3x + 7, what is the value of y when x = 4?
If the slope m of a line is negative, in which direction does the line head as you read it from left to right?

cards.title: Curves and the quadratic
cards.fact: Add an x² term and the straight line bends into a parabola.
cards.detail: \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) traces a parabola — a U-shaped curve. The coefficient \(a\) sets how narrow it is and which way it opens (up if \(a>0\), down if \(a<0\)); \(c\) shifts it vertically. To find where it crosses zero, the quadratic formula gives the answer for any quadratic: \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). Parabolas describe thrown objects, and the U-shape is exactly the kind of curve machine learning slides down to find its best fit.

media.caption: y = ax² + bx + c — change a, b, c to reshape the parabola.

cards.deploy: The first step beyond straight lines, and the shape of the cost surfaces optimisers descend.
cards.counter: The quadratic formula's discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac\) can be negative — then the curve never crosses zero and the (real) solutions don't exist.

quiz.q: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a…
choices: Straight line
Parabola
Circle
Spiral

quiz.q: Using the quadratic formula, find the larger root of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0.
For the parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c with a = -2, which statement is true?
choices: It opens downward
It opens upward
It is a straight line
It never has a maximum

quiz.q: Compute the discriminant b^2 - 4ac for the quadratic 2x^2 + 3x + 5.

cards.title: Sigma notation: add up a list
cards.fact: The symbol Σ is shorthand for 'add up all of these'.
cards.detail: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\) means add \(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\). The \(i\) is a counter that runs from the bottom number to the top one. For example \(\sum_{i=1}^{4} i = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10\). The average of \(n\) numbers is just \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\). This one symbol runs through all of statistics and machine learning: every total error, mean, and dot product is a sum written this way.

media.say: the sum of x-one, x-two, and so on up to x-n.
media.caption: Sigma says: run the counter and add.
Σ adds the bars: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

cards.deploy: Compresses 'add up many terms' into one symbol you'll meet in every quantitative field.
cards.counter: The limits and the index matter: \(\sum_{i=0}\) versus \(\sum_{i=1}\), or summing the wrong variable, silently changes the result.

quiz.q: What does Σ (from i=1 to 4) of i equal?
Evaluate the sum from i=1 to 5 of i (that is, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5).
The numbers 4, 8, 6, 2 are added with sigma notation and then averaged using (1/n) times their sum. What is the average?
In the expression sum from i=1 to n of x_i, what is the role of the letter i?

cards.title: The limit: getting infinitely close
cards.fact: A limit is the value a function heads toward as the input creeps up to a point.
cards.detail: Sometimes a function misbehaves exactly at one point but behaves perfectly all around it. \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) reads as \(0/0\) at \(x = 0\), yet as \(x\) shrinks toward zero the ratio heads steadily to 1. The limit, written \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\), captures that destination without ever dividing by zero. Making 'infinitely close' precise is the foundation the rest of calculus stands on.

media.caption: Undefined at 0, yet it heads to 1.
sin(x)/x has a hole at 0, yet heads to 1.

cards.deploy: Lets you reason about behaviour at a point a function can't actually reach — the gateway to derivatives and integrals.
cards.counter: A limit can fail to exist: if a function jumps, or approaches different values from the left and the right, there is no single destination.

quiz.q: A limit describes the value a function…
choices: Reaches exactly
Heads toward as the input approaches a point
Has at infinity only
Can never have

quiz.q: A function jumps to a different value when approached from the left than from the right at a point. What can be said about the limit there?
choices: The limit does not exist
The limit equals the average of the two sides
The limit equals zero
The limit always equals the function's value at that point

quiz.q: What is the limit of (sin x)/x as x approaches 0?
Why is a limit useful for evaluating (sin x)/x at x = 0?
choices: It finds the value the ratio heads toward without ever dividing by zero
It changes the function into a straight line
It forces the function to equal its slope
It removes the sine term entirely

cards.title: The derivative: the slope of a curve
cards.fact: The derivative is how fast something is changing right now — the slope of a curve at a point.
cards.detail: A straight line has one slope everywhere. A curve's steepness keeps changing. The derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) (also written \(f'(x)\)) is the slope of the tangent line that just grazes the curve at a single point. You find it by taking the slope between two nearby points and letting them slide together — a limit. For \(f(x) = x^2\), the derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\): at \(x = 3\) the curve climbs with slope 6. Speed is the derivative of distance; acceleration is the derivative of speed.

media.say: f-prime of x equals the limit, as h shrinks to zero, of the change in f divided by h.
media.caption: The slope between two points, as they merge.
Slide the point — the tangent's slope is the derivative.

cards.deploy: The universal tool for rates of change: speed, growth, marginal cost, and the direction to adjust a model.
cards.counter: A derivative needs a smooth curve. At a sharp corner or a jump the slope isn't defined — the function is not differentiable there.

quiz.q: The derivative of a function at a point is the…
choices: Area under it
Slope of its tangent line
Its highest value
Its average

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^2, the derivative is f'(x) = 2x. What is the slope of the curve at x = 7?
A car's position over time is given by a distance function. Which quantity equals the derivative of that distance function?
choices: The car's speed
The total distance travelled
The car's acceleration
The average position

quiz.q: At a sharp corner in a graph, the slope cannot be pinned to a single value. What one-word property does the function lack at that point?

cards.title: The integral: area under a curve
cards.fact: The integral adds up infinitely many thin slivers to measure the area under a curve.
cards.detail: To find the area under a graph, slice the region into thin rectangles, add their areas, then let the slices grow infinitely thin so the answer becomes exact. That limit is the integral, \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). The fundamental theorem of calculus ties it to the derivative: integration and differentiation undo each other. Distance is the integral of speed over time; in probability, the chance of landing in a range is the area under a curve.

media.caption: The shaded area is the integral ∫ f(x) dx.

cards.deploy: Turns a rate into a total: accumulate speed into distance, a density into a probability, a flow into a quantity.
cards.counter: Many functions have no tidy antiderivative formula — real integrals are often computed numerically rather than solved on paper.

quiz.q: An integral computes the…
choices: Slope at a point
Area under a curve
Highest point
Number of solutions

quiz.q: A theorem states that integration and differentiation undo each other. What is this theorem called?
choices: The fundamental theorem of calculus
The mean value theorem
L'Hopital's rule
The squeeze theorem

quiz.q: An object moves at a constant speed of 5 m/s. Using the fact that distance is the integral of speed over time, how many metres does it travel between t = 2 s and t = 10 s?
In probability, the chance that a continuous outcome lands within a given range equals the integral of which kind of function over that range?

cards.title: The chain rule: rates that pass through layers
cards.fact: To differentiate a function inside a function, multiply the two rates of change.
cards.detail: If \(y\) depends on \(u\), and \(u\) depends on \(x\), then a small nudge in \(x\) ripples through both: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\). Take \(y = (3x+1)^2\): the outer squaring contributes \(2(3x+1)\), the inner \(3x+1\) contributes \(3\), and the product is \(6(3x+1)\). The chain rule is how rates compose through nested steps — and it is exactly the mechanism that trains deep neural networks, where the error is passed back layer by layer (backpropagation).

media.say: the rate of f-of-g equals f's rate (at g) times g's rate.
media.caption: Outer rate times inner rate.
A chain x → u → y; the rates multiply along it.

cards.deploy: Differentiates any composition — and underpins backpropagation, the engine of modern AI training.
cards.counter: It's easy to forget the inner derivative \(g'(x)\); leaving it out is one of the most common calculus mistakes.

quiz.q: The chain rule differentiates f(g(x)) as…
Using the chain rule, differentiate y = (2x + 5)^2 and evaluate the derivative at x = 4. (Hint: dy/dx = 2(2x+5) times 2.)
The chain rule passing error backward layer by layer is the mechanism that trains deep neural networks. What is this training algorithm called?
When differentiating a composite function f(g(x)), what is the single most common mistake people make?
choices: Forgetting to multiply by the inner derivative g'(x)
Adding the two derivatives instead of multiplying
Using the quotient rule by mistake
Differentiating twice

cards.title: The gradient: which way is uphill
cards.fact: The gradient bundles a function's slopes in every direction into one arrow pointing straight uphill.
cards.detail: When a function has several inputs, say \(f(x, y)\), it has a separate slope in the x-direction and in the y-direction — its partial derivatives. The gradient \(\nabla f\) collects them into a vector: \(\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)\). That vector points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length tells you how steep. Walk in the opposite direction and you go downhill fastest — the single idea behind training almost every machine-learning model.

media.say: grad-f is the pair of slopes: how f changes along x, and along y.
media.caption: A vector of partial slopes, pointing uphill.
On the bowl f = x² + y², ∇f points outward — straight uphill.

cards.deploy: Gives the direction to step when tuning many numbers at once — the basis of gradient descent.
cards.counter: The gradient only shows the best local direction; on a bumpy surface, following it can stall in a dip that isn't the lowest point overall.

quiz.q: The gradient of a function points in the direction of…
choices: Steepest increase
Zero change
The nearest axis
Steepest decrease

quiz.q: For f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2, the gradient is (2x, 2y). At the point (3, 4), what is the length (magnitude) of the gradient vector?
Optimisation methods step in the direction opposite to the gradient to reduce a function as fast as possible. What is this method called?
choices: Gradient descent
Gradient ascent
Newton's method
The chain rule

quiz.q: Following the gradient downhill can get stuck in a dip that is not the overall lowest point. What is the name for such a non-global low point?

cards.title: A vector is an arrow and a list
cards.fact: A vector is at once an arrow with direction and length, and a list of numbers.
cards.detail: In the plane, a vector points from the origin to a spot: \(\vec v = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) means 'go 3 right and 2 up'. The arrow picture (direction and length) and the column of numbers are the same object — and holding both views at once is what makes linear algebra work. A data point with many features (age, height, income…) is simply a vector with many entries: a single point in a high-dimensional space.

media.caption: The vector [3, 2] as an arrow from the origin.

cards.deploy: The basic unit of data and geometry alike: one object you can picture as an arrow or compute with as numbers.
cards.counter: The arrow picture is honest only up to three dimensions; beyond that you must trust the numbers, since a 300-feature vector has no drawable shape.

quiz.q: The vector [3, 2] describes…
choices: 3 up and 2 right
3 right and 2 up
The number 32
A 3-by-2 grid

quiz.q: A dataset records each customer with 5 features: age, height, weight, income, and number of orders. As a vector, how many entries does one customer's data point have?
Why can the arrow picture of a vector not be drawn for a 300-feature data point?
choices: Arrows can only represent up to 3 dimensions visually; a 300-dimensional space has no drawable shape
Vectors with more than 3 entries are no longer valid vectors
The numbers become too large to fit on a page
Only vectors with whole-number entries can be drawn as arrows

quiz.q: A vector starting at the origin and going 4 units left and 7 units down would be written as a column of which two numbers (top entry, then bottom entry)?

cards.title: Adding and scaling vectors
cards.fact: Add vectors tip-to-tail; scale one by stretching or flipping it.
cards.detail: To add \(\vec a + \vec b\), set \(\vec b\)'s tail at \(\vec a\)'s tip; the sum runs from the very start to the very end. In numbers you just add matching entries: \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix}\). Multiplying by a plain number (a scalar) stretches or flips: \(2\vec a\) is twice as long, \(-\vec a\) points the other way. Any weighted mix \(c_1\vec a + c_2\vec b\) — a 'linear combination' — is the core move of the whole subject.

media.caption: a + b, tip-to-tail.

cards.deploy: The two operations every later idea is built from: combine vectors and rescale them.
cards.counter: You can only add vectors of the same length (same number of entries); a 2-D and a 3-D vector have no defined sum.

quiz.q: Compute the second (bottom) entry of the vector 3*[2, 1] + [-1, 4].
Which pair of vectors CANNOT be added together?
What is the name for a weighted mix of the form c1*a + c2*b, where c1 and c2 are scalars?

cards.title: The dot product: how aligned are two vectors
cards.fact: The dot product is one number saying how much two vectors point the same way.
cards.detail: Multiply matching entries and add them up: \(\vec a \cdot \vec b = \sum_i a_i b_i\). The same number also equals \(|\vec a|\,|\vec b|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors and the cosine runs from 1 (pointing the same way), through 0 (a right angle), to −1 (opposite). So the dot product is large when they align, zero when they're perpendicular, and negative when they oppose. It is the standard measure of similarity: search engines and language models compare meanings by taking dot products of vectors.

media.tex: \vec a \cdot \vec b = \sum_i a_i b_i = |\vec a|\,|\vec b|\cos\theta
media.say: a dot b: multiply matching entries and add — also the lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.
media.caption: Two views: entry-by-entry, and angle-based.
Swing θ: the dot product peaks when aligned, hits 0 at 90°.

cards.deploy: The workhorse of similarity and projection — and the operation inside every matrix multiply and attention score.
cards.counter: A dot product near zero means the vectors are merely perpendicular, not that either is small; alignment and magnitude are different things.

quiz.q: The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is…
choices: Their length
Zero
Negative
One

quiz.q: Compute the dot product of [2, -1, 3] and [4, 5, 1].
Two vectors each have length 5, and the angle between them is 60 degrees (cos 60 = 0.5). What is their dot product?
A dot product between two vectors comes out negative. What does this tell you?
choices: The angle between them is greater than 90 degrees, so they partly oppose each other
At least one of the two vectors has zero length
The two vectors are exactly perpendicular
The two vectors point in exactly the same direction

cards.title: Length and distance
cards.fact: A vector's norm is its length — and the gap between two points is the norm of their difference.
cards.detail: The norm \(\|\vec v\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots}\) is the Pythagorean theorem in any number of dimensions. The distance between two points is the norm of their difference, \(\|\vec a - \vec b\|\). 'Nearest neighbour' methods, clustering, and the size of an error all rest on this. Neatly, \(\|\vec v\|^2 = \vec v \cdot \vec v\): a vector's squared length is its dot product with itself.

media.say: the length of v is the square root of the sum of its squared entries.
media.caption: Pythagoras, in any number of dimensions.
‖[4, 3]‖ = √(16 + 9) = 5 — the hypotenuse.

cards.deploy: Defines size and closeness for data — the basis of distance, error magnitude and similarity searches.
cards.counter: The straight-line (Euclidean) norm is only one choice; others, like summing absolute values (the 'taxicab' norm), measure distance differently and suit different problems.

quiz.q: The norm of a vector measures its…
choices: Direction only
Length
Number of entries
Angle

quiz.q: What is the Euclidean norm (length) of the vector [6, 8]?
What is the Euclidean distance between the points [1, 2] and [4, 6]?
What name is given to the alternative norm that measures distance by summing the absolute values of a vector's entries rather than taking a straight line?

cards.title: A matrix is a grid of numbers
cards.fact: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers — a table, or a row of vectors side by side.
cards.detail: A matrix has rows and columns: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) is 2 by 2. You can read it as a spreadsheet — each row a record, each column a feature — or as several column vectors standing together. Its real power, though, is as an action: a matrix is a rule that takes a vector in and gives a transformed vector out, which is the next step.

media.caption: A 2×2 matrix: rows and columns.

cards.deploy: The container for data tables and for transformations alike — the central object of linear algebra.
cards.counter: Shape is everything: a 2×3 and a 3×2 matrix hold the same six numbers but behave completely differently, and most operations demand matching shapes.

quiz.q: A matrix is best described as…
choices: A single number
A grid of numbers in rows and columns
A curved line
An angle

quiz.q: A matrix has 4 rows and 7 columns. How many individual numbers does it contain in total?
You store a dataset as a matrix where each row is one customer and each column is one measured attribute (age, income, etc.). What do the columns represent?
choices: Features
Individual customers
The number of customers
Transformations of the data

quiz.q: Two matrices hold the same six numbers, one arranged 2x3 and one arranged 3x2. What single property distinguishes them and governs how they behave?

cards.title: A matrix transforms space
cards.fact: Multiplying a matrix by a vector moves the whole grid — it rotates, stretches and shears space.
cards.detail: \(A\vec x\) builds a new vector by combining \(A\)'s columns, each weighted by an entry of \(\vec x\). Picture it geometrically: the matrix moves every point of the plane at once, so the square grid tilts and stretches — yet straight lines stay straight and the origin stays fixed. That is a 'linear transformation'. The columns of \(A\) are nothing more than where the two basis arrows land after the move.

media.caption: Move the matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] — watch the grid transform.

cards.deploy: Reframes a matrix as a verb, not a table: it does something to space. This view unlocks the rest of the subject.
cards.counter: Only transformations that keep grid lines straight and evenly spaced, fixing the origin, are 'linear' — bends, curves and shifts of the origin are not matrix multiplication.

quiz.q: Multiplying a vector by a matrix geometrically…
choices: Leaves it unchanged
Transforms space (rotate/stretch/shear)
Adds a number
Bends lines into curves

quiz.q: A 2x2 matrix transformation moves every point of the plane, keeping grid lines straight and the origin fixed. Which of these effects would mean the operation is NOT a linear transformation?
choices: Every point is shifted 3 units to the right
The grid is stretched twice as wide horizontally
The grid is rotated 45 degrees about the origin
The grid is sheared so vertical lines tilt

quiz.q: For a 2x2 matrix A, the first column is where the basis vector [1,0] lands and the second column is where [0,1] lands. If A sends [1,0] to [3,0] and [0,1] to [0,5], what is the x-coordinate of A times the vector [2,4]?
Under a linear (matrix) transformation, which single point of the plane never moves?

cards.title: Matrix multiplication = doing one transform after another
cards.fact: Multiplying matrices means applying one transformation, then the next.
cards.detail: The product \(AB\) is the single transformation 'do \(B\) first, then \(A\)': \((AB)\vec x = A(B\vec x)\). Each entry of the product is a dot product of a row of \(A\) with a column of \(B\). Order matters — \(AB \neq BA\) in general, just as rotating then stretching differs from stretching then rotating. Chaining matrices this way is exactly how a neural network stacks its layers.

media.caption: The product is composition: B first, then A.

cards.deploy: Lets you collapse a whole pipeline of transformations into one matrix — and explains layered models.
cards.counter: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: swapping the order usually changes the result, and often isn't even allowed if the shapes stop matching.

quiz.q: In general, for matrices, AB is…
choices: Always equal to BA
Not the same as BA
Always zero
Undefined

quiz.q: The product AB acts on a vector x as (AB)x. In what order are the transformations applied?
choices: Apply B first, then A
Apply A first, then B
Apply A and B simultaneously and add the results
Apply whichever matrix has more columns first

quiz.q: A is the diagonal 2x2 matrix [[2,0],[0,1]] and B is [[1,0],[0,3]]. Their product AB is also diagonal. What is the bottom-right entry of AB?
What one-word property does matrix multiplication LACK, meaning AB and BA are generally different?

cards.title: Identity and inverse: undoing a transformation
cards.fact: The identity matrix changes nothing; the inverse runs a transformation backwards.
cards.detail: The identity matrix \(I\) has 1s down the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, so \(I\vec x = \vec x\) — the linear-algebra version of multiplying by 1. The inverse \(A^{-1}\) reverses whatever \(A\) did: \(A A^{-1} = I\). Not every matrix has one. If a transformation squashes space flat — collapsing a dimension — there is no way back, and no inverse exists. That collapse is detected by the determinant being zero.

media.say: A times A-inverse gives the identity — the do-nothing matrix.
media.caption: The inverse cancels the transformation.

cards.deploy: The formal 'undo' button — and the route to solving equations and reversing models.
cards.counter: Inverting a matrix that is nearly singular (almost flattening) is numerically unstable; in practice solvers avoid forming \(A^{-1}\) directly.

quiz.q: A matrix times its inverse gives the…
choices: Zero matrix
Identity matrix
Original matrix
Determinant

quiz.q: The 4x4 identity matrix has 1s on its diagonal and 0s elsewhere. How many of its 16 entries are equal to zero?
A 2x2 transformation squashes the entire plane onto a single line, collapsing one dimension. What does this tell you?
choices: It has no inverse and its determinant is zero
It is the identity matrix
Its inverse equals itself
It rotates space without changing area

quiz.q: What single quantity, when equal to zero, signals that a square matrix collapses a dimension and therefore has no inverse?

cards.title: Solving many equations at once: Ax = b
cards.fact: A pile of linear equations packs into one tidy matrix equation, Ax = b.
cards.detail: Two equations like \(2x + y = 5\) and \(x - y = 1\) fold into \(A\vec x = \vec b\), with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec b = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Solving asks: which input \(\vec x\) does \(A\) send to \(\vec b\)? If \(A\) is invertible, \(\vec x = A^{-1}\vec b\); otherwise there may be no solution, or infinitely many. Fitting a model, balancing a chemical equation and rendering 3-D graphics all reduce to solving \(A\vec x = \vec b\).

media.tex: A\vec x = \vec b \;\Rightarrow\; \vec x = A^{-1}\vec b
media.say: A times x equals b, so x equals A-inverse times b.
media.caption: When A is invertible, the system has one solution.
Two equations, two lines — they cross at the solution (2, 1).

cards.deploy: The standard form that an enormous range of practical problems gets rewritten into and solved.
cards.counter: Real systems are often 'overdetermined' — more equations than unknowns, no exact solution — so we settle for the closest fit instead (least squares).

quiz.q: In Ax = b, if A is invertible the solution is…
choices: x = Ab
x = b/A
x = A⁻¹b
x = b − A

quiz.q: Solve the system 3x + y = 11 and x - y = 1 by writing it as Ax = b. What is the value of x?
A factory has 5 unknown quantities but its constraints produce 9 linear equations with no single point satisfying all of them. What approach handles this overdetermined situation?
choices: Find the closest fit by least squares
Invert the 9-by-5 matrix directly
Compute the determinant to read off the answer
Throw away equations until the system is square, then invert

quiz.q: In the matrix equation Ax = b, what property of the square matrix A guarantees a unique solution exists for every b?

cards.title: The determinant: how much area gets scaled
cards.fact: The determinant says how much a transformation scales area — and zero means it flattens space.
cards.detail: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the determinant is \(\det A = ad - bc\). It is the factor by which areas grow or shrink under the transformation: \(\det = 2\) doubles every area, \(\det = 1\) preserves it, and a negative determinant flips orientation (like a mirror). When \(\det A = 0\) the grid has been squashed onto a line — a dimension is lost, information is destroyed, and the matrix has no inverse.

media.caption: The shaded unit square's area equals |det A|.

cards.deploy: A one-number test for whether a transformation is reversible, and by how much it expands or shrinks.
cards.counter: A large determinant doesn't mean a matrix is 'well-behaved' for computation; a separate measure (the condition number) governs numerical reliability.

quiz.q: If det A = 0, the transformation…
choices: Doubles area
Preserves area
Flattens space onto a line
Rotates only

quiz.q: For the 2x2 matrix with first row [4, 3] and second row [2, 5], compute the determinant ad - bc.
A 2x2 transformation has determinant -3. What does this tell you about its effect on the plane?
choices: It triples areas and flips orientation
It shrinks areas to one third and flips orientation
It triples areas while preserving orientation
It collapses the plane onto a line

quiz.q: A large determinant does NOT guarantee a matrix is numerically reliable to work with. What separate quantity actually governs that numerical reliability?

cards.title: Eigenvectors: the directions that don't turn
cards.fact: An eigenvector is a direction a transformation only stretches — it never rotates it.
cards.detail: Under a matrix \(A\), most vectors swing off to a new direction. A special few hold their direction and are merely scaled: \(A\vec v = \lambda\vec v\). Such a \(\vec v\) is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. These reveal a transformation's natural axes — the skeleton it acts along. Google's original PageRank found an eigenvector of the web's link matrix; principal component analysis finds the eigenvectors of data to compress it.

media.say: A times v equals lambda times v — the matrix only stretches v by the factor lambda.
media.caption: Same direction, scaled by λ.
Look for an arrow that stays on its own line — that's an eigenvector.

cards.deploy: Finds the hidden axes of a transformation or dataset — behind PCA, PageRank, and stability analysis.
cards.counter: Not every real matrix has real eigenvectors — a pure rotation turns every direction, so its eigenvalues are complex numbers, with no real axis it leaves alone.

quiz.q: For an eigenvector v of A, Av equals…
choices: A number
λv (v scaled)
Zero always
v rotated 90°
