quiz.q: A vector v is an eigenvector of matrix A with eigenvalue 4. If A is applied to v and the result is then scaled by 1/2, by what total factor has v been stretched compared to its original length?
Why does a matrix that rotates every vector in the plane by 90 degrees have no real eigenvectors?
choices: Every direction is turned, so no real direction is merely scaled
Its determinant is zero, destroying all directions
It scales every vector by zero
Rotations have infinitely many real eigenvectors, not none

quiz.q: Which data-compression technique works by finding the eigenvectors of a dataset to identify its dominant axes of variation?

cards.title: Probability: a number from 0 to 1
cards.fact: A probability scores how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
cards.detail: List everything that could happen — the 'sample space'. If each outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just the share that counts as a success: \(P(A) = \frac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}\). A fair die has six faces, so \(P(\text{roll a 4}) = \tfrac{1}{6}\). 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and 0.5 is an even chance. Everything else in probability builds on this.

media.caption: A fair die: six equally likely outcomes, each 1/6.

cards.deploy: Turns vague talk of 'likely' and 'rare' into a number you can compare and combine.
cards.counter: The 'equally likely' shortcut only works for symmetric setups like dice; for real events (rain tomorrow) probability means a long-run frequency or a degree of belief — a split between the frequentist and Bayesian schools.

quiz.q: A probability of 1 means an event is…
choices: Impossible
An even chance
Certain
Unlikely

quiz.q: A fair eight-sided die has faces numbered 1 through 8. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 5? Give the answer as a decimal.
The formula favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes assumes each outcome is equally likely. For which situation is this assumption valid?
choices: Drawing one card at random from a well-shuffled standard deck
Whether it rains in a particular city tomorrow
Whether a startup succeeds within five years
Which team wins an unevenly matched football game

quiz.q: Interpreting the probability of rain tomorrow as a personal degree of belief rather than a long-run frequency reflects which school of probability?

cards.title: Adding and multiplying probabilities
cards.fact: Use OR to add chances, AND to multiply them.
cards.detail: For the chance of A or B, add — then subtract the overlap so it isn't counted twice: \(P(A\text{ or }B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\text{ and }B)\). For A and B both happening, multiply — and if they're independent (one doesn't affect the other), it's simply \(P(A\text{ and }B) = P(A)\,P(B)\). Two fair coins both landing heads: \(\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14\).

media.say: the chance of both, when neither affects the other, is the two chances multiplied.
media.caption: Independent events: multiply.
Two fair coins: each combination is ½ × ½ = ¼.

cards.deploy: Lets you build the odds of complex events from simple ones.
cards.counter: The multiply rule fails when events are linked: P(rain) and P(I carry an umbrella) aren't independent, so multiplying understates the truth.

quiz.q: For two independent events, P(A and B) equals…
choices: P(A) + P(B)
P(A) − P(B)
P(A) × P(B)
P(A) / P(B)

quiz.q: A spinner has a 0.3 chance of landing red and a 0.5 chance of landing on an even number; the chance of landing on a red even number is 0.2. What is the chance it lands red OR on an even number?
You roll a fair six-sided die three times. What is the probability of getting a 6 on all three rolls? Give the answer as a decimal.
Why must you subtract P(A and B) when computing P(A or B) by adding P(A) and P(B)?
choices: Outcomes where both occur are otherwise counted twice
The two probabilities are always negatively correlated
Subtracting it makes the events independent
It corrects for the events being mutually exclusive

cards.title: Conditional probability: given that…
cards.fact: The probability of A changes once you know B has happened.
cards.detail: Written \(P(A \mid B)\) — 'the probability of A given B' — it narrows the world to the cases where B is true: \(P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}\). Knowing it rained (B) changes the chance the ground is wet (A). When \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\), knowing B told you nothing — that's exactly what independence means.

media.plain: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
media.say: the chance of A given B is the chance of both, divided by the chance of B.
media.caption: Restrict the world to the cases where B happened.
Knowing it rained lifts the chance the ground is wet.

cards.deploy: The formal way to update a probability when new information arrives.
cards.counter: People routinely confuse P(A|B) with P(B|A) — the 'prosecutor's fallacy'; the chance of a match given innocence is not the chance of innocence given a match.

quiz.q: P(A | B) is read as…
choices: A or B
A and B
A given B
A times B

quiz.q: In a deck, P(card is a face card) = 12/52 and P(card is a face card AND a spade) = 3/52. Given a card is a face card, what is the probability it is a spade? Give the answer as a decimal.
A medical expert notes the probability of a positive test given the patient is sick is high, then concludes a patient who tested positive is almost certainly sick. What error is this?
choices: Confusing P(positive | sick) with P(sick | positive)
Failing to subtract the overlap of the two events
Assuming the events are independent
Using a prior instead of a posterior

quiz.q: If learning that B has happened leaves the probability of A completely unchanged, so that P(A | B) = P(A), what relationship do A and B have?

cards.title: Bayes' theorem: updating beliefs with evidence
cards.fact: Bayes' rule flips a conditional probability — turning a test result into an updated belief.
cards.detail: It connects \(P(H \mid E)\) (a hypothesis given the evidence) to \(P(E \mid H)\) (the evidence given the hypothesis): \(P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}\). The starting belief \(P(H)\) is the 'prior'; the answer \(P(H \mid E)\) is the 'posterior'. Its sting is the base rate: a 99%-accurate test for a disease that 1 in 1000 people have still gives mostly false alarms, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.

media.say: the updated belief is the evidence's likelihood times the prior, divided by how likely the evidence was overall.
media.caption: Prior belief × evidence → updated (posterior) belief.
A rare disease (1%): even a positive test leaves you far from certain.

cards.deploy: The engine of rational updating — and of spam filters, medical screening and Bayesian machine learning.
cards.counter: Bayesians treat the prior as a real degree of belief to be updated; frequentists object that priors are subjective. The maths is agreed; what a probability *means* is not.

quiz.q: In Bayes' theorem, the starting belief P(H) before seeing evidence is the…
choices: Posterior
Prior
Likelihood
Margin

quiz.q: A disease affects 1 in 200 people. A test is positive for 100% of sick people and for 4% of healthy people. If someone tests positive, what is the probability they actually have the disease? Give the answer as a decimal rounded to two places.
In Bayes' theorem, the updated belief P(H | E) obtained after incorporating the evidence is called the what?
A 99%-accurate test for a rare disease produces mostly false alarms among positive results. What is the main reason?
choices: The low base rate means healthy people far outnumber sick ones
The test's accuracy is actually below 50% in practice
P(E | H) is smaller than P(H | E)
The prior and posterior must always be equal

cards.title: Random variables: numbers from chance
cards.fact: A random variable attaches a number to each uncertain outcome.
cards.detail: Call it \(X\). For one die roll, \(X\) is the face shown; for a coin, you might set heads \(= 1\), tails \(= 0\). A discrete random variable takes separate values (0, 1, 2…); a continuous one can be any value in a range (a height, a wait time). Its 'distribution' lists how much probability sits on each value — the bridge from single outcomes to averages and spread.
cards.deploy: Lets you do arithmetic — averages, sums, spreads — on the outcomes of chance.
cards.counter: The number you assign is a modelling choice: coding categories as 1, 2, 3 can smuggle in a false sense that the gaps between them are equal.

quiz.q: A random variable that can take any value in a range is…
choices: Discrete
Continuous
Constant
Binary

quiz.q: Which of these is best modelled as a continuous random variable?
choices: The exact time in seconds until a bus arrives
The number of emails received in an hour
The result of a single die roll
The count of heads in ten coin flips

quiz.q: What is the name for the description of how much probability sits on each value a random variable can take?
A survey codes the categories 'bus', 'train' and 'bike' as 1, 2 and 3. What hidden assumption does treating these numbers as a random variable risk smuggling in?
choices: That the gaps between the categories are equal and meaningful
That the categories are mutually exclusive
That the variable must be continuous
That each category has the same probability

media.caption: The distribution of a fair die: probability 1/6 sits on each value 1 through 6.

cards.title: Expected value: the long-run average
cards.fact: The expected value is the average you'd get from many repeats — each outcome weighted by its probability.
cards.detail: Multiply each value by its probability and add: \(E[X] = \sum_i x_i\,p_i\). A fair die's expected roll is \(\tfrac16(1+2+\dots+6) = 3.5\) — a value you can never actually roll, but the long-run average. It's the foundation of fair prices, insurance and betting: a bet is 'fair' when its expected gain is zero.

media.say: the expected value is each outcome times its probability, all added up.
media.caption: Each outcome, weighted by how likely it is.
Expected value is the probability-weighted average: E = 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) + 5(0.2) = 2.1 — the distribution's balance point.

cards.deploy: The single best summary of a random quantity — and the thing rational decisions try to maximise.
cards.counter: Expected value ignores risk: a 1-in-a-million shot at a billion has a high expectation, but few would stake their house on it. That gap is why utility, not raw money, often guides choices.

quiz.q: The expected value of a fair six-sided die is…
A game pays 10 dollars with probability 0.2, pays 3 dollars with probability 0.5, and pays 0 with probability 0.3. What is the expected payout in dollars?
A bet costs 4 dollars to enter and pays out an amount whose expected value is exactly 4 dollars. In the language of expected value, this bet is best described as:
choices: A fair bet
A bet you should always avoid
Guaranteed to break even on any single play
A bet with positive expected profit

quiz.q: A risky venture has a high expected monetary value yet almost everyone refuses it because it could ruin them. What concept, used instead of raw money, explains why people decline such bets?

cards.title: Variance and standard deviation: the spread
cards.fact: Variance measures how far outcomes typically stray from the average.
cards.detail: Take each value's distance from the mean \(\mu\), square it (so positives and negatives don't cancel), and average: \(\sigma^2 = E[(X-\mu)^2]\). The standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\) brings it back to the original units. Two classes can share a mean score of 60 yet feel completely different — one tightly bunched, the other spread from 20 to 95. That difference is the standard deviation.

media.say: variance is the average squared distance from the mean.
media.caption: Square the distances from the mean, then average.
Same mean, different spread: σ sets the width.

cards.deploy: Quantifies risk, noise and consistency — the second number (after the mean) you reach for.
cards.counter: Squaring makes variance hypersensitive to outliers; a single freak value can dominate it, which is why robust measures (like the interquartile range) are sometimes preferred.

quiz.q: The standard deviation is the…
choices: Square of the variance
Square root of the variance
Mean of the data
Largest value

quiz.q: A random variable takes the value 2 with probability 0.5 and the value 8 with probability 0.5. What is its standard deviation?
If every value in a dataset is multiplied by 3, how does the standard deviation change?
choices: It is multiplied by 3
It is multiplied by 9
It stays the same
It is multiplied by sqrt(3)

quiz.q: Because squaring distances makes variance react sharply to a single extreme value, analysts sometimes prefer a robust spread measure based on the 25th and 75th percentiles. What is that measure called?

cards.title: Distributions: uniform, Bernoulli, binomial
cards.fact: A distribution is the shape of how probability is spread across outcomes.
cards.detail: A few shapes recur everywhere. The uniform puts equal weight on each outcome (a fair die). The Bernoulli is a single yes/no trial with success probability \(p\) (one coin flip). The binomial counts successes in \(n\) independent trials — flip 4 coins and the number of heads follows it, peaking in the middle. Recognising the shape tells you what to expect.

media.caption: Heads in 4 coin flips (binomial): the middle is likeliest.

cards.deploy: Names the common patterns so you can pick the right model instead of starting from scratch.
cards.counter: Reaching for a textbook distribution can impose a shape the data doesn't have — real counts are often more skewed or heavy-tailed than the binomial or normal assume.

quiz.q: The number of heads in several independent coin flips follows the…
choices: Uniform distribution
Binomial distribution
Normal distribution
Bernoulli distribution

quiz.q: You flip 6 fair coins. On average, how many heads do you expect?
What distribution describes a single trial with only two outcomes, success or failure, with success probability p (for example, one coin flip)?
A spinner is divided into 8 equal sectors, and you record which sector it lands on. Which distribution best models this outcome?
choices: Uniform
Binomial
Bernoulli
Normal

cards.title: The normal (Gaussian) distribution
cards.fact: The bell curve: a smooth hump set by just two numbers — its mean and its spread.
cards.detail: The normal distribution's density is \(f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\). The mean \(\mu\) slides the peak left or right; the standard deviation \(\sigma\) makes it wide or narrow. About 68% of values land within one \(\sigma\) of the mean, 95% within two. It appears so often because sums of many small independent effects tend toward it — the reason it underpins so much of statistics.

media.caption: Slide μ to move the peak, σ to widen or narrow it.

cards.deploy: The default model for measurement error, natural variation and sample averages.
cards.counter: Assuming normality is dangerous in the tails: finance learned in 2008 that 'impossible' extreme moves happen far more often than the bell curve allows (fat tails).

quiz.q: Two numbers fully define a normal distribution: the mean and the…
choices: Median
Standard deviation
Maximum
Count

quiz.q: Adult heights are normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. Using the rule that about 95% of values fall within two standard deviations of the mean, what is the lower bound of that central 95% range, in cm?
Test scores are normal with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Approximately what fraction of scores fall between 400 and 600?
choices: About 68%
About 95%
About 50%
About 99.7%

quiz.q: What is the name of the result explaining why sums or averages of many small independent effects tend toward a normal distribution?

cards.title: Mean, median, and mode
cards.fact: Three ways to name the 'typical' value — and they can tell different stories.
cards.detail: The mean is the arithmetic average (add up, divide by how many). The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the most common value. They agree for symmetric data, but a few extreme values pull the mean while leaving the median put: most people earn below the mean income, because a handful of huge earners drag the average up. The median is the fairer 'typical' there.

media.caption: A long right tail (like incomes) drags the mean past the median.

cards.deploy: The first summary of any dataset — and choosing mean vs median can change the headline.
cards.counter: Any single number hides the shape: the same mean can describe steady data or wildly volatile data. Always ask about spread too.

quiz.q: For incomes with a few very high earners, the 'typical' value is best given by the…
choices: Mean
Median
Maximum
Sum

quiz.q: Five houses on a street sold for 200, 210, 220, 230, and 1140 (thousands). What is the median sale price, in thousands?
A dataset is heavily right-skewed by a few very large values. How will its mean and median typically compare?
choices: The mean is larger than the median
The median is larger than the mean
The mean and median are equal
The mode is always larger than both

quiz.q: For the values 3, 7, 7, 7, 9, 12, which single measure of central tendency equals 7 because it is the most frequently occurring value?

cards.title: Population vs sample: estimating from a piece
cards.fact: Statistics infers the whole from a part — and a biased part lies.
cards.detail: You rarely measure everyone (the 'population'), so you take a 'sample' and estimate. The catch is sampling error: any sample differs from the whole by chance, and that wobble shrinks roughly as \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — to halve the error you need four times the data. Worse than random error is bias: a sample that systematically over-represents some group. The 1936 Literary Digest poll surveyed millions yet called the US election wrongly, because its phone-and-car owners skewed wealthy.
cards.deploy: The basis of all polling, testing and science: how to learn about the many from the few.
cards.counter: A bigger sample cuts random error but not bias — a huge skewed sample is confidently wrong. Size is no substitute for representativeness.

quiz.q: To halve a sample's random error, you roughly need to…
choices: Double the sample
Quadruple the sample
Add 50%
Nothing — size doesn't matter

quiz.q: Random sampling error shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(n). If a sample of 400 people gives a certain error, how many people are needed to cut that error to one third of its size?
A survey collects 5 million responses but only from people who own both a phone and a car, a group skewed toward the wealthy. What is the main problem with this survey?
choices: Sampling bias, which a large sample size does not fix
Too small a sample, fixable by collecting more responses
Random sampling error, which 5 million responses cannot reduce
The mean was used instead of the median

quiz.q: What is the general term for the entire group you want to draw conclusions about, as opposed to the smaller subset you actually measure?

media.caption: Sampling error falls as 1/sqrt(n): going from n=4 to n=16 quarters the data but only halves the error.

cards.title: Hypothesis testing and the p-value
cards.fact: A p-value asks: if nothing were going on, how surprising would this data be?
cards.detail: Start with a 'null hypothesis' — no effect. The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null were true. A small p (often \(p < 0.05\)) means the data would be surprising under 'no effect', so researchers reject the null. It does not give the probability that the hypothesis is true, nor the size or importance of an effect.

media.tex: p = P(\text{data this extreme} \mid \text{null is true})
media.plain: p = P(data this extreme | null hypothesis true)
media.say: the p-value is the chance of data this extreme, assuming nothing is going on.
media.caption: Small p → the data is surprising if there's really no effect.

cards.deploy: The standard gatekeeper for 'is this result more than noise?' across the sciences.
cards.counter: The American Statistical Association warned in 2016 that p-values are widely misused: p < 0.05 is an arbitrary line, says nothing about effect size, and 'p-hacking' can manufacture it. A small p is not proof.

quiz.q: A small p-value means the data would be… if the null hypothesis were true.
choices: Expected
Surprising
Impossible
Certain

quiz.q: A study reports p = 0.5. Under the standard null hypothesis of no effect, what does this value indicate about the observed data?
choices: Data this extreme is quite ordinary under no effect, so there is no basis to reject the null
There is a 50% chance the hypothesis is true
The effect is large but uncertain
The null hypothesis is proven correct

quiz.q: What name is given to the default starting assumption in a significance test that there is no effect or no difference?
A researcher tries 20 different outcome measures and reports only the one that reached p < 0.05. What practice does this describe?
choices: p-hacking
Confidence interval estimation
Random sampling
Computing the effect size

cards.title: Confidence intervals: the margin of error
cards.fact: A confidence interval reports a range for an estimate, not a single false-precise number.
cards.detail: Rather than '52% support', a poll says '52% ± 3%'. The 95% confidence interval is built so that, across many repeated samples, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. A wider interval means more uncertainty; more data narrows it. It keeps you honest about how much the single estimate could be off.
cards.deploy: Communicates uncertainty alongside an estimate — essential for reading polls and studies.
cards.counter: The 95% refers to the long-run behaviour of the method, not to one interval: it's wrong to say 'there's a 95% chance the truth is in this particular range' — a subtlety frequentists stress and Bayesians sidestep with credible intervals.

quiz.q: A wider confidence interval indicates…
choices: More certainty
More uncertainty
A larger sample
A bigger effect

quiz.q: A poll reports 47% support with a 95% confidence interval of 47% plus or minus 4%. What is the upper bound of that interval, as a percentage?
What does the '95%' in a 95% confidence interval correctly refer to?
choices: The long-run fraction of such intervals, over many repeated samples, that would contain the true value
The probability that the true value lies inside this particular computed interval
The probability that the sample is unbiased
The fraction of the population that was surveyed

quiz.q: What is the name for the Bayesian counterpart to a confidence interval, for which it is valid to say there is a 95% probability the true value lies within the range?

cards.title: Least-squares regression: the best-fit line
cards.fact: Regression draws the straight line that comes closest to a cloud of points.
cards.detail: Fit a straight line \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) — an intercept and a slope — through a cloud of points. The standard method is ordinary least squares (OLS): pick the line that makes the total squared vertical gap between the points and the line as small as possible, \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\). Why square the gaps rather than just add them up? Squaring punishes big misses far more than small ones and — crucially — leaves exactly one best line. The fitted slope \(\beta_1\) then estimates how much \(y\) rises per unit of \(x\). It is the workhorse of empirical science and the simplest machine-learning model there is.

media.caption: The line that minimises the total squared gap to the points.

cards.deploy: The standard tool for measuring how one quantity moves with another, and predicting from it.
cards.counter: A fitted line can mislead: it assumes a straight relationship, is dragged by outliers, and — as the correlation/causation card warns — a good fit never proves x causes y.

quiz.q: Least-squares regression chooses the line that minimises the total…
choices: Number of points
Squared vertical distance to the points
Slope
Horizontal distance

quiz.q: A least-squares line is fit to four points. The fitted line gives predictions of 5, 8, 11, and 14, while the true y-values are 6, 7, 13, and 13. What is the sum of squared residuals that OLS minimizes for this fit?
Why does ordinary least squares minimize the sum of SQUARED vertical gaps rather than the sum of the raw signed gaps themselves?
choices: Raw signed gaps can cancel to zero for many different lines, while squaring penalizes large misses heavily and yields a single unique best line
Squaring is the only operation that keeps the fitted slope positive
Summing raw gaps is impossible to compute without calculus
Squaring guarantees the line passes through every data point

quiz.q: In the fitted model y-hat = b0 + b1*x, what does the coefficient b1 estimate about the relationship between x and y?
accept: the change in y per unit x
rise in y per unit increase in x
how much y rises per unit of x

cards.title: Machine learning: fitting a function to data
cards.fact: Instead of writing the rule by hand, you let the machine find a function that fits examples.
cards.detail: A model is a function \(f\) with adjustable numbers inside it, called parameters (or weights). 'Training' means tuning those numbers until \(f\) maps inputs to the right outputs on example data — learning the rule from cases rather than being told it. Show it thousands of labelled photos and it adjusts its weights until it separates cats from dogs. The input is a vector of features; the output is a prediction.

media.caption: Learning = finding the function that best fits the examples.

cards.deploy: The core idea behind modern AI: learn the function from data instead of programming it.
cards.counter: A model only learns patterns present in its training data — including the biases and gaps in that data, which it will faithfully reproduce and even amplify.

quiz.q: In machine learning, 'training' adjusts a model's…
choices: Inputs
Parameters (weights)
Outputs
Hardware

quiz.q: A team trains a hiring model only on resumes from past hires at a firm that historically favored one demographic. The deployed model strongly prefers that same group. What does this best illustrate?
choices: A model reproduces and can amplify the biases present in its training data
The model needs a larger learning rate
Squared error was the wrong loss to use
The model has too few parameters to learn the rule

quiz.q: In machine learning, what name is given to the adjustable internal numbers of the model that training tunes to fit the examples?
What is the key difference between traditional hand-coded programming and the machine-learning approach to building a classifier?
choices: In ML the rule is learned by adjusting a function to fit labelled examples, rather than written out explicitly by a programmer
ML never uses any numerical computation, only logic rules
Hand-coded programs require labelled data but ML does not
ML always produces a function with no inputs

cards.title: Linear regression as your first model
cards.fact: Predict with a weighted sum of the inputs: ŷ = w·x + b.
cards.detail: Give each input feature a weight, multiply, add them up, and add a bias: \(\hat{y} = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b\). That dot product is the whole model — a price predicted from size, location and age is just their weighted sum. 'Learning' means finding the weights \(\vec{w}\) and bias \(b\) that fit the data best, by making the error as small as possible. With a handful of features you can solve for them exactly with ordinary least squares; with millions you instead descend the error surface step by step (gradient descent) — both routes chase the same minimum. Simple, fast, and the template every fancier model extends.

media.say: the prediction is the weights dotted with the inputs, plus a bias.
media.caption: A prediction is a weighted sum of the features.
One feature: the model is just the best-fit line.

cards.deploy: The clearest place to see what 'a model' and 'weights' actually mean before things get deep.
cards.counter: A straight weighted sum can't capture curves or interactions; its honesty about that limit is also why it rarely overfits and stays easy to interpret.

quiz.q: In ŷ = w·x + b, the vector w holds the…
choices: Inputs
Weights
Outputs
Errors

quiz.q: A linear regression model predicts house price with weights w = (3, 5) on features x = (size, rooms) and bias b = 20. For a house with size 10 and 4 rooms, what price does y-hat = w·x + b give?
When a linear regression has only a handful of features versus millions, which pair of solution methods is typically used, respectively?
choices: Ordinary least squares (exact closed-form solve) for few features; gradient descent (iterative steps down the error surface) for very many
Gradient descent for few features; ordinary least squares for very many
Both cases require gradient descent because no exact solution exists
Both cases use ordinary least squares because it scales to any size

quiz.q: In the model y-hat = w·x + b, what is the single term 'b' called?

cards.title: The loss function: scoring how wrong you are
cards.fact: A loss function turns 'how bad is this model?' into a single number to minimise.
cards.detail: Compare each prediction \(\hat{y}_i\) to the truth \(y_i\), and summarise the misses in one number. The common choice for regression is the mean squared error: \(L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2\). Squaring punishes big mistakes harder and keeps the loss positive. Training becomes a clear goal: choose the weights that make this number as small as possible.

media.say: the loss is the average of the squared gaps between prediction and truth.
media.caption: Mean squared error: average of the squared misses.
Loss as the weight changes: a valley to roll into.

cards.deploy: Defines 'best' precisely, so training is just minimising one number.
cards.counter: The loss you pick is a value judgement: squared error chases outliers, while other losses (absolute error, cross-entropy) reward different behaviour — optimise the wrong loss and you get the wrong model.

quiz.q: Mean squared error squares the errors mainly to…
choices: Make them negative
Punish big mistakes more and stay positive
Speed up the computer
Remove the mean

quiz.q: A regression model makes 3 predictions with errors (prediction minus truth) of -2, 4, and 0. Using mean squared error L = (1/n) * sum of (y-hat - y)^2, what is the loss?

Two models have the same total absolute error, but model A makes one huge mistake while model B spreads the error evenly across many small misses. Under mean squared error, which is judged worse and why?
choices: Model A, because squaring penalizes a single large miss far more than several small ones
Model B, because more individual errors always raise squared loss
They tie, because squared error only depends on the total absolute error
Model A, because squared error ignores small errors entirely

quiz.q: Which loss function is commonly used to train a classifier (rather than the squared-error loss used for regression)?

cards.title: Gradient descent: rolling downhill to the best fit
cards.fact: Take small steps in the downhill direction of the loss until you reach the bottom.
cards.detail: The gradient \(\nabla L\) points uphill on the loss surface, so step the opposite way: \(\vec{w} \leftarrow \vec{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\). The learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size — too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges. Repeat, and the weights roll down into a valley of low loss. This one rule trains almost every model in modern machine learning.

layers.body: The gradient \(\nabla L\) points uphill on the loss surface, so step the opposite way: \(\vec{w} \leftarrow \vec{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\). The learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size — too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges. Repeat, and the weights roll down into a valley of low loss. This one rule trains almost every model in modern machine learning.

Say the loss is \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), so its slope is \(L'(w)=2(w-3)\). Start at \(w=0\) with learning rate \(\eta=0.1\).

Step 1: slope \(=2(0-3)=-6\), so \(w \leftarrow 0-0.1\times(-6)=0.6\). Step 2: slope \(=-4.8\), so \(w \leftarrow 1.08\). Step 3: \(w\approx1.46\)… each step slides \(w\) toward 3, where the slope is 0 — the bottom. Pick \(\eta=1.1\) instead and the steps overshoot and blow up.

media.say: new weights equal old weights minus the learning rate times the uphill gradient.
media.caption: Step against the gradient — downhill on the loss.
Press step: the ball rolls toward the minimum. Try a big η.

cards.deploy: The universal training algorithm — understand this and you understand how models learn.
cards.counter: On a bumpy, non-convex loss it can stall in a local dip or a saddle far from the best solution; momentum and adaptive methods (like Adam) are patches for that, not cures.

quiz.q: Gradient descent updates weights by stepping…
choices: Along the gradient (uphill)
Against the gradient (downhill)
Randomly
To zero

quiz.q: A weight currently equals 5.0. The gradient of the loss with respect to it is +8.0, and the learning rate is 0.1. What is the weight after one gradient-descent update?
Training loss oscillates wildly and then blows up to larger and larger values instead of settling. Which single change is the most direct fix?
choices: Decrease the learning rate
Increase the learning rate
Flip the sign of the gradient before stepping
Add more training examples

quiz.q: On a non-convex loss surface, gradient descent can get stuck at a point that is the lowest in its immediate neighborhood but not the globally lowest loss. What is the name for such a point?

cards.title: Logistic regression and the sigmoid
cards.fact: Squash a weighted sum through an S-curve to get a probability between 0 and 1.
cards.detail: For yes/no questions you want a probability, not an unbounded number. The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) takes any value and bends it into the range 0 to 1: large positive \(z\) → near 1, large negative → near 0, zero → exactly 0.5. Feed it the weighted sum \(z = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b\) and you have logistic regression — a classifier that outputs calibrated probabilities.

media.caption: The sigmoid squashes any number into a 0–1 probability.

cards.deploy: The standard way to turn a score into a probability — and the classic activation in a neuron.
cards.counter: Its probabilities are only as honest as the model: a confident sigmoid output can still be badly miscalibrated if the features or data are skewed.

quiz.q: The sigmoid function maps any input to a value between…
choices: −1 and 1
0 and 1
0 and 100
−∞ and ∞

quiz.q: A logistic regression neuron has a weighted sum plus bias of z = 0. Using the sigmoid 1/(1+e^-z), what probability does it output?
For a single feature x, a logistic model uses weight w = 2 and bias b = -1, so z = 2x - 1. Evaluate the output probability sigmoid(z) at x = 0.5. (e^0 = 1.)
A trained sigmoid classifier outputs 0.97 for an input, but among many inputs it scores at 0.97, only about 60% actually belong to the positive class. What does this reveal?
choices: The model's probabilities are poorly calibrated
The sigmoid was applied with the wrong sign
The learning rate during training was too small
The output cannot be a probability because it exceeds 0.5

cards.title: The artificial neuron
cards.fact: A neuron weighs its inputs, adds them up, and fires through an activation function.
cards.detail: The basic unit: take inputs \(\vec{x}\), weight and sum them with a bias, then pass the result through a non-linear activation: \(y = \sigma(\vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b)\). The weighted sum is a dot product; the activation (a sigmoid, or today usually a ReLU) lets the unit bend, not just draw a straight line. One neuron is a tiny logistic regression — the Lego brick everything bigger is built from.

media.say: the output is the activation of the weighted sum of inputs plus a bias.
media.caption: Weigh, sum, then squash: one artificial neuron.
Three weighted inputs feed one neuron.

cards.deploy: The atom of neural networks — every deep model is millions of these wired together.
cards.counter: The brain analogy is loose marketing: a biological neuron is vastly more complex, and this unit is better understood as a tunable mathematical function than as a model of a cell.

quiz.q: An artificial neuron applies an activation function to the…
choices: Raw inputs
Weighted sum of inputs plus bias
Output label
Learning rate

quiz.q: A neuron has weights (2, -1, 3) and bias 1. For input (1, 4, 2), compute the pre-activation value z = w.x + b.
If artificial neurons used no activation function (just the weighted sum plus bias), what single class of functions could a stack of such units ever represent?
Which statement best describes the relationship between a single artificial neuron with a sigmoid activation and logistic regression?
choices: A single sigmoid neuron computes exactly the same thing as logistic regression
A neuron has no bias term, unlike logistic regression
Logistic regression cannot output probabilities, but a neuron can
A neuron skips the weighted sum and applies the activation to raw inputs

cards.title: A neural network: layers of neurons
cards.fact: Stack neurons into layers and a network becomes matrices squashed through activations.
cards.detail: A layer computes many neurons at once: collect their weights into a matrix \(W\) and the whole layer is \(\vec{h} = \sigma(W\vec{x} + \vec{b})\) — a matrix-vector product, then an activation, applied entry by entry. Stack layers and the output of one feeds the next. Without the non-linear activations the stack would collapse into a single linear map; with them, the network can approximate almost any function. This is deep learning's core.

layers.body: A layer computes many neurons at once: collect their weights into a matrix \(W\) and the whole layer is \(\vec{h} = \sigma(W\vec{x} + \vec{b})\) — a matrix-vector product, then an activation, applied entry by entry. Stack layers and the output of one feeds the next. Without the non-linear activations the stack would collapse into a single linear map; with them, the network can approximate almost any function. This is deep learning's core.

Take one layer with 2 inputs feeding 3 neurons. The weights form a \(3\times2\) matrix \(W\); the inputs are a length-2 vector \(\vec x\). Then \(W\vec x\) is length-3 (one weighted sum per neuron), you add a length-3 bias \(\vec b\), and squash each of the 3 entries.

So '3 neurons on 2 inputs' is exactly: multiply by a \(3\times2\) matrix, add 3 numbers, squash 3 numbers. The next layer takes those 3 outputs as its own inputs — another matrix, another squash.

media.say: a layer is the activation of a matrix times the inputs, plus a bias vector.
media.caption: One layer: a matrix multiply, a bias, then a squash.
Inputs flow through hidden layers to outputs — every arrow is a weight.

cards.deploy: Explains why linear algebra and calculus are the language of AI: a net is matrices and activations composed.
cards.counter: 'Can approximate any function' is an existence result, not a recipe — it says nothing about how much data, compute, or luck it takes to actually find the right weights.

quiz.q: A neural-network layer is essentially a matrix multiply followed by…
choices: Another matrix
A non-linear activation
A sort
Nothing

quiz.q: A neural-network layer maps a 5-dimensional input vector to a 3-dimensional output vector via h = sigma(W x + b). How many entries does the weight matrix W contain?
Why does removing all non-linear activations from a deep network make extra layers pointless?
choices: The composition of linear maps is itself a single linear map
The matrices can no longer be multiplied together
The bias vectors cancel out to zero
Gradient descent can no longer compute a gradient

quiz.q: The result that a sufficiently large network with non-linear activations can approximate almost any continuous function goes by what name (the theorem)?

cards.title: Backpropagation: the chain rule that trains the net
cards.fact: Backprop sends the error backwards through the layers to find every weight's gradient.
cards.detail: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight — and a deep net has millions. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, from the output error back toward the input. Each layer passes the blame for the error to the one before it. It's just the chain rule, organised — and its rediscovery in the 1980s is what made training deep networks practical.

layers.body: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight — and a deep net has millions. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, from the output error back toward the input. Each layer passes the blame for the error to the one before it. It's just the chain rule, organised — and its rediscovery in the 1980s is what made training deep networks practical.

Chain one neuron: \(z=wx\), then \(a=\sigma(z)\), then loss \(L=(a-y)^2\). To adjust \(w\), multiply the rates along the chain:

\(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w}=\underbrace{2(a-y)}_{\text{loss}\to a}\cdot\underbrace{\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))}_{a\to z}\cdot\underbrace{x}_{z\to w}\).

Each layer passes that running product back to the layer before it — backprop just does this for every weight at once, output-side first.

media.say: a weight's effect on the loss is the chain of how it changes the output, times how that changes the loss.
media.caption: The chain rule, applied backwards through every layer.
Training sends the error backward, right to left, tuning every weight.

cards.deploy: The reason deep networks are trainable at all — the algorithm that powers the whole field.
cards.counter: Backprop finds gradients, not good solutions: it can suffer vanishing or exploding gradients in deep stacks, which architectures (ReLUs, residual connections, normalisation) were invented to tame.

quiz.q: Backpropagation is fundamentally an application of the…
choices: Quadratic formula
Chain rule
Dot product
Central limit theorem

quiz.q: Why is backpropagation needed at all, rather than just computing each weight's gradient independently?
choices: A deep net can have millions of weights, and the chain rule lets one backward pass reuse intermediate results to get every gradient efficiently
Independent gradients would point in the wrong direction, so the error must be reversed first
Gradients can only be defined for the output layer, so earlier layers must be approximated
Weights in different layers share the same gradient, so only one needs to be computed

quiz.q: Backprop can produce gradients that shrink toward zero as they travel back through many layers, stalling learning in early layers. What is this failure called (two words)?
Consider the chain y = f(g(h(x))). At the current point, dy/df = 2, df/dg = 0.5, and dg/dh = 3. Using the chain rule as backprop does, what is dy/dh?

cards.title: Softmax and cross-entropy
cards.fact: Softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that sum to 1; cross-entropy scores how good they are.
cards.detail: For many classes, softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the total: \(\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\). The biggest score gets the most probability, but all stay positive and sum to 1. Cross-entropy then measures the gap from the true label — heavily punishing confident wrong answers via the logarithm. Together they are the standard output and loss for classification, from image labels to the next-word predictions of a language model.

media.say: each score is exponentiated, then divided by the total — giving probabilities that add to one.
media.caption: Scores in, probabilities (summing to 1) out.
Raw scores → softmax probabilities that sum to 1.

cards.deploy: The standard final layer of a classifier — including the token probabilities an LLM samples from.
cards.counter: Softmax always returns a confident-looking distribution even on nonsense input; it never says 'none of the above', which is one root of AI models' overconfidence.

quiz.q: Softmax converts a list of scores into…
choices: A single number
Probabilities that sum to 1
Their squares
A sorted list

quiz.q: Softmax is applied to the scores [0, ln 2, ln 4]. What probability does the third score (ln 4) receive? Note e^0=1, e^(ln 2)=2, e^(ln 4)=4.
A classifier outputs probability 0.01 for the class that is actually correct. Why does cross-entropy penalise this so harshly?
choices: The loss is the negative log of the predicted probability, so -ln(0.01) is large; confident wrong answers get heavy penalties
The loss squares the gap between 0.01 and 1, which exceeds any other error
Cross-entropy multiplies all class probabilities, and a near-zero factor dominates
The penalty grows linearly as the probability drops, so 0.01 gives a fixed large value

quiz.q: A limitation of softmax is that it always returns a confident-looking distribution summing to 1, even on inputs that match no class — it can never express which option (three words)?

cards.title: Overfitting and the bias–variance trade-off
cards.fact: A model that memorises its training data can fail completely on new data.
cards.detail: Push a model hard enough and it fits the training points perfectly — including their noise. That's overfitting: low error on data it has seen, high error on data it hasn't. The opposite, underfitting, is a model too simple to catch the real pattern. This is the bias–variance trade-off: too simple misses the signal (bias), too flexible chases the noise (variance). You judge a model on held-out test data, and rein in flexibility with regularisation.

media.caption: The simple straight line generalises; a wiggly curve through every point would not.

cards.deploy: The central discipline of machine learning: build models that generalise, not memorise.
cards.counter: More data and bigger models complicate the neat trade-off — very large networks can fit noise yet still generalise ('double descent'), a phenomenon classical theory didn't predict.

quiz.q: A model with low training error but high test error is…
choices: Underfitting
Overfitting
Unbiased
Well-calibrated

quiz.q: Model A gets 1% error on training data but 30% on held-out test data. Model B gets 22% error on both. What does each diagnosis indicate?
choices: A is overfitting (high variance); B is underfitting (high bias)
A is underfitting (high bias); B is overfitting (high variance)
Both are overfitting, since both have nonzero training error
A generalises well because its training error is lowest

quiz.q: What technique deliberately constrains a model's flexibility to reduce overfitting (one word)?
Classical theory says test error rises once a model gets too flexible, yet very large networks can fit noise and still generalise well. What is this surprising phenomenon called (two words)?

cards.title: Attention and transformers: the maths behind LLMs
cards.fact: Attention lets each word pull in the others most relevant to it — by dot products and softmax.
cards.detail: A transformer represents each token as a vector and lets tokens look at one another. Each forms a query \(Q\), key \(K\) and value \(V\). The relevance of one token to another is their dot product (alignment); softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted blend of values: \(\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\). Stacked in layers, this is the architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) behind GPT and modern large language models.

layers.body: A transformer represents each token as a vector and lets tokens look at one another. Each forms a query \(Q\), key \(K\) and value \(V\). The relevance of one token to another is their dot product (alignment); softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted blend of values: \(\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\). Stacked in layers, this is the architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) behind GPT and modern large language models.

Three words, each with a query, key and value vector. To refresh word 3, score its query against every key with a dot product — say \(q_3\!\cdot\!k_1=2,\ q_3\!\cdot\!k_2=0,\ q_3\!\cdot\!k_3=4\).

Softmax turns \((2,0,4)\) into weights that sum to 1 — about \((0.11,0.02,0.87)\). The new word-3 vector is that weighted blend of the value vectors: mostly \(v_3\), a little \(v_1\). Score by similarity, soften into weights, mix the values.

media.say: score every pair by a dot product, soften the scores into weights, then blend the values.
media.caption: Dot-product similarity → softmax weights → weighted mix of values.
Attention weights: how much the blank word draws on each earlier word.

cards.deploy: Connects the whole maths ladder to today's AI: dot products, softmax and matrices are literally how an LLM reads.
cards.counter: Attention shows which tokens a model weighted, not why, and not whether it 'understands' — reading attention maps as explanations of a model's reasoning is contested (Jain & Wallace, 2019).

quiz.q: The core similarity score inside attention is computed with a…
choices: Determinant
Dot product
Derivative
Median

quiz.q: In scaled dot-product attention, scores are divided by sqrt(d) where d is the key dimension. If d = 144, what is the scaling divisor?
In attention, what role does each of query, key, and value play for a given token?
choices: The query is what a token is looking for; keys are what other tokens offer for matching; values are the content blended into the output by the resulting weights
The query is the token's final output; keys store the loss; values are the gradients sent backward
Queries and keys are identical copies; the value alone determines which token to attend to
The key is what a token seeks; the query is matched against it; the value is discarded after scoring

quiz.q: According to the card, what does an attention map actually reveal, and what is contested about it?
choices: It shows which tokens the model weighted, but not why or whether the model understands; treating it as an explanation of the model's reasoning is disputed
It proves exactly why the model made each decision, which is now settled fact
It measures the loss contributed by each token, replacing the need for cross-entropy
It records the gradient flowing to each token during the backward pass

cards.title: A dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow
cards.fact: Money now is worth more than the same money later, because it can be invested to grow.
cards.detail: Put a present value \(PV\) in at interest rate \(r\), and after \(n\) years it grows to \(FV = PV(1+r)^n\). At 5% a year, $100 today becomes \(100\times1.05 = 105\) next year — so a promise of $105 next year is worth only $100 now. Timing changes value. This one idea sits under every loan, investment, mortgage and valuation in finance.

media.say: future value is the present value times one-plus-the-rate, compounded for n years.
media.caption: Money today grows at rate r over n years.

cards.deploy: The root of interest, discounting and every 'what is it worth today?' calculation.
cards.counter: It assumes you can actually earn that rate safely; with negative real rates or high inflation, 'more later' can be worth less in real terms — the logic can invert.

quiz.q: Why is money today worth more than the same amount next year?
choices: Prices always fall
It can be invested to grow
Banks forbid waiting
It never is

quiz.q: At an interest rate of 8% per year, how much will $250 invested today be worth after 1 year?
A friend offers to repay a $1,000 loan either today or with the same $1,000 in two years. Why should you prefer repayment today?
choices: The $1,000 today can be invested to earn returns over the two years, so it is worth more
Inflation always falls over a two-year period, raising the dollar's value
Lenders are legally required to discount future payments
The future $1,000 would be taxed at a higher rate

quiz.q: Under what condition can 'more money later' actually be worth less than 'less money now' in real terms, inverting the usual logic?
accept: inflation higher than the rate earned

cards.title: Compound interest: interest on interest
cards.fact: Compounding pays interest on your interest, so growth feeds on itself and snowballs.
cards.detail: Simple interest pays only on the original sum. Compound interest pays on the sum plus all the interest earned so far, so it grows exponentially: \(FV = PV(1+r)^n\). The 'Rule of 72' is the handy shortcut — money doubles in roughly \(72/r\) years (about 12 years at 6%). Over decades the gap between simple and compound growth becomes huge, which is why starting to save early matters far more than saving a little extra later.

media.caption: Same 7% rate over 30 years: compound (curve) pulls away from simple (line).

cards.deploy: Explains why long-horizon saving, and long-horizon debt, both balloon.
cards.counter: Compounding cuts both ways: the same maths that builds a pension turns a 20%-APR credit-card balance into a trap. It rewards savers and punishes borrowers identically.

quiz.q: By the Rule of 72, money at 6% a year doubles in about…
choices: 6 years
12 years
36 years
72 years

quiz.q: Using the Rule of 72, in roughly how many years does money double at an annual interest rate of 9%?
Two accounts each start with $1,000 at 10% per year. One pays simple interest, the other compound. Why does the compound account pull ahead over time?
choices: Compounding pays interest on previously earned interest, not just the original sum
Compounding uses a higher stated rate than the simple account
Simple interest stops paying after the first year
Compound interest is paid out monthly instead of annually

quiz.q: What is the name of the shortcut that estimates the doubling time of money as 72 divided by the percentage interest rate?

cards.title: Present value: discounting the future
cards.fact: Present value runs compounding backwards — what is future money worth today?
cards.detail: Discounting is the reverse of compounding. To value \(FV\) received in \(n\) years, divide by the growth factor: \(PV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}\). Here \(r\) is the 'discount rate' — your required return or cost of capital. A higher discount rate shrinks the value of distant cash, which is exactly why rising interest rates hit long-dated bonds and growth stocks hardest: most of their value sits far in the future.

media.say: present value is the future amount divided by one-plus-the-rate, n times over.
media.caption: Discount future money back to today.
The discount factor: a dollar far in the future is worth little today.

cards.deploy: The core move in valuing anything that pays off over time — bonds, projects, companies.
cards.counter: The answer is only as good as the chosen \(r\): small changes in the discount rate swing long-term valuations wildly, so 'what's it worth' is often really a hidden argument about \(r\).

quiz.q: Raising the discount rate makes the present value of future cash…
choices: Larger
Smaller
Unchanged
Negative

quiz.q: What is the present value of $1,210 received in 2 years, discounted at 10% per year? Give the answer in dollars.
When market interest rates rise sharply, why do long-dated bonds and growth stocks tend to fall more than short-term assets?
choices: A higher discount rate shrinks distant cash flows the most, and their value sits far in the future
Long-dated assets are legally required to pay higher coupons when rates rise
Rising rates cause issuers of long-dated assets to default immediately
Short-term assets are exempt from discounting

quiz.q: In the present-value formula PV = FV / (1+r)^n, what name is given to the rate r, which reflects your required return or cost of capital?

cards.title: NPV and IRR: is an investment worth it?
cards.fact: NPV sums an investment's discounted cash flows; IRR is the rate at which it breaks even.
cards.detail: A project throws off cash \(CF_t\) over the years. Net present value discounts each back to today and adds them up, minus the upfront cost \(C_0\): \(NPV = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} - C_0\). If \(NPV > 0\), the project beats your discount rate, so take it. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the special rate that makes \(NPV = 0\) — the project's own break-even return. Together they are finance's standard 'should we do this?' test.

media.say: net present value is every future cash flow discounted to today and summed, minus the upfront cost.
media.caption: Discount every cash flow, add them, subtract the cost.

cards.deploy: The decision rule for capital projects, acquisitions and big purchases.
cards.counter: IRR misleads when cash flows change sign more than once (it can have several values) or when ranking projects of different size; Brealey & Myers' standard text argues NPV is the sounder rule.

quiz.q: A project should be accepted (on the NPV rule) when its NPV is…
choices: Negative
Zero
Greater than zero
Equal to the IRR

quiz.q: A project costs $100 today and pays a single cash flow of $110 in one year. Using a discount rate of 10%, what is its NPV in dollars?
What is the name for the discount rate that makes a project's net present value exactly equal to zero, i.e. its own break-even return?
When can IRR give misleading guidance compared with NPV?
choices: When cash flows change sign more than once, since IRR can then take several values
When the project's cash flows are all positive and equal
When the discount rate is exactly zero
When the upfront cost is paid in installments rather than at once

cards.title: Risk and return: no free lunch
cards.fact: Higher expected return is the reward for bearing more risk — you rarely get one without the other.
cards.detail: An asset's return is uncertain, so we summarise it with two numbers: the expected return (its mean \(\mu\)) and its risk (the standard deviation of returns \(\sigma\), called volatility). Treasury bills offer low \(\mu\) and low \(\sigma\); stocks offer higher \(\mu\) but a bumpier \(\sigma\). The extra expected return for taking on risk is the 'risk premium'. Plot \(\mu\) against \(\sigma\) and you see the trade-off every investor faces.

media.caption: Risk (σ, across) vs expected return (up): more of one tends to mean more of the other.

cards.deploy: The mental model behind every portfolio choice: what return am I paid for this risk?
cards.counter: The neat trade-off assumes investors are rational and that risk is fully captured by σ; behavioural economists (Kahneman, Thaler) show people feel losses about twice as hard as gains, so real 'risk' isn't symmetric.

quiz.q: In finance, an asset's 'volatility' usually refers to its…
choices: Expected return
Standard deviation of returns
Price
Dividend

quiz.q: Two assets have the same expected return, but asset A has a standard deviation of returns of 8% and asset B has 18%. A rational risk-averse investor should prefer:
choices: Asset A, because it offers the same expected return with less risk
Asset B, because higher volatility guarantees higher long-run gains
Asset B, because more risk always earns a larger risk premium
Either equally, since standard deviation does not affect choice

quiz.q: A Treasury bill yields 2% expected return. A stock is expected to return 9%. What is the stock's risk premium over the bill, in percentage points?
Behavioural economists like Kahneman and Thaler find that people psychologically feel a loss roughly how many times as intensely as an equal-sized gain? Give the number as a word or digit.

cards.title: Diversification: the only free lunch
cards.fact: Combining assets that don't move together cuts risk without cutting expected return.
cards.detail: Mix two assets and the portfolio's expected return is just the weighted average — but its risk is not. Variances combine through correlation: \(\sigma_p^2 = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1 w_2\,\rho\,\sigma_1\sigma_2\). When the correlation \(\rho\) is low or negative, that last cross term shrinks the total. Harry Markowitz (1952) built modern portfolio theory on this: spreading across uncorrelated assets is the closest thing to a free lunch in finance.

media.say: portfolio variance is each asset's weighted variance plus a cross term that shrinks when the correlation rho is low.
media.caption: Low correlation ρ shrinks the cross term — and the risk.

cards.deploy: The mathematical case for not betting everything on one stock, sector or country.
cards.counter: It only removes asset-specific risk; market-wide ('systematic') risk stays. Worse, in a crash correlations jump toward 1 — so diversification fails exactly when it's needed most (2008).

quiz.q: Diversification reduces a portfolio's risk most when the assets' returns are…
choices: Perfectly correlated
Uncorrelated or negatively correlated
Identical
Very volatile

quiz.q: A portfolio holds two assets, each with weight 0.5 and standard deviation 0.10. If their correlation is 0 (uncorrelated), what is the portfolio's variance? Use variance = w1^2*s1^2 + w2^2*s2^2 + 2*w1*w2*rho*s1*s2.
Why does combining two assets with negative correlation reduce portfolio risk more than combining two positively correlated ones?
choices: The cross term 2*w1*w2*rho*s1*s2 becomes negative, lowering total variance
Negative correlation raises the portfolio's expected return above the weighted average
Negative correlation eliminates systematic market risk entirely
The individual standard deviations s1 and s2 shrink when rho is negative

quiz.q: Diversification cannot remove the risk that affects the whole market at once and tends to spike correlations toward 1 in a crash. What term names this undiversifiable risk?

cards.title: CAPM: pricing risk with beta
cards.fact: An asset should be paid a return for its market risk — measured by beta — and nothing for risk you could diversify away.
cards.detail: Since diversification removes asset-specific risk, only market risk deserves a reward. The Capital Asset Pricing Model sets expected return as the risk-free rate plus a premium proportional to beta: \(E[R] = R_f + \beta\,(E[R_m] - R_f)\). Beta measures how strongly the asset swings with the market: \(\beta = 1\) moves with it, \(\beta > 1\) amplifies it, \(\beta < 1\) dampens it. William Sharpe won a Nobel for it, and it is still the workhorse for estimating the 'cost of equity'.

media.say: expected return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market's excess return.
media.caption: More market risk (beta) earns more expected return.
The security market line: expected return rises with beta.

cards.deploy: The standard way to turn 'how risky is this?' into a required return for valuing a company.
cards.counter: Empirically, beta predicts returns poorly. Fama & French (1992) showed company size and value explain more, and many quants treat single-factor CAPM as a teaching model rather than how markets really price risk.

quiz.q: In CAPM, an asset with beta greater than 1…
choices: Moves opposite the market
Amplifies market moves
Is risk-free
Pays no return

quiz.q: Using CAPM, an asset has beta 1.5, the risk-free rate is 3%, and the expected market return is 8%. What is the asset's expected return, in percent? Use E[R] = Rf + beta*(E[Rm] - Rf).
A stock has beta 0.6. According to CAPM, when the market rises or falls, this stock tends to:
choices: Move in the same direction but with smaller swings than the market
Move in the opposite direction to the market
Move in the same direction but with larger swings than the market
Stay flat regardless of market moves, like the risk-free asset

quiz.q: CAPM rewards only market risk and pays nothing for diversifiable risk. Which two researchers showed in 1992 that company size and value explain returns better than beta alone? Give both surnames.

cards.title: The efficient-market hypothesis
cards.fact: If prices already reflect all known information, you can't reliably beat the market.
cards.detail: Eugene Fama's efficient-market hypothesis (1970) holds that prices instantly absorb available information, so consistent outperformance is impossible without luck or inside knowledge. It comes in strengths: 'weak' (past prices don't predict future ones), 'semi-strong' (all public news is already priced in), and 'strong' (even private information is). It is the central argument for cheap, passive index funds over costly stock-picking.
cards.deploy: The case for index investing — and a sharp test to apply to anyone promising to beat the market.
cards.counter: Robert Shiller (who shared the 2013 Nobel with Fama) argues markets show 'excess volatility' and psychology-driven bubbles; the dot-com and 2008 housing manias look hard to square with efficiency. Fama's efficiency versus Shiller's behavioural view remains an open dispute.

quiz.q: The efficient-market hypothesis implies that beating the market consistently is…
choices: Easy with effort
Very hard without luck or inside information
Guaranteed
Illegal

quiz.q: An analyst claims to consistently beat the market by spotting patterns in past price charts. Which form of the efficient-market hypothesis does this claim most directly contradict?
choices: Weak form, which says past prices cannot predict future returns
Semi-strong form, which says public news is already priced in
Strong form, which says even private information is priced in
None, since chart-reading is consistent with all three forms

quiz.q: Which form of the efficient-market hypothesis holds that even private, inside information is already reflected in prices? Give the one-word strength label.
Which finding would most strongly support Robert Shiller's challenge to market efficiency rather than Fama's view?
choices: Stock prices swing far more than the eventual changes in underlying dividends justify
An index fund matches the market return at very low cost
A fund manager beats the market for one year then underperforms
Prices adjust within seconds of an earnings announcement

cards.title: Random walks: why prices resist prediction
cards.fact: If today's price already holds all information, tomorrow's move depends on tomorrow's news — which is random.
cards.detail: When prices reflect what's known, the next change is driven by the next surprise, so prices wander like a 'random walk': each step is a random shock added to the last. Finance models this as geometric Brownian motion — the continuous-time random walk underneath option pricing. Burton Malkiel popularised the provocation that a blindfolded monkey throwing darts could pick stocks about as well as many professionals.
cards.deploy: Explains why short-term price forecasts and most 'technical' chart-reading fail to beat chance.
cards.counter: Pure randomness is an idealisation: documented momentum and mean-reversion effects, and the fat-tailed jumps Benoit Mandelbrot and Nassim Taleb emphasise, mean real prices are not a tidy Gaussian random walk.

quiz.q: A 'random walk' in prices means the next change is mostly…
choices: Predictable from the trend
An unpredictable shock
Always upward
Zero

quiz.q: Under a strict random-walk view of prices, what is the best forecast of tomorrow's price given today's price and all public information?
choices: Today's price (the next move is an unpredictable shock)
Today's price plus the average of the last ten days' gains
The price implied by extending the recent upward trend line
A weighted average of the last month's highs and lows

quiz.q: What continuous-time process does finance use to model the random walk of asset prices that underlies option pricing?
Documented momentum, mean-reversion, and sudden large jumps in real markets are evidence against which idealised assumption of the basic random-walk model?
choices: That price changes are independent, Gaussian shocks with no fat tails
That prices can be quoted in a single currency
That markets are open every business day
That investors prefer higher returns to lower returns

cards.title: Options: the right, not the obligation
cards.fact: An option is the right — but not the duty — to buy or sell at a fixed price.
cards.detail: A call option lets you buy an asset at a fixed 'strike' price \(K\); a put lets you sell at \(K\). You exercise only if it pays. A call's payoff at expiry is \(\max(0,\ S - K)\), where \(S\) is the market price: worthless if \(S < K\), then climbing one-for-one above \(K\) — the famous 'hockey stick'. Options let you hedge a risk or speculate with a capped, known downside: the premium you paid.

media.caption: A call's payoff vs price S: flat until the strike K, then a 45° climb.

cards.deploy: The building block of hedging and of every structured payoff in modern markets.
cards.counter: The capped downside is sold by someone with uncapped risk: option sellers can lose far more than any premium, as 2008 and the 2021 meme-stock squeezes showed.

quiz.q: A call option's payoff at expiry is max(0, S − K). If S is below the strike K, the payoff is…
choices: S − K (negative)
Zero
K
Unlimited

quiz.q: A call option has a strike of 50. At expiry the underlying trades at 62. Using payoff = max(0, S - K), what is the payoff per share?
What is the name for the option contract that gives the holder the right to SELL the underlying at a fixed strike price?
You buy a call for a premium of 3 and the stock finishes below the strike at expiry. What is the most you can lose on the position?
choices: The 3 premium paid, and nothing more
The full strike price, since you must still buy
The difference between strike and market price
An unlimited amount as the stock falls

cards.title: Black–Scholes: pricing an option
cards.fact: A formula prices an option using the bell curve and the idea that you can hedge it perfectly.
cards.detail: Fischer Black, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton (1973) found the fair value of a call before expiry. It blends the stock price, strike, time, interest rate and volatility, weighting outcomes by the normal distribution: \(C = S\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rt} N(d_2)\), where \(N(\cdot)\) is the normal cumulative probability. The deep insight: you can replicate an option by continuously rebalancing stock and cash, so no-arbitrage pins down its price. It won the 1997 Nobel and launched the modern derivatives industry.

media.say: the call value is the stock weighted by a normal probability, minus the discounted strike weighted by another.
media.caption: Outcomes weighted by the normal curve N(·).
Black–Scholes weights future outcomes by the normal (Gaussian) curve.

cards.deploy: The foundation of derivatives pricing — and a clean example of the no-arbitrage idea.
cards.counter: Its assumptions — constant volatility, no jumps, a Gaussian world — break in crises: 1987 and 2008 revealed far fatter tails, and the market's 'volatility smile' prices in exactly what the formula omits. LTCM's 1998 collapse, with Scholes and Merton aboard, is the cautionary tale.

quiz.q: The Black–Scholes formula weights outcomes using which distribution?
choices: Uniform
Binomial
Normal (Gaussian)
Power law

quiz.q: The Black-Scholes price is justified by arguing that an option can be reproduced by continuously rebalancing a portfolio of stock and cash, so its price is fixed by the absence of free profit. What is the name of this no-free-profit principle?

In the Black-Scholes call formula C = S*N(d1) - K*exp(-r*t)*N(d2), suppose S = 100, K = 100, r = 0.05, t = 1, and you are told N(d1) = 0.6368 and N(d2) = 0.5359. What is the call price C? (use exp(-0.05) = 0.9512)
The market's 'volatility smile' is widely read as evidence that one core Black-Scholes assumption is wrong. Which assumption?
choices: That volatility is constant across strike prices
That interest rates are positive
That the option can be exercised only at expiry
That the stock pays no dividends

cards.title: Bonds: price and yield seesaw
cards.fact: A bond's price and its yield always move in opposite directions.
cards.detail: A bond pays fixed coupons plus its face value at maturity, so its price is the present value of those cash flows: \(P = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+y)^t}\). Because \(y\) sits in the denominator, a higher yield means a lower price — they are locked on a seesaw. 'Duration' measures how sharp the seesaw is: long-dated bonds swing far more when yields move, which is why a rate rise punishes 30-year bonds much harder than 2-year ones.

media.caption: Bond price falls (and convexly) as the yield rises.

cards.deploy: The key to reading the bond market and why central-bank rate moves ripple through everything.
cards.counter: The seesaw is exact only for default-free bonds held to maturity; credit risk, inflation and call features complicate it — 2022's bond rout caught many who underestimated how hard duration bites.

quiz.q: When market yields rise, existing bond prices generally…
choices: Rise
Fall
Stay flat
Double

quiz.q: A zero-coupon bond pays 1000 at maturity in exactly 2 years. If its yield is 5% per year, its price is 1000 / (1.05)^2. What is that price, to the nearest dollar?
What single measure tells you how sharply a bond's price will swing for a given change in yield, and is larger for longer-dated bonds?
Two bonds have the same yield, but one matures in 2 years and the other in 30 years. If yields rise by 1%, what happens to their prices?
choices: Both prices fall, and the 30-year bond falls much more
Both prices rise, and the 30-year bond rises much more
The 2-year falls while the 30-year rises
Both fall by the same amount since the yield change is equal

cards.title: Leverage and tail risk
cards.fact: Borrowing to invest magnifies gains and losses alike — and can wipe you out entirely.
cards.detail: Leverage means investing with borrowed money. Put in $1 of your own plus $9 borrowed, and a 10% gain on the $10 doubles your stake — but a 10% loss erases it. The multiplier runs both ways. 'Value at Risk' (VaR) tries to cap the danger by estimating the most you'd lose, say, 99 days in 100 — but it says nothing about the 100th day. Long-Term Capital Management (1998) and the 2008 banks were destroyed by leverage meeting a tail event.

media.caption: Leverage steepens the line: bigger gains, and bigger losses.

cards.deploy: Why a 'safe' strategy plus heavy borrowing can still blow up — the anatomy of financial crises.
cards.counter: Nassim Taleb argues VaR is dangerous precisely because it ignores the fat tail beyond its cutoff, breeding false confidence; most firms that blew up in 2008 were inside their VaR limits.

quiz.q: Value at Risk (VaR) is criticised mainly because it…
choices: Overstates everyday risk
Ignores the extreme tail beyond its cutoff
Is illegal
Only works for bonds

quiz.q: You invest with 5x leverage: $1 of your own money plus $4 borrowed, for $5 of exposure. If the position falls 18%, what percent of your own $1 stake is wiped out?
Name the hedge fund that collapsed in 1998 when its highly leveraged positions met a market shock it had judged extremely unlikely.
A bank reports a 1-day 99% Value at Risk of $10m. What does this figure actually claim?
choices: On the worst 1% of days, losses are expected to be exactly $10m
There is at most a 1% chance of losing more than $10m on a given day, with no statement about how bad that worst 1% gets
The maximum possible loss in any single day is $10m
Average daily losses over the year will be about $10m

cards.title: The mortgage: borrow now, repay for decades
cards.fact: A mortgage spreads a big purchase into level payments — mostly interest at first, mostly principal later.
cards.detail: A mortgage is a loan secured on the property. You repay it in equal instalments, but the split shifts over time. Each payment first covers the interest owed on the outstanding balance; whatever's left chips away at the principal. Early on the balance is huge, so most of the payment is interest; only near the end does it become mostly principal. The level payment on a loan \(P\) at periodic rate \(r\) over \(n\) periods is \(M = P\,\dfrac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}\).

media.say: the level payment is the loan times a factor built from the rate and the number of payments.
media.caption: The fixed monthly payment that exactly clears the loan in n periods.
Across a 30-year loan, each payment shifts from mostly interest to mostly principal.

cards.deploy: Explains why early mortgage years build little equity, and why overpaying early saves so much interest.
cards.counter: The level-payment picture assumes a fixed rate; adjustable-rate mortgages reset with market rates, which is how many 2000s borrowers were caught when payments jumped.

quiz.q: In the early years of a standard mortgage, each payment is mostly…
choices: Principal
Interest
Fees
Taxes

quiz.q: A mortgage of $200,000 is repaid monthly over 360 months at a monthly rate of 0.005 (0.5%). Using M = P*r*(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n - 1), what is the level monthly payment? (1.005^360 is about 6.0226)
On a loan with an outstanding balance of $150,000 at a monthly rate of 0.4%, if the level monthly payment is $900, how many dollars of that payment go toward reducing the principal?
What type of mortgage has an interest rate that periodically resets to track market rates, so payments can jump after an initial period?

cards.title: Loan-to-value: how leverage swings your equity
cards.fact: Put 10% down and a 10% price move doubles — or wipes out — your stake.
cards.detail: Your equity is the property's value minus the debt. The loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is the debt as a share of value: a 20% deposit means an 80% LTV. Because most of the purchase is borrowed, small price moves swing your equity hugely. Buy a $500k home with $50k down (90% LTV); a 10% price rise ($50k) doubles your equity, while a 10% fall erases it — 'negative equity', where the loan exceeds the home's worth.
cards.deploy: Shows why housing feels so lucrative on the way up and so ruinous on the way down.
cards.counter: Lenders treat the home as collateral, so the downside isn't symmetric for them: in a crash they can force a sale, and in non-recourse US states the owner can walk away — shifting the loss back to the bank.

quiz.q: With a 90% loan-to-value, a 10% fall in the property's price leaves your equity at roughly…
choices: Unchanged
Half
Zero
Doubled

quiz.q: You buy a $400,000 property with a $40,000 deposit and the rest borrowed. If the price falls 15%, what is your remaining equity in dollars (it can be negative)?
A buyer purchases a home for $600,000 with a $150,000 down payment. What is the loan-to-value ratio?
What is the term for the situation where the outstanding loan balance exceeds the current market value of the property?

media.caption: Equity (in $thousands) against the home-price change (%) at 90% LTV: a 10% rise doubles the $50k stake to $100k; a 10% fall wipes it to zero. The steep slope is leverage at work.

cards.title: NOI and the cap rate: a property's yield
cards.fact: The cap rate is a property's annual income as a percentage of its price — its rental yield.
cards.detail: Net operating income (NOI) is the rent a property earns minus its running costs (maintenance, taxes, insurance), before any mortgage. The capitalisation rate expresses that as a yield: \(\text{Cap rate} = \dfrac{\text{NOI}}{\text{Price}}\). A $1m building with $60k NOI has a 6% cap rate.
