The board hires more auditors to double-check the earnings figure

quiz.q: Stock options are commonly given to managers chiefly because they:
choices: Make the manager's payoff rise and fall with the share price the owners care about
Guarantee the manager a fixed income regardless of company performance
Transfer the firm's tax liability from shareholders to the manager
Let shareholders directly observe every decision the manager makes

cards.title: Wages and the labour market
cards.fact: A wage is a price — set, roughly, by the supply of and demand for labour.
cards.detail: Treat labour like any market: firms hire workers up to the point where an extra worker's output value equals the wage, and people offer hours by weighing pay against leisure. The wage clears the two. But labour is special — it's people — so minimum wages, unions, discrimination and unequal bargaining power all bend the simple model. Whether a minimum wage costs jobs is among economics' most-tested questions.

media.caption: The wage (up) settles where the supply of labour meets the demand for it.

cards.deploy: The starting frame for debates on wages, unions, immigration and the minimum wage.
cards.counter: The textbook prediction that a minimum wage cuts jobs was upended by David Card and Alan Krueger (1994), who found little to no employment loss; Card shared the 2021 Nobel. Critics reply that effects appear at higher minimums or over longer horizons. The question stays live.

quiz.q: Card and Krueger's famous finding challenged the idea that a minimum wage…
choices: Raises prices
Always cuts employment
Helps firms
Lowers taxes

quiz.q: A firm treats labour like any input and hires workers up to the point where an extra worker's output value equals the wage. If hiring one more worker would add 240 dollars of output value per day and the daily wage is 200 dollars, by how many dollars per day does that extra worker raise the firm's profit?
Which economist, who shared the 2021 Nobel Prize, co-authored the famous 1994 study finding that a minimum-wage increase caused little to no job loss?
An individual worker decides how many hours to offer for sale. In the simple labour-market model, the worker chooses that amount by weighing:
choices: The pay from extra work against the value of the leisure time given up
The firm's total profit against the firm's total revenue
The national inflation rate against the local unemployment rate
The price of consumer goods against the cost of producing them

cards.title: Inflation: when money buys less
cards.fact: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level — each unit of money buys a little less.
cards.detail: Inflation is measured by tracking a basket of goods over time, usually as the consumer price index (CPI). A 3% inflation rate means prices are, on average, 3% higher than a year ago. Mild, steady inflation is the target of most central banks (around 2%); the danger is at the extremes — deflation (falling prices) can freeze spending, while runaway inflation destroys savings and trust.
cards.deploy: The number behind 'cost of living', wage demands and every central-bank rate decision.
cards.counter: A single index hides wide variation — the inflation a renter or a car-buyer feels can differ sharply from the headline — and economists dispute how much of any given burst is demand, supply shocks, or expectations.

quiz.q: Inflation means that over time, a unit of money…
choices: Buys more
Buys less
Stays equal
Disappears

quiz.q: A basket of goods costs 100 dollars and the annual inflation rate is 4%. Assuming the inflation rate stays constant, what will the same basket cost two years later, in dollars?
What is the macroeconomic term for a sustained FALL in the general price level, which can freeze spending as people wait for things to get cheaper?
Most major central banks target an inflation rate of roughly 2% per year rather than 0%. Why deliberately aim for mild positive inflation instead of perfectly stable prices?
choices: It keeps a safety buffer away from deflation, which can stall spending and is hard to escape
Higher inflation directly increases the real value of people's savings
A 2% rate guarantees that every household faces the same cost-of-living change
Positive inflation automatically eliminates supply shocks and price volatility

media.caption: A price index rising year after year; the upward slope means each unit of money buys a little less over time.

cards.title: Real vs nominal: stripping out inflation
cards.fact: A 'nominal' figure is in today's money; a 'real' one is adjusted for inflation — and only real numbers compare across time.
cards.detail: A 5% pay rise feels good until you learn prices rose 7% — your 'real' wage fell. Nominal values are the raw money amounts; real values divide them by a price index so you compare apples to apples. The same split gives the real interest rate: roughly the nominal rate minus inflation, \(r \approx i - \pi\). A 6% loan during 4% inflation costs about 2% in real terms.

media.say: the real interest rate is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation.
media.caption: The Fisher relation: real return after inflation.

cards.deploy: The correction that stops you being fooled by figures that aren't adjusted for inflation.
cards.counter: Which price index you deflate by changes the answer, and the real rate uses expected inflation, which nobody knows in advance — so 'real' figures are estimates, not hard facts.

quiz.q: If your wage rises 5% but prices rise 7%, your real wage…
choices: Rose 5%
Fell about 2%
Rose 12%
Was unchanged

quiz.q: You take out a loan at a nominal interest rate of 9% in a year when inflation runs at 3%. Using the approximation real rate = nominal rate - inflation, what is the real cost of the loan in percent?

A worker's nominal salary rises from 40,000 to 42,000 over a year (a 5% raise), while the price index rises 8%. By approximately what percent did the worker's real wage change? Give a negative number for a fall.
An investor locks in a 5% nominal return but inflation turns out far higher than expected. Which statement about the real interest rate is correct?
choices: The realized real return is lower than expected, because higher inflation eats into the nominal return
The real return is unchanged, since the nominal rate was fixed in advance
The real return rises, because nominal returns and inflation move together
The real return equals the nominal return, since inflation only affects prices not interest

cards.title: Unemployment and its types
cards.fact: Not all unemployment is the same — some is people between jobs, some is the economy falling short.
cards.detail: The unemployment rate is the share of people who want work and are looking but can't find it. Economists split it: 'frictional' (briefly between jobs), 'structural' (skills or location don't match the jobs), and 'cyclical' (a slump means too few jobs overall). Some unemployment is normal even in a healthy economy — the 'natural rate'. It's cyclical unemployment that policy tries to fight in a recession.
cards.deploy: Distinguishes the unemployment policy can fix (cyclical) from the kind it can't easily (structural).
cards.counter: The headline rate misses discouraged workers who've stopped looking and the underemployed stuck in part-time work, so it can understate real distress — and the 'natural rate' is estimated after the fact, not observed.

quiz.q: Unemployment caused by a general economic downturn is called…
choices: Frictional
Structural
Cyclical
Natural

quiz.q: A coal-mining region loses its mines and the laid-off miners lack the skills for the software jobs now available elsewhere. Which type of unemployment is this?
A central bank cuts interest rates to stimulate spending during a recession. Which type of unemployment is this policy primarily aimed at reducing?
choices: Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
The natural rate of unemployment

quiz.q: A country's labour force is 25 million people, of whom 1.5 million want work and are actively looking but cannot find a job. What is the unemployment rate in percent?

cards.title: The Phillips curve and its breakdown
cards.fact: Lower unemployment once seemed to buy higher inflation — until the 1970s broke the deal.
cards.detail: A.W. Phillips (1958) found an inverse relation: when unemployment fell, wage inflation rose, suggesting a menu policymakers could pick from. Then the 1970s delivered 'stagflation' — high unemployment and high inflation together. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had predicted it: once people expect inflation, they bake it into wages and prices, so the trade-off vanishes in the long run. Only the short-run curve, with expectations fixed, still tilts.

media.caption: The original short-run trade-off: lower unemployment (left), higher inflation.

cards.deploy: A caution against any 'we can just trade a bit more inflation for jobs' claim — it's temporary at best.
cards.counter: Friedman and Phelps argued there's no long-run trade-off because expectations adjust; yet the curve's recent flatness (inflation barely moving as unemployment swung) has economists debating whether it's even useful any more.

quiz.q: The 1970s 'stagflation' undermined the Phillips curve by combining high inflation with high…
choices: Growth
Unemployment
Exports
Savings

quiz.q: What single word names the combination of high unemployment and high inflation occurring together, which discredited the original Phillips curve in the 1970s?
According to Friedman and Phelps, why does the inflation-unemployment trade-off disappear in the long run?
choices: People come to expect inflation and build it into wages and prices, neutralizing the trade-off
Governments eventually run out of money to stimulate the economy
Unemployment cannot physically fall below zero, capping the curve
Central banks legally commit to a fixed inflation target

quiz.q: Which economist's 1958 study first documented the inverse relationship between unemployment and wage inflation?

cards.title: Where money comes from
cards.fact: Most money isn't printed by the state — it's created by commercial banks when they lend.
cards.detail: Physical cash is a small slice of the money supply (measured as M0, M1, M2…). The bulk is bank deposits, and these are created when banks make loans: lend you money and they simply credit your account, conjuring a new deposit. Central banks influence how much through interest rates and reserve rules. The Bank of England spelled this out in 2014, correcting the textbook story that banks just lend out savers' deposits.
cards.deploy: Demystifies 'money printing' — and explains why credit booms expand the money supply.
cards.counter: How much control the central bank really has is disputed: monetarists see it steering money tightly, while post-Keynesians argue money is 'endogenous' — driven by demand for loans, with the central bank mostly following.

quiz.q: In modern economies, most new money is created when…
choices: The mint prints cash
Commercial banks make loans
People save
Taxes are paid

quiz.q: Under the modern understanding of money creation, what happens when a commercial bank approves a new loan?
choices: It credits the borrower's account, creating a brand-new deposit and thus new money
It hands over cash that savers previously deposited, leaving the money supply unchanged
It requests the central bank to print physical notes equal to the loan
It transfers reserves from another bank, so total deposits stay constant

quiz.q: Which central bank published a 2014 explanation correcting the textbook idea that banks simply lend out savers' deposits?
What term describes the view, held by post-Keynesians, that the money supply is driven by demand for loans rather than tightly controlled by the central bank?

media.caption: Physical cash is only a small slice of the money supply; most money is bank deposits created when banks lend (shares schematic).

cards.title: The quantity theory of money
cards.fact: Print far more money than the economy grows, and prices tend to rise to match.
cards.detail: The identity \(M V = P Y\) links the money supply \(M\), how fast it circulates (velocity \(V\)), the price level \(P\) and real output \(Y\). If velocity and output are roughly stable, extra money \(M\) shows up as higher prices \(P\). Milton Friedman built monetarism on this: 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.' It's the clearest reason why printing money to fund deficits risks inflation.

media.say: the money supply times its velocity equals the price level times real output.
media.caption: More money, with stable velocity and output, means higher prices.

cards.deploy: The core monetarist argument linking money growth to inflation.
cards.counter: Velocity is not stable — it collapsed after 2008 and during QE, when huge money creation produced little inflation — so Keynesians argue the link is loose and context-dependent, not mechanical.

quiz.q: In MV = PY, if money (M) surges while velocity and output hold steady, then…
choices: Prices (P) rise
Output (Y) doubles
Velocity falls
Nothing changes

quiz.q: In a year the money supply grows 9% and velocity is unchanged. If the quantity theory holds and real output grows 3%, what is the inflation rate, in percent?
Which quantity in the equation of exchange measures how often a unit of money is spent in a year?
Central banks created huge amounts of money via quantitative easing after 2008, yet inflation stayed low. Which assumption of the quantity theory does this episode most directly call into question?
choices: That velocity is roughly stable
That money can be measured at all
That output is positive
That prices are quoted in money

cards.title: The business cycle
cards.fact: Economies don't grow smoothly — they swing through booms and busts around a long-run trend.
cards.detail: Output, employment and spending rise in an expansion, peak, fall in a recession, hit a trough, and recover — the business cycle. A recession is commonly marked by two straight quarters of falling GDP (though official bodies judge it more broadly). The swings come from shifts in demand, credit, confidence and shocks. Smoothing them is a central aim of monetary and fiscal policy.

media.caption: Output swings above and below its long-run trend: boom, bust, repeat.

cards.deploy: The frame for reading 'are we heading into recession?' and what policy can do about it.
cards.counter: Schools disagree on the cause: Keynesians blame swings in demand, monetarists blame money, 'real business cycle' theorists (Kydland & Prescott) blame technology shocks and call the cycle efficient — not something to fight.

quiz.q: A recession is commonly identified by consecutive quarters of falling…
choices: Inflation
GDP
Population
Exports

quiz.q: In the standard sequence of business-cycle phases, what is the name of the lowest point, where output stops falling before recovery begins?
Real GDP falls 0.4% in Q1 and another 0.2% in Q2, then rises in Q3. By the common rule-of-thumb definition, this economy has experienced:
choices: A recession (two consecutive quarters of falling GDP)
An expansion the whole time
A peak followed by a boom
Stagflation by definition

quiz.q: Which economic school, associated with Kydland and Prescott, attributes cyclical swings to technology shocks and regards the cycle as an efficient response rather than something to fight?

cards.title: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
cards.fact: Scale supply and demand up to the whole economy and you get the model behind output and inflation.
cards.detail: Aggregate demand (AD) is total spending across the economy at each price level — it slopes down. Aggregate supply (AS) is total output firms will produce — upward in the short run, vertical in the long run at the economy's capacity. Their intersection sets national output and the price level. A demand slump (AD shifts left) causes recession and disinflation; a supply shock (AS shifts left) causes the nastier mix of falling output and rising prices — stagflation.

media.caption: Output (across) and the price level (up): where aggregate demand meets aggregate supply.

cards.deploy: The workhorse diagram for tracing how shocks and policy move output and prices.
cards.counter: It papers over deep disputes: how steep is short-run AS, how fast do prices adjust, and are the 'curves' stable enough to use? Different schools draw them very differently.

quiz.q: A negative supply shock (AS shifts left) tends to cause…
choices: Lower prices and more output
Higher prices and less output
No change
A boom

quiz.q: A sharp drop in consumer and business confidence cuts total spending across the economy. In the AD-AS model, the immediate effect is:
choices: Aggregate demand shifts left, lowering output and the price level
Aggregate supply shifts left, raising the price level
Aggregate demand shifts right, raising output and prices
The long-run AS curve becomes flatter

quiz.q: What single word names the combination of falling output and rising prices produced when aggregate supply shifts left?
Why does an increase in aggregate demand raise the price level but NOT real output once the economy is on its long-run aggregate supply curve?
choices: Long-run AS is vertical at the economy's capacity, so only the price level can adjust
Long-run AS slopes downward, absorbing the demand
Aggregate demand is vertical in the long run
Velocity falls to offset the demand

cards.title: The multiplier: spending begets spending
cards.fact: One person's spending is another's income — so an injection can ripple into a larger rise in output.
cards.detail: When you spend, the shopkeeper earns; they spend part of it, the next person earns, and so on. How much each round re-spends is the 'marginal propensity to consume' \(c\). Summing the fading rounds gives the multiplier \(\dfrac{1}{1-c}\): if people re-spend 0.6 of each dollar, a dollar of new spending eventually adds about 2.50 to output. It's the engine behind Keynesian stimulus.

media.say: the multiplier is one divided by one minus the fraction people re-spend.
media.caption: A higher propensity to spend means a bigger ripple.

cards.deploy: Shows why a given stimulus can move GDP by more than its sticker price.
cards.counter: The simple multiplier ignores leakage to imports and savings, crowding-out of private spending, and the state of the economy; its real size is hotly contested (see the fiscal-multiplier debate).

quiz.q: If people re-spend 0.5 of each extra dollar, the simple multiplier is…
Households re-spend 0.8 of each extra dollar of income (marginal propensity to consume = 0.8). What is the simple spending multiplier?
With a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75, by roughly how many dollars does total output eventually rise from 200 dollars of new government spending?
Which factor would make the actual size of a stimulus multiplier SMALLER than the simple 1/(1-c) formula predicts?
choices: Households spending part of their income on imports rather than domestic goods
A higher marginal propensity to consume
More rounds of re-spending occurring
Lower interest rates that encourage borrowing

cards.title: Long-run growth: the Solow model
cards.fact: In the long run, living standards rise mainly through technology — not just piling up more capital.
cards.detail: Robert Solow's growth model writes output as \(Y = A\,K^{\alpha} L^{1-\alpha}\): it depends on capital \(K\), labour \(L\), and a productivity term \(A\) for technology. Capital has diminishing returns — the tenth machine per worker adds less than the first — so saving and investing alone can't grow income forever. Sustained growth in income per person must come from rising \(A\): better technology and know-how. It also predicts poorer countries can grow faster and 'converge'.

media.caption: Diminishing returns to capital: more machines per worker help less and less.

cards.deploy: Explains why technology and education, not mere investment, drive long-run prosperity.
cards.counter: Solow leaves the key driver — technology \(A\) — unexplained, falling 'like manna from heaven'. Paul Romer's endogenous growth theory (2018 Nobel) made ideas and R&D the engine, and convergence has been patchy in practice.

quiz.q: In the Solow model, sustained growth in income per person comes mainly from…
choices: More capital alone
Technological progress
Population growth
Higher prices

quiz.q: In a Solow production function Y = A * K^0.3 * L^0.7, a country doubles its capital K while A and L stay fixed. By what factor does output Y increase? (Give the multiplier, e.g. 1.5 means 50% more output.)
What is the name of the term A in the Solow output equation Y = A * K^alpha * L^(1-alpha) that captures the level of technology and know-how?
Two countries are identical except one starts much poorer (less capital per worker). Because capital has diminishing returns, the Solow model predicts that, all else equal, the poorer country should:
choices: Grow faster and tend to catch up to the richer one
Grow more slowly and fall further behind
Grow at exactly the same rate forever
Never grow because it lacks technology

cards.title: Exchange rates: fixed, floating, and PPP
cards.fact: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another — and how it's set shapes a whole economy.
cards.detail: Under a 'floating' rate, markets set the price by supply and demand for the currency; under a 'fixed' (pegged) rate, the government holds it at a target, spending reserves to defend it. One anchor is purchasing-power parity (PPP): in the long run, rates should drift so a basket of goods costs the same everywhere (the basis of the Big Mac index). A peg gives stability but surrenders control of monetary policy.
cards.deploy: The key to reading currency moves, trade competitiveness and why pegs sometimes shatter.
cards.counter: PPP fails badly in the short and medium run — rates 'overshoot' (Rudiger Dornbusch) and can stay 'wrong' for years — and defended pegs invite speculative attacks, as the 1992 ERM crisis and 1997 Asian crisis showed.

quiz.q: Purchasing-power parity says exchange rates should adjust so that…
choices: Rates never change
A basket of goods costs the same across countries
Exports always rise
Inflation is zero

quiz.q: A burger costs 6 US dollars in the US and 240 pesos in another country. According to purchasing-power parity, what is the implied exchange rate in pesos per US dollar?
A central bank pegs its currency above the rate markets would set, and demand for the currency keeps falling. To hold the peg, what must the central bank do?
choices: Sell foreign-exchange reserves to buy back its own currency
Print more of its own currency and sell it
Buy foreign currency with newly printed domestic money
Raise import tariffs to reduce trade

quiz.q: Which economist is associated with the idea that exchange rates 'overshoot' their long-run equilibrium in the short run?

media.caption: Under a float, currency supply (rising) and demand (falling) cross to set the exchange rate; a peg holds it away from that point using reserves.

cards.title: The balance of payments
cards.fact: A country's dealings with the world split into a current account (trade) and a capital account (investment) that must balance.
cards.detail: The balance of payments records every transaction with the rest of the world. The current account tracks trade in goods and services plus income; the financial/capital account tracks flows of investment and assets. By construction they offset: a country running a current-account deficit (importing more than it exports) must be a net borrower from abroad — money flows in on the capital account to match. A 'trade deficit' is thus also a capital-account surplus.
cards.deploy: Cuts through 'trade deficit' panic: a deficit is mirrored by foreign investment flowing in.
cards.counter: Whether persistent deficits are dangerous is disputed — they can signal either a vibrant magnet for investment (the US) or a fragile dependence on foreign lending that can reverse suddenly (the 'sudden stops' of emerging-market crises).

quiz.q: A country with a current-account (trade) deficit must be a net…
choices: Lender to the world
Borrower from the world
Exporter
Saver

quiz.q: A country imports 700 billion dollars of goods and services and exports 520 billion, with income flows netting to zero. By how many billion dollars must net foreign investment flow IN on the financial/capital account to balance the books?
A country records a large surplus on its financial/capital account (net investment flowing in). What does this imply about its current account?
choices: It is running a current-account deficit of matching size
It is running a current-account surplus of matching size
Its current account must be exactly zero
Its current account is unrelated to capital flows

quiz.q: What two-word term describes the abrupt reversal of foreign capital inflows that triggered several emerging-market crises?

cards.title: The liquidity trap
cards.fact: When interest rates hit zero, cutting them further does nothing — monetary policy runs out of road.
cards.detail: Normally a central bank fights a slump by cutting rates. But rates can't fall much below zero: at that point people and banks just hold cash rather than lend, so extra money piles up unused and rate cuts lose their bite — a 'liquidity trap'. Keynes named it in the 1930s; Japan lived it from the 1990s and much of the West did after 2008. The standard escape is fiscal policy — direct government spending.
cards.deploy: Explains why, after 2008, central banks turned to QE and economists called for fiscal stimulus.
cards.counter: Monetarists like Friedman denied a true liquidity trap, arguing a determined central bank can always create inflation (via QE or 'helicopter money'); the post-2008 experience is read by both sides as supporting their view.

quiz.q: A liquidity trap occurs when interest rates are so low that…
choices: Inflation soars
Further rate cuts stop working
Banks lend freely
Output booms

quiz.q: An economy is in a deep slump with its policy interest rate already at zero, and further easing is doing nothing. Which policy is the standard textbook escape from this situation?
choices: Direct government spending (fiscal stimulus)
Another cut in the policy interest rate
Raising bank reserve requirements
Imposing tariffs to protect domestic industry

quiz.q: Which economist, writing in the 1930s, named the situation in which interest rates are so low that extra money is simply held as cash and rate cuts lose their effect?
Which monetarist economist denied that a true liquidity trap exists, arguing a determined central bank can always create inflation through measures like 'helicopter money'?

cards.title: Hyperinflation: when money dies
cards.fact: Once people lose faith in a currency, prices can double in days and the money becomes worthless.
cards.detail: Hyperinflation — often defined as 50%+ inflation per month — strikes when governments print money to cover spending they can't fund, and confidence collapses. People rush to spend before prices rise again, velocity explodes, and the spiral feeds itself: Weimar Germany (1923), Zimbabwe (2008) and Venezuela (2010s) all printed their way into it. It usually ends only with a new currency or a hard fiscal anchor.
cards.deploy: The cautionary extreme of monetary finance — and why central-bank independence is prized.
cards.counter: Pure monetarists blame the money printing alone; others (the 'fiscal theory of the price level') argue hyperinflation is ultimately a collapse of confidence in the government's solvency, with printing the symptom rather than the root cause.

quiz.q: Hyperinflation is typically triggered by governments…
choices: Raising taxes
Printing money to fund spending
Cutting spending
Pegging the currency

quiz.q: If a currency loses value so fast that prices double every 4 days, by what factor have prices risen after 12 days (assuming the doubling holds steady)?

What economic theory holds that hyperinflation is fundamentally a collapse of confidence in the government's ability to repay its debts, with money-printing being a symptom rather than the root cause?
quiz.answer: fiscal theory of the price level
accept: fiscal theory of the price level

quiz.q: During a hyperinflation, why does the speed at which money changes hands (velocity) tend to surge?
choices: People rush to spend cash immediately because holding it means watching its value evaporate
Banks are legally required to lend out reserves faster during a crisis
The central bank deliberately raises interest rates to circulate money
Foreign investors flood in to buy the cheap local currency

cards.title: What GDP misses
cards.fact: GDP counts market output — not wellbeing, unpaid work, inequality, or the environment.
cards.detail: GDP adds up the market value of what a country produces, and it rises whether the spending is on schools or on cleaning up an oil spill. It ignores unpaid care and housework, says nothing about how income is shared, and treats depleting forests or fisheries as pure gain. Even Simon Kuznets, who helped build it, warned in 1934 that 'the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from' it. Alternatives include the Human Development Index and the Genuine Progress Indicator.
cards.deploy: Arms you to question 'growth = progress' and to ask what a rising GDP is actually counting.
cards.counter: Defenders (the IMF, most statisticians) reply that GDP was never meant to measure welfare, that it correlates strongly with health and education, and that the proposed alternatives are more subjective and harder to compare. The debate is about what to measure, not whether to.

quiz.q: Which does GDP NOT capture?
choices: Market output
Unpaid care work
Government spending
Exports

quiz.q: A massive oil spill occurs, and a country spends billions on the cleanup. What does standard GDP accounting do with this spending?
choices: It adds the cleanup spending as output, so GDP rises
It subtracts the environmental damage, so GDP falls
It records the spill and cleanup as a net wash with no effect on GDP
It excludes the spending because it produces no marketable good

quiz.q: Name one of the alternative welfare measures the card lists as a supplement or replacement for GDP that tries to account for things like health, education, or environmental costs.
A common defense of GDP is that the harshest critique somewhat misses its design. What is that defense?
choices: GDP was never intended to measure welfare, only market output
GDP already fully includes unpaid care work in its totals
GDP is impossible to compute, so all alternatives are equally flawed
GDP measures inequality more accurately than any other indicator

cards.title: Growth vs degrowth
cards.fact: Can a finite planet sustain endless economic growth — or must rich economies stop chasing it?
cards.detail: The mainstream view holds that growth lifts living standards and can be 'decoupled' from environmental harm through clean technology and efficiency. 'Degrowth' scholars like Jason Hickel and Giorgos Kallis argue that absolute decoupling at the needed scale isn't happening, so rich countries should deliberately shrink resource use and reorganise around wellbeing rather than GDP. Ecomodernists counter that technology and growth are the way out, not the problem.
cards.deploy: Frames the deepest argument in environmental economics: grow greener, or grow less?
cards.counter: The dispute is empirical and contested: defenders of growth point to falling emissions per dollar in some rich economies (relative decoupling), while degrowthers stress that absolute global resource use keeps rising. Neither side has settled the evidence.

quiz.q: 'Degrowth' advocates argue that rich economies should…
choices: Maximise GDP
Deliberately reduce resource use
Print more money
Cut all taxes

quiz.q: What term describes growth continuing while environmental harm (such as emissions or resource use) falls in absolute terms, breaking the historical link between the two?
An economy's CO2 emissions per dollar of output fall, yet its total emissions keep rising because output grows even faster. Which concept does this illustrate?
choices: Relative decoupling without absolute decoupling
Absolute decoupling has been achieved
Degrowth has been successfully implemented
A complete failure of any decoupling whatsoever

quiz.q: What is the name of the position, opposed to degrowth, that holds technology and continued growth are the way out of environmental problems rather than the cause?

cards.title: Why nations fail: institutions
cards.fact: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson argue prosperity hinges on whether institutions include or extract.
cards.detail: Why are some countries rich and others poor? Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson (2024 Nobel) argue the decisive factor is institutions. 'Inclusive' institutions — secure property rights, broad political voice, rule of law — let ordinary people invest and innovate; 'extractive' ones funnel wealth to a narrow elite and choke growth. Their natural experiment: colonisers built inclusive institutions where they settled and extractive ones where they merely plundered, and that split still shapes incomes today.
cards.deploy: Shifts the development question from geography or culture to who holds power and how it's constrained.
cards.counter: Critics (Jeffrey Sachs) insist geography and disease still matter hugely, and others note the inclusive/extractive labels can be circular — defined partly by the prosperity they're meant to explain. China's growth under extractive politics is a standing puzzle for the theory.

quiz.q: Acemoglu and Robinson argue prosperity depends most on…
choices: Geography
Inclusive vs extractive institutions
Climate
Population size

quiz.q: Two neighboring regions were colonized by the same European power: one was densely settled by colonists, the other only plundered for resources. By the institutional theory of development, what would you predict about their incomes today?
choices: The densely settled region is richer, because settlers built inclusive institutions there
The plundered region is richer, because extraction concentrated capital efficiently
Their incomes are identical, since they share the same colonizer and culture
Income depends entirely on each region's climate and disease environment

quiz.q: Which economist does the card name as the leading critic of the institutions theory, arguing that geography and disease remain decisive in why nations are poor?
Which country's strong economic growth under extractive, non-inclusive politics does the card cite as a standing puzzle for the inclusive-institutions theory?
choices: China
Switzerland
Botswana
South Korea

cards.title: Dependency and world-systems theory
cards.fact: Dependency theorists argue poor countries stay poor because the global system is built to drain them.
cards.detail: Against the idea that poor nations simply lag behind, Latin American economists Raúl Prebisch and Andre Gunder Frank argued the world is split into a wealthy 'core' and a 'periphery' locked into supplying cheap raw materials, their terms of trade steadily worsening. Immanuel Wallerstein's world-systems theory generalised this into a single capitalist system that develops the core by underdeveloping the periphery. The prescription was often to industrialise behind tariffs rather than specialise in commodities.
cards.deploy: A counter to free-trade optimism: names who gains and who is structurally held back.
cards.counter: The East Asian 'tigers' — which grew rich through export-led trade, not withdrawal from it — are the standard rebuttal; mainstream economists also note that import-substitution policies often produced inefficient, protected industries. Dependency theorists reply that East Asia had unusual geopolitical backing.

quiz.q: Dependency theory describes the world economy as a…
choices: Level playing field
Wealthy 'core' and an exploited 'periphery'
Single nation
Random market

quiz.q: A small nation exports only cocoa and imports manufactured machinery. Over decades, each ton of cocoa buys fewer machines. Which dependency-theory concept does this trend most directly illustrate?
choices: Worsening terms of trade for the periphery
Comparative advantage paying off for both partners
Successful import substitution
The core voluntarily transferring technology

quiz.q: Which economist generalised core-periphery ideas into a single global 'world-systems' framework in which the core develops by underdeveloping the periphery?
Why are the East Asian 'tiger' economies the standard rebuttal to dependency theory?
choices: They grew rich through export-led integration into world trade, not withdrawal from it
They remained pure commodity exporters and still prospered
They proved that worsening terms of trade never occur
They refused all foreign investment and grew anyway

cards.title: The developmental state
cards.fact: Ha-Joon Chang and Joe Studwell argue today's rich countries got rich by guiding markets, not freeing them.
cards.detail: East Asia's rise — Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, then China — was led by an activist state: protecting infant industries, directing cheap credit, and forcing firms to export and compete abroad ('export discipline'). Ha-Joon Chang argues the now-rich West used the same protectionist tools while climbing, then 'kicked away the ladder' by preaching free trade to others. Joe Studwell adds that land reform and disciplined finance were decisive.
cards.deploy: A powerful case that industrial policy, not laissez-faire, built every late industrialiser.
cards.counter: Free-market economists reply that state direction also produced costly failures (much of Latin America, India's licence raj) and crony capitalism, and that East Asia succeeded partly despite, not because of, intervention. Picking winners is easy to romanticise after the fact.

quiz.q: Ha-Joon Chang's 'kicking away the ladder' accuses rich countries of…
choices: Sharing technology freely
Denying others the protectionist tools they themselves used
Always free-trading
Avoiding industry

quiz.q: What term describes a developmental state forcing subsidised firms to prove themselves by competing in foreign markets, withdrawing support if they fail?
A government grants cheap credit and tariff protection to a new steel firm but cuts it off unless the firm hits rising export targets within five years. This policy mix best fits which tradition?
choices: The developmental state model of guided markets
Laissez-faire free trade
Dependency-theory withdrawal from world trade
Pure import substitution with no export requirement

quiz.q: Beyond industrial policy, Joe Studwell singles out two factors as decisive in East Asia's rise: disciplined finance and one concerning agriculture. Name the agricultural one.

cards.title: Feminist economics: the work that doesn't count
cards.fact: The unpaid care that sustains every economy is invisible to the standard measures of it.
cards.detail: Feminist economists point out that mainstream economics ignores the enormous unpaid labour — childcare, cooking, eldercare, housework — done largely by women, without which no paid economy could function. Marilyn Waring showed national accounts count a forest only when it's felled, and a person only when they're paid; care work registers as nothing. The field also studies how gendered assumptions shape models of 'rational' choice and the household.
cards.deploy: Reframes 'the economy' to include the unpaid foundation it actually rests on.
cards.counter: Critics argue assigning market prices to care work is arbitrary and that including it would make GDP even noisier; feminist economists respond that leaving it at zero is the more distorting choice — the dispute is over what counts as economic value at all.

quiz.q: Feminist economics highlights that standard measures ignore…
choices: Exports
Unpaid care and domestic work
Taxes
Interest rates

quiz.q: Which economist argued that national accounts count a forest only when it is felled and a person only when they are paid, exposing how care work registers as nothing?
Feminist economists respond to the objection that pricing care work is 'arbitrary' by arguing that:
choices: Leaving care work valued at zero is itself the more distorting choice
Care work should be excluded because it has no market price
GDP is already a perfect measure of economic value
Only paid childcare counts as real economic activity

quiz.q: A household's measured (paid) output is 60,000 a year. Unpaid care work, if valued, would add another 45,000. By what percentage would including the unpaid care raise the household's recorded economic output?

cards.title: The colonial drain
cards.fact: Empires didn't just rule colonies — they ran them as engines of wealth extraction.
cards.detail: Colonial economies were reshaped to feed the metropole: land turned to cash crops, local industry suppressed, and surpluses siphoned abroad. The Indian nationalist Dadabhai Naoroji formulated the 'drain of wealth' thesis in the 19th century, estimating how much Britain pumped out of India each year; recent work by Utsa Patnaik puts the cumulative figure in the trillions. The mirror image is the Atlantic system, where enslaved labour built plantation wealth.
cards.deploy: Grounds 'why are some nations poor?' in a history of extraction, not just bad luck or culture.
cards.counter: The scale and lasting effect are debated: some economic historians (Tirthankar Roy) argue colonialism's impact is overstated relative to internal factors and that the counterfactual is murky, while others (Patnaik, the dependency school) see extraction as decisive. The numbers turn on contested assumptions.

quiz.q: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' described…
choices: Famine relief
Wealth siphoned from India to Britain
Free trade
Industrial growth

quiz.q: Which contemporary economist's research puts the cumulative wealth Britain extracted from India in the trillions, extending Naoroji's 19th-century thesis?
Which economic historian argues that colonialism's impact on India is overstated relative to internal factors, making him a counterweight to the drain school?
choices: Tirthankar Roy
Andre Gunder Frank
Dadabhai Naoroji
Immanuel Wallerstein

quiz.q: A colony's farmland is converted from food crops to cotton for export, local textile workshops are taxed out of business, and the trade surplus is remitted to the imperial capital. Which thesis does this pattern most directly support?
choices: The 'drain of wealth' / colonial extraction thesis
Comparative advantage benefiting the colony
The developmental-state export-discipline model
Free trade equalising incomes across the empire

cards.title: The East Asian miracle
cards.fact: In a generation, the 'Asian tigers' went from poor to rich — the fastest catch-up in history.
cards.detail: From the 1960s, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore (the 'Four Tigers'), followed by Southeast Asia and China, grew at extraordinary rates, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. The recipe is disputed but the ingredients recur: high savings and investment, mass education, land reform, and export-oriented industrialisation. The World Bank's 1993 report 'The East Asian Miracle' tried, awkwardly, to reconcile this with free-market orthodoxy.
cards.deploy: The central case study for every theory of development — and the rebuttal to dependency pessimism.
cards.counter: The 1997 Asian financial crisis exposed the model's fragility, and economists still split: the World Bank credits markets and openness, while Alice Amsden and Robert Wade credit the guiding hand of the state. Paul Krugman argued the growth was mostly 'perspiration' (more inputs), not 'inspiration' (productivity).

quiz.q: A common ingredient in the East Asian growth model was…
choices: Commodity exports only
Export-oriented industrialisation
Closed autarky
Low savings

quiz.q: Paul Krugman argued the East Asian growth boom was mostly 'perspiration, not inspiration.' What did he mean?
choices: Growth came from piling in more inputs (capital and labour) rather than from rising productivity
Growth was driven by rapid technological innovation that the West underestimated
Growth depended on cheap energy imports rather than domestic effort
Growth reflected lucky terms-of-trade gains rather than any deliberate policy

quiz.q: Which two economists are most associated with crediting an active, guiding state (rather than free markets) for East Asia's rise?
Suppose a 'tiger' economy grows real GDP per capita at a steady 7% per year. Using the rule of 70, roughly how many years does it take for living standards to double?

cards.title: The Washington Consensus
cards.fact: In the 1980s–90s, the IMF and World Bank prescribed one package to the developing world: liberalise, privatise, stabilise.
cards.detail: Coined by John Williamson in 1989, the 'Washington Consensus' named a set of market reforms — fiscal discipline, privatisation, deregulation, free trade and open capital markets — attached as conditions to IMF and World Bank loans (structural adjustment). It reshaped Latin America, Africa and the post-Soviet states. Results were mixed at best: growth often disappointed and inequality frequently rose.
cards.deploy: The label for the era when market liberalisation was exported worldwide as loan conditions.
cards.counter: Joseph Stiglitz attacked it for forcing premature liberalisation that triggered crises; William Easterly mocked top-down 'planning' for the poor. Defenders reply that the worst failures came where reforms were half-done or corruptly applied, not from the prescription itself. Even Williamson said his term was widely misused.

quiz.q: The Washington Consensus prescribed mainly…
choices: State ownership
Market liberalisation and privatisation
Higher tariffs
Currency pegs

quiz.q: Which economist coined the phrase 'Washington Consensus' in 1989?
A country accepts an IMF loan in the early 1990s on the standard reform conditions of the era. Which policy package best fits those 'structural adjustment' conditions?
choices: Cut budget deficits, privatise state firms, deregulate, and open up to trade and capital
Raise tariffs to protect infant industries while nationalising key banks
Expand public ownership and impose strict capital controls on outflows
Fix wages and prices centrally while subsidising domestic consumption

quiz.q: What was Joseph Stiglitz's central criticism of the Washington Consensus?
choices: Forcing premature liberalisation, especially of capital markets, helped trigger financial crises
It relied too heavily on central planning and ignored market signals
It funnelled aid to governments rather than directly to the poor
It protected domestic industries for too long, delaying competition

cards.title: The Marshall Plan
cards.fact: After 1945, the US poured aid into Western Europe — and helped rebuild both its economies and its alliances.
cards.detail: From 1948, the United States transferred some $13 billion (a vast sum then) to rebuild Western Europe under the European Recovery Program, named for Secretary of State George Marshall. It funded reconstruction, restarted trade, and was explicitly geopolitical — binding Western Europe to the US and against Soviet influence as the Cold War set in. Recipients were nudged toward cooperation, seeding what became the European common market.
cards.deploy: The canonical example of aid serving reconstruction and strategy at once.
cards.counter: Its size-of-effect is debated — Alan Milward argued Europe's recovery was already under way — but so is its framing. From Moscow the Plan was an instrument of US economic empire and dollar dominance, which is why Stalin forced Eastern Europe to refuse it and built Comecon in reply; dependency-school writers read conditional aid as binding recipients to American markets. The 'generous reconstruction' story is told mostly from Washington's side.

quiz.q: The Marshall Plan was US aid to rebuild…
choices: Japan
Western Europe
Latin America
Africa

quiz.q: The Marshall Plan transferred about $13 billion to Western Europe. If a later aid program instead gave $26 billion under otherwise comparable terms, how many times larger than the Marshall Plan would that program be, by dollars transferred?
What was the name of the economic bloc Stalin set up for the Eastern bloc after forcing those countries to refuse Marshall aid?
Historian Alan Milward's argument complicates the standard story of the Marshall Plan by claiming that:
choices: Western Europe's economic recovery was already under way before the aid arrived
The aid was far larger in real terms than commonly reported
The Soviet Union secretly accepted a share of the funds
The Plan was purely humanitarian with no strategic motive

cards.title: The CIA triad: what security protects
cards.fact: Security has three goals: confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
cards.detail: Almost every security measure serves one of three aims. Confidentiality keeps data secret from those who shouldn't see it (encryption, access control). Integrity keeps it from being altered without detection (hashes, signatures). Availability keeps it reachable when needed (backups, defence against denial-of-service). The three pull against each other — locking something down tighter can make it harder to reach — so security is always a balance, not a maximum.
cards.deploy: A checklist for any system: which of confidentiality, integrity and availability matters most here, and what threatens it?
cards.counter: The triad is a useful frame, not a complete one; practitioners add goals like authenticity, non-repudiation and privacy, and some argue it's too data-centric for modern threats like disinformation.

quiz.q: The 'A' in the CIA triad stands for…
choices: Authentication
Availability
Authorization
Anonymity

quiz.q: A hospital wants patient records to remain accessible to doctors at all hours, even during an outage. Which CIA-triad goal is the primary concern here?
choices: Availability
Confidentiality
Integrity
Authenticity

quiz.q: Which CIA-triad goal is most directly protected by using cryptographic hashes and digital signatures to detect unauthorised changes to data?
Encrypting a database and adding several layers of access control makes it slower and occasionally unreachable for legitimate users. What does this trade-off illustrate about the CIA triad?
choices: Strengthening confidentiality can come at the expense of availability, so security is a balance
Confidentiality and availability always reinforce each other
Integrity is irrelevant once confidentiality is maximised
The three goals can all be maximised simultaneously with enough resources

cards.title: Threat, vulnerability, risk
cards.fact: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is who'd exploit it; risk is the chance and cost if they do.
cards.detail: These three words are often muddled but mean different things. A vulnerability is a flaw — an unpatched server, a weak password. A threat is an actor or event that could exploit it — a criminal, an insider, a flood. Risk combines them: how likely is exploitation, and how bad would it be? The sum of all the ways in is the 'attack surface'. Security spends scarce effort where risk — not just vulnerability — is highest.
cards.deploy: Stops 'we found a flaw, panic' thinking: a vulnerability with no plausible threat or low impact may not be worth fixing first.
cards.counter: Risk numbers are estimates dressed as facts — probabilities of rare attacks are hard to know — so risk scoring can give false precision and miss the 'unknown unknowns' that cause the worst breaches.

quiz.q: An unpatched, exploitable flaw in software is a…
choices: Threat
Vulnerability
Risk
Patch

quiz.q: A hospital runs an old, unpatched database server, but it sits on an isolated network with no internet access and holds only public phone-directory data. In risk terms, why might this be low priority to fix despite the obvious flaw?
choices: The vulnerability exists, but there's little plausible threat path to it and the impact if exploited is minimal
An unpatched server cannot have a vulnerability if it's offline
Isolated networks have no attack surface of any kind
Public data automatically encrypts itself, removing the vulnerability

quiz.q: What single term names the sum of all the points and paths through which an attacker could try to get into a system?

A simple risk score is estimated as likelihood times impact. If an exploit has a 5 percent annual chance of occurring (likelihood 0.05) and would cost 800000 dollars, what is the expected annual loss in dollars?

cards.title: Authentication vs authorization
cards.fact: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you're allowed to do.
cards.detail: Logging in is authentication — proving identity by something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or token), or something you are (a fingerprint). Authorization is the next step: now that we know who you are, which files or actions may you access? Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two of those categories, so a stolen password alone isn't enough — one of the single most effective defences there is.
cards.deploy: Clarifies a constant confusion and explains why MFA blocks the bulk of account-takeover attacks.
cards.counter: Not all factors are equal: SMS codes can be intercepted (SIM-swapping), and 'push fatigue' attacks spam approval prompts until a tired user taps yes — so MFA reduces risk but doesn't end it.

quiz.q: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from…
choices: One category, twice
Two different categories (know/have/are)
Only passwords
Only biometrics

quiz.q: A web app lets users log in with a password, then checks their role to decide whether they can view the admin dashboard. Which step is authorization?
choices: Checking the role to decide if the admin dashboard may be viewed
Verifying the typed password matches the stored credential
Asking the user to enter their username
Sending a one-time code to the user's phone

quiz.q: A login that requires a password plus a fingerprint scan draws on two of the three authentication categories: something you know, something you have, and which third one (the biometric category)?
A security team classifies authentication factors into the three standard categories. To qualify as multi-factor authentication, a login must use factors from at least how many different categories?

cards.title: How passwords should be stored
cards.fact: Never store passwords as text — store a salted hash you can check but can't reverse.
cards.detail: A cryptographic hash turns any input into a fixed fingerprint that can't be run backwards. So a site stores the hash of your password, not the password; at login it hashes what you typed and compares. To stop attackers pre-computing hashes (rainbow tables), each password gets a unique random 'salt' mixed in before hashing, and a deliberately slow algorithm (bcrypt, Argon2) makes mass guessing expensive. A breach then leaks hashes, not your actual password.
cards.deploy: The reason a well-run site can be breached without your password itself leaking — and why reuse across sites is dangerous.
cards.counter: Hashing only buys time: weak or common passwords still fall to guessing, and NIST's 2017 guidance reversed old habits — it now advises against forced periodic changes and complexity rules, which pushed users toward predictable patterns.

quiz.q: A 'salt' is added before hashing a password to…
choices: Speed up login
Stop precomputed-hash (rainbow-table) attacks
Encrypt the database
Compress the password

quiz.q: Two users on the same site happen to choose the identical password. Each account stores a salted hash. Why will the two stored hash values differ?
choices: Each password is combined with its own unique random salt before hashing
Hash functions deliberately return a different output every time they run
The site re-encrypts one of the two passwords with a second key
Longer usernames force a longer hash output

quiz.q: Name one of the deliberately slow password-hashing algorithms designed to make mass guessing expensive (as opposed to a fast general-purpose hash).

Suppose adding a salt forces an attacker to build a separate guessing table per password instead of one shared table. If they must crack 250 stolen password hashes that each took one shared table before salting, how many separate tables must they now build, one per password?

cards.title: Symmetric encryption: one shared key
cards.fact: Symmetric encryption scrambles data with a key; the same key unscrambles it.
cards.detail: With a symmetric cipher like AES, sender and receiver share one secret key: the key plus the message produces ciphertext, and the same key reverses it. It's fast and used for the bulk of encrypted data — files, disks, the actual content of a secure connection. The hard part isn't the maths; it's the logistics: how do two parties who've never met agree on a shared secret key without an eavesdropper learning it? That problem is what public-key cryptography solves.
cards.deploy: The workhorse that actually encrypts your data; understanding its key-sharing snag motivates everything that follows.
cards.counter: A symmetric scheme is only as safe as its key handling: reuse a key or a 'nonce', or leak the key, and strong maths gives no protection — most real-world crypto failures are key-management failures, not broken ciphers.

quiz.q: In symmetric encryption, the key used to decrypt is…
choices: Different from the encryption key
The same as the encryption key
Public
Not needed

quiz.q: Why is the fundamental difficulty of symmetric encryption described as a logistics problem rather than a mathematical one?
choices: Two parties must somehow agree on the same secret key without an eavesdropper learning it
The AES algorithm has never been proven secure against any attack
Symmetric ciphers are too slow to encrypt large files in practice
Each message requires a fresh algorithm to be invented

quiz.q: What is the name of the widely used symmetric block cipher that encrypts the bulk of data such as files and disks?

In a purely symmetric setup, every pair of people who want to communicate privately needs its own shared secret key. For a group of 6 people who all want pairwise-private channels, how many distinct shared keys are required?

cards.title: Public-key cryptography
cards.fact: A public key locks; only the matching private key unlocks — so strangers can exchange secrets.
cards.detail: Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography gives everyone two linked keys: a public one they share freely and a private one they guard. Anyone can encrypt to you with your public key, but only your private key decrypts. It rests on 'one-way' maths — easy to do, brutally hard to reverse. RSA, for example, encrypts as \(c = m^{e} \bmod n\), and reversing it requires factoring a huge number, which is believed to be infeasible. This solves symmetric encryption's key-exchange problem.

media.say: the ciphertext is the message raised to the public exponent, wrapped around a big modulus n.
media.caption: RSA: easy to compute, hard to reverse without the private key.

cards.deploy: The breakthrough behind secure websites, signed software and encrypted messaging.
cards.counter: Its security rests on problems merely *believed* hard (factoring, discrete logs), not proven so — and a large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA outright, which is why post-quantum cryptography is being rolled out now.

quiz.q: In public-key cryptography, a message encrypted with your public key can be decrypted with…
choices: The same public key
Your private key
Anyone's key
A password

quiz.q: You want to receive a confidential message from someone you've never met, with no prior shared secret. What do you publish so they can send it securely?
choices: Your public key, which they use to encrypt; only your private key decrypts it
Your private key, which they use to encrypt the message
A shared password you both agree on in advance
Your public key, which they use to decrypt the reply

quiz.q: Using RSA-style encryption c = m^e mod n, encrypt the message m = 4 with public exponent e = 3 and modulus n = 33. What is the ciphertext c?
What hard mathematical problem must be solved to break RSA by recovering the private key from the public modulus?

cards.title: TLS: what the padlock means
cards.fact: HTTPS uses public-key crypto to agree a secret key, then switches to fast symmetric encryption.
cards.detail: When you connect to an HTTPS site, TLS does a 'handshake': the site presents a certificate (signed by a trusted authority) vouching for its identity and public key, the two sides use public-key crypto to agree on a fresh shared secret, and then they switch to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data. The padlock means the connection is encrypted and the site's certificate checks out — not that the site itself is honest.
cards.deploy: Explains exactly what the browser padlock does and doesn't promise.
cards.counter: The whole system trusts a web of certificate authorities; a compromised or coerced CA can issue fraudulent certificates, and a padlock on a phishing site only proves the connection is encrypted, not that the site is who you want.

quiz.q: The HTTPS padlock guarantees that…
choices: The website is trustworthy
The connection is encrypted and the certificate checks out
No one can hack the site
The site is malware-free

quiz.q: Why does TLS use public-key cryptography only at the start of a connection, then switch to symmetric encryption for the rest of the data?
choices: Symmetric encryption is much faster, so it's used once a shared secret has been safely agreed
Public-key crypto cannot encrypt large files at all
Symmetric encryption is more secure than public-key for any data size
Public-key crypto is only legal during the handshake phase

quiz.q: A bank-scam website shows a valid padlock in the browser. What does that padlock actually establish?
choices: The connection is encrypted and the certificate is validly signed for that domain
The website operator is honest and the site is not a scam
The website has been audited by a government regulator
Your data cannot be stolen once you submit it to the site

quiz.q: During a TLS handshake, what kind of trusted third party signs the certificate that vouches for a site's identity and public key?

cards.title: Hashes and digital signatures
cards.fact: A hash detects tampering; signing it with a private key proves who sent it.
cards.detail: A cryptographic hash (like SHA-256) reduces any file to a fixed fingerprint where the tiniest change yields a wildly different output and you can't work backwards — that gives integrity: re-hash a file and compare to spot tampering. A digital signature goes further: the sender encrypts the hash with their private key, and anyone can verify it with the matching public key, proving both that the file is unaltered and who signed it. This is how software updates and documents are authenticated.
cards.deploy: The mechanism behind 'verified' downloads, signed code, and tamper-evident records.
cards.counter: A signature only proves possession of a private key, not that the right person held it — stolen signing keys (as in the Stuxnet and SolarWinds attacks) let malware masquerade as trusted software.

quiz.q: A digital signature proves a message is unaltered AND…
choices: Encrypted
Who signed it
Compressed
Anonymous

quiz.q: You download a file and re-compute its SHA-256 hash, getting a value completely different from the publisher's listed hash. What can you conclude?
choices: The file has been altered or corrupted since it was published
The file is authentic but encrypted
The publisher used a different private key to sign it
Only the file's size changed, not its contents

quiz.q: To create a digital signature on a document, what does the sender encrypt with their private key?
choices: The hash (fingerprint) of the document
The entire document, byte for byte
The recipient's public key
A random session token unrelated to the document

quiz.q: Stuxnet and SolarWinds let malware pose as trusted software despite valid signatures. What had the attackers obtained to make this possible?

cards.title: Phishing and social engineering
cards.fact: The easiest way past strong security is to trick a human into opening the door.
cards.detail: Social engineering attacks people, not machines: a convincing email, text or call that pressures you into clicking a link, entering a password, or wiring money. Phishing casts a wide net; 'spear-phishing' targets a specific person with tailored detail; 'business email compromise' impersonates a boss or supplier. It works because it exploits trust, urgency and authority — and no firewall stops a user who volunteers their credentials.
cards.deploy: Names why training, verification habits and MFA matter as much as technical defences.
cards.counter: Blaming 'gullible users' is a cop-out: well-designed systems reduce the damage a tricked human can do (MFA, payment call-backs, least privilege), so repeated breaches often point to bad system design, not bad people.

quiz.q: Phishing primarily exploits…
choices: Software bugs
Human trust and urgency
Weak encryption
Network speed

quiz.q: An attacker sends a CFO an email tailored with the company's real project names and a specific vendor's invoice, impersonating the CEO. Which attack is this best described as?
choices: Spear-phishing / business email compromise
A brute-force password attack
A denial-of-service attack
Generic mass phishing with no targeting

quiz.q: After a phishing breach, which response best fits the view that repeated incidents reflect system design rather than 'gullible users'?
choices: Add MFA, payment call-backs and least privilege so a tricked user can do less damage
Publicly name and discipline the employee who clicked
Send more reminder emails warning staff to be careful
Remove all email access for non-technical staff

quiz.q: Beyond exploiting trust and authority, name one other psychological lever phishing attacks rely on to push a target into acting quickly.

cards.title: Malware: viruses, worms, ransomware
cards.fact: Malware is software written to harm — and its types differ by how they spread and what they do.
cards.detail: A virus attaches to a file and spreads when that file is run; a worm spreads by itself across networks with no help; a trojan hides inside something that looks useful; ransomware encrypts your files and demands payment for the key. Spyware watches, botnets hijack machines into a remote army. The category matters because it shapes the defence — patching for worms, backups for ransomware, vetting downloads for trojans.
cards.deploy: A taxonomy that tells you which defence fits which threat.
cards.counter: The neat categories blur in practice: modern attacks chain several types, and the bigger shift is economic — ransomware-as-a-service turned malware into a criminal industry, so the threat is now organised business, not lone hackers.

quiz.q: Which malware spreads across networks on its own, without user action?
choices: Virus
Worm
Trojan
Spyware

quiz.q: A hospital's accounting files are suddenly scrambled and a message demands Bitcoin to restore them. Which single defence would most directly let them recover without paying?
choices: Keeping offline backups of the files
Installing the latest network patches
Carefully vetting downloaded software
Running a packet sniffer on the network

quiz.q: What name is given to malware that disguises itself as a legitimate or useful program to trick a user into running it?
A piece of malware embeds itself in a spreadsheet and only activates when someone opens that spreadsheet. By how it spreads, what type is this?
choices: A virus
A worm
A botnet
Spyware

cards.title: Injection attacks: never trust input
cards.fact: If user input is treated as a command, attackers can rewrite what your program does.
cards.detail: Injection happens when data from a user is fed into an interpreter as if it were trusted code. The classic is SQL injection: type a crafted string into a login box and, if the app glues it straight into a database query, you can make the query return everything or delete the table. Cross-site scripting (XSS) does the same with JavaScript in a web page. The fix is the same idea everywhere: keep data and code separate (parameterised queries, output encoding).
cards.deploy: The root cause behind a huge share of web breaches — and why 'sanitise your inputs' is a mantra.
cards.counter: 'Sanitising' by blocklisting bad characters is fragile and keeps losing; the durable fix is structural (parameterised queries, safe APIs) — yet injection has topped the OWASP risk list for two decades because the unsafe pattern is so easy to write.

quiz.q: SQL injection works when user input is…
choices: Encrypted
Treated as part of a database command
Stored as a hash
Rejected

quiz.q: A web app glues a user's comment directly into the HTML page so that other visitors' browsers run any script the comment contains. Which attack class is this?
choices: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
SQL injection
Denial of service
Man-in-the-middle

quiz.q: What is the recommended structural defence against SQL injection that keeps the supplied data separate from the query's code instead of concatenating it into the query string?
Why is blocklisting 'bad characters' considered a fragile way to stop injection, compared with parameterised queries?
choices: Attackers keep finding new encodings and characters the list missed, so it must be patched forever
It encrypts the input so the database cannot read it
It blocks all legitimate users from logging in
It only works on web pages but not on databases

cards.title: Man-in-the-middle attacks
cards.fact: If an attacker sits between you and a server, they can read or alter everything — unless it's authenticated.
cards.detail: In a man-in-the-middle attack, the adversary secretly relays your traffic, posing as the server to you and as you to the server. On open Wi-Fi or a compromised router they can capture passwords and inject content. TLS defeats this by authenticating the server with a certificate and encrypting the channel — so even a relay in the middle sees only scrambled data and can't impersonate the real server without a valid certificate.
cards.deploy: Explains why public Wi-Fi without HTTPS is dangerous and why certificate warnings must never be clicked through.
cards.counter: TLS only helps if certificate checking is sound; 'SSL stripping', fake certificates from a rogue CA, or users who dismiss browser warnings all reopen the door — the maths is strong, the trust decisions around it are the weak point.

quiz.q: TLS stops a man-in-the-middle mainly by…
choices: Hiding your IP
Authenticating the server and encrypting the channel
Blocking Wi-Fi
Speeding up traffic

quiz.q: An attacker on an open Wi-Fi network relays a victim's traffic, pretending to be the bank's server. Which property of TLS prevents the attacker from successfully impersonating the real server?
choices: The server is authenticated with a certificate the attacker cannot forge
The connection is faster than the attacker's relay
The browser hides the URL from the network
The password is stored only on the user's device

quiz.q: What is the name of the attack technique that downgrades or removes the secure HTTPS layer so a victim's connection silently falls back to plain HTTP, reopening a man-in-the-middle position?
Even with strong TLS cryptography, a man-in-the-middle can still succeed in which situation?
choices: The user clicks through a browser certificate warning
The server uses a longer encryption key than the client
The traffic passes through more than one router
The page loads images from a separate domain

cards.title: Denial of service
cards.fact: You don't have to break in to take a service down — just drown it in traffic.
cards.detail: A denial-of-service attack overwhelms a system so real users can't reach it, attacking the 'availability' leg of the CIA triad. A distributed version (DDoS) uses a botnet of thousands of hijacked devices to flood a target from everywhere at once, which makes it hard to block by source. Defences absorb or filter the flood (content-delivery networks, scrubbing services, rate limits) rather than stopping the attackers directly.
cards.deploy: Explains outages that aren't 'hacks' in the data-theft sense, and why big sites sit behind traffic-scrubbing networks.
cards.counter: DDoS is increasingly a smokescreen or extortion tool rather than the goal itself, and the rise of insecure IoT devices (the Mirai botnet) has made huge attacks cheap — defence is now an arms race of capacity, not a one-time fix.

quiz.q: A DDoS attack targets which part of the CIA triad?
choices: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication

quiz.q: A DDoS botnet has 80,000 hijacked devices, and each sends 25 requests per second at the target. How many requests per second does the target receive in total, in millions?
What is the name of the botnet, built largely from insecure internet-connected (IoT) devices, that launched some of the largest DDoS attacks?
Why is a distributed denial-of-service attack much harder to stop by simply blocking the source than a single-machine flood?
choices: The traffic comes from thousands of different hijacked devices at once
It encrypts each request so the source is hidden
It steals data rather than sending traffic
It exploits a software bug in the target's database

cards.title: Buffer overflows and memory safety
cards.fact: Write past the end of a memory buffer and you can overwrite the program's own instructions.
cards.detail: Low-level languages like C let a program write data into a fixed-size block of memory without checking the size. Feed in more than fits and the excess spills into adjacent memory — including, classically, the address the program will jump to next. A crafted overflow can redirect execution into the attacker's own code. It's one of the oldest and most powerful bug classes; modern defences (stack canaries, ASLR, non-executable memory) and memory-safe languages (Rust) blunt it.
cards.deploy: Explains a whole family of severe vulnerabilities and the industry push toward memory-safe languages.
cards.counter: Mitigations raise the bar but get bypassed (return-oriented programming defeats non-executable memory); agencies like the NSA and CISA now argue the real fix is rewriting critical code in memory-safe languages, which is slow and contested for legacy systems.

quiz.q: A buffer overflow lets an attacker overwrite…
choices: The screen
Adjacent memory, including control data
The keyboard
The network

quiz.q: Why is return-oriented programming (ROP) significant as an attack technique?
choices: It defeats non-executable memory by chaining together snippets of code already present in the program
It exploits flaws that exist only in memory-safe languages like Rust
It guesses the random memory layout that ASLR introduces, always succeeding on the first try
It removes the need for an overflow because it edits the program's source code

quiz.q: Which programming language does the card name as memory-safe and promoted as a replacement for C to eliminate buffer overflows?

A program has a 64-byte buffer at the start of its stack frame, immediately followed by an 8-byte saved frame pointer, then the saved return address. An attacker copies 80 bytes of input into the buffer with no bounds checking. How many bytes of that input reach the saved return address or beyond?

cards.title: Zero-days and the exploit market
cards.fact: A zero-day is a flaw the defenders don't yet know about — so there's no patch on day zero.
cards.detail: A zero-day vulnerability is one unknown to the software's maker, giving defenders 'zero days' to have fixed it before attacks begin. Because they're unpatched, they're extremely valuable — there's a market where brokers and governments pay six or seven figures for working exploits. 'Responsible disclosure' asks researchers to tell the vendor and allow time to patch before going public; not everyone does.
cards.deploy: Explains why even fully-updated systems can be breached and why patch speed matters so much.
cards.counter: Governments face a dilemma: stockpiling zero-days for spying leaves everyone exposed, since the same flaw can be found or stolen by others — the NSA's hoarded EternalBlue exploit leaked and powered the 2017 WannaCry ransomware that hit hospitals worldwide.

quiz.q: A 'zero-day' vulnerability is one that…
choices: Was patched today
Is unknown to the vendor, so unpatched
Lasts zero days
Affects no one

quiz.q: Name the NSA-developed exploit that leaked publicly and was then used to power the 2017 WannaCry ransomware outbreak.
A government agency discovers a zero-day in widely used software. Which outcome best illustrates the core danger of stockpiling it rather than reporting it for a patch?
choices: An adversary independently finds or steals the same flaw and uses it against the agency's own citizens
The vendor releases a patch faster than it otherwise would have
The flaw automatically expires after a fixed number of days
Other researchers are legally barred from looking for the same bug

quiz.q: Under 'responsible disclosure', what should a researcher who finds a new vulnerability do first?
choices: Privately notify the software's vendor and give them time to issue a fix before going public
Publish full exploit code immediately so users can defend themselves
Sell the working exploit to the highest-bidding broker
Wait until an attacker uses it in the wild before saying anything

cards.title: Defence in depth
cards.fact: Don't rely on one wall — stack independent layers so a single failure isn't fatal.
cards.detail: Defence in depth assumes any one control will eventually fail, so it layers many: a firewall, then network segmentation, then strong authentication, then least-privilege access (everyone gets the minimum rights they need), then logging and encryption of the data itself. An attacker who slips past one layer still faces the next. The aim isn't perfection at any layer but resilience across all of them.
cards.deploy: The organising principle of real-world security architecture — no single point of failure.
cards.counter: Layers add cost, complexity and friction, and poorly chosen ones give 'security theatre' — the feeling of protection without the substance; more controls aren't automatically more security if they don't address the real risks.

quiz.q: The principle of 'least privilege' means giving each user…
choices: Admin rights
The minimum access they need
No access
Shared accounts

quiz.q: Which design choice best embodies the philosophy of defence in depth?
choices: Layering a firewall, network segmentation, strong authentication, and data encryption so breaching one still leaves others
Investing the entire security budget in one extremely strong perimeter firewall
Granting every employee full administrative rights to avoid access friction
Disabling logging so attackers have nothing to tamper with

quiz.q: What two-word term describes security measures that create a feeling of protection without actually reducing real risk?
A database administrator only needs to read one table to run reports, yet is given full write and delete rights across all databases. Which principle does this violate?
choices: Least privilege
Defence in depth
Responsible disclosure
Network segmentation
