Some veto players are institutional — a president, a second chamber, a constitutional court — and some are partisan, like the parties in a coalition. Using spatial models of bargaining, where each actor has an ideal point in policy space and any change must be preferred by all of them, Tsebelis showed that policy stability rises as you add veto players and as the ideological distance between them grows. He also stressed that the count alone says little; what matters is how the number interacts with the distances between ideal points. This explains why a fragmented coalition or a divided US government produces gridlock, and why systems with few veto players can swing policy sharply. The framework deliberately cuts across the usual labels, letting you compare a presidential system and a parliamentary coalition on the same yardstick.
cards.deploy: Reach for it to predict where reform will stall: count who can say no and how far apart they are, rather than just asking whether a country is presidential or parliamentary.
cards.counter: The theory predicts stability but says little about the direction or quality of policy, and Tsebelis himself concedes that actors' preferences are hard to measure. Ellen Immergut, whose 1990 article and 1992 book on health-care politics introduced the rival language of 'veto points,' argued the blocking opportunities depend on shifting parliamentary majorities and the rules of each decision stage, not on a fixed roster of actors. Critics such as Mark Hallerberg point out that agenda-setting power and informal norms can let a determined government route around nominal veto players, so the same institutional map can yield very different reform records.

quiz.q: According to Tsebelis, policy is hardest to change when…
choices: There is a single strong leader
There are many veto players who are ideologically far apart
The economy is growing
Voters are well informed

quiz.q: A reform must be agreed by a president, a second chamber, a constitutional court, and the three parties of a governing coalition, each able to block change on its own. Counting each as one veto player, how many veto players must agree?
Two parliaments each have exactly three veto players. Tsebelis's framework predicts policy will be harder to change in the parliament where:
choices: the three players' ideal points are far apart ideologically
the three players' ideal points are very close together
one of the three players controls the agenda
the three players belong to the same party

quiz.q: Ellen Immergut introduced a rival concept stressing that blocking opportunities arise from shifting majorities and the rules at each decision stage, not a fixed roster of actors. What two-word term did she use?

cards.title: Bureaucracy
cards.fact: Max Weber described modern bureaucracy as rule-bound, hierarchical and impersonal — powerful precisely because it is predictable, yet hard for politicians to control.
cards.detail: Writing in the late 1910s (the work was published posthumously in 1921-22, after his death in 1920), Weber distinguished rational-legal authority — obeying impersonal rules — from rule by tradition or charisma, and saw bureaucracy as its purest form. Its features are an 'ideal type', a deliberate simplification rather than a snapshot of any real office: a clear hierarchy, fixed jurisdictions, decisions made by written rules and kept in files, officials hired for qualifications and paid salaries, and the separation of the office from the person who holds it, so you obey the post, not the individual. This makes administration calculable, which is why modern states and large firms are built on it. But it concentrates expertise and information in the officials' hands, creating a principal-agent problem: elected politicians (the principals) set goals, while the administrators (the agents) who carry them out know more and may quietly pursue their own ends, so steering them is genuinely hard. Weber also feared this efficiency could harden into an 'iron cage' (Talcott Parsons' rendering of Weber's stahlhartes Gehäuse) that even rulers cannot escape.
cards.deploy: Use it to see why a newly elected minister cannot just snap their fingers and change a department, and why sluggish or unresponsive agencies are partly a structural feature — concentrated expertise, fixed rules, career officials who outlast ministers — and not simply sabotage by a hostile 'deep state'.
cards.counter: Weber's bureaucracy is an ideal type, and named critics pull against it from different directions. Robert Merton ('Bureaucratic Structure and Personality', 1940) argued rules produce 'goal displacement', where obeying the rule becomes the goal and the actual purpose suffers. Michael Lipsky (Street-Level Bureaucracy, 1980) found that front-line staff — teachers, police, caseworkers — exercise wide discretion the hierarchy never sees, so policy is really made at the counter. William Niskanen (Bureaucracy and Representative Government, 1971) claimed agencies systematically over-expand their budgets; but Patrick Dunleavy's bureau-shaping model (1991) counters that senior officials prefer interesting, low-conflict work over raw budget size, so the budget-maximizing claim is overstated. From a feminist and anarchist angle, Kathy Ferguson (The Feminist Case Against Bureaucracy, 1984) rejects the whole frame: bureaucracy is not a neutral tool that occasionally malfunctions but a structure of domination that subordinates clients and officials alike, which adding women to management will not fix.

quiz.q: For Weber, what makes bureaucratic authority 'rational-legal'?
choices: Officials are obeyed personally because of their charisma
Authority rests on impersonal rules attached to offices, not on the person
Decisions are handed down by tradition over generations
Officials are elected by the public

quiz.q: A clerk processing a benefits claim follows the written rule so rigidly that an obviously deserving applicant is rejected on a technicality, defeating the program's purpose. Which named critique best describes this?
choices: Robert Merton's 'goal displacement'
Weber's 'iron cage'
Niskanen's budget maximization
Lipsky's street-level discretion

quiz.q: In the relationship where elected politicians set goals but better-informed career officials carry them out and may pursue their own ends, what is the standard two-word name for this control problem?
Against Niskanen's claim that agencies always try to maximize their budgets, Patrick Dunleavy's bureau-shaping model argues senior officials instead prefer:
choices: interesting, low-conflict work over raw budget size
the largest possible staff regardless of the work
to abolish their own agency to gain promotion
strict obedience to traditional authority over rules

cards.title: The rule of law
cards.fact: The rule of law means the government itself is bound by law applied equally and predictably — not just that it uses law to control everyone else.
cards.detail: The key contrast is with 'rule by law', where rulers use law as a tool to command subjects but stand above it themselves; the rule of law instead subjects the rulers to the same general, public, stable rules as everyone, enforced by independent courts. Theorists split it into two conceptions. A thin or formal/procedural conception asks only about form: are laws clear, public, prospective, consistent and impartially applied? Lon Fuller's eight principles (his 'inner morality of law') and Joseph Raz's account both sit here — though they disagree on whether meeting those formal demands is itself a moral achievement (Fuller) or just the law working efficiently as an instrument (Raz). On the thin view even a harsh regime can satisfy the rule of law if it follows its own rules. A thick or substantive conception adds content: the laws must also protect basic rights and human dignity, so a regime that lawfully oppresses (Arthur Chaskalson and Tom Bingham cite apartheid South Africa) fails the test. The thin version is more neutral and easier to agree on; the thick version captures more of what people want but builds in contested claims about which rights count.
cards.deploy: Use the thin/thick distinction to cut through debates about authoritarian states that have 'lots of law': they may score well on procedure while failing any rights-based test.
cards.counter: Joseph Raz defends the thin view, warning that loading every good thing (democracy, rights, social justice) into the rule of law empties the phrase of distinct meaning — for him it is 'just one of the virtues' a legal system can have. From the left, the Marxist historian E.P. Thompson (in Whigs and Hunters, 1975) and the critical legal studies movement note the ideal can mask power: equal rules can still entrench unequal property and class relations — yet Thompson still judged it 'an unqualified human good' worth defending. Postcolonial critics add a further angle: rule-of-law language was used to legitimise colonial administration, so its export today can carry the same imperial baggage.

quiz.q: What is the central difference between 'rule of law' and 'rule by law'?
choices: Rule of law requires a written constitution; rule by law does not
Under rule of law the government itself is bound by the law; under rule by law the rulers stand above it
Rule by law applies only in democracies
There is no real difference; the terms are synonyms

quiz.q: An authoritarian state enacts harsh laws that are clear, public, applied consistently in advance, and enforced by courts that follow them faithfully. Under a thin (formal) conception of the rule of law, this regime:
choices: can satisfy the rule of law despite the laws being oppressive
automatically fails because the laws are harsh
fails only because it lacks independent courts
satisfies it only if the laws also protect human dignity

quiz.q: Which legal theorist set out eight principles he called the 'inner morality of law' (laws must be clear, public, prospective, consistent, and so on)?
A state where rulers stand above the legal commands they issue to their subjects, using law purely as a tool of control, exemplifies:
choices: rule by law
the rule of law
a thick conception of the rule of law
subsidiarity

cards.title: The left–right spectrum
cards.fact: 'Left' and 'right' come from where deputies sat in France's 1789 National Assembly — supporters of revolution to the president's left, defenders of the old order to his right.
cards.detail: In 1789 the National Assembly debated how much power to leave the king — chiefly whether he should keep an absolute veto. Deputies who wanted to limit the monarchy and push change sat to the president's left; those loyal to the king and the old regime sat to his right. The deputy Baron de Gauville recorded that royalists took the right "to avoid the shouts" from the other side. The seating label stuck and spread worldwide. Three ideological families are usually placed along the line. Liberalism (rooted in John Locke) prizes individual liberty and limits on state power. Conservatism (whose founding figure is conventionally Edmund Burke, though some historians dispute the label) prizes order, tradition and gradual change, distrusting grand redesigns of society. Socialism (Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and many earlier figures) prizes equality and collective provision, willing to use state power to redress economic inequality. Roughly, the left favours equality and change while the right favours order and tradition — but compressing every political belief onto one line is a simplification, because it cannot separate economic views from social ones.
cards.deploy: Use it as quick shorthand, but watch its limits: a libertarian (economically 'right', socially permissive) or a religious socialist breaks the single line, which is why analysts often add a second axis.
cards.counter: The libertarian activist David Nolan — a co-founder of the US Libertarian Party, not a political scientist — popularised a two-axis 'Nolan chart' (1969) splitting economic freedom from personal freedom, arguing the single line hides where libertarians and authoritarians actually stand. Political scientists more broadly have long held that one axis is too crude to capture the real range of beliefs. And cross-national work like the World Values Survey finds that what counts as 'left' or 'right' shifts sharply across countries and eras, so the labels — born in revolutionary France — travel poorly outside that original European context.

quiz.q: Where do the political terms 'left' and 'right' originate?
choices: From the seating in France's 1789 National Assembly
From the layout of the British House of Commons
From Karl Marx's writings
From the US Constitution

quiz.q: A voter wants minimal economic regulation and low taxes but also strongly favours legalising drugs and same-sex marriage. Why is this person hard to place on a single left-right line?
choices: Their economically 'right' and socially permissive positions pull toward opposite ends of one axis, so a single line cannot represent both at once
They hold no consistent positions, so no point on the line applies
The left-right line only measures social issues, never economic ones
They must be centrist, since the two views average out to the middle

quiz.q: Which two-axis diagram, popularised by Libertarian Party co-founder David Nolan in 1969, separates economic freedom from personal freedom to fix the single line's limits?
Of the three ideological families usually placed on the spectrum, which one prizes order, tradition and gradual change while distrusting grand redesigns of society?
choices: Conservatism, associated with Edmund Burke
Liberalism, associated with John Locke
Socialism, associated with Karl Marx
Libertarianism, associated with David Nolan

cards.title: Nationalism
cards.fact: Modernist theorists argue nationalism is a recent invention that creates nations, not an ancient bond that nations naturally express.
cards.detail: A nation is a large group that imagines itself a single people deserving its own state. Benedict Anderson, in Imagined Communities (1983), called nations "imagined communities": members will never meet most of their compatriots, yet feel deep kinship, a feeling he tied to print capitalism and mass vernacular literacy that let strangers picture themselves as one public. Ernest Gellner (Nations and Nationalism, 1983) pushed the modernist claim further: industrial society needs a mobile, literate workforce sharing one standardised culture, so nationalism is a product of modernity that manufactures nations, rather than nations giving rise to nationalism. Against this, Anthony D. Smith's ethnosymbolism (The Ethnic Origins of Nations, 1986) argues modern nations did not appear from nowhere — they grow from older ethnic cores ("ethnies") with shared myths, memories and symbols, so the modern nation reworks genuinely old material. The debate is essentially about timing and roots: invented yesterday, or built on something ancient?
cards.deploy: Use it to read separatist and unification movements: ask whether a group's national identity is being newly constructed (Gellner/Anderson) or revived from deep ethnic memory (Smith), since each implies different politics.
cards.counter: Primordialists (the position Clifford Geertz described and Smith critiqued) hold that ethnic attachments are far older and more visceral than the modernists allow. Anthony D. Smith's ethnosymbolism is the disciplined middle position. From a postcolonial angle, Partha Chatterjee (The Nation and Its Fragments, 1993; his essay "Whose Imagined Community?") objects that Anderson's "modular" forms treat European and American nationalism as the template the colonised world merely borrows, leaving it "nothing left to imagine" — and misses how anticolonial nationalism first claims a sovereign spiritual or cultural domain of its own before the political fight.

quiz.q: What is the central claim of the modernist view of nationalism (Gellner, Anderson)?
choices: Nations are ancient and biologically rooted
Nationalism is a modern phenomenon that creates nations, rather than the reverse
Nationalism is always harmful
Every ethnic group inevitably becomes a nation

quiz.q: An analyst studying a separatist movement argues that its national identity grew from an older ethnic core of shared myths, memories and symbols that the modern movement reworks. Whose theory does this reflect?
choices: Anthony D. Smith's ethnosymbolism
Ernest Gellner's modernism
Benedict Anderson's print-capitalism account
Cas Mudde's thin-ideology framework

quiz.q: What two-word phrase did Benedict Anderson coin for a nation whose members feel deep kinship though they will never meet most of their compatriots?
Ernest Gellner claimed industrial society needs a mobile, literate workforce sharing one standardised culture. What conclusion did he draw about nations and nationalism?
choices: Nationalism is a product of modernity that manufactures nations, rather than nations giving rise to nationalism
Nations are ancient bonds that naturally produce nationalism once industry arrives
Nationalism and nations both arose simultaneously from ancient ethnic cores
Industrial society dissolves nationalism by making cultures interchangeable

cards.title: Populism
cards.fact: Populism is a 'thin' ideology that splits society into 'the pure people' against 'the corrupt elite', and says politics should enact the people's will.
cards.detail: Cas Mudde defines populism as a 'thin-centred ideology' that divides society into two morally opposed, homogeneous camps — 'the pure people' versus 'the corrupt elite' — and holds that politics should express 'the general will' of the people. 'Thin' means it carries no full programme of its own, so it attaches to a fuller 'host' ideology: paired with nationalism and anti-immigration on the right (Marine Le Pen, Donald Trump), or with anti-austerity and redistribution on the left (Hugo Chavez, Spain's Podemos). What unites them is the anti-elite, 'us versus them' frame, not a shared policy package. Because populists claim to be the sole voice of a unified people, Mudde and co-authors (e.g. Cristobal Rovira Kaltwasser) argue they are ambivalent toward democracy: they champion popular sovereignty and majority rule, yet often attack the checks — courts, an independent press, minority rights — that liberal democracy uses to restrain majorities.
cards.deploy: Lets you classify a movement by its frame ('people vs elite') rather than its policies, and see why left and right populists can look alike structurally while pushing opposite agendas.
cards.counter: Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe reject the ideational view. In their Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985), and Laclau's On Populist Reason (2005), populism is not a thin ideology but a 'logic' of politics: 'a people' is constructed by linking many unmet demands into a shared chain held together by an 'empty signifier'. They treat populism as a healthy democratic resource for contesting entrenched power, not a pathology — and charge that Mudde's framework quietly defends the liberal status quo. Latin American scholars such as Carlos de la Torre push back on the implicit Western frame too, noting that populism there (e.g. Peronism) has often been inclusionary, extending rights and recognition to previously excluded poor and indigenous majorities, not simply a threat to democracy.

quiz.q: In Cas Mudde's definition, what makes populism a 'thin-centred' ideology?
choices: It appeals only to a thin slice of the electorate
It has no full programme of its own and attaches to a fuller 'host' ideology
It is held only weakly by its followers
It avoids taking any position on the economy

quiz.q: Under Cas Mudde's definition, why can a right-wing anti-immigration party and a left-wing anti-austerity party both count as populist despite opposite agendas?
choices: They share the 'pure people versus corrupt elite' frame, while their differing policies come from the fuller host ideology each attaches to
They both reject popular sovereignty and majority rule
Populism requires a complete policy programme that happens to be identical for left and right
They both define 'the people' as a small, internally divided minority

quiz.q: In Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe's theory, what term names the element that links many unmet demands into a single shared chain?
Mudde and Rovira Kaltwasser call populists 'ambivalent' toward democracy because populists tend to:
choices: Champion popular sovereignty and majority rule yet attack the checks like courts, an independent press, and minority rights
Reject elections entirely in favour of rule by experts
Defend independent courts and minority rights against the majority
Abandon the claim to speak for the people in favour of pluralism

cards.title: Social movements
cards.fact: Movements turn grievance into sustained action through resources, political openings, and shared 'repertoires' of protest — not raw discontent alone.
cards.detail: A social movement is sustained, organised collective action by people outside formal power pushing for (or against) change. The puzzle is that grievances are everywhere but movements are rare, so theory asks what converts discontent into durable mobilisation. The resource-mobilization school (sociologists John McCarthy and Mayer Zald) argues movements need resources — money, members, organisations, media access, leadership — and that the supply of resources matters more than the level of grievance. Political-process theory (Doug McAdam, Sidney Tarrow) adds 'political opportunity structures': movements surge when the system opens up, through elite splits, new allies, or weakened repression. Charles Tilly contributes the 'repertoire of contention' — the limited menu of protest forms a society knows how to perform at a given time (the petition, the strike, the demonstration, the boycott), which actors draw on and slowly modify rather than inventing afresh.
cards.deploy: Explains why a movement erupts in one moment and not another: look for new resources or a political opening, and read its tactics as drawn from an inherited repertoire.
cards.counter: Cultural and 'new social movement' theorists such as Alberto Melucci and Francesca Polletta argue the resource/opportunity approach explains the 'how' of mobilization better than the 'why'. By treating interests as given and structural, it sidelines collective identity, emotion, meaning and the framing work by which people come to see a situation as unjust and themselves as the ones to fix it — the very things that motivate participation. Melucci makes collective identity, not resources, the central variable.

quiz.q: What does Charles Tilly's 'repertoire of contention' refer to?
choices: The list of demands a movement issues to the state
The limited menu of protest forms a society knows how to perform at a given time
The financial resources available to a movement
The set of allies a movement recruits among elites

quiz.q: A long-standing grievance suddenly sparks a major movement after a split appears among governing elites and a powerful new ally emerges. Which theory best explains this timing?
choices: Political-process theory, which credits political opportunity structures opening up
Resource-mobilization theory, which credits a rise in raw discontent
Ethnosymbolism, which credits revived ethnic memory
Primordialism, which credits ancient visceral attachments

quiz.q: What term did Charles Tilly use for the limited menu of protest forms (petition, strike, demonstration, boycott) a society knows how to perform at a given time?
Resource-mobilization theorists John McCarthy and Mayer Zald argue that what factor matters more than the level of grievance in producing a movement?
choices: The supply of resources such as money, members, organisations, media access and leadership
The depth of collective identity and shared emotion
The antiquity of the group's ethnic core
The number of unmet demands linked by an empty signifier

cards.title: Theories of revolution
cards.fact: Theda Skocpol argues social revolutions come from state breakdown plus peasant capacity to revolt — structures, not ideology — against the deprivation tradition that roots revolt in a rising-then-thwarted sense of frustration.
cards.detail: Why do revolutions happen? One tradition locates the cause in mass psychology. James C. Davies' 'J-curve' (in 'Toward a Theory of Revolution', 1962) holds that revolt erupts not in steady misery but when a long rise in expectations is suddenly reversed, opening an unbearable gap between what people expect and what they get; Ted Robert Gurr generalised this as 'relative deprivation' in 'Why Men Rebel' (1970) — rebellion tracks the felt gap between expectation and attainment. In 'States and Social Revolutions' (1979), Theda Skocpol mounts a structural counter-argument built on France (1789), Russia (1917) and China (1911 onward). Quoting Wendell Phillips, she insists revolutions 'are not made; they come': they require two structural conditions to coincide, neither of which anyone wills. First, the old regime's state breaks down — typically under international military and fiscal pressure it cannot meet, often blocked by a landed upper class. Second, peasants must have the autonomous community organisation and capacity to revolt once central control slips. Ideology and revolutionary intent, for Skocpol, are not the engine; they ride on structural openings.
cards.deploy: Gives you rival lenses for any uprising: ask whether expectations recently outran reality (deprivation, Davies/Gurr), whether the state was already cracking and society could exploit it (structural, Skocpol), or why individuals chose to join once revolt looked likely to win (Kuran's cascades).
cards.counter: Skocpol's structuralism drew sharp named replies. William H. Sewell Jr. argued she wrongly demotes ideology and culture, which do real causal work in the French Revolution rather than just decorating structural shifts (Skocpol answered him in 'Social Revolutions in the Modern World', 1994). Rational-choice scholars such as Timur Kuran stress individual decisions, preference falsification and information cascades — why a person joins once a revolt looks likely to win, and why the 1989 collapses surprised everyone — which a purely structural account leaves dark.

quiz.q: What two conditions must coincide for a social revolution, in Theda Skocpol's account?
choices: A charismatic leader and a unifying ideology
State breakdown and peasant capacity to revolt
Economic growth and an expanding middle class
Foreign invasion and religious schism

quiz.q: A country sees two decades of rising living standards, then a sudden sharp economic reversal, and protests erupt soon after. Which theorist's account best fits this pattern?
choices: James C. Davies' J-curve, where revolt follows a rapid reversal after a long rise in expectations
Theda Skocpol's structural account, since the state had clearly broken down
Timur Kuran's cascades, since preference falsification had ended
Wendell Phillips' view that revolutions 'are not made; they come'

quiz.q: How many primary cases did Skocpol build her structural argument on in 'States and Social Revolutions' (France, Russia and China)?
What did Ted Robert Gurr call his generalisation that rebellion tracks the felt gap between what people expect and what they actually get?

cards.title: Clientelism
cards.fact: Clientelism trades material favours — jobs, cash, services — for votes and loyalty, distributing benefits to supporters rather than by public policy.
cards.detail: Clientelism is politics run as an exchange: a patron (a politician, party or 'boss') gives clients material goods — public jobs, cash, food, building permits, help with the bureaucracy — and in return clients deliver votes and support. The relationship is asymmetric (patron above client), often mediated by 'brokers' who know the neighbourhood, and it is iterated and contingent: you keep getting benefits as long as you keep delivering, and can be cut off if you don't. Classic 'machine politics' — the patronage machines of 19th-century US cities, or party machines across Latin America, southern Italy and parts of Africa and Asia — runs on exactly this logic. The contrast, as political scientists Herbert Kitschelt and Steven Wilkinson frame it, is programmatic politics, where benefits flow by public, formalised rules (a pension everyone over 65 receives) regardless of how you voted. Clientelism tends to thrive where the state is weak, poverty makes small payments decisive, and parties can monitor or credibly enforce the bargain; it is corrosive of democratic accountability because it rewards loyalty over good policy.
cards.deploy: Lets you read a party that wins through favours and patronage networks rather than its platform, and explains why anti-poverty 'programmatic' reforms (universal transfers) are partly attempts to break clientelist machines.
cards.counter: Javier Auyero, in his study of Peronist survival networks in Argentina (Poor People's Politics, 2000), warns against the elite reflex of dismissing clientelism as mere vote-buying by ignorant poor: seen from the clients' side it can be a rational survival strategy and a real, reciprocal social relationship, not just a cash-for-vote trade. Susan Stokes adds a structural caveat: because the secret ballot hides how people actually vote, machines face a commitment problem and work best only where they can monitor voters — dense small towns and tight social networks — so the coercive 'perverse accountability' she models is conditional on surveillance, not automatic.

quiz.q: How does clientelism differ from programmatic politics?
choices: Clientelism uses public, rule-based benefits; programmatic politics uses favours
Clientelism trades targeted material favours for support; programmatic politics distributes benefits by public rules regardless of vote
Clientelism happens only in dictatorships; programmatic politics only in democracies
There is no real difference between the two

quiz.q: A national pension that every resident over 65 receives, regardless of which party they voted for, is an example of:
choices: programmatic politics, where benefits flow by formal public rules
clientelism, because the state distributes a material benefit
brokerage, because an intermediary delivers the benefit
perverse accountability, because voters are being monitored

quiz.q: In clientelist machines, what is the term for the local intermediary who knows the neighborhood and links patrons to clients?
Susan Stokes argues machines face a commitment problem because the secret ballot hides votes. Which condition does this imply machines need to make the bargain work?
choices: the ability to monitor voters, as in dense small towns and tight social networks
a strong, well-funded central state bureaucracy
a population that is generally wealthy and policy-oriented
formal, universal rules that apply to all citizens equally

cards.title: Political culture and social capital
cards.fact: A line from Almond & Verba to Putnam argues that citizens' shared attitudes — trust, civic engagement, dense association — are what make democracy work.
cards.detail: Political culture means the pattern of attitudes, beliefs and habits citizens hold toward politics. In 'The Civic Culture' (1963), Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba surveyed five countries and sorted orientations into three types: 'parochial' (barely aware of national politics), 'subject' (aware but passive, expecting things to be done to them), and 'participant' (active, expecting to help shape outcomes). Stable democracy, they argued, rests on a mixed 'civic culture' that blends participation with enough deference and trust to keep the system manageable. Robert Putnam pushed this into 'social capital' — the networks, norms of reciprocity and trust generated by people associating. In 'Making Democracy Work' (1993) he traced the better performance of northern and central over southern Italian regional governments to centuries of denser horizontal civic association; in 'Bowling Alone' (2000) he argued American social capital was eroding as people withdrew into private life. The through-line: self-governance depends less on formal institutions than on whether citizens trust and join with one another.
cards.deploy: Offers a cultural explanation for why two countries with identical constitutions can have very different democratic quality, and frames worries about declining trust and civic membership.
cards.counter: Critics attack the causal arrow and what it hides. Sidney Tarrow (American Political Science Review, 1996) argued Putnam reverses cause and effect: over centuries it may be institutions that built civic culture, not the other way round, and the historical reconstruction is hard to test. Carole Pateman, in 'Participation and Democratic Theory' (1970), argued the civic-culture tradition treats passive deference as healthy and quietly takes Anglo-American norms as the democratic ideal. Feminist scholars such as Vivien Lowndes show Putnam's measures are gendered — counting formal club membership while ignoring the informal care and community networks women generate — so that inequality and power, not a thin stock of 'trust', shape who counts as civically engaged.

quiz.q: In Almond and Verba's 'The Civic Culture', a 'participant' orientation describes citizens who…
choices: are barely aware of national politics
are aware of politics but passively expect things to be done to them
are active and expect to help shape political outcomes
reject the political system entirely

quiz.q: In 'The Civic Culture', Almond and Verba sorted citizens' political orientations into how many basic types?

A citizen is aware of national policies and feels their effects but expects nothing from getting involved and never tries to shape outcomes. Which orientation, in Almond and Verba's scheme, does this describe?
choices: subject
parochial
participant
civic

quiz.q: What is the term Robert Putnam uses for the networks, norms of reciprocity, and trust that people generate by associating with one another?

cards.title: Civil society
cards.fact: Civil society is the space of voluntary association between the state and the family — clubs, unions, churches, NGOs — where citizens organise on their own.
cards.detail: Civil society names the realm of organised life that is neither the state nor the household: voluntary associations people form themselves — sports clubs, trade unions, churches, charities, professional bodies, NGOs, neighbourhood groups. Watching 1830s America for 'Democracy in America' (1835/1840), Alexis de Tocqueville argued such associations are a school of democracy: by joining together for shared purposes, citizens learn cooperation and self-rule and build a counterweight to an overbearing state, guarding against the 'tyranny of the majority'. Jurgen Habermas adds a different strand — the 'public sphere' (from 'The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere', 1962): the arena (coffee houses, the press, now online forums) where private citizens come together to debate public matters and form public opinion through reasoned argument, which can then hold power to account. Robert Putnam's 'Bowling Alone' (2000) carries the Tocquevillean line into modern survey data, treating dense membership as 'social capital' that makes democracy work. All three treat civil society as a foundation for democratic life: a space where people build the trust, skills and collective voice that self-government needs.
cards.deploy: Gives you the middle layer between citizen and state, so you can ask whether a country's associations are dense and independent — a standard yardstick for democratic health and a first target of authoritarian crackdowns.
cards.counter: The benign picture has named critics. Sheri Berman ('Civil Society and the Collapse of the Weimar Republic', World Politics, 1997) showed that Weimar Germany had unusually dense civic associations, yet weak parties and a discredited state let those networks feed the Nazi rise rather than democracy — so association is not automatically pro-democratic. Antonio Gramsci instead split the capitalist order into 'political society' (the coercive state — army, police, courts) and 'civil society' (schools, churches, press, unions), where the ruling class wins 'hegemony', consent to its own dominance; civil society is a terrain of class struggle, not a neutral good. And the very category is a contested liberal export: scholars such as Partha Chatterjee argue it fits a narrow Western associational model and ignores the 'political society' of the postcolonial poor, who bargain with the state outside formal civic forms.

quiz.q: Civil society is best described as…
choices: the elected branches of the state
the space of voluntary association between the state and the family
the private market economy
the household and extended family

quiz.q: A new club for retired engineers, a parish church, and a neighborhood watch group all fall into which category, defined as the space between the state and the household?
choices: civil society
the public sphere
political society
the household economy

quiz.q: Which thinker used the term 'public sphere' for the arena — coffee houses, the press — where private citizens debate public matters and form opinion through reasoned argument?
Sheri Berman's study of Weimar Germany undercuts which assumption about civil society?
choices: that a dense web of civic associations is automatically good for democracy
that civil society is distinct from the family and the state
that voluntary associations teach citizens cooperation
that the public sphere depends on a free press

cards.title: Knowledge as justified true belief
cards.fact: On the classical analysis, you know something only if you believe it, it is true, and you are justified in believing it.
cards.detail: The idea traces to Plato's dialogue Theaetetus, where Socrates and Theaetetus test whether knowledge is 'true belief with an account (logos)' — though the dialogue ends in aporia, rejecting that definition rather than endorsing it. The modern slogan breaks knowledge into three conditions. Belief: you have to actually accept the claim — you can't know what you don't even think is so. Truth: a belief can't count as knowledge if it's false, however confident you are. Justification: a lucky true guess isn't knowledge; you need good reasons, evidence, or grounds for holding it. The point of the third condition is to rule out beliefs that just happen to be right. So 'the Earth is round' is knowledge for you only if it's true, you believe it, AND you have grounds (you've seen the evidence) rather than a coin-flip hunch.
cards.deploy: A clean three-part checklist for pressing any knowledge claim: is it actually true, do you really believe it, and what are your grounds?
cards.counter: Edmund Gettier (1963) showed all three conditions can be met without knowledge, when a justified belief is true only by luck. Timothy Williamson's 'knowledge-first' program goes further, arguing knowledge is a basic mental state that can't be built up from belief plus extra conditions at all. The tripartite analysis is also not uniquely Western: classical Indian Nyaya epistemology, systematized by Gangesa (14th c.), defines knowledge as cognition produced by a reliable source (pramana) and likewise rules out accidentally-true belief — locating the same anti-luck worry in a different framework. Per the SEP, no analysis of knowledge is widely accepted, so JTB is a contested starting point, not a settled definition.

quiz.q: On the classical 'justified true belief' analysis, which is NOT one of the three required conditions for knowledge?
choices: The proposition is true
You believe the proposition
You are certain beyond all possible doubt
You are justified in believing it

quiz.q: A weather forecaster flips a coin, predicts rain tomorrow, and it does rain. On the classical justified-true-belief analysis, why does this fail to count as knowledge?
choices: The belief is true and held, but lacks justification — there were no good grounds, just a lucky guess
The belief is justified and held, but turned out false
The belief is justified and true, but was never actually held
All three conditions are met, so it does count as knowledge

quiz.q: Which Platonic dialogue first tests the idea that knowledge is 'true belief with an account (logos)', though it ends without endorsing that definition?
In 14th-century classical Indian Nyaya epistemology, systematized by Gangesa, what is the term for a reliable source of cognition that, like justification, rules out accidentally-true belief?

cards.title: The Gettier problem
cards.fact: Edmund Gettier showed you can have a justified true belief that still isn't knowledge, because its truth is a matter of luck.
cards.detail: In a three-page 1963 paper, Edmund Gettier built cases where the belief, truth and justification conditions are all met yet we balk at calling it knowledge. In his Case I, Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get a job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, so Smith infers 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'. As it happens, Smith himself gets the job, and Smith too has ten coins in his pocket without realising it. Smith's inferred belief is true and was well justified, but it is true by accident: his justification ran through Jones, not through the man (himself) who made it true. The lesson is that justification can be disconnected from what makes the belief true, so justified-true-belief is not sufficient for knowledge. This launched decades of attempts to add a fourth condition that screens out luck.
cards.deploy: A precise tool for spotting 'right answer, wrong reasons' — cases where someone lands on the truth by accident, not by their evidence actually tracking it.
cards.counter: Whether the cases sink JTB is itself disputed. Linda Zagzebski (1994, 'The Inescapability of Gettier Problems') argues that any analysis allowing justification to fall short of guaranteeing truth will face such cases, so the fix must be structural, not a patch. On how universal the reaction is, the experimental-philosophy work of Weinberg, Nichols and Stich (2001) reported that intuitions about Gettier cases varied across cultures and groups, casting doubt on the 'we wouldn't call it knowledge' response — but later attempts to replicate them mostly failed, and the large cross-cultural study by Machery, Stich and colleagues (2017, 'Gettier Across Cultures', testing Brazil, India, Japan and the USA) found the core Gettier intuition fairly robust.

quiz.q: What do Gettier cases demonstrate?
choices: That true beliefs are always justified
That a belief can be justified and true yet fail to be knowledge
That nothing can ever be known
That justification is unnecessary for knowledge

quiz.q: Take the year Edmund Gettier's paper appeared and add the number of conditions in the classical justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge. What total do you get?
You glance at a stopped clock reading 3:00, form the belief 'it is 3:00', and it happens to actually be 3:00. Why is this a Gettier-style case rather than knowledge?
choices: Your belief is justified and true, but true only by luck — your grounds (the clock) didn't track the time that made it correct
Your belief is false, so it cannot be knowledge
You never genuinely believed it was 3:00
You had no justification at all for reading the time off a clock

quiz.q: Which philosopher argued in 1994 that any analysis allowing justification to fall short of guaranteeing truth will inevitably face Gettier-type cases, so the fix must be structural?

cards.title: Reliabilism
cards.fact: On Alvin Goldman's reliabilism, a belief is justified if it was produced by a reliable process — whether or not you can spell out your reasons.
cards.detail: Goldman's 1979 paper 'What Is Justified Belief?' proposed that justification depends on the track record of the cognitive process that formed the belief: perception, memory, and good inference tend to produce true beliefs, while wishful thinking and guessing don't. This is a form of EXTERNALISM — the thing that makes your belief justified (the process's reliability) is a fact about the world, and you needn't have any access to it. A child or an animal can have justified beliefs just by perceiving well, even with no story to tell about why. This contrasts with INTERNALISM — the position of evidentialists like Earl Conee and Richard Feldman — on which justification must consist of factors you could in principle become aware of by reflection: your evidence and reasons, accessible 'from the inside'. Reliabilism also offers a Gettier diagnosis: lucky true beliefs often come from unreliable or accidentally-right processes.
cards.deploy: A way to credit knowledge that can't be articulated — the expert's snap judgement or trained perception — by asking 'is the process that produced this belief actually reliable?' rather than 'can you justify it in words?'
cards.counter: Laurence BonJour's clairvoyant case is the famous counterexample: imagine Norman, a reliable clairvoyant who has no evidence he has the power and no reason to trust the resulting belief — reliabilism says he's justified, but intuitively he isn't. There's also the 'generality problem' (anticipated by Goldman and pressed by Richard Feldman and by Conee and Feldman): any belief is produced by a process describable at many levels of generality, some reliable and some not, and reliabilism gives no principled way to pick the relevant one.

quiz.q: What does Goldman's reliabilism say makes a belief justified?
choices: That you can articulate good reasons for it from the inside
That it was produced by a reliable belief-forming process
That it coheres with all your other beliefs
That it feels certain to the believer

quiz.q: An experienced radiologist instantly senses a scan looks abnormal but cannot articulate why, and is reliably correct. How does reliabilism, unlike internalist evidentialism, treat this belief?
choices: Justified, because it was produced by a reliable process, regardless of whether reasons can be stated
Unjustified, because the radiologist cannot give accessible reasons on reflection
Justified only if the radiologist can later reconstruct the evidence in words
Neither justified nor unjustified, since trained perception falls outside epistemology

quiz.q: What is the name of Laurence BonJour's counterexample to reliabilism, featuring a reliable clairvoyant named Norman who has no reason to trust his power?
What is the name of the objection that any belief is produced by a process describable at many levels of generality, leaving reliabilism without a principled way to pick the relevant one?

cards.title: Skepticism
cards.fact: If a perfect deception would feel exactly like reality, the skeptic asks how you could ever know you aren't being deceived.
cards.detail: In his First Meditation (1641), René Descartes imagined an 'evil demon' bent on deceiving him about everything — the external world, his own body, even simple arithmetic. The modern update is the 'brain in a vat': a brain kept alive and fed electrical signals that perfectly simulate ordinary life. The argument runs: if you can't tell the difference between the real world and the deception, then you don't know you're in the real one; and since you can't rule the deception out, you don't really know the everyday things you take for granted. This isn't idle paradox — Descartes used radical doubt as a method to find something indubitable to build knowledge on, and skeptical hypotheses set the agenda for what any theory of knowledge has to answer.
cards.deploy: A stress test for confidence: ask what would look the same whether a claim were true or false — if nothing distinguishes them, your grounds are thinner than they feel.
cards.counter: Descartes thought he defeated the demon (via the cogito and a non-deceiving God), but later philosophers answer differently. G. E. Moore simply insisted his knowledge that 'here is a hand' is more certain than any skeptical premise, so the argument should be run in reverse. Hilary Putnam argued from semantic externalism that 'I am a brain in a vat' is self-refuting — a vat-brain's words couldn't refer to real vats. And the ancient Pyrrhonists (Sextus Empiricus) treated skepticism not as a problem to solve but as a way of life: suspend judgement (epoché) and gain tranquillity (ataraxia).

quiz.q: What is the core move in Cartesian skeptical arguments like the evil demon or brain-in-a-vat?
choices: Proving that the external world does not exist
Showing that a perfect deception would be indistinguishable from reality, so you can't rule it out
Demonstrating that all beliefs are false
Arguing that knowledge requires no justification

quiz.q: In his First Meditation, what figure does René Descartes imagine as bent on deceiving him about the external world, his body, and even arithmetic?
A skeptic claims you can't know you have hands. G. E. Moore's response was to:
choices: Insist his knowledge that 'here is a hand' is more certain than any skeptical premise, so the argument should run in reverse
Argue that a deceived brain's words could not refer to real hands, making the hypothesis self-refuting
Suspend judgement entirely and seek tranquillity rather than answer the skeptic
Prove the existence of a non-deceiving God who guarantees his perceptions

quiz.q: In Pyrrhonist skepticism, what is the Greek term for the suspension of judgement that is meant to lead to tranquillity (ataraxia)?

cards.title: Rationalism vs empiricism
cards.fact: Rationalists say some substantive knowledge comes from reason alone; empiricists say all of it ultimately traces back to the senses.
cards.detail: The dispute is about the SOURCE of substantive knowledge. The rationalists usually grouped together — Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz — hold that reason can deliver truths about the world independently of experience, often via innate ideas the mind brings with it. In his New Essays (written 1704, published 1765), Leibniz answered Locke's 'blank slate' with the image of a veined block of marble: experience reveals a structure already latent in the mind. The empiricists usually paired against them — Locke, Berkeley and Hume — deny innate content; Locke's Essay (1689) argues the mind starts as a tabula rasa and every idea is built from sensation or reflection. Hume sharpened this: ideas are faded copies of impressions, so any concept that can't be traced to an impression (he targeted causation and the self) is suspect. The clash sets up Kant's later attempt to synthesise the two.
cards.deploy: A lens for any debate about where a belief comes from: is the claim being defended by appeal to what we can observe, or by appeal to what reason or 'common sense' supposedly delivers on its own?
cards.counter: The neat 'Continental rationalists vs British empiricists' textbook split is itself contested. Markie and Folescu's SEP entry warns that the labels oversimplify: the real disagreements are over specific theses (innate knowledge, innate concepts, a priori knowledge of the world), almost no thinker falls cleanly into one camp, and figures like Hobbes, Berkeley, Anne Conway, Émilie du Châtelet and Mary Shepherd resist the grouping. Kant argued both camps were half-right: knowledge requires sensory content AND the mind's own organising categories, so neither reason alone nor experience alone suffices. W. V. O. Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) later attacked the analytic/synthetic distinction that much of the a priori side leaned on.

quiz.q: What is the central disagreement between rationalists and empiricists?
choices: Whether the external world exists
Whether some knowledge can come from reason alone or must all ultimately trace to sense experience
Whether truth is objective
Whether God exists

quiz.q: An engineer insists a bridge design must be sound because pure mathematical proof guarantees the load calculations hold, with no need to physically test a prototype. Which epistemological stance does this reasoning most resemble?
choices: Rationalism, since it claims substantive knowledge from reason alone
Empiricism, since it ultimately rests on observed measurements
Skepticism, since it doubts all knowledge claims
Pragmatism, since it judges the claim by whether it works

quiz.q: Locke argued the mind starts with no innate content. What two-word Latin phrase names this 'blank slate' view of the mind at birth?
On Hume's account, why is a concept like causation suspect?
choices: It cannot be traced back to any sense impression
It is an innate idea the mind brings with it
It contradicts the principle of non-contradiction
It coheres poorly with our other beliefs

cards.title: A priori and the analytic–synthetic divide
cards.fact: Two cuts: knowable without experience vs only through it, and true-by-meaning vs true-about-the-world. Kant said some truths are both a priori and substantive; Quine doubted the second cut exists at all.
cards.detail: Two distinctions get tangled together. The first is about how a belief is justified: a priori means knowable independent of experience (you don't run an experiment to know 'all bachelors are unmarried'), a posteriori means justified by experience ('it rained yesterday'). The second is about what makes a sentence true: analytic means true purely by the meanings of its words ('a vixen is a female fox'), synthetic means its truth also depends on how the world is. Immanuel Kant, in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), claimed the interesting cases are 'synthetic a priori' — substantive truths known without experience, his examples being arithmetic ('7+5=12') and geometry, which he held were not mere unpacking of definitions yet needed no observation. W.V.O. Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (Philosophical Review, 1951) attacked the analytic side, targeting Rudolf Carnap's logical-empiricist program: Quine argued that 'analytic' can only be explained via a circle of equally unclear notions (synonymy, definition, meaning) with no non-circular grounding, and that our beliefs face experience 'only as a corporate body' — confirmation holism — so no statement is immune from revision, collapsing the supposedly sharp line.
cards.deploy: Lets you separate two questions people blur: 'how do you know that?' (a priori vs experience) from 'is that just a definition or a real claim about the world?' (analytic vs synthetic).
cards.counter: Quine's obituary for the distinction is contested. H.P. Grice and P.F. Strawson ('In Defense of a Dogma', 1956) argued that a notion ordinary speakers apply confidently and agree on can't be incoherent merely because it resists a tidy reductive definition. Many later philosophers (e.g. Frank Jackson's defense of conceptual analysis, and formal/lexical semanticists who build analytic meaning-relations into their theories) still treat analyticity as a workable notion. Georges Rey's SEP survey judges the debate genuinely open: Quine's challenge is serious but has not been shown to be decisive.

quiz.q: Kant's 'synthetic a priori' claims that some truths are…
choices: True by definition and learned through experience
Substantive (not mere definitions) yet knowable without experience
Both empirical and uncertain
Neither analytic nor a priori

quiz.q: The sentence 'a triangle has three sides' is true purely because of what the word 'triangle' means. Independently, you can know it without doing any measurement. How is this sentence best classified?
choices: Analytic and a priori
Synthetic and a priori
Analytic and a posteriori
Synthetic and a posteriori

quiz.q: What is Quine's term for the thesis that our beliefs face the test of experience as a single connected body rather than one statement at a time?
Grice and Strawson's 'In Defense of a Dogma' (1956) replied to Quine by arguing that:
choices: A distinction ordinary speakers apply confidently and agree on is not incoherent just because it resists a tidy reductive definition
Analyticity can be defined non-circularly through synonymy and meaning
All synthetic statements are ultimately analytic
Kant was wrong that any truths are synthetic a priori

cards.title: Hume's problem of induction
cards.fact: We assume the future will resemble the past, but David Hume showed any argument for that assumption either begs the question or relies on the very habit it's meant to justify.
cards.detail: Induction is reasoning from observed cases to unobserved ones: the sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow. David Hume (1748) pressed a simple question: what justifies that leap? He laid out a dilemma. You can't justify it by pure logic ('demonstrative reasoning'), because a future where nature changes its habits involves no contradiction — it's conceivable. And you can't justify it by experience ('probable reasoning'), because every appeal to 'it has always worked before' already assumes that past regularities carry over to the future — the Uniformity of Nature — which is exactly the principle in question. That makes any experiential defence circular. Hume's own diagnosis is psychological, not logical: induction isn't grounded in reason at all but in 'custom' or habit — repeated exposure conditions us to expect the usual, and we mistake that pull of habit for rational insight.
cards.deploy: A reminder that 'it's always worked so far' is a psychological habit, not a proof — useful for spotting overconfident extrapolation from track records.
cards.counter: Many think the problem dissolves rather than threatens. Karl Popper accepted that induction is unjustifiable but argued science doesn't need it — it proceeds by conjecture and falsification. Bayesians (developed from Frank Ramsey and Bruno de Finetti) recast the issue as updating rational degrees of belief, and Peter Strawson argued that demanding an external 'justification' of induction is a confusion, since being reasonable just means proportioning belief to evidence.

quiz.q: Why does Hume say you can't justify induction by appealing to its past success?
choices: Because the past is unknowable
Because doing so assumes the future resembles the past — the very point in question
Because induction always fails in practice
Because only deductive logic counts as reasoning

quiz.q: Hume calls the unproven background principle that past regularities will carry over to future cases the 'Uniformity of ___'. Fill in the blank with the word he uses.
A trader argues a stock will keep rising tomorrow because it has risen every day for a year. By Hume's reasoning, the flaw in this justification is that it:
choices: Already assumes the past pattern carries into the future, the very point in question
Uses demonstrative reasoning where probable reasoning is required
Relies on an innate idea rather than experience
Confuses a synthetic claim with an analytic one

quiz.q: Hume's positive diagnosis is that inductive expectation comes not from reason but from one psychological mechanism. What single word (also rendered 'habit') does he use for it?

cards.title: Theories of truth
cards.fact: Four rival answers to 'what makes a belief true?': it matches reality (correspondence), it coheres with a system (coherence), it works in inquiry (pragmatist), or 'true' adds nothing beyond asserting the claim (deflationary).
cards.detail: The question is what truth consists in, not how we check it. The correspondence theory (Aristotle, G.E. Moore, and Bertrand Russell from around 1910) says a belief is true when it matches the way things actually are — 'snow is white' is true because snow is white; truth is a relation between thought and world. The coherence theory (the British idealist H.H. Joachim, and later the American Brand Blanshard) says a belief is true when it fits into a maximally consistent, comprehensive web of beliefs, since on this view we can never step outside our beliefs to compare them with a 'naked' reality. The pragmatist theory (Charles Peirce, William James) ties truth to inquiry: for Peirce truth is the opinion inquiry would converge on in the long run, while James more loosely said true beliefs are those that 'work' — that prove useful and survive testing. Deflationism (anticipated by Frank Ramsey's redundancy theory, developed as 'minimalism' by Paul Horwich) denies truth is a substantive property at all: saying 'p is true' just re-asserts p, so the word 'true' is a convenient device for endorsing claims, not a deep nature to analyse.
cards.deploy: Helps you ask, when someone calls a claim 'true', which standard they mean — matching the facts, fitting a worldview, or just being useful — which are not the same test.
cards.counter: The theories trade objections rather than one winning. Russell objected that coherence can't distinguish reality from an internally consistent fairy tale; Russell also charged that 'useful' beliefs (in James's sense) can be false, so usefulness isn't truth. Defenders of substantive truth (e.g. realists about science) argue deflationism throws away truth's role in explaining why successful theories track the world, while deflationists like Horwich reply that no such heavyweight property is needed. Each camp answers in kind, and the field remains divided.

quiz.q: Deflationism about truth holds that…
choices: Truth is correspondence with reality
Calling 'p' true adds nothing beyond asserting p — 'true' isn't a deep property
Truth is whatever beliefs cohere best
Only useful beliefs are true

quiz.q: A detective says her account of the crime is true because every clue, alibi, and timeline knits together into one consistent overall picture, with no piece left dangling. Which theory of truth does this standard reflect?
choices: Coherence theory
Correspondence theory
Pragmatist theory
Deflationary theory

quiz.q: For Charles Peirce, truth is the opinion that inquiry would eventually arrive at over time. What word describes what such inquiry is said to do toward that final opinion?
Russell's classic objection that a perfectly self-consistent fairy tale could count as 'true' is aimed at which theory of truth?
choices: Coherence theory
Correspondence theory
Deflationary theory
Pragmatist theory

cards.title: Bayesian epistemology
cards.fact: Treat belief as a degree of confidence — a credence between 0 and 1 — that obeys the probability axioms and gets revised by Bayes' rule as evidence comes in. Dutch-book arguments show why deviating leaves you exploitable.
cards.detail: Instead of treating belief as all-or-nothing (you believe it or you don't), Bayesian epistemology models it as a credence: a number from 0 (certain false) to 1 (certain true). The view has two core norms. Probabilism says your credences should obey the probability axioms — be non-negative, sum to 1 over exhaustive alternatives, and add for mutually exclusive cases. Conditionalization says when you learn evidence E, you update by Bayes' rule, shifting toward hypotheses that predicted E and away from those that didn't, weighted by your prior confidence. Why obey the axioms? The Dutch-book argument (Frank Ramsey 1926, Bruno de Finetti 1937) shows that if your credences violate them, a clever bookmaker can offer you a set of bets you'll each accept as fair yet that together guarantee you lose money — incoherence is a practical defect, not just an aesthetic one. This is a modern reply to Hume: induction isn't a leap needing external proof but the rational updating of credences as data accumulates.
cards.deploy: Reframes 'do you believe X?' as 'how confident, and how should this evidence move you?' — and explains why ignoring base rates or refusing to update is literally incoherent.
cards.counter: The framework has real soft spots its own proponents debate. The 'problem of the priors' bites: Bayes' rule tells you how to update but not where your starting credences come from, so two reasonable agents can reach different conclusions from identical evidence. Subjective Bayesians (de Finetti, Savage) accept this, holding any coherent prior is permitted; objective Bayesians (Harold Jeffreys, E. T. Jaynes) try to pin priors down via principles like indifference or maximum entropy, which critics say are ill-defined or arbitrary. And the 'problem of old evidence' (Clark Glymour 1980) shows the rule struggles to credit evidence already known when a theory was proposed — Einstein's use of Mercury's long-known perihelion shift is the stock case.

quiz.q: A Dutch-book argument shows that if your credences violate the probability axioms…
choices: You will always make true predictions
A set of bets each acceptable to you can be combined to guarantee you lose
You cannot update on evidence
Your priors must be objective

quiz.q: A diagnostic test has a true-positive rate of 90% and a false-positive rate of 20%. The disease's base rate (prior) is 5%. If someone tests positive, what is the posterior probability (as a percentage) that they actually have the disease? Round to the nearest whole percent.
What is the name of the objection that Bayes' rule struggles to give evidential credit to data already known when a theory was first proposed, with Mercury's perihelion shift as the stock example?

Two careful reasoners begin with different starting credences, apply Bayes' rule correctly to the same evidence, and reach different conclusions. Which difficulty for Bayesian epistemology does this illustrate?
choices: The Dutch-book vulnerability, since their bets can be combined into a guaranteed loss
The problem of the priors, since the rule says how to update but not where starting credences come from
A violation of probabilism, since their credences fail to sum to 1
The problem of old evidence, since the data was known before the theories existed

cards.title: Testimony and social knowledge
cards.fact: Almost everything you know — history, geography, science — you were told. The fight is whether trust in testimony must be earned by track record (Hume) or is a basic source of knowledge in its own right (Reid).
cards.detail: Testimony is believing something because someone told you, whether in conversation, a textbook, or the news. Since you've personally verified almost none of what you know, testimony does enormous epistemic work, which raises the question of what justifies believing what others say. Reductionism, traced to David Hume (whose "Of Miracles" in the 1748 Enquiry is the standard source), says testimony is not a basic source: a hearer is entitled to believe a speaker only on the strength of independent reasons — chiefly one's own observed track record that testimony of that kind tends to be reliable. So trust must be earned and reduces to ordinary inductive evidence. Anti-reductionism (also called non-reductionism), traced to Thomas Reid's Inquiry into the Human Mind (1764), denies this: Reid says humans have an innate 'principle of credulity' — a disposition to believe what we're told, paired with a 'principle of veracity' to speak truly — and absent specific red flags (the speaker is shifty, the claim is implausible) the hearer has a default, defeasible entitlement to trust. On this view testimony is a basic source alongside perception and memory. Either way, the moral is that knowledge is irreducibly social: it lives in a web of speakers and hearers, not in the lone inquirer.
cards.deploy: Sharpens how you handle second-hand claims: do you (Humean) demand the source prove its track record, or (Reidian) extend default trust until something specific defeats it?
cards.counter: Both camps face pointed objections. C.A.J. Coady (Testimony: A Philosophical Study, 1992) argued the reductionist can't actually run the project — no individual has checked enough testimony first-hand to build the required track record, and you'd need testimony even to learn that others are generally reliable, making the inductive base circular. Against anti-reductionism, Elizabeth Fricker defends 'local reductionism': a blanket default right to believe is too permissive and licenses gullibility, so hearers should monitor each source for trustworthiness. A third option treats testimony as interpersonal: Richard Moran's 'assurance' view says a speaker, by asserting, gives the hearer their word and assumes responsibility, so trust rests on that relationship rather than on either inference or bare credulity.

quiz.q: On the anti-reductionist (Reidian) view of testimony, a hearer…
choices: Must first establish the speaker's track record before believing
Has a default, defeasible entitlement to believe absent specific red flags
Can never gain knowledge from testimony
Should treat all testimony as equally false

quiz.q: You read a fact in an encyclopedia from an author you have never encountered and immediately accept it, with no prior track record of that source's reliability. Which view of testimony best fits and licenses this default acceptance?
choices: Humean reductionism, because trust must be earned by observed reliability
Fricker's local reductionism, because you monitored this source's trustworthiness
Reidian anti-reductionism, because we have a default, defeasible entitlement to believe what we are told
Moran's assurance view, because the author personally gave you their word

quiz.q: Which philosopher argued in a 1992 study that reductionism is unworkable because no individual has personally checked enough testimony to build the required reliability track record?

On Richard Moran's interpersonal account of testimony, what does a speaker do, by the act of asserting something, that grounds the hearer's trust in a relationship rather than in inference or bare credulity?

cards.title: Fallibilism
cards.fact: Charles Peirce's stance: you can genuinely know things while admitting any of your beliefs might turn out wrong. Knowledge doesn't require certainty — and demanding certainty is what hands the skeptic an easy win.
cards.detail: Fallibilism, a term from the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce in the late 1800s, is the view that knowledge does not require certainty: a belief can count as knowledge even though it could, in principle, turn out false. Jason Stanley puts the standard version sharply — you can know that p even when your evidence for p is logically consistent with p being false. Peirce framed it against Cartesian foundationalism — René Descartes' project of rebuilding all knowledge on indubitable, certain foundations. Peirce argued no inquiry ever reaches that bedrock; science advances by self-correction, holding its best-tested results as provisionally settled while staying open to revision. The payoff is escaping a trap: if you assume knowing X means being unable to be wrong about X, the skeptic only has to show error is conceivable to deny you any knowledge at all. The fallibilist blocks the move by lowering the bar — knowledge needs good justification, not a guarantee — so ordinary empirical claims can qualify even though they fall short of certainty.
cards.deploy: Lets you hold a position firmly while genuinely conceding it might be wrong — defusing the bad-faith 'but can you be 100% sure?' demand without collapsing into 'so nobody knows anything'.
cards.counter: Fallibilism faces a sharp puzzle. If you can know p while granting p might be false, you seem committed to saying 'I know p, but possibly not-p' — what Patrick Rysiew (2001) named a 'concessive knowledge attribution', and what sounds like a contradiction. David Lewis (1996) calls such a sentence the plain, explicit statement of fallibilism; if so, its oddness suggests knowledge really must be infallible, the line infallibilists press. Rysiew's own reply is that these sentences can be true but are merely infelicitous to say — pragmatically awkward, not contradictory; other fallibilists deny the fallibilist is committed to their truth at all.

quiz.q: Fallibilism, as Peirce held it, says that knowledge…
choices: Requires absolute certainty
Can be genuine even though the belief might turn out false
Is impossible to attain
Must rest on indubitable foundations

quiz.q: Which 17th-century philosopher's foundationalist project of rebuilding all knowledge on indubitable, certain foundations did Peirce frame fallibilism against?
An engineer says 'I know this bridge can carry the load, though it is logically possible my calculations contain an error.' How does a fallibilist evaluate this claim?
choices: It can be genuine knowledge, because knowledge requires good justification, not a guarantee against error
It cannot be knowledge, because knowing X requires being unable to be wrong about X
It is a flat contradiction and therefore necessarily false
It is knowledge only if the engineer first refutes every skeptical scenario

quiz.q: What is the term, named by Patrick Rysiew in 2001, for a sentence of the form 'I know p, but possibly not-p' that seems to follow from fallibilism?

cards.title: Occam's razor
cards.fact: Among hypotheses that fit the evidence equally well, prefer the one that posits fewer entities or assumptions.
cards.detail: The razor is a rule of thumb for choosing between explanations: when two accounts cover the same data, lean toward the leaner one — the one that invents fewer unseen causes, forces or entities. It is named for William of Ockham, a 14th-century English Franciscan friar, who wrote "plurality must never be posited without necessity"; the famous Latin slogan "entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity" is not in his works but was coined by the Irish friar John Punch in 1639, and the idea itself goes back further (Aristotle, Ptolemy, Duns Scotus). It is best read as a tie-breaker, not a truth detector: a simpler theory may be easier to test, but reality is sometimes genuinely complicated, so the leaner story can be the wrong one. "Simpler" is also slippery — cutting entities can force messier equations, so fewer entities and fewer equations pull in different directions.
cards.deploy: When someone's explanation needs a pile of special add-ons to survive each objection, ask whether a plainer account fits the same facts — extra epicycles are a warning sign.
cards.counter: Philosophers split on what the razor is worth. Karl Popper defends it instrumentally: simpler theories say more and so are more falsifiable, easier to test and refute. Richard Swinburne goes further, calling simplicity "an ultimate a priori epistemic principle that simplicity is evidence for truth." Elliott Sober pushes back: there is no global justification for parsimony — its force depends on local, subject-specific background assumptions, and where those assumptions fail, preferring the simpler hypothesis tracks nothing about the world.

quiz.q: What does Occam's razor actually license you to do?
choices: Prove that simpler theories are true
Prefer the hypothesis with fewer assumptions among those that fit the evidence equally well
Reject any theory that posits unobservable entities
Accept whichever theory is most popular among experts

quiz.q: Two theories predict the same observations equally well, but one requires positing several additional unobserved forces to survive objections. What does Occam's razor license you to do?
choices: Conclude the leaner theory is definitely true, since simplicity detects truth
Prefer the leaner theory as a tie-breaker, while granting reality might be more complicated
Reject both theories until one makes a distinct, testable prediction
Prefer whichever theory uses fewer equations regardless of how many entities it posits

quiz.q: Which Irish friar coined the famous Latin slogan 'entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity' in 1639, a phrase not found in William of Ockham's own writings?
Karl Popper endorses Occam's razor on instrumental grounds. What is his reason for preferring simpler theories?
choices: Simpler theories are more likely to be true a priori
Simpler theories require fewer equations and so are easier to compute
Simplicity reflects subject-specific background assumptions about the world
Simpler theories say more and are therefore more falsifiable and easier to test

cards.title: Scientific realism vs anti-realism
cards.fact: Realists say science's unobservables (electrons, fields) are really out there; anti-realists say theories are just tools for predicting what we can observe.
cards.detail: Scientific realism is the view that our best mature theories are at least approximately true, including their claims about things no one can see directly — electrons, quarks, electromagnetic fields. Its headline argument is the 'no-miracles argument', named after Hilary Putnam's 1975 line that realism 'is the only philosophy that doesn't make the success of science a miracle': if electrons weren't real, why does electron theory keep working so well? Anti-realists push back from two directions. Larry Laudan's 1981 'pessimistic meta-induction' points out that the history of science is full of once-successful theories now known to be false (phlogiston, caloric, the luminiferous ether), so by induction today's best theories are probably also false about their deep posits. Instrumentalists go further: a theory is a calculating device for organizing observations, and asking whether its hidden machinery is 'real' is a question we needn't answer.
cards.deploy: When a debate turns on whether a model's hidden variables 'really exist' or just 'work', you're standing on the realism/anti-realism fault line — name which question is actually being asked.
cards.counter: Bas van Fraassen's constructive empiricism (The Scientific Image, 1980) offers a disciplined middle path: science aims only at theories that are 'empirically adequate' — true about the observable — while you stay agnostic, neither believing nor disbelieving, about the unobservable. You keep all the predictive power without betting that electrons are literally real, sidestepping both the no-miracles overreach and the pessimistic induction. Critics counter that van Fraassen's sharp observable/unobservable line is itself hard to draw and arguably arbitrary.

quiz.q: What does Laudan's 'pessimistic meta-induction' argue against scientific realism?
choices: No theory can ever be tested in isolation
Many past theories were empirically successful yet are now known to be false, so today's may be too
Simpler theories are always preferable to complex ones
Observation is always theory-laden

quiz.q: A team builds a neural-network weather model. It predicts brilliantly, but no one believes its internal hidden layers correspond to any real atmospheric mechanism; they treat it purely as a forecasting device. Which philosophical stance best matches this attitude toward the model's internals?
choices: Instrumentalism
Scientific realism
The no-miracles argument
Strong objectivity

quiz.q: Bas van Fraassen's constructive empiricism says science aims only at theories that are correct about the observable. What two-word property is the official goal of a theory on his view, rather than truth about unobservables?

Someone argues: 'Since past successful theories like phlogiston and the luminiferous ether turned out false, we should expect our current best theories to be false about their deep posits too.' This reasoning is an example of which argumentative move?
choices: An induction over the historical track record of science
A deduction from the no-miracles premise
A claim that observation and theory are incommensurable
An appeal to the empirical adequacy of current theories

cards.title: Kuhn's paradigms
