cards.fact: Kuhn argued science isn't steady accumulation but long stretches of 'normal science' inside a paradigm, broken by crises and revolutions.
cards.detail: In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Thomas Kuhn rejected the textbook picture of science as facts piling up steadily. Most science is 'normal science': puzzle-solving within an accepted 'paradigm' — a reigning framework of theory, exemplary problems and shared standards (think Newtonian mechanics) that tells researchers what counts as a question and a good answer. Anomalies that resist the paradigm accumulate until they trigger a 'crisis', and a 'scientific revolution' swaps in a new paradigm (relativity, quantum theory). Kuhn's most radical claim is 'incommensurability': rival paradigms don't share a neutral measuring stick, because they redefine key terms and even what scientists 'see', so the choice between them isn't settled by logic and evidence alone. This directly opposes Karl Popper, for whom a single decisive refutation should topple a theory; Kuhn replies that during normal science researchers don't try to falsify the paradigm at all — they protect it and blame the anomaly on themselves.
cards.deploy: When a field seems to ignore data that 'should' refute it, ask whether you're watching normal science defend a paradigm — and what crisis would have to build before it flips.
cards.counter: In his 1970 essay 'Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes', Imre Lakatos charged that Kuhn made theory change a matter of 'mob psychology' — an irrational conversion rather than a reasoned judgment — and proposed 'research programmes' that are appraised rationally over time by whether they keep predicting novel facts; Popper similarly held that even paradigm shifts can be defended with reasons, not just sociology.

quiz.q: On Kuhn's view, what mainly happens during 'normal science'?
choices: Scientists constantly try to falsify the reigning theory
Scientists solve puzzles within an accepted paradigm rather than testing it
Rival paradigms are compared on a neutral measuring stick
Theories accumulate steadily with no framework guiding them

quiz.q: Two researchers from competing frameworks both use the word 'mass', but each means something different by it, and they end up describing the same experiment in incompatible terms with no shared neutral yardstick to settle the dispute. Which Kuhnian concept does this illustrate?
choices: Incommensurability
Normal science
Falsification
Empirical adequacy

quiz.q: On Kuhn's account, what name is given to the build-up phase, driven by accumulating unresolved anomalies, that precedes a scientific revolution and the switch to a new paradigm?

Popper holds a single decisive refutation should topple a theory. How does Kuhn characterize what working scientists actually do when an experiment contradicts their reigning paradigm during normal science?
choices: They protect the paradigm and treat the anomaly as their own failure to solve a puzzle
They immediately abandon the paradigm as falsified
They declare the two paradigms incommensurable and stop comparing them
They appraise rival research programmes by their record of novel predictions

cards.title: Underdetermination
cards.fact: The evidence never fully pins down one theory: incompatible theories can fit exactly the same data.
cards.detail: Underdetermination is the claim that any body of evidence can be accommodated by more than one mutually incompatible theory, so data alone can't single out the true one. One root is the Duhem-Quine thesis (after the French physicist-historian Pierre Duhem and the American logician W.V.O. Quine): you never test a hypothesis in isolation, only bundled with auxiliary assumptions (the instrument works, no hidden forces, the background physics holds). So when a prediction fails, logic alone can't say which link in the web broke -- you can always save the cherished hypothesis by revising an auxiliary instead. Kyle Stanford, summarizing the debate, separates this 'holist' (confirmational) underdetermination from 'contrastive' underdetermination, where two whole rival theories fit identical evidence with no experiment that could ever decide between them; Duhem and Quine, he notes, ran the two problems together. Because evidence leaves slack, other factors must do the choosing -- which is why underdetermination is a lever both for anti-realists like Bas van Fraassen (believe only what the data fix; stay agnostic about unobservables) and for sociologists of science in the 'strong programme' (David Bloor, Barry Barnes) who hold that social interests fill the gap.
cards.deploy: Before treating 'the data prove it' as decisive, ask which auxiliary assumptions a contrary result could be pinned on instead -- the data rarely point at a single culprit.
cards.counter: Larry Laudan and Jarrett Leplin (1991) argue the threat is overblown: which empirical consequences a theory has depends on the auxiliaries currently available, so 'empirical equivalence' must be relativized to a state of science -- rivals tied today can come apart tomorrow as new auxiliaries are added. They add that equivalent theories can still differ in evidential support (e.g. one is derivable from a better-confirmed general theory), and that simplicity, explanatory power and consilience routinely break ties. On their view underdetermination is a logical possibility, not the standing scientific predicament anti-realists need.

quiz.q: Why does the Duhem-Quine point make a single failed prediction inconclusive?
choices: Because experiments can never be repeated
Because the hypothesis is tested bundled with auxiliary assumptions, so logic can't say which one failed
Because all observation is theory-laden and so unreliable
Because simpler theories must always be preferred

quiz.q: A physicist's prediction fails in the lab. She concludes the failure could be blamed on the core hypothesis, on a faulty instrument, or on a background assumption, and that logic alone cannot say which. Which thesis names this predicament?
choices: The Duhem-Quine thesis
The pessimistic meta-induction
The no-miracles argument
Constructive empiricism

quiz.q: Kyle Stanford distinguishes the holist or confirmational form of underdetermination from a second form in which two complete rival theories fit identical evidence with no experiment that could ever decide between them. What one-word label does he give that second form?
Laudan and Leplin (1991) argue underdetermination is overblown. Which claim is part of their rebuttal?
choices: Empirically equivalent theories can still differ in evidential support, e.g. one derives from a better-confirmed general theory
Social interests must fill the evidential gap, as the strong programme holds
Scientists should believe only what the data fix and stay agnostic about unobservables
Rival theories share no neutral measuring stick because they redefine key terms

cards.title: Standpoint epistemology
cards.fact: Knowledge is socially situated, and the marginalized can hold an epistemic advantage on truths about how power works.
cards.detail: Standpoint epistemology holds that what you can know depends on where you stand in society: your position shapes which questions occur to you and which facts are visible. Drawing on a Marxist idea that the worker sees the labour system more clearly than the boss, Nancy Hartsock (1983) and Sandra Harding argued that those marginalized along lines of gender, race or class can have an epistemic advantage about how systems of power actually operate, precisely because they have to navigate them. Harding's 'strong objectivity' turns the usual worry on its head: real objectivity requires examining the social position of the knower, including the invisible biases of the privileged, rather than pretending to a 'view from nowhere' (Thomas Nagel's phrase, which Harding rejects). Donna Haraway's 'situated knowledges' (1988) makes the parallel case that all vision is from a body and a location; she calls the pretence of detached neutrality 'the god trick', and argues that owning one's partiality yields more honest, accountable knowledge. Patricia Hill Collins extended the tradition to race: in 'Black Feminist Thought' (1990) she argues Black women's 'outsider within' position and their intersecting oppressions generate a distinctive standpoint, anticipating intersectional analysis. A standpoint here is an achievement, won through critical reflection and political struggle, not just an identity you are born with.
cards.deploy: When a claim of 'neutral' expertise overlooks how things look to the people affected, standpoint theory gives you the question: whose situated knowledge is missing from this 'view from nowhere'?
cards.counter: Susan Haack presses the objectivity worry head-on: she argues social disadvantage confers no automatic epistemic privilege, and that tying knowledge to political position risks turning inquiry into advocacy for a foregone conclusion. A separate internal problem, raised by Bat-Ami Bar On, is adjudication: if several oppressed groups' standpoints conflict, which is privileged, and how do we rule out internalized oppression distorting any one of them? Helen Longino keeps the social insight but relocates objectivity: in her critical contextual empiricism it comes from the critical scrutiny of a diverse community, not from any single privileged standpoint, since heterogeneous communities are better at exposing each other's hidden background assumptions.

quiz.q: What does Sandra Harding's 'strong objectivity' demand?
choices: Stripping all social context from inquiry to reach a view from nowhere
Critically examining the social position and biases of the knower, including the privileged
Accepting whatever the marginalized assert without scrutiny
Replacing evidence with personal lived experience

quiz.q: Donna Haraway argues that all vision comes from a particular body and location, and she gives a mocking name to the pretence of detached, view-from-nowhere neutrality. What is that two-word phrase?

A government convenes only credentialed economists to assess a welfare policy, never consulting the recipients who navigate it daily. A standpoint theorist's central critique would be that this 'neutral expertise':
choices: Omits the situated knowledge of those whose lives the system shapes
Fails because economics is not empirically adequate
Treats the policy as merely a calculating device, not as real
Confuses normal science with a paradigm crisis

quiz.q: Helen Longino keeps the social insight of standpoint theory but relocates where objectivity comes from. On her critical contextual empiricism, objectivity arises from:
choices: The critical scrutiny of a diverse community that exposes hidden background assumptions
The single most marginalized group's privileged standpoint
A detached view from nowhere free of any social position
The automatic epistemic privilege conferred by social disadvantage

cards.title: The regress problem
cards.fact: Every reason needs a reason — so how does justification ever stop? That regress is epistemology's oldest headache.
cards.detail: If a belief is justified by another belief, and that one needs justifying too, you face the regress problem — sharpened by the ancient skeptic Agrippa into a trilemma (also called Münchhausen): a chain of reasons must either run on forever, circle back on itself, or stop at something itself unjustified. The two main escapes name two camps. Foundationalists, in the spirit of Descartes, say the chain halts at 'basic' beliefs justified non-inferentially — by direct experience or self-evidence. Coherentists, such as the early Laurence BonJour, deny any belief is basic and locate justification in how well a belief coheres with the whole web of one's beliefs. Each accepts the cost the other calls fatal: an arbitrary stopping point, or a suspiciously circular web.
cards.deploy: When someone demands you 'justify' a claim all the way down, name the trilemma — every body of knowledge must either stop somewhere or loop.
cards.counter: Reliabilists like Alvin Goldman sidestep the regress entirely: a belief can be justified by being produced by a reliable process, even if the believer can articulate no chain of reasons at all — shifting the question from 'what reasons do you have?' to 'how was the belief formed?'.

quiz.q: Agrippa's trilemma says a chain of justifying reasons must do one of three things — which is NOT one of them?
choices: Run on infinitely
Circle back on itself
Stop at an unjustified point
Be proven by experiment

quiz.q: A scientist says she trusts her data because the sensor is calibrated, and trusts that the sensor is calibrated because the data looks sound. An epistemologist objects that her two beliefs prop each other up. Which horn of Agrippa's trilemma is she on, and which camp would most readily accept that structure as legitimate?
choices: The circular horn; coherentists
The infinite-regress horn; foundationalists
The arbitrary-stopping horn; foundationalists
The circular horn; reliabilists

quiz.q: Which approach to justification answers the regress not by finding a place for reasons to stop, but by asking instead whether the belief was produced by a dependable belief-forming method, so a person could be justified without being able to state any reasons at all?

Agrippa's trilemma presents three possible fates for a chain of justifying reasons. A foundationalist rejects exactly one of those fates (the circular one) and a coherentist rejects exactly one (the arbitrary-stopping one). Counting only the distinct fates rejected by at least one of these two camps, how many of the three are rejected?

cards.title: First-past-the-post
cards.fact: Under first-past-the-post, you mark one name and the candidate with the most votes wins, even on 40% while a majority wanted someone else.
cards.detail: Each voter picks a single candidate, and whoever piles up the most marks takes the seat, with no requirement to clear half the votes. Take three candidates and 100 voters: A gets 40, B gets 35, C gets 25, so A wins on 40%. But suppose every B voter and every C voter prefers B to A; then 60 of the 100 (a majority) would pick B over A head-to-head, yet A still wins. The 25 votes for C are 'wasted' in that they elect nobody, and C acts as a spoiler: had C not run and those 25 gone to B, B would win 60 to 40. Voters anticipating exactly this waste is the mechanism behind Duverger's law, which pushes voters and money toward the two front-runners.
cards.deploy: Use it to spot when a plurality winner lacks majority backing, and to predict tactical 'lesser evil' voting and the two-party squeeze under single-mark single-seat rules.
cards.counter: Maurice Duverger framed FPTP as a force toward two parties, but the UK and India keep strong regional and third parties under the same rule, so the two-party outcome is a tendency, not a guarantee.

quiz.q: In a single-seat first-past-the-post contest with three candidates and no other rules, what is the minimum support a winner can have?
choices: A simple majority, over 50% of the vote
Only a plurality, the most votes, which can be well under 50%
Exactly one third of the vote
A two-thirds supermajority

quiz.q: In a first-past-the-post race, candidate X receives 9,000 votes, Y receives 7,500, and Z receives 3,500, out of 20,000 total. What percentage of the total vote does the winner X take, to the nearest whole percent?
What term describes a vote cast for a losing candidate (or surplus beyond what a winner needed) that elects nobody under first-past-the-post?
A minor candidate C draws votes mostly from candidate B, letting A win even though more voters preferred B to A. What is this effect called?
choices: The spoiler effect
The bandwagon effect
The median voter theorem
Proportional representation

cards.title: The two-round runoff
cards.fact: The two-round system sends the top two to a runoff if nobody wins a majority first, which can eliminate a centrist who would have beaten either finalist.
cards.detail: In round one each voter marks one candidate; if no one passes 50%, the two highest go to a second round where the majority winner takes office. France elects its president this way. The flaw is a 'centre squeeze': a broadly acceptable centrist can place third in round one and be eliminated even though they would beat each finalist head-to-head. Worked example with 100 voters and first-round shares Left 36, Right 34, Centre 30: nobody has a majority, so Left and Right advance and Centre is dropped despite sitting between them. France in 2002 shows the vote-splitting half of this: the left vote was divided across many candidates, so Lionel Jospin (16.2%) came third behind Jacques Chirac (19.9%) and far-right Jean-Marie Le Pen (16.9%), sending Le Pen to a runoff Chirac won easily. Polling indicated Chirac was the genuinely majority-preferred candidate, so 2002 illustrates first-round splitting without being a clean centre-squeeze case.
cards.deploy: Use it where you want a clear majority mandate without ranked ballots, but watch for first-round vote-splitting that can eliminate a consensus candidate before the decisive round.
cards.counter: Voting theorists working from the Condorcet criterion point to the centre squeeze: the runoff can drop the candidate who beats every rival head-to-head, so the majority winner of the final round need not be the candidate a majority preferred over all others.

quiz.q: Under a two-round system, what triggers a second round of voting?
choices: No candidate wins more than half the first-round vote
Turnout falls below 50%
More than two candidates run
The top two candidates tie exactly

quiz.q: First-round shares are A 31%, B 29%, C 22%, D 18%. No one has a majority, so the top two advance. What is the combined first-round percentage of the two candidates who go to the runoff?
What is the named failure mode in which a moderate candidate who would defeat both finalists head-to-head is eliminated in the first round of a runoff?
In the 2002 French presidential election, which feature of the first round let the far-right candidate reach the runoff instead of the Socialist candidate?
choices: The left-wing vote was split across many candidates, dropping the Socialist to third
The far-right candidate won an outright first-round majority
A ranked ballot transferred votes to the far right
Only two candidates were allowed to run

cards.title: Ranked-choice (instant-runoff) voting
cards.fact: Instant-runoff voting eliminates the last-place candidate and transfers their ballots to next choices until someone clears a majority.
cards.detail: Voters rank the candidates instead of marking one. Count first choices; if nobody has over half, drop the candidate with the fewest first-place votes and move each of their ballots to its next-ranked surviving choice, repeating until someone passes 50%. Worked example with 100 voters and first choices A 40, B 35, C 25: no majority, so C is eliminated. If C's 25 ballots split 20 to B and 5 to A, the new totals are B 55, A 45, and B wins with a majority, reversing the plurality result where A led. The catch is that IRV is non-monotonic: in some elections a candidate can lose precisely because some voters ranked them higher, since that shifts who gets eliminated first and reroutes the transfers.
cards.deploy: Use it to elect a single winner with majority support from one round of ranked ballots, avoiding a separate runoff trip to the polls and blunting the simple spoiler effect.
cards.counter: Analysts of the 2009 Burlington, Vermont mayoral election point out IRV failed both monotonicity and the Condorcet criterion there: the candidate who beat every rival head-to-head, Andy Montroll, was eliminated, and Bob Kiss won despite a majority preferring Montroll over him.

quiz.q: In instant-runoff voting, what happens after a counting round in which no candidate has a majority of the remaining votes?
choices: The candidate with the fewest first-place votes is eliminated and their ballots transfer to next choices
The candidate with the most votes is declared the winner anyway
All candidates below 50% are eliminated at once
Voters return to the polls for a separate runoff

quiz.q: Sixty voters rank three candidates. First choices: A 25, B 20, C 15. No one has a majority, so C is eliminated and C's ballots transfer 12 to B and 3 to A. After the transfer, how many votes does B have?
What property does instant-runoff voting fail, whereby ranking a candidate higher on some ballots can cause that candidate to lose?
The 2009 Burlington, Vermont mayoral race is cited against instant-runoff voting because it eliminated which candidate?
choices: The Condorcet winner, who would have beaten every rival head-to-head
The candidate with the most first-place votes
Every candidate except the incumbent
The candidate who won the popular vote outright

cards.title: The Borda count
cards.fact: The Borda count scores each ballot by rank — top choice earns the most points — and the candidate with the highest sum wins.
cards.detail: With n candidates a first place is worth n-1 points, second n-2, and so on down to 0 for last; you sum the points each candidate collects across all ballots. Worked example with 3 candidates (points 2/1/0): 5 voters rank A>B>C and 4 voters rank B>C>A. A gets 5*2 + 4*0 = 10; B gets 5*1 + 4*2 = 13; C gets 5*0 + 4*1 = 4. B wins with 13, even though A has the most first-place votes, because Borda rewards candidates ranked highly by almost everyone, so it favours a broadly acceptable compromise over a polarising plurality leader. That same logic makes it gameable: a faction can run near-identical clones to soak up middle-rank points (teaming or cloning), and voters can rank a strong rival dead last to drag down their score (burying).
cards.deploy: Reach for Borda when you want a consensus pick that most people can live with rather than the option a narrow plurality loves and others hate: committee shortlists, sports MVP votes, picking a meeting time.
cards.counter: Jean-Charles de Borda himself conceded the method assumes sincerity: 'My scheme is intended for only honest men.' Because both burying and clone nomination pay off, the method rewards strategic ballots over honest ones whenever the stakes are high.

quiz.q: Three candidates use Borda points 2/1/0. Four voters rank X>Y>Z and three voters rank Y>Z>X. How many Borda points does the winner, Y, receive?
Name the strategic tactic in which a voter ranks a strong rival candidate artificially low to lower that rival's Borda total.
Why does the Borda count tend to elect a broadly acceptable compromise candidate rather than a polarising one?
choices: It only counts first-place votes, like plurality
It awards points for every rank, so a candidate ranked second or third by almost everyone accumulates a high total
It eliminates the lowest candidate each round
It requires a candidate to beat every rival one-on-one

cards.title: Condorcet winners and the voting paradox
cards.fact: A Condorcet winner beats every other candidate one-on-one, but majority preferences can cycle, so often no such winner exists.
cards.detail: Compare candidates pairwise: a Condorcet winner is the one who wins every head-to-head majority contest. The trouble is that majority rule over a group need not be transitive. Take the classic case of 3 voters and 3 candidates: Voter 1 ranks A>B>C, Voter 2 ranks B>C>A, Voter 3 ranks C>A>B. Check the pairs. A vs B: voters 1 and 3 prefer A, so A beats B 2-to-1. B vs C: voters 1 and 2 prefer B, so B beats C 2-to-1. C vs A: voters 2 and 3 prefer C, so C beats A 2-to-1. The majority prefers A to B, B to C, and C to A: a cycle with no top, so no Condorcet winner exists. This is Condorcet's paradox, where rational individual rankings aggregate into an irrational collective one, the kind of breakdown Arrow's theorem later proved no ranked method can fully escape.
cards.deploy: Use the pairwise test to spot whether a clear winner exists before trusting any single tally; when preferences cycle, expect the outcome to hinge on the agenda, since which pair gets voted on first can decide who wins.
cards.counter: Condorcet's contemporary rival Jean-Charles de Borda rejected pairwise majorities, arguing his points method gives a definite winner exactly when the Condorcet approach deadlocks, at the cost of sometimes overruling a candidate who would win every head-to-head.

quiz.q: Three voters rank candidates P, Q, R as follows: Voter 1: P>Q>R, Voter 2: Q>R>P, Voter 3: R>P>Q. In the head-to-head contest of P versus Q, how many of the three voters prefer P?
What is the term for a candidate who would win a one-on-one majority contest against every other candidate?
In Condorcet's paradox the majority prefers A to B, B to C, and C to A. What property of group preference does this violate?
choices: Unanimity
Transitivity
Anonymity
Monotonicity

quiz.q: When majority preferences form a cycle with no Condorcet winner, what most determines the eventual outcome under pairwise voting?
choices: The total number of voters
The order in which candidates are paired against each other (the agenda)
The alphabetical order of candidate names
Nothing, the election is automatically void

cards.title: Approval voting
cards.fact: Approval voting lets each voter mark as many candidates as they like, and the one with the most approvals wins.
cards.detail: Each ballot is a yes/no on every candidate, you may approve any number of them, and totals are just the counts of approvals. Worked example with 100 voters and candidates L, M, R: 45 voters approve only L; 30 approve both M and L; 25 approve both M and R. Tally: L = 45 + 30 = 75, M = 30 + 25 = 55, R = 25. L wins with 75 approvals. Because a voter can approve both a favourite and an acceptable backup, a minor candidate no longer splits the vote and sinks an ally, which is why approval voting defuses the spoiler problem that plagues plurality. The flaw is the same freedom seen from the other side: deciding where to draw your approval line is a strategic gamble.
cards.deploy: Good for low-stakes multi-candidate choices where simplicity matters and you want to avoid spoilers: club elections, picking a single winner from a crowded field, online polls with one machine-readable mark per name.
cards.counter: Jack H. Nagel named the Burr dilemma: when two allied candidates compete, each candidate's supporters face pressure to approve only their own favourite, since approving the ally can let that ally beat your favourite, so mutual support can collapse. The yes/no ballot also records no intensity, so a grudging approval counts the same as an enthusiastic one.

quiz.q: Under approval voting, 50 voters approve only candidate G, 20 approve both G and H, and 35 approve only H. How many approvals does the winner receive?

What is the name of the strategic dilemma in approval voting, named by Jack Nagel, in which supporters of two allied candidates are each tempted to approve only their own favourite, risking the collapse of mutual support?
How does approval voting reduce the spoiler problem found in plurality voting?
choices: It eliminates candidates round by round
It lets a voter approve both a favourite and an acceptable backup, so a minor candidate no longer splits support
It requires every voter to rank all candidates
It gives extra weight to first-place approvals

quiz.q: What is a standard criticism of approval voting as a way of capturing voter opinion?
choices: It always produces a tie
Its yes/no ballot records no intensity, so a grudging approval counts the same as an enthusiastic one
It cannot be counted by machine
It forces voters to approve every candidate

cards.title: Single transferable vote
cards.fact: STV makes ranked ballots proportional by setting a quota and recycling every vote above it or behind a loser.
cards.detail: Voters rank candidates in a multi-member district. A candidate is elected once they reach the Droop quota = floor(votes/(seats+1))+1, the smallest number that not enough other candidates can also reach. Say a 4-seat district casts 100 valid votes: quota = floor(100/5)+1 = 20+1 = 21, because at most four candidates can each gather 21. A candidate with 28 first preferences is elected with a surplus of 28-21 = 7, and those 7 votes transfer to the next preference marked on them so they are not wasted. When no one new meets the quota, the lowest candidate is eliminated and all their votes transfer to the next preference. Ireland, Malta, and the Australian Senate run elections this way, getting roughly proportional results from ranked ballots without party lists.
cards.deploy: Reach for STV when you want proportional outcomes but want voters choosing people, not just parties, and crossing party lines in their rankings.
cards.counter: Counting is slow and order-dependent: Ireland transfers a physical random sample of a candidate's ballots to represent the surplus, so which papers move is partly luck, and STV is non-monotonic (more support can hurt you). Electoral-reform groups like the UK's Electoral Reform Society back STV, while plurality defenders argue the count is too opaque to trust.

quiz.q: A 2-seat district receives 60 valid votes. Using the Droop quota floor(votes/(seats+1))+1, how many votes does a candidate need to be elected?
Under STV, what happens to the votes a candidate holds above the quota once they are elected?
choices: They transfer to the next preference marked on those ballots
They are discarded as wasted votes
They are split equally among all remaining candidates
They are returned to the voters to recast

quiz.q: What is the name of the quota, equal to floor(votes/(seats+1))+1, that a candidate must reach to win a seat under single transferable vote?
Which set of jurisdictions all elect representatives using the single transferable vote?
choices: Ireland, Malta, and the Australian Senate
Germany, France, and the United States
Canada, the United Kingdom, and India
Brazil, Japan, and South Africa

cards.title: Mixed-member proportional
cards.fact: MMP gives you a local representative and a party total that matches your second, party-wide vote.
cards.detail: You cast two votes: one for a local candidate won by first-past-the-post, and one for a party. List seats are then added as compensation so each party's total seat share matches its party vote. Example: a 120-seat parliament, a party wins 30% of the party vote, so it is entitled to 0.30 x 120 = 36 seats; if it already won 22 local districts, it gets 36 - 22 = 14 top-up seats from its list. Germany and New Zealand use MMP, combining a named local member with proportional overall results.
cards.deploy: Choose MMP when you want proportionality but voters still want one identifiable local representative to hold accountable, rather than only a party label.
cards.counter: Overhang seats break the match: if a party wins more districts than its party vote earns (as in Germany before its 2023 reform), it keeps the extra seats and the parliament swells or proportionality slips. Thresholds like New Zealand's 5% also lock small parties out, and decoy-list tactics (Lesotho 2007, Italy) have gamed the two-vote split. Germany's 2023 reform abolished overhang seats precisely because critics judged the swelling Bundestag indefensible.

quiz.q: In a 100-seat parliament under MMP, a party wins 40% of the party vote and 25 local district seats. How many list top-up seats does it receive to reach its proportional share?
What are the two votes a voter casts in a mixed-member proportional system?
choices: One for a local district candidate and one for a party
One for a president and one for a prime minister
Two ranked preferences for the same district
One in the morning and one in the evening

quiz.q: In MMP, what is the term for the extra seats a party keeps when it wins more local districts than its party-vote share alone would entitle it to?
Which pair of countries are standard examples of mixed-member proportional representation?
choices: Germany and New Zealand
Ireland and Malta
France and the United States
Brazil and India

cards.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite: no honest system
cards.fact: Gibbard and Satterthwaite proved every honest-looking ranked voting rule can be gamed by lying about your ranking.
cards.detail: For three or more possible winners, any deterministic ranked voting rule that is not a dictatorship has situations where some voter gets a better result by submitting a false ranking. This is the strategic twin of Arrow's theorem, and the proof reuses Arrow: a strategy-proof, non-dictatorial rule would force a social ranking obeying independence of irrelevant alternatives, which Arrow forbids. Plurality example, 7 voters: 3 rank a>b>c, 2 rank b>c>a, 2 rank c>b>a. First-choice tallies are a=3, b=2, c=2, so a wins. The two c>b>a voters most fear a, their last choice; if they insincerely vote b first, the tally becomes b=4, a=3, c=0, and b wins. They prefer b to a, so lying paid off. Strategic voting is built into the rule, not a defect you can patch.
cards.deploy: Use it to stop searching for a strategy-proof ranked ballot and instead ask how easy a given rule is to manipulate and how much that matters in practice.
cards.counter: Allan Gibbard's broader 1973 result and the mechanism-design literature note escape routes: the theorem assumes deterministic, single-winner, ranked rules over an unrestricted domain, so random tie-breaking, rated ballots, or restricting preferences to single-peaked can dodge it. Empirically, finding a profitable lie can be hard, so manipulability is not the same as routine manipulation.

quiz.q: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem applies once the number of possible winners (alternatives) is at least how many?
What does the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem establish about deterministic, non-dictatorial ranked voting rules with three or more outcomes?
choices: Every such rule is manipulable: some voter can do better by ranking dishonestly
Exactly one such rule is perfectly strategy-proof
Such rules always pick the Condorcet winner
Such rules eliminate the spoiler effect entirely

quiz.q: Which assumption, if dropped, lets a voting rule escape the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem?
choices: Determinism: random tie-breaking can make a rule strategy-proof
Having any voters at all
Counting the ballots correctly
Allowing candidates to run for office

quiz.q: Gibbard-Satterthwaite is often called the strategic counterpart of which earlier impossibility theorem in social choice, whose proof it reuses?

cards.title: May's theorem: why majority rule
cards.fact: For exactly two options, simple majority rule is the only fair rule there is.
cards.detail: Kenneth May proved in 1952 that with just two options, majority rule is the unique decision rule satisfying three conditions. Anonymity: swapping which voter cast which ballot never changes the outcome, so every voter counts equally. Neutrality: relabelling the options A and B just relabels the result, so no option gets a built-in edge and there are no tie-breaks favouring a status quo. Positive responsiveness: if the group was exactly tied and one voter shifts toward A, the group now picks A. Concrete check of responsiveness: take 6 voters tied 3 for A and 3 for B; majority rule outputs a tie. Move one B-voter to A and it is 4 for A, 2 for B, so A wins outright, as positive responsiveness demands. Each condition rules out alternatives: a two-thirds supermajority rule breaks neutrality because it favours one option (the status quo), and a rule that weights some voters more breaks anonymity. The payoff is that the famous impossibility results need 3 or more options to bite.
cards.deploy: Use it to answer 'why majority vote?' for any yes/no or two-candidate decision, and to explain why Arrow's theorem only attacks elections with three or more options.
cards.counter: Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem shows the guarantee collapses at three or more options: no ranked rule can be fair and consistent once cycles like A>B>C>A become possible, so May's clean uniqueness is a two-option special case.

quiz.q: Under simple majority rule with two options, 9 voters split 5 for B and 4 for A, so B wins. What is the smallest number of voters who must switch from B to A for A to win outright?
A voting rule requires a two-thirds supermajority to change the current law, otherwise the current law stands. Which of May's three conditions does this rule violate?
choices: Neutrality
Anonymity
Positive responsiveness
Unanimity

quiz.q: What is the name of the condition in May's theorem that says permuting which voter cast which ballot leaves the result unchanged, so all voters count equally?
May's theorem guarantees majority rule is the unique anonymous, neutral, positively responsive rule under what restriction?
choices: When there are exactly two options
When there are at least three options
When voters number an odd total
When preferences are single-peaked

cards.title: Apportionment and its paradoxes
cards.fact: Turning vote shares into whole seats is impossible to do perfectly, and every method picks its poison.
cards.detail: Seats are integers but vote shares are not, so some rounding rule must decide who gets the leftover seats. Largest-remainder (Hamilton) gives each party the floor of its quota, then hands spare seats to the largest fractional remainders. This can trigger the Alabama paradox: in the 1880 US census, Alabama would have got 8 seats in a 299-seat House but only 7 in a 300-seat House, because enlarging the chamber shifted the remainders. Divisor methods dodge that by ranking quotients instead. Take votes A=100, B=80, C=20 for 7 seats. D'Hondt divides each vote total by 1, 2, 3, and so on, then takes the 7 highest quotients: 100, 80, 50, 40, 33.3, 26.7, 25, giving A=4, B=3, C=0. Largest-remainder (quota 200/7 = 28.57) gives floors A=3, B=2, C=0, summing to 5; the two spare seats go to the largest remainders, B at 0.80 and C at 0.70, for A=3, B=3, C=1. Small party C wins a seat under largest-remainder but is shut out by D'Hondt, which favours large parties; Sainte-Lague/Webster (divisors 1, 3, 5, and so on) treats small parties more evenly.
cards.deploy: Reach for this when a proportional result has to become a fixed number of seats and you must pick a method, or when explaining why two proportional systems hand the same votes different seat counts.
cards.counter: Balinski and Young proved no method can satisfy quota (every party gets its share rounded up or down) and avoid the population paradox at once, so the choice is a value judgement: D'Hondt's pro-large-party tilt suits coalition-building, Sainte-Lague's even treatment suits small-party representation.

quiz.q: Using the largest-remainder method, allocate 10 seats among three parties with votes P=50, Q=30, R=20 (total 100). How many seats does party P receive?
Adding one seat to the total chamber causes a state to LOSE a seat. What is this effect called?
choices: The Alabama paradox
The Condorcet cycle
The efficiency gap
Duverger's law

quiz.q: Which divisor method, using the divisor sequence 1, 2, 3, and so on, systematically tends to favour large parties in seat allocation?
Why do divisor methods such as D'Hondt and Sainte-Lague avoid the Alabama paradox?
choices: They rank quotients rather than distributing leftover seats by fractional remainder
They give every party an equal number of seats
They round all shares up to the next integer
They forbid any party from holding more than half the seats

cards.title: Gerrymandering and the efficiency gap
cards.fact: Gerrymandering wins seats by wasting the other side's votes, and the efficiency gap puts a number on it.
cards.detail: Mapmakers shift seats without shifting opinion using two moves. Packing crams an opponent's voters into a few districts they win by huge margins, so those extra votes are wasted. Cracking splits an opponent thin across many districts so they narrowly lose each one. A vote is wasted if it goes to a loser or sits above the threshold a winner needed; the efficiency gap is one side's wasted votes minus the other's, divided by all votes cast. Take 5 districts of 100 voters each, 500 total, with Parties X and Y tied 250-250 statewide, and use a 51-vote winning threshold. Y packs X into one district (X wins 90-10) and cracks X across the other four (X loses 40-60 in each). X's wasted votes: 160 from the four losses (40 each) plus 39 surplus in its blowout win, totalling 199. Y's wasted votes: 9 surplus in each of four narrow wins plus 10 in its one loss, totalling 46. Efficiency gap = (199 - 46)/500 = 30.6% favouring Y, which takes 4 of 5 seats off a 50-50 vote. Responses include independent redistricting commissions (used in Canada, Australia, and the UK) and court challenges; Wisconsin's 2011 map drew a federal ruling that cited its efficiency gap.
cards.deploy: Use packing and cracking to read a suspicious district map, and the efficiency gap to argue in court or commission that a plan is skewed beyond what the vote split warrants.
cards.counter: Chief Justice Roberts, writing for the US Supreme Court majority in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), held that partisan gerrymandering claims are nonjusticiable political questions beyond the reach of federal courts, kicking the fix to states and legislatures; in the earlier Gill v. Whitford argument he had dismissed partisan-fairness metrics as 'sociological gobbledygook'.

quiz.q: Across 3 equal districts with 300 total voters, Party A's wasted votes total 120 and Party B's wasted votes total 30. Compute the efficiency gap as a percentage, equal to (120 - 30)/300 expressed as a percent.
A mapmaker concentrates almost all of the rival party's supporters into a single district that the rival then wins 85-15. Which tactic is this?
choices: Packing
Cracking
Malapportionment
Apportioning

quiz.q: What is the gerrymandering tactic of splitting an opponent's supporters thinly across many districts so they narrowly lose each one?
In the efficiency-gap calculation, which votes are counted as wasted for a party?
choices: Votes for its losing candidates plus its winners' votes above the needed threshold
Only votes cast for candidates who lost
Every vote cast in a district the party won
Votes from people who later moved away

cards.title: Voting power: the Banzhaf index
cards.fact: In a weighted vote, your power is how often your switch flips the result — not your seat share.
cards.detail: The Banzhaf power index measures a player by how many winning coalitions they are critical in: a player is critical when their leaving turns a winning coalition into a losing one. Each player's index is their count of critical memberships divided by the total over all players. Take three parties with weights 50, 49, 1 and a 51-out-of-100 majority threshold. The winning coalitions are {A,B}, {A,C}, and {A,B,C}. In {A,B} both A and B are critical (drop either and the rest fall below 51); in {A,C} both A and C are critical (A alone is 50, C alone is 1, neither reaches 51); in {A,B,C} only A is critical (without A the other two total 50, but B or C can leave and 51 still holds). So A is critical 3 times, B once, C once — power 3/5, 1/5, 1/5. The party with 49 votes and the party with 1 vote hold the same power, even though one is 49 times larger.
cards.deploy: Use it to judge real bargaining strength in any weighted-vote body — EU Council, shareholder blocs, the US Electoral College, coalition talks — before assuming a big bloc dominates or a small one is a pushover.
cards.counter: Lionel Penrose first defined this swing-based measure in 1946, and John Banzhaf reinvented it in 1965 to attack malapportioned county boards such as Nassau County. Lloyd Shapley and Martin Shubik's Shapley-Shubik index instead counts how often a player is pivotal as a coalition forms in random order, weighting each player by their order of arrival. The two indices can rank the same players differently, so 'voting power' has no single agreed number — the answer depends on which coalition model you adopt.

quiz.q: Under the Banzhaf index, a player is 'critical' in a winning coalition when:
choices: They have the largest weight in that coalition
Their leaving turns that winning coalition into a losing one
They voted first to form the coalition
Their weight exceeds the quota by itself

quiz.q: Three parties have weights 3, 2, and 2; a coalition wins if its total reaches the quota of 4. Enumerate the winning coalitions, find each member who is critical (whose leaving drops the total below 4), and report the Banzhaf power index of the weight-3 party as a decimal.
What name is given to a player who is never critical in any winning coalition and therefore has a Banzhaf power index of zero, regardless of how many votes they hold?
Which alternative index measures voting power by how often a player is pivotal as a coalition is built up in a random order of arrival?
choices: The Gini coefficient
The Shapley-Shubik power index
The Droop quota
The Borda count

cards.title: The SIR model and R0
cards.fact: Split a population into Susceptible, Infected, Recovered, and one ratio R0 = transmission/recovery decides whether the outbreak grows or fizzles.
cards.detail: The SIR model tracks three groups with rate equations: people flow S to I (at transmission rate beta times the chance a susceptible meets an infected) and I to R (at recovery rate gamma). R0 = beta/gamma is the average number of new cases one infected person makes in a fully susceptible population: you stay infectious for about 1/gamma time and infect at rate beta, so you produce beta/gamma cases. If R0 is above 1 each case more than replaces itself and infections climb; below 1 the chain shrinks and the outbreak dies out. Once enough people are immune the average case meets too few susceptibles to replace itself, which happens when the susceptible share drops to 1/R0, so the herd-immunity threshold is 1 - 1/R0. Worked example: R0 = 4 needs 1 - 1/4 = 0.75, so 75% of the population immune to halt spread.
cards.deploy: Use it to judge any outbreak fast: estimate R0, then 1 - 1/R0 tells you the vaccination or immunity coverage needed, and whether a control measure (which cuts beta, raising 1/R0) can push R0 below 1.
cards.counter: The plain SIR model assumes one well-mixed population with constant rates and lifelong immunity. Epidemiologists tracking COVID-19 found R0 is not a fixed constant of a pathogen: it depends on contact patterns, density, and behaviour, so a single number from one setting badly predicts another. Models with age structure, waning immunity (SIRS), or network contact (rather than uniform mixing) routinely override the simple threshold.

quiz.q: A pathogen has basic reproduction number R0 = 5. What fraction of the population must be immune to halt its spread, using the herd-immunity threshold 1 - 1/R0?
In the SIR compartments, by what single letter is the group labelled that has left the infected pool and can no longer transmit (the destination of the final flow)?
R0 in the SIR model is defined as the ratio of which two rates?
choices: transmission rate divided by recovery rate
recovery rate divided by transmission rate
birth rate divided by death rate
infected count divided by susceptible count

cards.title: Hardy–Weinberg: the null model of evolution
cards.fact: Random mating shuffles two alleles into genotype proportions p^2, 2pq, q^2 that never change on their own, so any drift away from them is evolution caught in the act.
cards.detail: Take one gene with two alleles at frequencies p and q where p + q = 1. Under random mating each offspring draws two alleles independently, so the chance of two copies of the first allele is p^2, two of the second is q^2, and one of each (the heterozygote) is 2pq because it can form two ways. These sum to p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = (p+q)^2 = 1. With no selection, mutation, migration, drift (an infinite population), or non-random mating, those frequencies hold generation after generation, so Hardy-Weinberg is the null model: predicted frequencies if nothing is happening. A measured deviation from p^2, 2pq, q^2 is the signal that one of those forces is at work. Worked example: p = 0.7, q = 0.3 gives heterozygote carriers 2pq = 2(0.7)(0.3) = 0.42, the two homozygotes 0.49 and 0.09.
cards.deploy: Use it as the baseline test in population genetics: compute expected genotype frequencies from allele frequencies, compare to observed counts, and read a significant mismatch as evidence of selection, inbreeding, drift, or a genotyping error.
cards.counter: G.H. Hardy framed the result as almost trivial algebra, and that is its limit: it is a null hypothesis, not a description of real populations. Real populations are finite, so genetic drift alone perturbs the frequencies, and assortative mating or selection are common. So passing the test does not prove no evolution (forces can cancel), and the model also assumes one locus with simple Mendelian inheritance.

quiz.q: A gene has two alleles with frequencies p = 0.6 and q = 0.4. Under Hardy-Weinberg, what is the expected frequency of heterozygotes (2pq)?
Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies stay constant across generations only under which condition?
choices: none of selection, mutation, migration, drift, or non-random mating is acting
natural selection is acting
genetic drift is acting
mating is non-random

quiz.q: When observed genotype frequencies match Hardy-Weinberg predictions, the principle is serving as which kind of statistical model (the baseline assuming no forces act)?
Why does the heterozygote term carry the factor of 2 (giving 2pq) while each homozygote term does not?
choices: a heterozygote can form two ways (the first allele from either parent), homozygotes only one way
heterozygotes are always twice as fit
p and q are each doubled before squaring
mutation doubles the heterozygote count each generation

cards.title: Predator and prey: the Lotka–Volterra model
cards.fact: Two rate equations make predators and prey chase each other in a permanent cycle, with predators always peaking a quarter-turn after the prey.
cards.detail: The Lotka-Volterra model couples two populations: prey x grow on their own but lose to predation, dx/dt = alpha*x - beta*x*y; predators y die off on their own but grow by eating prey, dy/dt = -gamma*y + delta*x*y. The cross terms x*y mean encounters between the two drive both losses and gains. The oscillation is built into this feedback, not forced from outside: plenty of prey lets predators multiply, the swollen predator population then eats the prey down, the now-scarce prey starve the predators, and with predators gone the prey rebound, restarting the loop. So predators lag prey by about a quarter period (90 degrees) because they respond to prey abundance rather than set it. The populations orbit a fixed equilibrium at x* = gamma/delta prey and y* = alpha/beta predators; the orbits are closed loops, so the cycle repeats forever without damping.
cards.deploy: Reach for it as the first toy model of any coupled consumer-resource system (predator-prey, herbivore-plant, even host-parasite) to explain why population cycles can be endogenous and why a predator peak trailing a prey peak does not need an external cause.
cards.counter: Ecologists since the 1920s have flagged the assumptions as unrealistic: prey grow exponentially with unlimited food and no carrying capacity, and predators have limitless appetite. The neutral closed orbits are also structurally fragile (any added realism, like logistic prey growth, collapses them to a damped spiral toward equilibrium), so real cycles such as the Canadian lynx-hare data fit better with carrying capacity and a saturating (Holling type-II) functional response.

quiz.q: For Lotka-Volterra parameters alpha = 1, beta = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, delta = 0.02, the equilibrium prey level is gamma/delta. What is that prey equilibrium?
In the Lotka-Volterra model, the predator population peak relative to the prey peak is:
choices: about a quarter period behind (90 degrees lagging)
exactly in phase
exactly half a period ahead
completely random in timing

quiz.q: What single assumption about the prey's food supply is the most cited unrealistic feature of the basic Lotka-Volterra model (the prey have how much food)?
Why is the Lotka-Volterra oscillation called intrinsic rather than externally driven?
choices: the predator-prey feedback alone generates the cycle, with no outside forcing
a seasonal climate signal forces the populations up and down
random shocks restart the cycle each year
predator and prey are independent and only appear to cycle together

cards.title: The logistic map: order into chaos
cards.fact: One line, x_next = r*x*(1-x), goes from a steady population to chaos as you turn a single knob.
cards.detail: Here x is the population as a fraction of carrying capacity (0 to 1) and r is the growth rate; the (1-x) term is crowding that pulls growth down as the population fills the space. For r below 3 the population settles to one steady level: with r=2.5, starting from x=0.4 the first step gives 2.5*0.4*0.6 = 0.6, and it stays at 0.6, which is exactly the predicted fixed point 1-1/r = 1-1/2.5 = 0.6. Past r=3 that single value splits into a 2-cycle (the population alternates between a high and a low year); at r=3.2 it bounces between about 0.80 and 0.51. Raise r more and the cycle doubles to 4, then 8, then 16, faster and faster, until near r=3.57 the doubling piles up and the orbit becomes deterministic chaos: no repeating cycle, and two starting values a hair apart soon diverge completely. Robert May used this in 1976 to argue that a simple, fully deterministic biological rule can produce irregular dynamics with no outside randomness.
cards.deploy: Reach for it to show that 'random-looking' need not mean 'random-caused' — a fixed deterministic rule with sensitive dependence on initial conditions can generate erratic data, so unpredictability alone is not evidence of noise or many hidden variables.
cards.counter: Robert May's own warning is the limit: the logistic map is a deliberate caricature with one species and no age structure, time lags, or spatial spread, so reading literal ecological forecasts off it overreaches. May pressed the modeling-and-teaching point rather than the prediction-of-real-populations point.

quiz.q: Using x_next = r*x*(1-x) with r=3 and x=0.5, compute x_next for one step.
For the logistic map x_next = r*x*(1-x) with r=2, the population settles to the fixed value 1-1/r. What is that value?
As the growth parameter r in the logistic map increases past 3, what happens to the long-run behaviour before chaos sets in?
choices: The single steady value splits into a 2-cycle, then a 4-cycle, doubling repeatedly
The population immediately becomes chaotic with no intermediate stage
The population goes extinct (settles to 0)
The fixed point simply grows larger but stays a single steady value

quiz.q: What term describes the property of the chaotic regime whereby two starting populations that differ by a tiny amount soon diverge completely, even though the rule is deterministic?

cards.title: The species–area relationship
cards.fact: The species count of a habitat grows as a power of its area, S = c*A^z, so shrinking land loses species far slower than you might guess at first.
cards.detail: S is the number of species, A is area, c is a constant for the region, and z is an exponent usually around 0.2 to 0.35. Because it is a power law, taking logs gives log(S) = log(c) + z*log(A), a straight line of slope z on a log-log plot. The exponent controls how harshly habitat loss bites: if a patch keeps a fraction f of its original area, it keeps roughly f^z of its species, so it loses 1 - f^z. With z=0.25 and 90% of the habitat destroyed, f=0.1 and the loss is 1 - 0.1^0.25 = 1 - 0.562 = about 0.44, so roughly 44% of species are committed to extinction even though 90% of the land is gone. The same math explains why losing half an area (f=0.5, z=0.25) costs only 1 - 0.5^0.25 = about 16% of species — the curve is concave, so the first hectares lost cost few species and the last ones cost many.
cards.deploy: Use it to turn a deforestation or land-conversion figure into a first-pass extinction estimate, and to counter the naive linear intuition that losing X% of habitat loses X% of species.
cards.counter: Conservation biologists led by Fangliang He and Stephen Hubbell (2011, Nature) argue the species-area curve systematically overestimates extinction: the area you must add to find the FIRST new species is smaller than the area whose loss eliminates the LAST individual of a species, so running the relationship backward inflates the predicted losses. They proposed using an endemics-area relationship instead.

quiz.q: Using the species-area rule, a habitat reduced to a fraction f of its area keeps f^z of its species. With z=0.3 and half the area lost (f=0.5), what fraction of species is lost (1 - f^z)? Give a decimal.
On a log-log plot of species count versus area, the species-area relationship S = c*A^z appears as a straight line. If z = 0.25, what is the slope of that line?
Why does destroying 90% of a habitat typically eliminate far less than 90% of its species under S = c*A^z?
choices: The relationship is a concave power law with exponent z below 1, so species fall much more slowly than area
Species simply migrate to the remaining 10% and all survive
The exponent z is greater than 1, so losses are amplified
The relationship is linear, so 90% area loss means 90% species loss

quiz.q: What is the name of the mathematical form, of which S = c*A^z is an example, that becomes a straight line when both axes are plotted on logarithmic scales?

cards.title: Map projections: every flat map lies
cards.fact: No flat map can keep both shapes and areas honest, so every projection chooses what to lie about.
cards.detail: A sphere has intrinsic curvature and a flat sheet does not, and Gauss's theorema egregium says curvature cannot change when you bend a surface without stretching it; so unrolling a globe onto paper must stretch something, and a projection can preserve angles (conformal) or areas (equal-area) but not both. The Mercator projection is conformal: it keeps angles and compass bearings correct, so a constant heading is a straight line, which is why sailors used it. The price is that it stretches everything toward the poles, inflating high-latitude land: Greenland appears about as large as Africa, yet Africa's roughly 30 million square kilometres is about 14 times Greenland's roughly 2.2 million. The Gall-Peters projection is equal-area, so it gets Africa's true size right, but it stretches shapes (countries look tall and thin). Choosing between them is one design trade-off — angles versus areas — not a verdict on which map is 'correct'.
cards.deploy: Use it whenever someone treats one map as the true picture: ask what the projection preserves and what it distorts, and match the projection to the task (navigation wants Mercator's bearings; comparing country sizes wants an equal-area map).
cards.counter: Arno Peters argued in the 1970s-80s that Mercator's pole-ward inflation is not a neutral side effect but a political distortion that visually enlarges and centres the wealthier global North while shrinking equatorial regions, and pushed his equal-area map as a corrective. Cartographers such as those in the American Cartographic Association replied that Peters' map distorts shapes badly and that the underlying area-versus-angle trade-off is a geometric necessity, not a Northern conspiracy.

quiz.q: Africa's area is about 30 million square kilometres and Greenland's is about 2.2 million square kilometres. About how many times larger than Greenland is Africa? Give a whole number.
What does the Mercator projection preserve, and what does it distort?
choices: It preserves angles and compass bearings but inflates areas toward the poles
It preserves areas but distorts angles near the equator
It preserves both angles and areas exactly
It preserves distances along every line but distorts colour

quiz.q: Why is it impossible for a flat map to preserve both shapes (angles) and areas everywhere at once?
choices: A sphere's curvature cannot be flattened without stretching, by Gauss's theorema egregium
Ink cannot represent two properties on one sheet
Map-makers have simply never managed it yet
Compass bearings always change the scale of a printed map

quiz.q: What single term describes a map projection that keeps areas true to scale (the property the Gall-Peters projection has and Mercator lacks)?

cards.title: Lanchester's laws of combat
cards.fact: Lanchester's square law says modern firepower scales with the SQUARE of how many units you field, so concentration of force wins decisively.
cards.detail: Frederick Lanchester modelled aimed, ranged combat with two coupled equations: each side loses units at a rate set by how many of the enemy are shooting, dA/dt = -b*B and dB/dt = -a*A, where a and b are per-unit firepower. Solving them gives a conserved quantity, a*A^2 - b*B^2, so with equal weapons the larger force A beats B and ends with sqrt(A^2 - B^2) survivors. Example: 5 units against 3, equal weapons, leaves sqrt(25 - 9) = sqrt(16) = 4 survivors, not the 2 you would get by plain subtraction. The squaring is why a 100 vs 70 fight is lopsided (the 100 keeps about sqrt(10000 - 4900) = 71 units while the 70 are wiped out) and why splitting your army in half is dangerous: each half fights at a quarter of the combined strength, since (1/2)^2 = 1/4. The older LINEAR law fits one-on-one melee, where each soldier engages exactly one enemy and the survivor count is just the plain difference A - B.
cards.deploy: Use it to argue for concentrating force rather than dividing it, and to estimate how a ranged engagement between unequal numbers ends: with equal kit the winner keeps about sqrt(A^2 - B^2) units.
cards.counter: The square law assumes every unit can fire on any target with full information; it breaks down for guerrilla and asymmetric war. Analysts of the Vietnam and counterinsurgency literature note that when one side hides among civilians and cannot be targeted freely, neither the square nor the linear model holds, and historians caution that Lanchester's clean attrition equations omit terrain, morale, logistics and command.

quiz.q: By Lanchester's square law, two forces have equal per-unit firepower. A force of 13 fights a force of 5. How many units does the winning side have left at the end?
Under Lanchester's square law for aimed ranged fire, a force's fighting strength is proportional to which quantity?
choices: The number of units it fields
The square of the number of units it fields
The square root of the number of units it fields
The logarithm of the number of units it fields

quiz.q: Which Lanchester law (square or linear) applies to ancient one-on-one melee combat, where the surviving force is simply the difference between the two army sizes?
Why does Lanchester's square law warn against splitting an army into two equal halves to face a single unified enemy?
choices: Each half fights at only a quarter of the combined force's strength because strength goes as the square of numbers
Two halves cannot share a single commander, which violates unity of command
Splitting doubles the supply lines and so doubles the casualty rate directly
The linear law takes over once a force is divided, making numbers irrelevant

cards.title: Richardson: modelling arms races and war
cards.fact: Lewis Fry Richardson turned an arms race into two coupled equations and found that war sizes obey a power law: many small clashes, rare catastrophes.
cards.detail: Richardson modelled two states' arms spending x and y as feeding back on each other: dx/dt = k*y - a*x + g and dy/dt = l*x - m*y + h. Each state arms up in proportion to the rival's stockpile (the fear terms k*y and l*x) and a fixed grievance (g, h), and arms down in proportion to its own cost burden (the fatigue terms a*x and m*y). When fatigue outweighs fear (a*m > k*l) the system settles to a stable balance; when fear wins it spirals into a runaway race. Separately, in Statistics of Deadly Quarrels he sorted conflicts from 1815-1950 by a base-10 log scale of battle deaths and found their frequency follows a heavy-tailed (Pareto) power law, while wars per year fit a Poisson distribution. He is treated as the initiator of quantitative conflict analysis.
cards.deploy: Cite Richardson as the founding case for using mathematics in IR: reach for the fear-vs-fatigue condition to ask whether a given rivalry is stabilising or escalating, and for the power law to argue that rare giant wars dominate the total death toll.
cards.counter: Hedley Bull, in his 1966 essay 'International Theory: The Case for a Classical Approach,' attacked exactly this kind of formalism, arguing that equations strip out the politics, judgement, intentions and meaning that drive states, so the model's coefficients hide rather than explain the real decisions. The recurring failure mode is treating armament as a mechanical reflex when leaders actually deliberate.

quiz.q: In Richardson's arms-race equations, what does the 'fatigue' term (for example -a*x in dx/dt) represent?
choices: A state arming up in proportion to its rival's stockpile
A state arming down in proportion to the cost burden of its own arms
A fixed grievance that pushes arming up regardless of the rival
Random shocks from domestic politics

quiz.q: In Richardson's model the stockpiles are stable when fatigue outweighs fear, i.e. when the product of the two fatigue coefficients exceeds the product of the two fear coefficients. Take fear coefficients k = 0.6 and l = 0.5, and fatigue coefficients a = 0.9 and m = 0.8. Compute the fatigue product a*m. (The fear product k*l is 0.30, so the system is stable because a*m exceeds it.)

Richardson found that the frequency of wars falls off with their death toll following what kind of heavy-tailed statistical distribution (many small conflicts, rare huge ones)? Name the distribution or the general law.
Which condition makes Richardson's coupled arms-spending system spiral into a runaway race rather than settle to a stable balance?
choices: The fear (response-to-rival) terms outweigh the fatigue (cost) terms
The fatigue terms outweigh the fear terms
The grievance terms are set to zero
Both states spend exactly the same amount

cards.title: Password entropy: counting the guesses
cards.fact: A password's strength against guessing is its entropy in bits, log2 of the number of possible passwords, and each extra bit doubles the attacker's work.
cards.detail: If a password is chosen at random with length L from an alphabet of N symbols, there are N^L possibilities, so its entropy is log2(N^L) = L*log2(N) bits. Worked example: 8 random lowercase letters draw on N = 26, giving 8*log2(26) = 8*4.7 = about 38 bits, which is 26^8 = about 2.1 x 10^11 possibilities (and 2^38 = about 2.7 x 10^11). A 5-word passphrase from a 7776-word list (a Diceware-style list) gives 5*log2(7776) = 5*12.9 = about 65 bits, far stronger, because the alphabet is 7776 'symbols' wide. Since one extra bit doubles the count of guesses, the 27-bit gap between 38 and 65 means the passphrase is about 2^27 (roughly 130 million) times harder to brute-force. The catch is that this formula assumes true randomness: a human-chosen 'P@ssw0rd' follows predictable substitution patterns, so its real guessing entropy is far below what its 8 characters suggest.
cards.deploy: Use L*log2(N) to compare schemes at a glance and to judge whether a policy actually buys security: lengthening the password or widening the alphabet adds bits, and a few random words beat a short tortured string.
cards.counter: NIST Special Publication 800-63B (Burr and colleagues) repudiated the old composition rules built on this counting, because the entropy formula models random passwords while people choose predictable ones; NIST now drops forced symbol-and-digit rules and periodic resets in favour of long passphrases and checks against breached-password lists. The named failure mode is mistaking theoretical entropy for the entropy of human-chosen passwords.

quiz.q: A password is 10 characters chosen at random from an alphabet of 64 symbols. Its entropy in bits is 10*log2(64). How many bits is that?
Adding one bit of entropy to a randomly chosen password has what effect on the number of guesses needed to brute-force it?
choices: It adds one extra guess
It doubles the number of guesses
It increases the guesses tenfold
It squares the number of guesses

quiz.q: The formula L*log2(N) for password entropy assumes the password was chosen with a particular property, which is exactly what a human-chosen string like 'P@ssw0rd' lacks. What is that property?
Why does a random 5-word passphrase from a 7776-word list (about 65 bits) beat 8 random lowercase letters (about 38 bits) on guessing strength?
choices: Each of the 5 picks draws from a much larger alphabet (7776 vs 26), so each contributes far more bits
Words are inherently unguessable in a way that letters are not
Passphrases are exempt from brute-force attacks
Longer strings always have more entropy regardless of the alphabet

cards.title: The birthday attack on hashes
cards.fact: Finding any two inputs that share a hash is far easier than hitting one target hash, so an n-bit hash gives only about n/2 bits of collision resistance.
cards.detail: The birthday problem says that among N equally likely values, a repeat becomes likely after only about sqrt(N) draws (more precisely about 1.18*sqrt(N) for even odds), not N draws. An attacker uses this by hashing many of their own messages and waiting for any pair to collide, rather than chasing a fixed digest. So an n-bit hash, with N=2^n possible outputs, falls to roughly sqrt(2^n) = 2^(n/2) work. A 128-bit hash like MD5 therefore needs only about 2^64 tries to collide, which is feasible, so MD5 is broken for digital signatures. To get 128 bits of real collision resistance you need a 256-bit hash, since 256/2 = 128.
cards.deploy: Use it to size a hash: if you want b bits of collision resistance against the birthday attack, pick a hash with at least 2b output bits. It also explains why you sign a long hash, not a short one, and why two PDFs can be forged to share an MD5 digest.
cards.counter: Bruce Schneier and the wider cryptographic community point out that collision resistance is only one property: for password storage or HMAC, second-preimage and preimage resistance matter more, and those stay at the full n bits, so a shorter hash is not automatically unsafe for every use. The birthday bound bites specifically when an attacker controls both messages, as in signature forgery.

quiz.q: A hash function outputs 80 bits. About how many bits of collision resistance does it give against a birthday attack?
Why is finding a collision easier than matching one specific target hash?
choices: A collision can be ANY matching pair, so the chance of some repeat grows much faster than the chance of hitting a fixed value
Collisions can be computed without running the hash function
Modern hashes deliberately produce frequent collisions
Matching a specific hash needs a quantum computer while a collision does not

quiz.q: Name the 128-bit hash function that is considered broken for digital signatures because a collision needs only about 2^64 work.
You need 128 bits of collision resistance against a birthday attack. What is the minimum hash output length in bits?

cards.title: P versus NP
cards.fact: P vs NP asks whether every problem whose answer can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly, and nobody can prove it either way.
cards.detail: P is the class of problems a computer can solve in polynomial time, where the work grows like n, n^2, or n^3 as the input size n grows. NP is the class where a proposed answer can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding it seems to need brute force. The gap is the difference between checking and finding: verifying that a given seating chart satisfies every guest is fast, but searching all charts may take 2^n steps. At n=50, n^3 is 125,000 while 2^n is over 10^15, so an exponential search is hopeless while the check stays trivial. Thousands of problems are NP-complete, meaning a fast algorithm for any one (Boolean satisfiability, traveling salesman) would give a fast algorithm for all of them; this is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize problems, with a 1,000,000 dollar award, and a 2018 poll found 88 percent of respondents believe P != NP.
cards.deploy: Use it to set expectations: once you recognize a task is NP-complete (scheduling, routing, packing), stop hunting for a guaranteed-fast exact algorithm and reach for heuristics, approximation, or special-case structure. It also explains why public-key cryptography is built on problems easy to verify but believed hard to solve.
cards.counter: Donald Knuth has argued the conventional wisdom may be wrong: he leans toward P = NP being true, though only via a nonconstructive proof that would yield no usable algorithm, which would leave practical cryptography intact even as it overturns the standard belief that P != NP.

quiz.q: What is the defining property of the class NP?
choices: Its problems can have a proposed solution VERIFIED in polynomial time
Its problems can never be solved by any computer
Its problems require exactly exponential time to verify
Its problems are all unsolvable like the halting problem

quiz.q: For an input of size n=20, how many steps does an exponential 2^n algorithm take?
What single word describes the hardest problems in NP, such that a fast algorithm for any one of them would give a fast algorithm for all NP problems?
If someone proved P = NP with a practical fast algorithm, what is the most direct consequence for cryptography?
choices: Much of modern cryptography would break, because it relies on problems being hard to solve but easy to verify
Cryptography would become permanently unbreakable
Nothing, since cryptography does not depend on computational difficulty
Only quantum cryptography would be affected

cards.title: PageRank: ranking by random surfing
cards.fact: PageRank scores a page by the long-run share of time a random web surfer spends on it, computed as the dominant eigenvector of the link matrix.
cards.detail: Picture a surfer who, at each step, follows a random outgoing link from the current page. The fraction of time spent on each page settles into a stationary distribution, which is the dominant eigenvector of the Markov chain built from the links: a page is important if important pages point to it, a recursive definition that the eigenvector resolves at once. The rule is PR(A) = (1-d)/N + d * sum over pages B linking to A of PR(B)/L(B), where N is the number of pages, L(B) is B's outbound link count, and d is the damping factor (about 0.85), modeling a 15 percent chance the surfer jumps to a random page instead of clicking a link, which guarantees a single well-defined answer even with dead ends. Worked example: page X has one inbound link, from page Y; Y has PR 0.4 and two outbound links, with d=0.85 and N=5. Then PR(X) = (1-0.85)/5 + 0.85*(0.4/2) = 0.03 + 0.17 = 0.20.
cards.deploy: Use it whenever you need to rank nodes in a network by endorsement flow: web search, citation analysis, recommending accounts to follow, or ranking proteins and roads. The damping/teleport trick is the general fix for stranding a random walk on sink nodes or disconnected components.
cards.counter: Search-spam practitioners and SEO researchers showed PageRank is gameable by link farms, large rings of pages that link to a target to inflate its rank; Google responded after 2007 by penalizing such schemes, but the manipulability is why raw link counts alone no longer decide rankings.

quiz.q: Page X has a single inbound link from page Y. Y has PageRank 0.6 and 3 outbound links. With damping factor d=0.85 and N=10 total pages, compute PR(X) = (1-d)/N + d*(PR(Y)/L(Y)).
In the random-surfer model, what does a page's PageRank represent?
choices: The long-run fraction of time a random surfer spends on that page
The total number of words on the page
How recently the page was updated
The number of images the page contains

quiz.q: What is the name of the parameter (about 0.85) that gives the surfer a chance to jump to a random page instead of following a link, guaranteeing a unique PageRank solution?
Which mathematical object is PageRank, viewed as the stationary distribution of the link Markov chain?
choices: The dominant (principal) eigenvector of the link matrix
The determinant of the adjacency matrix
The largest singular value of the data
The inverse of the transition matrix

cards.title: Expected utility and rational choice
cards.fact: A rational agent ranks gambles by expected utility, not expected money.
cards.detail: Expected utility of an option is the sum over its possible outcomes of (probability of the outcome) times (utility of that outcome), and you pick the option with the largest sum. The shift from money to utility matters because utility usually rises with diminishing returns: the millionth euro is worth less to you than the first. That dissolves the St. Petersburg paradox, a coin-flip bet paying 2 euros if heads comes on flip 1, 4 on flip 2, 8 on flip 3, and so on. Its expected MONEY value is 2 times one-half plus 4 times one-quarter plus 8 times one-eighth ... = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinite, yet nobody will pay much to play. With a utility that grows like log2(money), the payoff 2^n on flip n is worth n utils, so the expected UTILITY is the sum of n times (1/2^n), which equals exactly 2 utils, and a modest stake is rational. Von Neumann and Morgenstern proved that anyone whose preferences satisfy a few consistency axioms (completeness, transitivity, continuity, independence) behaves AS IF maximising some expected-utility function. Quick check: a sure 50 utils versus a gamble of 50 percent nothing and 50 percent 110 utils; the gamble's expected utility is 0.5 times 0 plus 0.5 times 110 = 55, so the axioms say take the gamble.
cards.deploy: Use it to value any decision under risk: convert each outcome to your own utility scale (not its cash value), weight by probability, and compare sums. It also flags when a 'huge expected payoff' is a mirage because the utility of the money is bounded.
cards.counter: Allais's paradox shows people reliably flip their choice between two gambles when a common component is added, violating the independence axiom; Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory replaces it with loss aversion and a probability-weighting curve that overweights small chances. These are documented, replicated descriptions of how real choosers depart from the axioms, not stylistic quibbles.

quiz.q: A gamble gives a 25 percent chance of 80 utils and a 75 percent chance of 40 utils. What is its expected utility, in utils?
Why does using utility instead of money dissolve the St. Petersburg paradox, where the bet's expected money value is infinite?
choices: Diminishing marginal utility makes the utility of ever-larger prizes grow slowly enough that the expected utility is finite
The probability of each later payoff is rounded down to zero
Utility is always exactly proportional to money, so the infinity cancels
The casino caps the payout, so the money sum is finite after all

quiz.q: What did von Neumann and Morgenstern establish about preferences that satisfy axioms like completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence?
choices: Such preferences can be represented as if the agent maximises an expected-utility function
