The experiment ended through a combination of Stalinist Republican suppression (the Barcelona May Days of 1937, when Communist-influenced police attacked CNT-controlled buildings) and eventual military defeat by Franco. Both Marxists and conservatives drew the lesson that the anarchists' rejection of political and military centralisation made them unable to sustain a war effort; anarchists drew the lesson that accepting Republican state structures led to their destruction by ostensible allies.

Murray Bookchin's **libertarian municipalism** (from the 1980s) proposed a synthesis: use local democratic assemblies — not unions or communes — as the vehicle for social transformation, building a 'dual power' alongside existing institutions until confederal assemblies can replace the state. This influenced the Kurdish political movement in Rojava (northern Syria), which implemented 'democratic confederalism' in its constitution. Internal anarchist debates include: whether property markets can co-exist with anti-capitalism (mutualism: yes; anarcho-communism: no); whether militant action ('propaganda of the deed') is compatible with anti-authoritarian principles; and how to coordinate complex production without market prices.

quiz.q: Anarcho-syndicalism's proposed mechanism for ending capitalism is:
choices: A vanguard party seizing state power on behalf of the working class
The general strike, with unions providing the organising skeleton of the new society
A gradual accumulation of cooperative economic power through mutual-aid societies
Electoral victory by a workers' party committed to immediate abolition of private property

quiz.q: The Barcelona May Days (1937) involved conflict between which two forces within the Republican side of the Spanish Civil War?
choices: Anarchist CNT-FAI forces and Trotskyist POUM militias
Communist-influenced Republican police and CNT-controlled institutions
The Spanish army and armed workers defending their factories
Basque nationalist troops and Catalan anarchist militias

quiz.q: Murray Bookchin's libertarian municipalism proposes which vehicle for social transformation, differing from both classical anarchism and Marxism?
choices: Revolutionary industrial unions leading a general strike
Local democratic assemblies building a confederal dual power alongside existing institutions
Armed rural communes organised on the model of the Spanish collectives
A libertarian political party competing in elections to win state power and then dismantle it

quiz.q: The main tension within anarcho-syndicalism over 'propaganda of the deed' (political violence) is:
choices: Whether it is tactically effective in building mass movements
Whether violence as a means is compatible with anti-authoritarian ends — does revolutionary violence reproduce the hierarchical logic anarchism opposes?
Whether it gives the state justification to increase repression
Whether it alienates middle-class sympathisers needed for a majority movement

cards.title: Lenin: the vanguard party and democratic centralism
cards.fact: In *What Is to Be Done?* (1902), Lenin argued that the working class by itself develops only 'trade union consciousness' — fighting for better wages within capitalism; a disciplined party of professional revolutionaries must bring revolutionary consciousness 'from without'.

layers.body: Lenin's central addition to Marxism was not economic theory but organisational: the working class needs a party that is distinct from it — not simply workers' representatives, but professional revolutionaries with theoretical clarity and strict discipline who lead the class rather than merely expressing its existing demands.

The 1902 pamphlet diagnoses why the Russian labour movement was stuck in economic demands (shorter hours, higher wages) rather than political revolution: workers, shaped by the immediate conditions of factory life, develop only 'trade union consciousness.' Revolutionary political consciousness must be introduced from outside the economic struggle, by a party with access to theory.

**Democratic centralism**: the party's operating principle. All members participate in debate before a decision; once a decision is made, all members implement it without further public dissent. This produces a party capable of coordinated action rather than fragmented local initiatives. Democratic centralism became the defining organisational form of all Communist parties after 1917.

The vanguard model has two distinct interpretations. In the 1902 context, it describes a small illegal organisation in Tsarist Russia where open organisation was impossible — the discipline was a response to repression, not a permanent principle. Some Leninists read it this way: the model is situationally appropriate, not universally prescribed. Others treat it as a permanent truth about the relationship between party and class.

Rosa Luxemburg (*Organisational Questions of the Russian Social Democracy*, 1904) responded immediately: centralising decision-making in a small leadership produces a party that substitutes itself for the working class rather than representing it. The 'ultracentralism' Lenin prescribed would result in the party blindly following its central committee, undermining the mass initiative that revolution actually requires.

The key long-run debate is whether democratic centralism is compatible with internal party democracy. Trotsky (later) and Luxemburg (immediately) argued that Lenin's model created structures that could not prevent the degeneration that occurred under Stalin — the central committee that was supposed to be democratically elected and accountable became self-perpetuating. Opponents from the libertarian left (council communists, Pannekoek) argued the vanguard model is inherently elitist and reproduces bourgeois hierarchical organisation within the workers' movement. Leninists reply that the alternative — waiting for spontaneous mass revolution — produces fragmentation and defeat.

quiz.q: What does Lenin mean by 'trade union consciousness'?
choices: Workers who join unions rather than political parties
Working-class demands focused on wages and conditions within capitalism, rather than challenging the system itself
Consciousness that develops from reading Marxist texts distributed through trade unions
A stage of political development that naturally leads to revolutionary consciousness over time

quiz.q: Democratic centralism means:
choices: Free debate at all times, with majority votes binding only on operational decisions
Open debate before a decision, then unified implementation without public dissent after it
Election of leaders by secret ballot, with no debate permitted before votes
Central committee decisions implemented locally with adaptations chosen democratically

quiz.q: Luxemburg's 1904 reply to Lenin argued that his model would produce what outcome?
choices: A party too indisciplined to survive Tsarist repression
A party that substitutes itself for the working class and eventually becomes self-perpetuating rather than accountable
A party split between intellectuals and workers, with neither able to lead
A party dominated by spontaneous mass uprisings with no central coordination

quiz.q: Council communists (Pannekoek) differed from Leninists on the party question by arguing:
choices: The party should be even more centralised than Lenin prescribed
Workers' own councils (soviets), not a party, should be the primary organ of revolutionary power
No organisation at all is needed — spontaneous action will produce revolution
The party must be a mass party with millions of members rather than a small professional cadre

cards.title: Leninism in practice: imperialism, 1917 and the Soviet state
cards.fact: Lenin's *Imperialism* (1916) explained WWI as a war among capitalist powers competing for colonial territories; his April Theses (1917) broke with the Mensheviks' two-stage theory and opened the path to October; the Soviet state that followed dissolved the Constituent Assembly when the Bolsheviks lost the election.

layers.body: Three moments define how Lenin translated revolutionary theory into practice: the imperialism analysis (why WWI was a capitalist war); the April Theses (the strategic break that made October possible); and the institutional choices of the first months of Soviet power.

Lenin's *Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism* (1916) argues that the advanced capitalist economies had reached monopoly stage — finance capital merging with industrial capital — and were exporting capital abroad to earn higher returns in less developed markets. Competing capitalist powers therefore went to war over access to colonial territories and investment zones. This explained WWI as a war among imperialist rivals rather than a defensive war by any party.

A political corollary: the reformism of European Social Democratic parties was partly funded by the super-profits flowing from colonial exploitation. Workers in imperial cores were receiving a share of colonial surplus, making them less revolutionary — they had a stake in the imperial system.

Lenin returned to Russia in April 1917 with a set of theses that surprised his own party. The mainstream Bolshevik position had been to give conditional support to the Provisional Government for completing the bourgeois-democratic stage of the revolution. Lenin broke with this: no support to the Provisional Government; all power to the Soviets (workers' and soldiers' councils); immediate peace with Germany. This directly contradicted the Menshevik 'two-stage' theory (bourgeois revolution first, socialist later) and isolated Lenin initially even within the Bolshevik leadership.

The October seizure of power (7 November 1917 in the new calendar) was followed by immediate decrees: peace, land redistribution, workers' control of factories. The Constituent Assembly elections (November 1917) produced a Socialist Revolutionary majority; the Bolsheviks came second. The Assembly met once (January 1918) and was dissolved by Red Guard soldiers. Lenin justified this: the Soviets were a higher form of democracy than a parliamentary assembly.

The dissolution of the Constituent Assembly is the single act most cited by non-Marxist critics as evidence that Leninism is incompatible with democracy: the Bolsheviks dissolved the only democratically elected institution in Russia when they lost the election. Leninists reply that the Soviets — direct representation of workers and soldiers — were a superior form of democracy to parliamentary representation, and that the counter-revolutionary conditions of 1917–18 made normal democratic procedure impossible. The imperialism thesis has been updated repeatedly: dependency theorists (Frank, Cardoso), world-systems theory (Wallerstein), and Rosa Luxemburg's own imperialism analysis provide alternatives that agree capitalism is inherently expansionary but differ on the mechanism.

quiz.q: Lenin's imperialism thesis explains WWI as caused by what structural dynamic?
choices: German militarism and the Kaiser's personal ambitions
Competing capitalist powers going to war over colonial territories and investment zones
Nationalist movements in the Balkans triggering the alliance system
A crisis of overproduction requiring new markets, leading all powers to expand simultaneously

quiz.q: The April Theses broke with what position held by most Bolsheviks before Lenin's return?
choices: That Russia needed a vanguard party before any revolutionary action was possible
That the Bolsheviks should give conditional support to the Provisional Government while the bourgeois-democratic stage of revolution was completed
That socialist revolution required prior industrialisation, making Russia not yet ready
That the Soviets should become advisory bodies to the Provisional Government rather than competing with it

quiz.q: The Constituent Assembly election of November 1917 produced what result, and what happened next?
choices: Bolshevik majority; they formed a government and implemented their programme through parliament
Socialist Revolutionary majority; the Bolsheviks dissolved the Assembly after one session when it did not support Soviet power
Menshevik majority; the Bolsheviks refused to recognise the result and called new elections
No clear majority; proportional coalition government was formed with Bolshevik participation

quiz.q: Lenin's corollary from the imperialism thesis — that European workers in imperial cores were less revolutionary — depended on what claim?
choices: Imperial workers were more educated and therefore more conservative
A share of colonial super-profits flowed to workers in imperial powers, giving them a stake in the imperial system
Industrial concentration in imperial cores produced a labour aristocracy that controlled trade unions
Universal male suffrage in imperial countries gave workers a peaceful route to change that colonial workers lacked

cards.title: Stalinism: socialism in one country
cards.fact: Stalin's 'socialism in one country' held that the USSR could build socialism alone without world revolution; combined with rapid forced industrialisation, collectivisation of agriculture, one-party totalitarian control and systematic elimination of opponents, this became the model Soviet socialist state.

layers.body: After Lenin's death (1924), Stalin won the succession struggle by arguing that the USSR did not need to wait for revolution elsewhere — it could build socialism within its own borders. This framed the Communist International as a tool of Soviet state policy rather than an organ of world revolution.

'Socialism in one country' was the key strategic doctrine distinguishing Stalin from Trotsky, who held that a socialist state could not survive in permanent isolation (the permanent revolution thesis). Stalin's position allowed the USSR to pursue its own economic development regardless of the fate of revolution elsewhere, and to frame Soviet foreign policy as state interest rather than internationalist obligation.

The Five-Year Plans (from 1928) drove industrialisation through centralised planning: production targets were set by Gosplan, enforced through party structures and the secret police. The USSR went from a largely agrarian economy to a major industrial power within two decades. Agriculture was collectivised by merging smallholdings into collective farms (kolkhozy) under state direction, accompanied by the 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class.'

The collectivisation campaign involved compulsory seizure of grain and livestock. The resulting famine of 1932–33 (known as the Holodomor in Ukraine) caused deaths estimated by historians at 3.5–7 million in Ukraine alone; other areas of the USSR were also affected. The kulak category was applied broadly; hundreds of thousands were executed or deported to labour camps.

The Great Purge (1936–38) involved show trials of former Bolshevik leaders producing public confessions (later attributed to sustained interrogation under coercion), mass executions, and the imprisonment of millions in the Gulag system of forced-labour camps. Most of the original revolutionary leadership was killed or imprisoned. Theoretically, this was the final consolidation of: party-state fusion (all institutions subordinated to the party, the party to Stalin); a **cult of personality** elevating Stalin as both practical leader and theoretical genius; **socialist realism** as the mandatory aesthetic doctrine; and ideological control over scientific inquiry (Lysenko's rejection of Mendelian genetics).

Hannah Arendt (*The Origins of Totalitarianism*, 1951) compared Stalinism and Nazism as two forms of **totalitarianism** — both distinct from ordinary authoritarianism by their aim at total social transformation through terror and ideology, and their destruction of all intermediate institutions between individual and state. This comparative framework is contested: critics argue the Holocaust's logic (racial annihilation as an end in itself) differs structurally from Stalinist terror (instrumental elimination of political enemies). Historians Hobsbawm and Deutscher contextualised Stalinist industrialisation as a response to genuine external threat and technological backwardness. Anti-Stalinist Marxists (Trotskyists) argue the system was a degeneration of the revolution's gains, caused by material isolation and the Bolshevik substitutionist party model.

quiz.q: Stalin's 'socialism in one country' doctrine was developed in opposition to whose competing thesis?
choices: Bukharin's 'right deviation' proposing slower industrialisation through NEP
Trotsky's 'permanent revolution' holding that socialism could not survive in isolation without world revolution
Zinoviev's 'left opposition' demanding faster industrialisation and less market tolerance
Kamenev's argument for a coalition government with Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries

quiz.q: The Five-Year Plans drove industrialisation through which institutional mechanism?
choices: Market incentives and private investment guided by indicative planning
Centralised targets set by Gosplan, enforced through party structures and the secret police
Worker-managed factories setting their own output targets under Soviet democracy
Joint ventures with Western companies bringing capital and technology

quiz.q: The Great Purge (1936–38) eliminated most of the original Bolshevik leadership. What method produced the public confessions seen in the Moscow show trials?
choices: Genuine ideological conviction after internal party investigation
Sustained interrogation under coercion, as later documented by survivors and NKVD archives
Secret ballot within the party Central Committee declaring these leaders enemies
Voluntary confession as a revolutionary duty to demonstrate loyalty to the party

quiz.q: Arendt's totalitarianism analysis distinguishes totalitarian regimes from ordinary authoritarianism by which characteristic?
choices: Totalitarian regimes are more violent; authoritarian regimes rely on consent

Totalitarian regimes aim at total social transformation through terror and ideology, destroying all intermediate institutions; ordinary authoritarian regimes want conformity but leave private life alone
Totalitarian regimes have charismatic leaders; authoritarian regimes are run by bureaucratic committees
Totalitarian regimes claim a scientific basis; authoritarian regimes rely on traditional or religious authority

cards.title: Trotskyism: permanent revolution and the degenerated workers' state
cards.fact: Trotsky argued in *The Revolution Betrayed* (1936) that the USSR under Stalin was neither capitalist nor genuinely socialist but a 'degenerated workers' state' — workers' property remained but a bureaucratic caste had captured political power and must be removed by political revolution.

layers.body: Permanent revolution: socialist revolution in backward countries cannot wait for a bourgeois phase — the workers must lead both stages without pause, and the revolution must spread internationally or degenerate. Degenerated workers' state: this degeneration already happened in the USSR — not into capitalism, but into bureaucratic caste rule over a socialist economic base.

Developed from 1905, the thesis holds: in late-developing countries where capitalism arrived recently and the bourgeoisie is too weak and tied to imperial capital to lead a democratic revolution, the proletariat must lead. But if the proletariat leads the democratic revolution (against feudalism and imperial domination), it will not stop there — it will push toward the socialist stage. Therefore: no 'two stages' (bourgeois-democratic first, socialist later), just a continuous process. And: the revolution must spread internationally or it will be isolated, distorted and eventually crushed by surrounding capitalism.

In *The Revolution Betrayed* (1936), Trotsky analyses the USSR: the basic achievement of the revolution — nationalised, planned production — remains. The social revolution (transforming property relations) is not reversed. But political power has been captured by a bureaucratic caste. This caste is not a class, because it does not own property individually — it holds power through its position in the party-state apparatus. It is a parasitic caste that defends its privileges through the police state but does not own the means of production.

The implication: the USSR requires a **political revolution** — replacing the bureaucracy with genuine Soviet democracy — but not a social revolution (property relations remain socialist). Trotskyists should therefore defend the USSR against capitalist imperialism (because the social gains remain worth defending) while opposing the Stalinist regime politically.

Trotsky founded the **Fourth International** in 1938. He was killed in Mexico City in August 1940 by a Stalinist agent.

Three main alternatives emerged within the Marxist tradition. Tony Cliff (founder of the International Socialists): the USSR is **state capitalist** — the bureaucracy functions as a collective capitalist class, and the law of value operates through military competition between states. Milovan Đilas (*The New Class*, 1957): the bureaucracy is a genuine **new ruling class** — it exercises effective ownership through its control of state property. Max Shachtman: **bureaucratic collectivism** — a new mode of production distinct from both capitalism and socialism. The choice between these analyses carries practical consequences: it determines whether socialist organisations should critically defend the USSR against imperialism (Trotsky's position) or oppose it unconditionally (Cliff and Shachtman's positions).

quiz.q: The 'two-stage' theory (bourgeois revolution first, socialist second) was associated with the Mensheviks. Trotsky's 'permanent revolution' rejected it by arguing:
choices: Both stages must happen simultaneously, not sequentially
In backward countries, the proletariat must lead both stages without pause, as the bourgeoisie is too weak to complete even the democratic stage
The socialist stage must come first, with the democratic stage following automatically from it
There are no stages — revolution happens all at once or not at all

quiz.q: Trotsky argues that restoring Soviet democracy requires a 'political revolution', not a 'social revolution'. What is the distinction?
choices: Political revolution changes who rules; social revolution changes economic relations. Since Soviet property is still nationalised, changing the political superstructure suffices
Political revolution is peaceful; social revolution involves violence. Only peaceful change is permissible
Political revolution changes the constitution; social revolution changes culture and everyday life
Social revolution is already complete under Stalin; only the political forms need updating

quiz.q: Tony Cliff's 'state capitalism' thesis differs from Trotsky's 'degenerated workers' state' in which crucial respect?
choices: Cliff argues property was privatised under Stalin, completing the capitalist restoration Trotsky denied
Cliff argues the bureaucracy functions as a collective capitalist class and the law of value operates through military competition, making the USSR capitalist despite formal nationalisation
Cliff argues the Fourth International should support Soviet foreign policy unconditionally against imperialism
Cliff denies the bureaucracy exists as a distinct social stratum — he sees the USSR as a genuine workers' state

quiz.q: Trotsky was assassinated in Mexico City in August 1940. Who organised the killing?
choices: The Nazi Gestapo, which feared his anti-fascist agitation in exile
A faction within the Fourth International that disagreed with his analysis of the Soviet state
Stalin's NKVD, which recruited Ramón Mercader to infiltrate Trotsky's household
The Mexican government, which accused him of fomenting communist revolution

cards.title: Maoism: mass line and people's war
cards.fact: Mao adapted Marxism-Leninism to a predominantly peasant country: the peasantry — not the urban proletariat — became the primary revolutionary force, led through the 'mass line' method, fighting through prolonged rural guerrilla war.

layers.body: Classical Marxism expected revolution in the most industrialised countries, led by urban workers. China in the 1920s–40s had a tiny urban proletariat and a vast peasantry under semi-colonial conditions. Mao's strategic innovations addressed this gap.

**The mass line** (*On the Mass Line*, 1943): the party gathers dispersed, unformed ideas from the masses, concentrates them through Marxist analysis into a correct political line, then returns that line to the masses to test and propagate until the masses embrace it as their own. This is a cycle — from the masses, to the masses — distinguishing Maoist leadership from both top-down command and unled spontaneity. The party learns from the people while leading them.

**People's war** (*Problems of Strategy in China's Revolutionary War*, 1936): surround the cities from the countryside; build base areas in rural regions; engage in protracted guerrilla warfare while building political support among the peasantry; gradually extend control. This reverses the classical Leninist model of urban insurrection and became a template for liberation movements in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

**New Democracy**: Mao proposed that for semi-colonial countries not yet ready for direct socialist transition, a bloc of four classes — proletariat, peasantry, urban petty bourgeoisie and national bourgeoisie — under Communist Party leadership should first complete the anti-imperialist and anti-feudal tasks. This justified alliances with nationalist forces (the Guomindang in the United Front) during the war against Japan. The national bourgeoisie was a temporary ally, not an enemy; it would become an enemy only after the democratic stage was complete.

The people's war strategy succeeded: the People's Liberation Army, starting from rural base areas, encircled and defeated the Guomindang forces, proclaiming the People's Republic on 1 October 1949.

The applicability of Mao's strategy outside China is contested. In Vietnam, the NLF combined people's war with urban political work in a different mix. The Shining Path in Peru and the Naxalite movement in India applied the strategy with very different outcomes. Debray's *Revolution in the Revolution?* (1967) argued that the Cuban experience showed the guerrilla *foco* could work without a mass party base, contradicting Mao's emphasis on political work. Post-Maoist Chinese Communist Party historiography maintains the strategic correctness of the people's war period while criticising the Cultural Revolution phase that followed.

quiz.q: The mass line method has three steps. Which of these correctly describes the full cycle?
choices: Issue directives from the centre, monitor compliance through cadres, punish deviation
Gather ideas from the masses, concentrate them through Marxist analysis, return the resulting line to the masses to test and spread
Read Marxist theory, apply it to local conditions, report outcomes to party leadership
Identify the most oppressed group, build their political consciousness, lead them in armed struggle

quiz.q: People's war reverses the classic Leninist model of revolution. What is the spatial reversal?
choices: Strike rural areas first to cut off the cities' food supply
Surround the cities from the countryside, building strength through rural base areas and guerrilla warfare
Begin with a naval blockade, then land urban insurrectionists from the sea
Capture the capital first by infiltrating the military, then use state power to pacify the countryside

quiz.q: Mao's 'New Democracy' thesis justified temporary alliances with which class that Leninist theory typically treated as an enemy?
choices: The landlord class, to prevent them joining the Japanese
The national bourgeoisie, as a temporary anti-imperialist partner before the socialist stage
The urban petty bourgeoisie, which controlled small retail and artisan production
Western imperialist powers, whose rivalry with Japan made them potential allies

quiz.q: The people's war strategy's central logistical advantage over the classical urban insurrection model is:
choices: Urban workers are more politically developed than peasants and therefore more reliable
Rural base areas allow the revolutionary force to grow gradually and survive setbacks without being destroyed in a single urban confrontation
The peasantry is the majority class and will always vote for the revolution democratically
Cities have strong garrison forces; rural areas have fewer troops and are easier to hold

cards.title: Maoism: continuous revolution and the Sino-Soviet split
cards.fact: Mao's later theory held that bourgeois elements persist inside the Communist Party itself after the revolution — requiring continuous struggle against them; this produced the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) and the Sino-Soviet split over Khrushchev's 'revisionism'.

layers.body: Classical Marxism treats revolution as the transition to power; Mao added a theory of what happens after power is achieved. The class struggle does not end with the seizure of state power — it continues inside the party itself, requiring ongoing mobilisation to prevent 'capitalist restoration.'

By the 1950s–60s, Mao developed the theory that **cadres** (full-time party officials) and **intellectuals** who acquired power after the revolution tend toward conservatism and privilege — becoming 'capitalist roaders' who would restore capitalism without a revolutionary push. The solution: continuous mass mobilisation to keep the revolution alive against internal bureaucratic consolidation. This was directed both at the Soviet Union (Khrushchev's 'revisionism') and at Mao's rivals within the CCP leadership (Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping).

The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) was launched to attack the 'Four Olds' (old customs, culture, habits, ideas) and 'capitalist roaders' within the party. Red Guards — student youth organisations — mobilised in millions to denounce teachers, officials and intellectuals. Universities and secondary schools were closed for years. Books, artworks and cultural heritage were destroyed. Officials (including Deng Xiaoping twice) were removed, publicly humiliated and sent to the countryside for 're-education through labour.'

Estimates of deaths range from several hundred thousand to over a million; millions more were imprisoned, persecuted or had their careers permanently disrupted. The movement was factional and chaotic despite official guidance; the People's Liberation Army eventually had to restore order in 1969, and some Red Guard factions were sent to the countryside en masse.

The **Sino-Soviet split** (formally 1960): after Khrushchev's 1956 'secret speech' denouncing Stalin, Mao accused Soviet leadership of revisionism — abandoning revolutionary principles for accommodation with capitalism and imperialism. China and the USSR competed for influence over Communist parties worldwide; the split divided the international communist movement.

The CCP's 1981 resolution called the Cultural Revolution a 'comprehensive, long-drawn-out and grave blunder' while maintaining Mao's overall historical importance ('70% positive, 30% negative'). Historians Frank Dikötter (*The Cultural Revolution*, 2016) and MacFarquhar and Schoenhals (*Mao's Last Revolution*, 2006) document the violence and factional chaos in detail. Outside China, Maoist parties that adopted continuous revolution as a permanent principle (Shining Path in Peru, Communist Party of India Marxist-Leninist factions) produced very different outcomes from the Chinese model. The mass line method has been extracted from the Cultural Revolution context and used in community organising traditions globally, separate from Maoism's Chinese political history.

quiz.q: The Cultural Revolution's key theoretical premise was that:
choices: A foreign capitalist threat required cultural mobilisation to prepare for war
Bourgeois elements persist inside the Communist Party after the revolution, requiring continuous mass struggle to prevent capitalist restoration
The Soviet model of economic planning should be replaced with a Chinese model developed through mass participation
China's traditional culture was incompatible with communism and had to be replaced before the socialist transition could complete

quiz.q: The Sino-Soviet split (1960) was triggered by which event or speech?
choices: Stalin's death in 1953, which created a power vacuum Mao sought to fill
Khrushchev's 1956 'secret speech' denouncing Stalin, which Mao attacked as revisionist abandonment of revolutionary principles
The Soviet refusal to share nuclear weapons technology with China in 1959
Disagreement over the Korean War ceasefire terms and Soviet support for negotiations

quiz.q: Red Guards — the main instrument of the Cultural Revolution — were primarily composed of which social group?
choices: Factory workers seeking to extend workers' control to political institutions
Student youth mobilised to attack 'capitalist roaders' in the party, intellectuals and traditional culture
Peasants who had benefited from land reform and were loyal to Mao personally
Veteran PLA soldiers demobilised after the Korean War and assigned to political education

quiz.q: The CCP's official 1981 assessment of Mao's overall historical record described it as:
choices: Wholly positive — the Cultural Revolution was necessary despite its costs
70% positive, 30% negative — maintaining his importance while designating the Cultural Revolution a blunder
Negative overall — the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution negated his earlier achievements
Ambiguous — the party declined to make a definitive assessment to avoid factional conflict

cards.title: Fascism: the nation reborn
cards.fact: Roger Griffin's definition: fascism is a 'palingenetic ultranationalism' — a political myth of national rebirth from decadence, positioning the nation above all divisions of class or individual and rejecting both liberal individualism and Marxist class conflict as national disintegration.

layers.body: Fascism's organising idea is national rebirth: the nation was once great, has been corrupted or humiliated by internal enemies (liberals, Marxists, ethnic minorities depending on variant), and is now called to regenerate through collective will, struggle and sacrifice under strong leadership.

Fascism takes its name from the *fasces* (bundle of rods bound around an axe — Roman symbol of collective strength) adopted by Mussolini's *Fasci di Combattimento*, founded March 1919. Key features: **ultranationalism** — the nation is the supreme value, overriding individual rights and class interests; **rejection of liberal individualism** — parliamentary debate and individual liberty produce weakness and national disunity; **rejection of Marxist class conflict** — dividing the nation into opposing classes serves the enemies of national unity; **glorification of will and action** — struggle and sacrifice are presented as expressions of national vitality; **authoritarian leadership** — the leader embodies the national will rather than representing competing interests.

**Corporatism**: workers and employers are organised into state-supervised 'corporations' that mediate relations nationally, replacing class conflict with managed collaboration. Independent trade unions were abolished.

Studies of fascism's social base (Seymour Martin Lipset and others) identify the lower middle class — small shopkeepers, artisans, rural proprietors, clerks — as disproportionately represented, though fascism attracted support across class lines. The lower middle class is particularly susceptible to 'status anxiety': threatened economically from above by big capital and from below by organised labour.

Italian fascism in practice (Mussolini, 1922–45): preserved capitalist property relations while subordinating business to state economic direction; abolished independent unions; controlled press, education and cultural life; was less doctrinally rigid than Nazism. The racial laws adopted in 1938 were imported from Germany rather than arising from foundational Italian fascist ideology. The March on Rome (October 1922): King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini Prime Minister to forestall potential unrest — not a military conquest.

Griffin's 'palingenetic ultranationalism' is the most widely cited academic definition, allowing identification of fascist movements across different national contexts by their shared mythic structure rather than surface features. Robert Paxton (*The Anatomy of Fascism*, 2004) shifted analysis from ideology to practice: fascism is better understood through what it does than what it claims — its characteristic modes of action (squadrism, seizure of state power, use of state power against labour while preserving capitalism) define it more reliably than its incoherent doctrine. Marxist interpretations (Thalheimer, Gramsci) analyse fascism as the resolution of a class stalemate — the state appearing autonomous while serving capital against a labour movement too strong to be defeated by normal means. The debate about which contemporary movements qualify as fascist vs 'merely' authoritarian nationalist is active in current scholarship.

quiz.q: Griffin defines fascism as 'palingenetic ultranationalism'. What does 'palingenetic' specifically mean?
choices: Passed down through biological inheritance — the nation as a racial organism
A myth of rebirth — the nation portrayed as called to regenerate from decadence and humiliation
Derived from pagan pre-Christian traditions rather than Enlightenment rationalism
Produced by the same conditions in different countries simultaneously — hence all variants share core features

quiz.q: Fascist corporatism replaces independent trade unions with:
choices: Worker-controlled enterprises under state supervision
State-supervised corporations combining workers and employers of the same industry under a national unity framework
A free market in labour with government arbitration for wage disputes
Party cells within workplaces reporting directly to the ministry of labour

quiz.q: The March on Rome (October 1922) is often described as a coup. What actually happened?
choices: Mussolini's Blackshirts fought and defeated the Italian army in street battles across three days
King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini Prime Minister to forestall potential unrest — no military conquest occurred
The Italian parliament voted Mussolini into power by a constitutional two-thirds majority
A military mutiny handed power to Mussolini, who had not organised the march personally

quiz.q: Paxton argues fascism is better defined by what it does than what it claims. Which feature does he most emphasise?
choices: The palingenetic myth of national rebirth that unifies its adherents ideologically
The characteristic pattern of squadrism, seizure of power and then use of state power against labour while preserving capitalism
The leader cult that concentrates decision-making in a single charismatic figure
The corporate state structure that eliminates class conflict through managed collaboration

cards.title: Nazism: race and the Holocaust
cards.fact: National Socialism differs from other fascisms by placing biological race — not nation, class or state — at its centre: history is a racial struggle, the 'Aryan' race is threatened by Jews who simultaneously control capitalism, communism and liberal democracy, and physical destruction of the enemy is a necessity, not an expedient.

layers.body: Fascism defines the nation politically and culturally; Nazism defines it biologically, by blood. This difference is structural, not incidental — it produces a different kind of enemy, a different internal logic, and an exterminatory rather than merely repressive relationship with designated groups.

Hitler's *Mein Kampf* (1925–26) is the primary text. Its worldview: races are the fundamental historical actors, competing in a zero-sum struggle for *Lebensraum* (living space); racial mixing causes civilisational decline; the 'Aryan' race faces a unique threat from the Jews, who are portrayed as a biologically cohesive force working through capitalism, communism and liberal democracy simultaneously to undermine racial communities. This is a conspiratorial worldview in which apparently opposed systems (capitalism and communism) are unified as instruments of Jewish power.

Nazism differs from Italian fascism in three structural ways: **race over nation** as the central category; **foundational** rather than adopted antisemitism; and an **exterminatory** logic rather than a repressive one — designated enemies are not suppressed and exiled but physically eliminated.

The **Holocaust**: the systematic murder of approximately 6 million Jews and approximately 5–6 million others (Roma, people with disabilities, Soviet prisoners of war, gay men, political prisoners, Jehovah's Witnesses). This was carried out through a bureaucratically organised process: registration, concentration, deportation via the railway network, and killing through mass shootings (Einsatzgruppen) and purpose-built extermination camps (Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno, Majdanek).

Hannah Arendt's *Eichmann in Jerusalem* (1963) introduced the concept of the **'banality of evil'**: the Holocaust was administered by ordinary bureaucrats — officials like Eichmann who processed paperwork and organised logistics — not by monsters. Mass atrocity does not require extraordinary sadism; it requires ordinary people willing to follow orders within a system that defines the moral framework.

The conditions enabling Nazism: hyperinflation (1923), the Great Depression from 1929, proportional representation fragmenting parliament, emergency governance under Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution, and Hindenburg's appointment of Hitler as Chancellor in January 1933 within a conservative coalition intended to 'tame' him.

The **intentionalist vs functionalist** debate: intentionalists (Lucy Dawidowicz) argue Hitler planned extermination from early on; functionalists (Mommsen, Broszat) argue the Holocaust emerged from the competitive chaos of Nazi institutions rather than a master plan. Most current historians (Kershaw, Browning) hold a 'cumulative radicalisation' or 'functionalist' synthesis — Hitler's ideological goal was always the elimination of the Jews but the specific mechanism evolved through escalation.

Arendt's 'banality of evil' is contested: Christopher Browning (*Ordinary Men*, 1992) confirmed from Reserve Police Battalion 101 that ordinary men committed mass murder without ideological conviction; Daniel Goldhagen (*Hitler's Willing Executioners*, 1996) countered that perpetrators were motivated by specifically German 'eliminationist antisemitism', not merely conformism. Saul Friedländer argues Hitler's 'redemptive antisemitism' — the belief that destroying Jews would save civilisation — had no structural parallel in Stalinist terror, distinguishing the Holocaust from other 20th-century mass atrocities.

quiz.q: The core structural difference between Italian fascism and Nazism is:
choices: Nazism was more democratic internally; fascism was more centralised around Mussolini
Nazism places biological race as the central category; fascism defines the national community politically and culturally
Fascism emerged earlier and had more time to develop a coherent ideology than Nazism
Nazism accepted market capitalism; fascism used state economic direction

quiz.q: Arendt's concept of the 'banality of evil' holds that:
choices: Evil on a mass scale requires an extraordinary ideology that dehumanises victims completely
Mass atrocity is administered by ordinary people following orders within a system that defines the moral framework — extraordinary sadism is not required
Evil is banal because it is irrational and self-defeating, whereas rational actors would not commit atrocities
The Holocaust was uniquely evil in 20th-century history; all other mass atrocities were comparatively banal

quiz.q: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution enabled what, and how did this facilitate the Nazi rise?
choices: It permitted proportional representation, which fragmented parliament into coalitions Hitler could exploit
It allowed the President to govern by emergency decree, enabling Hindenburg to bypass parliament — normalising executive rule before Hitler was appointed
It required a two-thirds majority to remove a Chancellor, making Hitler difficult to dislodge once appointed
It allowed the Chancellor to dissolve parliament and call new elections — which Hitler used to consolidate power in March 1933

quiz.q: Christopher Browning's *Ordinary Men* (1992) studied Reserve Police Battalion 101 to test Arendt's thesis. What did he find?
choices: The perpetrators were predominantly fanatical antisemites who had volunteered for the killing assignments
Most perpetrators were ordinary men without strong ideological conviction who participated due to conformism, peer pressure and the structure of the situation
The killers showed clinical signs of psychological disorders, confirming that atrocity requires psychological deviance
The battalion's officers were committed Nazis, but ordinary members were coerced by threat of execution

cards.title: Neoliberalism: Hayek, the Mont Pelerin Society and the market order
cards.fact: Friedrich Hayek's *The Road to Serfdom* (1944) argued that any state economic planning tends toward totalitarianism; his 'Use of Knowledge' (1945) argued that price signals aggregate dispersed information no planner can replicate — together founding the post-WWII case for market order against planning.

layers.body: Hayek's key move was epistemological: markets are not just efficient, they are the only mechanism capable of aggregating the dispersed, local, tacit knowledge that exists in an economy. Central planning cannot replicate this, not because planners are corrupt or malicious, but because the information they need does not exist in any form a planner can access.

layers.t: Hayek, Friedman and the Mont Pelerin Society
layers.body:
The **Mont Pelerin Society** (1947, founded by Hayek): an international intellectual network bringing together Hayek, Milton Friedman, Wilhelm Röpke, Ludwig von Mises and others to rebuild the case for markets and limited government after WWII. It became the institutional infrastructure through which neoliberal ideas spread into economics departments, think tanks and eventually policy.

**The Road to Serfdom** (1944): any state economic planning — including social democratic — tends toward totalitarianism. The planner must decide who gets what; this requires coercion to override market outcomes; those who administer the coercion accumulate power; and power corrupts. Planning therefore tendentially produces, not just inefficiency, but despotism.

**'The Use of Knowledge in Society'** (1945): economic knowledge is dispersed, local and tacit — it exists in the practices of millions of producers, consumers and traders, not in any centralised form. The price mechanism aggregates and transmits this knowledge better than any planner could, because prices incorporate the actions of all these dispersed agents.

Milton Friedman's Chicago School added several key propositions to Hayek's framework. **Monetarism**: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon — the price level is determined by the money supply. The right policy is a stable, predictable rule for money growth, not Keynesian discretionary intervention. **The natural rate of unemployment**: there is a minimum rate of unemployment consistent with stable inflation (the NAIRU); attempts to push unemployment below this through demand stimulus only produce accelerating inflation. **Negative income tax** as an alternative to the welfare state: a universal floor income provided through the tax system, replacing complex welfare bureaucracies with a simple cash transfer that does not distort incentives.

Quinn Slobodian (*Globalists*, 2018) argues the neoliberals were never primarily interested in *minimal* government but in the right *kind* of government — specifically, strong international institutions (GATT, IMF, later WTO) to *insulate* markets from democratic redistribution. The goal was not less government but governance at a level above democratic reach. David Harvey (*A Brief History of Neoliberalism*, 2005) argues neoliberalism is a class project: its real achievement was redistributing income upward, and the rhetoric of market efficiency was cover for that. Philip Mirowski (*Never Let a Serious Crisis Go to Waste*, 2013) argues that neoliberalism's resilience — its ability to survive and strengthen after the 2008 financial crisis it arguably caused — shows it functions as a thought collective with self-reinforcing institutional infrastructure.

quiz.q: Hayek's 'knowledge problem' is his argument against central planning. What does it claim?
choices: Planners lack the mathematical tools to solve economic optimisation at scale
Economic knowledge is dispersed, local and tacit — it cannot exist in any centralised form a planner can access; only price signals can aggregate it
Planners are inevitably captured by special interests and make politically rather than economically rational decisions
Central planning worked in the USSR for a period but cannot scale to full economic complexity

quiz.q: *The Road to Serfdom* argues that economic planning tends toward totalitarianism. What is the mechanism?
choices: Planners are drawn from the professional class, which is naturally authoritarian
Planning requires coercion to override market outcomes; administering coercion concentrates power; concentrated power corrupts
Planned economies grow more slowly and fall behind, creating conditions for militarist authoritarian regimes
The bureaucracies needed for planning inevitably grow until they consume all resources, starving the productive economy

quiz.q: Slobodian's *Globalists* argues that Hayek and the Mont Pelerin neoliberals wanted not minimal government but:
choices: Free trade without any supranational institutions, relying on bilateral agreements
Strong international institutions (GATT, IMF, WTO) to insulate markets from democratic redistribution at the national level
A world government with the power to enforce market principles across all nations
National governments that restrict their own powers through constitutional amendments

quiz.q: Friedman's 'natural rate of unemployment' (NAIRU) concept implies which limit on macroeconomic policy?
choices: Governments can reduce unemployment to zero if they accept high enough inflation
There is a minimum rate of unemployment consistent with stable inflation; pushing below it only produces accelerating inflation
Unemployment is caused by unions and minimum wages, not by macroeconomic conditions
Fiscal policy cannot affect unemployment at all — only monetary policy matters

cards.title: Neoliberalism as governmentality: Foucault and the entrepreneurial self
cards.fact: Foucault's *Birth of Biopolitics* lectures (1978–79) argue neoliberalism is not a withdrawal of government but its transformation: citizens are remade as 'human capital' who govern themselves as competitive enterprises — the state does not retreat but changes what it does.

layers.body: The standard account says neoliberalism = less government. Foucault's account says: neoliberalism = a different *form* of government — one that works not by commanding people but by structuring incentives so that people govern themselves in market-rational ways.

Foucault studied the German **ordoliberals** (Walter Eucken, Wilhelm Röpke, Franz Böhm) alongside the Chicago School. The ordoliberals made a crucial move: markets are not natural phenomena that emerge when governments step back. They are artificial orders that must be actively constructed and maintained by law and institutional design. A strong state is required — not to direct the economy, but to produce and protect the conditions for competitive markets. The German postwar *Soziale Marktwirtschaft* (social market economy) is ordoliberalism in practice.

This is different from classical laissez-faire, which imagined markets as natural and government as intrusion. Ordoliberalism imagined markets as achievements requiring institutional support.

layers.t: Human capital and the entrepreneurial self
layers.body:
The Chicago School extended market rationality beyond economics into social life. Gary Becker's **human capital theory**: individuals can be analysed as investing in themselves (education, skills, health, social networks) as enterprises invest in assets. Rational agents should treat themselves as portfolios of human capital to be optimised over a lifetime.

Foucault's analysis of this: it transforms the political subject. Classical liberalism's subject is a rights-bearing citizen. Welfarist social democracy's subject is a class member with social rights. Neoliberalism's subject is an **entrepreneur of the self** — permanently responsible for their own outcomes, investing in their own capacity, governing themselves through market calculations. This is not the absence of governance but a particular mode of it: the state shapes incentive structures so that individuals do the governing work on themselves.

This explains why neoliberalism is compatible with an active, interventionist state: workfare (social support conditional on seeking employment), performance management (public institutions governed by targets and competition), tuition fees (making students investors in their own human capital), health savings accounts — all are techniques of neoliberal governance, not its absence.

Dardot and Laval (*The New Way of the World*, 2013): neoliberalism has become a **rationality** reproduced through subjectivity — it shapes how people think about themselves and their responsibilities, making it harder to dismantle than a mere policy regime. Wendy Brown (*Undoing the Demos*, 2015): homo oeconomicus, the entrepreneurial self, is incompatible with democratic citizenship — it erodes the political subject who acts from values and judgment rather than self-interested calculation, undermining democracy from within. Critics from the right (Michael Sandel, communitarians): market rationality applied to non-market domains (education, healthcare, civic life) crowds out non-market values and relationships that market logic cannot generate or replace.

quiz.q: The ordoliberals (Eucken, Röpke) differed from classical laissez-faire by arguing that competitive markets are:
choices: Natural phenomena that emerge when governments step back
Artificial orders that must be actively constructed and maintained by law and institutional design
Impossible in practice and must be replaced by coordinated state planning
Only stable with monopoly firms, which the state should regulate rather than break up

quiz.q: Foucault argues that neoliberal government works 'through' markets rather than 'against' them. What does this mean in practice?
choices: The government buys and sells on markets to achieve policy goals
The state structures incentives so that individuals govern themselves in market-rational ways, rather than commanding them directly
Markets are used as performance metrics to evaluate the success of government programmes
Government policy is set by market actors through lobbying, rather than by democratic deliberation

quiz.q: Gary Becker's human capital theory transforms citizens into which kind of subject?
choices: Rights-bearing political citizens who can make claims on the state for welfare provision
Investors in themselves — 'entrepreneurs of the self' who optimise their education, health and skills as portfolio decisions
Members of class collectives whose welfare depends on collective bargaining and solidarity
Consumers maximising utility from a bundle of goods purchased in competitive markets

quiz.q: Wendy Brown's *Undoing the Demos* argues that the neoliberal subject (homo oeconomicus) threatens democracy by:
choices: Concentrating wealth so that money buys political power directly
Replacing the political citizen who acts from values with a market actor who calculates self-interest, eroding the subject democracy requires
Creating such economic inequality that democratic legitimacy is lost
Privatising public institutions and removing them from democratic accountability

cards.title: Libertarianism: the minimal state and the entitlement theory
cards.fact: Robert Nozick's *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* (1974) argued that any state larger than a 'nightwatchman' — preventing force, fraud and enforcing contracts — violates individual rights without consent; taxation for redistribution is, structurally, a form of forced labour.

layers.body: Libertarianism treats individual rights not as goals to be maximised but as side-constraints — limits that cannot be crossed even to produce better aggregate outcomes. If an action would violate someone's rights, it is impermissible regardless of how much good it would do overall.

Nozick wrote *Anarchy, State, and Utopia* (1974) directly against Rawls's *A Theory of Justice* (1971). Three central claims:

**Entitlement theory**: a distribution is just if it arose through just acquisition of previously unowned things and just voluntary transfer between persons. There is no pattern — no formula of equality or merit — that a just distribution must satisfy. If people make free transactions starting from a just distribution, the resulting distribution is just whatever it looks like.

**Anti-redistribution**: taxation of earnings for redistribution forces some people to labour for the benefit of others. 'This is equivalent to forced labour.' Taking earnings compels a person to devote some working hours to others' purposes without their consent.

**Minimal state**: the only legitimate state is one that protects against force, theft and fraud, and enforces contracts. A 'nightwatchman state'. Anything beyond this — welfare provision, regulation, public education — uses coercion against non-consenting individuals and is therefore illegitimate.

Libertarianism occupies a distinct position among adjacent ideologies. From **classical liberalism**: classical liberals (Mill) accepted some state action (public goods, externalities); libertarians push rights-based constraints to exclude nearly all such action. From **conservatism**: libertarians defend personal lifestyle freedoms (drug legalisation, sex work, same-sex relationships) that social conservatives oppose. From **neoliberalism**: neoliberals use the state to construct market competition; libertarians want categorically to shrink it. From **anarcho-capitalism** (Murray Rothbard): libertarians accept the minimal state; anarcho-capitalists want to privatise even police and courts.

**Left-libertarianism** (Peter Vallentyne, Michael Otsuka, Hillel Steiner): accepts self-ownership but argues that unlimited private appropriation of natural resources violates others' equal claims on the earth. If natural resources belong to all equally, redistribution of resource rents is compatible with — even required by — rights theory. This produces a libertarian case for some redistributive taxation.

G.A. Cohen (*Self-Ownership, Freedom and Equality*, 1995): accepts Nozick's self-ownership premise but attacks the Lockean proviso that allows unlimited private appropriation of land and natural resources. If others already own all the land, self-ownership is formal — you cannot move or eat without their permission. Most actual property derives from conquest, enclosure and colonial expropriation, not from the labour-mixing acquisition Nozick assumes. Will Kymlicka: the market distribution Nozick defends is itself maintained by state-enforced institutions (contract law, property law, courts, police). The distinction between a 'natural' market and a 'coercive' redistributive state is false — both depend on coercive enforcement. Objections from hard cases: does pollution (imposing costs on others without consent) constitute initiation of force under the non-aggression principle? If so, libertarianism implies strong environmental regulation.

quiz.q: Nozick's entitlement theory holds that a distribution is just if it satisfies what condition?
choices: It maximises the welfare of the least-advantaged group
It arose through just acquisition of previously unowned things and just voluntary transfers between persons
It conforms to a pattern — equal shares, or shares proportional to contribution
It was approved by a constitutional assembly representing all affected parties

quiz.q: Nozick argues that redistributive taxation is 'equivalent to forced labour'. What is the analogy?
choices: Tax collectors visit homes like slave masters visiting plantations
Taking earnings compels people to work some hours for others' purposes without consent — the coerced portion of their working time is effectively forced labour
Taxation reduces the incentive to work, pushing people to labour less than they otherwise would
Redistribution forces people to produce goods they do not want and would not freely provide

quiz.q: Left-libertarians (Vallentyne, Otsuka) accept self-ownership but reach redistributive conclusions by arguing:
choices: Self-ownership implies collective ownership of the products of labour
Natural resources belong equally to all persons; unlimited private appropriation violates others' claims and redistribution of resource rents is therefore required
Self-ownership requires a guaranteed minimum income to make it real rather than formal
Historical injustices in appropriation justify reparations that overwhelm the entitlement theory's conclusions

quiz.q: G.A. Cohen's counter-argument accepts Nozick's self-ownership premise. What does he attack instead?
choices: The non-aggression principle — Cohen shows it is internally self-contradictory
The Lockean appropriation proviso — if others own all the resources, self-ownership is formal because you cannot act without their permission
The minimal state — Cohen argues even nightwatchman functions require taxation that violates self-ownership
The entitlement theory — Cohen shows that no actual distribution satisfies its conditions because all involve historical injustice

cards.title: Rousseau: the general will
cards.fact: Rousseau distinguishes the 'will of all' (the sum of private interests) from the 'general will' (what citizens would choose reasoning from the common good) — only the latter makes law legitimate.

layers.body: In *The Social Contract* (1762) Rousseau argues that legitimate authority cannot simply rest on consent to protect private interests, as Locke held. Laws must express the general will — what we would will if we set aside self-interest and asked what the community as a whole needs.

The general will is not what most people happen to want. The majority can be wrong. It is what each citizen would choose if reasoning as a citizen rather than as a private individual. This requires civic equality: no one so rich they can buy others, no one so poor they must sell themselves. Obeying the general will is compatible with freedom because you are obeying a law you gave yourself as a member of the sovereign body.

Isaiah Berlin and Jacob Talmon warned that if the general will can be discerned by leaders even against popular wishes — the notorious phrase 'forced to be free' — then any government can claim to embody the true will of the people. Defenders reply that Rousseau requires direct participation and civic equality as preconditions, and that the general will cannot be delegated to a party or a leader.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po] Challenges liberal individualism: genuine self-governance requires citizens capable of civic virtue, not just rational preference-aggregation.
cards.counter: The general will has no reliable institutional mechanism. In practice, claims to embody it have served authoritarian populism as readily as genuine democracy.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Rousseau's 'will of all' and 'general will'?
choices: The will of all requires unanimity; the general will only a majority
The will of all sums private interests; the general will is what citizens would choose reasoning from the common good
The general will belongs to elected leaders; the will of all to ordinary citizens
They are synonyms in Rousseau's usage

cards.title: Hegel: the state as ethical life
cards.fact: For Hegel, freedom is not freedom from the state but freedom realised within it — the state is the form in which ethical life (Sittlichkeit) reaches its highest expression.

layers.t: Freedom through, not against, the state
layers.body: Liberal theory treats the state as a necessary constraint on natural freedom. Hegel inverts this in the *Philosophy of Right* (1820): individuals are only fully free inside a rational state. Outside of social institutions, there is no self to be free — identity and freedom are constituted through family, civil society, and the state.

Hegel's social philosophy moves through three levels. *Family* is the immediate ethical unit, held together by feeling. *Civil society* is the market and corporations, where individuals pursue their own interests and collide with others. *The state* is not a contract but an organic ethical community that mediates these interests and expresses the rational general will — not Rousseau's popular will, but the will of reason embodied in constitutional institutions, a civil service, and law.

Marx accepted Hegel's relational account of the self but inverted the conclusion: civil society (the economy) is not mediated by the state — rather, the state is an instrument of civil society's dominant class. Where Hegel saw rational synthesis, Marx saw ideological cover. This 'materialist inversion' of Hegel is the foundation of Marxist state theory.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Distinguishes liberal individualism (state as constraint) from communitarian and idealist traditions (state as constitutive of freedom); also crucial for understanding Marx.
cards.counter: Hegel's identification of the rational with the real can slide into apologetics for existing institutions. His philosophy of right gave intellectual cover to both reformist liberalism and, in distorted form, 20th-century statism.

quiz.q: Hegel's concept of Sittlichkeit ('ethical life') includes which three levels?
choices: Church, army, and parliament
Individual, society, and nature
Family, civil society, and the state
Custom, law, and morality

cards.title: Habermas: deliberative democracy
cards.fact: Habermas argues that legitimate political decisions require unconstrained public reasoning — not just voting, but the force of the better argument in an open public sphere.

layers.body: For Habermas, a norm is legitimate only if all those affected could agree to it through free and fair public deliberation. Democracy is not simply aggregating preferences by voting; it requires a public sphere where citizens reason together under conditions approaching the ideal speech situation: only the force of the better argument, not power or money, should determine outcomes.

In *Between Facts and Norms* (1992) Habermas describes a two-track model. Informal public opinion-formation occurs in civil society — media, associations, social movements — where issues are first raised and debated. This feeds into formal decision-making in parliament and courts. Legitimacy is the circulation between these tracks: parliament is legitimate when it remains connected to an active public sphere.

Critics note that real public spheres are shaped by money, media ownership, and social inequalities that the ideal speech situation abstracts away. Nancy Fraser argues Habermas's model assumes a unitary bourgeois public sphere and excludes counter-publics. Deliberative theory has also been criticised for ignoring agonistic dimensions of politics: genuine value conflicts cannot always be resolved by better arguments.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Grounds a normative case for civic education and free press as conditions for democratic legitimacy, not just nice extras.
cards.counter: Deliberation theory can become an idealist ideal that depoliticises real conflicts of interest. Chantal Mouffe argues that adversarial contestation, not consensus, is democracy's lifeblood.

quiz.q: What does Habermas mean by 'the ideal speech situation'?
choices: A utopia of universal literacy
Conditions where only the force of the better argument counts — no coercion, no strategic deception
A setting where all citizens vote directly on every law
A parliamentary debate with strict time limits and neutral chairing

cards.title: Pettit: republicanism and non-domination
cards.fact: Pettit's republicanism defines freedom as non-domination — the absence of anyone's arbitrary power over you — not merely non-interference. A master who treats a slave kindly still dominates.

layers.body: Liberal freedom (Berlin's negative liberty) means absence of actual interference. Pettit argues this misses the key threat: the capacity for arbitrary interference, whether or not it is exercised. A benevolent master, a deferential employee, a battered spouse who is not currently being beaten — all are dominated even if not currently interfered with.

Non-domination requires not just constitutional rights but institutions that make domination structurally impossible: an independent judiciary, a free press, electoral accountability, and social rights (since poverty creates dependence). The republican tradition running from Rome through Machiavelli, Harrington, and the American founders is united by this concern with structures, not just acts.

Isaiah Berlin defined freedom as non-interference and was suspicious of 'positive' liberty accounts he saw as leading to coercion in freedom's name. Pettit insists non-domination is a third concept — neither Berlin's negative liberty nor positive self-mastery. Critics ask whether the line between domination and mere vulnerability is clear enough to ground policy: all relations of dependence involve some vulnerability.

cards.deploy: [Cambridge / Sciences Po] Non-domination distinguishes freedom as merely formal (no interference) from genuine freedom; grounds the labour movement, welfare rights, and anti-monopoly policy.
cards.counter: Quentin Skinner and the neo-Roman tradition focus on non-arbitrary rule without Pettit's social-rights implications. Some libertarians argue that non-interference is the correct liberty concept and non-domination collapses into positive liberty.

quiz.q: How does Pettit's non-domination differ from Berlin's negative liberty (non-interference)?
choices: They are the same concept expressed differently
Non-domination requires the absence of any capacity for arbitrary power over you, even when that power is not exercised
Non-domination means positive self-governance; non-interference means mere absence of state action
Non-interference is Pettit's term; non-domination is Berlin's

cards.title: Tocqueville: democracy in America
cards.fact: Tocqueville saw equality of conditions as democracy's defining social fact — and its greatest danger: it can breed conformism, individualism, and a 'soft despotism' that makes citizens dependent on the state.

layers.body: Alexis de Tocqueville visited the United States in 1831 and published his analysis in two volumes (1835, 1840). His central observation was that democracy is above all a social condition — the equality of conditions — not just a political system. This equality shapes manners, tastes, and the mind as much as it shapes government.

Tocqueville identified two risks peculiar to democracies. First, the *tyranny of the majority*: majority opinion, amplified by a free press and social conformism, can silence minorities more effectively than an aristocratic court ever could. Second, *soft despotism*: as citizens retreat into private life and delegate everything to the state, they become 'timid and industrious animals of which government is the shepherd.' His remedy was voluntary associations, local government, and free press — forms of civic life that exercise democratic muscles.

Tocqueville is the godfather of communitarianism (Putnam's social capital) and of conservative warnings about bureaucratic overreach. But critics note his analysis was shaped by a romanticised view of New England towns and a blindness to slavery — the equality he observed excluded Black Americans entirely. His insights about democratic conformism resonate with research on social media and opinion homogenisation.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po] Connects democratic theory to sociology: institutions alone do not sustain democracy — civic culture, associations, and media do.
cards.counter: Tocqueville's alarm about soft despotism has been used by conservatives against the welfare state, but Tocqueville himself was not a pure laissez-faire liberal — he favoured civic engagement over either statism or atomism.

quiz.q: What does Tocqueville mean by 'soft despotism'?
choices: A military dictatorship that is less violent than traditional despotism
Citizens who delegate all public life to the state and become passive dependents — tyranny without terror
A monarchy that grants civil liberties but retains executive power
Democratic majorities that silence minorities through public opinion

cards.title: Weber: the monopoly on legitimate violence
cards.fact: Weber's definition of the state: the human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.

layers.body: In 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919) Max Weber defines the state not by its purposes (welfare, justice) but by its means. What distinguishes the state from every other association is that it alone can legitimately use — or authorise others to use — physical coercion. This definition is now the standard starting point for comparative politics.

Weber adds two crucial qualifications. First, *legitimacy*: the monopoly only works when the population believes the state has the right to coerce. Second, *territory*: the monopoly is spatially bounded. This generates three dimensions of statehood: empirical control of violence (capacity), territorial reach (extent), and recognised right (legitimacy). A state can fail on any of these: gangster states fail on legitimacy, failed states on capacity, stateless zones on both.

The definition is descriptive, not normative — it tells us what states do, not what they should do. Critics note it privileges the state's own perspective: rebels and oppressed groups dispute the legitimacy of the monopoly. Feminist scholars point out that the state has historically tolerated male violence in the private sphere, de facto limiting its own monopoly claim.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] The cleanest entry point for any comparative analysis of statehood, state failure, or regime type — the definition grounds everything else.
cards.counter: The definition is functionalist and circular (the state legitimates itself) and says nothing about justice. A state can hold the monopoly on violence while being tyrannical.

quiz.q: Which element does Weber's definition of the state NOT include?
choices: A claim to the monopoly on the use of physical force
Territorial delimitation
A constitution or written law
The requirement of legitimacy

cards.title: Tilly: war makes states
cards.fact: Charles Tilly's thesis: European states were built as a by-product of making war — rulers who needed armies built tax systems, and rulers who built tax systems built states.

layers.body: Tilly inverted the standard story of state-building. States did not emerge because societies wanted order; they emerged because rulers wanted to survive militarily. Fielding an army required money; raising money required extracting taxes; extracting taxes required administration; administration required legitimation. The state is, at its origin, a protection racket that worked.

Tilly compared European state formation from 990 to 1992. Where capital and coercion were both concentrated (France, England), durable centralised states emerged. Where capital was concentrated but coercion dispersed (Italian city-states), commercial republics but not great powers. Where coercion was concentrated but not capital (eastern Europe), large but relatively weak states. The European state form spread globally through colonialism — imposed, not home-grown.

Tilly's model explains European state-building but poorly predicts outcomes in Africa and Asia, where colonial powers drew arbitrary borders, suppressed indigenous political formations, and then departed. Jeffrey Herbst applied Tilly to Africa: low population density meant no military pressure to build tax systems, producing states with nominal sovereignty but weak capacity. The 'war makes states' logic does not transfer to a world with protected borders.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] Explains why states vary so dramatically in capacity — the historical conditions for strong state-building are unusual, not the default.
cards.counter: Tilly's model is contested by scholars who emphasise ideology, religion, or trade as independent drivers of state formation. It also generates an uncomfortable implication: if war builds states, then prolonged peace may weaken state capacity.

quiz.q: What is Tilly's central thesis about European state formation?
choices: Democratic revolutions built nation-states through popular mobilisation
States emerged from rulers' need to finance war through taxation, which drove bureaucratic centralisation
Commercial trade routes generated the wealth that allowed rulers to build state institutions
Religious authority gave rulers the legitimacy needed to centralise power

cards.title: Lipset-Rokkan: cleavage theory
cards.fact: Lipset and Rokkan showed that today's party systems are 'frozen' reflections of the social conflicts of the 1920s — four cleavages from the national and industrial revolutions still structure most Western party politics.

layers.body: In 'Party Systems and Voter Alignments' (1967) Lipset and Rokkan argued that European party systems are not accidental — they map onto four deep social cleavages formed in two historical revolutions: the National Revolution (centre vs periphery; church vs state) and the Industrial Revolution (land vs industry; owners vs workers).

The *centre-periphery* cleavage pits national culture against regional minorities (Flemish vs Belgian, Catalan vs Spanish). The *church-state* cleavage divides secular liberals from religious conservatives — still the basis of Christian Democrat parties. The *land-industry* cleavage set agrarian interests against industrial urban ones. The *owner-worker* cleavage produced socialist and labour parties on one side, conservative and liberal parties on the other. By the 1920s these were institutionalised in stable party systems — and stayed that way.

Subsequent scholarship debates whether cleavages have 'unfrozen' since the 1970s. Ronald Inglehart argued a post-materialist value shift — from economic security to self-expression — created new conflicts (green parties, feminism, gay rights) that cross-cut class. More recently, 'demography is destiny' arguments suggest an education cleavage is replacing the class cleavage, with university-educated voters moving left and non-graduates moving right — the pattern behind Brexit, Trump, and Le Pen.
