cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] Explains why party systems look so different across countries and why they change slowly — historical path dependence structures political competition.
cards.counter: The freezing hypothesis is contested: turnout volatility has risen, new parties (Greens, populists) have entered, and Rokkan's model was built on Western Europe and fits non-European democracies poorly.

quiz.q: According to Lipset and Rokkan, which two historical revolutions generated the four main cleavages in European party systems?
choices: The French Revolution and the Russian Revolution
The National Revolution and the Industrial Revolution
The Enlightenment and the Reformation
The Agricultural Revolution and the Democratic Revolution

cards.title: O'Donnell & Schmitter: transitology
cards.fact: O'Donnell and Schmitter's model of democratic transition has three stages: liberalisation (opening up the authoritarian regime), democratisation (installing competitive procedures), and consolidation (making democracy 'the only game in town').

layers.body: In *Transitions from Authoritarian Rule* (1986) O'Donnell and Schmitter argued that transitions to democracy are uncertain, strategic processes — not inevitable results of modernisation. The key actors are 'hardliners' and 'softliners' within the authoritarian coalition, and 'moderates' and 'radicals' in the opposition.

*Liberalisation* is the authoritarian regime allowing some political space — press freedom, reduced repression — often to manage elite splits. *Democratisation* is the installation of democratic procedures: elections, civil rights, competitive party formation. *Consolidation* is when democracy is internalised by all major actors as the only legitimate framework — no player calculates that a coup or uprising would pay off. The stages can stall or reverse.

Earlier modernisation theory (Lipset) held that economic development produces democracy — 'no bourgeoisie, no democracy.' O'Donnell and Schmitter rejected structural determinism: elite bargaining and contingency matter. This 'transitology' approach was later criticised by Thomas Carothers, who argued it assumes all countries are 'in transition' when many are stuck in grey-zone hybrid regimes with no transition underway.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Frames democracy as a political achievement requiring strategic action by elites, not an automatic dividend of economic growth.
cards.counter: Transitology has been accused of ethnocentrism — assuming all politics tends toward liberal democracy. It also underspecifies which institutional choices make consolidation more likely.

quiz.q: In O'Donnell and Schmitter's model, what does democratic 'consolidation' mean?
choices: A constitution has been ratified
The first free election has been held
All major actors accept democracy as the only legitimate framework — no one calculates that a coup would pay
The military has been formally subordinated to civilian control

cards.title: Linz: the perils of presidentialism
cards.fact: Juan Linz argued that presidential systems are more prone to democratic breakdown than parliamentary ones — because fixed mandates and dual legitimacy produce constitutional crises that parliamentary systems resolve with a vote of no confidence.

layers.body: In 'The Perils of Presidentialism' (1990) Linz noted that presidentialism creates two independently elected power centres — the president and the legislature — each claiming democratic legitimacy. When they deadlock there is no constitutional mechanism to resolve it short of military intervention or constitutional crisis.

In a parliamentary system, a prime minister who loses legislative support falls through a no-confidence vote — the system is self-correcting. A president who loses support cannot be removed until the term ends, which may be years away. Linz also stressed the *zero-sum* character of presidential elections: the winner takes all, the loser nothing — unlike parliamentary coalition-building, which distributes power more broadly and loses less for the loser.

Horowitz, Mainwaring, and others pushed back: US presidentialism has survived over two centuries; many parliamentary systems have also failed. The US case is often attributed to exceptional factors (federalism, checks, culture). Cross-national studies (Przeworski et al.) found that presidentialism per se is not fatal — institutional design details and party system fragmentation matter more. Still, Latin America and Africa provide many cases consistent with Linz's worry.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Grounds the institutional design debate: when advising post-conflict constitution-making, the choice between presidential and parliamentary is not arbitrary.
cards.counter: The UK's parliamentary system has not prevented Brexit-level dysfunction; Japan's parliamentary system produced decades of LDP dominance. Presidentialism may be less the cause than a contributing factor to breakdown when parties are highly polarised.

quiz.q: What is Linz's main structural objection to presidentialism?
choices: Presidents concentrate too much power in one person, enabling despotism
Fixed terms and dual legitimacy produce deadlock that parliamentary systems resolve through no-confidence votes
Presidential elections are more vulnerable to fraud than parliamentary ones
Presidentialism requires a two-round system that produces unstable coalitions

cards.title: Levitsky & Ziblatt: guardrails of democracy
cards.fact: Levitsky and Ziblatt argue that formal institutions alone do not protect democracy — informal norms of mutual toleration and institutional forbearance are the real guardrails, and they can erode without a single constitutional violation.

layers.body: In *How Democracies Die* (2018) Levitsky and Ziblatt identify two informal norms that underpin democratic stability. *Mutual toleration*: treating opponents as legitimate rivals, not existential enemies. *Institutional forbearance*: using formal powers with restraint — not every legal power needs to be used at every opportunity.

Most 21st-century democratic breakdowns are not coups — they are incremental erosions by elected governments. A president packs courts, uses emergency powers, delegitimises the press, and intimidates opponents — all technically within legal bounds. Because no single act is clearly unconstitutional, established players hesitate to name it as a breakdown. Only informal norms stand between legal authority and abuse of that authority.

Some critics argue the guardrails framework is too US-centric and that the authors underestimate how often democratic norms have historically excluded entire groups. Others note that 'institutional forbearance' can be an argument for inaction when the other side is transgressing: asymmetric norm-keeping favours the norm-breaker. The framework also focuses on elites — it has less to say about the societal conditions that make norm-breaking popular.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Explains why constitutions alone do not protect democracy — the informal political culture around institutions matters as much as written rules.
cards.counter: Informal norms are by nature unenforceable; calling for their protection is a political move, not a neutral legal one. What counts as 'forbearance' is itself contested.

quiz.q: What does 'institutional forbearance' mean in Levitsky and Ziblatt's framework?
choices: Courts that refuse to strike down unconstitutional laws
The norm of not using every legal power available — restraint in the exercise of formal authority
Opposition parties that accept electoral defeat without protest
Constitutional amendments that limit presidential term lengths

cards.title: Mill's comparative methods
cards.fact: John Stuart Mill's three canons of comparative causal inference — agreement, difference, and concomitant variation — are still the logical foundation of most comparative politics.

layers.body: In *A System of Logic* (1843) Mill specified methods for identifying causes by comparison. The *method of agreement*: if cases that share an outcome also share one prior condition, that condition is a candidate cause. The *method of difference*: if two cases differ only in one condition and one has the outcome, that condition is the cause. The *method of concomitant variation*: if the outcome varies systematically with a condition, they are causally linked.

These methods generate two strategies for case selection. The *most-similar systems design* (MSSD) selects cases that share as many background conditions as possible (e.g. Scandinavia), so differences in the outcome can be traced to the few conditions that differ. The *most-different systems design* (MDSD) selects cases that differ on everything except the outcome, to isolate its necessary conditions. MSSD is the workhorse of comparative politics; MDSD tests universality.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] Underlies case selection arguments: researchers must justify why their comparison controls for alternative explanations.
cards.counter: Mill's methods assume causes are necessary and sufficient; most social causes are probabilistic and interacting. Multivariate statistics and process tracing fill the gap, but the logic of comparison still rests on Mill.

quiz.q: In a most-similar systems design (MSSD), researchers select cases that…
choices: Differ on as many background conditions as possible
Share as many background conditions as possible, so variation in outcomes can be traced to a few differing factors
Have the same outcome, to confirm a hypothesis
Come from the same region to control for cultural variables

cards.title: Selection on the dependent variable
cards.fact: Studying only successful cases (or only failures) produces biased causal inference — if you only look at cases with the outcome you want to explain, you have no variation on the outcome to explain.

layers.body: If you want to know why states become democratic and study only democracies, you cannot identify the cause — all your cases have the same outcome. You need variation: some that democratised and some that did not, with different prior conditions.

David Collier and James Mahoney formalized the critique. Studying only OECD successes to explain economic development (Przeworski and Limongi's concern) misses the many countries with the same initial conditions that failed. Studying only democratic breakdowns misses the many democratic regimes that faced similar stresses and survived. The problem is not just statistical: it reflects a deeper failure to think clearly about what the comparison is meant to establish.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Key methodological critique: always ask what the counterfactual comparison set is — what cases with and without the outcome are being compared.
cards.counter: Studying rare events (coups, revolutions, genocides) may require selecting on the outcome simply because negative cases are too numerous. Process tracing within selected cases can partially compensate.

quiz.q: Why is 'selecting on the dependent variable' a methodological problem?
choices: It uses too many cases to identify a single cause
It removes variation in the outcome being explained, making causal inference impossible
It focuses on process rather than outcomes
It relies on qualitative rather than quantitative methods

cards.title: Process tracing
cards.fact: Process tracing establishes causation within a single case by testing whether the predicted causal chain — the 'fingerprints' of a mechanism — is actually present in the evidence.

layers.body: Correlation across many cases tells us that X and Y co-vary. Process tracing asks: *how* does X produce Y? It identifies the mechanism — the chain of events linking cause to outcome — and then looks for observable evidence of each step in a single case.

Bennett and Checkel distinguish four tests borrowed from scientific evidence standards. A *hoop test*: the mechanism evidence must be present (failing it eliminates the hypothesis). A *smoking gun*: rare evidence that, if present, confirms the mechanism (passing it is sufficient). A *straw in the wind*: weak evidence, neither necessary nor sufficient but directionally informative. A *doubly decisive* test: both necessary and sufficient. Good process tracing stacks multiple hoop tests and seeks a smoking gun.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Answers the criticism that case studies cannot establish causation — they can, by testing the predicted mechanism step by step.
cards.counter: Process tracing depends on the researcher's prior theory of the mechanism and can be manipulated by selecting favourable evidence. It works within a case but cannot generalise without cross-case comparison.

quiz.q: A 'smoking gun' test in process tracing is evidence that is…
choices: Necessary but not sufficient — it must be present to keep the hypothesis alive
Rare and, if present, sufficient to confirm the causal mechanism
Weak and directional — informative but neither necessary nor sufficient
Both necessary and sufficient to confirm the hypothesis

cards.title: Gramsci: hegemony
cards.fact: Gramsci argued that the ruling class maintains power primarily through cultural consent — hegemony — not just coercion; winning in civil society matters as much as controlling the state.

layers.body: Antonio Gramsci, writing in Mussolini's prisons (1929–35), asked why the working class in advanced capitalist societies did not revolt as Marx predicted. His answer: the ruling class governs not just through the state's coercive apparatus but through hegemony — a cultural dominance in which subaltern classes internalise ruling-class values as common sense.

In Russia, the state was the whole fortress; capturing it (the 'war of manoeuvre') brought down the regime. In Western Europe, civil society — schools, churches, media, unions — forms a dense network of consent that must be won over before state power can be seized. This is the 'war of position': building counter-hegemony through a long campaign in the cultural and intellectual sphere. The party must become an 'organic intellectual' that articulates subaltern experience into a coherent worldview.

Laclau and Mouffe (*Hegemony and Socialist Strategy*, 1985) revised the concept: hegemony is not class-based but contingent — any social group can construct a hegemonic project by articulating different demands (workers, feminists, greens) into a chain of equivalence. This post-Marxist move was influential in left strategy but criticised for abandoning class analysis. The concept was also adopted by IR scholars (Cox) to describe American hegemony as ideological, not just military.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / Harvard Government] Explains why ideas and institutions, not just interests, matter in politics — and why electoral victories alone do not transform society.
cards.counter: Hegemony can become an unfalsifiable explanation: if the working class consents to capitalism, that is hegemony; if it revolts, that is a crack in hegemony. The concept needs operationalisation to be empirically useful.

quiz.q: What does Gramsci mean by a 'war of position' (as opposed to a 'war of manoeuvre')?
choices: Military strategy using defensive trenches rather than offensive advance
A long-term cultural and institutional struggle to build counter-hegemony in civil society before taking state power
Electoral politics in proportional representation systems
Coercive control of civil society through surveillance and censorship

cards.title: Bourdieu: the political field
cards.fact: Bourdieu treats politics as a semi-autonomous field where professional politicians compete for the monopoly on legitimate political speech — and in doing so, tend to dispossess ordinary citizens of the means to speak politically.

layers.body: For Bourdieu, the political field is a structured space in which political actors hold different amounts of political capital (credibility, party positions, name recognition) and compete for the authority to represent the social world. Like other fields, it has specific rules, a doxa (what goes without saying), and a logic that insiders must master.

As the political field professionalises, the cost of political competence rises. Party activists, pollsters, speechwriters, and commentators constitute a political field from which ordinary citizens are increasingly excluded. The layperson delegates political opinion formation to professionals — and those professionals increasingly respond to the internal logic of the field (career, reputation) rather than to the constituents they represent. This structural dispossession explains political disengagement without pathologising voters.

Bourdieu's model captures elite reproduction well but is criticised for underplaying agency: social movements, populist leaders, and digital platforms have repeatedly disrupted the field's closure. It also struggles with non-Western political contexts where the field's autonomy is much lower — where economic or military capital directly dominates political capital.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po] Explains why political professionalisation produces disengagement — not voter apathy, but structural dispossession of citizens' capacity to speak politically.
cards.counter: The field metaphor can make political outcomes seem determined by structural position. Bourdieu himself was a highly influential public intellectual who broke the rules of field theory through direct political intervention.

quiz.q: What does Bourdieu mean by the 'dispossession' of ordinary citizens in the political field?
choices: Citizens are literally excluded from voting by property requirements
The professionalisation of politics raises the competence cost, structurally excluding non-specialists from legitimate political speech
Media ownership concentrates in elite hands, making propaganda the main political tool
Citizens are dispossessed of economic capital by taxation and inflation

cards.title: The seat-vote curve
cards.fact: Under FPTP the relationship between votes and seats is non-linear — a party winning 40% of votes may win a majority of seats, while one winning 35% may win almost none, because votes are distributed unevenly across constituencies.

layers.body: In single-member plurality systems, seats are won constituency by constituency. A party that piles up huge majorities in safe seats 'wastes' votes; one that wins narrowly in many seats converts votes efficiently into seats. This creates a cube law relationship in two-party competition: the leading party tends to get its vote share cubed as its seat share.

layers.t: The cube law and swing amplification
layers.body: If Party A leads Party B 55:45 in votes, the cube law predicts a seat split closer to 63:37. A small national swing in votes produces a large swing in seats. This is why UK general elections can produce large parliamentary majorities from modest vote leads, and why a party's vote share often dramatically understates or overstates its parliamentary representation. The disproportionality is a structural feature of the system, not a malfunction.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / Harvard Government] Makes disproportionality concrete: electoral reform debates are ultimately arguments about which distortions of the seat-vote curve are acceptable.
cards.counter: The cube law is an empirical regularity, not a law — it holds when votes are distributed roughly uniformly across constituencies. Geographic concentration of a party's vote (like the SNP in Scotland) can produce much higher seat-to-vote ratios.

quiz.q: The 'cube law' in two-party FPTP systems predicts that the winning party's seat share…
choices: Roughly equals its vote share
Is the cube root of its vote share
Exceeds its vote share — the leading party gets its vote share cubed relative to the trailing party
Depends solely on constituency boundary design

cards.title: Katz & Mair: the cartel party
cards.fact: Katz and Mair argued that mainstream parties have colonised the state — using public funding and media access to entrench themselves — producing a cartel that insulates them from societal demands and fuels anti-party populism.

layers.body: In 'Changing Models of Party Organization' (1995) Katz and Mair identified a shift from mass parties embedded in civil society to 'cartel parties' embedded in the state. Public funding, guaranteed media access, and regulatory barriers to new entrants allow established parties to survive even as their memberships collapse.

The cartel model predicts a self-reinforcing cycle: established parties set the rules of party competition, giving themselves advantages in state resources and ballot access. They converge ideologically on a manageable centre, reducing voter choice. Voters disengage from party membership (which has collapsed across Western democracies) and turn to outsider vehicles — populist parties, social movements, or direct democracy demands. The rise of Macron, the Five Star Movement, and various right-populist parties fits the prediction.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po] Explains the paradox of low voter turnout and rising anti-establishment politics in stable democracies — the formal infrastructure of parties has survived, but their representative function has atrophied.
cards.counter: The cartel thesis may overstate convergence: plenty of mainstream parties offer genuine ideological contrasts. And public funding of parties can be defended as preventing capture by wealthy donors — the alternative to a cartel may be a plutocracy.

quiz.q: What is the core claim of the 'cartel party' thesis?
choices: Parties form electoral cartels to fix vote shares and prevent new entrants
Established parties have colonised the state — using public funding and regulation to entrench themselves and insulate from societal pressure
Digital media allows parties to bypass traditional civil-society organisations
Party cartels are illegal under EU competition law but persist in practice

cards.title: Path dependence in politics
cards.fact: Path dependence means that early institutional choices constrain later ones — even after the original reasons for a choice have disappeared, switching costs lock in the status quo.

layers.body: Path dependence, imported from economics (David's QWERTY keyboard study) into political science by North and Pierson, means that the sequence of events matters: what happened first shapes what is possible later. Early choices create constituencies, sunk costs, and cognitive lock-ins that make reversal increasingly expensive.

Pierson identifies three mechanisms. *Increasing returns*: the more an institution is used, the more the complementary arrangements adapt to it (common law vs civil law; QWERTY keyboards). *Veto players*: beneficiaries of existing institutions block reform. *Cognitive lock-in*: the institution becomes the taken-for-granted framework, so alternatives become literally unimaginable. The welfare state's different structures in the UK vs Sweden are not just policy choices — they reflect path-dependent trajectories from early 20th-century insurance arrangements.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Explains why rational policy proposals often fail in practice — not from irrationality, but because the institutional context that evolved around the old policy makes switching expensive for those who adapted to it.
cards.counter: Path dependence can become a general-purpose explanation that explains nothing: anything can be said to be 'locked in' post-hoc. It needs to specify scope conditions for when paths can shift — critical junctures, exogenous shocks, and the role of agency in breaking lock-in.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Pierson's mechanisms of path dependence?
choices: Increasing returns from complementary adaptations to an institution
Veto players who block reform to protect institutional benefits
Cognitive lock-in where alternatives become unimaginable
External shocks that force rapid institutional change

cards.title: Consociationalism: governing divided societies
cards.fact: Consociationalism is Arend Lijphart's model for stable democracy in deeply divided societies — using elite power-sharing, mutual veto rights, proportionality in appointments, and segmental autonomy rather than majority rule.

layers.body: In societies divided by religion, language, or ethnicity, majority rule can mean permanent exclusion of minorities — and is likely to produce ethnic outbidding and conflict. Lijphart argued that stable democracy in such societies requires not competitive majoritarianism but consociationalism: structured power-sharing among group elites.

Lijphart's four elements: (1) *Grand coalition* — a government that includes representatives of all major segments (Switzerland's Federal Council, Lebanon's confessional formula). (2) *Mutual veto* — each group can block decisions affecting its vital interests. (3) *Proportionality* — civil service appointments, public funding, and parliamentary seats allocated proportional to group size. (4) *Segmental autonomy* — groups govern their own schools, media, and social welfare. Belgium, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and post-1998 Northern Ireland are the canonical cases.

Critics argue consociationalism institutionalises and freezes the very divisions it manages — making ethnic or religious identity the permanent basis of politics, crowding out cross-cutting cleavages. In Lebanon, the confessional system that prevented civil war in the 1940s became a mechanism for political paralysis and warlordism by the 1970s. Horowitz favours centripetalism (electoral incentives for cross-group appeals) over consociationalism as a long-term strategy.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] Offers an institutional design toolkit for post-conflict or divided societies where Westminster-style majoritarianism is dangerous.
cards.counter: Consociational systems tend toward gridlock (see Lebanon, Bosnia, Belgium's record government-formation times) and can entrench group identities that might otherwise erode. The elite-pact logic also undermines popular accountability.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Lijphart's four pillars of consociationalism?
choices: Grand coalition government including all major segments
Mutual veto rights for each group on vital interests
Proportional allocation of public offices and resources
Winner-take-all elections to generate clear governing mandates

cards.title: The French republican model
cards.fact: France's republican tradition demands colourblind, universalist citizenship — the state recognises only individuals, not communities; laïcité bans religious expression in public institutions; assimilation is the expected path for immigrants.

layers.body: The French Republic is constitutionally 'one and indivisible.' This is not only a statement about territorial unity: it means the state recognises no intermediate communities — no ethnic groups, no confessional bodies, no regional identities — between the individual citizen and the Republic. Rights are universal and individual, not communal.

Laïcité (secularism) is the institutional expression of the republican model: religious practice is strictly private; public schools and state offices must be religiously neutral. The logic of integration is assimilationist — immigrants are expected to become republican citizens, adopting French language, norms, and civic identity. This contrasts with Anglo-Saxon multiculturalism, which accepts and accommodates cultural difference.

Critics argue universalist republicanism is a form of covert particularism: it universalises French majority culture and forces minorities to erase their identities to access citizenship. The ban on the hijab in schools (2004) and burkini debates exposed the tension. Todd and others argue French integration has in practice failed for post-colonial minorities — producing formal citizenship without genuine inclusion, which makes the universalist ideal hollow.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po] Provides the framework for French debates on immigration, secularism, and identity — and a contrast case for Anglo-Saxon multiculturalism debates.
cards.counter: The universalist model has produced a genuine civic culture and avoided some communal conflicts visible in consociational states. Its defenders argue the alternative — institutionalised ethnic categories — itself produces discrimination.

quiz.q: What is the core principle of the French republican model of citizenship?
choices: Cultural diversity should be publicly celebrated and institutionally protected
The state recognises only individual citizens — not communities, ethnicities, or religions — between the person and the Republic
Religious identity should be integrated into civic life through official representation
Regional governments should enjoy broad autonomy to accommodate cultural differences

cards.title: State capacity
cards.fact: State capacity is the state's ability to actually implement policy in its territory — to collect taxes, enforce laws, deliver services. It is distinct from state authority: many states claim sovereignty they cannot exercise.

layers.t: The gap between authority and capacity
layers.body: A state may have formal sovereignty, a constitution, and international recognition, yet lack the administrative apparatus to implement any of it. Millions of people live under states that cannot reliably provide security, collect tax, or enforce contracts — 'nominal states' in Joel Migdal's phrase. State capacity is what separates these from effective states.

Political scientists distinguish several components. *Coercive capacity*: the state monopolises force and enforces law. *Extractive capacity*: it collects taxes. *Administrative capacity*: it delivers services and implements regulations. *Legal capacity*: courts enforce contracts and property rights. These dimensions are correlated but distinct — the US has high administrative capacity but middling legal capacity for the poor; China has high extractive capacity but selective legal capacity. Fragile states may hold territory without any consistent delivery.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government] Explains why institutional reform fails in developing countries — not because institutions are badly designed on paper, but because the state lacks the capacity to implement them.
cards.counter: High state capacity without accountability produces predatory states (North Korea, DRC). The development literature now emphasises that capacity must be paired with responsive institutions — capable autocracies are not a development model.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best definition of 'state capacity'?
choices: The formal constitutional authority a state claims over its territory
The state's ability to actually implement policy — to tax, enforce law, and deliver services
The size of the state's military relative to its population
The degree to which a state's legal system is independent of the executive

cards.title: Frege: sense and reference
cards.fact: Frege showed that two expressions can refer to the same thing (same reference) while meaning something different (different sense) — 'the Morning Star' and 'the Evening Star' both pick out Venus, but discovering this is informative, not trivial.

layers.body: If 'the Morning Star = the Morning Star' is trivial, but 'the Morning Star = the Evening Star' is a genuine astronomical discovery, the two expressions must differ in something beyond what they pick out. Frege called the object picked out the *reference* (Bedeutung) and the mode of presentation the *sense* (Sinn).

Every expression has a sense — the way it presents its reference — and that sense determines which object it refers to. Two expressions can share a reference while differing in sense (as above). Some expressions have sense but no reference: 'the present King of France' presents an object but there is none. For Frege, the meaning of a sentence is its truth-value, determined compositionally from the senses of its parts.

Russell argued that senses are mysterious entities: what are they, exactly? He replaced Frege's account with the theory of descriptions, analysing 'the Morning Star' as a quantificational claim rather than a name with a sense. Kripke later attacked both, arguing that names are *rigid designators* — they pick out the same object in every possible world, not via a sense but via a causal-historical chain.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Foundational for philosophy of language and logic: any argument about meaning, reference, or propositional content has to navigate Frege's distinction.
cards.counter: The sense-reference distinction multiplies entities (every expression now has two levels) and generates puzzles about oblique contexts (where substitution of co-referential terms fails, e.g. in 'Lois believes Superman can fly').

quiz.q: The discovery that 'the Morning Star' and 'the Evening Star' both refer to Venus is informative. What does Frege conclude from this?
choices: The two expressions have the same reference but different senses
The two expressions are synonymous
Reference is unimportant; only sense matters for meaning
Venus has two names, which is merely a linguistic accident

cards.title: Russell: theory of descriptions
cards.fact: Russell's 'On Denoting' (1905) showed that 'the present King of France is bald' is not meaningless but false — by analysing definite descriptions as quantificational claims rather than names.

layers.body: If 'the present King of France' were a name, the sentence 'The present King of France is bald' would fail to say anything (there is no such king). Russell argued it is instead an *existential claim in disguise*: 'There exists exactly one thing that is currently king of France, and it is bald.' That claim is false, not meaningless.

Paraphrased formally: ∃x(KingOfFrance(x) ∧ ∀y(KingOfFrance(y) → y=x) ∧ Bald(x)). This eliminates the description entirely — no 'present King of France' appears in the logical form. Apparent reference to non-existent entities is analysed away. Russell called descriptions 'incomplete symbols': they have no meaning in isolation, only in sentential context.

P.F. Strawson argued Russell was wrong: 'The present King of France is bald' is neither true nor false but *lacks a truth value*, because the sentence presupposes (rather than asserts) that there is a King of France. If the presupposition fails, the sentence does not make a false claim — it misfires. This initiated the presupposition vs. assertion debate still alive in linguistics.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] The theory of descriptions is a model for philosophical analysis: apparent puzzles dissolve when expressions are shown to have a different logical form than their surface grammar suggests.
cards.counter: The theory gets complex for belief contexts ('George believes the present King of France is bald') and for names that lack a descriptive backing. Kripke's causal theory of names bypasses the descriptivist assumptions entirely.

quiz.q: On Russell's theory, 'The present King of France is bald' is…
choices: Meaningless, because there is no present King of France
False, because it asserts existence and uniqueness of a King of France, which fail
True, because it is trivially satisfied by the empty domain
Neither true nor false, because it presupposes a referent that doesn't exist

cards.title: Early Wittgenstein: the picture theory
cards.fact: The Tractatus argues that language pictures the world — a proposition is a logical picture of a fact; meaningful language represents possible facts, and the limits of meaningful language are the limits of what can be said.

layers.body: Wittgenstein's *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (1921) proposes a stark vision: the world is the totality of facts, not things. Language represents facts by picturing them — the logical form of a proposition mirrors the logical form of a possible fact. If proposition and world share no logical form, the 'proposition' says nothing.

layers.t: What can be said vs shown
layers.body: The limits of meaningful language are the limits of what can be said: only propositions that can be either true or false count as meaningful. Ethics, aesthetics, metaphysics, and the logical form of language itself cannot be said — they can only be *shown*. The Tractatus ends: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' Wittgenstein believed this dissolved most traditional philosophy as meaningless.

The Tractatus's own propositions appear to violate the picture theory — they make claims about logical form that the theory says cannot be said. Wittgenstein acknowledged this: the propositions of the Tractatus are 'elucidatory nonsense' that one kicks away like a ladder once one has climbed it. His later work (*Philosophical Investigations*) rejected the picture theory entirely.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Establishes the positivist-adjacent principle that meaningful claims must in principle have conditions of truth and falsity — basis for the logical positivists' verificationism and for dismissing much metaphysics.
cards.counter: The picture theory cannot account for commands, questions, exclamations, or performatives — all meaningful speech that doesn't represent facts. Wittgenstein himself abandoned it.

quiz.q: According to the Tractatus, what determines whether a proposition is meaningful?
choices: Whether it expresses a feeling or value
Whether it can in principle be verified by observation
Whether it pictures a possible fact — shares a logical form with a possible state of the world
Whether it is grammatically well-formed

cards.title: Late Wittgenstein: meaning as use
cards.fact: Philosophical Investigations rejects the picture theory: the meaning of a word is its use in a language-game — and there is no private language, only public rule-following practices.

layers.body: The *Philosophical Investigations* (1953) opens by attacking the picture theory: language is not a uniform mirror of reality — it is a vast collection of 'language games,' each with its own rules and purposes (giving orders, telling stories, guessing riddles, singing, acting). 'The meaning of a word is its use in the language.'

Can there be a language that only one person can understand — a language for purely private inner states? Wittgenstein argues no. A word gains meaning from its use in a shared practice; without the possibility of correction by others, there is no difference between following a rule correctly and merely thinking you are. Language requires a community of practice. This has profound implications for how we talk about sensations, mental states, and introspection.

Kripke's *Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language* (1982) gave a sceptical reading: nothing about past practice determines the correct future application of a rule — there is always a deviant interpretation that fits all past cases. The 'solution' is that the practice of the community provides a standard, but this is a 'sceptical solution,' not a refutation of the scepticism. This reading was hotly contested but enormously influential.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Grounds the ordinary-language philosophy movement: philosophical puzzles often arise from language gone idle — language taken out of the form of life in which its use makes sense.
cards.counter: Critics (Davidson) argue that if meaning is use, there is no non-circular account of what makes a use the *correct* one. Chomsky objected that understanding language cannot be reduced to mastery of social practices.

quiz.q: What is the 'private language argument' in Philosophical Investigations?
choices: The argument that sign languages are private and cannot be translated into spoken language
The claim that a language known only to one person is impossible, because meaning requires public, correctable rule-following
The view that inner thoughts are meaningful even though they cannot be expressed
The proof that all language is ultimately private, based on individual interpretation

cards.title: Austin: speech act theory
cards.fact: Austin showed that language does not just describe — it does things: when a judge says 'I sentence you' or a couple says 'I do,' they are not reporting facts but performing actions.

layers.body: J.L. Austin in *How to Do Things with Words* (1962) distinguished *constatives* (statements that describe and can be true or false) from *performatives* (utterances that perform the action they name — 'I promise,' 'I apologise,' 'I hereby open this meeting'). Performatives are not true or false; they can be *felicitous* (succeed) or *infelicitous* (misfire).

Austin later generalised into three dimensions of any utterance. The *locutionary act* is the act of saying something with meaning. The *illocutionary act* is the conventional force — what is done in saying it (asserting, promising, ordering, warning). The *perlocutionary act* is the effect produced in the hearer (persuading, alarming, embarrassing). Searle systematised Austin's illocutionary acts into five categories (assertives, directives, commissives, expressives, declarations).

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Foundational for linguistics, legal philosophy, and communication theory — many legal disputes hinge on whether an utterance was an assertion or a promise, a warning or a threat.
cards.counter: The distinction between constatives and performatives became unstable (Austin himself dissolved it): even 'it is raining' has an illocutionary force (assertion). Speech act theory catalogues acts but struggles to explain how context determines force.

quiz.q: In Austin's framework, the 'illocutionary act' is…
choices: The effect the utterance produces in the hearer (persuading, alarming)
The conventional force of the utterance — what is done in saying it (asserting, promising, ordering)
The sounds and words produced in the act of speaking
Any utterance that describes an action rather than performing one

cards.title: Grice: implicature and the cooperative principle
cards.fact: Grice showed that we constantly communicate more than we literally say — by recognising that speakers are cooperative, hearers infer implicatures from apparent violations of conversational maxims.

layers.body: H.P. Grice observed that conversation is vastly underdetermined by sentence meaning. When someone asks 'can you pass the salt?' the literal meaning is a question about ability; what is communicated is a request. This 'implicature' is inferred because both parties know they are cooperating.

Grice formalised a *cooperative principle* — 'make your contribution appropriate to the conversation' — and four maxims: *Quantity* (say neither too little nor too much); *Quality* (be truthful); *Relation* (be relevant); *Manner* (be clear, brief, orderly). Implicatures arise when a speaker *ostentatiously* violates a maxim: saying 'X is a fine friend' of a betrayer implicates the opposite by violating Quality.

Sperber and Wilson's relevance theory (1986) reduced Grice's four maxims to one principle: communication aims to produce the greatest cognitive effect for the least processing effort. They argued this explains implicature more economically and accounts better for metaphor, irony, and loose use of language. Relevance theory is now dominant in cognitive pragmatics.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Establishes that meaning is not just sentence meaning but speaker meaning, context-dependent — crucial for legal interpretation, political rhetoric, and AI language understanding.
cards.counter: Gricean maxims assume cooperative, rational speakers. Much real communication — advertising, manipulation, irony, ritual speech — operates by strategic exploitation of the maxims rather than compliance.

quiz.q: What is a conversational 'implicature' in Grice's theory?
choices: A claim that is explicitly stated in a sentence
A logical entailment of a sentence
What is communicated beyond literal sentence meaning, inferred because speakers are assumed to be cooperative
A sentence whose meaning is ambiguous without context

cards.title: Kripke: rigid designators and a posteriori necessity
cards.fact: Kripke argued that proper names are rigid designators — they pick out the same object in every possible world — not bundles of descriptions; and that some necessary truths are known only empirically, e.g. 'water is H₂O'.

layers.body: On the Fregean-Russellian view, 'Aristotle' means something like 'the man who taught Alexander and wrote the Nicomachean Ethics.' Kripke's *Naming and Necessity* (1980) argues names are not descriptions: they are *rigid designators* fixed by a historical baptism and passed on through a causal chain. Even in a world where Aristotle never taught anyone, 'Aristotle' still refers to that very man.

Kripke distinguished two axes: epistemic (a priori/a posteriori) and metaphysical (necessary/contingent). Traditional philosophers assumed these aligned: necessary = a priori, contingent = a posteriori. Kripke showed they can come apart. 'Water is H₂O' is metaphysically necessary (water cannot be anything other than H₂O in any possible world) but a posteriori (we discovered this by chemistry). This is 'a posteriori necessity' — and it shatters the traditional picture.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / NYU analytic tradition] Transformed philosophy of language and metaphysics — showed that essence ('what a thing necessarily is') is an empirical question, not just an a priori one.
cards.counter: The causal theory of reference faces cases where the causal chain goes wrong (misidentification) or is incomplete (mathematical objects, fictional entities). Descriptivists have developed sophisticated replies (two-dimensional semantics, Jackson, Chalmers).

quiz.q: Why are proper names 'rigid designators' according to Kripke?
choices: They are defined by a fixed description that cannot change
They pick out the same object in every possible world, not via a description but via a causal-historical chain
They are the most precise form of reference in natural language
They always refer to physical objects rather than abstract ones

cards.title: Kant: categorical imperative (universalizability)
cards.fact: Kant's first formulation: act only according to the maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law — if universalising your maxim leads to contradiction, the act is impermissible.

layers.body: In the *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785) Kant argues that morality must be based on reason alone, not inclination. The first formulation of the categorical imperative: 'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' You must check whether your maxim could be universalised without contradiction.

Suppose you want to make a false promise to borrow money. Your maxim: 'When in need, I will make a false promise to borrow money.' Could this be a universal law? No — if everyone made false promises whenever convenient, the institution of promising would collapse; no one would believe promises, so your false promise would fail to secure the loan. The maxim is self-defeating when universalised: a *contradiction in conception*.

Critics argue the test is too permissive (one can always describe the maxim narrowly enough to pass) and too restrictive (many intuitively fine acts fail). Hegel objected that the universalizability test is merely formal — it can generate substantive conclusions only by smuggling in empirical assumptions about how the world works. Korsgaard's Kantian response: the test works because it tests whether your maxim could constitute its own success conditions.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] The core deontological move: moral worth comes from acting from duty, from a principle you could endorse for everyone, not from consequences.
cards.counter: The test generates counterintuitive results without supplementary principles. A maxim like 'always tell the truth, even to murderers seeking your friend' passes the universalizability test — but many argue this shows the test is incomplete without consequences.

quiz.q: Why can't the maxim 'I will make false promises when convenient' pass Kant's universalizability test?
choices: It would make everyone dishonest, producing bad consequences
Universalised, it would destroy the institution of promising, making the very maxim self-defeating
It violates the Golden Rule of treating others as you would be treated
It cannot be stated as a universal law without grammatical contradiction

cards.title: Kant: categorical imperative (humanity formula)
cards.fact: Kant's second formulation: act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in any other person, always as an end and never merely as a means.

layers.body: The second formulation of the categorical imperative shifts from logic to persons. Rational beings (persons) have dignity — unconditional worth not reducible to price. To treat a person merely as a means is to use them as a tool for your own ends without respecting their capacity for rational self-governance. Manipulation, coercion, and deceit paradigmatically violate this formula.

The formula says *merely* as a means — not 'never as a means.' You use a taxi driver as a means to your transport, but you do not use her merely as a means provided you don't deceive or coerce her and she consents to the arrangement. What is forbidden is treating rational beings as if their interests and rational agency were of no account. The formula grounds human rights: rights are protections of persons as ends.

Kant's formula applies to rational beings — which historically Kant restricted more narrowly than most contemporary philosophers accept. Does it apply to severely cognitively impaired humans? Animals? Future generations? Contemporary Kantians (Christine Korsgaard) have extended the formula, arguing that having a perspective from which things matter is sufficient for moral consideration — a move that includes many animals.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] Grounds human rights, medical ethics, and the prohibition on torture directly — persons cannot be sacrificed for aggregate utility because they are not mere receptacles of value.
cards.counter: The humanity formula gives no guidance when respecting one person's rational agency requires harming another's. Trolley problems and triage expose the formula's silence on trade-offs.

quiz.q: What is the key distinction in Kant's humanity formula between permissible and impermissible treatment of persons?
choices: Permissible: never using persons as means; impermissible: using them as ends
Permissible: using persons as means with consent; impermissible: treating them merely as means, ignoring their rational agency
Permissible: using rational persons; impermissible: using non-rational beings
Permissible: using persons for public benefit; impermissible: using them for private gain

cards.title: Kant: kingdom of ends
cards.fact: Kant's third formulation: act according to maxims of a legislative member of a possible kingdom of ends — a community of all rational beings each treating the others as ends.

layers.body: The third formulation synthesises the first two. Imagine a 'kingdom of ends': a community where all members are both subject to and legislators of the moral law, treating each other as ends. Morally permissible acts are those whose maxims could be endorsed by all members of such a community. This unifies universalisability and dignity.

The kingdom of ends formulation makes Kant's ethics explicitly social and procedural: morality is not a monologue (am I contradicting myself?) but a dialogue (could everyone rationally endorse this?). It prefigures later contractualist ethics (Scanlon, Habermas): legitimacy comes from the ability to justify one's actions to all those affected. It also grounds the idea that even citizens are legislators of the moral and political law — Kant's connection between ethics and democracy.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] Bridges Kantian deontology and social contract theory; grounds the idea that legitimate political authority requires justification to citizens as co-legislators.
cards.counter: The kingdom of ends is a regulative ideal, not a procedure. Kant does not specify who participates or how disagreements are resolved — later philosophers (Habermas, Rawls) had to develop the institutional and procedural machinery Kant left implicit.

quiz.q: What does Kant mean by a 'kingdom of ends'?
choices: A theocracy where God's commands are the moral law
An ideal community of all rational beings, each treating others as ends and serving as co-legislators of the moral law
A democracy where majority votes determine ethical principles
A utilitarian community optimised for aggregate happiness

cards.title: Bentham: the greatest happiness principle
cards.fact: Bentham's utilitarianism holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness of the greatest number — and that pleasure and pain are the only real values.

layers.body: Jeremy Bentham's *Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation* (1789) begins: 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' The utilitarian principle follows: the right act is that which maximises the sum of pleasure minus pain across all those affected. Each person counts as one and no more.

Bentham proposed a *hedonic calculus* for measuring pleasures: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity (tendency to produce more pleasure), purity (tendency not to produce pain), and extent (number of people affected). The calculus is meant to make morality scientific and democratic — every person's pleasure counts equally, regardless of birth or status. Bentham applied it to prison reform, animal welfare, and democratic politics.

If utility is simply additive, a sufficiently large gain for the many can justify serious harm to a few. This generates notorious counterexamples: could we torture one person to provide mild pleasure to millions? Bentham's answer — that the numbers justify it — strikes most people as monstrous. This led Mill to distinguish higher and lower pleasures, and later philosophers (Rawls, Nozick) to reject aggregation as incompatible with individual rights.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] Grounds the strongest consequentialist argument in policy — that interventions should be judged by their total effect on wellbeing, not by rule-following or rights.
cards.counter: Pure hedonistic utilitarianism cannot explain why certain acts feel intrinsically wrong regardless of consequences. It also requires interpersonal utility comparisons that may be theoretically impossible.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental principle of Bentham's utilitarianism?
choices: Act as you would want others to act toward you
Maximise the greatest happiness of the greatest number — the sum of pleasure minus pain
Follow rules that, if universally adopted, would produce the best outcomes
Respect the rights of every individual, regardless of consequences

cards.title: Mill: higher pleasures and the harm principle
cards.fact: Mill modified Bentham by distinguishing higher (intellectual, moral) from lower (bodily) pleasures — 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied' — and by limiting social interference to self-regarding actions.

layers.body: John Stuart Mill accepted Bentham's utilitarian framework but rejected pure hedonism: not all pleasures are equal in kind, only in quantity. Intellectual, aesthetic, and moral pleasures are higher; bodily pleasures lower. A person who has experienced both will prefer the higher, even when it involves more dissatisfaction. This qualitative distinction rescues utilitarianism from the 'pig satisfied' objection.

In *On Liberty* (1859) Mill argued that the only legitimate basis for society's coercive interference with individual liberty is to prevent harm to others. Self-regarding actions — that affect only the agent — are beyond law and social pressure. This harm principle grounds modern liberal politics: drug policy, sexual freedom, paternalism debates. Mill intended it to protect autonomy and individuality as preconditions for human flourishing.

The higher/lower pleasure distinction sits uneasily with utilitarian aggregation: if quality matters, utility sums may be incomparable. And the harm principle is notoriously hard to apply — almost every action harms someone indirectly. Devlin argued that Mill's individualism ignores social fabric; Feinberg extended harm to include offence, endangerment, and liberalism itself. Contemporary debates on hate speech, pornography, and paternalism all replay the harm principle.

cards.deploy: [Oxford ethics] The harm principle is the standard liberal argument against paternalism and moralistic legislation — still the baseline reference in any debate about what law may prohibit.
cards.counter: Mill never satisfactorily explained how higher pleasures are measured; if they cannot be aggregated with lower ones, the utilitarian calculus breaks down. The harm principle is vaguer in practice than in theory.

quiz.q: According to Mill's harm principle, society may coercively interfere with individual action only when…
choices: The action offends the majority's sense of morality
The action harms only the agent themselves
The action causes harm to others
The action violates a rule whose universal adoption would decrease total utility

cards.title: Rule vs act utilitarianism
cards.fact: Act utilitarianism evaluates each action by its own consequences; rule utilitarianism evaluates actions by whether they follow rules whose general acceptance would maximise utility.

layers.body: Act utilitarianism (AU): for each action, calculate expected utility and choose the act that maximises it. This leads to counterintuitive results — promise-breaking, punishment of the innocent, lying, may all be permitted if they produce better consequences. Rule utilitarianism (RU): follow the rules whose general adoption would maximise utility. Keeping promises is a rule that, generally followed, produces better outcomes than case-by-case utility calculation.

The sharpest objection to RU is that it collapses into AU. For any rule, the RU utilitarian should add an exception clause for cases where breaking the rule maximises utility. A rule 'keep promises, except when breaking them produces more utility' is just act utilitarianism in rule clothing. Brandt and others responded by specifying that RU rules must be adopted in a world where full compliance is expected — a different calculation from AU.

cards.deploy: [Oxford ethics] Distinguishes two versions of consequentialism — understanding which version is being invoked is essential to any policy or ethics debate.
cards.counter: RU faces the collapse objection (above) from AU, and the charge of being insufficiently consequentialist from Kantians: if utility is what matters, why follow rules that sometimes produce less of it?

quiz.q: The 'collapse objection' to rule utilitarianism claims that…
choices: Rule utilitarianism is indistinguishable from Kantian deontology
Adding exception clauses to every rule for utility-maximising cases reduces rule utilitarianism to act utilitarianism
Rules cannot be specified precisely enough to guide action
Utility cannot be measured for groups of people, only individuals

cards.title: Aristotle: virtue ethics
cards.fact: Aristotle argued that the goal of human life is eudaimonia (flourishing), achieved by cultivating virtues — stable character traits like courage, justice, and practical wisdom — that lie between excess and deficiency.

layers.body: While Kant asks 'What should I do?' and Bentham 'What produces most good?', Aristotle asks 'What kind of person should I be?' The *Nicomachean Ethics* argues that the good life is *eudaimonia* — active exercise of the soul in accordance with virtue. Virtue is not a single act but a stable disposition: the courageous person acts courageously because of who they are.

Each virtue is a mean between two vices — excess and deficiency. Courage is the mean between cowardice (deficiency) and recklessness (excess). Justice is the mean between taking too little and too much. But the mean is relative to the person and the situation, not arithmetically fixed. Crucially, virtues are acquired through practice: we become courageous by doing courageous acts. Character is a second nature formed by habituation.

Virtue ethics was largely dormant after Kant until Elizabeth Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958) argued that deontological ethics presupposes a divine lawgiver and needs replacing with an Aristotelian character ethics. MacIntyre's *After Virtue* (1981) diagnosed modernity as having lost the narrative and communal context that makes virtues intelligible. Virtue ethics is now one of the three main normative frameworks in analytic ethics.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] Shifts ethical focus from acts and rules to character formation — important for medical ethics, professional ethics, and educational philosophy.
cards.counter: Virtue ethics says little about what to do in specific dilemmas; 'what would a courageous person do?' is not always action-guiding. It is also historically tied to particular conceptions of human flourishing that may be culturally specific.

quiz.q: According to Aristotle, what is the relationship between virtue and habituation?
choices: Virtue is innate and cannot be developed through practice
Virtues are acquired by performing virtuous acts repeatedly, forming stable character dispositions
Virtue is knowledge — understanding the good is sufficient for acting well
Virtue is feeling the right emotions; action follows automatically

cards.title: MacIntyre: After Virtue
cards.fact: MacIntyre argued that modern moral philosophy is incoherent because it uses the vocabulary of virtue and obligation without the Aristotelian teleological framework that gave those terms their meaning — like speaking a language whose grammar has been lost.

layers.body: *After Virtue* (1981) opens with an analogy: imagine a civilisation that destroys its scientific knowledge but retains the fragments. Later generations use the words 'electron' and 'mass' without the theoretical framework that gave them content. MacIntyre argues that is the position of modern ethics: the language of rights, duties, and virtues persists, but the teleological framework (humans have a natural end, a *telos*) that justified it has been abandoned.

MacIntyre defines a virtue as a quality needed to achieve the *goods internal to a practice* — those goods achievable only through the practice itself (chess mastery can only be experienced through chess, not bought). Practices are sustained by *traditions*, which supply the narrative context within which individual lives have meaning. Without participating in tradition-constituted practices, virtues cannot be learned or exercised — which is why modernity produces emotivism (the view that ethical claims are just expressions of preference).

cards.deploy: [Oxford ethics] Grounds communitarian critiques of liberal individualism — the self is not prior to its ends; character is formed within and by communities, not chosen from behind a veil of ignorance.
cards.counter: MacIntyre's appeal to Aristotelian teleology is rejected by most analytic philosophers as metaphysically committed in a way modern science cannot sustain. His communitarianism has been criticised for making it hard to critique the tradition one inhabits.

quiz.q: What are 'goods internal to a practice' in MacIntyre's account?
choices: Financial rewards that practices provide to their participants
Goods achievable only through participation in the practice itself — like chess mastery or musical excellence
Moral rules that apply only within specific communities
The emotional satisfactions of belonging to a social group

cards.title: Scanlon: contractualism
cards.fact: Scanlon's contractualism grounds morality in what we owe to each other: an act is wrong if its performance under the circumstances would be disallowed by any set of principles that no one could reasonably reject.

layers.body: T.M. Scanlon's *What We Owe to Each Other* (1998) grounds morality in our standing as beings who can give and demand reasons from each other. An act is wrong if it is forbidden by principles that no one could reasonably reject as the basis for mutual governance.

Scanlon shares Kant's contractualist structure but replaces the categorical imperative with reasonable agreement. Unlike Rawls, who uses the veil of ignorance to derive principles of justice for social institutions, Scanlon's contractualism governs individual morality — what I owe you personally. Reasonable rejection is not majority rejection: a principle can be reasonably rejected by one person even if the many benefit from it.

Scanlon's contractualism handles aggregation differently from utilitarianism. Can the minor benefits to many outweigh serious harm to one? Scanlon says no: each individual has the right to reject a principle that sacrifices her for aggregate benefit. This produces the 'numbers don't count' objection — critics like John Taurek and contractualists themselves debate how to handle cases where we must choose between saving one or five.

cards.deploy: [NYU/Oxford ethics] The main non-consequentialist, non-Kantian alternative: grounds moral prohibitions in what individuals can reasonably reject rather than in abstract categorical principles or utility sums.
cards.counter: Critics argue 'reasonable rejection' is too indeterminate — what counts as reasonable? Without a theory of reasonable preferences, contractualism risks circularity (reasonable = morally appropriate, which presupposes the morality being defined).

quiz.q: On Scanlon's contractualism, an act is morally wrong if…
choices: It produces less utility than the available alternatives
It treats persons merely as means
It would be disallowed by principles no one could reasonably reject
A majority of affected parties would vote against it

cards.title: Singer: expanding the moral circle
cards.fact: Peter Singer's drowning child argument: if you could save a child drowning before you, you would; distance and statistical vs identifiable victims do not change the moral obligation — we are required to give until giving more would make us significantly worse off.

layers.body: In 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972) Singer argues: if it is in my power to prevent something very bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral significance, I ought to do it — regardless of whether it is a drowning child in front of me or a starving child in a distant country. Distance and nationality are morally irrelevant.

The argument generates radical obligations: affluent people should give to the most effective causes until giving more would cost them something of comparable moral importance. This is the philosophical foundation of the effective altruism movement — the idea that we should choose which causes to support based on evidence of impact, not emotional salience. Singer later applied the argument to animal suffering: if sentience is what matters morally, the species of the sufferer is as arbitrary as its geography.

Critics raise two objections. The *demandingness objection*: the principle demands too much — it would require giving away almost all wealth. Singer replies that most people give almost nothing, so the demandingness objection rationalises inaction. The *partiality objection*: we are permitted to prioritise those close to us — family, compatriots — and Singer's impartiality erases morally important special obligations. Singer responds that partiality is a bias analogous to racism.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] The sharpest philosophical case for radically increasing foreign aid and charitable giving; regularly used in applied ethics and international development debates.
cards.counter: William MacAskill's 'longtermism' extends Singer's logic temporally — future people matter as much as present ones. But critics argue this can justify sacrificing present welfare for speculative future benefits, inverting Singer's original practical focus.

quiz.q: What is Singer's central argument in 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality'?
choices: Governments, not individuals, are responsible for global poverty
If we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral significance, we ought to — regardless of geographic distance
Only immediate, identifiable suffering creates genuine moral obligations
Charitable giving is morally supererogatory — praiseworthy but not required

cards.title: Descartes: Cartesian dualism
cards.fact: Descartes argued that mind and body are two entirely different substances — res cogitans (thinking substance) and res extensa (extended substance) — and the mind can in principle exist without the body.

layers.body: Descartes's famous *cogito* — 'I think, therefore I am' — establishes that the thinking self is known with certainty even while doubting the external world. From this he argues the mind is a substance entirely different from matter: the mind has no extension in space; the body has no capacity for thought. They are metaphysically distinct.

If mind and body are entirely distinct substances, how do they causally interact? Descartes proposed the pineal gland as the site of interaction — an answer immediately ridiculed. More seriously: if the mental is non-physical, how does a thought cause a physical movement (raising my arm)? This *mind-body problem* drives all subsequent philosophy of mind. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed it on Descartes in their famous correspondence.

Despite its problems, dualism captures something important: mental states (pain, beliefs, desires) seem fundamentally unlike physical states (neural firing). This is the intuitive basis for Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness. Property dualism — not substance dualism — is the contemporary version: there is only one substance, but mental properties are not reducible to physical ones.

cards.deploy: [Oxford philosophy of mind] The historical starting point for the philosophy of mind: every subsequent position (identity theory, functionalism, eliminativism, property dualism) is defined in relation to the Cartesian picture.
cards.counter: Neuroscience has accumulated extensive evidence for the tight correlation of mental and physical states — brain damage alters personality and cognition in predictable ways. The burden of proof lies with dualists to explain how mental and physical can interact if they are distinct.

quiz.q: What is the 'interaction problem' for Cartesian dualism?
choices: How can the pineal gland generate consciousness?
If mind and body are entirely distinct substances, how can a mental event (a thought) cause a physical event (raising an arm)?
How can two people share mental states if minds are private substances?
How can the brain store the infinite complexity of conscious experience?

cards.title: Type identity theory
cards.fact: Type identity theory holds that mental state types are identical to brain state types: pain = C-fibre firing; beliefs = specific neural patterns. There is no separate mental substance.

layers.body: U.T. Place ('Is Consciousness a Brain Process?', 1956) and J.J.C. Smart proposed a radical simplification: mental states are not distinct from physical brain states — they are identical. 'I am in pain' just means 'my C-fibres are firing.' This eliminates the mind-body problem by denying there are two distinct things to interact.

*Type identity* says every mental state type (pain-in-general) is identical to a physical type (C-fibre firing). This is a strong claim: pain is always and everywhere C-fibre firing, in all creatures. *Token identity* is weaker: each individual mental state token is identical to some physical token, but different creatures might realise pain in different physical ways. Hilary Putnam's multiple realizability argument demolished type identity but left token identity viable.

cards.deploy: [Oxford philosophy of mind] The clearest physicalist position — grounds neuroscience's assumption that mental phenomena are explicable in physical terms.
cards.counter: Multiple realizability: Martians, octopuses, and AI systems could be in pain without C-fibres. If pain can be realised differently in different systems, it cannot be identical to any single physical type.

quiz.q: What is the multiple realizability objection to type identity theory?
choices: Pain is too variable in intensity to identify with a single neural state
Different creatures could be in the same mental state (pain) without sharing the same physical brain state, so pain cannot be identical to any single physical type
Brain states are observable; mental states are not — so they cannot be identical
Type identity requires that all tokens of a type be physically identical, which no two brain cells are

cards.title: Functionalism
cards.fact: Functionalism defines mental states by their causal-functional role — pain is whatever state is caused by tissue damage and causes avoidance behaviour — not by their physical makeup. This allows multiple realizability.

layers.t: What something does, not what it is made of
layers.body: Hilary Putnam's functionalism (1967) defines mental states by their functional role: their causal relations to inputs, outputs, and other mental states. Pain is not C-fibre firing — it is whatever state is caused by damage and causes avoidance. A Martian whose pain is realised in silicon still has pain, provided the causal role is the same.

Functionalism is inspired by the computer analogy: a program can run on different hardware while remaining the same program. Mental states are like software — realised in biological neural networks now, but in principle realisable in other physical systems. This opened the possibility of artificial intelligence as genuine cognition, and grounded the computational theory of mind (Fodor's *Language of Thought*).

Chalmers argues there could be a being functionally identical to you — same inputs, same outputs, same causal structure — but with no subjective experience. Such a 'philosophical zombie' is conceivable. If so, functional organisation does not suffice for consciousness. Functionalism accounts for cognition but may leave the qualitative feel of experience — qualia — unexplained.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU philosophy of mind] The dominant framework in cognitive science and AI — grounds the possibility of machine cognition and sets up the debate about consciousness vs computation.
cards.counter: Ned Block's inverted qualia (your red may be my green, though we behave identically) and absent qualia (functionalism without phenomenal consciousness) arguments suggest functional organisation doesn't determine inner experience.

quiz.q: What does functionalism say that type identity theory denies?
choices: That mental states are causally efficacious
That the same mental state type can be physically realised in different ways in different systems
That consciousness can be explained scientifically
That artificial intelligence is possible

cards.title: Searle: the Chinese room
cards.fact: Searle's thought experiment: a person in a room follows rules to manipulate Chinese symbols without understanding Chinese — just like a computer. Syntax (symbol manipulation) is not sufficient for semantics (understanding).

layers.body: John Searle's Chinese room (1980): imagine you are locked in a room with a rulebook for responding to Chinese symbols. You pass the Turing test — your outputs are indistinguishable from a Chinese speaker's. But you don't understand a word of Chinese. A computer that processes symbols perfectly is in the same position: syntax does not give rise to semantics.

Searle distinguishes *weak AI* (computers simulate cognitive processes) from *strong AI* (computers have genuine cognitive states). He accepts weak AI but argues the Chinese room refutes strong AI: no matter how sophisticated the simulation, symbol manipulation alone cannot produce genuine understanding, intentionality, or consciousness. The room as a whole may pass the test, but nothing in it understands Chinese.

The main reply: the person doesn't understand Chinese, but the *system* as a whole does. Searle's response: if the person memorises the rulebook, they are the whole system — and they still don't understand. A second reply: the robot reply (embed the system in a robot body with sensors) — consciousness may require causal connection to the world. Large language models have renewed this debate: do GPT-class systems 'understand' in any sense?

cards.deploy: [Oxford philosophy of mind] The standard argument against strong AI and computational theories of mind — tests any claim that a system 'understands' or 'thinks' purely by virtue of its computational behaviour.
cards.counter: Most cognitive scientists and functionalists find the systems reply compelling. The Chinese room assumes an implausibly sharp syntax/semantics distinction; in connectionist networks, 'symbol manipulation' and 'understanding' may not be cleanly separable.

quiz.q: What is the 'systems reply' to the Chinese room argument?
choices: The person does understand Chinese after practicing long enough
The entire system — rules, person, and room together — understands Chinese, even if no individual component does
The Chinese room is not a fair simulation of how computers actually work
Understanding Chinese requires a biological brain, not a paper rulebook

cards.title: Chalmers: the hard problem of consciousness
cards.fact: The hard problem: explaining why physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective experience — why there is something it is like to see red, feel pain — not merely how the brain processes information.

layers.body: David Chalmers (1995) distinguished easy problems of consciousness (explaining attention, reportability, perception, memory — all are hard scientifically but tractable in principle by functional/computational explanation) from the *hard problem*: why does any of this physical processing feel like anything from the inside? Why is there subjective experience at all?

Even a complete neuroscientific account of pain — which neurons fire, how signals propagate, how behaviour results — seems to leave out the *painfulness* of pain: the raw feel, the quale. This 'explanatory gap' between physical description and phenomenal experience is the hard problem. Chalmers argues it cannot be solved by adding more neuroscience: the problem is conceptual, not empirical.

Dennett's eliminativism: qualia are an illusion; the intuition that there is a hard problem is itself a cognitive error. Type-B materialism: the explanatory gap is real but epistemological, not metaphysical — there is no gap in the world, only in our concepts. Chalmers's own property dualism: phenomenal properties are real, non-physical, and supervene on physical properties without being reducible to them.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU philosophy of mind] The central live debate in philosophy of mind and increasingly in AI ethics — distinguishes the question of cognitive function from the question of consciousness.
cards.counter: Dennett argues the hard problem presupposes a Cartesian theatre — a central observer of experience — that neuroscience shows does not exist. Once the confusion is cleared up, the hard problem dissolves.
