quiz.q: What distinguishes the 'hard problem' of consciousness from what Chalmers calls the 'easy problems'?
choices: The hard problem is harder empirically — it requires more experiments to solve
The easy problems concern cognitive functions (attention, memory) tractable to functional explanation; the hard problem asks why any physical process gives rise to subjective experience at all
The hard problem concerns unconscious processing; easy problems concern conscious experience
The hard problem is only a problem for dualists; materialists have already solved it

cards.title: Nagel: what is it like to be a bat?
cards.fact: Nagel's 1974 paper argues that the subjective character of experience — what it is like to be a bat — cannot be captured by any objective, third-person physical description, so physicalism must be incomplete.

layers.t: The irreducibility of the first person
layers.body: We know bats navigate by echolocation. But what is it *like* to experience the world through echolocation? Thomas Nagel argues we cannot know — not because of ignorance but because the subjective character of experience is inherently first-personal. Any objective description abstracts away from the perspective of the subject.

If physicalism were true, an objective physical description of a brain would capture everything about mental states. But no physical description captures *what it is like* to be the creature having those states. There is a fact about bat sonar experience that lies beyond any third-person description. Therefore, physicalism as currently formulated is incomplete. Nagel is not arguing for dualism but for the limits of the objective-subjective framework we have.

cards.deploy: [Oxford philosophy of mind] Grounds the intuition that subjective experience is not fully captured by science — essential context for debates about consciousness, AI sentience, and animal welfare.
cards.counter: Paul Churchland argues the 'mystery' of qualia rests on a failure of imagination: as neuroscience develops, we will develop new concepts that make the subjective character of experience scientifically tractable — just as we did for heat, colour, and other apparently non-physical qualities.

quiz.q: What does Nagel mean when he says we cannot know what it is like to be a bat?
choices: Bats are too neurologically different from us to study scientifically
The subjective character of bat experience is inherently first-personal and cannot be captured by any objective physical description
Our cognitive limitations prevent us from imagining echolocation
Bat experience is simpler than human experience and therefore not phenomenally rich

cards.title: The problem of universals
cards.fact: Do abstract properties like redness or justice exist independently of the things that have them? Realists say yes; nominalists say only particular things exist; conceptualists say universals exist in the mind.

layers.body: Two roses are both red. What makes that true? *Realism* (Plato, Armstrong): there is a universal Redness that both roses instantiate — it exists independently of any rose. *Nominalism*: only the two roses exist; 'red' is just a word we apply to similar things. *Conceptualism*: universals exist as concepts in the mind, not in the world.

The debate has downstream consequences for mathematics (do numbers exist?), science (do natural kinds exist?), and ethics (do moral properties exist mind-independently?). Armstrong's *in re* realism — universals exist but only instantiated in particulars — is the dominant contemporary position in analytic metaphysics. It grounds scientific realism: laws of nature hold because they express genuine universal properties of things.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Foundational metaphysics: the debate about abstract objects (numbers, laws, propositions) is a version of the universals debate with major implications for philosophy of mathematics and science.
cards.counter: Nominalism is ontologically parsimonious (Occam's razor: don't multiply entities beyond necessity), but struggles to explain what makes similarity claims true without invoking the very universals it wants to eliminate.

quiz.q: What is Armstrong's 'in re' realism about universals?
choices: Universals exist independently in a Platonic realm, separate from all particulars
Universals are mere names (nomina) for patterns of similar particulars
Universals exist, but only instantiated in particular things — not in a separate realm
Universals are mental concepts that we project onto the world

cards.title: Possible worlds semantics
cards.fact: Modal logic — the logic of necessity and possibility — is given a semantics via possible worlds: 'necessarily P' means P is true in all possible worlds; 'possibly P' means P is true in at least one.

layers.body: 'It is necessarily true that 2+2=4' and 'It is possible that Napoleon won at Waterloo.' These modal claims differ from ordinary claims: what makes them true? Possible worlds semantics says: a proposition is *necessarily* true if and only if it is true in all possible worlds; *possibly* true if true in at least one.

David Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds*, 1986) took the ontological jump: possible worlds are *concrete realities*, as real as the actual world — they just don't stand in any spatio-temporal relation to us. Other philosophers use *ersatz* possible worlds: maximally consistent sets of propositions, or abstract structures. Lewis's realism is parsimonious in one sense (no extra primitives) but radically counterintuitive (infinite concrete worlds exist).

Possible worlds semantics is used in: logic (soundness and completeness proofs for modal logics); linguistics (conditionals, presuppositions); philosophy (causation, counterfactuals, essence, de re vs de dicto modality). Kripke's rigid designators are defined in terms of possible worlds. Chalmers uses two-dimensional semantics (two sets of possible worlds) to analyse the relationship between conceivability and possibility.

cards.deploy: [Oxford analytic tradition] Provides the formal tools for reasoning about necessity, possibility, counterfactuals, and hypotheticals — used in logic, linguistics, AI, and ethical reasoning.
cards.counter: Lewis's modal realism is widely found too ontologically extravagant. And 'possible worlds' may be viciously circular for explaining modality: to say a world is possible already presupposes a notion of possibility.

quiz.q: In possible worlds semantics, 'it is necessarily true that P' means…
choices: P is true and cannot be doubted
P is logically provable from first principles
P is true in all possible worlds
P is true in the actual world and most nearby worlds

cards.title: Lewis: counterfactual causation
cards.fact: Lewis analyses causation counterfactually: C caused E if and only if, had C not occurred, E would not have occurred — evaluated across the closest possible worlds where C is absent.

layers.body: Hume analysed causation as constant conjunction plus temporal priority. Lewis's improvement uses possible worlds: C causes E if in the closest possible worlds where C doesn't occur, E doesn't occur either. This captures the intuition that causation is about what *would have happened* in the relevant counterfactual scenario.

The main difficulties: *preemption* (two events both sufficient for E, but C fires first — E counterfactually depends on C, but only because D was preempted); *overdetermination* (two independent events, each sufficient for E — the building burns from both arson and lightning). Lewis developed a sophisticated 'chancy' counterfactual theory to handle these cases, and later moved to an 'influence' account. Causal inference in statistics and machine learning faces the same problems.

cards.deploy: [Oxford metaphysics] Foundational for legal and scientific reasoning about causation — and directly relevant to causal inference debates in statistics (Pearl's do-calculus formalises a similar idea).
cards.counter: Counterfactual theories face preemption and overdetermination (above); they also rely on a notion of 'closeness' between possible worlds that may be obscure or circular.

quiz.q: On Lewis's counterfactual theory, what makes it true that C caused E?
choices: C and E are constantly conjoined in our experience
C temporally precedes E and is spatially contiguous with it
In the closest possible world where C doesn't occur, E doesn't occur either
C is a necessary condition for E given background conditions

cards.title: Personal identity: continuity and what matters
cards.fact: What makes you the same person over time? Locke said memory (psychological continuity); physical/bodily continuity theorists said the body; Parfit argued personal identity is not what matters — survival of psychological continuity matters even without strict identity.

layers.body: Locke (1689): personal identity consists in continuity of *consciousness* — memory links present to past self. You are the same person as the five-year-old who has your memories. The *body* theorist: you are your organism; memory and personality can change but the biological continuity is identity. Both face cases: amnesia, teletransportation, fission (one brain divided into two people).

Derek Parfit (*Reasons and Persons*, 1984) argued that personal identity is a further fact beyond physical and psychological continuity — and it may not be what matters. In the fission case, your brain is divided and transplanted into two bodies: both are psychologically continuous with you. Which is you? Parfit: neither, or both — and neither answer matters much. What matters is psychological continuity itself, not whether it constitutes strict identity.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] Personal identity matters for punishment (same person as the criminal?), healthcare (advanced directives), population ethics (future persons), and the ethics of early-life interventions.
cards.counter: Marya Schechtman's 'narrative self-constitution' view and Eric Olson's animalism (you are your organism, period) both challenge psychological continuity accounts on different grounds.

quiz.q: What is Parfit's key claim about personal identity?
choices: Personal identity is grounded in the continuity of the physical body
Personal identity is what matters — without it, nothing of importance survives
Personal identity may not be what matters; psychological continuity matters even without strict identity
Personal identity is unknowable and should be dropped from philosophy

cards.title: Lakatos: scientific research programmes
cards.fact: Lakatos proposed that science advances through competing research programmes, each with a 'hard core' of inviolable assumptions protected by a 'protective belt' of auxiliary hypotheses — a programme is scientific if progressive, degenerate if shrinking.

layers.body: Popper said science advances by falsifying theories. Kuhn said scientists protect their paradigms from refutation. Lakatos aimed to split the difference: scientists rationally protect a *hard core* of foundational assumptions by redirecting refutations onto *auxiliary hypotheses*. This is legitimate — if new auxiliary hypotheses predict novel facts, the programme is *progressive*. If they only explain away existing anomalies, it is *degenerative*.

Newtonian mechanics: the hard core (Newton's laws) was protected for centuries by adding auxiliary hypotheses (new planets, new forces) when anomalies appeared. Kuhn saw this as paradigm incommensurability; Lakatos saw it as rational protection of a progressive programme. The Newtonian programme became degenerative only when it stopped predicting new phenomena and merely explained anomalies post hoc. This is the difference between explaining why Mercury's orbit deviated (Einsteinian) and inventing a new unseen planet (Vulcan).

cards.deploy: [Oxford philosophy of science] More realistic than naive Popperian falsificationism — scientists do and should protect their best theories while the programme is progressive.
cards.counter: The progressive/degenerative distinction is hard to apply in real time — one person's protection of a progressive programme is another's irrationality. Feyerabend argued Lakatos's criteria, applied strictly, would condemn major scientific advances as dogmatic.

quiz.q: In Lakatos's model, a scientific research programme becomes 'degenerative' when…
choices: The hard core is directly falsified by experimental evidence
The programme only generates post hoc explanations of anomalies, not novel predictions
Scientists stop publishing within the programme
The auxiliary hypotheses contradict the hard core

cards.title: Feyerabend: against method
cards.fact: Feyerabend argued that science has no single rational method — every major advance involved violating the rules of the day; the only principle that does not inhibit progress is 'anything goes'.

layers.body: Paul Feyerabend's *Against Method* (1975) is the most radical philosophy of science: there is no methodological rule that science has always followed. Galileo's successes required violating inductive and falsificationist norms. The only consistent principle of scientific practice is *epistemological anarchism* — 'anything goes' — not as a positive prescription but as a description of how science actually advances.

Feyerabend argued Galileo succeeded not by following the scientific method but by *propaganda*, rhetorical skill, and an appeal to telescope observations that were theoretically contaminated by optics Galileo did not fully understand. The Church's objections were not simply irrational. Feyerabend was not anti-science — he was arguing against the mythologised image of science as uniquely rational, which he saw as an ideology that unjustifiably marginalises alternative traditions.

cards.deploy: [Oxford philosophy of science] Useful corrective to naive Popperian accounts — science's actual history is messier than its self-image; acknowledges the role of rhetoric, social factors, and non-rational elements in scientific change.
cards.counter: Most philosophers of science reject 'anything goes' as too permissive — it gives no basis to prefer Einstein over astrology. Feyerabend's own historical case studies have been challenged; and his conclusions are more provocative than his arguments warrant.

quiz.q: Feyerabend's 'anything goes' is best understood as…
choices: A positive recommendation to abandon all scientific standards
A description of the actual historical diversity of methods that have produced scientific advances — no single method has been consistently followed
A defence of pseudoscience and alternative medicine on equal footing with science
A critique of Kuhn's paradigm theory from a rationalist perspective

cards.title: Parfit: reasons and persons
cards.fact: Parfit's Reasons and Persons argues that personal identity is less deep than we assume, that this matters for ethics (future people, obligations to future generations, population ethics), and that consequentialism, contractualism, and Kantianism may converge.

layers.t: The most important book in ethics
layers.body: *Reasons and Persons* (1984) is unusual in analytic philosophy — it pursues several interconnected theses across 540 pages. Its core insight: our ordinary beliefs about personal identity are false in a philosophically significant way, and recognising this should change our ethical and practical reasoning.

A policy that causes climate change harms future people — but those people would not have existed under a different policy (different events, different people meet and conceive). How can we harm people by causing them to exist in worse conditions, when the alternative is their non-existence? This *non-identity problem* (a better policy causes different people to exist) threatens to undermine obligations to future generations. Parfit explored multiple solutions — total vs average views of population ethics, person-affecting principles — without reaching a fully satisfying answer.

cards.deploy: [Oxford/NYU ethics] Foundational for population ethics, climate ethics, and intergenerational justice — forces precise thinking about obligations to people who don't yet exist.
cards.counter: Parfit concluded *Reasons and Persons* in aporia — the non-identity problem and the repugnant conclusion (maximise total utility even with very large populations at barely-livable conditions) have no solution he could endorse. The field remains unresolved.

quiz.q: What is the 'non-identity problem' as Parfit poses it?
choices: Future people cannot be identified precisely, so we have no obligations to them
A policy that harms future people may be required if those people would not have existed under an alternative policy, making the harm impossible to compare to non-existence
Personal identity across time makes it unclear whether our future selves are owed the same obligations as present selves
Different individuals have non-identical interests, making interpersonal utility comparisons impossible

cards.title: Athenian democracy
cards.fact: Athens from Cleisthenes (507 BCE) was a direct democracy — male citizens voted in the assembly on laws and decisions, and most offices were filled by sortition (lottery), not election.

layers.body: Cleisthenes' reforms (507 BCE) created the world's first democracy: the *ekklesia* (assembly) met 40 times a year and all male citizens could speak and vote. The *boule* (council of 500) prepared assembly business, its members chosen by lot from citizens over 30. Most magistracies were filled by lottery — election was considered oligarchic.

At its height, Athens had perhaps 30,000–60,000 adult male citizens, of whom maybe 6,000 attended a typical assembly. Women, slaves (up to a third of the population), and *metics* (foreign residents) were excluded entirely. Payment for jury service and assembly attendance was introduced to enable poor citizens to participate. This was a democracy for citizens only — built on slave labour.

Athens was a direct democracy — citizens legislated and judged directly, not through representatives. Modern liberal democracy is representative and separates legislation from administration. Athenian democracy had no written constitution protecting individual rights against the demos: it condemned Socrates by majority vote. The Athenian precedent is simultaneously the ideal of participatory democracy and a warning about majoritarian tyranny.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The reference point for all democratic theory — and for critiques of both representation (too remote from direct rule) and majoritarian democracy (no minority protections).
cards.counter: The Athenian model was compatible with brutal imperialism, chattel slavery, and female exclusion. Romanticising it as an ideal requires filtering out most of who lived under it.

quiz.q: How were most magistracies filled in Athenian democracy?
choices: By popular election in the assembly
By hereditary succession from noble families
By sortition (lottery) from eligible citizens — election was considered oligarchic
By appointment from the council of 500

cards.title: The Persian Wars
cards.fact: The Greek city-states, led by Athens and Sparta, repelled two Persian invasions (490 BCE: Marathon; 480 BCE: Salamis, Thermopylae) — establishing Athens's naval power and the myth of Greek freedom defending against Eastern despotism.

layers.body: The Persian wars are the first great self-defining myth of Western civilisation: free Greek citizens defeating the vast Persian empire. Marathon (490 BCE) — 10,000 Athenians defeat a larger Persian force. Thermopylae (480 BCE) — 300 Spartans hold the pass. Salamis (480 BCE) — the Athenian fleet destroys the Persian navy. Each battle became a cultural touchstone.

Athens's naval victory at Salamis established Athenian sea power. The Delian League, formed to continue the Persian war, became an Athenian empire: allies paid tribute to Athens, which used it to build the Parthenon. Herodotus, writing after the wars, created the first prose history — analysing causes, comparing cultures, and establishing the narrative genre that shaped Western historical writing. The wars generated the freedom vs despotism binary that haunts Western political thought.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Introduces the Persian Wars as a historical event and as a constructed myth — essential for understanding how Western civilisational identity was narrated and contested.
cards.counter: The 'freedom vs despotism' framing was Athenian propaganda: Persian governance was sophisticated and often tolerant; Greek slavery was more brutal than Persian. Herodotus himself was more nuanced than his later reception.

quiz.q: Which Athenian victory at the Persian Wars was most decisive for establishing Athenian sea power?
choices: Marathon (490 BCE)
Thermopylae (480 BCE)
Salamis (480 BCE)
Plataea (479 BCE)

cards.title: The Peloponnesian War
cards.fact: The 27-year war between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BCE), recorded by Thucydides, is the first analysis of power politics: Athens fell not to Persian invasion but to imperial overreach, plague, and strategic failure.

layers.body: Thucydides, an Athenian general exiled for a battlefield failure, wrote the war's history as a permanent possession — a model for understanding politics freed from myth and divine causation. His Melian Dialogue (416 BCE), where Athenians tell a small island 'the strong do what they can; the weak suffer what they must,' became the founding text of realism in international relations.

Athens entered the war as the stronger naval power; Sparta as the stronger land force. Pericles's strategy: stay behind walls, use the fleet, avoid land battle. It collapsed when plague killed Pericles and a third of Athens. The disastrous Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) — Athens invading Sicily at enormous cost — destroyed the Athenian fleet. By 404 BCE, the walls of Athens were torn down. The lesson Thucydides drew: imperial power generates fear that drives rivals to coalition against you.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The origin of power-political analysis in historical writing — Thucydides is the ancestor of both international relations realism and political science.
cards.counter: Thucydides' realism has been criticised for overdetermining power and underestimating norms, domestic politics, and accident. Athens's defeat was not inevitable — a different Sicilian decision would have changed the war's outcome.

quiz.q: What does the Melian Dialogue in Thucydides illustrate?
choices: The importance of negotiation and diplomatic compromise
That the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must — the realist logic of power
That small states can resist great powers through moral appeals
That democratic Athens was more just than oligarchic Sparta

cards.title: The Roman Republic
cards.fact: The Roman Republic (509–27 BCE) developed mixed government — consuls (executive), Senate (aristocratic advisory), assemblies (popular) — plus tribunes with veto power to protect plebeians, a constitution Polybius called the model of balanced rule.

layers.body: Founded in 509 BCE after expelling the kings, Rome developed a complex constitution over centuries. Two annually elected *consuls* shared executive power and checked each other; the *Senate* (ex-magistrates, life membership) gave advice with enormous informal authority; tribal and centuriate *assemblies* voted on laws and elected magistrates. *Tribunes of the Plebs* could veto any magistrate's action — the first institutionalised veto.

The Greek historian Polybius argued Rome's constitution was uniquely stable because it mixed monarchy (consuls), aristocracy (Senate), and democracy (assemblies). Each element checked the others. Cicero, Machiavelli, and the American Founders drew on the Roman model: Madison's *Federalist No. 51* on checks and balances is directly Polybian. The *mos maiorum* — the custom of the ancestors — functioned as an unwritten constitutional norm.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The model for mixed constitutionalism, separation of powers, and republican government that shaped early modern and modern constitutional design.
cards.counter: The Republic was oligarchic in practice: the Senate dominated through wealth and social prestige; popular assemblies voted by property class, so the wealthy voted first and often decided everything. The 'balance' was heavily weighted toward the elite.

quiz.q: What made Roman tribunes constitutionally distinctive?
choices: They commanded the legions in wartime
They could veto any magistrate's action — an institutionalised check to protect plebeians
They were elected annually by the Senate rather than by popular assemblies
They served for life as permanent constitutional guardians

cards.title: Rome's civil wars
cards.fact: A century of civil war (133–27 BCE) — triggered by Tiberius Gracchus's land reform, continuing through Marius, Sulla, Caesar, and Octavian — destroyed the Republic by making military commanders rather than the Senate the ultimate source of power.

layers.body: Rome's military expansion created wealth that concentrated in elite hands; dispossessed peasants could no longer afford the equipment to serve in the legions. Tiberius Gracchus (133 BCE) proposed redistributing public land — the Senate had him killed, the first political murder in Roman history and the opening of a century of violence.

Marius reformed the army, recruiting from the landless poor who owed loyalty to the general, not the state. Soldiers expected land grants on demobilisation — which the general had to deliver. The result: personal armies. Sulla, Pompey, Caesar, Antony, and Octavian used their armies as political instruments. The Senate could not resist. Caesar crossed the Rubicon (49 BCE) — using his army inside Italy, forbidden by law — and the Republic never recovered. Octavian won the last civil war at Actium (31 BCE) and became Augustus.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Shows how institutional breakdown begins at the margins: the Senate's willingness to use violence against reformers normalised force in politics, a spiral the Republic could not reverse.
cards.counter: Syme argued the Republic's fall was structural — too much territory for city-state institutions — not the result of individual ambition. The Augustan settlement maintained republican forms while changing their content.

quiz.q: Why did Marius's army reforms undermine the Republic?
choices: They made the army too large to fund from taxes
Soldiers recruited from the landless poor owed personal loyalty to their general rather than to the state — generals became warlords
They transferred Senate control over military appointments to the assemblies
They required tribunes to approve all military commands

cards.title: Augustus and the Principate
cards.fact: Augustus (27 BCE–14 CE) ended the civil wars by disguising a monarchy as a reformed republic — retaining Senate, consuls, and assembly, while holding permanent control of the armies, provinces, and treasury.

layers.body: Octavian took the title *Augustus* (revered one) and *Princeps* (first citizen) — not king or dictator, which were politically toxic. He controlled the frontier provinces (where the armies were), the treasury, and religious offices, while allowing the Senate to keep its traditional forms. The Senate was grateful for order after a century of civil war.

The two centuries after Augustus (Pax Romana) saw the Empire at its height: internal peace, expanding trade, enormous building programs, and legal codification. Roman law — the concept of legal personhood, contracts, property, inheritance — became the foundation of European civil law. By 100 CE the Empire held perhaps 70 million people across three continents. The institutional innovation was the *emperor* as commander-in-chief and supreme judge, not as arbitrary tyrant.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Shows how authoritarian consolidation can be disguised in republican forms — a pattern that Levitsky and Ziblatt identify in modern democratic backsliding.
cards.counter: The Principate was eventually succeeded by more openly autocratic Dominate (from Diocletian); the republican fiction gradually eroded. The question of whether Rome needed the Principate or whether the Republic could have survived is a major debate.

quiz.q: Why did Augustus avoid the title 'king' or 'dictator'?
choices: He lacked the legal authority to claim those titles under Roman law
Both titles were politically toxic after the civil wars — he preferred 'Princeps' (first citizen) to disguise his monarchical power in republican forms
The Senate refused to grant him any title beyond his birth name
He genuinely believed Rome should remain a republic and exercised only temporary emergency powers

cards.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
cards.fact: The Western Roman Empire formally ended in 476 CE when Odoacer deposed the last emperor Romulus Augustulus — but the 'fall' was a centuries-long transformation, not a sudden collapse.

layers.body: Gibbon's *Decline and Fall* (1776) attributed Rome's fall to Christianity (weakening civic virtue) and 'barbarian' invasions. Modern historians prefer 'transformation': Germanic kings maintained Roman institutions, Latin continued as the church's language, Roman law persisted in the church courts. The Eastern Empire survived as Byzantium until 1453.

Historians have proposed over 200 causes for Rome's decline. Main contenders: military overextension and frontier defence costs; economic decline (debasement of currency, declining trade); political instability (25 emperors in 50 years, 235–285 CE); the 'Crisis of the Third Century'; plague; and migration pressure from the Hunnic invasions pushing Germanic peoples into Roman territory. Bryan Ward-Perkins argues genuine economic collapse is detectable in archaeological evidence — pottery, building size, animal bone evidence of declining livestock quality.

The 'fall' remains a proxy debate about whether great civilisations can truly decline and collapse, or only transform. Paul Kennedy's *The Rise and Fall of Great Powers* (1987) applied Gibbonian logic to modern empires, arguing imperial overstretch — military commitments exceeding economic base — is the recurring pattern. The Soviet collapse and debates about American decline revisit the same question.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The paradigm case for studying imperial decline — and a warning that 'transformation' narratives can understate genuine disruption.
cards.counter: Ward-Perkins's archaeological evidence of material decline is contested by Peter Heather, who argues for a more abrupt military collapse. The historiographical debate between continuity and collapse positions has not closed.

quiz.q: The modern historiographical consensus on Rome's 'fall' leans toward…
choices: Gibbon's thesis: Christianity weakened civic virtue and caused collapse
A sudden military catastrophe in 476 CE that destroyed all Roman institutions at once
A centuries-long transformation in which Roman institutions adapted and persisted — though with genuine material decline in many regions
A purely economic collapse driven by monetary debasement

cards.title: Feudalism
cards.fact: Feudalism was the political-economic system of medieval Europe: lords granted land (fiefs) to vassals in exchange for military service; peasants worked the land in exchange for protection — and the entire system rested on personal bonds, not territorial sovereignty.

layers.body: In a world where central states had collapsed, political order was reconstructed through personal bonds. A king granted land to a duke; the duke granted portions to barons; barons to knights. Each granted land (a *fief*) in exchange for military service (knight's fee) and counsel. Peasants (*serfs*) were tied to the land and owed labour services to the lord in exchange for protection.

layers.t: The debate about whether feudalism existed
layers.body: Historians have debated whether 'feudalism' is a useful concept at all. Elizabeth Brown (1974) argued it was a historians' construct imposed on a much messier reality. Susan Reynolds argued the medieval reality was dominated by communal tenure and royal law, not the tidy hierarchy of lord-vassal-serf. What is clear: Western Europe from ~800 to ~1300 CE had decentralised political authority, land-based wealth, and military obligations rooted in personal loyalty rather than territorial state sovereignty.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The contrast case for modern statehood: what the transition from feudal to territorial sovereignty involved — the replacement of personal bonds with impersonal institutional authority.
cards.counter: Feudalism was never a uniform system: Italian cities remained commercial; Byzantine Empire had a fully centralised state; Islamic caliphates operated differently. The concept risks imposing a Western European template on global medieval history.

quiz.q: What was the core exchange in feudal relationships?
choices: Money taxes in exchange for legal protection
Land (a fief) granted to a vassal in exchange for military service and counsel
Church land granted to nobles in exchange for crusading
Royal monopolies granted to merchants in exchange for financial loans

cards.title: The Islamic Golden Age
cards.fact: From ~750 to 1258 CE the Islamic world — centred on Baghdad's House of Wisdom — led global knowledge production: preserving Greek philosophy, advancing algebra, optics, medicine, and astronomy while Europe was in its 'Dark Ages'.

layers.body: Under the Abbasid Caliphate (750–1258 CE), Baghdad's *Bayt al-Hikma* (House of Wisdom) was the world's leading intellectual centre. Scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts and built on them. Al-Khwarizmi formalised algebra; Ibn al-Haytham founded optics; Ibn Sina's medical canon was used in European universities until the 18th century.

The Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258 CE) is the traditional terminus: the caliph was killed, the House of Wisdom destroyed, the irrigation system wrecked. But the decline was gradual and contested: the Islamic world remained scientifically active in Egypt, Spain (Al-Andalus), and Persia. What changed was the shift of intellectual initiative back to European universities — which had absorbed the Islamic transmissions — from the 13th century onward. The Reconquista's completion (1492) marks the end of Islamic Spain's scientific contribution to Europe.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Corrects the Eurocentric 'Dark Ages' narrative — the gap between ancient Greece and the European Renaissance was filled by Islamic scholarship; European universities built on that inheritance.
cards.counter: The idea of a single 'Islamic Golden Age' may homogenise diverse traditions. Iranian, Arab, Jewish, and Central Asian scholars all contributed, often in tension. And the Mongol sack's intellectual impact is debated — the Islamic world did not immediately collapse.

quiz.q: What was the primary role of Baghdad's House of Wisdom in the Islamic Golden Age?
choices: A royal treasury and administrative centre
A translation centre and research institution where Greek, Persian, and Indian texts were translated and developed
A theological school for training Islamic jurists
A military academy for training Abbasid generals

cards.title: The Mongol Empire
cards.fact: Under Genghis Khan and his successors, the Mongols created the largest contiguous land empire in history — and the Pax Mongolica unified the Silk Roads, but the conquests killed tens of millions and permanently weakened Central Asian civilisations.

layers.body: Temüjin unified the Mongol clans and was proclaimed Genghis Khan (1206). His armies conquered from China to Poland — the largest land empire ever. The Mongol conquests were extraordinarily violent: cities that surrendered were spared; those that resisted were destroyed. Baghdad (1258), Samarkand, and Nishapur were sacked with mass killing.

The paradox: Mongol destruction enabled the Pax Mongolica — a century of relative peace across Eurasia in which the Silk Roads were unified under Mongol rule. Trade, disease, and ideas moved at unprecedented speed. The Black Death (1347) spread along these same routes from Central Asia to Europe. Marco Polo travelled from Venice to China. Mongol postal relay systems moved messages faster than any previous state. The Mongol Empire fragmented into four khanates after Genghis Khan's grandsons quarrelled.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Shows that empire can simultaneously destroy and integrate — the Mongols are a case where catastrophic violence and trade globalisation were two sides of the same coin.
cards.counter: Jack Weatherford's *Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World* argues the Mongols enabled religious tolerance, rule of law, and global commerce. Critics argue he romanticises mass killing; the demographic collapse in Iran and Central Asia was not offset by trade benefits.

quiz.q: What was the 'Pax Mongolica'?
choices: A peace treaty between the Mongols and the Chinese Song Dynasty
A period of relative stability across Eurasia under Mongol rule that unified the Silk Roads and enabled unprecedented long-distance trade
The Mongol policy of sparing conquered peoples who converted to Islam
A diplomatic agreement between Mongol khanates to divide territory and end internal warfare

cards.title: Black Death: structural break
cards.fact: The Black Death (1347–51) killed a third to half of Europe's population — and the labour scarcity it created undermined serfdom, raised wages, and accelerated the end of feudalism.

layers.body: The plague arrived in Sicily in 1347, spread via the Mongol trade routes, and killed perhaps 25 million Europeans in five years — maybe a third of the continent's population. The immediate effect was devastation. The long-term effect was structural: with labour scarce, surviving peasants had bargaining power. Serfdom, which depended on an abundance of desperate labour, became economically unworkable.

Real wages rose significantly after the plague — surviving workers could demand better terms. Lords attempted to freeze wages by statute (English Statute of Labourers, 1351) but could not enforce it against labour mobility. The resulting Peasants' Revolt (1381) in England and similar uprisings across Europe reflected the new leverage of commoners. The plague thus accelerated Europe's transition from feudal labour coercion to wage labour — a shift that took centuries but whose demographic foundation was laid in the Black Death.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] A model case for demographic shocks as drivers of institutional change — analogous to how the post-WWII labour shortage contributed to the welfare state in some accounts.
cards.counter: Serfdom did not disappear equally across Europe: in eastern Europe it was reimposed more harshly after the plague, as lords responded to labour scarcity by binding peasants more tightly. The Black Death accelerated western European wage labour while deepening eastern European serfdom.

quiz.q: What was the main long-term economic effect of the Black Death on feudal labour relations?
choices: Lords strengthened serfdom to maintain control over the reduced labour supply
Labour scarcity gave surviving peasants bargaining power, undermining serfdom and raising wages
The plague destroyed agricultural knowledge, causing permanent economic decline
Kings used the crisis to nationalise land and eliminate feudal tenure

cards.title: Hundred Years' War and nationalism
cards.fact: The Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) between England and France contributed to the emergence of French and English national identities — Joan of Arc became the first figure to articulate popular mobilisation around national rather than dynastic loyalty.

layers.body: The war began as a dynastic dispute over the French throne. What changed over its course: the emergence of national sentiment. Joan of Arc's (1429) appeal was not to the Valois dynasty's legal claim but to a divinely mandated French nation. This is one of the earliest popular expressions of something like national identity in European history.

The war also transformed warfare. English longbowmen at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415) devastated armoured cavalry — undermining the military superiority of feudal knights. The introduction of gunpowder artillery (by the war's end) made castle walls obsolete. These changes reduced the military monopoly of the armoured aristocracy and contributed to the rise of the professional, nationally conscripted army — which would later become a vehicle for nationalism.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Early evidence for Tilly's thesis: war-making and taxation built national political identity; the Hundred Years' War forced English and French populations to fund, fight, and identify with 'their' side.
cards.counter: Historians debate how far the war created nationalism vs how far dynastic-religious loyalty remained the dominant frame. Most people on both sides identified primarily with their locality, lord, or church, not with 'France' or 'England'.

quiz.q: What made Joan of Arc's mobilisation historically significant?
choices: She was the first woman to command a professional army under modern law
Her appeal was to a divinely mandated French nation — one of the earliest popular expressions of national rather than purely dynastic identity
She established the principle that commoners could be knighted for military service
Her victory at Orléans ended feudal military obligations and introduced conscription

cards.title: The Renaissance
cards.fact: The Renaissance (c. 1350–1600) was a cultural movement centred in Italian city-states that recovered classical texts and placed human dignity at the centre of learning — producing a transformation in art, literature, and eventually politics.

layers.body: Renaissance humanists — Petrarch, Boccaccio, Pico della Mirandola — recovered Greek and Latin texts, argued that classical antiquity modelled human excellence, and placed man as the 'measure of all things.' The Italian city-states (Florence, Venice, Milan) provided wealthy patrons. What emerged was not anti-Christian but a shift in the centre of gravity from theology to humanity.

Machiavelli's *Prince* (1513) and *Discourses* (1517) broke from medieval political thought by analysing politics as it is, not as it should be — *virtù*, *fortuna*, and necessity replace moral virtue as explanatory categories. The Florentine republican tradition (Bruni, Machiavelli, Guicciardini) developed secular political analysis and set the terms of subsequent political philosophy. The Renaissance spread from Italy to northern Europe via printing, producing Erasmus, Thomas More, and eventually Shakespeare.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The origin of secular humanism and modern political analysis — Machiavelli is the first modern political scientist in the sense of analysing power empirically rather than normatively.
cards.counter: Jacob Burckhardt's classic thesis that the Renaissance invented modern individualism has been heavily revised: medieval individuals were also complex; the Renaissance's continuities with the medieval are as striking as its breaks.

quiz.q: What made Machiavelli's political thought distinctively modern?
choices: He argued for democratic government and popular sovereignty
He analysed politics as it actually operates — power, necessity, virtù — rather than as it should operate according to Christian morality
He developed the first systematic theory of international law
He rejected all classical models and based his analysis entirely on contemporary Italian politics

cards.title: The Protestant Reformation
cards.fact: Luther's 95 Theses (1517), enabled by the printing press, shattered Western Christianity's unity — and by giving believers direct access to scripture, established the principle of individual conscience against institutional authority.

layers.body: Martin Luther's argument was simple but revolutionary: the Bible alone (*sola scriptura*), not the Pope or the Church's traditions, is the final authority in faith. Every Christian can read it. This direct relationship between the believer and God — without institutional mediation — was made possible by Gutenberg's printing press: by 1520 Luther's pamphlets had circulated 300,000 copies across Europe.

The Reformation fragmented Europe. Princes adopted Lutheranism partly for theological reasons, partly to seize Church property and assert authority against Rome — the *cuius regio, eius religio* principle (Peace of Augsburg, 1555) gave each ruler the right to set his territory's religion. This contributed to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) and ultimately to the Westphalian settlement. Weber argued that Calvinist predestination and inner-worldly asceticism generated the economic ethos of capitalism.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The Reformation is the origin of individual conscience as a political principle — from Luther's 'Here I stand' to Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration.
cards.counter: The Reformation did not straightforwardly liberate: Calvin's Geneva was authoritarian; Protestant states persecuted dissenters as readily as Catholic ones. The pluralism the Reformation produced came through exhaustion after the wars of religion, not from its original intentions.

quiz.q: What political principle did the Peace of Augsburg (1555) establish?
choices: Religious tolerance for all faiths within the Holy Roman Empire
Cuius regio, eius religio — each ruler determines his territory's religion
Freedom of conscience for all citizens regardless of their ruler's faith
Papal authority over religious questions, secular authority over political ones

cards.title: The Scientific Revolution
cards.fact: From Copernicus's heliocentric model (1543) to Newton's laws (1687), European natural philosophers rebuilt knowledge on observation, experiment, and mathematics — replacing the authority of Aristotle and the Church as arbiters of how the world works.

layers.body: Copernicus (*De Revolutionibus*, 1543) displaced Earth from the centre of the universe. Galileo used the telescope, developed a mathematical physics, and confronted the Inquisition. Kepler showed planetary orbits are ellipses. Newton's *Principia* (1687) unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics in a single mathematical framework. The revolution was not just new findings but a new method: hypothesis, observation, experiment, mathematical law.

The Scientific Revolution created new institutions: the Royal Society (1660), Académie des Sciences (1666) — early forms of peer review. It disrupted religious authority (Galileo's house arrest) and ultimately made the separation of natural knowledge from theological authority a practical necessity. The Enlightenment was downstream of the Scientific Revolution: if Newton could explain the cosmos by natural law, perhaps Locke could explain politics and Montesquieu society by natural law too.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The historical foundation of the modern relationship between science, authority, and society — and of the Enlightenment's confidence in reason.
cards.counter: The 'revolution' metaphor overstates the break: Copernicus used Ptolemaic circular motions; Newton acknowledged medieval predecessors. Kuhn's paradigm model (normal science → crisis → revolution) was itself inspired by but does not perfectly fit the history.

quiz.q: What distinguished the Scientific Revolution's method from medieval natural philosophy?
choices: It rejected all previous knowledge and started from scratch
It grounded knowledge in observation, experiment, and mathematical law rather than in textual authority
It separated theology entirely from natural inquiry for the first time
It relied on collective peer review rather than individual genius

cards.title: The Columbian Exchange
cards.fact: Columbus's arrival in 1492 triggered the permanent biological integration of the Old and New Worlds: maize, potatoes, and tomatoes transformed Eurasian diets; European diseases killed up to 90% of indigenous American populations.

layers.body: Alfred Crosby coined 'Columbian Exchange' for the transfer of plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia after 1492. The Americas gained horses, cattle, wheat, and smallpox. Afro-Eurasia gained maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco, and syphilis. This was the greatest biological exchange since the separation of Gondwana.

The most devastating transfer was disease: indigenous Americans had no immunity to smallpox, measles, influenza, or typhus. In some regions, 90% of the population died within a century of contact. This depopulation made large-scale European colonisation possible — vast territories appeared 'empty' to European eyes. The potato and maize transformed European and African food production: Ireland's population quintupled 1600–1840 on potatoes; West African states grew more powerful on maize. The potato famine of 1845 reversed Ireland's growth catastrophically.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds environmental and biological history — shows that the most transformative force of European colonialism was not armies but pathogens.
cards.counter: Disease was not weaponised deliberately in most cases — it was an unintended consequence. But European colonisers rapidly exploited the resulting labour vacuum through enslaved African labour, so the causal chain from disease to slavery is direct.

quiz.q: What made European diseases so devastating to indigenous American populations?
choices: Europeans deliberately introduced smallpox-contaminated blankets as a weapon
Indigenous Americans had no prior exposure and therefore no immune defences to Old World pathogens
Indigenous American populations were smaller and less densely organised
European diets were nutritionally superior, giving their immune systems an advantage

cards.title: The Atlantic slave trade
cards.fact: Between 1500 and 1900 roughly 12.5 million Africans were enslaved and shipped to the Americas — the largest forced migration in history — two million dying during the Middle Passage, the rest forming the labour foundation of New World plantation economies.

layers.body: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database documents about 36,000 slave voyages carrying 12.5 million Africans between 1500 and 1866. About 10.7 million survived to arrive in the Americas, principally Brazil, the Caribbean, and North America. The 'triangle trade' shipped manufactured goods from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, and plantation produce (sugar, cotton, tobacco) back to Europe.

Eric Williams (*Capitalism and Slavery*, 1944) argued that the profits from slavery and the plantation economy funded the British Industrial Revolution — a thesis now widely accepted in modified form (the connection is real but slavery's contribution is one factor among many). The slave trade required and produced African political transformations: coastal states like Dahomey and Asante grew wealthy supplying captives, creating political incentives that perpetuated the trade. Its abolition required both moral campaigning and economic arguments.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds any analysis of Western economic development, the origins of racial capitalism, and postcolonial reparations debates in the structural history of slavery.
cards.counter: The Williams thesis on industrial revolution funding remains debated quantitatively — Joseph Inikori strengthened the connection; critics argue slavery's British GDP contribution was too small to have been decisive. The moral case for abolition stands independently of the economic argument.

quiz.q: Approximately how many Africans were enslaved and transported in the Atlantic slave trade?
choices: 1–2 million
5–6 million
12–13 million
20–25 million

cards.title: Thirty Years' War and Westphalia
cards.fact: The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) devastated Central Europe and ended with the Peace of Westphalia — institutionalising the principle of state sovereignty and non-interference in internal religious affairs that still underlies international order.

layers.body: What began as a conflict between Protestant and Catholic princes within the Holy Roman Empire became a general European war when France (Catholic) allied with Protestant states against the Habsburgs for balance-of-power reasons. By the 1640s religion was secondary to dynastic and territorial competition — a transformation in the logic of European politics.

The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the war with two treaties: the principle *cuius regio, eius religio* was retained but extended and softened. More importantly, the settlement embodied the principle that sovereign states are equal and do not have the right to interfere in each other's internal affairs — including religion. This 'Westphalian system' is still the operating principle of international law: sovereignty means exclusive domestic jurisdiction.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The historical foundation of the modern state system — shows that sovereignty and non-interference emerged from a specific European religious crisis, not from timeless logic.
cards.counter: The 'Westphalian system' as a founding moment of state sovereignty is partly a historians' retrospective construction: the treaties dealt primarily with specific territorial and religious settlements; the principle was systematised later. 1648 is a useful landmark, not a founding moment.

quiz.q: What principle did the Peace of Westphalia (1648) enshrine?
choices: Freedom of religion for all individuals within Europe
State sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs, including religion
The supremacy of the Holy Roman Emperor over all European rulers
Parliamentary governance as the required form of government for Christian states

cards.title: The Enlightenment
cards.fact: The Enlightenment (c. 1680–1790) held that reason, not tradition or revelation, should govern human affairs — producing liberalism, secularism, and the revolutions that remade the political world.

layers.body: The *Enlightenment* (French: *Lumières*; German: *Aufklärung*) was the intellectual movement arguing that reason could improve human life as Newton's laws had improved knowledge of nature. Voltaire attacked the Church; Montesquieu analysed governments comparatively; Rousseau challenged inequality; Diderot and d'Alembert compiled the *Encyclopédie* — an attempt to capture all human knowledge in rational form.

Jonathan Israel distinguishes a 'radical Enlightenment' (Spinoza, d'Holbach) that drew egalitarian, atheist, and democratic conclusions, from a 'moderate Enlightenment' (Locke, Voltaire, Hume) that accepted religion and monarchy while advocating reform. The American and French Revolutions drew primarily on the moderate tradition. The radical tradition — equality, abolition of hereditary privilege, democracy — took longer to become politically dominant.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The ideological source of liberal democracy, human rights, and secular government — understanding the Enlightenment is required for understanding the subsequent political history of the West.
cards.counter: The Enlightenment's universalism was partial: rights were for white property-owning men; slavery was defended by Enlightenment figures; women were mostly excluded. Postcolonial critics argue its universalism was imperial.

quiz.q: What distinguishes Jonathan Israel's 'radical Enlightenment' from the 'moderate Enlightenment'?
choices: The radical Enlightenment was religious; the moderate Enlightenment was secular
The radical Enlightenment drew egalitarian, democratic, and atheist conclusions; the moderate Enlightenment accepted monarchy and religion while advocating reform
The radical Enlightenment was French; the moderate Enlightenment was English and Scottish
The radical Enlightenment focused on economics; the moderate on political theory

cards.title: The American Revolution
cards.fact: The American Revolution (1776) was the first successful application of Enlightenment principles — natural rights, consent of the governed — producing a republic with constitutional separation of powers that became the model for subsequent revolutionary movements.

layers.body: The Declaration of Independence (1776) articulated Lockean natural rights — 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' — as the basis for political authority. The Constitution (1787) translated Montesquieu's separation of powers into a working government with federalism (federal-state division), checks and balances, and a bill of rights.

Gordon Wood argued the Revolution was genuinely radical — it replaced deference and aristocratic hierarchy with a democratic culture of self-making. Others stress continuity: American colonists were already subjects with common law rights; they were defending existing liberties, not creating new ones. The Revolution's limits: slavery was preserved; women were excluded; Native Americans lost land. Hannah Arendt contrasted the American and French Revolutions: the American avoided the Terror because it was about founding free institutions, not ending social misery.

cards.deploy: [Harvard History] The founding case for liberal constitutionalism — and a reference point for all subsequent debates about whether revolutions can produce stable free institutions.
cards.counter: The American founding was deeply shaped by slave-owning elites protecting their property. The Constitution's 3/5 compromise and property requirements for voting qualify the claim to universal rights.

quiz.q: Hannah Arendt argued the American Revolution avoided the Terror because…
choices: Americans were more virtuous than the French
The American Revolution was about founding free institutions, not ending social misery — which spared it the dynamic of radical resentment that drove the French Terror
The American Constitution was written by professional lawyers rather than philosophers
The Revolution was led by moderate Whigs rather than radical democrats

cards.title: The French Revolution: causes and legacy
cards.fact: The French Revolution (1789–1799) destroyed the ancien régime, declared universal rights, guillotined the king, and ended in Napoleon's dictatorship — combining Enlightenment ideals, radical terror, and popular nationalism in a volatile mix.

layers.body: The Revolution began with a fiscal crisis (the state was bankrupt from American war debts), social tension (bourgeoisie excluded from power, peasants crushed by taxes and seigneurial dues), and Enlightenment ideas about rights. The Estates-General of 1789 became the National Assembly, the Declaration of the Rights of Man followed, the monarchy was abolished (1792), and Louis XVI was guillotined (1793). The Terror (1793–94) executed 17,000 and imprisoned hundreds of thousands.

First, *universal rights*: the Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) declared rights belong to all humans, not just Frenchmen — inspiring every subsequent human rights movement, including the Haitian Revolution. Second, *nationalism*: the Revolution created the concept of the nation as a political community, conscripting citizens rather than mercenaries. Third, *revolutionary politics*: the precedent that a society could be remade by political will — the model for all subsequent revolutionary movements from 1848 to 1917.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The watershed event in modern political history — the origin of the left-right spectrum, modern nationalism, and the concept of universal human rights.
cards.counter: The Revolution's universalism was immediately limited in practice: women were denied political rights (Olympe de Gouges guillotined); slavery was abolished, then reimposed. The Revolution's democratic promise recurrently gave way to centralised dictatorship.

quiz.q: What was the 'Reign of Terror' (1793–94) during the French Revolution?
choices: The period when peasants massacred aristocrats across the French countryside
The government's systematic use of the guillotine against perceived counter-revolutionaries, executing ~17,000 people in a year
The invasion of France by the Austrian and Prussian monarchies
Napoleon's coup that ended the revolutionary republic

cards.title: The Haitian Revolution
cards.fact: Haiti (1791–1804) was the only successful slave revolt in history and the only country founded by formerly enslaved people — exposing the contradiction between the French Revolution's universal rights and its maintenance of colonial slavery.

layers.body: Saint-Domingue (Haiti) was France's most profitable colony — producing a third of Europe's sugar and half its coffee on the labour of 500,000 enslaved Africans. When the French Revolution declared the Rights of Man, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue demanded their application. Toussaint Louverture led the revolution from 1791; after French, British, and Spanish interventions, Haiti declared independence in 1804.

The Haitian Revolution terrified slave societies globally: it demonstrated that enslaved people could defeat European armies and establish a republic. France, the US, and Britain refused to recognise Haiti for decades — the US until 1862. France extorted 150 million francs in 'reparations' for lost colonial property as a condition for diplomatic recognition, a debt Haiti did not finish paying until 1947. C.L.R. James's *The Black Jacobins* (1938) made the Haitian Revolution central to anti-colonial and Black political thought.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Exposes the limits of Enlightenment universalism: the rights declared in 1789 were not meant to include enslaved Africans; Haiti's revolution forced the contradiction into the open.
cards.counter: Haiti's post-independence history of instability and poverty has been attributed to the weight of the indemnity and to US and French interference — but also to internal political fragmentation. The revolution's success was military; building a stable state proved far harder.

quiz.q: Why did France demand 150 million francs from Haiti after independence?
choices: As war reparations for the French soldiers killed during the revolution
As 'compensation' to slaveholders for lost colonial property — a condition for French diplomatic recognition
To fund French construction projects in the Caribbean
As a trade tariff on Haitian sugar exports to France

cards.title: The Industrial Revolution
cards.fact: Britain's Industrial Revolution (c. 1760–1840) shifted economic production from agriculture to manufacturing driven by steam power — transforming not just technology but the social fabric, concentrating workers in cities and generating the labour question.

layers.body: Steam engines, textile machinery, iron and coal: Britain industrialised first for a combination of reasons: coal deposits near water; secure property rights; an empirical scientific culture; a global colonial market; and absence of internal tariffs. By 1850, Britain produced half the world's iron and cotton cloth.

Urbanisation was rapid: Manchester grew from 25,000 (1772) to 300,000 (1850). Living conditions in industrial cities were catastrophic — Engels's *Condition of the Working Class in England* (1845) documented Manchester's slums in detail. Child labour in mines and factories became a political scandal. Life expectancy in industrial cities initially fell. The working class created trade unions, Chartism (mass movement for democratic rights), and eventually socialist parties. The Industrial Revolution thus generated both capitalism's productive power and its political antagonist.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The historical baseline for all subsequent economic development, labour relations, and political economy — nothing in modern social science makes sense without it.
cards.counter: The 'standard of living debate' is unresolved: McCloskey and others argue real wages rose after an initial dip; Thompson and others stress the degradation of craft skill and autonomous work. The average masks huge distributional variation.

quiz.q: Which combination of factors does most economic history cite for Britain industrialising first?
choices: Superior military technology allowing colonial exploitation of resources
Coal near waterways, property rights, empirical culture, colonial markets, and absence of internal tariffs
A uniquely Protestant work ethic that drove savings and investment
Royal state investment in manufacturing, analogous to a developmental state

cards.title: The New Imperialism
cards.fact: The New Imperialism (1870–1914) divided Africa and Asia among European powers — driven by industrial competition, nationalist rivalries, and the need for markets, raw materials, and strategic bases.

layers.body: Between 1870 and 1914 European powers acquired 23 million square kilometres of new territory, mostly in Africa and Asia. The Berlin Conference (1884–85) set the rules for European partition of Africa — without African representation. Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, and Portugal competed for colonies.

J.A. Hobson (*Imperialism*, 1902): surplus capital in Britain needed overseas investment outlets, so the state used imperial force to secure them. Lenin refined this into a Marxist theory: imperialism is the highest stage of monopoly capitalism. Joseph Schumpeter counter-argued that imperialism was an atavistic social structure driven by pre-capitalist warrior classes, not capitalism's logic. Robinson and Gallagher emphasised 'peripheral' factors: British imperial expansion was often driven by local crises requiring intervention, not metropolitan capital needs.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds postcolonial economics and the dependency theory debate — whether colonial underdevelopment was a deliberate outcome or a side effect of integration into the world economy.
cards.counter: The economic causation of imperialism is contested: much colonial territory was economically worthless; strategic rivalry and nationalist prestige often outweighed economic calculation.

quiz.q: What was J.A. Hobson's economic explanation for the New Imperialism?
choices: Population pressure drove European states to seek new territories for settlement
Surplus capital in industrial economies needed overseas investment outlets that could not be found at home
Colonial resources were essential to industrialisation and could not be obtained by trade alone
National prestige rather than economic interest drove colonial acquisition

cards.title: WWI: causes and character
cards.fact: WWI (1914–1918) killed 20 million and was caused by the interaction of the alliance system, imperial competition, mobilisation timetables, and the miscalculation that a short war was possible — no single state wanted the catastrophe that followed.

layers.t: No one planned it; everyone caused it
layers.body: Sarajevo (June 1914) triggered the alliance system: Austria-Hungary vs Serbia → Russia mobilises → Germany declares war on Russia → France in by alliance → Germany invades Belgium → Britain in. Christopher Clark's *Sleepwalkers* (2012) argues no power planned the war; all were trapped by alliances, mobilisation timetables, and domestic political pressures. The old 'German war guilt' thesis oversimplifies.

WWI was the first industrialised total war: machine guns, artillery, gas, submarines, aircraft. The Western Front stalemate was a product of the defensive advantage of trenches and machine guns over offensive infantry. 10 million soldiers died, 21 million wounded. Industrial production was redirected entirely to war. The war created the modern state's capacity for mass mobilisation — conscription, rationing, propaganda, censorship — that shaped 20th-century state power.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The event that made the 20th century — the war's outcome (Versailles, Russian Revolution, collapse of empires) set the stage for fascism, WWII, and the Cold War.
cards.counter: The 'sleepwalkers' thesis has been criticised for distributing responsibility too evenly. John Röhl's biography of Kaiser Wilhelm II argues Germany bears primary responsibility for pushing Austria-Hungary to war. The debate continues.

quiz.q: Why did the Schlieffen Plan require Germany to invade Belgium even though it wanted to focus on France?
choices: Belgium held strategic coal deposits Germany needed for the war economy
The plan required encircling France rapidly, and the fastest route went through Belgium — which brought Britain into the war
Germany feared Belgium would ally with Russia if not occupied first
The Kaiser personally ordered the invasion against military advice

cards.title: The Russian Revolution
cards.fact: 1917 produced two revolutions: the February Revolution (March 1917 NS) ended the Tsar and created a liberal provisional government; the October Revolution (November 1917 NS) brought the Bolsheviks to power — the first communist state.

layers.body: February 1917: workers and soldiers in Petrograd overthrew the Tsar; a Provisional Government shared power with the Petrograd Soviet. October 1917: Lenin's Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government with the slogan 'Peace, Land, Bread' — promising to end the war, redistribute land, and supply food. Why then? Three years of catastrophic war, 1.7 million military dead, economic collapse, and a government that refused to end the fighting.

Lenin's theory (built on Kautsky and Luxemburg) was that a small disciplined vanguard party could seize state power and hold it while the European working class also revolted. When European revolution failed to materialise, the Bolsheviks were isolated in a backward agrarian country. This produced the paradox of 'socialism in one country' — and the subsequent debates between Trotsky (permanent revolution) and Stalin (building socialism domestically first) that defined Soviet ideology.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The founding event of 20th-century communist politics — explains Leninism, Stalinism, and the Cold War's ideological structure.
cards.counter: The Bolshevik seizure of power was a coup by a minority party against a democratically elected constituent assembly (dissolved January 1918). Whether October was a revolution or a coup is a political question that shaped subsequent communist self-understanding.

quiz.q: What were the three main Bolshevik slogans in 1917 that drove their popular support?
choices: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Peace, Land, Bread
All Power to the Soviets, No War, No Tsar
Revolution, Redistribution, Republic

cards.title: Versailles and its consequences
cards.fact: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed war guilt, reparations, and territorial losses on Germany — and Keynes's prediction that it would cause economic and political catastrophe proved correct within 15 years.

layers.body: The Paris Peace Conference (1919) produced the Treaty of Versailles, forcing Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war (Article 231, the 'war guilt clause'), pay 132 billion gold marks in reparations, cede territory (Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor), and limit its military. John Maynard Keynes resigned from the British delegation and published *The Economic Consequences of the Peace* (1919), arguing the terms were economically ruinous and would produce political disaster.

The *Dolchstoßlegende* (stab-in-the-back myth) — that Germany had not been militarily defeated but betrayed by Jews and socialists — was false but politically powerful. Hyperinflation (1923) destroyed middle-class savings. The Great Depression (1929) collapsed the Weimar Republic's support. Hitler's appeal rested directly on reversing Versailles. The diplomatic consensus since WWII: the lesson is that peace settlements must allow defeated nations a viable future, not humiliate them into resentment.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The case that links war settlement, economic policy, and subsequent political radicalism — used in debates about post-conflict reconstruction, sanctions, and reparations.
cards.counter: Historians have revised Keynes: German reparations were restructured repeatedly (Dawes Plan 1924, Young Plan 1929) and Germany actually paid a small fraction of the total. The economic argument against Versailles may be weaker than the political argument.

quiz.q: What was Keynes's prediction about Versailles in 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'?
choices: Germany would quickly industrialise and become the dominant European power
The punitive economic terms would cause German economic collapse and political extremism
The treaty was too lenient and Germany would rearm within five years
American withdrawal from the peace process would doom the League of Nations

cards.title: The rise of fascism
cards.fact: Fascism arose in interwar Europe as a response to three combined shocks: the humiliation and instability of the Versailles settlement, the Bolshevik threat from the left, and the mass mobilisation of WWI that produced a new political actor — the combat veteran turned political soldier.

layers.body: Robert Paxton (*The Anatomy of Fascism*, 2004) defines fascism by its practice rather than its doctrine: a politics of emotional mobilisation, contempt for liberal democracy, violence against enemies, and a national rebirth narrative. It emerged where the combination of national humiliation (Germany: Versailles; Italy: 'mutilated victory'), communist fear, and weak liberal institutions created space.

Mussolini (1922) came to power first — through the threat of a 'March on Rome,' followed by King Victor Emmanuel III appointing him Prime Minister legally. Hitler (1933) was appointed Chancellor legally by Hindenburg after electoral rises; the Reichstag fire and enabling act followed. Both used democratic procedures to dismantle democracy. The key enablers were conservative elites who thought they could control the fascists — they could not.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds the Levitsky-Ziblatt argument: fascism came to power through legal means and the failure of conservative institutions to stop it, not through a sudden military coup.
cards.counter: Hannah Arendt (*Origins of Totalitarianism*) argued fascism and Stalinism shared a 'totalitarian' structure despite their ideological opposition — both mobilised mass movements to destroy civil society. This 'totalitarianism' category has been debated: it risks equating very different regimes.

quiz.q: Why did conservative elites support fascist leaders' appointment to government?
choices: They shared fascism's racial ideology and wanted to implement it through state power
They believed they could control the fascists and use them as a bulwark against communist revolution — but were wrong
They were coerced by fascist paramilitary threats and had no choice
They genuinely believed fascist mass movements represented the popular will

cards.title: Decolonisation
cards.fact: Between 1945 and 1975 over 80 new states emerged from European colonial empires — driven by anti-colonial nationalism, colonial contradictions exposed by WWII, and Cold War competition for Third World allegiance.

layers.body: European empires had dominated most of Asia and Africa since the 19th century. Decolonisation came rapidly after WWII for several reasons: the war discredited European racial hierarchy; Asian and African soldiers who fought for empires returned demanding rights; nationalist movements matured; the US and USSR both officially opposed European colonialism (for different reasons); and economic exhaustion meant empires were no longer profitable to defend.

Decolonisation was uneven. India (1947): negotiated transfer with partition violence killing 500,000–1,000,000. French Indochina (1945–54): brutal war ending at Dien Bien Phu. Algeria (1954–62): 1 million Algerians killed. Kenya: Mau Mau uprising, British torture camps. Africa south of Sahara: mostly negotiated by 1965, but with coups and Cold War proxy wars immediately following. The Bandung Conference (1955) established the Non-Aligned Movement — rejecting both Cold War blocs.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds postcolonial theory and the debates about whether decolonisation produced genuine independence or merely a change of the exploiting class.
cards.counter: Frantz Fanon argued that political decolonisation without economic decolonisation produces neocolonialism — the same structures of extraction persist under new flags. This 'dependency' critique was confirmed in many cases.

quiz.q: What was the Bandung Conference (1955) and why was it significant?
choices: A UN conference that set the rules for transferring colonial territories to self-governance
A meeting of 29 Asian and African states that established the Non-Aligned Movement — rejecting alignment with either Cold War bloc
A French-British conference that agreed the terms for Algerian independence
A UN General Assembly vote that declared colonialism illegal under international law

cards.title: The Cold War
cards.fact: The Cold War (1947–1991) was an ideological and geopolitical contest between the US-led liberal capitalist order and the Soviet-led communist bloc — fought through proxy wars, arms races, and competition for the Third World, but never directly between the superpowers.

layers.t: Not a war, but not peace
layers.body: George Orwell coined 'cold war' in 1945: neither hot war (nuclear deterrence made it too costly) nor peace (the ideological competition was total). The US strategy was 'containment' (George Kennan's 1946 Long Telegram): prevent Soviet expansion without going to war. The USSR pursued expansion of its sphere while avoiding nuclear confrontation.

The Cold War had a clear structure: US-led NATO vs Soviet-led Warsaw Pact in Europe; proxy conflicts in Korea, Vietnam, Angola, Afghanistan globally; nuclear deterrence (MAD) as the underlying constraint. Key crises: Berlin Blockade (1948–49), Korean War (1950–53), Cuba (1962), Vietnam (1965–75). John Lewis Gaddis's 'Long Peace' argument: the Cold War's nuclear logic produced the longest period without great-power war in modern history.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The structural frame for post-WWII history — almost no regional conflict, independence movement, or economic policy from 1947–1991 can be understood without the Cold War context.
cards.counter: The Cold War's 'long peace' for great powers came at enormous cost in proxy wars — Korea (3 million dead), Vietnam (3 million dead), Angola, Afghanistan. Calling it a 'peace' requires ignoring its hot peripheries.

quiz.q: What was the US policy of 'containment' during the Cold War?
choices: Rolling back Soviet influence by supporting anti-communist insurgencies globally
Preventing Soviet expansion without direct military confrontation — through alliances, economic aid, and proxy support
Containing nuclear weapons to existing arsenals through arms control treaties
Confining Soviet influence to Eastern Europe in exchange for recognising US dominance of Latin America

cards.title: 1989 and the end of the Cold War
cards.fact: In 1989, communist regimes in Eastern Europe fell in rapid succession without Soviet military intervention — driven by a combination of Gorbachev's reforms, economic stagnation, and mass mobilisation that exposed the systems' total loss of legitimacy.
