layers.body: Poland (Solidarity electoral victory, August), Hungary (opened its border to Austria, September), East Germany (Berlin Wall, November 9), Czechoslovakia (Velvet Revolution, November), Romania (violent revolution, December). Each fell within months. Gorbachev's 'Sinatra Doctrine' — letting each country go its own way — was decisive: 1956 Hungary and 1968 Czechoslovakia had shown that Soviet tanks would hold the line; in 1989 they didn't come.

Structural factors: Soviet economic stagnation, the arms race cost, Afghanistan's failure, Gorbachev's reform programme (glasnost, perestroika). Proximate factor: cascading information — when East Germans saw on television that Hungary had opened its border, others followed. Francis Fukuyama's 'end of history' thesis (1989) argued liberal democracy had no remaining ideological competitor. This proved premature: illiberal nationalism, Islamism, and authoritarian capitalism emerged as alternatives.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The end of the Cold War defined the post-1989 world — and 1989's contradictions (liberal triumphalism followed by authoritarianism's return) frame contemporary global politics.
cards.counter: Fukuyama's end of history thesis failed to anticipate the resilience of authoritarian alternatives. The unipolar moment of 1989–2008 gave way to great-power competition — suggesting the Cold War's end was a pause, not a resolution.

quiz.q: What was Gorbachev's 'Sinatra Doctrine' and why was it decisive in 1989?
choices: A policy of cultural exchange with the West that undermined communist ideology
Allowing Eastern European states to choose their own path — not intervening militarily as in 1956 and 1968, which made 1989's revolutions possible
A unilateral disarmament offer to NATO that demonstrated Soviet weakness
The decision to withdraw Soviet troops from Afghanistan, signalling imperial exhaustion

cards.title: The Annales school
cards.fact: The Annales school (founded 1929) shifted history from great events and individuals to long-term structures — Braudel's longue durée of geography, climate, and economy underlying the short-term 'froth' of political events.

layers.body: Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre founded the *Annales d'histoire économique et sociale* (1929) in opposition to event-driven political and diplomatic history. Their manifesto: history must study all aspects of human life — economy, society, mentalities — not just kings and battles. Fernand Braudel's *The Mediterranean* (1949) gave this a theoretical framework.

Braudel distinguished three temporal scales. The *longue durée*: geographical and structural time — the rhythms of climate, technology, population that change over centuries. The *conjoncture*: medium-term economic and social cycles of decades. The *événement*: individual events and short-term political history — the 'froth on the waves.' Braudel's hierarchy inverted traditional historical attention: the longue durée is most fundamental; événements are almost irrelevant.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] The most important methodological movement in 20th-century historiography — grounds any argument for structural vs. agential explanations of historical change.
cards.counter: The Annales school's structuralism was later criticised for underplaying agency, narrative, and the specificity of events. The 'return of the event' (Paul Ricoeur, cultural turn) reasserted the importance of contingency and meaning that the structural approach marginalised.

quiz.q: What did Braudel mean by the 'longue durée'?
choices: The long narrative history of a civilisation from ancient times to the present
The slow-moving geographical and structural time of climate, technology, and population — which underlies and constrains short-term events
The medium-term duration of economic cycles lasting 50–100 years
The lifespan of historical institutions like churches and universities

cards.title: Social history: history from below
cards.fact: E.P. Thompson's 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) established 'history from below' — recovering the experience of ordinary people rather than elites, and treating class as a process of formation rather than a structural category.

layers.body: Traditional historiography told the story of rulers, statesmen, and generals. E.P. Thompson, Eric Hobsbawm, and the British Marxist historians argued that history must recover the agency of workers, women, peasants, and the poor. Thompson's *Making* (1963) showed how the English working class was not produced by industrialisation but actively made itself through experience and struggle.

Thompson's key theoretical move: class is not a structural category (workers who share an economic position) but a historical relationship — class happens when people with shared interests experience their situation as a class and act on it. This shifted historical attention from structure (Annales, Marxist base) to agency (how people made sense of and responded to their conditions). The 'cultural turn' in the 1980s–90s took this further: identity, meaning, and discourse became primary historical objects.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds social history methodology: history must include the perspectives of those who left fewer written records, using other sources — oral history, material culture, statistics.
cards.counter: Scott and the cultural turn criticised Thompson for still centering class (an economic category) rather than the full range of identities. The proliferation of 'histories from below' (gender history, queer history, subaltern studies) has enriched but also fragmented the field.

quiz.q: What was E.P. Thompson's innovation in *The Making of the English Working Class*?
choices: He showed that the working class was created by the Industrial Revolution's structural forces, with no agential input
He argued class is a historical relationship actively made through shared experience and struggle — not a pre-given structural category
He traced the origins of labour unions from medieval craft guilds without a break
He proved that capitalists deliberately designed the factory system to prevent class consciousness

cards.title: Postcolonial historiography
cards.fact: The Subaltern Studies collective (1982) argued that Indian history written from an elite or nationalist perspective erased subaltern experience — and Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Provincialising Europe' challenged the assumption that European history is the universal template.

layers.body: Ranajit Guha founded the Subaltern Studies collective to recover the voices of Indian peasants, workers, and women erased from both colonial and nationalist historiography. 'Subaltern' (from Gramsci) means those excluded from the power to narrate history. The project extended Said's *Orientalism* into historical practice.

Dipesh Chakrabarty's *Provincialising Europe* (2000) made the methodological point explicit: European concepts — the nation-state, capitalism, the individual, secular time — are assumed to be universal categories, but they emerged from a particular European historical experience. To 'provincialise' Europe is to see these as local, partial concepts rather than universal benchmarks against which non-European history must be measured.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard History] Grounds the methodological critique of Eurocentrism in historical writing — relevant to any analysis of 'development,' 'modernisation,' or comparative political science.
cards.counter: Critics argue Subaltern Studies' epistemological relativism makes it impossible to make claims about what actually happened. And the project's own elite academic position (mostly written by scholars at Western universities) is itself a form of subaltern-for-others.

quiz.q: What does Chakrabarty mean by 'provincialising Europe'?
choices: Reducing European history to a minor thread within a global narrative
Treating European historical concepts (nation-state, capitalism, secular time) as local and partial rather than universal templates for all histories
Arguing that European civilisation was inferior to Asian civilisations
Decentralising Europe geographically by focusing on its provinces rather than capital cities

cards.title: Indifference curves
cards.fact: An indifference curve shows all consumption bundles giving a consumer equal utility — they slope downward (more of one good means less of the other at constant utility) and bow inward (diminishing marginal rate of substitution).

layers.body: An indifference curve is the set of consumption bundles a consumer is indifferent among — all giving the same utility. Higher curves represent higher utility. The slope at any point is the *marginal rate of substitution* (MRS): how much of good Y the consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of X.

Indifference curves are convex to the origin because the MRS diminishes: when you have lots of X and little Y, you value Y highly (you'll give up a lot of X for a little Y). As you acquire more Y, it becomes less valuable to you relative to X — the MRS falls. This reflects *diminishing marginal utility* translated into preference space.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] The foundation of consumer theory — indifference curves represent preferences without requiring cardinal utility measurement; only ordinal rankings are needed.
cards.counter: Revealed preference theory (Samuelson) dispenses with indifference curves by inferring preferences from observed choices — no need for the mental construct of equal satisfaction.

quiz.q: Why do indifference curves bow inward (are convex to the origin)?
choices: Because goods are perfect substitutes at a constant rate
Because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes — as you get more of X, each additional unit is worth less Y to give up
Because higher utility requires consuming more of both goods
To reflect the budget constraint's linear shape

cards.title: The budget constraint
cards.fact: The budget constraint shows all consumption bundles a consumer can afford — it is a straight line with slope equal to minus the price ratio (−P_x/P_y), shifting outward with income increases.

layers.body: With income M and prices P_x and P_y, the consumer can buy any bundle where P_x·x + P_y·y ≤ M. The boundary (the budget line) has slope −P_x/P_y: to get one more unit of X, you must give up P_x/P_y units of Y. This slope is the *opportunity cost* of X in terms of Y.

An income increase shifts the budget line outward in parallel. A price change for X rotates it: if X becomes cheaper, the X-intercept rises (you can buy more X with all your income) while the Y-intercept stays fixed. Tax and subsidy policies work by changing the effective price, shifting the budget constraint and therefore the feasible consumption set.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] Combines with indifference curves to derive consumer demand — policy analysis of taxes, subsidies, and price controls begins here.
cards.counter: The static budget constraint ignores time, uncertainty, and borrowing constraints. Life-cycle models extend it to an intertemporal budget constraint where current and future consumption are the choice variables.

quiz.q: What determines the slope of the budget line?
choices: The consumer's marginal utility of income
The ratio of the prices of the two goods (−P_x/P_y) — the opportunity cost of X in terms of Y
The consumer's income level
The marginal rate of substitution at the optimal bundle

cards.title: Consumer optimum
cards.fact: The consumer maximises utility where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line — at this point MRS = P_x/P_y: the subjective trade-off equals the market trade-off.

layers.body: At the optimum, the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: MRS = P_x/P_y. Intuition: if MRS > P_x/P_y, you are willing to give up more Y for X than the market requires — so buy more X. If MRS < P_x/P_y, buy less X. At equality, there is no profitable reallocation.

The optimum condition MRS = P_x/P_y means that at the margin, the last unit of every good provides equal utility per pound spent: MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y. This is the *equalising marginal utility* condition. It generates the demand curve: as P_x falls, the budget line rotates and the optimum shifts — tracing out how quantity demanded changes with price.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] The first-order condition for consumer choice — underlies all demand analysis and is the building block for welfare economics.
cards.counter: The optimum assumes fully rational preferences and complete information. Behavioural economics shows that real consumers systematically deviate: they anchor, frame, and satisfice rather than maximise.

quiz.q: At the consumer optimum, why is MRS = P_x/P_y?
choices: Because the consumer has spent all their income
Because any deviation would mean the consumer is willing to trade at a different rate than the market offers — a profitable reallocation would exist
Because the budget line and indifference curve have the same curvature
Because preferences are convex at the optimum

cards.title: Income and substitution effects
cards.fact: A price fall has two components: the substitution effect (X is now relatively cheaper, so substitute X for Y) and the income effect (you are effectively richer, so you may buy more or less of X depending on whether it is normal or inferior).

layers.body: When P_x falls: (1) X is relatively cheaper compared to Y — even at the same real income, you substitute toward X. (2) You are effectively richer — the fall in price increases real purchasing power. For a *normal good*, both effects push toward more X. For an *inferior good*, the income effect pushes toward less X.

A *Giffen good* is one where a price fall causes less consumption — the income effect dominates and works against the substitution effect (because the good is strongly inferior and commands a large share of the budget). Potatoes in famine-era Ireland are the canonical example (disputed). This violates the 'law of demand' but is theoretically consistent. The Slutsky decomposition formalises the separation: the total effect = substitution effect + income effect.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] Essential for tax and subsidy policy analysis: VAT on food has income and substitution effects that hit poor households harder (food is a larger budget share).
cards.counter: Giffen goods are extremely rare in practice — the income effect must dominate the substitution effect and the good must be a large budget share. The potato-Ireland example is historically contested.

quiz.q: What is a 'Giffen good'?
choices: A good whose demand rises with income
A luxury good with an income elasticity greater than one
A good for which a price fall leads to less consumption — the income effect dominates and reverses the substitution effect
A good supplied by a monopolist with a downward-sloping demand curve

cards.title: Revealed preference (Samuelson)
cards.fact: Samuelson's revealed preference: if a consumer chooses bundle A when B is also affordable, A is revealed preferred to B — preferences are inferred from choices, not from hypothetical utility functions.

layers.body: Paul Samuelson proposed that economics need not assume utility functions — preferences can be derived from observed choices. If a consumer buys bundle A (say, 5 apples, 2 oranges) when bundle B (3 apples, 4 oranges) was also affordable, A is *revealed preferred* to B. No introspection required.

The *Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference* (WARP): if A is revealed preferred to B, then B cannot be revealed preferred to A when A was affordable. This is a testable consistency condition. The *Strong Axiom* (SARP) requires transitivity across multiple choices. Demand data that violate WARP indicate inconsistent preferences — or measurement error. WARP and SARP form the empirical foundation for testing consumer rationality.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics — Chicago price theory] Makes consumer theory empirically testable: you can test whether purchasing behaviour is consistent without observing utility.
cards.counter: Revealed preference theory assumes choices reveal stable preferences. Behavioural economics shows choices are heavily context-dependent — the same preference 'revealed' in one framing differs from another. The theory may measure behaviour, not underlying preferences.

quiz.q: What does the Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP) require?
choices: That consumers always prefer more to less
That if bundle A is chosen when B was affordable, B cannot be chosen when A is affordable
That preferences are independent of income
That utility is measurable on a cardinal scale

cards.title: Cost curves
cards.fact: A firm's short-run costs split into fixed (do not vary with output) and variable (do vary); marginal cost (MC) is the cost of one more unit; when MC is below average cost (AC), AC is falling; when MC is above AC, AC is rising.

layers.body: In the short run, some costs are fixed (rent, capital). Variable costs rise with output. *Average Cost* (AC = total cost/quantity) is U-shaped: it falls at first because fixed costs are spread over more units, then rises because diminishing marginal productivity increases variable cost per unit. *Marginal cost* (MC) cuts the AC curve at its minimum.

The relationship between MC and AC is mathematical: if MC < AC, producing one more unit costs less than the average — the average falls. If MC > AC, producing more costs above the average — the average rises. So MC always cuts AC at AC's minimum. This is analogous to your exam score: if your last score is below your average, your average falls.

cards.deploy: [MIT / Chicago Microeconomics] Foundational for all firm behaviour analysis — profit maximisation, entry, and pricing all depend on the structure of costs.
cards.counter: Real cost curves are rarely clean U-shapes — economies of scale may persist, technology affects cost structures, and multi-product firms have joint costs that cannot be cleanly attributed.

quiz.q: At what point does marginal cost intersect the average cost curve?
choices: At the point where fixed costs become negligible
At the minimum of the average cost curve
At the point where variable costs equal fixed costs
At the profit-maximising level of output

cards.title: Profit maximisation: P = MC
cards.fact: A profit-maximising firm produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC) — for a price-taking competitive firm, MR = P, so the rule becomes P = MC. It shuts down if price falls below average variable cost.

layers.body: If producing one more unit adds more to revenue than to cost (MR > MC), produce it. If it adds more to cost than revenue (MR < MC), produce less. Profit is maximised where MR = MC — the last unit breaks even on the margin.

A firm should continue operating in the short run as long as price covers *variable* costs (P ≥ AVC), even if it is making a loss — because fixed costs must be paid regardless. It should shut down if P < AVC: operating would lose more than shutting down. In the long run, the firm exits if price falls below *average total* cost (P < AC).

cards.deploy: [MIT / Chicago Microeconomics] The universal rule for firm supply — generates the supply curve and grounds all market analysis.
cards.counter: The P = MC efficiency result assumes no externalities. When production imposes costs on others (pollution), the social optimum requires P = social marginal cost > private MC — the basis for carbon taxes.

quiz.q: When should a firm shut down in the short run?
choices: When it is making a loss (price below average total cost)
When price falls below average variable cost — because operating would lose more than simply stopping production
When marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue
When fixed costs exceed variable costs

cards.title: Pareto efficiency
cards.fact: An allocation is Pareto efficient if no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off — a necessary condition for social optimality, but silent on equity.

layers.body: An allocation is *Pareto efficient* if there is no feasible reallocation that makes at least one person better off and no one worse off. Any allocation that can be improved is *Pareto inefficient* — there is 'waste' on the table. Pareto improvements are unambiguous welfare gains: no one loses.

Pareto efficiency is a minimal criterion. An allocation where one person has everything and everyone else has nothing can be Pareto efficient (you cannot take from the one without making them worse off). The concept says nothing about fairness, equality, or distributive justice. It is a *floor* — identifying waste — not a ceiling. Amartya Sen and Rawls both criticise relying on Pareto as the sole welfare criterion.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] The standard welfare benchmark — any policy that creates a Pareto improvement is unambiguously good; any that is Pareto inefficient wastes potential.
cards.counter: Most real policies create winners and losers — Pareto improvements in the strict sense are rare. The Kaldor-Hicks criterion (potential Pareto improvement: winners could compensate losers) is used instead but makes distributional trade-offs.

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid Pareto-efficient allocation?
choices: One where total output could be increased by reallocating resources
One where trade between two people would make both better off
One where no reallocation can make someone better off without making someone else worse off — even if very unequal
One where everyone has equal shares of all goods

cards.title: First welfare theorem
cards.fact: Every competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient — the 'invisible hand' formalised: given no externalities, no public goods, and no information asymmetries, markets waste nothing.

layers.body: The First Welfare Theorem (Arrow & Debreu, 1954): under competitive markets with complete markets, no externalities, and no public goods, every equilibrium is Pareto efficient. Each consumer optimises at MRS = price ratio; each producer optimises at MC = price; so MRS = MC across all goods — no reallocation can improve someone's welfare without harming another.

The theorem is a conditional statement: *if* markets are competitive *and if* there are no externalities, public goods, information asymmetries, or missing markets. Each assumption failure is a *market failure* justifying intervention. The theorem precisely identifies where markets fail: not everywhere, but specifically where its assumptions break down. This is the rigorous basis for distinguishing when government intervention is and is not warranted.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] The formal foundation for market liberalism — and for its limits: the theorem tells you exactly when markets fail.
cards.counter: The theorem assumes complete markets and no transaction costs — neither holds in reality. Coase argued transaction costs prevent markets from being complete; Arrow showed insurance markets are systematically incomplete due to moral hazard and adverse selection.

quiz.q: The First Welfare Theorem says that competitive equilibria are Pareto efficient only if…
choices: The government regulates prices to prevent monopoly
Markets are complete and there are no externalities, public goods, or information asymmetries
All consumers have equal income
Technology exhibits constant returns to scale

cards.title: Second welfare theorem
cards.fact: Any Pareto-efficient allocation can be achieved as a competitive equilibrium after an appropriate lump-sum redistribution — efficiency and equity can in principle be separated.

layers.body: The Second Welfare Theorem: for any Pareto-efficient allocation you want to achieve (including highly equal ones), there exists a redistribution of initial endowments after which competitive markets will deliver it. Desired equity does not require price distortions — redistribute first, then let markets work.

The redistribution required is *lump-sum* — transfers independent of behaviour (like a one-time wealth tax). Real redistributions (income taxes, VAT) distort behaviour and produce deadweight losses. This is the 'second-best' problem: lump-sum transfers are rarely feasible politically or informationally. The theorem is therefore more a theoretical benchmark than a practical policy tool — it shows that the efficiency-equity trade-off is not logically necessary, even if practically unavoidable.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] Refutes the claim that redistribution must sacrifice efficiency — under idealised conditions, equity and efficiency are separable. Grounds the progressive tax debate.
cards.counter: Lump-sum taxes are theoretically ideal but practically impossible to design without distorting incentives. Mirrlees's optimal tax theory showed that income taxation necessarily trades off efficiency and equality — the second welfare theorem's ideal cannot be realised.

quiz.q: What does the Second Welfare Theorem tell us about the efficiency-equity trade-off?
choices: Equity and efficiency are always in conflict — you can never have both
Any desired Pareto-efficient allocation (including equal ones) can be achieved by competitive markets after lump-sum redistribution — separating equity from efficiency in principle
Progressive income taxes can achieve equity without any efficiency loss
Only market outcomes are efficient; government redistribution always reduces total welfare

cards.title: Public goods
cards.fact: A public good is non-rival (one person's use doesn't reduce availability for others) and non-excludable (you can't prevent anyone from benefiting) — private markets under-provide them because free-riders benefit without paying.

layers.body: National defence, street lighting, and basic research are public goods: non-rival (one person's protection doesn't reduce another's) and non-excludable (you can't exclude non-payers). Private markets fail: each person can free-ride on others' contributions, so no one wants to pay — leading to under-provision or no provision at all.

Samuelson's taxonomy: *public goods* (non-rival, non-excludable: lighthouses); *private goods* (rival, excludable: apples); *club goods* (non-rival but excludable: Netflix, golf clubs); *common-pool resources* (rival but non-excludable: fish in the ocean). Ostrom's work on commons showed that non-excludable rival goods are not inevitably over-exploited ('tragedy of the commons') — communities develop governance rules.

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] Grounds the economic case for public provision of defence, basic research, and public health — not ideology, but market failure.
cards.counter: Public goods provision does not require government — clubs, private communities, and voluntary agreements can provide public goods in some cases (Coase). The difficulty is identifying truly non-excludable goods: most historical lighthouses were privately financed.

quiz.q: A 'club good' is best characterised as…
choices: Non-rival and non-excludable
Non-rival but excludable — many people can enjoy it simultaneously but access can be restricted
Rival but non-excludable
Rival and excludable

cards.title: The Coase theorem
cards.fact: Coase's theorem: if property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are zero, private bargaining will internalise externalities and achieve the efficient outcome regardless of the initial assignment of rights.

layers.body: A factory pollutes a river; a fisherman downstream is harmed. If the factory has the right to pollute, the fisherman may pay the factory to reduce pollution to the efficient level. If the fisherman has the right to clean water, the factory will pay the fisherman for permission to pollute up to the efficient level. Either way, the outcome is the same level of pollution — the efficient one.

Coase was not arguing for laissez-faire. His point was diagnostic: externality problems arise from *transaction costs* and *ill-defined property rights*, not from market failure per se. This implies two policy instruments: define property rights clearly and reduce transaction costs (mediation, courts) — rather than imposing a Pigouvian tax. Real-world externalities often have too many parties or too high transaction costs for bargaining to work (climate change: 7 billion emitters). The theorem identifies the conditions under which markets can self-correct.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Microeconomics] The most important theorem in law and economics — grounds property rights approaches to environmental policy, contract design, and liability rules.
cards.counter: Transaction costs are rarely zero and property rights over the environment are rarely well-defined — the real world is the negation of Coase's assumptions. The theorem tells us why markets fail more than why they succeed.

quiz.q: The Coase theorem says externalities will be internalised through bargaining, but only if…
choices: The government assigns property rights to the polluter rather than the victim
Property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are zero
Both parties have equal bargaining power and equal information
The externality affects no more than two parties

cards.title: Mechanism design
cards.fact: Mechanism design asks: given an allocation you want to achieve, what rules (mechanism) will induce self-interested agents to reveal information truthfully and produce that outcome?

layers.body: Mechanism design is 'reverse game theory': instead of analysing outcomes given rules, you design the rules to achieve desired outcomes. The fundamental challenge is *private information* — agents know things (their type, valuation, cost) that the designer does not. The mechanism must induce truthful revelation.

The *revelation principle* (Myerson, 1979): any outcome achievable by any mechanism is achievable by a *direct mechanism* where agents report their types truthfully. This means you can restrict attention to incentive-compatible direct mechanisms without loss of generality. Applications: optimal auctions (Myerson), optimal regulation (Baron-Myerson), public goods provision (Clarke-Groves), matching markets (Gale-Shapley).

cards.deploy: [MIT Microeconomics] The foundation of auction design, matching markets, regulation, and AI alignment — whenever you want agents to reveal private information, mechanism design is the framework.
cards.counter: Mechanism design assumes agents optimise and have well-defined types. Behavioural evidence shows agents deviate systematically from optimal play; designed mechanisms can fail when real behaviour doesn't match the theory.

quiz.q: The revelation principle in mechanism design says…
choices: Governments must reveal the design of their regulatory mechanisms to the public
Any outcome achievable by any mechanism is also achievable by a direct mechanism where agents truthfully report their private information
Agents will always lie about their private information unless threatened with penalties
Optimal mechanisms require agents to have complete information about each other's preferences

cards.title: Cournot oligopoly
cards.fact: In Cournot competition, two or more firms simultaneously choose quantities, each maximising profit given the other's output — the Nash equilibrium lies between monopoly (firms collude) and perfect competition (firms price at cost).

layers.body: Augustin Cournot (1838) analysed two firms each choosing how much to produce, taking the other's quantity as given. Each firm's best-response function slopes downward: the more your rival produces, the less you should produce (lower price from rival output reduces your incentive). The Nash equilibrium is where the two best-response curves intersect.

layers.t: Market power between monopoly and competition
layers.body: With N symmetric Cournot firms, the market approaches perfect competition as N → ∞ and approaches monopoly as N → 1. For two firms, the equilibrium price is between competitive and monopoly levels, and each firm earns positive profit. The deadweight loss is positive but less than monopoly. This provides the microeconomic foundation for competition policy: merger from 3 to 2 firms has a large effect on market power.

cards.deploy: [MIT / Chicago Microeconomics] The standard model for oligopoly and competition policy analysis — merger review, market concentration indices (HHI), and antitrust all build on Cournot intuition.
cards.counter: Cournot competition assumes firms choose quantities simultaneously; Bertrand competition assumes they choose prices. Under Bertrand, two firms drive price to marginal cost — the 'Bertrand paradox.' Real markets involve both price and quantity decisions.

quiz.q: What happens to the Cournot equilibrium price as the number of firms increases?
choices: It rises toward the monopoly price
It falls toward the competitive price (marginal cost)
It stays constant regardless of the number of firms
It first falls then rises, creating a U-shaped relationship

cards.title: The IS curve
cards.fact: The IS curve shows all combinations of interest rate and output where the goods market is in equilibrium — it slopes downward because lower interest rates stimulate investment, increasing equilibrium output.

layers.body: Investment is interest-sensitive: when rates fall, firms borrow more to invest. Via the multiplier, higher investment raises equilibrium income/output. The IS curve traces the (r, Y) pairs where saving = investment: it slopes downward — lower r → higher I → higher Y.

Government spending (G) and taxes (T) shift the IS curve. Higher G raises autonomous demand → multiplier raises equilibrium Y at every interest rate → IS shifts right. A tax cut raises disposable income → higher consumption → IS shifts right. The size of the shift equals the fiscal multiplier times the change in autonomous spending. Crowding out (higher G raises r, reducing private investment) is modelled by the subsequent LM adjustment.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] The foundation of Keynesian fiscal policy analysis — IS-LM is the workhorse model for policy analysis from central bank textbooks to IMF programs.
cards.counter: The IS-LM model assumes a short run where prices are fixed. It is not a model of the long run. Microfoundations critics (Lucas) argued the IS curve is not derived from optimising behaviour and is unstable under policy changes — motivating the New Keynesian DSGE models.

quiz.q: Why does the IS curve slope downward?
choices: Lower output increases household saving, which lowers interest rates
Lower interest rates stimulate investment, which via the multiplier raises equilibrium output
Higher interest rates reduce inflation, which raises real GDP
The central bank raises output when interest rates fall by printing money

cards.title: The LM curve
cards.fact: The LM curve shows all combinations of interest rate and output where the money market is in equilibrium — it slopes upward because higher output increases money demand, which raises interest rates given a fixed money supply.

layers.body: Money demand (liquidity preference) depends on output (transactions demand: more income → more spending → more money needed) and the interest rate (opportunity cost of holding money: higher r → hold less money). Money supply is fixed by the central bank. LM shows (r, Y) pairs where money supply = money demand: it slopes upward — higher Y → higher money demand → r must rise to restore equilibrium.

An increase in the money supply shifts LM right: at every output level, r is lower. This is expansionary monetary policy — lower rates stimulate investment, raising output. Quantitative easing operates by increasing the money supply even at the zero lower bound. At very low interest rates the LM curve becomes horizontal (liquidity trap): people hold any additional money rather than buying bonds, so monetary policy loses effectiveness.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] Completes the IS-LM framework for simultaneous goods and money market analysis — the interaction between fiscal and monetary policy is the LM's key role.
cards.counter: Modern central banks set interest rates directly (rather than targeting money supply), making the LM redundant as usually specified. The New Keynesian model replaces it with a Taylor Rule.

quiz.q: Why does the LM curve slope upward?
choices: Higher interest rates reduce investment, lowering output
Higher output raises transactions demand for money, requiring higher interest rates to reduce money demand back to the fixed supply
The central bank raises money supply when output rises
Higher output increases inflation, reducing the real money supply

cards.title: IS-LM model
cards.fact: IS-LM simultaneously solves goods and money market equilibrium — fiscal policy shifts IS; monetary policy shifts LM; their interaction determines both the interest rate and output level.

layers.body: The IS-LM model finds the (r, Y) pair that simultaneously clears both the goods market (IS) and the money market (LM). The intersection is macroeconomic equilibrium. Fiscal expansion (shift IS right) raises both r and Y. Monetary expansion (shift LM right) lowers r and raises Y. The mix of fiscal and monetary policy determines the composition of demand.

When government spends more (IS shifts right), output rises but so does r. Higher r crowds out private investment — partially offsetting the fiscal stimulus. The degree of crowding out depends on LM's slope: if LM is steep (money demand is interest-inelastic), fiscal policy is largely crowded out; if LM is flat (liquidity trap), there is no crowding out and the multiplier is full.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] The standard policy framework for short-run analysis — used by central banks, IMF, and treasury economists to assess fiscal-monetary mixes.
cards.counter: Lucas's critique: IS-LM is not derived from microeconomic optimisation; its parameters shift when policy changes, making it unreliable for policy evaluation. The DSGE revolution replaced IS-LM in academic macro, though it remains the practitioner's workhorse.

quiz.q: What is 'crowding out' in the IS-LM model?
choices: Government spending crowds out private consumption directly
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates, which reduces private investment and partially offsets the stimulus
Monetary tightening crowds out fiscal expansion by reducing the money multiplier
Higher taxes crowd out private saving

cards.title: The impossible trinity
cards.fact: A country cannot simultaneously have a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and independent monetary policy — it must give up one of the three.

layers.body: The trilemma (Mundell-Fleming): if capital moves freely across borders and the exchange rate is fixed, the central bank must hold the rate by buying or selling currency whenever capital flows disturb it — and this requires setting interest rates to prevent flows, eliminating independent monetary policy.

The Bretton Woods system (1944–71): fixed rates + capital controls → monetary independence. Post-1971 floating rates: monetary independence + free capital → flexible exchange rates. The Eurozone: fixed rates (single currency) + free capital → no monetary independence for member states. China: monetary independence + capital controls → managed exchange rate. The trilemma explains why exchange rate crises occur when countries try to maintain all three: Thailand 1997, Argentina 2001, UK 1992 (ERM crisis).

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics / LSE IR] Fundamental constraint on international economic policy — explains every exchange rate crisis as a failure to choose.
cards.counter: Rey's 'global financial cycle' hypothesis (2013) argues that even with floating exchange rates, capital flows from the US dollar system limit monetary independence — a 'dilemma' not a trilemma. The constraint may be even tighter than Mundell-Fleming implies.

quiz.q: Which combination did Bretton Woods (1944–71) choose?
choices: Fixed exchange rates + free capital mobility → no monetary independence
Fixed exchange rates + capital controls → monetary independence
Free capital mobility + monetary independence → floating exchange rates
All three: fixed rates, free capital, and independent monetary policy

cards.title: Mundell-Fleming model
cards.fact: Mundell-Fleming extends IS-LM to the open economy — fiscal policy is most effective under fixed exchange rates; monetary policy is most effective under floating rates.

layers.t: Open economy adds a third curve
layers.body: The Mundell-Fleming model (1963) adds a *BP curve* (balance of payments equilibrium) to IS-LM. With perfect capital mobility, the BP curve is horizontal at the world interest rate: the domestic rate must equal the world rate, or capital flows will restore it.

Under *fixed exchange rates*: monetary expansion is ineffective — it pushes r below world rate, causing capital outflows, which forces the central bank to buy domestic currency, contracting money supply back to baseline. But fiscal expansion is fully effective — no crowding out, because the exchange rate stays fixed. Under *floating exchange rates*: fiscal expansion crowds out completely via exchange rate appreciation reducing net exports. Monetary expansion is fully effective — lower r causes depreciation, stimulating exports.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] The standard open-economy macro framework — explains why eurozone fiscal austerity had no monetary offset and why floating-rate countries have more policy space.
cards.counter: The model assumes perfect capital mobility and prices fixed in the short run. With imperfect capital mobility or exchange rate overshooting, the policy conclusions are more nuanced.

quiz.q: Under floating exchange rates, why is fiscal expansion ineffective in the Mundell-Fleming model?
choices: Higher government spending directly crowds out private investment
Fiscal expansion raises interest rates, causing capital inflows and exchange rate appreciation that reduces net exports, fully offsetting the stimulus
Monetary policy automatically contracts when fiscal policy expands
The BP curve shifts to neutralise any IS shift

cards.title: The golden rule of capital accumulation
cards.fact: The 'golden rule' saving rate is the one that maximises steady-state consumption per worker — an economy saving too much (above the golden rule) or too little (below) can increase consumption by adjusting its saving rate.

layers.t: Not too much, not too little
layers.body: The Solow model has many steady states (one for each saving rate). Edmund Phelps showed that consumption per worker is maximised at the saving rate where the *marginal product of capital = depreciation rate* — the 'golden rule.' Save more, and you invest more than the capital that depreciates: net capital and output grow, but you consume less today. The golden rule trades off present consumption against steady-state consumption.

A country above the golden rule saving rate (overaccumulating capital) is *dynamically inefficient*: it could consume more today and in steady state by reducing its saving rate. Empirical estimates suggest advanced economies are below the golden rule (underaccumulating), meaning additional saving would raise steady-state consumption. But transitional costs — you must sacrifice current consumption to reach the higher steady state — create a political economy constraint.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] Shows that the optimal saving rate is not the highest one — a critique of 'save more, grow faster' policy advice that ignores steady-state consumption.
cards.counter: The golden rule applies in the long run. In the short run, any increase in saving involves a sacrifice of current consumption; the political economy of intergenerational redistribution means democratic governments rarely pursue the golden rule deliberately.

quiz.q: The 'golden rule' saving rate in the Solow model is the one where…
choices: Growth rate equals the depreciation rate
Consumption per worker is maximised in steady state — the marginal product of capital equals the depreciation rate
Investment equals consumption in the steady state
The economy reaches the highest possible GDP per capita

cards.title: Romer: endogenous growth
cards.fact: Romer's endogenous growth theory explains why growth need not peter out: ideas are non-rival (everyone can use them) and accumulate, generating sustained increasing returns — so R&D investment is the engine of long-run growth.

layers.body: The Solow model predicts convergence: diminishing returns to capital mean growth eventually stops without technological progress — which Solow treated as exogenous (unexplained). Romer (1990) endogenised technology: ideas are *non-rival* (a recipe, a formula, a drug molecule can be used by everyone simultaneously without being used up) and *partially excludable* (patents protect their monetisation). Non-rivalry means no diminishing returns to the stock of ideas.

If ideas drive long-run growth, subsidise R&D. Because ideas are non-rival, private returns to research are below social returns (others benefit from your innovation without paying) — markets under-invest. Government funding for basic research, universities, and patent systems all address this externality. Romer's framework also explains why knowledge industries (tech, pharma, media) have increasing returns and winner-take-most dynamics.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] The modern foundation for industrial policy in knowledge sectors — if ideas are the engine of growth and private markets under-provide them, active technology policy is warranted.
cards.counter: Empirically, convergence across countries is conditional on institutions (Acemoglu), not just knowledge diffusion. Ideas spread slowly across borders due to intellectual property regimes, tacit knowledge, and institutional barriers.

quiz.q: What makes ideas 'non-rival' and why does this matter for growth theory?
choices: Ideas cannot be owned, so they have zero economic value
Ideas can be used by everyone simultaneously without depletion — meaning no diminishing returns to the stock of ideas, enabling sustained growth
Ideas are non-rival because they are produced by governments rather than markets
Ideas depreciate more slowly than physical capital

cards.title: NAIRU and the vertical long-run Phillips curve
cards.fact: Friedman and Phelps (1968): there is a natural rate of unemployment (NAIRU) below which inflation accelerates indefinitely — attempts to hold unemployment below NAIRU through monetary expansion generate ever-rising inflation, not a stable trade-off.

layers.body: The short-run Phillips curve offers a trade-off: lower unemployment at the cost of higher inflation. Friedman argued this is an illusion. Workers expect future inflation; when their expectations adjust, they demand higher wages — shifting the Phillips curve upward. To keep unemployment below NAIRU, the central bank must continuously accelerate inflation to stay ahead of expectations.

Actual inflation = expected inflation + α(u* − u), where u* is NAIRU and u is actual unemployment. In the long run, expectations adjust: actual = expected, so u = u*. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at NAIRU. The 1970s stagflation was the empirical confirmation: the trade-off broke down when inflationary expectations became entrenched. Modern inflation targeting was designed to anchor expectations.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] The foundation of modern central banking — central banks target inflation, not unemployment, because the long-run trade-off does not exist.
cards.counter: NAIRU is unobservable and non-constant — estimates varied from 6% to 4% in the 1990s US as unemployment fell without inflation. Blanchard and others argue NAIRU is more volatile than Friedman assumed, giving central banks more room to support employment.

quiz.q: Why is the long-run Phillips curve vertical at NAIRU?
choices: In the long run, wages and prices are fully flexible, eliminating unemployment
Workers' inflation expectations adjust, so any attempt to hold unemployment below NAIRU requires accelerating inflation — there is no stable long-run trade-off
Central banks target a fixed inflation rate, anchoring the curve at one point
Unemployment cannot fall below NAIRU because structural barriers prevent labour market clearing

cards.title: Fiscal multiplier: size and constraints
cards.fact: The fiscal multiplier is larger when the economy is in recession, monetary policy cannot offset (zero lower bound), and trade leakage is low — but near zero when interest rates rise freely or Ricardian equivalence holds.

layers.body: The simple Keynesian multiplier is 1/(1−MPC). In practice, the actual fiscal multiplier varies widely: near zero in normal times (if monetary policy offsets by raising rates) to above one in deep recessions (when the economy is far below potential and rates are at zero).

During the Eurozone austerity debate, the IMF's chief economist Olivier Blanchard admitted (2013) that the Fund had systematically underestimated multipliers — using estimates of ~0.5 when the actual multipliers were 1.5–2.5 at the zero lower bound with coordinated multi-country austerity. The consequences: fiscal consolidation in 2010–12 caused greater output losses than forecast. *Ricardian equivalence* (Barro 1974) claims the multiplier is zero: households anticipate future taxes and save the stimulus. Empirical evidence suggests Ricardian equivalence holds poorly in practice.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] Key for evaluating austerity and stimulus debates — the multiplier is not fixed; its size depends critically on the economic context.
cards.counter: Measuring the fiscal multiplier is methodologically hard — isolating fiscal shocks from confounding factors. Estimates range from negative (Alesina) to strongly positive (Blanchard). Political economy shapes which estimates are cited in policy debates.

quiz.q: When is the fiscal multiplier largest?
choices: In a boom when monetary policy is tightening
At the zero lower bound in a recession — when monetary policy cannot offset fiscal expansion and the output gap is large
In small open economies with floating exchange rates
When government debt is low

cards.title: Secular stagnation
cards.fact: Larry Summers's secular stagnation thesis (2013): advanced economies face a persistent shortfall of investment demand relative to saving — keeping interest rates near zero — not a temporary business cycle problem but a structural shift.

layers.t: When the zero lower bound binds persistently
layers.body: After 2008, advanced economies saw weak investment, low inflation, and near-zero interest rates persisting for years — unlike typical recessions. Summers revived Alvin Hansen's 1938 'secular stagnation' concept: the equilibrium real interest rate may have fallen permanently below zero, making monetary policy structurally insufficient.

Proposed causes: aging demographics increase desired saving and reduce investment. Rising inequality concentrates income among high-savers. Technological change is less capital-intensive (software vs factories). Bernanke's 'global savings glut' (China and oil exporters) suppresses global rates. The policy implication: fiscal policy and public investment must fill the investment gap that private markets cannot, even in normal times — not just in recessions.

cards.deploy: [MIT Macroeconomics] Grounds the case for permanent activist fiscal policy and public investment — not just as recession-fighting but as structural macroeconomic management.
cards.counter: Goodhart and Pradhan argue that the end of globalisation and aging demographics will reverse the savings glut and raise inflation and interest rates — the secular stagnation was a temporary demographic phase, not a permanent trap.

quiz.q: What is the core claim of the secular stagnation thesis?
choices: Economic growth rates have permanently declined due to productivity slowdown
The equilibrium real interest rate has fallen persistently below zero — investment demand falls short of desired saving even at zero rates, making monetary policy structurally insufficient
Government debt has risen to levels that crowd out private investment
Demographic aging reduces labour supply, shrinking potential GDP

cards.title: Strategic form game
cards.fact: A strategic form (normal form) game is defined by: a set of players, for each player a set of strategies, and a payoff function mapping strategy combinations to outcomes.

layers.body: A game consists of: (1) *Players* — who is making decisions; (2) *Strategy sets* — what each player can choose; (3) *Payoff functions* — what each player receives for each combination of strategies. For two players with finite strategies, the game is represented as a matrix (rows for player 1's strategies, columns for player 2's, cells for payoffs).

A *pure strategy* is a definite choice. A *mixed strategy* is a probability distribution over pure strategies. Players choose simultaneously in the strategic form — they commit to strategies without knowing what the other will do. This contrasts with the *extensive form* where the sequence of moves matters.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] The entry point for all strategic reasoning — any situation with multiple decision-makers whose payoffs depend on each other's choices can be modelled as a game.
cards.counter: The normal form loses information about the *order* of moves and about what players know when they move — for sequential games with private information, the extensive form is needed.

quiz.q: What are the three components of a strategic form game?
choices: Agents, actions, outcomes
Players, strategy sets, and payoff functions
Principals, agents, contracts
States, transitions, utilities

cards.title: Dominant strategies and IESDS
cards.fact: A dominant strategy is one that is best regardless of what others do — if you have one, play it. Iterated elimination of dominated strategies (IESDS) extends this: eliminate dominated strategies for all players, repeatedly, until only rationalizable strategies remain.

layers.body: Strategy X *strictly dominates* Y if X gives a higher payoff than Y for every strategy the opponent might play. If you have a strictly dominant strategy, rational play is immediate: play it, regardless of what you believe the opponent will do.

IESDS: if player 1 has a dominated strategy, rational player 2 knows player 1 won't play it. This may now make one of player 2's strategies dominated. Eliminate it. Continue until no more eliminations are possible. The strategies that survive IESDS are *rationalizable*. In some games IESDS gives a unique prediction (as in many simple coordination and competition games). In others many strategies survive.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] The simplest rational solution concept — sufficient for many applied models (advertising, pricing, voting) without requiring complex belief-formation.
cards.counter: IESDS requires not just rationality but common knowledge of rationality — I know you're rational, you know I know you're rational, etc. This is a strong assumption; bounded rationality can interrupt the chain.

quiz.q: Strategy X strictly dominates strategy Y if…
choices: X gives a higher payoff than Y for at least one opponent strategy
X gives a higher payoff than Y for every strategy the opponent might play
X is chosen more frequently than Y by experimental subjects
X is the Nash equilibrium and Y is not

cards.title: Mixed strategy Nash equilibrium
cards.fact: In a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, players randomise over pure strategies — each player is indifferent between the strategies they mix over, because the opponent's mix makes each equally good.

layers.body: Nash proved that every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium if mixed strategies are allowed. In a mixed NE, player 1 mixes over strategies A and B — not because randomising is inherently good, but because player 2's mixing makes player 1 exactly indifferent. Player 1 is willing to randomise because they are indifferent.

layers.t: How to find a mixed NE
layers.body: To find player 1's mixed strategy: choose the mix that makes player 2 *indifferent* between player 2's strategies. The equilibrium mix does not maximise player 1's payoff given player 2's strategy — player 1 is exactly indifferent. Classic example: Matching Pennies — player 1 wants to match, player 2 wants to differ; the unique NE has each mixing 50:50. Penalty kicks in football approximate a mixed strategy equilibrium.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Explains randomisation in competitive situations: poker bluffing, penalty kick direction, audit frequency — anywhere predictability is exploitable.
cards.counter: Mixed strategy equilibria are psychologically awkward: players must be made exactly indifferent by the opponent's mix. Experiments show players often deviate systematically from the equilibrium mix (matching pennies studies).

quiz.q: In a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, player 1 randomises because…
choices: Randomisation makes player 1 better off than any pure strategy
Player 2's mixing makes player 1 exactly indifferent — no pure strategy is strictly better
Player 1 cannot compute the pure strategy Nash equilibrium
Random play prevents player 2 from best-responding

cards.title: Coordination games and multiple equilibria
cards.fact: Coordination games have multiple Nash equilibria — players prefer to coordinate, but there are several ways to coordinate; the challenge is selecting one equilibrium without explicit communication.

layers.body: In the *Battle of Sexes*, both players want to attend the same event but prefer different ones (he prefers football, she prefers opera). Both attend football is a NE; both attend opera is a NE; neither attending is not. The players' problem: which equilibrium to coordinate on without communication?

Thomas Schelling's *The Strategy of Conflict* (1960): players solve coordination problems by converging on a *focal point* — a salient option that stands out by virtue of convention, tradition, or shared context. 'Meet in New York at noon': the top of the Empire State Building emerges as a focal point, even without communication. Standards (metric vs imperial), currencies (dollar as reserve), and legal defaults all serve as coordination focal points.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Explains why standards, norms, and conventions are economically valuable — they are focal point solutions to coordination problems that markets cannot solve by price.
cards.counter: Focal points require shared cultural context; what is focal for one group may not be for another. This complicates international coordination: different countries have different historical focal points (common law vs civil law, dollar vs euro).

quiz.q: What is a 'Schelling focal point'?
choices: The Nash equilibrium selected by iterated elimination of dominated strategies
A salient coordination point that players converge on without communication, by virtue of shared context or convention
The equilibrium that maximises total social welfare
A mixed strategy that makes each player indifferent in a coordination game

cards.title: Extensive form and game trees
cards.fact: The extensive form represents sequential games as a tree: nodes are decision points, branches are actions, leaves are outcomes — it captures the order of moves and what players know when they move.

layers.body: When moves are sequential rather than simultaneous, the extensive form is more informative than the normal form. A *game tree*: nodes represent where a player makes a decision; branches represent available actions; terminal nodes show payoffs. *Information sets* group nodes the current player cannot distinguish — modelling what they know when they move.

With *perfect information* (chess: both players see the full board), every information set is a singleton — every node is distinguishable. With *imperfect information* (card games: you don't see the opponent's hand), some nodes are grouped in the same information set. A *strategy* in the extensive form specifies an action at every information set — not just at nodes you'll actually reach.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Essential for modelling any sequential interaction: entry deterrence, arms races, negotiations, repeated games — all require the extensive form.
cards.counter: Real sequential games rarely have perfectly specified trees: bounded recall, communication complexity, and strategy space explosion make the extensive form an idealisation rather than a complete model.

quiz.q: What does an 'information set' represent in the extensive form?
choices: The information a player has received in previous rounds
A group of decision nodes the player cannot distinguish — modelling uncertainty about where in the tree they are
The set of strategies available to a player
The payoffs at a terminal node

cards.title: Backward induction
cards.fact: Backward induction solves finite games by reasoning from the end: at the last decision node, the player chooses their best action; then the previous player anticipates this and chooses accordingly, working back to the first move.

layers.body: In the final stage, the last mover picks the action that maximises their payoff. The player before anticipates this and picks to maximise their payoff given the last mover's anticipated action. Continue backward to the first move. The resulting strategy profile is the unique backward induction outcome.

The Centipede game: two players alternately choose to take a growing pot or pass. Backward induction predicts the first player takes on the first move — but experiments show players cooperate for many rounds. This 'unravelling problem' (common in repeated games, wage negotiations, and political brinksmanship) shows backward induction can produce paradoxical predictions when it requires implausibly long chains of rationality assumptions.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] The basis for solving sequential games — underlies entry deterrence models, take-or-leave bargaining, and legislative agenda-setting.
cards.counter: Backward induction requires *common knowledge of rationality* in arbitrarily long chains. Experimental evidence (Centipede game) shows real players deviate, often cooperating when theory predicts immediate defection.

quiz.q: What does backward induction require that makes it controversial in long games?
choices: Players must have perfect information throughout the game
Common knowledge of rationality through arbitrarily long chains — I know you're rational, you know I know you're rational, etc.
Players must be able to commit to strategies in advance
The game must have a unique Nash equilibrium

cards.title: Subgame perfect equilibrium
cards.fact: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE) is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame — it eliminates non-credible threats by requiring rational play even at nodes the path of play never reaches.

layers.body: A Nash equilibrium can be sustained by threats that would never be carried out. SPE (Selten, 1965) requires Nash equilibrium in every subgame — including off-path nodes. An empty threat (e.g. a firm threatening to start a price war if a rival enters) is ruled out if following through would be irrational: the rival knows the firm won't actually start a price war, so the threat deters nothing.

An incumbent monopolist threatens to fight any entrant with a price war. If this is credible, entrants stay out. SPE analysis: would the incumbent actually fight if entry happened? If fighting is costly (it is — price wars destroy profit), the threat is empty. A rational entrant recognises this and enters. The monopolist cannot credibly commit to fighting without a pre-commitment device (excess capacity, irreversible investment). This is the Spence signalling argument applied to entry deterrence.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] The standard solution concept for sequential games — used in industrial organisation, contract theory, political science, and international bargaining.
cards.counter: SPE requires rationality at all nodes, including unreached ones — and real players sometimes do follow through on irrational threats for reputational reasons. Reputation models (Kreps-Wilson) restore the rationality of seemingly irrational commitments.

quiz.q: Why does subgame perfect equilibrium rule out Nash equilibria sustained by empty threats?
choices: It requires all strategies to be dominant
It requires Nash equilibrium in every subgame — so threats that would be irrational to carry out cannot sustain equilibrium
It eliminates mixed strategies from sequential games
It assumes players have perfect recall of all previous moves

cards.title: Credible commitment
cards.fact: Credible commitment means binding yourself to a future action (even a costly one) to influence others' behaviour now — cutting off options to gain strategic advantage: burning the boats, signing inflation targets, putting up sunk costs.

layers.body: Counterintuitively, *limiting your options* can make you better off. If you can commit to fighting a price war regardless of cost, the threat becomes credible and rivals won't enter. The key: the commitment must be irreversible or costly to reverse. Burning your own boats prevents retreat — which makes the army fight harder and the enemy knows it.

Central bank independence: a government that can override the central bank faces high inflation expectations; independence commits the government credibly to low inflation. NATO Article 5: the collective defence clause makes the commitment credible because defection from it would destroy the alliance. Nuclear 'dead man's switches': an automated retaliation system removes the option not to retaliate — making the deterrent credible even if retaliation would be suicidal.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Unifies monetary policy credibility, deterrence theory, and business strategy — anywhere that the inability to commit undermines your strategic position.
cards.counter: Commitment devices can backfire: North Korea's extreme threats are partly credible but reduce its room for diplomatic manoeuvre. Schelling noted the danger of being too committed — it can trigger the crisis you were trying to prevent.

quiz.q: Why does limiting your own options sometimes give you a strategic advantage?
choices: Fewer options means faster decision-making
By committing irreversibly to an action, you make a threat credible — others change their behaviour in anticipation
Limiting options signals that you are rational and will not make costly mistakes
Constraint forces creativity and leads to better strategic solutions

cards.title: Bayesian games and incomplete information
cards.fact: Harsanyi's Bayesian game models situations where players have private information (types) — a player's type determines their payoffs, and strategies map types to actions.

layers.body: John Harsanyi (1967) showed how to model games where players have private information. Each player has a *type* (their private information: valuation, cost, quality) drawn from a prior distribution. Strategies now map types to actions. Bayesian Nash equilibrium requires each player to maximise expected payoff given the prior distribution over opponents' types.

Auctions: bidders have private valuations. Insurance: clients have private risk levels. Bargaining: parties have private reservation prices. Entry games: an entrant is uncertain whether the incumbent has high or low costs. In all these cases, equilibrium strategies depend on what each player believes about the distribution of types and how that shapes strategic interaction.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] The foundation of all information economics — auctions, contracts, signaling, screening, and mechanism design all build on Bayesian game theory.
cards.counter: Bayesian game theory requires a common prior — all players agree on the probability distribution of types. This is a strong assumption; Disagreement games and robust mechanism design relax it.

quiz.q: What is a player's 'type' in a Bayesian game?
choices: Their level of strategic sophistication
Their private information — valuation, cost, risk level — that affects their payoffs and that others cannot directly observe
Their dominant strategy in the normal form
The probability distribution they use to randomise in mixed strategies

cards.title: Signaling games
cards.fact: In Spence's education signaling model, education signals productivity even if it adds nothing to it — high-ability workers get degrees to distinguish themselves, creating a separating equilibrium where the signal is credible because it is too costly for low-ability workers to mimic.

layers.body: Michael Spence's education signaling (1973): employers cannot observe workers' ability. High-ability workers signal their type by getting a degree — not because education makes them more productive, but because the cost of getting the degree is lower for high-ability types. In equilibrium, employers offer high wages to graduates and low wages to non-graduates. It is a *separating equilibrium* because low-ability workers find mimicking the signal too costly.

A *separating equilibrium*: different types choose different signals → receivers can infer types. A *pooling equilibrium*: all types choose the same signal → receivers learn nothing. Signaling is used in: peacock tails (fitness signals), warranties (quality signals), advertising (profitability signals), criminal trials (credibility signals). The key is that the signal must be *differentially costly* — more costly for low-quality types to send than high-quality types.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Explains credentials, warranties, advertising, and biological displays — any situation where one party has private information and wants to communicate it credibly.
cards.counter: If education is pure signaling rather than human capital formation, it is socially wasteful — a signaling equilibrium is efficient only if the signal is also productively valuable. Empirically disentangling signaling from human capital is methodologically very difficult.

quiz.q: Why is education a credible signal in Spence's model even if it adds no productivity?
choices: Employers cannot verify productivity directly and must rely on observable credentials
The cost of getting a degree is lower for high-ability types, so only high-ability types find it worth getting — low-ability types won't mimic it
Governments mandate degrees for high-skill jobs, making credentials legally required
Education is valuable because it provides networking opportunities that increase earnings

cards.title: Nash bargaining solution
cards.fact: Nash's axiomatic bargaining solution uniquely pins down how two rational agents split a surplus: the product of their utility gains is maximised — the 'Nash product' — reflecting efficiency, symmetry, and invariance.

layers.t: From axioms to a unique solution
layers.body: Nash (1950) asked: given a bargaining problem (a set of feasible outcomes and a disagreement point), what solution satisfies basic rationality axioms? His four axioms: (1) Pareto efficiency; (2) symmetry (equal bargainers get equal shares); (3) invariance to equivalent utility representations; (4) independence of irrelevant alternatives. The unique solution satisfying all four maximises the Nash product: (u₁ − d₁)(u₂ − d₂), where d is the disagreement payoff.

The Nash solution depends on the *disagreement point* (threat point) — what each player gets if negotiation fails. A better outside option raises your share. Rubinstein's alternating-offers model provides a non-cooperative foundation: when offers alternate and players discount time, the equilibrium converges to the Nash solution as the time between offers → 0. More patient players get a larger share.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Standard framework for union-firm wage bargaining, international trade negotiations, and contract theory — the Nash product is the canonical benchmark.
cards.counter: The independence of irrelevant alternatives axiom is disputed. Kalai-Smorodinsky replace it with a monotonicity axiom, generating a different solution. Which axiom is more normatively compelling is contested.

quiz.q: In Nash's axiomatic bargaining solution, what is maximised?
choices: The sum of the two players' utility gains over the disagreement point
The product of the two players' utility gains over the disagreement point (the Nash product)
The equal division of the surplus, regardless of utility functions
The minimax regret of both players

cards.title: Rubinstein alternating-offers bargaining
cards.fact: Rubinstein's model: two players alternate making offers; the unique SPE gives the first mover a larger share, with the split determined by relative patience — more patient players get more.

layers.body: Ariel Rubinstein (1982): player 1 makes an offer, player 2 accepts or rejects and makes a counter-offer, and so on. Each rejection delays agreement — both players discount the future (δ₁, δ₂). The unique SPE gives player 1 a share of 1/(1 + δ₂/(1 − δ₁)). More patient players (higher δ) get more; the first mover's advantage disappears as offers alternate faster.

As the delay between offers → 0, the Rubinstein outcome converges to the Nash bargaining solution. This provides a *non-cooperative foundation* for the axiomatic Nash solution: the axioms are justified by the strategic structure of alternating offers. Applications: union-firm wage bargaining, bilateral monopoly, international treaty negotiation.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Grounds the intuition that patience is power in bargaining — explains why creditors in debt renegotiations seek to induce impatience, and why timing of sanctions matters in diplomacy.
cards.counter: The unique SPE requires common knowledge of rationality and discount factors. Empirically, bargaining outcomes are heavily influenced by norms, framing, and fairness concerns — the 50-50 split is a strong behavioural focal point.

quiz.q: In Rubinstein's bargaining model, what determines each player's share?
choices: The number of rounds they are willing to bargain
Their relative patience — more patient players (higher discount factors) get a larger share of the surplus
Who has the legal property right over the object being divided
The Nash product of their utility functions

cards.title: Vickrey second-price auction
cards.fact: In a sealed-bid second-price auction, each bidder's dominant strategy is to bid their true value — you win if your bid is highest, but pay only the second-highest bid.

layers.body: Vickrey auction: each bidder submits a sealed bid; the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. Dominant strategy: bid your true valuation. Proof: if you bid above your value and win, you may pay more than it's worth. If you bid below your value, you risk losing an auction you would have profited from winning. Bidding truthfully always does weakly better than any other strategy.

The *revenue equivalence theorem* (Vickrey 1961, generalised by Myerson): under symmetric risk-neutral bidders with independent private values, all standard auction formats (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch) yield the same expected revenue. Despite this, mechanisms differ in simplicity: second-price auctions are strategically simple (truth is dominant); first-price require calculation. Google's ad auctions, eBay, spectrum auctions all use variants of the second-price design.

cards.deploy: [MIT Mechanism Design] The canonical auction design result — any well-designed auction should elicit honest preferences; the Vickrey design does so by making truthfulness dominant.
cards.counter: Revenue equivalence breaks down with risk aversion, correlated values, or multiple objects. Combinatorial auctions (spectrum) require extensions (VCG) because items have complementarities that single-item Vickrey doesn't handle.

quiz.q: Why is it a dominant strategy to bid your true value in a Vickrey second-price auction?
choices: Because the auctioneer will verify your valuation and disqualify dishonest bids
Because bidding above your value risks paying more than the item is worth; bidding below risks losing an auction you would have profited from — truthfulness avoids both
Because the payment rule punishes any deviation from true value
Because all bidders know each other's valuations

cards.title: The folk theorem
cards.fact: In infinitely repeated games, any individually rational payoff (above the minmax) can be sustained as a Nash equilibrium — cooperation, punishment, and anything in between — if players are patient enough.

layers.body: The prisoner's dilemma has a unique NE (defect) in the one-shot game. But in an infinitely repeated game, cooperation can be sustained if players are patient (discount factor δ close to 1). The *grim trigger* strategy: cooperate until the other defects, then defect forever. Each player prefers cooperation (getting C each period) over defection (getting D once, then punishment forever) if the gain from deviation is outweighed by the discounted stream of lost cooperation.

The folk theorem is a double-edged result. It shows repetition can sustain cooperation — good. But it also shows that almost *any* outcome (including very bad ones) can be an equilibrium in an infinitely repeated game. The theorem doesn't predict *which* equilibrium will be played. This is the main limitation: theory says cooperation is possible but doesn't tell us when it will actually occur.

cards.deploy: [Princeton / MIT Game Theory] Explains why firms in oligopolies can sustain tacit collusion, why countries comply with international treaties, and why communities maintain norms — repetition with punishment potential changes incentives fundamentally.
cards.counter: The folk theorem requires infinite (or uncertain) repetition, sufficient patience, and the ability to observe each other's actions (or use probabilistic punishment). With finite horizons, backward induction unravels cooperation in the last period, then the second-to-last, etc.

quiz.q: Why does the folk theorem have a 'dark side'?
choices: It proves that cooperation is impossible in most real games
It shows that almost any outcome — including bad ones — can be an equilibrium, so it provides little predictive power about which equilibrium is actually played
It requires players to be irrational in one-shot games
It only applies when both players use grim trigger strategies

cards.title: Prospect theory
cards.fact: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory: people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point; losses loom larger than equivalent gains (loss aversion); the value function is S-shaped — concave for gains, convex for losses.

layers.body: Expected utility theory evaluates outcomes by total wealth. Prospect theory evaluates them by *gains and losses relative to a reference point*. The value function is: S-shaped (concave in gains → diminishing sensitivity; convex in losses → risk-seeking to avoid losses); steeper in losses than gains (loss aversion: a $100 loss hurts more than a $100 gain pleases).

Prospect theory also transforms probabilities: people *overweight small probabilities* (why people buy lottery tickets and insurance simultaneously) and *underweight large probabilities* (why people are overconfident about near-certain events). The combination explains a range of anomalies: the Allais paradox, the preference for certainty (certainty effect), and simultaneous gambling and insurance purchase.
