cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] The dominant descriptive theory of decision under risk — has replaced expected utility theory as the empirical benchmark in finance, insurance, and policy.
cards.counter: Prospect theory is descriptive, not normative — it describes how people behave, not how they should. The reference point is under-theorised: people form reference points in context-dependent ways that are hard to predict.

quiz.q: The value function in prospect theory is 'S-shaped.' What does the convex portion in the loss domain imply?
choices: People are risk-averse when facing losses, just as they are with gains
People become risk-seeking when facing losses — they prefer a gamble to a certain loss of the same expected value
The marginal pain of additional losses decreases at an accelerating rate
People overweight small losses just as they overweight small probabilities

cards.title: Framing effect
cards.fact: The framing effect: logically equivalent descriptions of the same choice elicit different preferences — '90% survival rate' and '10% mortality rate' are identical but survival framing induces more treatment acceptance.

layers.body: Kahneman and Tversky's Asian Disease problem: if a disease kills 600 people and you must choose between programmes, choosing 'save 200 people' (certain) vs '1/3 chance to save 600' (risky) shows risk-aversion. But describing the same choice as '400 die' (certain) vs '2/3 chance 600 die' (risky) reverses the preference — because 'die' frames the choice in the loss domain, inducing risk-seeking.

Rational agents should have preferences independent of the description of identical outcomes (the *invariance axiom* of expected utility theory). Framing effects violate this. They have major policy implications: how a pension scheme, health warning, or tax is described affects uptake regardless of the underlying incentive. Choice architects can manipulate outcomes through framing without changing any objective feature of the choice.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] Explains why identical policies get different responses depending on how they are communicated — framing is a policy lever as powerful as incentives.
cards.counter: Framing effects are robust in laboratory settings but their magnitude varies in field settings where stakes are higher and people have more time to deliberate. Highly numerate individuals are more resistant to framing.

quiz.q: What does the Asian Disease framing experiment demonstrate?
choices: People are systematically overconfident about medical treatments
Describing outcomes in terms of gains (lives saved) versus losses (deaths) reverses preferences, even though the options are objectively identical
Risk aversion increases when stakes involve human lives
People prefer certainty in all domains involving public health

cards.title: System 1 and System 2
cards.fact: Kahneman's dual-process theory: System 1 is fast, automatic, heuristic, and emotion-driven; System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytical, and effortful — most errors arise when System 1 gives an answer that System 2 fails to override.

layers.body: System 1 operates automatically and quickly with no sense of voluntary control — it handles routine perception, fast reactions, social intuition. System 2 allocates attention to effortful mental activities — logical reasoning, arithmetic, deliberate consideration of alternatives. System 1 drafts most of our thoughts; System 2 sometimes edits.

Cognitive biases arise when System 1 substitutes an easier question for the hard one (attribute substitution), uses a heuristic that fails in a particular case, or gives an answer System 2 lacks the capacity or motivation to override. The famous CRT (Cognitive Reflection Test) bat-and-ball problem (bat + ball = $1.10, bat costs $1 more than ball — most answer $0.10, not $0.05) measures System 2 override capacity. Dual-process theory underlies nudge design: target System 1 defaults.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] The organising framework for understanding when and why people deviate from rationality — grounds policy designs that make good choices easy (defaults) rather than requiring deliberation.
cards.counter: The System 1/2 distinction is a conceptual metaphor, not a neurological fact — there is no single 'System 1' region in the brain. Critics argue it oversimplifies cognition and that many 'System 1' processes are also responsive to incentives.

quiz.q: According to dual-process theory, when do cognitive biases typically arise?
choices: When System 2 is overactive and introduces too much deliberation
When System 1 produces a fast intuitive answer and System 2 fails to override it
When people switch between System 1 and System 2 mid-decision
When emotional states shut down System 1 entirely

cards.title: Heuristics and biases
cards.fact: Tversky and Kahneman's three heuristics: representativeness (judging probability by similarity), availability (judging frequency by ease of recall), and anchoring (adjusting insufficiently from a starting value).

layers.body: Heuristics are mental shortcuts that work well on average but systematically fail in predictable ways. Three main ones: (1) *Representativeness*: estimate probability by how similar something is to a prototype — leads to the base-rate neglect (the conjunction fallacy, the 'Linda problem'). (2) *Availability*: estimate frequency by how easily examples come to mind — plane crashes feel more likely after media coverage. (3) *Anchoring*: adjust from a starting value but not enough.

Linda is described as a feminist bank teller. When asked whether it is more probable that (a) Linda is a bank teller or (b) Linda is a bank teller and a feminist, most people choose (b). This violates probability theory — a conjunction cannot be more probable than either conjunct. The *representativeness heuristic* makes (b) seem more 'Linda-like,' overriding the probability calculation. This is the *conjunction fallacy*.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] Each heuristic has specific policy implications: availability bias means salience of risks drives insurance; anchoring explains why initial salary offers anchor negotiations.
cards.counter: Gigerenzer argues Tversky-Kahneman overstate the bias story — heuristics are often *ecologically rational*: they work well in the real environment even if they fail in artificial lab problems. The biases-and-heuristics literature may be measuring lab performance, not general cognition.

quiz.q: The conjunction fallacy (Linda problem) illustrates which heuristic?
choices: Availability — Linda comes to mind easily when thinking of feminists
Representativeness — people judge probability by how similar the description is to a prototype, ignoring the probability rule that conjunctions are less probable
Anchoring — initial description of Linda anchors the probability estimate
Overconfidence — people are too confident that Linda is a feminist

cards.title: Anchoring and adjustment
cards.fact: Anchoring: when making numerical estimates, people start from an initial value (anchor) and adjust — but typically adjust insufficiently, so the final estimate is biased toward the anchor even when the anchor is arbitrary.

layers.body: In Tversky and Kahneman's classic experiment, participants were asked: is the percentage of African countries in the UN more or less than [a randomly spun wheel showing 65 or 10]? Then: what is the actual percentage? Those anchored at 65 guessed ~45%; those at 10 guessed ~25%. The anchor was clearly arbitrary — a spinning wheel — but still distorted estimates substantially.

Anchoring is pervasive in negotiations (first offer sets the anchor), legal sentencing (asking juries to consider a longer sentence before deliberating raises actual sentences), real estate pricing (listing price anchors buyers' valuations), and salary negotiation. It is not just availability: anchoring occurs even when the anchor is obviously irrelevant. Counter-strategy: generate your own anchor before seeing the other side's offer.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] One of the most robust findings in psychology — applies to any quantitative estimate or negotiation. Legal, medical, and financial decision-making are all affected.
cards.counter: The robustness of anchoring depends on context: when people have strong prior knowledge (experts) or when stakes are very high, anchoring effects shrink. Ariely's work suggests market experience can reduce anchoring.

quiz.q: What makes the classic anchoring experiments so striking?
choices: The anchors were always accurate, proving that initial estimates are correct
Clearly irrelevant anchors (a random spinning wheel) still biased numerical estimates substantially
Experts were immune to anchoring while novices were not
Anchoring only occurred when participants were stressed or time-pressured

cards.title: Overconfidence and the planning fallacy
cards.fact: Overconfidence: people systematically overestimate the accuracy of their knowledge and the success probability of their plans; the planning fallacy is a specific form — projects take longer and cost more than forecast.

layers.body: Three forms of overconfidence: (1) *Overprecision* — 90% confidence intervals are too narrow (they actually contain the true value less than 90% of the time). (2) *Overplacement* — most people think they are above-average drivers (impossible). (3) *Overestimation* — forecasting your own performance above base rates.

The planning fallacy (Kahneman-Tversky 1979): people predict that their own projects will proceed as planned, discounting base rates of similar projects. Cure: use the *reference class forecasting* (outside view) — ask how long similar projects actually took, rather than constructing a plan from scratch (inside view). Used by Bent Flyvbjerg to explain cost overruns in infrastructure projects: the Sydney Opera House was budgeted at $7m, cost $102m.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] Planning fallacy explains systematic cost overruns in public projects, business plans, and personal schedules — reference class forecasting is the practical corrective.
cards.counter: Optimism bias is not always costly — it motivates start-ups and social movements that would not have been attempted if success probabilities were accurately assessed. Some overconfidence may be instrumentally rational.

quiz.q: What is 'reference class forecasting' and why does it correct the planning fallacy?
choices: Building forecasts from first principles using expert opinion rather than statistical data
Asking how long similar projects actually took historically, instead of constructing a plan from the project's specific details — which avoids inside-view optimism
Adjusting forecast intervals by a standard overconfidence correction factor
Using multiple independent forecasters and averaging their estimates

cards.title: Hyperbolic discounting and present bias
cards.fact: Hyperbolic discounting: people discount the near future much more steeply than the far future — creating time-inconsistency. You prefer €100 today over €110 tomorrow, but prefer €110 in 31 days over €100 in 30 days.

layers.body: Exponential discounting (standard economics): the discount factor between any two equally-spaced periods is constant. Hyperbolic discounting: the discount factor drops steeply from 'now' to 'soon' but gently between any two future periods. This creates *time inconsistency*: you plan to exercise tomorrow but when tomorrow arrives, you prefer to start next week.

A *naive* present-biased agent doesn't realise their preferences will change — they over-optimistically believe future-self will follow today's plan. A *sophisticated* agent knows they'll procrastinate and uses commitment devices (joining gyms with cancellation fees, automatic pension enrollment). Policy implications: default enrollment in pension plans exploits present bias — workers benefit from an automatic saving decision they could override but don't.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] Grounds the entire nudge/default architecture literature — explains why people undersave, underexercise, and overeat despite 'knowing better.'
cards.counter: Hyperbolic discounting may reflect rational preferences rather than a bias — if near-term future is genuinely more uncertain, higher near-term discounting is rational. Measuring present bias separately from risk aversion is methodologically hard.

quiz.q: What makes hyperbolic discounting 'time-inconsistent'?
choices: People apply the same discount rate to all future periods
Today's preferences over future trade-offs change when you arrive at the future date — what looks like a small sacrifice tomorrow looks much larger when tomorrow arrives
People cannot form consistent beliefs about future interest rates
Future preferences are inconsistent with current utility functions

cards.title: Nudge and choice architecture
cards.fact: Thaler and Sunstein's nudge: small, low-cost changes to the choice environment (defaults, framing, ordering) reliably shift behaviour without restricting options or changing incentives.

layers.body: Any environment in which people make choices has a *choice architecture* — the arrangement of options matters. A *nudge* exploits predictable cognitive biases (defaults, framing, social norms) to shift behaviour in a desired direction while preserving freedom of choice ('libertarian paternalism'). Defaults are the most powerful nudge: organ donation opt-in rates are ~15%; opt-out rates ~85%.

UK's Behavioural Insights Team ('Nudge Unit'), SAVE MORE TOMORROW (Thaler-Benartzi): automatic pension escalation doubled savings rates without requiring active decisions. Social norm nudges: 'your neighbours use less energy than you' reduces energy use by 2%. *Criticism*: nudges are paternalistic (even if libertarian); they may substitute for structural change; the effects are often small; and some nudges can be manipulated by corporations (junk food as the default cafeteria option).

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics / Government policy] The most policy-relevant behavioral economics output — governments worldwide use nudge units; UK, US, Australia, and Germany all have official behavioral insights teams.
cards.counter: Nudges work on System 1 — they are most effective when stakes are low. For consequential decisions (medical treatments, major financial choices), people deliberate more, reducing nudge effectiveness. Critics also argue nudges address symptoms without changing the environment that creates bad defaults.

quiz.q: Why is the opt-out default for organ donation more effective than opt-in?
choices: Opt-out is legally mandatory in most countries
Present bias and inertia mean people rarely actively change defaults — the default becomes the outcome for most people
Opt-out provides a financial incentive for organ donation
People prefer opt-out systems on normative grounds

cards.title: Mental accounting
cards.fact: Thaler's mental accounting: people mentally separate money into non-fungible accounts (entertainment, savings, food) and treat them differently — spending the 'entertainment' budget freely while feeling bad spending 'savings' on the same item.

layers.t: Money is not fungible in the mind
layers.body: Economic theory: $100 is $100, regardless of source. Behavioural reality: people are more willing to spend a 'bonus' than equivalent regular income; casino gamblers play riskier with 'house money' (winnings); people keep money in a low-interest savings account while carrying high-interest credit card debt — rational only if the accounts feel psychologically different.

The *sunk cost fallacy*: spending money or effort already lost influences future decisions — 'I already paid for the theatre ticket so I'll go even though I feel terrible.' Rational agents should ignore sunk costs (irreversible) and consider only marginal costs going forward. Mental accounting creates loss aversion around sunk investments: stopping feels like realising a loss. This explains project escalation and holding losing stocks too long.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics] Explains household finance anomalies (simultaneous saving and borrowing), corporate budgeting waste, and the sunk cost fallacy in project management.
cards.counter: Some mental accounting is rational: separate budgets create commitment devices (ring-fencing savings prevents it being spent on consumption). The same feature that looks like a 'bias' in a lab can be a self-control device in practice.

quiz.q: What is the 'sunk cost fallacy' and why does mental accounting reinforce it?
choices: Treating future costs as if they were already spent, leading to underinvestment
Continuing an activity because of past (irrecoverable) investment, even when the marginal returns are negative — mental accounting frames stopping as realising a loss
Overestimating the future cost of a project because of previous overruns
Allocating too many resources to profitable accounts and too few to losing ones

cards.title: Social preferences: fairness and reciprocity
cards.fact: Experimental economics shows people reject unfair offers, punish defectors at personal cost, and cooperate more than self-interest predicts — Fehr-Schmidt inequity aversion: people dislike being worse-off or better-off than others.

layers.body: The *ultimatum game*: a proposer splits $10 with a responder; the responder can accept or reject. Self-interested responders accept any positive offer (better than nothing). Actual responders reject offers below ~30%, even at personal cost — punishing unfairness. This 'costly punishment' cannot be explained by self-interest.

Fehr-Schmidt (1999): people have utility functions that include not just own payoff but the *difference* between their payoff and others'. They dislike being worse off (envy) but also dislike being better off (guilt). *Reciprocity*: people reward kind behaviour and punish unkind behaviour, even when there is no strategic future interaction. These preferences support cooperation in public goods games and help explain wage fairness norms and labour market puzzles.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Behavioral Economics / Sociology] Grounds the behavioral economics of labour markets, taxation fairness, and redistribution — 'fair wages' motivate effort independently of monitoring.
cards.counter: Laboratory ultimatum games use small stakes; in high-stakes field settings, people show more self-interested behaviour. Cross-cultural experiments (Henrich et al.) show wide variation in fairness norms — the WEIRD lab subjects (Western, Educated, Industrial, Rich, Democratic) are not representative.

quiz.q: The ultimatum game demonstrates that people have social preferences by showing…
choices: Proposers always offer 50/50 splits to avoid conflict
Responders reject offers below ~30% even at personal cost — punishing unfairness when self-interest would accept any positive sum
Both players cooperate to maximise the joint surplus
Offers decline toward zero as the game is repeated

cards.title: What is development economics?
cards.fact: Development economics analyses why some countries are rich and others poor, and what can be done about it — covering structural transformation, institutions, poverty, human capital, and the political economy of reform.

layers.body: Why do countries differ so vastly in income? Development economics addresses this through: growth theory (why does capital accumulate?), structural transformation (how do economies shift from agriculture to industry to services?), poverty analysis (who is poor and why?), and institutions (what rules and norms shape economic behaviour?). The field spans decades-long grand theory (Rostow, Prebisch) and micro-level field experiments (Banerjee, Duflo).

A structural tradition (Lewis dual economy, Prebisch-Singer, dependency theory) sees development as structural transformation requiring industrial policy and trade protection. A neoclassical tradition (World Bank structural adjustment, Washington Consensus) emphasises markets, openness, and price signals. The post-2000 'new development economics' is more empirical — measuring impact through RCTs and natural experiments rather than deriving policy from ideology.

cards.deploy: [MIT/Harvard Development Economics] The field sits at the intersection of macroeconomics, microeconomics, political science, and history — any poverty/inequality policy debate requires its tools.
cards.counter: There is no unified 'development theory' — debates over institutions vs geography vs culture vs policy are unresolved. Rodrik argues the best response is a toolkit of context-specific diagnostics rather than one-size-fits-all prescriptions.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the 'new development economics' (post-2000) from earlier grand theories?
choices: It focuses exclusively on institutional reform rather than economic growth
It uses empirical methods (RCTs, natural experiments) to measure what actually works, rather than deriving policy from macro-level growth theory
It prioritises market liberalisation over state-led development
It measures development through non-monetary indicators like happiness and freedom

cards.title: Institutions and development (Acemoglu-Robinson)
cards.fact: Acemoglu and Robinson's thesis: inclusive economic institutions (property rights, rule of law, open markets) and inclusive political institutions (constrained elites, broad participation) are the fundamental causes of prosperity — extractive institutions trap countries in poverty.

layers.body: *Inclusive economic institutions* allow all citizens to participate in markets, enforce contracts, protect property, and accumulate capital. *Extractive* institutions concentrate power and wealth — rulers appropriate rather than invest. The same dichotomy applies politically: *inclusive* political institutions constrain elites; *extractive* ones allow elites to dominate. The key claim: sustained growth requires *both* economic and political inclusivity.

Why do countries get bad institutions? Acemoglu-Robinson's colonial origins paper (2001) shows that settler mortality determined colonisation strategy: where Europeans could not settle (high malaria/yellow fever), they set up extractive institutions; where they settled, they built inclusive ones. This path-dependent institutional legacy persists and explains current income differences. Counterargument: North Korea and South Korea started from the same base — institutions diverged through political choices, not just colonial history.

cards.deploy: [MIT Development Economics / Harvard Government] The dominant 2000s framework for explaining cross-country income differences — underpins World Bank, IMF, and OECD governance reform programmes.
cards.counter: Geography (Sachs: disease burden, tropical climate) and culture (Weber: Protestant ethic) offer alternative explanations. Acemoglu-Robinson's causal identification has been challenged: institutions may be endogenous to income levels, and settler mortality may be a poor instrument in some contexts.

quiz.q: What does Acemoglu-Robinson argue is the fundamental cause of prosperity vs poverty?
choices: Geographic location and natural resources
Inclusive political and economic institutions — which protect property, enforce contracts, and constrain elites — vs extractive institutions that concentrate power
Human capital investment in education and health
Cultural values of hard work and saving

cards.title: Sen's capability approach
cards.fact: Amartya Sen's capability approach: development is the expansion of *freedoms* — people's real ability to do and be what they have reason to value. GDP per capita is an inadequate proxy; what matters is *capabilities* (substantive freedoms) and *functionings* (things people can do and be).

layers.body: Sen distinguishes: *functionings* (what a person actually does or is — being well-nourished, being educated, participating in community life) from *capabilities* (the real opportunities to achieve these functionings). A person who fasts has the same functioning as a person who starves, but different capabilities. Development should expand the set of real choices people have, not just raise income.

The Human Development Index (HDI, UNDP 1990, with Sen) operationalises the capability approach: income + life expectancy + education. But the capability approach is richer than HDI: it includes political freedoms, social opportunities, transparency guarantees, and protective security. Martha Nussbaum developed a specific list of ten central capabilities (life, health, bodily integrity, senses, emotions, practical reason, affiliation, other species, play, political control). Sen resisted a fixed list.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Development Economics] The philosophical foundation of the HDI and human development paradigm — a critique of purely growth-oriented development policy.
cards.counter: The capability approach is hard to operationalise: whose capabilities, and who decides which capabilities matter? The approach risks imposing Western liberal conceptions of the good life on non-Western communities.

quiz.q: In Sen's capability approach, what is the difference between a 'functioning' and a 'capability'?
choices: Functionings are economic outputs; capabilities are institutional inputs

A functioning is what a person actually does or is; a capability is the real freedom to achieve that functioning — a fasting person and a starving person have the same functioning but different capabilities
Capabilities are measured by income; functionings by health and education indicators
Functionings are basic needs; capabilities are advanced freedoms only relevant to wealthy societies

cards.title: Poverty traps and the big push
cards.fact: A poverty trap is a self-reinforcing mechanism where the poor cannot save or invest enough to escape poverty — Sachs argues a 'big push' of coordinated investment (foreign aid) can break the trap; critics say it ignores incentives.

layers.body: With a poverty trap, the production function has an S-shape: below a threshold level of capital, returns to investment are too low to outpace depreciation — the economy stagnates. Above the threshold, growth is self-sustaining. Poor households cannot save enough to cross the threshold, so they stay poor. The state or external aid must inject enough capital to jump over.

Jeffrey Sachs (*The End of Poverty*, 2005) argued the poorest countries are in a poverty trap requiring a large coordinated aid push — $100bn/year — to escape. William Easterly (*The White Man's Burden*, 2006) argued aid without incentive reform perpetuates dependence and corrupt institutions. The RCT evidence (Banerjee-Duflo) finds that micro-level poverty traps are rare — most poor households are responsive to small incentives without a structural trap, though some asset-level traps do exist.

cards.deploy: [MIT/Harvard Development Economics] Central to the foreign aid debate — whether poor countries need a big external push or better domestic incentives is still contested.
cards.counter: Empirical evidence for macro poverty traps is weak — most poor countries' economies move, sometimes rapidly (East Asia, China, Bangladesh). Traps may exist at the micro level (health-poverty interactions) without preventing macro growth.

quiz.q: What is the central disagreement between Sachs and Easterly on the poverty trap?
choices: Sachs thinks geography determines poverty; Easterly thinks culture does
Sachs argues poor countries are in a structural trap requiring a big aid push; Easterly argues aid without incentive reform perpetuates dependence
Sachs favours microfinance; Easterly favours foreign direct investment
Sachs wants recipient-led aid; Easterly wants donor-led conditionality

cards.title: Randomised controlled trials in development
cards.fact: Banerjee and Duflo's J-PAL pioneered RCTs in development economics: randomly assign aid programmes to some villages or individuals and not others — this identifies causal effects and tests what actually works.

layers.body: Before RCTs, development policy was guided by macro theory (Washington Consensus) or country case studies. The problem: selection bias — countries that received aid tended to be different from those that didn't. Randomised assignment removes this: if villages are randomly assigned to receive a new programme, any outcome difference is caused by the programme.

RCTs changed development policy: conditional cash transfers work better than in-kind aid; deworming in Kenya dramatically increased school attendance at low cost; free bed nets increase malaria prevention; teacher incentive pay alone doesn't improve learning. But critiques: external validity (does what works in Kenya work in Bangladesh?); scale (lab conditions vs. government programs); and ethical concerns about withholding treatment from control groups.

cards.deploy: [MIT Development Economics] The Nobel-winning methodological shift in development research — now the gold standard for programme evaluation in health, education, and poverty reduction.
cards.counter: RCTs identify average treatment effects in specific contexts; they cannot tell you whether a policy will work at national scale or in a different country. Development is a complex adaptive system — interventions that work in trials may be undermined by political economy or institutional constraints at scale.

quiz.q: What is the primary advantage of RCTs over observational studies in development economics?
choices: They are faster and cheaper to conduct than large-scale surveys
Random assignment eliminates selection bias — differences between treatment and control groups are caused by the programme, not by pre-existing differences
They allow researchers to test many interventions simultaneously
They capture long-run dynamic effects that cross-country regressions miss

cards.title: Colonial legacy and comparative development
cards.fact: Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson (2001): where European colonisers settled (low disease mortality), they built inclusive institutions that persist; where they couldn't settle, they built extractive institutions — settler mortality centuries ago predicts current GDP.

layers.body: The AJR (2001) paper uses *settler mortality* (historical data on European soldiers' death rates from malaria and yellow fever) as an instrument for institutional quality: low mortality → dense settlement → inclusive property rights and rule of law → higher current income. High mortality → extractive institutions (plantation economies, mining enclaves) → lower current income. The IV strategy attempts to separate institutions from geography and culture.

The 'reversal of fortune' (AJR 2002): among ex-colonies, the richest in 1500 (Aztec/Mughal civilisations) are now the poorest — colonisers imposed extractive institutions precisely where the indigenous population was densest (more labour to exploit). Countries with sparse indigenous populations (North America, Australia) got settlement-type institutions. This reversal cannot be explained by geography (tropics are poor) because the geography didn't change.

cards.deploy: [MIT Development Economics / Harvard Government] The empirical foundation for the 'institutions hypothesis' — colonialism's institutional legacy explains much of today's income inequality across countries.
cards.counter: The settler mortality instrument has been contested: historical disease records may be endogenous to institutional quality; the mechanism requires many assumptions. Putterman and Weil show that settler populations' own origins matter — the AJR effect may partly reflect human capital migrants brought.

quiz.q: Why did Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson use 'settler mortality' as an instrument for institutions?
choices: Settler mortality directly measures colonial violence, which destroyed existing institutions

High settler mortality meant Europeans couldn't settle and set up extractive institutions; low mortality led to settlement and inclusive institutions — mortality predates and is unaffected by current economic outcomes
Settler mortality proxies for geographic factors like climate and disease burden that directly affect productivity
Colonial-era settlement patterns are correlated with current educational attainment

cards.title: Dutch disease and the resource curse
cards.fact: Dutch disease: a natural resource boom raises the exchange rate, making other export sectors uncompetitive — countries with large natural resource endowments often have slower industrial development and worse institutions than comparable resource-poor countries.

layers.body: When the Netherlands discovered North Sea gas in the 1960s, energy exports raised the guilder's value — making Dutch manufacturing uncompetitive ('Dutch disease'). The mechanism: resource export revenues raise demand for non-tradables (services, construction), bidding up wages and the real exchange rate, which crowds out manufacturing exports.

Empirically, resource-rich countries have grown more slowly than resource-poor ones (Sachs-Warner 1995). Beyond the exchange rate: resource rents reduce the need for taxation, weakening state-society bargains that historically build accountable government ('no taxation without representation'). Rents also create predatory incentives: elites fight over control rather than building productive capacity. Norway escaped the curse through the Petroleum Fund (sovereign wealth), transparent governance, and pre-existing strong institutions.

cards.deploy: [MIT/Harvard Development Economics] The resource curse explains why oil and mineral wealth correlates with poor governance and low diversification — institutional design (sovereign wealth funds, revenue transparency) is the counter.
cards.counter: The 'curse' is not inevitable: Botswana (diamonds), Norway (oil), and Malaysia (oil) all grew strongly. The key variable is institutional quality at the time of resource discovery, not the resource itself.

quiz.q: What is the exchange-rate mechanism in Dutch disease?
choices: Resource exports are priced in foreign currency, reducing domestic money supply
Resource export revenues raise demand and bid up wages and the real exchange rate, making non-resource exports uncompetitive
Resource wealth reduces investment in human capital, lowering productivity in other sectors
Multinational resource companies repatriate profits, creating a capital account deficit

cards.title: Structural transformation
cards.fact: Lewis's dual economy model: development is the transfer of surplus labour from low-productivity subsistence agriculture to high-productivity modern industry — the 'Lewis turning point' is when the surplus is exhausted and wages begin to rise.

layers.t: The shift from farm to factory
layers.body: W. Arthur Lewis (1954): developing economies have two sectors — a traditional agricultural sector with surplus labour (marginal product near zero) and a modern industrial sector with higher productivity. Industrial wages are just above subsistence. As the industrial sector expands, it draws in surplus workers — keeping wages low and profits high, which fund further investment. Growth continues until the surplus labour is exhausted.

layers.t: The Lewis turning point and East Asia
layers.body: The *Lewis turning point* is when surplus agricultural labour runs out — wages begin to rise and profit-led growth slows. China reached its turning point around 2010–15: factory wages began rising faster than urban productivity. East Asian growth was the canonical realisation of the Lewis model — Japan in the 1950s–60s, South Korea 1960s–80s, China 1980s–2010s. The policy implication: support manufacturing, maintain a competitive exchange rate, invest in education and infrastructure.

cards.deploy: [MIT Development Economics / LSE] The classic framework for understanding East Asian growth and for assessing whether late-industrialisation is still possible for today's poor countries.
cards.counter: The Lewis model assumes tradeable manufacturing can absorb unlimited labour — but premature deindustrialisation (Rodrik) means many poor countries are losing manufacturing before the Lewis turning point, moving from agriculture into low-productivity services instead.

quiz.q: What is the 'Lewis turning point' in development?
choices: When a country transitions from agricultural exports to industrial exports
When surplus agricultural labour is exhausted — wages begin to rise because industry must now bid workers away from productive farming
When GDP per capita crosses the middle-income threshold
When foreign direct investment exceeds domestic savings

cards.title: The security dilemma
cards.fact: The security dilemma: when one state builds up arms for defensive purposes, it appears threatening to others — who then arm in response — leaving everyone less secure despite no one intending aggression.

layers.body: State A, fearing attack, builds more ships. State B, uncertain of A's intentions, interprets this as preparation for aggression — and builds more ships itself. State A now feels less safe and builds still more. Neither intended war, but both end up in an arms race. The security dilemma is the structural cause of conflict in an anarchic world: under uncertainty, defensive arming cannot be distinguished from offensive arming.

Jervis (1978): the security dilemma is less intense when: (a) offence is distinguishable from defence (troops in deep rear positions vs. border deployments); (b) defence is favoured over offence (trenches in WWI made defence dominant — but all sides misread this). When offence and defence look the same, intentions are unreadable and spirals are more likely. Confidence-building measures (transparency, arms control, hotlines) attempt to reduce the security dilemma directly.

cards.deploy: [Oxford IR] Explains arms races, unintended escalation, and the challenge of signalling defensive intent — used in analysis of China-US naval competition, Russia-NATO, and Israeli-Iranian nuclear dynamics.
cards.counter: Not all arms buildups are misinterpreted — some states genuinely plan aggression. Distinguishing malign from defensive intent is the core intelligence challenge. The dilemma logic can be used to excuse aggression by portraying all buildups as defensive.

quiz.q: What structural feature of the international system creates the security dilemma?
choices: The offensive nature of modern weaponry, which makes defence impossible
Anarchy: without a world government to verify intentions, defensive military buildup looks identical to offensive preparation, triggering reactions
The tendency of leaders to misperceive threats due to cognitive biases
The imbalance of power between states

cards.title: Neoliberal institutionalism
cards.fact: Keohane's neoliberal institutionalism: international institutions help states overcome collective action problems by providing information, monitoring, and reducing transaction costs — even without a hegemon.

layers.body: Keohane: states can cooperate even under anarchy if *institutions* reduce the barriers. The problem is not that states don't want to cooperate but that they fear defection (prisoner's dilemma, collective action, monitoring costs). Institutions — WTO, IMF, IAEA — lower these costs by: monitoring compliance, establishing expectations, facilitating repeated interaction, and providing information.

Keohane (1984) asked: can cooperation persist even when the US hegemon declines? His answer: yes, because institutions persist and create their own constituencies. This debates hegemonic stability theory (cooperation requires a hegemon). The WTO, GATT, and Bretton Woods institutions were built when the US was dominant but continue to shape trade policy decades later, long past peak US hegemony.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Kennedy School / Oxford IR] The analytical foundation for studying international organisations, multilateral cooperation, and global governance — why states build and maintain international institutions.
cards.counter: Mearsheimer's critique: institutions are epiphenomenal — states follow them when it's in their interest and abandon them when it isn't. Great powers use institutions as instruments rather than following them as constraints.

quiz.q: How does neoliberal institutionalism differ from neorealism in explaining cooperation?
choices: Neoliberalism says cooperation requires hegemony; neorealism says it doesn't
Neoliberalism argues institutions reduce transaction costs and monitoring problems, enabling cooperation even under anarchy and without a hegemon
Neorealism explains economic cooperation; neoliberalism explains security cooperation
Neoliberalism requires states to have shared values; neorealism only requires shared interests

cards.title: Median voter theorem
cards.fact: The median voter theorem: in a two-party majoritarian system with single-peaked preferences, both parties converge on the position of the median voter — whoever captures the median wins.

layers.body: Hotelling (1929) showed that in a competitive market with two sellers, both locate at the centre. Downs (1957) applied this to politics: in a two-party system with a one-dimensional policy space and majority rule, parties converge on the median voter's preference. Moving left or right loses more votes than it gains.

The theorem requires: one-dimensional policy space, single-peaked preferences, all voters vote, and two parties. Violations: multi-dimensional issues (trade-off between economic and social positions), primary elections (parties must first win their base before the general election — pulling parties from the centre), third parties, abstention, and expressive voting. Empirically, parties do not fully converge: polarisation is a stylised fact of 21st-century democracies — contradicting the simple theorem.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] Explains centrist tendencies in two-party systems and why primary elections push parties toward their base — a central tool of electoral analysis.
cards.counter: Polarisation is the empirical puzzle the median voter theorem cannot explain. Explanations: ideological sorting, primary elections, media fragmentation (Fox News), party activists, and geographic clustering of voters by ideology.

quiz.q: Under what conditions does the median voter theorem predict party convergence?
choices: Proportional representation with many parties competing
Two parties, single-peaked voter preferences on one dimension, and majority rule — so the median voter is decisive
High voter turnout and low party polarisation
Open primaries that allow independents to participate

cards.title: Rent-seeking
cards.fact: Rent-seeking: spending resources to obtain existing transfers (monopoly privileges, subsidies, tariffs) rather than creating new value — the social cost includes not just the deadweight loss of the policy but also the resources spent lobbying for it.

layers.body: Economic rent is income above opportunity cost — a monopolist earns rents. Rent-seeking is the activity of obtaining rents through political means rather than productive activity. Krueger (1974): import licences in developing countries created rents; competitors spent resources competing for them — these resources (lawyers, lobbyists, bribes) were socially wasted.

Standard analysis: a monopoly creates a deadweight loss triangle (lost consumer surplus and producer surplus). Rent-seeking adds to this: the monopoly's profit rectangle (transfers from consumers) is the prize being competed for. If competition to obtain the monopoly is fully dissipative, resources worth the entire monopoly rent are wasted — the 'rectangle' disappears into lobbying costs, not profit. Total social cost of monopoly = triangle + rectangle.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Chicago PE] Explains why trade protection, agricultural subsidies, and occupational licences persist even when they are welfare-reducing — political economy of the status quo.
cards.counter: Not all rent-seeking dissipates the full rectangle — competition for rents is often imperfect and political connections, not resource expenditure, determine outcomes. The full dissipation result (Tullock) requires implausible assumptions about competitive lobbying.

quiz.q: Why does Tullock argue the social cost of monopoly is larger than the standard deadweight loss triangle?
choices: Monopolists spend on innovation that is socially wasteful
Resources are spent competing for the monopoly rent (lobbying, legal fees) — in the extreme case the entire profit rectangle is dissipated in rent-seeking activity
Monopoly creates negative externalities that are not captured in the demand curve
Monopoly power compounds over time, raising the cost in future periods

cards.title: Public choice theory
cards.fact: Buchanan and Tullock's public choice theory: politicians and bureaucrats pursue self-interest (votes, budgets, power) just like private actors — applying economic analysis to political actors reveals systematic failures of democratic governance.

layers.body: Public choice takes the homo economicus assumption seriously about government. Voters are rationally ignorant (the probability of casting the decisive vote is near zero, so it pays little to be informed). Politicians maximise votes (electoral cycle distortions). Bureaucrats maximise budgets. Interest groups concentrate benefits and disperse costs — enabling them to organise and capture regulation while the diffuse public cannot.

Stigler's *Theory of Economic Regulation* (1971): regulation is typically acquired by the regulated industry and shaped to serve its interests. Regulatory agencies gradually come to be dominated by those they regulate — the 'revolving door.' This predicts that regulation produces concentrated benefits for industry and diffuse costs for consumers. Public choice: the market failure that regulation is meant to correct may be less damaging than the government failure of regulatory capture.

cards.deploy: [Chicago Political Economy] The foundation of the 'government failure' critique — used to argue against naive market correction policies and to design better institutions (independent central banks, constitutional rules).
cards.counter: Public choice theory assumes politicians and bureaucrats are purely self-interested; evidence shows many are motivated by ideology, duty, or policy goals. The theory also struggles to explain the welfare state and Bismarckian social insurance, which redistributed without obvious interest group pressure.

quiz.q: What is 'rational ignorance' in public choice theory?
choices: Politicians are rationally ignorant of economics and therefore make bad policy
Voters have little incentive to be informed about politics because the probability of their vote being decisive is near zero — the expected benefit is below the information cost
Bureaucrats ignore rational policy advice because they maximise budgets
Voters rationally ignore politicians' stated positions because they know they will not be followed

cards.title: Political business cycle
cards.fact: Nordhaus's political business cycle: governments expand the economy before elections (reducing unemployment) and tighten after (controlling inflation) — creating a predictable electoral stimulus cycle driven by political incentives, not economic need.

layers.body: Nordhaus (1975): governments stimulate the economy pre-election (expanding fiscal policy, pushing the central bank to ease) to minimise unemployment and maximise popularity. Post-election, they tighten to control the inflation that results. This generates a predictable electoral cycle in output and inflation — not an economic cycle, but a politically induced one.

Hibbs (1977) adds a partisan dimension: left governments tolerate more inflation to keep unemployment low (their core voters are workers); right governments accept higher unemployment to control inflation (their core voters are creditors). So the cycle is not just electoral but ideological. Empirical evidence for both types of cycles is mixed in developed economies — central bank independence was partly designed to break the political business cycle by removing monetary policy from electoral politics.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] Explains why central bank independence is an institutional solution to a political economy problem, not just a technocratic one.
cards.counter: Rational expectations theory (Lucas): if voters and markets anticipate the cycle, they will price in the pre-election stimulus and it won't have real effects. Central bank independence has reduced the PBC in many countries — the institutional fix worked.

quiz.q: What is the main argument for central bank independence from a political economy perspective?
choices: Central banks have superior macroeconomic expertise compared to elected governments
Independent central banks cannot be pressured to create pre-election stimulus — removing the political business cycle distortion from monetary policy
Central bank independence ensures compliance with international monetary commitments
Independent central banks avoid the 'too big to fail' problem in banking regulation

cards.title: Varieties of capitalism
cards.fact: Hall and Soskice's VoC: liberal market economies (US, UK) coordinate through competitive markets; coordinated market economies (Germany, Japan) coordinate through non-market institutions (unions, industry associations). Each type has comparative institutional advantages.

layers.body: Liberal market economies (LMEs: US, UK) have flexible labour markets, short-term capital (stock markets), general education, and competitive inter-firm relations — suited to radical innovation. Coordinated market economies (CMEs: Germany, Sweden, Japan) have employment protection, patient capital (bank-based finance), vocational training, and industry coordination — suited to incremental innovation. Each type is internally coherent and competitively viable.

The key claim: CME institutions that look 'inefficient' by LME standards (employment protection, union co-determination) are actually complementary — they enable long-term investment in firm-specific skills and incremental innovation. German engineering and Japanese manufacturing required these apparently rigid institutions. Policy implication: there is no single 'best practice' institutional model — LME-style deregulation imposed on CMEs destroys their institutional advantages.

cards.deploy: [Oxford Political Economy / Sciences Po] The analytical foundation for comparative capitalism research — counters the Washington Consensus's one-size-fits-all liberalisation agenda.
cards.counter: VoC has been criticised for being static: it doesn't explain institutional change (how Sweden moved from high to lower employment protection after the 1990s crisis). Also, Mediterranean/mixed economies don't fit cleanly into either type.

quiz.q: What is 'comparative institutional advantage' in the varieties of capitalism framework?
choices: Countries with better institutions grow faster than those with weaker ones
Different types of market economies have distinct institutional configurations suited to different sectors — CME rigidities that look inefficient by LME standards enable incremental innovation
Coordinated market economies outperform liberal ones in international trade
Institutional advantage reflects a country's colonial heritage and legal origin

cards.title: The Washington Consensus
cards.fact: Williamson's 1989 ten-point programme: fiscal discipline, tax reform, trade liberalisation, deregulation, privatisation, and property rights — presented as the consensus among Washington institutions (IMF, World Bank, US Treasury) on what developing countries need.

layers.body: John Williamson (1989) coined 'Washington Consensus' to describe common advice to Latin American reformers: (1) fiscal discipline; (2) reorienting public spending; (3) tax reform; (4) interest rate liberalisation; (5) competitive exchange rate; (6) trade liberalisation; (7) FDI liberalisation; (8) privatisation; (9) deregulation; (10) property rights. This became the template for IMF structural adjustment programmes globally.

The Consensus had partial successes (Latin America's macroeconomic stabilisation) and major failures (Russia's 'shock therapy,' the 1997 Asian crisis, Argentina 2001). Stiglitz (*Globalisation and its Discontents*, 2002) argued sequencing matters — capital account liberalisation before strong institutions caused crises. Rodrik's critique: the Consensus ignored institutions, political economy, and the need for industrial policy. Post-consensus development economics is more heterodox and context-specific.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Development / Sciences Po] The canonical example of how ideology dressed as technocracy shapes development policy — understanding it is essential for analysing IMF conditionality, structural adjustment, and globalisation debates.
cards.counter: Williamson later clarified that 'Washington Consensus' was misused — his original formulation was narrower than the sweeping neoliberal agenda it came to represent. The label conflated sensible macroeconomic stabilisation with controversial market fundamentalism.

quiz.q: What was Stiglitz's main critique of the Washington Consensus?
choices: It focused too much on fiscal discipline and not enough on monetary policy
It ignored sequencing and institutional preconditions — capital account liberalisation before strong banks and regulatory capacity caused financial crises rather than growth
It was too cautious about privatisation and market liberalisation
It overestimated the role of foreign direct investment in development

cards.title: Gramscian hegemony
cards.fact: Gramsci's hegemony: ruling class dominance is maintained not only through coercion but through cultural and ideological consent — the dominant class shapes what appears 'natural' and 'commonsense,' making alternatives seem unrealistic.

layers.body: Antonio Gramsci (Prison Notebooks, 1929–35): dominant classes don't only rule by force (coercion, state apparatus). They exercise *hegemony* — cultural leadership that makes their worldview appear natural and universal. The dominated classes *consent* to their own domination because they have internalised the ruling class's values, norms, and common sense.

Because hegemony is cultural and ideational, it can be challenged culturally. The *organic intellectual* emerges from the subordinate class and articulates its interests in ways that challenge hegemonic common sense. Gramsci's *war of position* (long cultural-ideological struggle) vs *war of manoeuvre* (frontal assault). Applied to contemporary politics: neoliberalism as hegemony (TINA — 'There Is No Alternative' — makes market ideology appear as natural fact); populism as counter-hegemony.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / Oxford Political Economy] The framework for analysing ideological power, media, and cultural politics — used in international relations (Cox), media studies, and social movements.
cards.counter: Gramsci's framework is analytically rich but empirically hard to operationalise — it is difficult to distinguish genuine consent from strategic deference or simple ignorance. The concept can become unfalsifiable.

quiz.q: How does Gramsci distinguish 'hegemony' from simple coercion?
choices: Hegemony is enforced by international institutions rather than national states
Hegemony is maintained through cultural and ideological consent — the dominated classes internalise the dominant worldview and accept subordination voluntarily, not just under threat
Hegemony describes the military dominance of one state over others
Hegemony operates through market mechanisms rather than political institutions

cards.title: Collective action problem (Olson)
cards.fact: Olson's *The Logic of Collective Action*: large groups fail to provide themselves with collective goods because each member prefers to free-ride — small groups with selective incentives are more effective, explaining why producer lobbies defeat consumers in policy fights.

layers.body: Mancur Olson (1965): a large group with a common interest (consumers wanting low prices, citizens wanting clean air) will not act to achieve that interest unless some members are coerced or unless special incentives are provided. Each member can benefit from the group good without contributing — free-riding. The group's optimal provision requires costly individual action, but each individual's contribution is tiny and the benefit is shared regardless.

Why do producer lobbies (e.g. steel manufacturers: 10 firms, high per-firm stakes, concentrated benefits) dominate consumer interests (millions of consumers, diffuse low per-person costs)? Small groups with concentrated interests can: monitor free-riding, provide selective incentives for participation, and coordinate more easily. Olson explains the political economy of trade protection, agricultural subsidies, and occupational licences — all concentrated benefits, diffuse costs.

cards.deploy: [Harvard Government / Sciences Po] The fundamental model of interest group politics — explains the systematic bias of political systems toward producer interests over consumer interests.
cards.counter: Ostrom showed that large groups can and do solve collective action problems through institutions, norms, and graduated sanctions — without coercion or privatisation. The pessimism of Olson's model is overstated for groups with repeated interaction.

quiz.q: Why do small producer lobbies often defeat large consumer groups in policy fights, according to Olson?
choices: Producers have more money to spend on lobbying
Small groups with concentrated per-member stakes can coordinate and monitor free-riding; large groups with diffuse interests cannot — collective goods logic favours the small concentrated group
Democratic systems are structurally biased toward business over labour
Consumers rationally prefer low-information politics, ceding the field to producers

cards.title: Social democracy and welfare state regimes
cards.fact: Esping-Andersen's three worlds of welfare capitalism: liberal (US/UK: means-tested, market-dependent), conservative-corporatist (Germany/France: status-preserving, employment-based), and social-democratic (Scandinavia: universal, decommodifying).

layers.body: Esping-Andersen (1990) classifies welfare states by *decommodification* (to what extent social rights free citizens from dependence on the market) and *stratification* (whether benefits reinforce or equalise class differences). Liberal: residual welfare, maximum market exposure. Corporatist: Bismarckian insurance tied to employment status. Social-democratic: universal benefits, high decommodification, status equality.

Each regime type is politically self-reinforcing. Liberal welfare states create middle-class dependence on private insurance (US health insurance), which builds a constituency against public provision. Social-democratic regimes build universal programmes that generate broad cross-class coalitions supporting them. Path dependence explains why Beveridge-style universalism (UK) and Bismarckian insurance (Germany) diverged despite similar industrialisation, and why the welfare state does not converge under globalisation.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / Oxford Politics] The foundational comparative welfare state framework — used in every debate about NHS reform, pension systems, and post-austerity reconstruction.
cards.counter: Esping-Andersen's typology is white, Western, male, and Northern: it poorly fits the East Asian developmental states, Mediterranean 'family-based' welfare, and post-colonial welfare systems. Gender critics (Lewis) note it ignores care work.

quiz.q: What does Esping-Andersen mean by 'decommodification'?
choices: The removal of goods from market pricing, as in public ownership
The extent to which social rights allow citizens to maintain a livelihood without dependence on market wages — how much the welfare state frees people from commodity status
The reduction of economic inequality through redistribution
The replacement of private insurance by state provision in healthcare and pensions

cards.title: What is sociology?
cards.fact: Sociology is the scientific study of society — how social structure, institutions, norms, and relationships shape human behaviour. It asks: what holds society together? What generates inequality? How does change happen?

layers.body: The three founding questions: Durkheim's solidarity (what holds society together?), Marx's conflict (who benefits from social arrangements?), and Weber's rationalisation (how does modernity transform meaning and authority?). Each maps onto a distinct methodology: Durkheim's positivism (social facts as things), Marx's historical materialism, Weber's interpretive sociology (verstehen).

A central tension in sociology: does social structure determine behaviour (structuralism: Marx, Durkheim, Parsons), or do individuals create social reality through meaningful action (agency: Weber, symbolic interactionism, ethnomethodology)? Giddens's *structuration theory* attempts synthesis: structure both constrains and is reproduced through individual action.

cards.deploy: [LSE Sociology] The entry point for any sociological analysis — specifying whether you are explaining social structure or individual action determines your method and theory.
cards.counter: Sociology's explanatory scope is contested: rational choice sociologists (Coleman) argue that macro-level social facts can always be explained by individual-level rational action; structuralists argue individuals are the product of social forces that cannot be reduced to psychology.

quiz.q: What is the 'structure vs agency' debate in sociology?
choices: Whether social policy should focus on structural poverty or individual behaviour
Whether social outcomes are primarily determined by structural forces (class, institutions, norms) or by individuals' meaningful choices and interpretations
Whether quantitative or qualitative methods are better for sociological research
Whether sociology should be value-free or politically engaged

cards.title: Durkheim's social facts
cards.fact: Durkheim's 'social facts' are ways of acting, thinking, and feeling that are external to the individual and exercise coercive power over them — social facts cannot be reduced to individual psychology; they are the proper subject of sociology.

layers.body: Durkheim argued sociology requires its own subject matter: *social facts* — social phenomena that exist independently of any individual's will or consciousness. Language, law, suicide rates, religious norms: these have an existence external to me and constrain my behaviour. They cannot be explained by psychology — they require a social explanation.

Durkheim's *Suicide* (1897) demonstrated the social-fact method: suicide rates vary systematically across social groups (Protestants vs Catholics, married vs unmarried, peacetime vs wartime) — proof that what seems most individual is socially shaped. His causal variable: *social integration* (how tightly the individual is bound to a social group) and *moral regulation* (the norms constraining individual desires). Altruistic suicide (over-integration), egoistic (under-integration), anomic (under-regulation), fatalistic (over-regulation).

cards.deploy: [LSE / Sciences Po Sociology] The methodological foundation for treating social phenomena as having their own causal logic — independent of psychology.
cards.counter: The reduction of individual action to social causation is methodologically challenged: micro-level studies show that even suicide has complex individual-biographical components that aggregate statistics erase. Boudon's 'methodological individualism' argues all social facts must ultimately be explained through individual action.

quiz.q: What does Durkheim's study of suicide demonstrate about social facts?
choices: That suicide is caused by psychological disorders that are socially transmitted
That even the most individual act varies systematically with social conditions — social integration and moral regulation shape suicide rates, making it a social fact
That Protestants have higher individualism than Catholics due to religious doctrine
That suicide rates are determined by economic conditions rather than social integration

cards.title: Mechanical and organic solidarity
cards.fact: Durkheim: pre-modern societies have mechanical solidarity (similarity — everyone shares the same beliefs and roles); modern societies have organic solidarity (difference — specialised interdependence binds people who are unlike each other).

layers.body: *Mechanical solidarity* (traditional societies): cohesion through sameness — strong collective consciousness, low individuality, harsh punishment for deviation. *Organic solidarity* (modern industrial societies): cohesion through interdependence of differentiated roles — like organs of a body each performing a different function. High individuality, weak collective consciousness, restitutive rather than punitive law.

layers.t: Anomie as the risk of modern solidarity
layers.body: The transition from mechanical to organic solidarity is dangerous: when specialisation outpaces the moral norms that should regulate interdependence, *anomie* results — normlessness, where individual desires are insufficiently constrained by social rules. Modern economic growth can generate anomic conditions: rising aspirations without the moral framework to satisfy them → social pathology, mental illness, suicide. Durkheim was not a conservative — he supported occupational corporations as modern institutions for organic solidarity.

cards.deploy: [LSE Sociology] Explains why social disruption (rapid modernisation, migration, economic upheaval) generates pathology — and why institutions matter for binding individuals to social norms.
cards.counter: Organic solidarity assumes functional interdependence is inherently cohesive. But specialised industrial societies can also produce intense class conflict — Durkheim's framework downplays conflict and power, which Marx placed at the centre.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between mechanical and organic solidarity?
choices: Mechanical solidarity is rational; organic solidarity is traditional
Mechanical solidarity binds through social sameness and shared beliefs; organic solidarity binds through interdependence of specialised and differentiated roles
Mechanical solidarity is characteristic of urban societies; organic of rural ones
Mechanical solidarity relies on the state; organic solidarity on civil society

cards.title: Anomie and strain theory
cards.fact: Anomie (Durkheim): normlessness caused by rapid social change that outpaces moral regulation. Merton's strain theory: anomie results from the gap between culturally approved goals (wealth) and structurally available means — producing deviance when legitimate means are blocked.

layers.body: Merton (1938) adapted Durkheim's concept: in America, all are told to pursue success (the cultural goal), but the legitimate means (education, hard work) are unequally distributed. Those blocked from legitimate means experience 'strain' and adapt in several ways: *innovation* (pursue goal by illegitimate means — crime), *ritualism* (abandon goal but keep the rules), *retreatism* (abandon both — vagrancy, addiction), *rebellion* (challenge both — revolution).

Strain theory suggests crime is not a product of individual pathology but of structural inequality — if legitimate paths to success are blocked, some proportion will find illegitimate ones. Policy implication: reducing crime requires expanding access to legitimate opportunities (education, jobs), not just punishment. Cloward and Ohlin extended Merton: access to *illegitimate* opportunity structures also varies — the type of deviance depends on the available subculture (organised crime vs gang violence vs drug culture).

cards.deploy: [LSE / Chicago Sociology] The sociological explanation for crime as a structural phenomenon — grounds social policy arguments for opportunity expansion over punishment.
cards.counter: Strain theory struggles to explain white-collar crime (Sutherland) — highly successful people who have legitimate means still commit fraud and embezzlement. Opportunity isn't the only driver.

quiz.q: In Merton's strain theory, what causes innovation (crime) as an adaptive response?
choices: Lack of internalisation of social norms during childhood socialisation
A gap between culturally approved goals (success, wealth) and the legitimate means available — those with blocked access to legitimate paths may pursue goals through illegitimate ones
Social disorganisation in urban areas where monitoring is low
Subcultures that positively value deviant behaviour and provide status for it

cards.title: Weber: verstehen and ideal types
cards.fact: Weber's sociology is interpretive (Verstehende Soziologie): the sociologist must understand the subjective meaning actors attach to their actions — using 'ideal types' (theoretical constructs that capture core features of social phenomena) as analytical tools.

layers.body: Weber: social science is different from natural science because the subject matter is meaningful action. The sociologist must *understand* (verstehen) the meaning actors give to their behaviour — why they do what they do from their own perspective. This does not mean being sympathetic; it means reconstructing the actor's meaningful orientation.

Weber's method: *ideal types* are analytical constructs that capture the logical essence of a social phenomenon, not empirical averages or normative ideals. 'Bureaucracy,' 'capitalism,' 'charismatic authority' are ideal types — they do not describe any actual case perfectly, but they provide yardsticks against which reality can be measured. No actual bureaucracy has all the features of Weber's ideal type; but the construct allows you to ask: in what ways and to what degree does this organisation approximate a bureaucracy?

cards.deploy: [Oxford / LSE Sociology] Weber's methodological contribution — used in comparative historical sociology (state formation, capitalism, religion) and organisation theory.
cards.counter: The verstehen method is criticised for making sociology dependent on the sociologist's interpretive imagination — it is difficult to verify whether you have correctly understood actors' meanings. Survey-based sociology and ethnography represent alternatives.

quiz.q: What is a 'Weberian ideal type'?
choices: The normatively ideal form of a social institution — what it should look like
An analytical construct capturing the logical essence of a social phenomenon, used as a yardstick to compare empirical cases — not a description of any actual case
A statistical average of the characteristics of a social type
A case study of the typical member of a social class

cards.title: Weber: rationalisation and the iron cage
cards.fact: Weber's thesis on rationalisation: modernity increasingly substitutes rule-based calculation for tradition and emotion — producing bureaucracy, capitalism, and ultimately an 'iron cage' in which technical rationality becomes an end in itself, draining life of meaning.

layers.body: Weber identified a master process in modernity: *rationalisation* — the replacement of traditional, emotional, and mystical orientations by calculation, predictability, and formal rules. It produces: capitalism (systematic profit calculation), science (systematic empirical method), bureaucracy (rule-governed administration), and formal law (positive, systematised legal codes).

The Protestant Ethic (Weber, 1904): Calvinist predestination created anxiety that was relieved by treating worldly success as a sign of grace → systematic capital accumulation as a calling → capitalism. Once capitalism is established, the original religious motivation falls away but the economic structure remains and compels the same behaviour. The *iron cage*: the rational organisation of capitalist production constrains individuals who can no longer escape it — not coercion, but the logic of a system that reproduces itself.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / LSE Sociology] The framework for analysing bureaucratic creep, managerialism, and the 'disenchantment of the world' — from Weber's understanding of why modern institutions feel both powerful and meaningless.
cards.counter: Weber presented rationalisation as progressive and unidirectional; in practice, modern societies contain large irrational elements — nationalism, religious revivals, populism. The iron cage metaphor may overstate the closure of modern societies.

quiz.q: What did Weber mean by the 'iron cage' of capitalism?
choices: The oppressive conditions of factory work in industrial capitalism
A system of rational economic organisation that, once established, compels behaviour regardless of the moral or religious motivations that originally created it
The legal and regulatory framework that constrains capitalist firms
The psychological state of alienation experienced by workers under capitalism

cards.title: Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy
cards.fact: Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy: hierarchical authority, specialised roles, rules-based decision-making, separation of office from person, written records — the most technically efficient form of administration in large organisations.

layers.body: Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy: (1) hierarchy of authority; (2) specialised jurisdictions with defined competence; (3) formal rules governing procedures; (4) office/person separation — the official does not own the position; (5) appointment by merit (examination, credentials); (6) full-time salaried officials. This rational-legal authority type is more reliable and less capricious than charismatic or traditional authority.

Weber admired bureaucracy's technical efficiency but feared its consequences: 'specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart.' Modern states and corporations require bureaucracy, but bureaucracy can also become *rigid*, self-perpetuating, and an end in itself ('bureau-pathology'). Later sociologists (Merton: bureaucratic dysfunction, goal displacement) studied how bureaucracies subvert their own goals.

cards.deploy: [LSE / Oxford Sociology] The foundational concept in organisation theory — public administration, corporate management, and state capacity all build on Weber's framework.
cards.counter: Weber's ideal type captures one mode of organisation. Network organisations, flat hierarchies, and informal coordination in complex environments (military special forces, startups) show that bureaucracy is not always the most effective form — only in stable, predictable environments.

quiz.q: What does 'separation of office from person' mean in Weber's bureaucracy?
choices: Officials cannot hold office in more than one organisation
The position belongs to the organisation, not the incumbent — officials have no ownership of the role and cannot appropriate its resources or pass it on
Office-holders are physically separated from clients they serve
Personal relationships are prohibited within the bureaucratic hierarchy

cards.title: Marxian class theory
cards.fact: Marx's class analysis: in capitalism, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production; the proletariat owns only labour power and must sell it to survive. Exploitation is structural — workers produce more value than they receive in wages (surplus value).

layers.body: Class in Marx is defined by *relationship to the means of production*: the bourgeoisie owns factories, land, capital; the proletariat owns only their labour. This generates exploitation not through bad employers but structurally: workers produce more value in a day than they are paid — the difference is *surplus value*, appropriated as profit.

layers.t: Class in itself vs for itself
layers.body: Marx distinguished: *class in itself* (objective class position defined by economic relations) and *class for itself* (class consciousness — recognition of shared interests and antagonism with the opposing class). The proletariat exists as a class in itself (objectively exploited) but may not be a class for itself (false consciousness — they may not recognise their position). Revolutionary change requires class consciousness; capitalism generates conditions (immiseration, polarisation) that eventually produce it.

cards.deploy: [LSE Sociology] The foundational conflict theory of stratification — any analysis of inequality, economic power, and labour relations begins with Marx's class framework.
cards.counter: The two-class model (bourgeoisie/proletariat) fails to capture the complexity of modern stratification — the growth of the middle class, credentialed professionals, managers, and the precariat. Weber's multidimensional class-status-party framework captures this better.

quiz.q: What is 'surplus value' in Marxian economics?
choices: The profit made from selling goods at above their cost of production
The value workers produce above and beyond what they are paid in wages — appropriated by the capitalist as profit
The value added through technological innovation
The difference between market price and use value of commodities

cards.title: Bourdieu: forms of capital
cards.fact: Bourdieu expands capital beyond the economic: economic capital (money, assets), cultural capital (education, tastes, credentials), social capital (social connections and network resources) — all three can be converted into each other and reproduce class position.

layers.body: Pierre Bourdieu: the accumulation of resources that confer social advantage operates through three convertible forms: *economic capital* (directly convertible to money), *cultural capital* (embodied in tastes and dispositions [habitus], objectified in cultural goods, or institutionalised in credentials), and *social capital* (resources from durable networks — 'who you know'). A fourth form, *symbolic capital*, is the prestige and recognition that any of the three accrue when socially recognised.

Capital forms convert into each other: economic capital buys private schooling → cultural capital (credentials); social capital (elite networks) → economic capital (jobs). Class is reproduced because upper-class parents transmit embodied cultural capital to children through early socialisation — this 'cultural inheritance' is invisible (it looks like 'merit') but systematically advantages the children of the already privileged. Education legitimises inequality by presenting cultural capital as natural talent.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / LSE Sociology] The dominant framework for explaining how privilege reproduces across generations through non-economic means — underpins cultural sociology, educational inequality research, and elite studies.
cards.counter: Bourdieu's framework has been criticised for underestimating the possibility of social mobility and the agency of those with low capital — his model can appear deterministic. DiMaggio's work on cultural mobility shows cultural capital is not perfectly correlated with class origin.

quiz.q: Why does Bourdieu argue cultural capital is central to class reproduction?
choices: Because the wealthy spend more on arts and culture than the poor

Because upper-class children inherit cultural dispositions, tastes, and knowledge through early socialisation, which are then rewarded by educational institutions — appearing as 'merit' but actually transmitting class advantage
Because cultural industries directly employ upper-class graduates
Because credentials have replaced inherited wealth as the primary determinant of class position
