cards.title: Bourdieu: habitus and field
cards.fact: Bourdieu's habitus is the system of durable dispositions (perceptions, appreciations, practices) acquired through early socialisation — it generates behaviour without conscious calculation, 'feeling at home' in the social position one was born into.

layers.body: Habitus: the socially inculcated system of dispositions that shape how you perceive the world, what you find tasteful, how you speak, carry yourself, and interact — acquired in childhood, largely below the threshold of consciousness. The working-class child develops a habitus suited to their social position: modest expectations, practical orientations. The middle-class child develops a habitus of entitlement and ease. Neither chooses this — it is the class structure made flesh.

A *field* is a structured social space with its own rules, valued resources, and positions (academic field, economic field, political field). Each field has specific 'rules of the game.' Capital is effective only within the relevant field: high cultural capital (knowing art history) confers advantage in the academic field but not the business field. Habitus matches (or mismatches) different fields: the working-class student feels like a 'fish out of water' in elite academic settings — *hysteresis* when habitus and field are misaligned.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / LSE Sociology] Bourdieu's analytical framework for explaining how inequality is reproduced through the body and everyday social practice — widely applied in education, cultural, and political sociology.
cards.counter: Habitus is a dispositional concept — it is difficult to observe directly and risks becoming a circular explanation (habitus explains behaviour, behaviour reveals habitus). Agency is undertheorised: Bourdieu's actors appear largely trapped in their social position.

quiz.q: What does Bourdieu mean by 'hysteresis' in the habitus-field relationship?
choices: The tendency of social fields to resist change over long periods
The mismatch between habitus (shaped by one social position) and a different field — the dispositions appropriate to one context feel wrong and perform poorly in another
The lag between economic capital accumulation and cultural capital formation
The way high-status groups use delay to maintain distinction from arrivistes

cards.title: Social capital
cards.fact: Social capital: resources available through social networks — Coleman's bonding social capital (dense, trust-generating networks within a group) vs Putnam's bridging social capital (weak ties across groups); both enable collective action.

layers.body: Social capital refers to the value of social networks — the norms of reciprocity, trust, and information flows that networks enable. Coleman (1988): dense closed networks generate trust (the diamond dealer can leave gems on approval because the community will punish defectors). Putnam (1993, 2000): civic participation and associational life generate generalised trust — Italy's north-south development divide tracks civic participation over centuries.

*Bonding capital*: strong ties within a group (family, ethnic community) — provides support and solidarity but can be insular and exclude outsiders. *Bridging capital*: weak ties across diverse groups — generates information, opportunities, and innovation (Granovetter: 'the strength of weak ties'). *Linking capital* (Woolcock): vertical ties to power and institutions — matters for social mobility. Over-reliance on bonding at the expense of bridging produces fragmented, insular communities — the 'dark side' of social capital.

cards.deploy: [LSE / Harvard Sociology] The framework for analysing community, trust, and collective action — applied to development economics, public health, education, and crime prevention.
cards.counter: Social capital is conceptually diffuse: when it explains everything from economic development to health, it risks explaining nothing. The Putnam-Fukuyama-type empirical claims (civic life → economic growth) have been contested on methodological grounds.

quiz.q: What is Granovetter's 'strength of weak ties' thesis?
choices: Strong personal bonds produce more reliable information than casual acquaintances
Weak ties to people outside your close circle provide access to novel information and opportunities — new jobs, ideas, and contacts come through acquaintances, not close friends
The weakening of social ties in modern societies reduces collective action capacity
Trust is more efficiently built through indirect than direct social interaction

cards.title: Social network analysis
cards.fact: Social network analysis maps social structure as nodes (actors) and ties (relations) — key concepts: degree centrality, betweenness centrality, structural holes (Burt), and small-world networks (Watts-Strogatz).

layers.body: Network analysis treats social position not by individual attributes but by patterns of connection. *Degree centrality*: how many connections (popular). *Betweenness centrality*: how often you appear on shortest paths between others (broker). *Structural holes* (Burt 1992): gaps between clusters — actors bridging structural holes control information flows and gain brokerage advantages.

Watts-Strogatz (1998): most real networks are 'small worlds' — clustering is high (you know clusters of friends) but average path lengths are short (six degrees of separation). This structure accelerates information diffusion, social contagion, and disease spread — a few 'connector' nodes link separate clusters. Applications: disease epidemiology, rumour spread, organisational knowledge management.

cards.deploy: [LSE / Columbia Sociology] Essential for any social structure analysis — explains why who you know shapes outcomes, how information and diseases spread, and where strategic brokerage positions are.
cards.counter: Network analysis describes structure but does not easily explain how networks form, why ties persist or dissolve, or what happens inside nodes. It can reduce agency to positional effects.

quiz.q: What are 'structural holes' in social network analysis (Burt)?
choices: Missing data in network surveys that create gaps in the analysis
Gaps between clusters in a network — actors who bridge these holes control information flows between disconnected groups and gain brokerage advantages
Weak ties that create vulnerabilities in social solidarity
Nodes with very low degree centrality that are isolated from the main network

cards.title: Social stratification
cards.fact: Stratification refers to the hierarchical arrangement of society into layers (strata) based on class, status, and power (Weber's three dimensions) — determining life chances in health, education, income, and justice.

layers.body: Weber distinguished three dimensions of social inequality: *class* (economic position — market capacity), *status* (social honour and prestige — often not aligned with class: a professor may have high status but low income), and *party* (power — organised capacity to achieve goals). These dimensions can reinforce or cut across each other.

Social mobility is movement between strata. *Absolute mobility* rose in the 20th century (everyone moved up as the economy grew). *Relative mobility* (who moves up relative to whom) is more contested — most countries have similar rates, except Nordic ones with higher relative mobility. Weber's *social closure*: groups monopolise resources by defining eligibility criteria (credentials, race, gender) and excluding outsiders — naturalising inequality.

cards.deploy: [LSE / Sciences Po Sociology] The foundational framework for all inequality analysis — used in every policy debate about social mobility, educational meritocracy, and class.
cards.counter: Class-based stratification analyses have been challenged by the growing importance of consumption-based identities, cultural capital differences within classes, and the fragmentation of traditional class groupings (the 'death of class' debate — Pakulski and Waters).

quiz.q: What is 'social closure' in Weber's stratification theory?
choices: The process by which social classes become rigidly fixed over generations
The monopolisation of social resources by a group through defining exclusionary eligibility criteria (credentials, race, gender) — preventing outsiders from accessing the group's advantages
The collapse of status differences in modern meritocratic societies
The tendency of elites to move into different sectors to avoid taxation

cards.title: Goffman: dramaturgical sociology
cards.fact: Goffman's dramaturgical sociology: social life is a performance — individuals are actors managing impressions on a 'front stage' for an audience; the 'back stage' is where they prepare and relax their presentation of self.

layers.body: Erving Goffman (*Presentation of Self in Everyday Life*, 1959): social interaction is like theatrical performance. The *front stage*: where you perform for an audience — managing your appearance, manner, and setting to create a desired impression. The *back stage*: where you prepare, rehearse, and relax with colleagues — the 'real' behaviour that would undermine the performance if seen.

*Stigma* (Goffman, 1963): social identities that are discrediting — the bearer manages 'spoiled identity' through concealment, disclosure strategy, or 'passing.' *Total institutions* (asylums, prisons, military): places that completely manage both front and back stage — the inmate's entire identity is subjected to institutional control. Goffman's work highlighted how social control operates at the micro-level of everyday interaction — not only through law and state power.

cards.deploy: [Chicago / Columbia Sociology] The foundational microsociology of everyday life — applied in disability studies, prison sociology, gender performance theory, and online self-presentation.
cards.counter: Goffman's dramaturgical model implies that social selves are entirely performed — but doesn't there have to be a 'real' self doing the performing? The theory is criticised for not specifying the relationship between performed self and authentic identity.

quiz.q: What does Goffman mean by 'impression management'?
choices: The psychological process of maintaining a positive self-image
The active management of social performance — controlling appearance, manner, and setting to influence how others perceive and respond to you
The way institutions control information about their policies
The process by which dominant groups manage their social reputation

cards.title: Intersectionality
cards.fact: Kimberlé Crenshaw's intersectionality: race, gender, class, and other categories of identity are not independent — they interact and compound to produce experiences that cannot be understood by analysing each dimension separately.

layers.body: Crenshaw (1989): a Black woman's experience of discrimination is not simply 'race discrimination' plus 'gender discrimination' — the intersection creates a unique position not captured by either lens alone. Analysing only race (using Black men as the reference) or only gender (using white women) makes the specific experience of Black women invisible. Discrimination is multiplicative, not additive.

Intersectionality challenges single-axis frameworks in law, social policy, and social movements. It implies that the 'woman problem' or 'race problem' cannot be solved by one-size-fits-all policies — solutions must account for their interaction. Methodologically, it requires examining *combinations* of identities, not just their effects separately. Critics argue it can lead to ever-finer categorisation, making comparative analysis difficult and political coalitions unstable.

cards.deploy: [Columbia Sociology / Critical Race Theory] Essential for understanding systematic discrimination, equality policy, and identity politics — used in law, education, public health, and social movements.
cards.counter: Critics of intersectionality argue the framework can proliferate identity categories indefinitely, making systematic empirical analysis difficult. McCall distinguishes anti-categorical, inter-categorical, and intra-categorical approaches to operationalise the concept.

quiz.q: Why does Crenshaw argue that analysing race and gender separately is insufficient?
choices: Because race and gender are both socially constructed and therefore equally arbitrary

Because the intersection creates a specific position (e.g. Black women) that is invisible in both the 'race discrimination' frame (which uses Black men as reference) and the 'gender discrimination' frame (which uses white women as reference)
Because most people experience multiple identities and cannot be placed in single categories
Because race and gender have the same legal status under anti-discrimination law

cards.title: Gender as social construction
cards.fact: Simone de Beauvoir: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' — gender is not a biological given but a social construction produced through norms, socialisation, and performance (Butler's performativity).

layers.body: The sociological distinction: *sex* is biological (chromosomes, anatomy); *gender* is social (the meanings, roles, and behaviours attributed to sex categories). Beauvoir (1949): 'femininity' is not a natural essence but a social category imposed on those with female bodies. This distinction opened the sociological analysis of gender inequality as a social and political, not natural, phenomenon.

Judith Butler (*Gender Trouble*, 1990): gender is not a role that pre-existing individuals perform — there is no pre-social subject behind the performance. Gender identity is constituted *through* the repetitive performance of gendered acts (dress, gesture, language). The appearance of a stable binary gender is produced by these repetitions and enforced by social norms. This implies: gender can be subverted through parody, transgression, or non-normative performance.

cards.deploy: [LSE / Yale Sociology] The theoretical foundation of gender sociology and queer theory — applied in policy analysis of gender pay gaps, care work, sexual harassment, and trans rights.
cards.counter: Butler's performativity theory has been criticised for underweighting the material and embodied dimensions of gendered experience — it risks reducing gender to discourse. Feminist materialists (Fraser, Skeggs) emphasise economic and bodily dimensions that discourse theory brackets.

quiz.q: What does Butler mean by gender 'performativity'?
choices: That gender is a performance individuals consciously put on, like acting a role
That gender identity is constituted through the repetition of gendered acts — there is no pre-social subject before the performance; the performance produces the subject
That gender differences are performed in public but authentic in private
That gender norms are reproduced through media and popular culture

cards.title: Symbolic interactionism
cards.fact: Mead and Blumer's symbolic interactionism: people act toward things based on the meanings those things have for them; meanings arise from social interaction; meanings are modified through interpretive processes.

layers.body: George Herbert Mead (*Mind, Self & Society*, 1934) and Herbert Blumer: human behaviour is not stimulus-response but *meaning-driven*. We act toward objects (people, institutions, things) based on the meanings we attribute to them. Meanings are not fixed — they emerge from interaction with others and are continuously revised through our interpretations.

Mead: the *self* has two components — the 'I' (spontaneous, subjective self) and the 'me' (the social self, internalised from others' responses). The *generalised other* is the internalised view of the community as a whole — when you imagine how 'people in general' would see your action. This social self is the mechanism by which society enters the individual: social control is internal, not just external. Applications: labelling theory (Becker: deviance is a label applied by others, not an intrinsic property of acts).

cards.deploy: [Chicago Sociology] The microsociology of meaning and interaction — grounds labelling theory, ethnomethodology, and qualitative research methods.
cards.counter: Symbolic interactionism is criticised for ignoring structural constraints — it focuses on micro-interaction without explaining why some meanings dominate over others (power, class, ideology). It can slide into voluntarism: as if actors are free to negotiate meanings without structural limits.

quiz.q: What is the 'generalised other' in Mead's symbolic interactionism?
choices: The statistical average of others' views toward any social act
The internalised perspective of the community as a whole — the imagined view of 'people in general' that regulates behaviour from within
The most powerful other person in any social interaction
The symbolic representations of social norms in culture and media

cards.title: Foucault: power/knowledge and discipline
cards.fact: Foucault: power is not only repressive but productive — it produces knowledge, subjects, and truth claims. Modern discipline operates through surveillance and normalisation, not primarily violence — the Panopticon as the model of modern power.

layers.t: Power produces, it doesn't only prohibit
layers.body: Foucault (*Discipline and Punish*, 1975): modern power is productive — it creates subjects (the 'delinquent,' the 'homosexual,' the 'patient'), generates knowledge (psychiatry, criminology, medicine), and establishes what counts as truth (discourses). Power is not held by a sovereign but dispersed throughout social institutions — schools, prisons, clinics, the army all exercise power through discipline.

Foucault used Bentham's *Panopticon* as a metaphor for modern disciplinary power: a prison where inmates can be observed at any moment but cannot see the guard — they eventually internalise surveillance and discipline themselves. Modern institutions (schools, factories, hospitals) work similarly: constant potential observation produces self-regulation. *Biopolitics* (later Foucault): power operates not just on individual bodies but on populations — through public health, demography, sexuality. This frames contemporary debates about surveillance capitalism and data.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / LSE Sociology] The framework for analysing power beyond formal institutions — used in security studies, medical sociology, education, and surveillance studies.
cards.counter: Foucault's concept of power is so diffuse that it can seem to explain everything — making it hard to explain how resistance is possible or how dominant discourses can change. His work is historically rich but empirically contested.

quiz.q: What does the Panopticon metaphor illustrate about modern disciplinary power?
choices: That authoritarian states use mass surveillance to suppress dissent
That the mere possibility of being observed — without actual surveillance — induces self-discipline, making direct coercion unnecessary
That knowledge about individuals is always used to control them
That institutional power is concentrated in the hands of a visible authority

cards.title: Urbanisation and urban sociology
cards.fact: Louis Wirth's 'Urbanism as a Way of Life' (1938): size, density, and heterogeneity of cities produce a characteristic way of life — impersonal, segmented, secondary relations replace primary community ties.

layers.body: Wirth (Chicago School): cities are not just large villages. Size (many strangers) + density (close proximity to different others) + heterogeneity (diversity) produce: impersonal and formal relationships; role segmentation (you only interact with a person as driver/customer/colleague, not as a whole person); reliance on formal institutions (law, police, bureaucracy) instead of community norms.

layers.t: From Chicago School to global cities
layers.body: Park and Burgess's concentric zone model (Chicago School, 1920s): cities organise spatially into zones — CBD, transition, working-class housing, middle-class residences, commuter suburbs. Gentrification (Sassen, Zukin): global cities (New York, London, Tokyo) are command-and-control centres of the global economy — attracting high-skilled finance/tech workers and displacing working-class residents through rising rents. Today 56% of the world's population lives in cities (UN 2023); the global urban transition is ongoing.

cards.deploy: [LSE / Columbia Sociology] Essential for housing policy, urban planning, segregation analysis, and understanding the social conditions of contemporary capitalism.
cards.counter: Wirth's urbanism thesis overstates the impersonality of city life — urban villages (Gans), ethnic enclaves, and neighborhood networks show that strong community ties persist within cities. The 'loss of community' narrative is partial.

quiz.q: What three features does Wirth identify as producing the urban way of life?
choices: Economic inequality, geographic mobility, and cultural diversity
Size, density, and heterogeneity — together producing impersonal, segmented, secondary social relations
Immigration, industrialisation, and class stratification
Anonymity, noise, and pollution

cards.title: What is anthropology?
cards.fact: Anthropology studies human diversity — cultural, biological, archaeological, linguistic — through a comparative and holistic lens. Its core method is ethnography: long-term participant observation in the field.

layers.body: Four sub-fields: *cultural/social anthropology* (meaning, society, practice), *biological/physical anthropology* (human evolution, primates), *archaeology* (material culture across time), *linguistic anthropology* (language and culture). The American four-field tradition (Boas) integrates these; British social anthropology focuses on the social/cultural. The unifying question: what does it mean to be human, and how do human societies differ and why?

The traditional distinction: sociology studied 'complex' (Western) societies with quantitative methods; anthropology studied 'simple' (non-Western) societies with qualitative methods. This distinction has collapsed — anthropology now studies finance (Maurer), science (Latour), the state (Gupta), and globalisation (Appadurai). The defining method remains ethnography: immersive, qualitative, long-term fieldwork — making the familiar strange and the strange familiar.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] The field that studies human difference without reducing it to the familiar — essential for cross-cultural analysis, development, and global governance.
cards.counter: Anthropology's founding method (ethnography) generates rich but non-generalisable findings — the 'n=1' problem. Its earlier tradition of studying 'primitive' societies reflected colonial power relations that contemporary anthropology is still working to decolonise.

quiz.q: What distinguishes ethnography as an anthropological method?
choices: Large-scale survey methods applied across many cultures simultaneously
Long-term immersive participant observation — living with a community, learning language and practice from the inside
Systematic comparison of cultural traits across many societies using coded data
Analysis of material remains to reconstruct past societies

cards.title: Ethnography and participant observation
cards.fact: Malinowski's participant observation: the ethnographer lives in the field for an extended period, learns the language, participates in daily life, and documents the society from the inside — producing data unavailable to the outside observer.

layers.body: Malinowski (*Argonauts of the Western Pacific*, 1922): the anthropologist must not rely on informants at a distance but must live in the village, observe daily life, participate in activities, and earn the community's trust. This produces: the *imponderabilia of daily life* (routines, gestures, moods that would not be reported to an outsider), the *corpus inscriptionum* (observable data: gardens, canoes, ceremonies), and *native's own statements* (what people say about their lives).

*Reflexivity*: the ethnographer is part of the field — her gender, race, nationality, and personality shape what she sees and what people say to her. Feminist anthropologists (Rosaldo, Strathern) and the 'writing culture' critique (Clifford-Marcus, 1986) challenged the pretence of objectivity: ethnography is a *written* product, shaped by rhetorical choices. Postcolonial critique: ethnography was embedded in colonial administration and surveillance.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] The gold standard of qualitative research — used in organisational studies, design research, policy evaluation, and healthcare.
cards.counter: Participant observation produces data that is specific to the ethnographer's position — replication is impossible. The 'observer effect' is irreducible: presence changes behaviour. Long fieldwork may also create excessive investment in the community's self-presentation.

quiz.q: What is 'reflexivity' in ethnographic research?
choices: The method of going back to fieldwork to check earlier interpretations
The recognition that the researcher's identity and position shape what they observe and how — making the ethnographer part of the data, not a neutral recorder
The process of reflecting on theoretical frameworks after fieldwork is complete
The ethical requirement to reflect on the uses of anthropological knowledge

cards.title: Cultural relativism
cards.fact: Boas's cultural relativism: cultures must be understood on their own terms, not ranked by an evolutionary hierarchy — each culture is the product of its unique historical circumstances, not a stage in a universal progression.

layers.body: 19th-century evolutionary anthropology (Morgan, Spencer) ranked societies from 'savagery' to 'civilization' — placing Western Europe at the top. Boas rejected this: *historical particularism* holds that each culture has a unique history that cannot be fitted into universal stages. Cultural relativism: to understand a custom, start from the culture's own logic, not from Western standards of rationality, aesthetics, or morality.

*Methodological relativism*: suspend your own evaluative standards when doing fieldwork (heuristic). *Moral relativism*: there are no universal moral standards — cultures cannot be morally evaluated from outside. The distinction matters: most anthropologists practice methodological relativism (bracket judgment to understand) without endorsing moral relativism (which would make critique of practices like torture or female genital mutilation impossible). Herskovits and others blurred this distinction, drawing criticism from Lévi-Strauss and contemporary human rights scholars.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] The methodological foundation of ethnography and cross-cultural analysis — and the source of ongoing debate about human rights universalism.
cards.counter: Taken to an extreme, cultural relativism makes it impossible to criticise practices that violate human rights. It can also romanticise 'other' cultures as static and coherent, denying internal conflict and dynamism.

quiz.q: What is the difference between 'methodological relativism' and 'moral relativism' in anthropology?
choices: Methodological relativism is practised by American anthropologists; moral relativism by British social anthropologists

Methodological relativism brackets judgment to understand a culture from within; moral relativism claims there are no universal moral standards — the first is a research heuristic, the second is a normative position
Methodological relativism applies to material culture; moral relativism to values and beliefs
They are the same: Boas's relativism was always both methodological and normative

cards.title: Geertz: thick description and interpretive anthropology
cards.fact: Geertz's interpretive anthropology: culture is a web of significance; the anthropologist's task is 'thick description' — interpreting not just what a behaviour does but what it means within the cultural system.

layers.body: Geertz: 'Man is an animal suspended in webs of significance he himself has spun; I take culture to be those webs.' To understand a wink vs a twitch: both are physically identical, but a wink has meaning (a cultural code), a twitch doesn't. *Thick description* (from Gilbert Ryle): describing not just the observable behaviour but the context, codes, and meanings that make it intelligible.

Geertz's Balinese cockfight essay: the cockfight is not about money (the bets are not economically rational) — it is a *story* Balinese tell themselves about themselves (masculinity, prestige, fate, hierarchy). The anthropologist reads cultures as *texts* — the goal is interpretation, not explanation through causal laws. This humanistic approach marked a turn away from the scientific aspirations of structural-functionalism.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] The interpretive turn's manifesto — grounds qualitative, hermeneutic approaches to culture in anthropology, sociology, and policy analysis.
cards.counter: Geertz's interpretive approach has been criticised for reducing culture to text — ignoring material conditions, power, and conflict. Abu-Lughod: 'culture' talk can reify and homogenise groups, hiding internal diversity and domination.

quiz.q: What does Geertz mean by 'thick description'?
choices: Describing a culture in exhaustive empirical detail
Interpreting behaviour at the level of its cultural meaning — not just what is done but what it signifies within the cultural system
Using multiple sources to triangulate a single cultural fact
Providing historical context for contemporary cultural practices

cards.title: Lévi-Strauss: structural anthropology
cards.fact: Lévi-Strauss: beneath the diversity of cultures lie universal structures of the human mind — myths, kinship rules, and totems all operate through binary oppositions (raw/cooked, nature/culture) that reveal deep cognitive patterns.

layers.body: Claude Lévi-Strauss applied Saussurean linguistics to anthropology: meaning arises from difference and relation, not from the intrinsic properties of elements. Myths and kinship rules across cultures are like languages — they vary infinitely in content but operate by the same structural logic. Binary oppositions (raw/cooked, sacred/profane, nature/culture) are the building blocks of all cultural systems.

Lévi-Strauss on kinship: the incest taboo is universal — not a natural aversion but a cultural rule that forces groups to *exchange* women (or, mutually, partners), creating alliances. Exchange, not production, is the foundation of social life (*The Elementary Structures of Kinship*, 1949). This structural universal generates the diversity of kinship systems observed across cultures. Feminist critique: the exchange model treats women as objects exchanged between men, not as subjects.

cards.deploy: [Sciences Po / Oxford Anthropology] The bridge between French structuralism and anthropology — foundational for understanding kinship, myth, and cultural logic.
cards.counter: Structural anthropology has been criticised for: imposing Western binary logic on non-Western thought; being unfalsifiable (any data can be fitted into binary structures); and treating living cultures as static texts rather than dynamic practice.

quiz.q: In Lévi-Strauss's theory, why is the incest taboo universal?
choices: Because inbreeding causes genetic defects that reduce survival
Because it is a cultural rule that forces groups to exchange partners, creating inter-group alliances — exchange, not production, is the foundation of social structure
Because all human societies have internalised a natural aversion to incest through evolution
Because children raised in the same household develop Westermarck aversion

cards.title: Kinship systems
cards.fact: Kinship systems — the culturally specific rules for reckoning descent, defining kin, and regulating marriage — are the organisational backbone of most pre-industrial societies, structuring inheritance, alliance, and social solidarity.

layers.body: Kinship is not simply biology — cultures reckon 'who counts as kin' in very different ways. *Descent* rules: *patrilineal* (descent through men: Bedouin, Chinese lineages), *matrilineal* (through women: Trobriand Islanders), *bilateral* (through both parents: most Western societies). *Residence*: *patrilocal* (wife moves to husband's family), *matrilocal* (reverse), *neolocal* (new household: common in industrial societies).

*Exogamy* (must marry outside the group) vs *endogamy* (must marry within). *Cross-cousin marriage* (marry your father's sister's child) is common in many societies — it maintains alliances between patrilineages while keeping descent clear. These rules are not arbitrary — they serve social functions: controlling property transmission, creating inter-group alliances, regulating labour. Schneider's radical critique (1984): 'kinship' as a universal category is a Western ethnocentric construct — other cultures organise social relations through categories that don't map onto Euro-American 'kinship.'

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] Essential for understanding family policy, inheritance law, marriage regulation, and demographic change in non-Western societies.
cards.counter: New reproductive technologies, same-sex kinship, adoption, and donor conception challenge kinship systems globally — showing that the categories of 'parent,' 'sibling,' and 'family' are more flexible and culturally negotiated than classic kinship theory acknowledged.

quiz.q: What is the difference between 'patrilineal' and 'matrilineal' descent?
choices: Patrilineal means the father is the head of household; matrilineal means the mother is
Patrilineal descent traces group membership through the male line (father to son); matrilineal through the female line (mother to child) — determining inheritance, authority, and group identity
Patrilineal systems practice exogamy; matrilineal systems practice endogamy
Patrilineal is found in agricultural societies; matrilineal in hunter-gatherer ones

cards.title: Mauss: the gift
cards.fact: Mauss's theory of the gift: in non-market societies, gifts are not free — they obligate the recipient to reciprocate. Gift exchange creates social bonds, status, and hierarchy; it is the foundation of social solidarity, not market exchange.

layers.body: Marcel Mauss (*The Gift*, 1925): in Melanesian, Polynesian, and Northwest Coast Indian societies, objects are exchanged as gifts — but with deep obligations attached. The recipient must reciprocate (comparable but not identical value), must accept (refusing a gift is an insult), and must give in the same spirit. The gift creates a *social bond* and establishes hierarchy (the more you give, the higher your status — potlatch).

Malinowski's *kula ring* (Trobriand Islands): shell armbands circulate clockwise, necklaces counter-clockwise, across a ring of islands. No practical use — but the exchange creates long-distance alliances, trust, and fame. The objects accrue value through the history of hands they have passed through. This illustrates: (1) exchange is social, not merely economic; (2) objects carry social histories; (3) the economy is embedded in social relations (Polanyi). Derrida and Bourdieu critique: a truly free gift — which creates no obligation — is impossible; it would destroy the gift economy by breaking the cycle.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] The foundation of economic anthropology — challenges the universality of market rationality; applied in development economics (credit relationships) and gift economy debates.
cards.counter: The obligation to reciprocate in Mauss's analysis may be an emic Western misreading of what indigenous people described as 'free' giving. Annette Weiner showed that in the Trobriands, some objects are 'inalienable possessions' that must NOT be given — complicating the pure circulation model.

quiz.q: What does the potlatch ceremony (Northwest Coast Indians) illustrate about gift exchange?
choices: That market economies are universal — even 'primitive' societies have price mechanisms
That giving can confer status and create hierarchy — the chief who gives away most demonstrates superior wealth and generosity, obligating others and raising his prestige
That gift exchange is economically irrational and leads to the destruction of surplus
That reciprocity is a moral duty in all human societies

cards.title: Hunter-gatherers and the 'original affluent society'
cards.fact: Sahlins's thesis: hunter-gatherers are not in perpetual scarcity — they work fewer hours than agricultural or industrial workers and meet their needs with ease. Affluence is achieved either by producing much or by desiring little.

layers.body: Marshall Sahlins (*Stone Age Economics*, 1972): the conventional view — hunter-gatherers are in chronic want, driving them to eventually adopt agriculture — is wrong. !Kung San of the Kalahari work ~15 hours/week for subsistence and have leisure for socialising, rituals, and sleeping. Scarcity is not a natural condition but a *product of the market economy*, which multiplies wants faster than means.

If hunter-gatherers are 'affluent,' why did agriculture emerge? Agriculture provides higher caloric yield per acre but requires more labour per person and produces monotonous, less nutritious diets. Most archaeologists now agree that the transition to agriculture was gradual, context-dependent, and not obviously 'progress' in terms of quality of life (Diamond: 'the worst mistake in the history of the human race'). Climate change (Younger Dryas) and population pressure are the main drivers in the archaeological consensus.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] Challenges the narrative of linear progress and market rationality — relevant to debates about working hours, consumerism, degrowth, and economic anthropology.
cards.counter: The '15 hours' figure has been challenged: it measures direct food procurement but not food processing, childcare, tool maintenance, and knowledge transmission. The romantic vision of hunter-gatherer affluence may understate the precariousness of pre-agricultural life.

quiz.q: What is the 'Zen road to affluence' in Sahlins's framework?
choices: Accumulating material goods to the point where all wants are satisfied
Achieving affluence by having few wants — so that available resources always exceed desires, without needing to maximise production
Using spiritual practice to transcend material scarcity
Sharing resources communally so that poverty is eliminated through redistribution

cards.title: Anthropology of religion
cards.fact: Geertz's definition of religion: a system of symbols that establishes powerful, pervasive moods and motivations by formulating conceptions of a general order of existence and clothing these with an aura of factuality.

layers.t: Religion as a system of meaning
layers.body: Geertz: religion does two things simultaneously — it provides a *model of* reality (a cognitive map) and a *model for* action (prescriptions for behaviour). Sacred symbols make the world intelligible and motivate behaviour by connecting cosmology to ethics. This is functionalism in interpretive clothing: religion makes suffering meaningful, integrates communities, and motivates action.

layers.t: Tylor, Durkheim, and Weber on religion
layers.body: Tylor: religion begins with *animism* (attributing spirit to natural objects — intellectualist explanation, religion as proto-science). Durkheim: religion is society worshipping itself — the sacred/profane distinction reflects the distinction between group and individual. Weber: *theodicy* (how religions account for suffering and inequality) shapes economic and political behaviour (Protestant ethic). These three strands — cognitive, social, and motivational — still structure the anthropology of religion.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Chicago Anthropology] The framework for analysing religion in any policy context — from Islamism to evangelical politics to new age movements — without ethnocentrism.
cards.counter: Geertz's definition is Western-secular: not all societies distinguish a 'religion' domain from practical or political life. Talal Asad argues that 'religion' as a universal category was invented by Enlightenment secularism — it is not a cross-cultural natural kind.

quiz.q: What does Durkheim mean when he says religion is 'society worshipping itself'?
choices: Religious institutions serve the interests of ruling elites
The sacred represents the social — when people worship the divine, they are actually venerating the power and authority of their social group, which produces collective moral solidarity
Societies develop religion to justify their own existence and particular institutions
Religious symbols are created by the state to produce ideological conformity

cards.title: What is jurisprudence?
cards.fact: Jurisprudence (legal philosophy) asks: what is law? What makes law valid? What is the relationship between law and morality? The three dominant traditions are legal positivism, natural law, and legal realism.

layers.body: Jurisprudence (legal philosophy) addresses: (1) *What is law?* — the nature and definition of legal systems. (2) *What makes law valid?* — the source of legal authority (is it the sovereign's command? social facts? moral content?). (3) *What is the relation between law and morality?* — must law be morally acceptable to be law? Can an unjust law still be law?

*Natural law*: law derives its validity from morality — an unjust law is not truly law. *Legal positivism* (Austin, Hart): law is a social fact — it is valid law if it was enacted by the proper authority through the right procedures, regardless of moral content. *Legal realism*: law is what courts actually do — judicial decisions are the real law, and legal rules merely rationalise prior decisions. These debates shape constitutional interpretation, legal education, and judicial appointments.

cards.deploy: [Oxford Law / Harvard Law] The meta-level framework for any legal argument — every constitutional or statutory interpretation debate involves implicit jurisprudential commitments.
cards.counter: Some legal theorists (Endicott) argue the jurisprudential debates are irresolvable because they rest on conceptual disagreements rather than empirical ones — the field has been spinning its wheels. Others (Leiter) think legal realism is the only scientifically defensible position.

quiz.q: What is the central disagreement between natural law theory and legal positivism?
choices: Whether courts or legislatures should have the final say on law's content
Whether law's validity depends on moral content (natural law) or only on being enacted through proper social procedures (positivism) — whether 'unjust law' is still law
Whether common law or civil law systems are more efficient
Whether legal interpretation should be textualist or purposivist

cards.title: Legal positivism: Hart
cards.fact: Hart's legal positivism: law is a system of rules — primary rules (what you must do) and secondary rules (rules about rules: how to change, adjudicate, and recognise valid law). The 'rule of recognition' determines what counts as valid law in a given system.

layers.body: Hart (*The Concept of Law*, 1961): law is a union of primary rules (imposing duties and conferring rights — don't steal, you may make a will) and secondary rules (meta-rules: rules of change [how to legislate], adjudication [courts], and recognition [what counts as law]). The *rule of recognition* is the master rule specifying what makes a rule valid law — in the UK, 'whatever Parliament enacts.'

layers.t: Hard cases and the open texture
layers.body: Hart conceded that law has an *open texture* — words have settled core meanings and a penumbra of uncertainty. In hard cases, judges must exercise discretion. Hart: they are not bound by existing law and must make a new rule. Dworkin's critique: even in hard cases, there is always one right answer because judges must apply *principles* (not just rules), which are morally weighted and do determine outcomes. This debate about discretion vs. determinate answers drives constitutional interpretation theory.

cards.deploy: [Oxford Law] The foundational positivist theory — grounds legal certainty, rule-of-law analysis, and the separation of law from morality in institutional analysis.
cards.counter: Dworkin: Hart's positivism cannot account for the role of principles in legal reasoning — legal systems contain not just rules (all-or-nothing) but principles (weighted toward outcomes). You cannot identify law by social facts alone.

quiz.q: What is the 'rule of recognition' in Hart's theory?
choices: The constitutional provision that defines the boundaries of legislative power
The master secondary rule specifying the criteria for legal validity in a given system — what counts as law (e.g., in the UK: whatever Parliament enacts in proper form)
The judicial rule requiring courts to recognise foreign judgments
The rule determining when common law precedent must be followed

cards.title: Natural law theory
cards.fact: Natural law theory (Aquinas, Finnis): law derives its authority from morality or reason — an unjust law is no law at all (lex iniusta non est lex). Modern natural law grounds universal human rights in the intrinsic moral order.

layers.body: Aquinas: law is 'an ordinance of reason for the common good.' A law that contradicts the natural moral order lacks the essential nature of law — citizens have no obligation (and may have a duty) to disobey it. This was the jurisprudential foundation of resistance to Nazi law at Nuremberg and the philosophical basis of Martin Luther King's distinction between just and unjust laws.

John Finnis (*Natural Law and Natural Rights*, 1980): natural law does not depend on a theological foundation — it is grounded in *basic goods* (life, knowledge, friendship, practical reason, religion, play, aesthetic experience) that can be rationally recognised as intrinsically valuable. Law is morally obligatory when it coordinates action to achieve these goods. Finnis's framework grounds both the critique of unjust law and the justification of rights without requiring religious premises.

cards.deploy: [Oxford Law / Harvard Law] The philosophical foundation of constitutional rights, human rights law, and civil disobedience theory — invoked whenever legality and legitimacy are distinguished.
cards.counter: Positivists argue: even if law should conform to morality, the question of what IS law (its definition) and what law OUGHT to be are distinct. Conflating them risks making citizens' legal duties depend on each individual's moral judgement — producing legal uncertainty.

quiz.q: What does 'lex iniusta non est lex' mean for civil disobedience?
choices: That unjust laws should be legally challenged but obeyed in the meantime
That an unjust law has no binding authority — citizens are morally permitted (or required) to disobey laws that violate the natural moral order
That injustice in law is always a procedural failure, not a substantive one
That legal positivists cannot justify civil disobedience on their own terms

cards.title: Dworkin: law as integrity
cards.fact: Dworkin's anti-positivism: law includes not just rules but *principles* — morally weighted standards. The judge must find the interpretation that best 'fits' past legal decisions and best 'justifies' them morally: there is always one right answer.

layers.body: Dworkin: rules apply in an all-or-nothing way; *principles* have a 'dimension of weight' — they pull toward a conclusion but can be outweighed by competing principles. Legal systems contain both. When rules conflict or run out, judges don't have discretion — they must reason from principles, and there is always a best interpretation: the 'right answer thesis.'

Dworkin's ideal judge Hercules: infinitely wise and knowledgeable, Hercules reads all past law as an attempt to express a coherent vision of justice (*law as integrity*). He constructs the interpretation that best *fits* the legal record and best *justifies* it morally — like the best next chapter added to a collaborative novel. Rights are 'trumps' — they cannot be overridden merely because it would be useful or efficient to do so.

cards.deploy: [Oxford Law / Harvard Law] The dominant anti-positivist jurisprudential theory — drives constitutional interpretation debate (originalism vs living constitutionalism) and human rights adjudication.
cards.counter: Hart's response: there is no reason to think there is always one right answer in hard cases — judges do exercise discretion and that is legitimate. The claim that law has a single right answer even in genuinely contested cases is implausible.

quiz.q: What is Dworkin's 'right answer thesis'?
choices: That courts always reach the right decision when properly constituted
That even in hard cases there is always one legally correct answer — found by interpreting the whole body of law as expressing the best coherent moral and political theory
That legal rights are absolute and cannot be balanced against each other
That Hercules would use utilitarian calculus to determine the outcome in hard cases

cards.title: Constitutional law and judicial review
cards.fact: Constitutional law establishes the supreme law of a state — the structure of government, the distribution of power, and the protection of fundamental rights. Judicial review is the court's power to invalidate legislation that violates the constitution.

layers.body: A constitution is *higher law* — it constrains even the legislature. *Judicial review* (US since Marbury v. Madison, 1803): courts can strike down legislation as unconstitutional. In the UK, there is no constitutional entrenchment — Parliament is sovereign (parliamentary supremacy). Continental systems have dedicated constitutional courts (Kelsenian model: Germany's Bundesverfassungsgericht, France's Conseil Constitutionnel).

Bickel's *counter-majoritarian difficulty*: if democracy means majority rule, why should unelected judges be able to override elected legislatures? Justifications: (1) constitutions protect minorities from majority tyranny (fundamental rights as countermajoritarian protections); (2) courts enforce the pre-committed constitution that the founding generation democratically enacted; (3) deliberative democracy requires certain conditions (rights to speech, vote, due process) that courts protect. These justifications ground different theories of constitutional interpretation.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard Law] The framework for understanding judicial power, constitutional rights, and democracy — grounds every constitutional design debate.
cards.counter: Waldron's democratic objection: in societies with reasonable disagreement about rights, the decision should be made by democratically elected legislatures, not by judicial elites with lifetime tenure. Judicial review may protect elite interests more than minority rights.

quiz.q: What is the 'counter-majoritarian difficulty' in constitutional law?
choices: The problem that constitutional courts have fewer resources than legislatures
The tension between judicial review (unelected judges overriding elected legislatures) and democratic self-government — if democracy means majority rule, judicial supremacy appears anti-democratic
The difficulty of achieving a constitutional majority for amendments in diverse societies
The conflict between federal and state courts over constitutional interpretation

cards.title: Theories of justice
cards.fact: Justice has three main conceptions: procedural (justice is fair process), distributive (justice requires certain outcomes — equality, sufficiency, desert), and retributive/corrective (justice restores balance after wrong). Rawls, Nozick, and Walzer represent major 20th-century accounts.

layers.body: *Procedural justice* (Nozick): whatever outcome results from fair procedures is just — redistribution to correct outcomes is unjust 'patterning.' *Distributive justice* (Rawls): justice requires distributing primary goods fairly — allowing inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged. *Corrective justice* (Aristotle, tort law): repairs damage done to a victim by an injurer — aims to restore the status quo ante.

Rawls: behind the 'veil of ignorance' (not knowing your position in society), rational agents choose two principles: (1) equal basic liberties; (2) inequalities are just only if they benefit the worst-off (difference principle) and are attached to positions open to all (fair equality of opportunity). Nozick: the state has no right to redistribute — if you earned it through legitimate acquisition or voluntary transfer, it is yours. Any taxation is akin to forced labour.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard Law] The philosophical foundation of taxation, welfare state, and redistribution debates — every policy argument about 'fairness' implicitly invokes one of these theories.
cards.counter: Communitarian critics (Sandel, Walzer): justice cannot be determined from behind a veil of ignorance — we are situated beings, and our conceptions of justice are embedded in particular communities and traditions. There is no Archimedean point from which to derive universal principles.

quiz.q: What is Rawls's 'difference principle'?
choices: Social inequalities are just only if they make the least advantaged members of society as well off as possible
All differences in wealth must be eliminated for justice to obtain
The difference between Rawls and Nozick on redistribution can be resolved by the veil of ignorance
Fundamental liberties take priority over economic equality in all cases

cards.title: Rawls: veil of ignorance
cards.fact: Rawls's 'original position': rational agents choosing principles of justice behind a 'veil of ignorance' (not knowing their place in society, talents, or conception of the good) would choose principles that benefit everyone — especially the worst-off.

layers.body: Rawls's thought experiment: imagine choosing the basic structure of society without knowing who you will be in it — your class, race, gender, talents, or conception of the good life. Behind this *veil of ignorance*, you would not design a system favouring any particular group (since you might end up at the bottom). The principles chosen under such conditions are fair — they are 'justice as fairness.'

Behind the veil, Rawls argues rational agents would choose: (1) equal basic liberties for all (freedom of speech, conscience, political participation — lexically prior to (2)); (2a) fair equality of opportunity — social positions open to all with genuine equal access; (2b) the difference principle — social and economic inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged. The difference principle grounds a welfare state: inequalities (executive salaries) must 'trickle down' to benefit the worst-off, or they are unjust.

cards.deploy: [Oxford / Harvard Law] The most influential political philosophy of the 20th century — grounds progressive redistribution, constitutional rights, and international justice debates.
cards.counter: Nozick: historical entitlement matters — what is just depends on how things came about, not just on the current distribution. The veil of ignorance strips away the very information needed to apply justice correctly. Sen: a full theory of justice requires comparing actual real-world alternatives, not deriving principles from an imaginary original position.

quiz.q: Why does Rawls use the 'veil of ignorance' device?
choices: To model actual policy-making under conditions of uncertainty
To ensure that principles of justice are chosen without self-interest — if you don't know your place in society, you will choose principles that are fair to all positions, especially the worst-off
To show that inequality is always unjust because no one would choose it in advance
To abstract from cultural differences and produce universal principles valid across all societies

cards.title: Critical Legal Studies
cards.fact: CLS (1970s Harvard): law is indeterminate — for any legal outcome, a plausible legal argument can be constructed in its favour. Legal reasoning does not produce determinate outcomes; it rationalises power. Law is politics by other means.

layers.body: Critical Legal Studies scholars (Unger, Kennedy, Tushnet): law is not a neutral technical system producing determinate outcomes. For any case, competent lawyers can construct plausible legal arguments for opposed conclusions. The outcome is determined by political and ideological choices, not by legal logic. Law *legitimates* existing power arrangements by making them appear necessary and natural.

CLS methodology: 'trashing' — taking any legal doctrine and showing the contradictions beneath its surface (contract law simultaneously promotes individual freedom and enforces status; property rights protect both the wealthy's accumulations and the poor's subsistence). Law rests on *fundamental contradictions* (freedom vs security, individual vs community) that legal doctrine cannot resolve. CLS connects to Gramsci's hegemony: law makes contingent power arrangements appear inevitable. Critical Race Theory (Crenshaw, Bell) extended this to analyse how legal doctrine perpetuates racial hierarchy.

cards.deploy: [Harvard / Yale Law] The radical critique of legal reasoning — used in human rights, labour law, and constitutional interpretation to expose the political choices embedded in apparently neutral legal rules.
cards.counter: The indeterminacy thesis, if taken seriously, would undermine the rule of law entirely — if law can support any outcome, it provides no guidance. Mainstream jurisprudence argues that while some cases are hard, legal systems do produce determinate results in the vast majority of cases.

quiz.q: What is the 'legal indeterminacy' thesis in CLS?
choices: Legal outcomes are unpredictable because judges have wide discretion
For any legal conclusion, a competent legal argument can be constructed for the opposite conclusion — law does not determine outcomes; political and ideological choices do
Legal rules are so complex that ordinary citizens cannot understand or predict them
Legal systems are always changing, making prior decisions unreliable guides

cards.title: Habermas: deliberative democracy and law
cards.fact: Habermas's *Between Facts and Norms*: law is legitimate when it arises from communicatively rational discourse — all affected parties must be able to participate freely in the discourse that produces legal norms. Law co-originates with politics through deliberative democracy.

layers.body: Habermas: law faces a 'tension between facticity (law is effective because it is backed by sanctions) and validity (law is legitimate because it is rationally acceptable).' His resolution: law is legitimate when produced through *communicative rationality* — public deliberation where the only force is the force of the better argument. Citizens are both addressees of law and its authors (through democratic processes).

Habermas rejects both natural law (law derives legitimacy from morality independently of democratic process) and legal positivism (law's validity is purely procedural, indifferent to content). Instead: private autonomy (individual rights) and public autonomy (democratic self-legislation) are *co-original* — you cannot have one without the other. Rights enable democratic participation; democratic discourse produces and revises rights. This grounds both constitutional rights and democratic legitimacy simultaneously.

cards.deploy: [Frankfurt School / Oxford Law] The major democratic legitimation theory — relevant to EU democratic deficit debates, constitutional democracy, and global governance legitimacy.
cards.counter: Critics argue that Habermas's ideal speech situation — where only the force of the better argument counts — is an impossible idealisation that ignores power, strategic action, and the impossibility of fully rational public discourse.

quiz.q: What does Habermas mean by law's 'tension between facticity and validity'?
choices: The gap between what the law says and what courts actually decide

Law is effective through coercive enforcement (facticity) but only legitimate when rationally acceptable to those it governs (validity) — the challenge is to close this gap through democratic deliberation
Constitutional law (validity) often conflicts with ordinary legislation (facticity)
International law has normative authority (validity) but lacks enforcement mechanisms (facticity)

cards.title: What is psychology?
cards.fact: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour — from neurons to social groups. Its major schools are psychoanalysis, behaviourism, cognitive psychology, evolutionary psychology, and social psychology.

layers.body: Psychology's development: *psychoanalysis* (Freud, 1890s–): unconscious drives; *behaviourism* (Watson, Skinner, 1913–1960s): only observable behaviour; *humanistic* (Maslow, Rogers, 1950s): growth and self-actualisation; *cognitive* (1960s–): mental representation and information processing; *evolutionary* (1980s–): behaviour shaped by natural selection; *social* (Asch, Milgram, 1950s–): situational influences on individual behaviour.

Psychology operates at multiple levels: biological (neurons, neurotransmitters, hormones), cognitive (attention, memory, decision-making), developmental (how minds change across the lifespan), social (how others influence thought and behaviour), clinical (abnormal behaviour and mental health). A complete explanation of any behaviour typically requires multiple levels — reductionist (neuroscience) and emergent (social) approaches are complementary, not competing.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] The entry point — understanding which level and which school is relevant determines what evidence and methods apply.
cards.counter: Psychology's unit of analysis (the individual) may be too narrow for phenomena that are fundamentally social (mental health, addiction, violence). Cultural psychology and cross-cultural psychology challenge the universality of findings based on WEIRD samples.

quiz.q: What was the key argument of behaviourism against psychoanalysis?
choices: That unconscious processes are the primary drivers of all behaviour
That scientific psychology should study only observable behaviour — internal mental states (like the unconscious) are not directly observable and should be excluded from scientific explanation
That behaviour is determined by biological instincts, not learning
That social context matters more than individual mental states

cards.title: Freud: psychoanalysis
cards.fact: Freud's psychoanalytic theory: the mind is divided into conscious and unconscious; the id (instinctual drives), ego (reality principle), and superego (moral authority) are in dynamic conflict; mental illness arises from unresolved unconscious conflict.

layers.body: Freud: most mental life is unconscious — outside awareness but influencing behaviour. The *id* contains primitive drives (sex, aggression — the 'pleasure principle'). The *ego* navigates reality ('reality principle'). The *superego* internalises moral norms and punishes violations with guilt. Neurotic symptoms are the ego's compromise: expressing drive energy in disguised form that avoids superego punishment.

Ego *defence mechanisms* protect against anxiety from id impulses or superego demands: *repression* (pushing threatening thoughts out of consciousness), *projection* (attributing your own unacceptable impulses to others), *rationalisation* (constructing post-hoc justifications), *displacement* (redirecting impulse to a safer target), *sublimation* (channelling drives into socially acceptable activities). Anna Freud systematised these. Many defence mechanism concepts have been validated empirically outside the psychoanalytic framework.

cards.deploy: [Vienna / Columbia Psychoanalysis] The framework for understanding defence mechanisms, the therapeutic relationship, and unconscious motivation — despite empirical limitations, psychoanalytic concepts permeate clinical psychology and cultural theory.
cards.counter: Freud's theory is largely unfalsifiable — any disconfirming evidence can be explained away as resistance, projection, or repression. Eysenck and others showed psychoanalytic therapy was no more effective than no treatment in early studies. Modern neuroscience has validated some aspects (unconscious processing) while rejecting others (specific drive theory).

quiz.q: What is 'sublimation' as a defence mechanism?
choices: Redirecting unacceptable impulses toward socially valued activities (e.g. aggression → competitive sport)
Suppressing threatening thoughts by pushing them into unconsciousness
Projecting your own unacceptable impulses onto other people
Constructing rational justifications for impulses after the fact

cards.title: Behaviourism
cards.fact: Watson's behaviourism: psychology should study only observable behaviour, not internal mental states. Behaviour is shaped by the environment through conditioning — Pavlov's classical conditioning and Skinner's operant conditioning are the foundational mechanisms.

layers.body: Watson (1913): psychology should be a natural science of behaviour, not a science of consciousness. The basic unit: stimulus (S) → response (R). All complex behaviours are chains of conditioned S-R associations. Skinner extended this: the environment selects behaviours through reinforcement and punishment, much as natural selection selects traits.

Behaviourism dominated American psychology until the 1960s but was undone by: (1) Chomsky's critique of Skinner's *Verbal Behavior* (1959): language acquisition cannot be explained by conditioning — children generate novel grammatical sentences they have never heard; (2) Tolman's cognitive maps: rats learn the spatial layout of mazes, not just S-R chains; (3) Garcia's taste aversion: not all conditioning is equal — some associations are formed after one trial, violating the equipotentiality assumption. The *cognitive revolution* shifted psychology toward internal mental representations.

cards.deploy: [Harvard / Stanford Psychology] The foundation of applied behaviour analysis (ABA), token economy programmes, and cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) — behaviourism's practical applications outlasted its theoretical dominance.
cards.counter: Behaviourism's neglect of cognitive processes and biological constraints made it inadequate for explaining language, planning, and insight learning. But its methodological legacy — observable, measurable behaviour — remains foundational to empirical psychology.

quiz.q: What did Chomsky's critique of Skinner demonstrate about behaviourism's limits?
choices: That reinforcement cannot explain why some behaviours persist without reward
That children generate novel grammatical sentences they have never heard — language cannot be explained by conditioning, implying an innate language acquisition device beyond S-R mechanisms
That animals can solve problems through insight, not trial-and-error alone
That behaviour is primarily determined by biological drives rather than environmental contingencies

cards.title: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
cards.fact: Pavlov's classical conditioning: a neutral stimulus (bell) repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus (food) eventually elicits the conditioned response (salivation) on its own — the basis of phobias, advertising, and emotional learning.

layers.body: Pavlov: dogs salivate at food (unconditioned stimulus → unconditioned response). Bell (neutral stimulus) repeatedly precedes food → bell alone elicits salivation (*conditioned stimulus → conditioned response*). The conditioned response is an acquired prediction — the CS signals the imminent US.

*Extinction*: conditioned stimulus repeatedly without the unconditioned stimulus → conditioned response weakens. *Spontaneous recovery*: after extinction, a rest period → conditioned response reappears. *Generalisation*: stimuli similar to the CS also elicit the response (Little Albert feared all white furry objects). *Discrimination*: training the organism to distinguish CS from similar stimuli. Applications: phobias (fear conditioned to trauma-associated stimuli), advertising (product paired with attractive models), taste aversions (chemotherapy nausea conditioned to food).

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] The basis of exposure therapy (systematic desensitisation), fear learning, and advertising psychology.
cards.counter: Classical conditioning doesn't always require temporal contiguity — Garcia's taste aversion forms after hours between CS (taste) and US (illness). The biological constraints on conditioning (preparedness: snakes and spiders are more easily conditioned as fear stimuli than flowers) show that conditioning is not a universal, content-free learning mechanism.

quiz.q: What is 'spontaneous recovery' in classical conditioning?
choices: The reappearance of the unconditioned response without further training
After a conditioned response has been extinguished, a rest period leads to its reappearance — suggesting extinction involves suppression rather than unlearning
The ability of organisms to generalise conditioned responses to new stimuli
The recovery of conditioning ability after brain injury

cards.title: Operant conditioning (Skinner)
cards.fact: Skinner's operant conditioning: behaviour is shaped by its consequences — reinforcement (positive or negative) increases behaviour; punishment decreases it. Variable ratio reinforcement schedules (unpredictable rewards) produce the most persistent behaviour.

layers.body: *Positive reinforcement*: add a reward → behaviour increases (pay, praise). *Negative reinforcement*: remove an aversive stimulus → behaviour increases (taking aspirin removes pain → you take aspirin again). *Positive punishment*: add aversive stimulus → behaviour decreases. *Negative punishment*: remove a reward → behaviour decreases (take away phone). Reinforcement always *increases* behaviour; punishment always *decreases* it.

Fixed ratio: reward after every N responses (piecework) — high steady rate, short pause after reward. Variable ratio: reward after an unpredictable number of responses (slot machines) — the highest, most persistent response rate — and very resistant to extinction. Fixed interval: reward after a fixed time (salary) — scalloped pattern with low rate then burst near payday. Variable interval: reward after unpredictable time (checking email). Variable ratio produces gambling-like addictive patterns — the basis of social media and app engagement design.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] Applied in CBT, token economies, parenting, management, and app design — variable ratio schedules underpin social media addiction by design.
cards.counter: Instinctive drift (Breland & Breland): operantly conditioned behaviours can drift back toward species-typical instincts over time, showing that biology constrains what can be trained. Also, intrinsic motivation can be undermined by extrinsic rewards (overjustification effect).

quiz.q: Why do variable ratio reinforcement schedules produce the most persistent behaviour?
choices: Because the organism knows exactly when to expect the reward and prepares efficiently
Because unpredictable reward timing prevents the organism from discriminating when to stop — every response might be the one that gets rewarded, maximising response rates and resistance to extinction
Because variable rewards are larger on average than fixed rewards
Because variability reduces the biological constraints on conditioning

cards.title: The cognitive revolution
cards.fact: The cognitive revolution (1960s) replaced behaviourism with an information-processing model of the mind — the computer metaphor: the brain takes inputs, processes information through representations, and outputs behaviour.

layers.t: From black box to information processing
layers.body: The cognitive revolution restored mental representations to psychology. Neisser's *Cognitive Psychology* (1967): the mind processes information — attending to stimuli, encoding them in memory, retrieving, reasoning, problem-solving. The computer metaphor: software (cognitive processes) running on hardware (brain). This opened the study of attention, memory, perception, language, and reasoning as scientific topics.

*Attention*: selective processing — filter model (Broadbent: early selection), late selection (Deutsch-Norman). *Memory*: Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model (sensory, short-term, long-term); Baddeley's working memory (central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad). *Schemas* (Bartlett): prior knowledge structures that organise new information. *Cognitive development* (Piaget): sensorimotor → preoperational → concrete operational → formal operational — stages of increasingly sophisticated reasoning.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] The foundation of modern cognitive science, AI, and educational psychology — the information-processing model of learning underlies most instructional design.
cards.counter: Embodied cognition critics (Lakoff, Varela): the computer metaphor is misleading — cognition is not just in the head but distributed across brain, body, and environment. Cognitive processes depend on perception and action, not just internal symbol manipulation.

quiz.q: What was the core insight of the cognitive revolution against behaviourism?
choices: That emotions, not cognitions, are the primary driver of human behaviour
That internal mental representations — attention, memory, reasoning — are scientifically measurable and necessary to explain behaviour; the behaviourist 'black box' must be opened
That human behaviour is fundamentally different from animal behaviour
That the unconscious mind is more important than conscious reasoning

cards.title: Memory: types and processes
cards.fact: Memory divides into explicit (declarative: episodic + semantic) and implicit (procedural, conditioning, priming); encoding, storage, and retrieval are the three processes; memories are reconstructed on recall, not replayed — Elizabeth Loftus showed how easily they distort.

layers.body: The key insight of modern memory research: memory is not a recording but a reconstruction. Each retrieval is an active process of reassembly — it can be influenced by post-event information, leading questions, and source confusion. Loftus's misinformation effect: eyewitnesses shown post-accident footage with 'smashing' cars vs 'contacted' cars later recalled higher speeds and broken glass.

*Episodic*: autobiographical events ('what I did last Tuesday'). *Semantic*: general world knowledge ('Paris is the capital of France'). *Procedural*: motor skills ('how to ride a bike') — implicit, survives amnesia (H.M.: could learn new motor skills, couldn't form new episodic memories). *Working memory*: limited capacity online workspace (7±2 chunks: Miller 1956). The distinction between declarative (explicit, hippocampus-dependent) and non-declarative (implicit, intact in amnesia) is foundational for clinical neuropsychology.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] Applied in eyewitness testimony reform, educational design, and clinical neuropsychology — memory's reconstructive nature is a major finding for the legal system.
cards.counter: The misinformation effect's implications have been contested: some flashbulb memories (9/11, Kennedy assassination) appear more robust than ordinary reconstruction would suggest. The ecological validity of laboratory memory research for traumatic and emotionally significant memories is debated.

quiz.q: What does Loftus's misinformation effect show about memory?
choices: That memories decay exponentially over time unless rehearsed
That memories are reconstructed on recall and can be distorted by post-event information — false details inserted after the event become incorporated into the memory
That traumatic memories are encoded more strongly than ordinary ones
That implicit memory is more reliable than explicit memory

cards.title: Attachment theory (Bowlby, Ainsworth)
cards.fact: Bowlby's attachment theory: infants form emotional bonds with caregivers that are biologically based (not just learned through feeding). Ainsworth's Strange Situation identified three (later four) attachment styles: secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant, disorganised.

layers.body: Bowlby: attachment behaviour (clinging, crying, following) is a behavioural system that keeps infants close to caregivers for protection — it is adaptive, not neurotic. The caregiver serves as a *secure base* for exploration: infants venture out and return. The quality of the early attachment relationship shapes an *internal working model* of self-other relationships.

Ainsworth's Strange Situation test: observe infant's response to separation from caregiver and reunion. *Secure* (65%): distressed at separation, easily comforted at reunion. *Anxious-ambivalent* (10–15%): highly distressed, resistant at reunion. *Avoidant* (20%): minimally distressed, ignores caregiver at reunion. *Disorganised* (~15%, Main-Solomon): no consistent strategy — associated with frightening or abusive caregiving and worst outcomes. Internal working models predict adult attachment style (Hazan-Shaver), though with significant plasticity.

cards.deploy: [Yale / Oxford Psychology] The foundation of developmental psychology and child welfare policy — early attachment security predicts social, emotional, and cognitive outcomes across the lifespan.
cards.counter: Attachment theory is culturally variable: the distribution of attachment styles differs across cultures (German infants appear more avoidant by US norms — but German parenting values independence). The Strange Situation was developed and validated in Western middle-class samples.

quiz.q: What is an 'internal working model' in attachment theory?
choices: A child's model of their own cognitive development stage
A mental model of self-other relationships built from early attachment experiences — shaping expectations about whether others will be available and responsive in future relationships
The caregiver's mental model of how to respond to infant distress signals
A psychological test for measuring attachment quality in clinical settings

cards.title: Social influence: conformity and obedience
cards.fact: Social psychology's core finding: people are far more influenced by social context than they (or observers) expect — Asch's conformity experiments and Milgram's obedience experiments showed the power of the situation over individual character.

layers.body: The *fundamental attribution error*: we over-attribute behaviour to character (personality) and under-attribute it to situation. Social psychologists showed that ordinary people conform to false group consensus (Asch) and administer lethal electric shocks to strangers when ordered to by authority (Milgram) — not because they are evil, but because the *situational pressure* is powerful.

Two mechanisms of social influence: *normative* (conform to be liked, fit in, avoid social censure — you know the group is wrong but comply anyway) and *informational* (conform because you genuinely believe the group has better information — ambiguous situations). Asch: in an unambiguous line-matching task, 76% of participants conformed to an obviously wrong group consensus at least once. Dissent by one other member dramatically reduced conformity — social support breaks the spell.
