cards.deploy: [Stanford / Columbia Psychology] The foundation of political propaganda, advertising, and organisational psychology — explains crowd behaviour, obedience in organisations, and media influence.
cards.counter: The situationist conclusion (persons don't matter, situations do) was overcorrected — meta-analyses show both personality and situation matter. The 'fundamental attribution error' itself may be culturally variable: collectivist cultures make more situational attributions.

quiz.q: What is the 'fundamental attribution error' in social psychology?
choices: The tendency to blame others for negative outcomes and credit ourselves for positive ones

The tendency to over-attribute behaviour to character (dispositional factors) and under-attribute it to the situation — assuming a person's behaviour reflects stable traits rather than contextual pressures
The systematic error in perception that leads to racial and gender bias
The misattribution of emotional arousal to the wrong source

cards.title: Milgram's obedience experiments
cards.fact: Milgram (1963): 65% of participants administered what they believed were lethal 450-volt shocks to a screaming stranger when ordered by an experimenter in a white coat — obedience to authority overrode moral judgement.

layers.body: Milgram's original study: participants were told they were administering learning trials to a 'learner' (a confederate) — with shocks escalating for each wrong answer. The experimenter (authority) instructed them to continue despite screaming and eventually silence. 65% went to 450 volts (marked 'Danger — Severe Shock'). Before the study, psychologists predicted <1% would reach this level — they massively underestimated situational power.

layers.t: Conditions that increase and decrease obedience
layers.body: Obedience *decreased* when: authority figure left the room (distance), participant was in the same room as the learner (proximity increased moral discomfort), a peer also refused (social support), or when participant witnessed another person refuse. *Increased* when: authority was in the same room, learner was remote, settings were more official/prestigious. Milgram's agentic state theory: people in hierarchies shift moral responsibility to the authority — they become instruments rather than agents. Applied to: Nazi genocide, Abu Ghraib, corporate misconduct.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Columbia Psychology] The most important finding in social psychology for understanding obedience, authority, and moral disengagement — applied in military psychology, organisational ethics, and genocide studies.
cards.counter: The replication of Milgram has been partial and contested; full replication is ethically prohibited. Some scholars (Haslam, Reicher) argue Milgram's participants weren't blindly obedient but actively identified with the scientific mission — obedience was identity-driven, not authority-driven.

quiz.q: What did Milgram's 'agentic state' theory propose about obedience?
choices: That obedient participants felt powerful and in control of the situation
That participants shifted moral responsibility to the authority figure — entering an 'agentic state' where they see themselves as instruments of authority rather than autonomous moral agents
That conformity to authority is a product of individual personality traits
That authority figures activate the survival instinct, overriding rational decision-making

cards.title: Cognitive dissonance
cards.fact: Festinger's cognitive dissonance: holding contradictory cognitions produces psychological discomfort — which motivates attitude change, rationalisation, or avoidance of disconfirming information to restore consistency.

layers.body: Festinger: *cognitions* (beliefs, attitudes, behaviours) that are inconsistent produce *dissonance* — an unpleasant tension that motivates reduction. Three reduction strategies: (1) change one of the cognitions to make them consistent; (2) add new cognitions that reduce the conflict; (3) reduce the importance of one cognition.

The $1/$20 experiment: participants paid $1 to tell the next participant a boring task was interesting subsequently rated it as more interesting than participants paid $20. Why? $20 provides sufficient justification for lying — no dissonance. $1 doesn't — participants reduce dissonance by actually changing their attitude toward the task. *Post-decision dissonance*: after choosing between two attractive options, we upgrade the chosen option and degrade the rejected one — reducing regret. *Effort justification*: initiation rituals that require suffering produce greater group loyalty (hazing, medical training).

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] Explains post-hoc rationalisation, confirmation bias, cult persistence after failed prophecy, and consumer brand loyalty.
cards.counter: Self-perception theory (Bem): cognitive dissonance may not involve internal tension — people simply observe their own behaviour and infer their attitudes ('I ate broccoli so I must like broccoli'). The two theories predict the same outcomes but invoke different processes; distinguishing them experimentally is difficult.

quiz.q: In the $1/$20 experiment, why did the $1 group rate the boring task as more enjoyable?
choices: They had more time to complete the task and were therefore less bored
They lacked sufficient external justification for lying, so they reduced dissonance by genuinely changing their attitude — convincing themselves the task was interesting
The smaller payment created a sense of intrinsic motivation and engagement
Participants paid $20 were aware of the study's true purpose and rated tasks lower

cards.title: Big Five personality traits
cards.fact: The OCEAN model: Openness to experience, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — the five major dimensions of personality that predict behaviour, wellbeing, and life outcomes. Stable across cultures and partially heritable.

layers.body: *Openness*: curiosity, creativity, aesthetic sensitivity. *Conscientiousness*: self-discipline, organisation, goal-directedness (the strongest predictor of academic and job performance). *Extraversion*: sociability, assertiveness, positive affect. *Agreeableness*: cooperativeness, trust, altruism. *Neuroticism*: emotional instability, anxiety, tendency to negative affect. Each is a continuum, not a type.

Twin studies: Big Five traits are 40–60% heritable. Traits are fairly stable across adulthood but show characteristic mean-level changes: agreeableness and conscientiousness rise; neuroticism declines (the 'maturity principle'). Extraversion and neuroticism are the most strongly linked to wellbeing. Conscientiousness predicts longevity, job performance, and relationship quality. Social media personality tests (Cambridge Analytica's psychographic profiling) used Big Five data for targeted political advertising — raising ethics concerns about personality-targeted manipulation.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Oxford Psychology] The standard personality framework for personnel selection, clinical assessment, and behavioural prediction — any discussion of individual differences uses OCEAN.
cards.counter: The Big Five is derived from factor analysis of English-language personality adjectives — cross-cultural validity is imperfect. Some non-Western cultures show different factor structures. The lexical hypothesis (personality is captured in language) may miss biologically grounded traits not yet in the English dictionary.

quiz.q: Which Big Five trait is the strongest predictor of job performance and academic achievement?
choices: Openness to experience — because creativity and intellectual engagement drive performance
Conscientiousness — self-discipline, organisation, and goal-directedness predict performance across many domains
Extraversion — because social skills and assertiveness are essential in most jobs
Agreeableness — because cooperation and trust are valued in team settings

cards.title: Motivation: Maslow and self-determination theory
cards.fact: Maslow's hierarchy of needs (1943): physiological → safety → belonging → esteem → self-actualisation. Self-determination theory (Deci-Ryan): intrinsic motivation (autonomy, competence, relatedness) is more sustaining than extrinsic reward.

layers.body: Maslow: human needs form a hierarchy — lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones become motivating. Physiological (food, sleep) → Safety (security, stability) → Belonging (love, connection) → Esteem (achievement, recognition) → Self-actualisation (realising potential). While the strict hierarchy is not empirically supported, the framework captures the qualitatively different character of basic vs growth motives.

Deci and Ryan's *Self-Determination Theory* (SDT): three universal psychological needs — *autonomy* (acting from one's own values), *competence* (effective engagement), and *relatedness* (meaningful connection). When these are satisfied, intrinsic motivation flourishes. *Overjustification effect*: adding extrinsic rewards (money, grades) to an intrinsically motivating activity can undermine intrinsic interest — the person shifts from 'I'm doing this because I enjoy it' to 'I'm doing this for the reward.' Implications: management practices that over-incentivise performance can crowd out intrinsic motivation.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] Applied in education (intrinsic motivation in learning), management (employee motivation), and health behaviour (autonomous motivation for exercise predicts adherence).
cards.counter: Maslow's hierarchy lacks empirical support: the specific ordering of needs is not universal and deficiency motivation (lower needs) and growth motivation (higher needs) can coexist. The 'self-actualisation' concept is poorly defined and reflects Western individualist values.

quiz.q: What is the 'overjustification effect' in motivation research?
choices: The tendency to over-reward employees, leading to escalating wage demands
Adding extrinsic rewards to an already intrinsically motivating activity reduces intrinsic interest — the person shifts attribution from enjoyment to reward
The way high expectations create self-fulfilling prophecies of high performance
The effect of social comparison on reducing motivation through unfavorable comparisons

cards.title: Attribution theory
cards.fact: Attribution theory: we explain others' behaviour as due to their dispositions (internal causes) or the situation (external causes). The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to over-attribute others' behaviour to character while under-attributing our own to situation.

layers.body: Heider (1958): we attribute behaviour to *internal* (dispositional: personality, ability, effort) or *external* (situational: luck, social pressure, environmental factors) causes. *Locus of control* (Rotter): people differ in whether they generally attribute outcomes to internal or external causes — internal locus predicts higher achievement and better health.

*Actor-observer bias*: as an actor, I attribute my own behaviour to the situation ('I was rude because I was stressed'); as an observer of others, I attribute their behaviour to their character ('she is a rude person'). This asymmetry: observers lack information about the actor's situation and focus on the visible person (not the invisible context). *Self-serving bias*: attributing successes to internal causes ('I worked hard') and failures to external ones ('the exam was unfair') — protects self-esteem.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] Applied in conflict resolution (misattribution drives escalation), clinical psychology (depressive attributional style), and social policy (blaming the poor for poverty).
cards.counter: The fundamental attribution error is stronger in individualist cultures — collectivist cultures (East Asian) show more situational attributions, suggesting the error is culturally mediated, not a universal cognitive bias.

quiz.q: What is the 'actor-observer asymmetry' in attribution?
choices: Actors perceive the world differently from observers due to different angles of view
When we observe our own behaviour we tend to attribute it to the situation; when we observe others' behaviour we tend to attribute it to their character — creating systematic asymmetric explanations
Actors are more accurate than observers in attributing the causes of behaviour
Observers always attribute positive outcomes to actors' ability and negative ones to bad luck

cards.title: Developmental psychology: Piaget
cards.fact: Piaget's stage theory: cognitive development proceeds through four stages — sensorimotor (0–2), preoperational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11), formal operational (11+) — driven by assimilation and accommodation as children adapt schemas to experience.

layers.body: Piaget's fundamental insight: children think *qualitatively differently* from adults — they are not simply less informed but use different cognitive structures. *Schemas*: mental frameworks for understanding the world. *Assimilation*: fitting new experience into existing schemas. *Accommodation*: modifying schemas to fit new experience. *Equilibration*: the driving force — resolving the tension between assimilation and accommodation.

*Object permanence* (sensorimotor, ~8–12 months): the understanding that objects continue to exist when not perceived — tested by hiding a toy. *Egocentrism* (preoperational): difficulty taking another's perspective — the three mountains task. *Conservation* (concrete operational): understanding that quantity doesn't change when form changes — water poured between differently shaped containers. *Formal operations*: systematic hypothetical reasoning, abstract thought. Vygotsky's challenge: learning is socially mediated — the Zone of Proximal Development (what you can do with guidance) precedes independent achievement.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] The foundational model for educational psychology — understanding what reasoning children at each stage can and cannot do guides teaching.
cards.counter: Piaget underestimated infants' and young children's competencies — looking-time methods show object permanence appears earlier than Piaget thought. Stages are more continuous and context-dependent than the strict stage theory implies. Neo-Piagetian theorists retain the insight while revising the mechanisms.

quiz.q: What does Piaget mean by 'conservation'?
choices: The child's ability to conserve learned material in long-term memory
The understanding that quantity remains constant even when its appearance changes — e.g. water poured into a taller container is the same amount, not more
The ability to maintain a consistent self-concept despite changing experiences
Environmental preservation attitudes that develop in the concrete operational stage

cards.title: Neuroplasticity
cards.fact: Neuroplasticity: the brain changes its structure and function in response to experience — Hebb's rule: 'neurons that fire together wire together'; synaptic connections strengthen through use and weaken through disuse.

layers.body: The classical view: the brain is fixed after development. Modern view: the brain retains substantial plasticity throughout life. *Synaptic plasticity*: individual synapse strengths change with use (long-term potentiation [LTP] and long-term depression [LTD]). *Structural plasticity*: new dendritic spines, synapses, and even new neurons (neurogenesis in hippocampus) form in response to learning and experience.

*Critical periods*: windows in development when the brain is especially receptive — language acquisition, binocular vision (Hubel-Wiesel: depriving one eye in kittens during the critical period causes permanent vision loss in that eye). After critical periods, plasticity decreases but never disappears. London taxi drivers: the posterior hippocampus (spatial navigation) is larger than matched controls — and grows during the Knowledge (the memorisation test). Adult learning causes measurable structural brain changes, grounding the case for lifelong education.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] The neuroscience foundation for learning, rehabilitation (stroke, TBI), and educational policy — the brain is never 'finished' but responds to environment throughout life.
cards.counter: The popular interpretation of neuroplasticity ('you can rewire your brain for success') is often oversimplified. Most studies show modest, specific effects; generalised 'brain training' programmes (N-back tasks) often don't transfer to real-world cognitive performance.

quiz.q: What does Hebb's rule ('neurons that fire together wire together') imply for learning?
choices: That cognitive load should be minimised to preserve neural resources
That repeated co-activation of neurons strengthens their synaptic connection — learning and memory form through use-dependent changes in synaptic strength
That emotional arousal is necessary for long-term memory formation
That the hippocampus is the only brain region involved in memory

cards.title: Wellbeing: hedonic vs eudaimonic
cards.fact: Hedonic wellbeing: subjective wellbeing (SWB) = high positive affect + low negative affect + high life satisfaction (Diener). Eudaimonic wellbeing: flourishing through meaning, growth, and relationships (Seligman's PERMA: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Achievement).

layers.body: Hedonic: wellbeing as pleasure and life satisfaction — measured by the Satisfaction With Life Scale. Eudaimonic (Aristotle's eudaimonia): wellbeing as living well — realising human potential, relationships, meaning, virtue. Kahneman distinguishes *experienced utility* (in-the-moment affect, measured by Day Reconstruction Method) from *remembered utility* (global satisfaction ratings) — they often diverge due to the peak-end rule.

The Easterlin paradox: within a country at a given time, richer people are happier; but over time, rising average income does not raise average happiness. Recent reanalysis (Stevenson-Wolfers): the paradox may be a statistical artifact — happiness does rise with income throughout the income range, but diminishing returns set in. Kahneman and Deaton: day-to-day emotional wellbeing plateaus around $75,000 (US, 2010); but life satisfaction continues rising with income.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] The conceptual foundation for happiness economics, positive psychology, and wellbeing policy — used by UK Office for National Statistics, OECD 'Better Life Index', and Bhutan's GNH.
cards.counter: Wellbeing research relies heavily on self-report — which is susceptible to framing, mood, and cultural norms for expressing happiness. Nordic countries score high on life satisfaction; but survey norms for expressing satisfaction differ, making cross-national comparisons problematic.

quiz.q: What is the 'peak-end rule' in Kahneman's wellbeing research?
choices: Wellbeing peaks at middle age and declines at the end of life

People evaluate past experiences largely by their most intense moment (peak) and how they ended — not the average — so duration neglect causes short painful experiences to be rated the same as longer ones if the ending is the same
Happiness peaks when both income and social relationships are maximised simultaneously
The first and last items in a sequence are remembered better than those in the middle

cards.title: The replication crisis
cards.fact: The Open Science Collaboration (2015): only 36–39% of replicated psychology findings replicated at the same effect size — social priming, power pose, ego depletion, and many other high-profile findings failed to replicate.

layers.body: The 2015 OSC study replicated 100 published psychology findings: only ~39% had comparable effect sizes to the originals. High-profile casualties: social priming (subliminally activating 'professor' → better test scores — largely failed), power pose (Amy Cuddy: expanding body posture → testosterone, confidence — failed large replication), ego depletion (willpower is a limited resource — failed registered replications).

Causes: *publication bias* (journals publish positive results — the file drawer); *p-hacking* (testing multiple analyses until p < .05); *HARKing* (hypothesising after results known); *small samples* (underpowered studies); *flexibility in analysis* (garden of forking paths). Remedies: pre-registration (specify hypotheses and analyses before data collection), open data and materials, registered reports, larger samples, multi-site replications. The crisis has transformed methodology — effect sizes matter more than p-values; open science norms are spreading.

cards.deploy: [Stanford / Harvard Psychology] Essential for evaluating any psychological claim — the replication crisis should raise scepticism about single small-sample studies with surprising findings.
cards.counter: The 'crisis' has been exaggerated: not all findings fail to replicate, and the affected areas are concentrated in social and cognitive psychology, less so in clinical, cognitive neuroscience, and developmental psychology. The OSC's binary 'replicated/not' metric is crude.

quiz.q: What is 'p-hacking' in psychological research and why does it inflate false positives?
choices: Hacking into p-value databases to adjust published statistics

Running multiple analyses until finding p < .05 — by testing many combinations, the probability of finding a 'significant' result by chance alone rises above the nominal 5%, inflating false positive rates
Adjusting sample sizes mid-study to achieve the desired level of significance
Using powerful computers to run Monte Carlo simulations of null hypothesis distributions

cards.title: Banerjee & Duflo: Good Economics for Hard Times
cards.fact: Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo argue that on migration, trade and growth the textbook intuitions are often wrong — and that good policy should follow the evidence and protect people's dignity, not just GDP.
cards.detail: Written by the 2019 Nobel laureates who pioneered randomised trials in development, 'Good Economics for Hard Times' (2019) turns the empirical, humble method on the rich world's biggest fights. Its through-line: economies are 'sticky', not the frictionless markets of the textbook, so people and resources don't smoothly reallocate. Migration: more migrants rarely depress local wages — labour markets don't behave like a simple supply curve, and migrants add demand as well as supply (Card's Mariel boatlift study). Trade: Ricardian gains from trade are real but smaller than advertised, and the losses fall hard and permanently on specific places and workers who cannot just move to the next opportunity. Growth: nobody reliably knows how to manufacture GDP growth in rich countries, so chasing it by cutting taxes for the top is a bad bet. Preferences aren't fixed and people aren't only money-maximisers — respect, identity and dignity drive behaviour, which is why cash transfers don't make people lazy and why redistribution done well can restore agency. The recurring move is to replace a confident model with a measured fact.
cards.deploy: Use it to puncture three 'common sense' claims at once — that immigrants undercut wages, that free trade is painless, and that tax cuts buy growth — by pointing to the evidence that labour markets are sticky and the gains/pains are unevenly distributed.
cards.counter: Critics note the book leans on a curated set of studies and that some findings (e.g. the wage effects of immigration) remain genuinely contested — George Borjas reads the same Mariel data as showing real wage losses for low-skilled locals. Growth-pessimism is also disputed: Robert Gordon sees a true innovation slowdown, while techno-optimists expect AI to lift productivity, so 'we can't engineer growth' may be premature.

quiz.q: What is the central recurring claim Banerjee and Duflo make about how real economies behave?
choices: Markets clear instantly, so policy should never interfere
Economies are 'sticky' — people and resources do not smoothly reallocate, so shocks land hard on specific places and workers
Growth is easy to engineer through tax cuts for high earners
Money is the only thing that reliably motivates behaviour

quiz.q: On immigration, what do Banerjee and Duflo argue the evidence shows about its effect on local wages?
choices: Immigration sharply and permanently lowers wages for everyone
More migrants rarely depress local wages much — labour markets aren't a simple supply curve, and migrants add demand as well as supply
Immigration only affects wages in developing countries
Wages always rise immediately when migrants arrive

quiz.q: The book accepts that free trade produces net gains but stresses one big problem with them. Which?
choices: The gains are illusory and trade always makes a country poorer
The gains are large but accrue only to foreigners
The gains are smaller than advertised and the losses fall hard and permanently on specific places and workers
Trade gains can only be measured decades later

quiz.q: Banerjee and Duflo cite a famous natural experiment — a sudden wave of Cuban migrants to Miami in 1980 — to argue immigration need not cut local wages. What is this study commonly called? (Two words.)
In what year was 'Good Economics for Hard Times' published?

cards.title: 125,000 migrants hit Miami — and wages barely moved
cards.fact: In 1980 the Mariel boatlift swelled Miami's workforce by about 7% almost overnight, yet David Card found no measurable fall in the wages or jobs of low-skilled locals.
cards.detail: Over six months in 1980, around 125,000 Cubans arrived in Miami after Castro briefly opened the port of Mariel. Roughly half stayed, enlarging the city's labour force by about 7% — and its low-skilled labour force by far more — in an instant. The textbook supply-and-demand prediction is obvious: a surge in supply should push wages down. David Card's classic 1990 study compared Miami's low-skilled and Black workers against similar workers in Atlanta, Houston and other cities, and found essentially no negative effect on wages or unemployment. Banerjee and Duflo use it as their headline example that labour markets are 'sticky', not the smooth supply curve of the textbook: migrants spend money too, adding demand as well as supply, and local firms and workers adjust in ways a one-market diagram misses.
cards.deploy: Drop this when someone treats 'more workers ⇒ lower wages' as automatic — a natural experiment that should have shown the textbook effect plainly, and didn't.
cards.counter: Contested. George Borjas (2015) re-cut the same data to a narrow slice — non-Hispanic male high-school dropouts — and reported sharp wage losses; Peri and Yasenov rebutted that the slice is tiny and noisy. The honest reading is that the wage effect is small, not that it is provably zero.

quiz.q: What makes the Mariel boatlift such a powerful natural experiment about immigration and wages?
choices: Migrants were randomly assigned to different US cities
A sudden ~7% jump in Miami's workforce should have shown the textbook wage drop plainly — yet Card found essentially none
Wages were tracked for fifty years afterward
The migrants were all high-skilled professionals

quiz.q: Banerjee and Duflo read the Mariel result as evidence that labour markets are…
choices: perfectly competitive and fast-clearing
'sticky' — migrants add demand as well as supply, and adjustment is messier than a single supply-demand diagram
irrelevant to wage determination
driven mainly by the minimum wage

quiz.q: Which economist re-analysed the Mariel data on a narrow subgroup and argued it did show wage losses?

cards.title: The China Shock: the towns hit by trade never bounced back
cards.fact: Autor, Dorn and Hanson found Chinese import competition cost the US on the order of a million-plus manufacturing jobs — and the local labour markets that took the hit stayed depressed for over a decade.
cards.detail: The gains-from-trade theorem says open trade makes a country richer on net, with displaced workers moving to new opportunities. The 'China Shock' studies (Autor, Dorn & Hanson, starting with their 2013 'China Syndrome' paper) tracked what actually happened as Chinese imports surged from 1990 to 2007. Net gains were real — but the adjustment story failed. Estimates run from about one million manufacturing jobs lost directly to roughly 2.4 million once knock-on effects are counted, and crucially the regions that lost factories did not recover: unemployment stayed high, wages stayed low, and disability rolls rose for ten-plus years. Workers mostly did not pack up and move to booming areas. Banerjee and Duflo use it to show trade's gains are diffuse and its pains are concentrated, permanent and place-based — which is why 'the winners can compensate the losers' rarely happens in practice.
cards.deploy: Use it against the glib 'free trade lifts everyone' line: the gains are real but thin and spread out, while the losses pile onto specific towns that never recover.
cards.counter: Cheaper imported goods and stronger US export sectors did benefit consumers and other workers broadly — those gains just don't show up in one factory town. Some economists also argue automation destroyed more manufacturing jobs than trade did, so the 'China Shock' label can be overstated.

quiz.q: What did the China Shock studies show that contradicts the simple gains-from-trade story?
choices: Trade made the US poorer overall
Displaced workers and hard-hit towns did NOT smoothly recover — unemployment and depressed wages persisted for over a decade
Chinese imports had no effect on US manufacturing
Every laid-off worker quickly found a higher-paying job

quiz.q: Why does this finding undercut the 'winners can compensate the losers' defence of free trade?
choices: Because trade produced no winners at all
Because the losses were concentrated, place-based and permanent, while the gains were diffuse — so compensation rarely actually happened
Because compensation is illegal under WTO rules
Because the losers were wealthier than the winners

quiz.q: Roughly how many total US manufacturing jobs do the higher China Shock estimates attribute to Chinese import competition (in millions)?

cards.title: Give poor people cash and they don't stop working (or drink it away)
cards.fact: Across a string of randomised trials, giving poor households unconditional cash did not make them work less or spend more on alcohol and tobacco — directly refuting the 'lazy welfare recipient' stereotype.
cards.detail: A persistent argument against helping the poor with cash is that handouts breed idleness and vice. The evidence says otherwise. Banerjee, Hanna, Kreindler and Olken (2017) reviewed seven randomised cash-transfer programmes and found no systematic drop in work. GiveDirectly's randomised trials in Kenya (Haushofer & Shapiro, 2016) found recipients raised their assets, consumption and psychological wellbeing — with no increase in spending on alcohol or tobacco. Banerjee and Duflo lean on this to make a broader point: people are not simple money-maximisers waiting for an excuse to quit, and treating the poor as suspects designs bad, demeaning policy. Cash respects agency, and the evidence — not the stereotype — should drive the rules.
cards.deploy: Bring this when someone assumes welfare or basic income will 'make people lazy' — the randomised evidence repeatedly fails to find the work disincentive the stereotype predicts.
cards.counter: Most of the strongest evidence is from poor countries and from time-limited transfers; a permanent, universal income in a rich economy is less tested. Finland's UBI trial, for instance, improved recipients' wellbeing but produced only a small employment effect — encouraging, not decisive.

quiz.q: What does the randomised evidence on unconditional cash transfers consistently find?
choices: Recipients stop working and spend the money on alcohol
No systematic fall in work and no rise in alcohol/tobacco spending — contradicting the 'lazy recipient' stereotype
Recipients become permanently dependent on aid
Cash transfers only help if tied to strict work requirements

quiz.q: What broader point do Banerjee and Duflo draw from the cash-transfer evidence?
choices: People are pure money-maximisers who need monitoring
Treating the poor as suspects produces bad, demeaning policy — respecting agency works, and evidence should beat stereotype
Only conditional aid can ever change behaviour
Cash transfers are too expensive to ever scale

quiz.q: Which organisation's randomised cash-transfer trials in Kenya are a key part of this evidence base?

cards.title: Most growth comes from the part we can't measure
cards.fact: Solow found that roughly seven-eighths of the rise in US output per worker-hour from 1909 to 1949 came not from more machines or workers, but from a residual he labelled 'technical change'.
cards.detail: When Robert Solow decomposed US growth (1957), he expected capital — more and better machines per worker — to explain most of the rise in output per hour. It didn't. Only about one-eighth (~12.5%) traced to capital deepening; the other seven-eighths (~87.5%) was a leftover his equations couldn't account for, which he attributed to 'technical change'. Economists now call this leftover the Solow residual, or total factor productivity. It is less an explanation than a confession: it is the measure of our ignorance about why economies actually grow — better ideas, organisation, and know-how that no capital-and-labour bookkeeping captures. This finding is exactly why later theorists (Romer) tried to drag technology inside the model rather than leave it as a residual.
cards.deploy: Use it to deflate any growth story built purely on 'invest more capital': the historical record says the bulk of growth is the stuff we can't directly measure — ideas and know-how.
cards.counter: The residual is a measure of ignorance, not a thing: it sweeps in mismeasurement, human capital, and reallocation. Calling it 'technical change' names the gap without explaining it — which is the whole motivation for endogenous growth theory.

quiz.q: What did Solow's growth decomposition reveal about the source of US growth 1909–1949?
choices: Almost all of it came from accumulating more capital per worker
Only about an eighth came from more capital — the rest was an unexplained 'residual' attributed to technical change
Growth was driven entirely by population increase
Output per hour did not actually rise over the period

quiz.q: Why is the Solow residual sometimes called 'a measure of our ignorance'?
choices: Because Solow admitted his data were fabricated
Because it is the leftover growth the capital-and-labour model can't explain — a gap labelled, not understood
Because it can never be positive
Because it only applies to the United States

quiz.q: Roughly what percentage of the growth did Solow attribute to the residual (technical change)?

cards.title: The Fed let a third of the money supply vanish
cards.fact: Friedman and Schwartz showed the US money stock collapsed by about a third between 1929 and 1933 as some 9,000 banks failed — and argued Federal Reserve passivity turned a recession into the Great Depression.
cards.detail: In 'A Monetary History of the United States' (1963), Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz assembled a century of monetary data and zeroed in on 1929–1933. As waves of bank runs hit, roughly 9,000 banks failed and the money supply shrank by about a third. The Federal Reserve — created precisely to be a lender of last resort — mostly stood aside. Their verdict: the Depression was not proof that capitalism is inherently unstable but a man-made monetary catastrophe; an active Fed could have stemmed the collapse. The finding reshaped macroeconomics and central banking — and Ben Bernanke, a Depression scholar, invoked it directly when the Fed flooded the system with liquidity in 2008, telling Friedman at his 90th birthday: 'You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.'
cards.deploy: Cite it whenever a slump is blamed on 'markets failing': the canonical case study says the central bank's inaction, not the market, did the damage — and that the lesson was applied in 2008.
cards.counter: Keynesians (and later Bernanke himself) argue money wasn't the whole story — collapsing demand, debt deflation and broken credit channels mattered too. Pure monetarism over-credits the money stock and under-weights the real economy's downward spiral.

quiz.q: What did Friedman and Schwartz identify as a key driver of the Great Depression's depth?
choices: Excessive government spending in the 1920s
A collapse of about a third in the money supply that the Federal Reserve failed to prevent
A sudden surge in the money supply causing hyperinflation
The gold standard being abandoned too early

quiz.q: Why does this finding matter for 2008?
choices: It showed central banks should never intervene in crises
Bernanke, a Depression scholar, used the lesson to justify flooding the system with liquidity rather than standing aside
It proved fiscal stimulus is always ineffective
It led the Fed to raise interest rates aggressively

quiz.q: Approximately how many US banks failed during 1929–1933 according to the account?

cards.title: One city, one border, two destinies: Nogales
cards.fact: Nogales is a single city split by the US–Mexico border. Same desert, same climate, same founding population — yet the Arizona side is about three times richer than the Sonora side.
cards.detail: Acemoglu and Robinson open 'Why Nations Fail' with the perfect natural experiment. Nogales straddles the US–Mexico line: the people on both sides share ancestry, food, music and a brutal desert climate. Hold geography and culture constant, and what's left is institutions. North of the fence: higher incomes (roughly triple), longer lives, better schools, the rule of law, and accountable government. South of the fence: lower incomes, worse health and schooling, more crime and corruption. Since nothing physical differs across the street, the gap can only come from the rules — secure property rights, broad political voice, reliable courts — that the two national systems impose. It's the book's whole thesis compressed into one town you can walk across.
cards.deploy: The cleanest one-line rebuttal to geographic or cultural determinism about poverty: identical place and people, opposite outcomes — so the cause must be institutions.
cards.counter: A single vivid case can't prove a general law: critics like Jeffrey Sachs argue geography and disease still matter hugely at the global scale, and the inclusive/extractive labels risk being defined by the prosperity they're meant to explain.

quiz.q: Why is the Nogales example such a clean test of the institutions theory?
choices: The two halves have completely different climates and ethnic groups
It holds geography and culture constant — same desert, same founding population — so the income gap must come from differing institutions
It compares a city to a rural region
Both sides are governed by the same country

quiz.q: Roughly how much richer is the Arizona side of Nogales than the Sonora side?
choices: About 10% richer
About the same
About three times richer
About fifty times richer

quiz.q: Which economist is named as the leading critic, arguing geography still matters at the global scale?

cards.title: The Nobel-laureate hedge fund that blew up
cards.fact: Long-Term Capital Management — with Black–Scholes co-creators Scholes and Merton on its board — used vast leverage and lost about $4.6 billion in months in 1998, forcing a $3.6 billion Fed-organised bailout.
cards.detail: LTCM was the dream team: founded 1994, its board included Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the 1997 Nobel for option-pricing theory. The fund made highly-leveraged bets that small pricing gaps would converge, its models calibrated on historical volatility. The models assumed those bets were nearly independent and that extreme moves were vanishingly rare. Then in 1998 Russia defaulted, correlations across the world snapped to one, and 'impossible' losses cascaded. The fund lost about $4.6 billion in under four months; with derivative positions in the trillions, its collapse threatened the whole financial system, and the New York Fed organised a roughly $3.6 billion rescue by fourteen banks. The lesson sits right beside the Black–Scholes card: a model is only as good as its assumption that the past describes the tails — and it usually doesn't.
cards.deploy: The go-to cautionary tale for over-trusting elegant models: even the people who invented the maths were sunk by the rare event their model treated as negligible.
cards.counter: Some argue the failure was leverage and liquidity, not the option-pricing maths as such — LTCM could have survived its positions with less borrowing and more capital. The models flagged risk; human bets on their precision did the damage.

quiz.q: What broke LTCM's models in 1998?
choices: A bug in the Black–Scholes formula
Russia's default made supposedly independent bets move together and triggered 'impossible' losses the models treated as near-impossible
Regulators banned its trading strategy
Interest rates fell to zero

quiz.q: What is the broader lesson the LTCM collapse teaches about quantitative models?
choices: Models with Nobel laureates behind them are always safe
A model is only as good as its assumption that past data describe extreme 'tail' events — and they usually don't
Leverage eliminates risk if the model is correct
Diversification guarantees survival in a crisis

quiz.q: Roughly how large (in $ billion) was the Fed-organised rescue of LTCM?

cards.title: Smith's pin factory: 1 pin alone, 4,800 together
cards.fact: Adam Smith reckoned a lone untrained worker could barely make one pin a day — but ten workers splitting the job into about eighteen steps turned out roughly 48,000 a day, some 4,800 each.
cards.detail: On the first page of The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith reaches for a humble example to explain why nations grow rich: the pin. A single worker, ignorant of the trade and its machinery, 'could scarce make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty.' But break pin-making into its parts — one draws the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts, a fourth points, a fifth grinds the head, and so on through about eighteen distinct operations — and ten people could make upwards of 48,000 pins a day. That's roughly a four-thousand-fold leap in output per person from nothing but reorganisation. The division of labour, Smith argued, is the original engine of productivity: specialisation breeds dexterity, saves the time lost switching tasks, and invites machinery. The catch he also saw: a man who spends his life pointing pins may have his mind dulled by it.
cards.deploy: The founding illustration of why specialisation — not just working harder — drives wealth; reach for it to explain productivity gains from the assembly line to the global supply chain.
cards.counter: Smith himself warned of the dark side later in the book: extreme division of labour can make work mindless and the worker 'as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become' — an early statement of alienation Marx would amplify.

quiz.q: What point does Smith's pin factory illustrate?
choices: That machines always outperform human workers
That dividing work into specialised steps multiplies output per person enormously — the division of labour drives productivity
That pin-making was the most important industry in 1776
That trade between nations lowers prices

quiz.q: What downside of extreme division of labour did Smith himself warn about?
choices: It raises prices for consumers
It can make work mindless and dull the worker's mind — a precursor to the idea of alienation
It always leads to unemployment
It makes nations dependent on imports

quiz.q: Roughly how many pins a day could ten specialised workers make, in Smith's example?

cards.title: The top 1% took 95% of the recovery
cards.fact: Emmanuel Saez's data show the top 1% of US earners captured about 95% of all income gains in the first years of the post-2008 recovery (2009–2012).
cards.detail: After the 2008 crash the US economy began growing again — but the gains went almost entirely to the top. Using tax records, economist Emmanuel Saez calculated that between 2009 and 2012 the top 1% of households captured about 95% of the rise in total income, while the bottom 99% saw their incomes barely move. This is the kind of statistic Joseph Stiglitz marshals to argue that inequality is a policy choice, not a natural market outcome: a 'recovery' can be real in the aggregate yet leave almost everyone behind, depending on the rules governing pay, taxation, and finance. It reframes the headline 'the economy is growing' question into 'growing for whom?'
cards.deploy: Deploy it against 'a rising tide lifts all boats': here the tide rose and 95% of the lift went to the top 1% — aggregate growth and broad prosperity are not the same thing.
cards.counter: The figure is sensitive to the window: measured over a longer recovery the top 1%'s share of gains falls well below 95%, and pre-tax tax-record income misses transfers and benefits that cushion the bottom. Greg Mankiw also argues top incomes substantially reflect productivity, not just rule-rigging.

quiz.q: What did Saez find about the early post-2008 US recovery (2009–2012)?
choices: Income gains were shared roughly equally across households
The top 1% captured about 95% of the income gains, while the bottom 99% barely moved
The bottom 99% gained more than the top 1%
Total income did not grow at all

quiz.q: Why does Stiglitz use figures like this?
choices: To argue that aggregate growth automatically benefits everyone
To argue inequality is shaped by policy choices — a real recovery can leave almost everyone behind depending on the rules
To prove that taxes should be cut for top earners
To show that recessions hurt the rich most

quiz.q: Which economist's tax-record analysis produced the '95% of gains to the top 1%' figure?

cards.title: The paper rejected three times — then won a Nobel
cards.fact: Akerlof's 'The Market for Lemons', which founded the economics of asymmetric information, was rejected by three journals as trivial or wrong before it was finally published — and helped win him the Nobel.
cards.detail: George Akerlof's 1970 paper showed something the prevailing theory had missed: when sellers know more than buyers about quality — as with used cars, where the bad ones are 'lemons' — the bad can drive out the good, and a market can shrink or collapse even when willing buyers and sellers exist. Reviewers didn't see it. Three journals turned it down: some said the argument was trivial, one said that if it were correct economics would have to change and therefore it must be wrong. The Quarterly Journal of Economics finally published it. It became one of the most-cited papers in all of economics, opened the entire field of information economics, and was central to Akerlof's 2001 Nobel Prize (shared with Spence and Stiglitz). The episode is a double treat: it teaches adverse selection and how badly gatekeepers can misjudge a genuinely new idea.
cards.deploy: Use it both ways: to explain why information gaps can kill otherwise viable markets (insurance, used cars, credit), and as a caution that peer review and 'expert consensus' can flatly reject ideas that later reshape a field.
cards.counter: Real markets evolve institutions — warranties, certifications, reputation, inspections — that blunt the lemons problem, so total collapse is rarer than the bare model implies. The rejection story is also partly the system working: extraordinary claims do warrant scrutiny, even when the scrutineers get it wrong.

quiz.q: What does the 'market for lemons' show?
choices: That used cars are always overpriced
When sellers know more about quality than buyers, bad goods can drive out good ones and the market can shrink or collapse
That buyers always have more information than sellers
That markets always reach efficient outcomes

quiz.q: What happened to Akerlof's paper before it was published?
choices: It was an instant hit accepted by the first journal
It was rejected by three journals — as trivial, or as so consequential it 'must be wrong' — before the QJE published it
It was published but ignored for decades
It was withdrawn by Akerlof himself

quiz.q: How many journals rejected 'The Market for Lemons' before publication?

cards.title: Why no planner can set every price
cards.fact: Soviet central planners had to set output and prices for millions of distinct goods by hand — the exact task Hayek argued is impossible, because no central mind can gather the dispersed local knowledge that market prices aggregate automatically.
cards.detail: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) reframed the planning debate. The hard problem of an economy, he argued, isn't allocating known resources to known ends — it's that the relevant knowledge never exists in one place. It's scattered across millions of people: which machine is idle, which worker is skilled, that a frost hit one region, that tastes are shifting. A price system solves this without anyone knowing the whole: when tin gets scarce, its price rises, and everyone who uses tin economises — without being told why. Soviet Gosplan tried to do by hand what prices do automatically, drawing up balances and prices for an ever-growing list of goods (estimates run into the millions of distinct products). The informational load was crushing, the signals chronically wrong, and shortages and gluts endemic. The market's 'magic' is that it is a giant, decentralised information processor.
cards.deploy: The core argument for prices over planning: not that planners are stupid or evil, but that the knowledge an economy runs on is dispersed and local, and prices aggregate it in a way no central office can.
cards.counter: Hayek's argument bites less against modern data and computation, and markets fail badly where prices misfire — externalities, public goods, monopoly, climate. The lesson is about the limits of central planning, not a blanket case that unregulated markets always get prices right.

quiz.q: What is the core of Hayek's 'knowledge problem'?
choices: Planners are less intelligent than entrepreneurs
The knowledge an economy needs is dispersed across millions of people and never available to any central authority — but prices aggregate it automatically
Computers cannot perform arithmetic fast enough
Markets always set perfectly correct prices

quiz.q: In Hayek's example, what happens when tin becomes scarce?
choices: A central office orders everyone to use less tin
Its price rises and everyone who uses tin economises — without needing to know the cause
Production halts until the shortage is investigated
The government rations tin equally to all users

quiz.q: Against which real-world system does the card contrast Hayek's argument?

cards.title: Piketty: r > g, so wealth piles up
cards.fact: Thomas Piketty's central finding: across two centuries of data, the return on capital (r, ~4–5%) has usually run ahead of the economy's growth rate (g, ~1–2%) — so inherited wealth grows faster than wages, and fortunes concentrate.
cards.detail: In 'Capital in the Twenty-First Century' (2013), Piketty and collaborators assembled tax and wealth records stretching back over 200 years — an empirical haul economics had never had. The pattern: the rate of return on capital r tends to exceed the growth rate of the economy g. When r > g, money already owned grows faster than money earned from work, so wealth concentrates at the top and the past (inheritance) dominates the present (effort). The mid-20th century looked equal only because two world wars and the Depression destroyed capital and high taxes held it down; by his data, wealth-to-income ratios in Europe have since climbed back toward the extreme levels of the Belle Époque (~600–700% of national income). His proposed remedy — a global progressive wealth tax — is openly utopian, but the diagnosis reframed the inequality debate around capital, not just wages.
cards.deploy: Use r > g to explain why inequality can widen even in a fair labour market: if owned wealth compounds faster than the economy grows, inheritance outpaces work regardless of how wages are set.
cards.counter: Heavily debated. Matt Rognlie showed most of the rising capital share is housing, not the factories-and-finance Piketty emphasises; a Financial Times investigation (Chris Giles) alleged data errors in the wealth series; and many economists doubt r > g mechanically implies ever-rising inequality without strong assumptions about saving and inheritance.

quiz.q: What does Piketty's inequality 'r > g' mean?
choices: Government revenue exceeds spending
The return on capital usually exceeds the economy's growth rate, so owned wealth grows faster than wages and fortunes concentrate
Real interest rates always exceed nominal ones
Rich countries grow faster than poor ones

quiz.q: Why does Piketty say the equal mid-20th century was the exception, not the rule?
choices: Because globalisation had not yet begun
Because two world wars, the Depression and high taxes destroyed and held down capital — temporarily compressing wealth before it climbed back
Because computers had not yet automated production
Because trade unions were illegal

quiz.q: Which critic argued that most of the rising capital share Piketty highlights is actually housing?

cards.title: New Jersey raised the minimum wage — and jobs didn't fall
cards.fact: When New Jersey raised its minimum wage in 1992 and neighbouring Pennsylvania didn't, Card and Krueger found fast-food employment in NJ didn't drop — it edged up — defying the textbook prediction.
cards.detail: The standard supply-and-demand story is unambiguous: set a wage floor above the market rate and employers will hire fewer workers. David Card and Alan Krueger ran the natural experiment in 1994. New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05; just across the river, Pennsylvania didn't. They surveyed hundreds of fast-food restaurants on both sides before and after. Employment in New Jersey didn't fall relative to Pennsylvania — if anything it rose slightly. The result was explosive because it contradicted a near-sacred prediction, and it pushed economists toward the 'monopsony' view: employers often have wage-setting power, so a modest minimum-wage rise can raise pay without killing jobs (and can even draw more people into work). Card shared the 2021 Nobel partly for pioneering exactly this kind of credible natural-experiment design.
cards.deploy: The headline rebuttal to 'minimum wages always cost jobs': a clean natural experiment found no job loss — and seeded the monopsony view that employers have wage-setting power.
cards.counter: Fiercely contested: Neumark and Wascher re-ran it with payroll records and reported job losses. The modern consensus is narrower than either side — modest minimum-wage rises in low-wage labour markets show little disemployment, but very large or economy-wide floors may still cost jobs.

quiz.q: What did Card and Krueger's New Jersey–Pennsylvania study find?
choices: A minimum-wage rise sharply cut fast-food employment in New Jersey
Raising the minimum wage in NJ did not reduce fast-food employment relative to PA — it edged up
Pennsylvania's employment collapsed after the change
Wages rose but prices fell to compensate

quiz.q: What theory did the result push economists toward?
choices: Perfect competition in labour markets
Monopsony — employers often have wage-setting power, so a modest minimum-wage rise can lift pay without cutting jobs
Rational expectations
The Laffer curve

quiz.q: Who re-analysed the data with payroll records and reported job losses, contradicting Card and Krueger?

cards.title: The austerity number undone by an Excel error
cards.fact: Reinhart and Rogoff's hugely influential claim — that growth falls off a cliff once government debt tops 90% of GDP — turned out to rest partly on a spreadsheet error a graduate student uncovered.
cards.detail: In 2010 Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff published a finding politicians seized on worldwide: when public debt exceeds about 90% of GDP, economic growth drops sharply (they reported median growth turning slightly negative). It became the empirical backbone of austerity programmes across Europe and the US. In 2013 a UMass graduate student, Thomas Herndon, tried to replicate it for a class assignment and couldn't. When he got the authors' spreadsheet, he found three problems: a literal Excel coding error that omitted five countries from a key average, questionable data exclusions, and an unusual weighting scheme. Fix them and the cliff largely vanishes — high-debt countries grow more slowly, but there is no magic 90% threshold and no negative-growth precipice. The episode is a double lesson: about the weak causal basis for austerity, and about how a single un-replicated number can steer real policy until someone checks the cells.
cards.deploy: Cite it to puncture any hard debt 'threshold' argument for austerity — the famous 90% cliff didn't survive replication, and correlation (slow growth and high debt move together) was being sold as causation.
cards.counter: Reinhart and Rogoff argued the coding slip barely moved their central estimate and that high debt and slow growth really are correlated — which is true. The deeper unsettled question is causation: does debt slow growth, or does slow growth pile up debt? The error story doesn't settle that.

quiz.q: What was the influential Reinhart–Rogoff claim, and what undid it?
choices: That low debt causes inflation — undone by new inflation data
That growth collapses above 90% debt-to-GDP — undermined when a student found a spreadsheet error and questionable data choices behind it
That austerity always boosts growth — disproven by the IMF
That deficits don't matter — refuted by the eurozone crisis

quiz.q: What is the deeper question the Excel error does NOT resolve?
choices: Whether spreadsheets should be used in research
Causation — whether high debt slows growth, or slow growth piles up debt
Whether 90% is the right threshold after the fix
Whether Reinhart and Rogoff acted in bad faith

quiz.q: Above roughly what debt-to-GDP percentage did Reinhart and Rogoff claim growth falls sharply?

cards.title: Kansas cut taxes to spark growth — and had to reverse it
cards.fact: Governor Brownback's 2012 Kansas tax cuts were sold as a growth engine that would 'pay for themselves'; instead growth lagged neighbours and budgets cratered, and a Republican legislature repealed them in 2017.
cards.detail: Supply-side theory says cutting taxes can unleash so much extra activity that revenue barely falls — or even rises (the Laffer-curve idea). In 2012 Kansas ran the experiment in the open: Governor Sam Brownback slashed income taxes and abolished tax on certain business 'pass-through' income, predicting a shot of adrenaline to the economy. It didn't come. Job and income growth trailed neighbouring states and the national average; revenues fell roughly $700 million a year, forcing cuts to schools, roads and pensions and repeated credit downgrades. By 2017 the shortfalls were so severe that Kansas's own Republican-controlled legislature voted to roll the cuts back, overriding Brownback's veto. The episode is a clean real-world data point that you can't reliably conjure growth — or pay for tax cuts — from the top of the Laffer curve when you're nowhere near it.
cards.deploy: The go-to case against 'tax cuts pay for themselves': a state ran the supply-side play deliberately and had to reverse it when growth didn't show and the budget broke.
cards.counter: Defenders argue Kansas botched the execution (the pass-through loophole invited gaming) and that national-level cuts in a different setting could perform differently. A single state over a few years also can't separate the tax change from the wider economy — though the contrast with neighbours is hard to wave away.

quiz.q: What did the Kansas tax-cut experiment test, and how did it end?
choices: Whether higher taxes reduce inequality — and they did
Whether deep tax cuts would spark self-funding growth — growth lagged, budgets cratered, and the cuts were repealed
Whether a state could run a balanced budget — and it succeeded
Whether minimum wages cut jobs — and they did

quiz.q: What Laffer-curve idea did Kansas put to the test?
choices: That tax cuts can generate enough extra activity to largely pay for themselves
That higher taxes always raise more revenue
That deficits cause hyperinflation
That tariffs protect domestic jobs

quiz.q: In what year did Kansas's legislature reverse the Brownback tax cuts?

cards.title: The fading American Dream: 90% to 50%
cards.fact: Using tens of millions of tax records, Raj Chetty found the share of children who grow up to out-earn their parents fell from about 90% for those born in 1940 to about 50% for those born in 1980.
cards.detail: The 'American Dream' has a measurable version: what fraction of children end up earning more than their parents did at the same age? Raj Chetty and colleagues computed it from anonymised tax data covering tens of millions of people. For the 1940 birth cohort the answer was about 90% — almost everyone out-earned their parents. For the 1980 cohort it had fallen to roughly 50% — a coin flip. The decline is driven less by slower growth than by how unequally that growth is now shared: when the gains pool at the top, fewer children clear their parents' bar. Chetty's mobility maps add a second jolt — a child's odds of climbing from the bottom fifth to the top vary enormously by the neighbourhood they grow up in, sometimes between adjacent counties. Mobility, in other words, is local and has been fading.
cards.deploy: Use it to make inequality concrete and personal: the odds of doing better than your parents have roughly halved in two generations, mostly because growth's gains now pool at the top.
cards.counter: The exact figures depend on how you measure income (household vs individual, before vs after taxes and transfers) and on price adjustments; some economists argue the absolute-mobility decline is real but milder once benefits and household size are accounted for. The direction, though, is robust.

quiz.q: What did Chetty find about absolute income mobility across birth cohorts?
choices: It stayed constant at about 90%
The share of children out-earning their parents fell from ~90% (1940 cohort) to ~50% (1980 cohort)
It rose as the economy grew richer
It was always around 50%

quiz.q: What is the main driver of the decline, according to the work?
choices: Children working less hard than their parents
Growth's gains being shared far more unequally — pooling at the top so fewer children clear their parents' bar
Falling population growth
Rising immigration

quiz.q: Roughly what share of children born in 1980 out-earn their parents, per Chetty (percent)?

cards.title: The elephant curve: who won globalisation
cards.fact: Branko Milanovic charted global income growth from 1988 to 2008 and got a shape like an elephant: huge gains for the emerging-Asia middle and the global top 1%, but near-stagnation for the working and middle classes of rich countries.
cards.detail: Plot how much each slice of the world's income distribution gained over the two decades of hyper-globalisation (1988–2008) and the line traces an elephant: a high, arched back over the middle of the global distribution — hundreds of millions of Chinese and Indian workers whose incomes surged — then a deep dip near the 80th–90th percentile, and a flick up at the very end. That dip is the lower-middle class of the rich world, whose real incomes barely moved. The raised trunk-tip is the global top 1%, who captured a disproportionate share. Branko Milanovic and Christoph Lakner's picture reframed inequality as a single global story: globalisation lifted the world's poor and the world's richest at the same time, while squeezing the Western working class — which helps explain both the fall in global poverty and the populist backlash in rich democracies.
cards.deploy: Use it to cut through 'globalisation is good / bad' shouting: the same process that lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty also stalled the rich-world working class — both halves of the populism story in one curve.
cards.counter: The elephant shape is sensitive to choices: the Resolution Foundation showed that adjusting for population changes (China's huge weight) and country composition flattens the dip — the rich-world middle did better than the raw curve suggests. Within-country and between-country inequality also move in opposite directions here.

quiz.q: What does the 'elephant curve' show about global income growth 1988–2008?
choices: Everyone's income grew at the same rate
Big gains for the emerging-Asia middle and the global top 1%, but near-stagnation for the rich-world working/middle class
Only the global poor gained; everyone else lost
Incomes fell across the whole distribution

quiz.q: Why does the curve help explain populism in rich democracies?
choices: It shows immigrants caused all the income gains
The 'dip' is the rich-world lower-middle class whose incomes barely moved while others surged — a grievance globalisation left behind
It proves globalisation made everyone poorer
It shows the global top 1% lost out

quiz.q: Which economist is most associated with the elephant curve?

cards.title: The Great Gatsby Curve: inequality freezes mobility
cards.fact: Across countries, the more unequal a society's incomes, the less likely a child is to escape the class they were born into — more inequality goes hand in hand with less mobility.
cards.detail: Economist Miles Corak plotted income inequality against intergenerational mobility for a set of rich countries, and Alan Krueger — then chair of the White House Council of Economic Advisers — named it the 'Great Gatsby Curve' in 2012. The relationship is strikingly tidy: high-inequality countries (the US, UK, Italy) show low mobility — a poor child's economic fate is tightly tied to their parents'; low-inequality countries (Denmark, Norway, Finland) show high mobility. The intuition is mechanical: when the rungs of the income ladder are far apart (high inequality), the distance a child must climb is greater, and the advantages the well-off can buy — schools, networks, housing — loom larger. It links two findings that might seem separate: societies that are unequal now tend to stay unequal across generations. It's the cross-country backdrop to Chetty's fading American Dream.
cards.deploy: The rebuttal to 'inequality is fine as long as there's opportunity': across countries, more inequality is precisely where opportunity (mobility) is lowest — the two are not independent.
cards.counter: It's a cross-country correlation, not proof of cause: unobserved factors (education systems, family structure, how mobility is measured) could drive both. And the US is an outlier pulling the line; drop it and the relationship weakens.

quiz.q: What relationship does the Great Gatsby Curve show?
choices: More inequality goes with higher economic growth
More income inequality goes with lower intergenerational mobility — unequal societies tend to stay unequal across generations
More inequality goes with more mobility
Inequality and mobility are unrelated across countries

quiz.q: What is the intuitive mechanism behind the curve?
choices: Poor children are less talented in unequal societies
When the ladder's rungs are far apart, the climb is longer and the advantages the rich can buy matter more — freezing children near their parents' position
Unequal societies ban social mobility by law
Equal societies have no income ladder at all

quiz.q: Who popularised the name 'Great Gatsby Curve' in 2012?

cards.title: The Spirit Level: unequal countries do worse on almost everything
cards.fact: Wilkinson and Pickett found that among rich countries, the more unequal ones score worse across a whole battery of outcomes — life expectancy, mental illness, obesity, homicide, teen births, imprisonment — even though they're all wealthy.
cards.detail: Epidemiologists Richard Wilkinson and Kate Pickett asked a simple question in 'The Spirit Level' (2009): among countries rich enough that absolute poverty isn't the issue, does the gap between rich and poor itself matter? They built an index of health and social problems and plotted it against income inequality across developed nations and US states. The correlation was strong and consistent: more-unequal places (US, UK, Portugal) clustered at the bad end across many measures at once, more-equal ones (Japan, the Nordics) at the good end. Their bold claim is that inequality harms everyone, not just the poor — even the well-off in unequal societies do worse than their counterparts in equal ones, because steep hierarchies raise status anxiety, erode trust, and stress whole populations. It shifts the inequality debate from fairness to public health.
cards.deploy: Use it to argue inequality is a collective harm, not just a moral complaint: across rich countries the unequal ones do worse on health, crime, and trust — affecting the comfortable too, not only the poor.
cards.counter: Heavily criticised on method: Christopher Snowdon and Peter Saunders argue the results hinge on which countries are included and which problems are picked, and that correlation is being read as causation — richer-but-more-equal cultures may differ in many ways besides inequality.

quiz.q: What is the central claim of The Spirit Level?
choices: Poor countries always have worse health than rich ones
Among rich countries, more-unequal ones score worse across many health and social outcomes — inequality itself, not just poverty, does harm
Inequality only affects the poorest 10%
Equality reduces economic growth

quiz.q: What is the book's most provocative argument?
choices: That only the poor are harmed by inequality
That inequality harms everyone — even the well-off do worse in unequal societies, via status anxiety and eroded trust
That redistribution always reduces total wealth
That health is determined purely by genetics

quiz.q: On what grounds do critics like Snowdon attack the book's findings?

cards.title: The IMF admitted it got the austerity maths wrong
cards.fact: In 2013 the IMF's chief economist showed that fiscal multipliers during the post-2008 austerity were far bigger than forecasters assumed — so the spending cuts shrank economies by much more than predicted.
cards.detail: When Europe imposed austerity after 2010, the official models assumed a fiscal multiplier of about 0.5 — cut government spending by a euro and output falls only 50 cents, so consolidation looked relatively painless. In a 2013 IMF analysis, chief economist Olivier Blanchard and Daniel Leigh checked the forecasts against what actually happened: countries that cut harder suffered systematically worse growth than the IMF had projected. Backing out the implied multiplier, they found it was closer to 0.9–1.7 in the depressed, zero-interest-rate conditions of the time — two to three times the assumed value. The practical meaning is stark: the austerity programmes were self-defeating in part, deepening recessions (and in some cases barely improving debt ratios because the denominator, GDP, was falling too). For the IMF — an architect of those programmes — to publish the correction was a remarkable institutional admission.
cards.deploy: The insider's evidence that austerity backfired: the IMF itself found multipliers 2–3× larger than assumed, so cuts deepened recessions instead of the gentle adjustment the models promised.
cards.counter: Some economists argue the forecast errors reflected other shocks (the euro crisis itself, banking stress) not just underestimated multipliers, and that multipliers really are small in normal times — the big-multiplier result is specific to a depressed economy at the zero lower bound, not a general law.

quiz.q: What did Blanchard and Leigh's 2013 IMF analysis find about fiscal multipliers during the austerity years?
choices: They were near zero, so austerity was costless
They were far larger than the assumed ~0.5 (closer to 0.9–1.7), so spending cuts shrank economies more than predicted
They were exactly as forecast
They were negative, so cuts boosted growth

quiz.q: Why was this finding institutionally remarkable?
choices: It came from a fringe think tank
The IMF — an architect of the austerity programmes — was publicly admitting its models had understated the damage
It was published anonymously
It contradicted Keynes

quiz.q: Roughly what multiplier value had forecasters assumed before the correction?

cards.title: Greece's austerity depression: a quarter of GDP gone
cards.fact: Under the austerity attached to its post-2010 bailouts, Greece's economy shrank by about a quarter and unemployment passed 27% — youth unemployment topped 50% — a slump on the scale of the Great Depression.
cards.detail: After 2010, Greece received bailouts from the 'troika' (IMF, ECB, European Commission) conditional on severe austerity: deep cuts to pensions, wages and public services, and tax rises, all while locked inside the euro so it could not devalue its currency to soften the blow. The aim was to restore debt sustainability. Instead the economy collapsed — real GDP fell roughly 25% from its peak, unemployment climbed above 27% (and over 50% for the young), and the debt-to-GDP ratio actually rose, because GDP (the denominator) was shrinking faster than the debt. It became the most extreme illustration of the big-multiplier problem: cutting hard into a depressed economy that can't devalue can be self-defeating. The IMF later conceded it had underestimated the damage — the Blanchard-Leigh multiplier story made flesh in one country.
cards.deploy: The starkest real-world austerity case: cuts meant to fix Greece's debt ratio instead shrank the economy a quarter and pushed the ratio higher — austerity defeating its own goal.
cards.counter: Defenders argue Greece had no painless option — it had borrowed unsustainably, lost market access, and needed reform; the alternative (disorderly default and euro exit) might have been worse. Some of the depth also reflects Greece's weak institutions and tax collection, not austerity alone.

quiz.q: What happened to Greece's economy under post-2010 bailout austerity?
choices: It grew steadily as confidence returned
It shrank about a quarter, with unemployment over 27% — and the debt-to-GDP ratio rose because GDP fell faster than debt
It stagnated but avoided recession
It recovered within two years

quiz.q: Why did austerity push Greece's debt-to-GDP ratio UP rather than down?
choices: Because the government kept borrowing more
Because the cuts shrank GDP (the denominator) faster than they cut the debt (the numerator)
Because interest rates rose to 50%
Because Greece left the euro

quiz.q: Being inside the euro removed which crisis tool from Greece?

cards.title: 1937: tightening too soon reignited the Depression
cards.fact: As the US was clawing back from the Great Depression, a premature turn to balanced budgets and tighter money in 1937 sent output and employment plunging again — the 'Roosevelt recession'.
cards.detail: By 1936 the US economy had been recovering for three years; output and employment were climbing back toward pre-1929 levels. Then policymakers, worried about deficits and inflation, hit the brakes on every front at once: Roosevelt cut spending to balance the budget, new Social Security payroll taxes pulled money out of paychecks, and the Federal Reserve doubled bank reserve requirements to mop up 'excess' reserves. The recovery cracked. Industrial production fell about a third, and unemployment, which had been falling, jumped back up by several million. The lesson economists draw is about sequencing: withdrawing fiscal and monetary support before a recovery is self-sustaining can abort it. The 1937 episode is the historical companion to the modern austerity debate — and was invoked repeatedly as a warning against tightening too early after 2008.
cards.deploy: The historical trump card against tightening too soon: in 1937 the US balanced the budget and tightened money mid-recovery, and promptly fell back into deep recession.
cards.counter: The relative blame is debated: monetarists (Friedman) stress the Fed's reserve-requirement hike and a sterilisation of gold inflows over the fiscal cuts, while others emphasise the spending side. Either way the moral — don't tighten prematurely — survives, but 'which lever did it' is unsettled.

quiz.q: What caused the 'Roosevelt recession' of 1937–38?
choices: A stock market crash like 1929
A premature turn to balanced budgets, new payroll taxes, and tighter money while the economy was still recovering
A sudden surge in government spending
An oil price shock

quiz.q: What general lesson do economists draw from 1937?
choices: Recoveries are always self-sustaining once they begin
Withdrawing fiscal and monetary support too early — before a recovery is self-sustaining — can abort it
Inflation should always be fought immediately
Balanced budgets guarantee growth

quiz.q: Which 20th-century economic episode does 1937 serve as a historical warning for, in the modern debate?

cards.title: Anatomy of an argument
cards.fact: An argument isn't a strong opinion said loudly — it's a claim, a reason the claim is true, the evidence behind the reason, and why it matters.

layers.body: Take any argument apart and you find up to four parts. The CLAIM is what you want me to accept (‘we should ban X’). The WARRANT is the reason it follows (‘because X causes harm’). The EVIDENCE backs the warrant (‘here are the numbers on the harm’). The IMPACT says why it matters (‘so banning it saves lives’). A claim with no warrant is just an assertion; a warrant with no impact wins a point nobody cares about.

Philosopher Stephen Toulmin laid this out in 1958 to describe how real arguments work, as opposed to tidy formal syllogisms. His core trio is claim, grounds (evidence) and warrant — the warrant being the often-unstated bridge that licenses going from the grounds to the claim. Most weak arguments fail at the warrant: the speaker states a fact and a conclusion but never says why one gives you the other. Naming the missing part is the fastest way to answer an argument — ‘that's a claim, where's the warrant?’

‘Remote work should be permanent.’ That's a bare claim. Add a warrant: ‘because it lets people work when they focus best.’ Add evidence: ‘output per hour rose in trials where teams chose their hours.’ Add impact: ‘so the firm ships more for the same payroll.’ Now it's an argument you have to engage with, not just disagree with. Each part is attackable on its own — you can grant the evidence and still deny the warrant (‘focus isn't the bottleneck, coordination is’).

cards.deploy: Before you argue, name your claim, warrant, evidence and impact — and when answering, attack the part that's actually missing.
cards.counter: Real exchanges rarely separate this cleanly; the parts blur, and over-formalising can make you sound like a textbook instead of a person.

quiz.q: In the claim–warrant–evidence–impact model, what is the 'warrant'?
choices: The reason the evidence supports the claim
The conclusion you want accepted
The data or examples cited
Why the claim matters in the end
