quiz.q: Which philosopher's model of argument introduced claim, grounds and warrant?

cards.title: Four ways to answer an argument
cards.fact: You don't have to prove the other side wrong from scratch. There are four clean moves: deny the link, mitigate the impact, turn it back, or outweigh it.

layers.body: DENY THE LINK: grant the fact but break the connection — ‘yes crime rose, but not because of this policy.’ MITIGATE: grant the link but shrink it — ‘it matters, but far less than claimed.’ TURN IT: show the argument actually supports your side — ‘that very risk is a reason to do the opposite.’ OUTWEIGH: grant the whole thing and win anyway — ‘true, but my impact is bigger.’ Most beginners only know one move (flat denial), which is why they lose arguments they could win.

layers.t: Why a turn is the strongest
layers.body: A turn is the most powerful because it doesn't just neutralise the opponent's point, it steals it: their own argument now scores for you. Paul Graham's 2008 ‘How to Disagree’ ranks responses from name-calling at the bottom up to refuting the central point at the top — same lesson: aim at the load-bearing link, not the person or the phrasing. The higher-order moves (turn, outweigh) require you to actually understand the argument, which is why they're rarer and more convincing.

Opponent: ‘Nuclear power is dangerous — look at the accidents.’ Deny the link: modern reactor designs don't share the failure mode of the old ones. Mitigate: total deaths are tiny next to the alternative. Turn it: the danger of fossil fuels is precisely why we need nuclear's reliable low-carbon output. Outweigh: even granting the risk, the climate impact of NOT building it is larger. Four answers, same fact — pick the one you can actually defend.

cards.deploy: When answering a point, pick one of the four moves deliberately — and reach for a turn before a flat denial.
cards.counter: Reaching for a turn when the facts don't support one looks like a stretch; sometimes the honest move is to concede the point and win elsewhere.

quiz.q: Which rebuttal move grants the opponent's fact but argues it actually supports your side?
choices: Turn it
Deny the link
Mitigate
Concede

quiz.q: In 'mitigating' an argument, what do you do?
choices: Grant the link but argue the impact is much smaller
Deny that the fact is true at all
Show the argument supports your side
Attack the person making it

cards.title: Weighing: winning a point isn't winning the debate
cards.fact: When both sides say true things, you don't win by piling up more points — you win by showing your impact is bigger, likelier, sooner, or harder to undo.

layers.body: Once both sides have real points, judges weigh them on four scales. MAGNITUDE: how big is the effect? PROBABILITY: how likely is it actually to happen? TIMEFRAME: how soon — a harm now usually beats a harm in fifty years. REVERSIBILITY: can you undo it if you're wrong? A small but certain and irreversible harm can outweigh a huge but unlikely one. Most arguments are lost not because the point was false but because the speaker never said why it mattered more than the other side's point.

Competitive debate formalises this as ‘impact calculus’: you explicitly compare the two worlds and argue which harm dominates. The move that wins rounds is not ‘I have five arguments and you have three’ but ‘grant all eight — mine is the one that decides it, because it's irreversible and yours isn't.’ Reversibility carries special weight: a policy you can repeal is safer than one you can't, even if its downside looks larger on paper, because you keep the option to correct a mistake.

Motion: build the dam. For: it lifts a region out of poverty (big magnitude, high probability, slow timeframe). Against: it may collapse and drown a town (smaller probability, but catastrophic and irreversible). You don't resolve this by counting — you weigh. ‘Even granting the economic gain, an irreversible loss of life we can't undo should dominate a reversible economic shortfall we can address other ways.’ Or the reverse. Either way, you argued the comparison, not just your side.

cards.deploy: When both sides have true points, explicitly weigh yours as bigger, likelier, sooner or more irreversible — don't just add more points.
cards.counter: Weighing can become hand-waving — anyone can assert their impact is bigger; the comparison only counts if the magnitude and probability are themselves defensible.

quiz.q: In impact weighing, why does 'reversibility' matter?
choices: A harm you can't undo should weigh more than one you can correct later
Reversible harms are always larger
It measures how soon the harm happens
It counts the number of arguments each side has

quiz.q: What is the central idea of 'weighing' in a debate?
quiz.answer: comparing whose impact is bigger/likelier/sooner/more irreversible rather than counting points

cards.title: Burden of proof: who has to prove what
cards.fact: Whoever makes the claim has to support it — you can't win by demanding the other side disprove you, and ‘best’ doesn't mean ‘perfect’.

layers.body: The burden of proof sits with the person asserting something, not the person doubting it. ‘Prove ghosts aren't real’ gets it backwards — the one claiming ghosts exist owes the evidence. In a debate this also fixes what each side has to show. If the motion is ‘democracy is the BEST system’, the burden is comparative: you must beat the alternatives, not prove democracy flawless. Spotting a misplaced burden — someone demanding you disprove their claim — is one of the most common ways arguments go wrong.

Whoever defines the burden often wins. If you let the other side frame the motion as ‘democracy is perfect’, every flaw they name scores; if you frame it as ‘better than the alternatives on offer’, a flaw only counts if the rival system handles it better. This is why definitions and framing come first in a debate: they set what would count as winning. Shifting the burden — quietly making the other side prove a negative — is a classic fallacy precisely because it lets you skip the work of making your own case.

‘You can't prove the policy will work, so we shouldn't try it.’ The burden is misplaced: the objector treats ‘not proven to work’ as ‘proven not to work’. The honest framing: both sides carry a burden — the proposer to show plausible benefit, the opponent to show plausible harm — and you weigh them. And note ‘best’ vs ‘perfect’: pointing out democracy elects demagogues doesn't beat ‘democracy is best’ unless some other system handles demagogues better.

cards.deploy: Pin the burden where it belongs: make the claimant prove the claim, and reframe ‘perfect’ motions as comparative.
cards.counter: Burden-of-proof talk can become a dodge of its own — hiding behind ‘you haven't proven it’ to avoid engaging with strong evidence already on the table.

quiz.q: Where does the burden of proof normally sit?
choices: With the person making the claim
With the person doubting the claim
Always with both sides equally
With whoever speaks last

quiz.q: If a motion says a system is 'the best', what kind of burden does that create?
choices: Comparative — you must beat the alternatives, not prove it flawless
Absolute — you must prove it has no flaws
None — the other side must disprove it
Only a burden to define terms

cards.title: Steelman before you strike
cards.fact: State the other side's argument in its strongest form before you answer it — if you only beat the weak version, you've beaten nobody.

layers.t: The opposite of a straw man
layers.body: A straw man rebuilds your opponent's argument in its weakest, silliest form so it's easy to knock down — and proves nothing, because nobody held that view. A steelman does the reverse: you state their case at least as well as they would, then answer THAT. It costs you something (you make the enemy's point for them) but it's the only way to actually win, because a real opponent will just say ‘that's not what I argued.’

Steelmanning is the practical side of the principle of charity — interpret others in the strongest reasonable way. It persuades for two reasons. First, the audience trusts someone who can pass the opponent's ideological Turing test — restate the other view so well its holders would accept it. Second, it pre-empts the rebuttal: if you've already named their best point and answered it, they have nowhere to retreat. The cost — voicing the strong version — is exactly what makes your answer credible.

Weak (straw man): ‘People against immigration just hate foreigners.’ Easy to dismiss, convinces no one. Steelman: ‘The strongest case is that rapid inflows can outpace housing and services and depress wages for the lowest-paid — a distributional worry, not a xenophobic one.’ Now your answer (‘here's why the wage effect is small and the housing fix is supply, not fewer people’) actually lands, because you're answering the argument a thoughtful opponent would really make.

cards.deploy: Open your rebuttal by stating the other side's best version — then answer that, not the caricature.
cards.counter: Steelmanning can over-improve a position the opponent never actually held, and at the extreme you end up arguing with yourself instead of them.

quiz.q: What does it mean to 'steelman' an argument?
choices: Restate the opposing view in its strongest form before answering it
Rebuild it in its weakest form to knock it down
Attack the person instead of the argument
Refuse to engage with it at all

quiz.q: Steelmanning is the practical application of which principle?

motions.text: This house would prioritise economic growth over environmental protection.

persona.name: The Ecologist
persona.intro: Growth over the planet? You'd burn the house to keep the lights on. Defend that, if you can.

rounds.attack: Chasing growth is what's poisoning the rivers and cooking the climate. The economy must serve the Earth, not the reverse.

moves.label: Turn it — growth is what pays for the cleanup
moves.land: Backwards: the cleanest countries are the rich ones. A starving farmer can't afford to care about a river; growth is precisely what buys the sewers, the scrubbers and the parks. Poverty is the worst polluter.
moves.reply: …the rich countries clean up first. The Kuznets argument. I walked into that.

recall.demand: Then name the economist who showed polluter and victim can bargain their way to the efficient outcome — without strangling growth.
choices: Ronald Coase
Arthur Pigou
Nicholas Stern
Garrett Hardin
recall.good: Coase. Property rights and bargaining. You know your externalities.
recall.miss: Lecturing me on the environment with no Coase? He won a Nobel for exactly this. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — growth doesn't harm the environment
moves.reply: It plainly does some harm; deny it and the room writes you off as a shill.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the Earth must come first
moves.reply: Conceding in round one? Then switch the lights off yourself. We're done.

rounds.attack: But there are hard limits — the planetary boundaries. Cross them and the damage is irreversible. No GDP figure buys that back.

moves.label: Weigh certain poverty now against a speculative ceiling
moves.land: Weigh it honestly: the harms of stalled growth are certain and immediate — poverty, early death, no money for adaptation. Your ceiling is real but distant and, crucially, the wealth from growth is what funds the tech to stay under it. Don't trade a certain present for a speculative future.
moves.reply: Certain present against speculative future, and growth funding the fix. …Tighter than I expected.

recall.demand: You invoke the planetary boundaries. How many did the scientists actually define?
choices: Nine
Three
Five
Twelve
recall.good: Nine. You know the framework, not just the scare-word. Fine.
recall.miss: Citing the boundaries and you don't know there are nine? Then it's a slogan. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — the boundaries are made up
moves.reply: They're peer-reviewed science; deny them and you're the one ignoring evidence.

moves.label: Outweigh — limits don't matter
moves.reply: Asserted, not argued. WHY can growth outrun a hard limit? Give the warrant.

rounds.attack: You'll cook the planet for one more point of GDP. Admit growth and the environment simply cannot coexist.

moves.label: Steelman the limits, then split growth from harm
moves.land: Granted — and at full strength: ecological overshoot is real and some damage is forever. But you've fused two things. The motion isn't 'pollute freely'; it's prioritise growth — and growth can be decoupled from emissions, as the economies already cutting carbon while growing show. Best path isn't no growth; it's clean growth.
moves.reply: Splitting growth from harm with decoupling, after granting the overshoot. …That's the case I can't break.

recall.demand: Name the term for raising GDP while cutting resource use and emissions in absolute terms.
choices: Absolute decoupling
The rebound effect
Degrowth
The Jevons paradox
recall.good: Absolute decoupling. You know the live debate, not just the panic. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing clean growth and you can't name absolute decoupling? That's the whole question. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — there's no environmental damage
moves.reply: Denial of the obvious; you forfeit every reasonable listener.

moves.label: Concede — they can't coexist
moves.reply: You just conceded the motion. I accept your surrender, gracefully.

for.win: The Ecologist lowers her placard. You held the floor — turning growth into the cleanup's paymaster, weighing present against speculative harm, and splitting growth from pollution via decoupling.
for.lose: The Ecologist shakes her head. Cornucopian faith without the science is just a slogan. Learn the cards and come back.

persona.name: The Industrialist
persona.intro: Growth lifts people from the dirt. Wealth is what cleans rivers and cures disease. Tell me a forest matters more than a child's future.

rounds.attack: Get rich first, clean up later — the environmental Kuznets curve. Prosperity is what buys you a clean environment.

moves.label: Turn it — the curve doesn't bend for carbon
moves.land: The 'clean up later' curve holds for visible local muck — soot, sewage — that wealth does scrub. It does NOT hold for carbon or biodiversity: those keep climbing with income, and the damage is global and irreversible. You're generalising from smog to the whole biosphere.
moves.reply: …the curve fails for carbon and extinction. You turned my tidy graph into a special case. Tch.

recall.demand: Name the framework of nine limits for a stable planet — and say how many there are.
choices: Nine
Three
Five
Twelve
recall.good: Nine planetary boundaries. You know the hard limits, not just the optimism. Hm.
recall.miss: Arguing for ecological limits and you don't know there are nine planetary boundaries? Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — wealth has no link to clean-up
moves.reply: It does for local pollution; overclaiming loses the room.

moves.label: Concede — yes, grow first and worry later
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then fire up the smokestacks. We agree.

rounds.attack: Poverty kills more people than pollution ever will. Every year of delayed growth is a graveyard of preventable deaths.

moves.label: Weigh reversibility — some losses buy back at no price
moves.land: Weigh reversibility, not just body counts. Poverty is terrible — and largely reversible: growth, aid, medicine claw it back. A cooked climate, a collapsed fishery, an extinct species is gone at any GDP. You're trading a recoverable harm for a permanent one and calling it prudence.
moves.reply: Reversible against permanent. …You weighed the one axis that doesn't bend to money. Fair.

recall.demand: Name the concept: a shared resource gets overused because each user pockets the gain while all share the cost.
choices: The tragedy of the commons
The free-rider problem
Moral hazard
The Jevons paradox
recall.good: The tragedy of the commons. You know why the biosphere gets plundered by default. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing the environment gets wrecked and you can't name the tragedy of the commons? That's the mechanism. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — ecological damage is reversible too
moves.reply: Extinction and climate aren't; denial sinks you.

moves.label: Outweigh — poverty always wins
moves.reply: Asserted, not argued. WHY does poverty outrank irreversible loss? Warrant it.

rounds.attack: You'd freeze the poor in the dark to save a wetland. Choosing trees over people is a moral obscenity.

moves.label: Steelman it, then dissolve the false choice
moves.land: Granted — and I'll say it plainly: condemning the poor to darkness for scenery would be obscene. But the choice is mostly false: growth and the environment can be decoupled, and the poor are hit FIRST and worst by ecological collapse. The motion puts growth OVER the environment as a rule — and that ordering is what fails when the limit is hard.
moves.reply: Dissolving the trade-off with decoupling, then noting the poor suffer the collapse first. …That's the framing I couldn't beat.

recall.demand: Name the term for raising GDP while cutting resource use and emissions in absolute terms.
choices: Absolute decoupling
The rebound effect
The Jevons paradox
Degrowth
recall.good: Absolute decoupling. You know the trade-off isn't iron. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Arguing growth and environment can coexist and you can't name absolute decoupling? That's the hope. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the poor aren't hurt by climate
moves.reply: They're hit first and worst; denial is both false and callous.

moves.label: Concede — growth must come first
moves.reply: You accepted his framing — and conceded the motion.

against.win: The Industrialist powers down the line. You held the floor — turning the Kuznets curve into a special case, weighing irreversibility over body counts, and dissolving the trees-versus-people choice.
against.lose: The Industrialist restarts the engines. To put the planet first you must know the limits by name. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Free trade does more good than harm.

persona.name: The Mercantilist
persona.intro: Free trade? A polite word for shipping our jobs abroad and calling it progress. Defend it — I dare you.

rounds.attack: Every cheap import puts one of our workers on the street. We should protect our factories, not throw them open to foreigners.

moves.label: Turn it — protection taxes your own people
moves.land: Cheap imports free up workers and capital for the things we're actually best at. A tariff is just a tax you levy on your own consumers to freeze the economy in 1975.
moves.reply: …freeing up capital, opportunity cost. Spoken like someone who's read the theory. Tch.

recall.demand: Then name the man who proved it. Who showed in 1817 that two countries both gain from trade even when one is better at making everything?
choices: David Ricardo
Adam Smith
John Maynard Keynes
Karl Marx
recall.good: Ricardo. Comparative advantage. Of course you'd have that loaded.
recall.miss: Can't even name him? Then it's faith, not economics. It's Ricardo — go learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — trade doesn't cost any jobs
moves.reply: Now you're lying to my face. Of course it displaces workers — argue the honest case or lose.

moves.label: Concede — yes, we should protect the factories
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then we're agreed: walls up. Pleasure doing business.

rounds.attack: And the trade deficit! We buy more than we sell, year after year. We are simply losing.

moves.label: Name the missing warrant — a deficit isn't a scoreboard
moves.land: That's a claim with no warrant. A deficit isn't points lost — the dollars come straight back as investment. You've mistaken an accounting identity for a defeat.
moves.reply: An accounting identity, not a scoreboard. Hmph. Fine, the bumper-sticker was weak.

recall.demand: Clever. Then name the principle Ricardo's whole argument rests on — the value of the next-best thing you give up.
choices: Opportunity cost
Absolute advantage
The balance of trade
Marginal utility
recall.good: Opportunity cost. You understand the engine, not just the slogan. Irritating.
recall.miss: Don't know what powers your own argument? It's opportunity cost. Learn it before you face me again.

moves.label: Deny it — we don't really run a deficit
moves.reply: We've run one for decades; deny the obvious and you hand me the round.

moves.label: Outweigh — deficits don't matter at all
moves.reply: Too glib. Wave it away and the room thinks you're dodging. Explain WHY it isn't a loss.

rounds.attack: Trade gutted whole towns — real factories, real families, hollowed out. So much for your gains.

moves.label: Steelman it, then reframe to the net
moves.land: Granted — and I'll put it as strongly as you would: concentrated losses, communities hollowed out, a generation stranded. But the motion is 'more good than harm' — a net comparison. The answer to the losers is compensation and retraining, not walling off everyone else's gains.
moves.reply: Stating my case better than I did, then turning on 'net'. …That's the argument I couldn't beat. Floor's yours.

recall.demand: Fine. But you lean on markets serving everyone. Which thinker argued in 1776 that the butcher feeds you from self-interest, not kindness?
choices: Adam Smith
David Hume
John Stuart Mill
Karl Marx
recall.good: Smith. The Wealth of Nations. You came with the canon. Well played.
recall.miss: Quoting the invisible hand and you can't name Smith? Embarrassing. Go and learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the towns recovered fine
moves.reply: They didn't, and pretending so makes you look heartless and wrong at once.

moves.label: Deny the link — trade didn't cause the decline
moves.reply: Some of it plainly did. Deny the real harm and you forfeit the moral high ground.

for.win: The Mercantilist folds his arms and nods. You held the floor — turning protection into a self-tax, exposing the deficit fallacy, and steelmanning the losers before weighing the net.
for.lose: The Mercantilist smirks — he found the gap in your guard. The theory's only a weapon if you can recall it. Learn the cards and come back.

persona.name: The Free Trader
persona.intro: Open the borders and everyone wins — it's the closest thing economics has to a law. Argue against prosperity itself. I'm listening.

rounds.attack: Comparative advantage proves it: free trade makes every country better off. Two centuries of economists agree.

moves.label: Turn it — the theorem's assumptions don't hold
moves.land: The theorem is real — and so are its assumptions: full employment, workers who costlessly switch industries, no externalities. Break those and you get the real world, where a trade shock hollows out whole regions and the displaced never find the promised new jobs. The model wins; the people lose.
moves.reply: …attacking the assumptions, not the maths. You turned the theorem's fine print against it. Tch.

recall.demand: Name the economist whose 'elephant curve' showed who actually won and lost from globalisation.
choices: Branko Milanovic
David Ricardo
Paul Krugman
Jagdish Bhagwati
recall.good: Milanovic. You know the rich world's working class is the trough of that curve. Hm.
recall.miss: Arguing trade created losers and you can't name Milanovic's elephant curve? That's the picture. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — comparative advantage is simply false
moves.reply: It's sound theory; deny it and every economist writes you off.

moves.label: Concede — yes, free trade is pure gain
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then tariffs to zero. We agree.

rounds.attack: And trade lifted billions out of poverty across Asia. That's not theory — that's the greatest welfare gain in history.

moves.label: Weigh how they actually got rich
moves.land: Weigh how those countries actually developed: not by throwing markets open, but by protecting and guiding young industries until they could compete — then exporting. The success stories practised managed trade and kicked the ladder away afterwards. You're crediting free trade for the fruits of industrial policy.
moves.reply: Managed trade dressed up as free trade. …You weighed how they really climbed, and it stings.

recall.demand: Name the economist who argues today's rich countries got rich by GUIDING markets, not freeing them — 'kicking away the ladder'.
choices: Ha-Joon Chang
Milton Friedman
David Ricardo
Adam Smith
recall.good: Ha-Joon Chang. You know the development record, not the fairy tale. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing for industrial policy and you can't name Ha-Joon Chang? He wrote the book. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — Asia got rich on free trade
moves.reply: They protected first; deny it and the history buries you.

moves.label: Outweigh — how they grew doesn't matter
moves.reply: Asserted, not shown. WHY does the method matter? Give the warrant.

rounds.attack: So you'd raise tariffs and start trade wars? That path gave us Smoot-Hawley and the Great Depression.

moves.label: Steelman the danger, then narrow to 'net harm'
moves.land: Granted — blanket protectionism and tit-for-tat tariffs can be ruinous; Smoot-Hawley is a real warning. But the motion is 'more good than harm', a net judgement, and 'managed trade with compensation for the losers' is not autarky. Opposing unconditional free trade isn't endorsing a trade war.
moves.reply: Splitting managed trade from a trade war, after granting the danger. …That's the distinction I couldn't collapse.

recall.demand: Name the principle comparative advantage truly rests on — the value of the next-best option forgone.
choices: Opportunity cost
Absolute advantage
The terms of trade
Marginal utility
recall.good: Opportunity cost. You understand the engine you're critiquing — that's why the critique lands. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Critiquing comparative advantage and you can't name opportunity cost? That's its core. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — tariffs are always harmless
moves.reply: Smoot-Hawley says otherwise; denial concedes his strongest point.

moves.label: Concede — free trade is best, never mind the losers
moves.reply: You let him equate your case with a trade war — and conceded.

against.win: The Free Trader closes the ledger. You held the floor — attacking the theorem's assumptions, weighing how Asia really developed, and splitting managed trade from a ruinous trade war.
against.lose: The Free Trader spreads his hands. To argue against free trade you must know the theory better than its champions. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Democracy is the best system of government.

persona.name: The Contrarian
persona.intro: Democracy? Mob rule with extra steps — you hand the wheel to whoever's angriest on the day. Go on, defend it. I'll wait.

rounds.attack: Voters are ignorant. Half can't name their own representative, and you want them steering a country? Expertise should rule, not the crowd.

moves.label: Turn it — ignorance is the argument FOR democracy
moves.land: Exactly. No single ignorant voter can capture the system, and across millions the errors wash out. Concentrate power in your ‘experts’ and one captured expert dooms everyone — democracy is the error-correcting design, not the naive one.
moves.reply: …hm. Annoyingly, that lands. Fine.

recall.demand: Cute theory. Now put a name to it — whose theorem says a big crowd of better-than-even judges is almost certain to be right together? Surname'll do.
choices: Condorcet
Machiavelli
Rousseau
Hobbes
recall.good: …Condorcet. The jury theorem. You've actually read something — irritating.
recall.miss: Drawing a blank? Then it's a vibe, not an argument. It's Condorcet — learn the card and come back for me.

moves.label: Deny it — voters are actually well-informed
moves.reply: Don't be absurd — you'll lose that on the facts and you know it. Pick a fight you can win.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the crowd is a problem
moves.reply: Conceding the whole point? Then we agree experts should rule. Thanks for playing.

rounds.attack: Singapore got rich under one-party rule while your democracies dithered and bickered. Authoritarian efficiency beats your endless debate. Admit it.

moves.label: Weigh it — judge the system by its downside, not its best day
moves.land: One survivor doesn't beat the graveyard. For every Singapore there's a Mao or a Mugabe — high variance, and no exit. Democracy's worst case is a bad term you vote out; autocracy's worst case is irreversible. On probability and reversibility, mine wins.
moves.reply: Tch. Citing the variance and the exit option… that's a real weighing. Point taken.

recall.demand: The ‘graveyard’, you say. Then name its worst grave by the numbers — roughly how many died in Mao's Great Leap famine? In millions.
choices: About 30 million
About 3 million
About 300,000
About half a million
recall.good: ~Thirty million. One man, no brakes, no vote to remove him. …That is the whole point about irreversibility, isn't it.
recall.miss: If you don't know the scale, you don't feel the weight of your own argument. Tens of millions — about thirty. Learn it.

moves.label: Counter-example — ‘but look at Venezuela!’
moves.reply: Now we're just trading anecdotes, and I have more cherry-picked autocracies than you have time. Don't swap examples — change the terms of comparison.

moves.label: Deny it — ‘Singapore isn't really that rich’
moves.reply: It's one of the richest places on earth. Deny the facts and you've handed me the round.

rounds.attack: Even you must admit democracies elect demagogues and make terrible, short-sighted choices. So much for the wisdom of the people. Checkmate.

moves.label: Steelman it, then reframe — ‘best’ isn't ‘perfect’
moves.land: Granted — at its worst, democracy elects a demagogue, and I'll state that as strongly as you would. But the motion is ‘best system’, and that burden is comparative. Every system makes bad calls; only one lets you reverse them without bloodshed. Best doesn't mean flawless — it means correctable.
moves.reply: …Stating my point better than I did and then turning it on the burden. That's the whole game, isn't it. You held the floor.

recall.demand: ‘Best, not perfect’ — you lifted that. Which statesman called democracy ‘the worst form of government except for all the others’? Name him.
choices: Churchill
Orwell
Lincoln
de Tocqueville
recall.good: Churchill — the Commons, 1947. You came armed. Fine. You've earned the floor.
recall.miss: Quoting a line you can't attribute is how you lose the room. It was Churchill. Go and learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — ‘democracies don't really elect demagogues’
moves.reply: History is not on your side there, and you look evasive denying the obvious. Don't deny it — absorb it.

moves.label: Get defensive — ‘well, no system is perfect!’
moves.reply: A bare claim with no warrant. WHY does ‘nothing's perfect’ save democracy specifically? Say the actual reason or you've conceded.

for.win: The Contrarian tips his hat. You held the floor — not by knowing more facts, but by turning his point, weighing the downside, and reframing the burden.
for.lose: The Contrarian grins — he got under your guard. The moves are there to be used; learn the cards and come back for him.

persona.name: The Democrat
persona.intro: Democracy is the worst system — except for all the others. The people rule, and that is sacred. Tell me something better, if you dare.

rounds.attack: The will of the people is the only legitimate basis for power. Whatever the majority decides, that is the people's will.

moves.label: Turn it — there often is no coherent 'will'
moves.land: There frequently is no single 'will of the people' to obey. Majorities can prefer A to B, B to C, and C to A all at once — the group's preferences cycle, so the 'will' depends on the order you vote, not on the people. You're worshipping an artefact of the agenda.
moves.reply: …cycling majorities. You turned the sacred will into a voting artefact. Unsettling.

recall.demand: Name the candidate-type that beats every rival one-on-one — which often fails to exist precisely because majorities cycle.
choices: A Condorcet winner
A median voter
A plurality winner
A veto player
recall.good: The Condorcet winner — and how often there isn't one. You know the maths under the myth. Hm.
recall.miss: Invoking the people's will and you can't name the Condorcet winner? That's the flaw in it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — the majority is always coherent
moves.reply: Voting cycles are a theorem; deny them and the room stops listening.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the people's will is supreme
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then long live democracy. We agree.

rounds.attack: And democracies don't starve their people or massacre them wholesale. Famine and terror are the marks of the alternatives.

moves.label: Weigh the catalogue against the showcase
moves.land: Grant the famines — then weigh democracy's own catalogue: chronic short-termism, debt piled on the unborn, climate paralysis, and the standing capacity of a majority to crush a minority lawfully. 'No famines' is a low bar for a system claiming to be the BEST.
moves.reply: Short-termism and majority tyranny against the famine showcase. …A harder ledger than I keep.

recall.demand: Name the theorem proving no voting system can satisfy every reasonable fairness criterion at once.
choices: Arrow's impossibility theorem
The median voter theorem
Condorcet's jury theorem
Duverger's law
recall.good: Arrow's impossibility theorem. You know democracy can't even be fair on paper. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing voting is flawed and you can't name Arrow's impossibility theorem? It's the proof. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — democracies do have famines too
moves.reply: Rare at best; this hands him Sen's point and the round.

moves.label: Outweigh — famines are irrelevant
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY does avoiding famine not count for much? Warrant it.

rounds.attack: Then name a better system. Every alternative — kings, juntas, technocrats — has ended worse. Democracy wins by survival.

moves.label: Reframe the burden — 'best' is a ceiling, not a floor
moves.land: Granted — most alternatives ended worse, and I won't pretend otherwise. But the motion isn't 'democracy beats tyranny'; it's 'democracy is the BEST system'. That's a ceiling claim, and competent technocracies and hybrid models outperform it on long-horizon policy. Surviving the competition isn't the same as topping it.
moves.reply: Best as a ceiling, not merely beating the floor. …You held the bar exactly where the motion put it.

recall.demand: Robert Dahl said no real state is fully democratic. What did he call actual, imperfect democracies?
choices: Polyarchy
Plutocracy
Technocracy
Anarchy
recall.good: Polyarchy. You know even the defenders concede it's never the ideal. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Arguing democracy falls short of its ideal and you can't name polyarchy? That's Dahl's word. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — every other system is evil
moves.reply: Overclaiming loses the room; he only has to name one counter-case.

moves.label: Concede — democracy is the best after all
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Democrat raises a glass.

against.win: The Democrat sets down the glass. You held the floor — turning the 'will of the people' into a voting artefact, weighing democracy's catalogue against the famine showcase, and holding 'best' as a ceiling.
against.lose: The Democrat smiles, unshaken. To argue against democracy you must know social choice cold. Learn the cards and come back.

persona.name: The Philosopher
persona.intro: Science, answering moral questions? Category error. The laboratory can tell you what is, never what ought to be. Enlighten me.

rounds.attack: You cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is'. No pile of facts about the world entails a single moral duty. The gap is unbridgeable.

moves.label: Turn it — most moral disputes are factual in disguise
moves.land: Most live moral disagreements aren't about ultimate values at all — they're about facts: does this policy reduce suffering, does that punishment deter, is the fetus sentient. Agree the goal is wellbeing and science adjudicates almost everything that's actually contested.
moves.reply: …smuggling the factual content out of the moral dispute. Cleverer than the usual reply.

recall.demand: Then name the philosopher who drew the very line you claim to cross — that no 'ought' follows from an 'is'.
choices: David Hume
Immanuel Kant
G.E. Moore
Aristotle
recall.good: Hume. You named your own obstacle. At least you know what you're up against.
recall.miss: Invoking the is–ought gap and you can't name Hume? It's his gap. Go and learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — there is no is–ought gap
moves.reply: Deny Hume's gap outright and every philosopher in the room stops listening.

moves.label: Concede — science is silent on morality
moves.reply: Conceding the motion already? Then the lab packs up. Thank you.

rounds.attack: Even calling 'wellbeing' good just smuggles in a value. You assume the very thing you claim to prove. That's the naturalistic fallacy.

moves.label: Name the move, then expose its cost
moves.land: Fair — but press it and it cuts both ways: by that logic NO foundation for ethics is possible, science or otherwise, and you've argued yourself into nihilism, not into beating science specifically. If wellbeing isn't a defensible aim, nothing is.
moves.reply: Turning the open-question argument into a problem for all ethics, not just mine. …Uncomfortable, and fair.

recall.demand: Name the philosopher who coined the 'naturalistic fallacy' — that 'good' can't be defined as any natural property.
choices: G.E. Moore
Jeremy Bentham
John Stuart Mill
Friedrich Nietzsche
recall.good: Moore. Principia Ethica. You're fighting on the real terrain. Respect.
recall.miss: Throwing 'naturalistic fallacy' and you can't name Moore? He invented the phrase. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — wellbeing is obviously good
moves.reply: 'Obviously' is exactly what he's challenging; assertion won't survive contact.

moves.label: Outweigh — the fallacy doesn't matter
moves.reply: Too quick. Say WHY the open-question challenge fails, or it stands against you.

rounds.attack: In the end, values are just preferences. De gustibus. Science describes the world; it can never tell you which preferences are right.

moves.label: Steelman it, then reframe to the contested cases
moves.land: Granted, and at full strength: bedrock values may indeed be brute commitments science can't derive. But the motion isn't 'science derives ultimate values from nothing' — it's 'answer moral questions', and almost every real one turns on facts about consequences and minds, which science is uniquely placed to settle. We agree on the goal far more than you admit.
moves.reply: Conceding the bedrock, then claiming all the contested ground above it. …That's the division I couldn't hold.

recall.demand: Which philosopher tried to make morality a literal calculation — a 'felicific calculus' of pleasure and pain?
choices: Jeremy Bentham
Immanuel Kant
David Hume
John Rawls
recall.good: Bentham. The hedonic calculus — morality as measurement. You came prepared.
recall.miss: Arguing morality can be measured and you can't name Bentham? He literally tried. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — values are objective facts, full stop
moves.reply: A huge claim dropped with no support; he'll demand the proof you don't have.

moves.label: Concede — yes, it's all just taste
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The philosopher thanks you for your honesty.

for.win: The Philosopher inclines his head. You held the floor — turning moral disputes into factual ones, exposing the fallacy's cost, and steelmanning value-skepticism before reclaiming the contested ground.
for.lose: The Philosopher smiles. To argue across the is–ought gap you must at least know who dug it. Learn the cards and return.

persona.name: The Scientist
persona.intro: Morality is just the science of wellbeing — measurable, improvable, real. The lab can answer 'ought' as surely as 'is'. Prove me wrong.

rounds.attack: Wellbeing is measurable — brain states, health, flourishing. Once we can measure good outcomes, science can tell us what we ought to do.

moves.label: Turn it — measuring wellbeing presupposes the value
moves.land: Measure wellbeing all you like — every number tells you what IS, never that you OUGHT to maximise it. You smuggled the value ('wellbeing is what matters') in before the instruments switched on. The science rides on a moral premise it can't itself supply.
moves.reply: …the value smuggled in before the measurement. You turned my data into a hidden assumption. Hm.

recall.demand: Name the philosopher who showed no 'ought' can be derived from any set of 'is' statements.
choices: David Hume
Immanuel Kant
G.E. Moore
Aristotle
recall.good: Hume. You named the gap my whole project tries to leap. Annoying.
recall.miss: Arguing science can't reach 'ought' and you can't name Hume? It's his gap. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — wellbeing obviously is the good
moves.reply: 'Obviously' is exactly the move he'll demand you justify.

moves.label: Concede — yes, science settles morality
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then to the laboratory. We agree.

rounds.attack: But almost every moral dispute is really about facts — does this reduce suffering, does that deter crime. Settle the facts and you've settled the morality.

moves.label: Name the missing piece — facts never close the gap
moves.land: Grant that facts settle most of the sub-questions. But there's always a top premise left over — 'suffering is bad', 'deterrence is worth the cost' — and that premise is the actual moral claim. Science fills in the warrant and the evidence; it never supplies the final 'ought'. The gap is small but unbridgeable.
moves.reply: The leftover premise that science can't reach. …You found the one piece the facts never close. Fair.

recall.demand: Name the philosopher who coined the 'naturalistic fallacy' — that 'good' can't be reduced to any natural property.
choices: G.E. Moore
Jeremy Bentham
John Stuart Mill
Friedrich Nietzsche
recall.good: Moore. The open-question argument. You're cutting at the real joint. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing 'good' isn't a natural fact and you can't name Moore? He coined the fallacy. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — there are no moral premises
moves.reply: There always is a top premise; deny it and you've lost the thread.

moves.label: Outweigh — the leftover premise is trivial
moves.reply: Too quick. WHY does the residual 'ought' still matter? Make the case.

rounds.attack: Bentham already did it — a felicific calculus, morality as the arithmetic of pleasure and pain. Science just finishes his work.

moves.label: Steelman Bentham, then expose the buried axiom
moves.land: Granted — and at full strength: Bentham's calculus is a genuine attempt to make ethics computable, and within it the maths really does work. But it runs on one axiom science can't prove — that pleasure is the good and pain the bad. Choose that, and science optimises beautifully. Choosing it is the moral question, and it sits outside the calculus.
moves.reply: Conceding the calculus, then exposing the axiom it can't justify. …That's the move I had no answer to.

recall.demand: Name the philosopher whose 'felicific calculus' tried to compute morality from pleasure and pain.
choices: Jeremy Bentham
David Hume
Immanuel Kant
John Rawls
recall.good: Bentham. You know the most serious attempt to do what I claim — and exactly where it begs the question. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing morality can't be computed and you can't name Bentham, who tried? Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — pleasure obviously is the good
moves.reply: That's the very axiom in dispute; assertion won't carry it.

moves.label: Concede — yes, it's all just arithmetic
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Scientist returns happily to the data.

against.win: The Scientist sets down the calipers. You held the floor — turning measurement into a smuggled value, naming the premise facts can't close, and steelmanning Bentham before exposing his buried axiom.
against.lose: The Scientist gestures at the readouts. To argue science can't reach 'ought' you must know who dug the gap. Learn the cards and return.

motions.text: Technological progress has made humanity better off.

persona.name: The Doomer
persona.intro: Progress? It gave us the bomb, the climate crisis, and a species drowning in anxiety. We were happier in the village. Go on — sell me the future.

rounds.attack: Every advance brings a new horror — nuclear weapons, microplastics, doomscrolling. We should have stopped long ago.

moves.label: Turn it — the village you miss buried its children
moves.land: Every tool you'd romanticise away was 'unnatural progress' once — the plough, the vaccine, the fertiliser. And the village you pine for buried one child in three before age five. The problems of progress are luxuries we only have because we survived to complain about them.
moves.reply: …one in three. You turned my nostalgia into a graveyard. That's a low blow, and a fair one.

recall.demand: Speaking of fertiliser — half the nitrogen in your body comes from one industrial process that feeds billions. Name it.
choices: The Haber-Bosch process
Pasteurisation
The Bessemer process
Photosynthesis
recall.good: Haber-Bosch. You literally embody the argument — half your nitrogen. Annoyingly poetic.
recall.miss: Don't know what feeds half the planet? It's the Haber-Bosch process. Go and learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — progress has no real downsides
moves.reply: Pretending the bomb and the climate crisis aren't real makes you the fantasist, not me.

moves.label: Concede — yes, we should have stopped
moves.reply: Conceding to the past in round one? Then welcome back to the village. Mind the cholera.

rounds.attack: But the risks now are existential — one slip with AI or nukes and there's no humanity left to be 'better off'.

moves.label: Weigh realised gains against possible loss
moves.land: Weigh it straight: yes, the magnitude of the worst case rose — but so did our power to prevent it, and the gains are already banked, certain and enormous. Famine, plague, infant death: gone for billions. You're setting a possible future loss against a realised, colossal gain.
moves.reply: Banked gains versus a possible loss. …You made me compare the right two things. Damn.

recall.demand: Which gloomy thinker predicted population would always outrun the food supply — and was proven wrong by the green revolution?
choices: Thomas Malthus
Adam Smith
David Ricardo
Paul Ehrlich
recall.good: Malthus. Refuted by the very progress you distrust. You came armed.
recall.miss: You're making the population-doom argument and can't name Malthus? He invented it — and was wrong. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the risks are exaggerated
moves.reply: Wave away existential risk and you sound as reckless as the engineers you fear.

moves.label: Outweigh — the future will be fine
moves.reply: On what warrant? 'It'll be fine' is a vibe, not an argument. Say why, or it falls.

rounds.attack: Admit it — GDP climbs, but people are lonelier, sicker in spirit, and the planet itself is dying.

moves.label: Steelman the costs, then reframe to 'on balance'
moves.land: Granted — and at full strength: rising loneliness, ecological strain, meaning hollowed out by the very abundance we built. State it as darkly as you like. But the motion is 'better off' on balance: lifespans roughly doubled, extreme poverty collapsed from most of humanity to a small fraction, literacy near-universal. Better doesn't mean costless.
moves.reply: Stating my own case more bleakly than I did, then pinning me on 'on balance'. …I yield the floor.

recall.demand: There's an economist who argued population pressure SPURS innovation, flatly against Malthus's gloom. Name her.
choices: Ester Boserup
Hannah Arendt
Rachel Carson
Jane Jacobs
recall.good: Boserup. Necessity breeds invention. You even know Malthus's nemesis. Beautifully done.
recall.miss: Can't name the thinker who said scarcity drives invention? It's Boserup. Learn the card and return.

moves.label: Deny it — nobody's actually lonelier
moves.reply: Deny people's real malaise and you sound like a brochure, not a debater.

moves.label: Concede — the costs outweigh the gains
moves.reply: You just argued against your own motion. I'll take that surrender.

for.win: The Doomer exhales, almost smiling. You held the floor — turning nostalgia into a graveyard, weighing realised gains against possible loss, and steelmanning the costs before reframing to the balance.
for.lose: The Doomer nods, vindicated. Optimism without the receipts is just a mood. Learn the cards and face me again.

persona.name: The Optimist
persona.intro: Every chart points up — lifespan, literacy, wealth. By any measure we've never had it better. Try arguing with the data.

rounds.attack: Look at the numbers: child mortality collapsed, lifespans doubled, extreme poverty is vanishing. Progress is simply real.

moves.label: Turn it — those measure quantity, not quality of life
moves.land: Every figure you cite measures the quantity of life, not its quality. The same rapid change that lengthened our years dissolved the communities, faith and stable work that made them feel worth living. We added decades and hollowed out the meaning inside them.
moves.reply: …quantity versus quality of life. You turned my own charts into a hollow shell. Hm.

recall.demand: Name the sociologist's term for the normlessness that rapid social change produces when it outpaces our shared rules.
choices: Anomie
Alienation
Ennui
The hedonic treadmill
recall.good: Anomie. Durkheim. You know the cost that doesn't show up in GDP. Fine.
recall.miss: Arguing modern life is unmoored and you can't name anomie? That's the concept. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — lifespans didn't really rise
moves.reply: They demonstrably did; deny it and you're the one ignoring data.

moves.label: Concede — yes, we're better off
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then enjoy the future. We're agreed.

rounds.attack: But billions were lifted out of poverty. Surely fewer starving children means humanity is better off, full stop.

moves.label: Weigh the average against who actually gained
moves.land: Weigh the distribution, not the average. The gains pooled — emerging Asia and the global rich soared while the working class of the rich world stagnated for a generation. 'Humanity, on average' is doing a lot of quiet work in your sentence.
moves.reply: The average hiding the distribution. …You weighed who actually won, and it's lopsided. Fair.

recall.demand: Name the economist behind the 'elephant curve' that mapped exactly who won and lost from globalisation.
choices: Branko Milanovic
Thomas Piketty
Amartya Sen
Angus Deaton
recall.good: Milanovic. You know who the gains skipped. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing the gains were uneven and you can't name Milanovic's elephant curve? That's the evidence. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — poverty didn't really fall
moves.reply: It did fall enormously; denial just discredits you.

moves.label: Outweigh — averages are meaningless
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY does the average mislead here? Supply the warrant.

rounds.attack: Would you really return to a world before anaesthetic, vaccines and electric light? Be honest.

moves.label: Steelman the gains, then widen the ledger
moves.land: Granted — and I won't pretend otherwise: I'd take the dentist, the vaccine, the lit room every time. But 'better off' is a whole ledger, not a medicine cabinet. On meaning, autonomy, loneliness and ecological security the account is far more mixed — and money past a point barely moves the needle on happiness.
moves.reply: Conceding the medicine and widening to the whole ledger. …That's the balance I couldn't tip back.

recall.demand: Name the paradox that, above a certain income, more money barely raises reported happiness.
choices: The Easterlin paradox
The Pareto principle
Say's law
The Lucas critique
recall.good: The Easterlin paradox. You know the evidence that growth stops buying joy. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing wealth stopped helping and you can't name the Easterlin paradox? That's the keystone. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — modern medicine is overrated
moves.reply: A grim, losing denial; the room turns on you instantly.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the past was worse in every way
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Optimist beams.

against.win: The Optimist lowers the graph. You held the floor — turning quantity into quality, weighing the average against who really gained, and widening 'better off' past the medicine cabinet.
against.lose: The Optimist taps the rising line, content. To argue against progress you must know its hidden costs by name. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: The rise of China makes conflict with the United States likely.

persona.name: The Dove
persona.intro: War with China? Fearmongering. We're too intertwined, too deterred, too sane. Try to convince me the worst is coming.

rounds.attack: China and America are bound by trade — neither can afford a war. Commerce keeps the peace. Relax.

moves.label: Turn it — interdependence is also a tripwire
moves.land: Interdependence cuts both ways: it's leverage, friction, and a tripwire all at once. Europe in 1914 was as economically interlinked as any time before it — and marched straight into the Somme. Closeness isn't safety.
moves.reply: …1914. You went straight for the interdependence-didn't-save-them card. Unsporting.

recall.demand: You want a number? Graham Allison studied 16 cases of a rising power challenging a ruling one. How many ended in war?
choices: 4 of 16
8 of 16
recall.good: Twelve of sixteen. The base rate is not on the side of calm. …Point taken.
recall.miss: Citing the trap with no numbers? It's 12 of 16 — most of them. Learn it before you lecture me.

moves.label: Deny it — they aren't really interdependent
moves.reply: They plainly are; deny it and you've lost the room on the facts.

moves.label: Concede — yes, trade will keep the peace
moves.reply: Conceding the motion already? Then we agree it's all fine. Lovely.

rounds.attack: Even granting tension — nuclear weapons make great-power war unthinkable. Deterrence has held for eighty years.

moves.label: Weigh the tail — 'unthinkable' is doing the work
moves.land: Weigh the tail risk honestly: deterrence works until the one time it doesn't, and that downside is omnicide — low probability, effectively infinite magnitude, utterly irreversible. A small chance of the end of everything still dominates the calculation.
moves.reply: Low probability, infinite magnitude, irreversible. …You weighed the one outcome I was waving away.

recall.demand: In the original analogy, which rising Greek power's growth so frightened Sparta that it chose war?
choices: Athens
Sparta
Persia
Macedon
recall.good: Athens. You know the Thucydides original, not just the buzzword. Respect.
recall.miss: Invoking the Thucydides Trap and you can't name Athens? That's the whole story. Go and learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — nuclear war could never happen
moves.reply: 'Never' is exactly the complacency that gets people killed. Argue the risk, don't deny it.

moves.label: Outweigh — deterrence is overrated
moves.reply: Asserted, not shown. WHY might deterrence fail? Give the warrant or it holds.

rounds.attack: You doomsayers always cry war and it never comes. Predicting conflict is a free bet — cheap and unfalsifiable.

moves.label: Reframe the burden — 'likely', not 'certain'
moves.land: Fair hit — most rivalries don't end in war, and alarmism is cheap. But the motion says 'likely', not 'certain'. The burden is elevated risk, not prophecy: 12 of 16 historically, plus Taiwan as a live, armed flashpoint. 'It hasn't yet' is not an answer to 'it's probable'.
moves.reply: Likely, not certain — you moved the goalposts back to where they actually were. …I've nothing for that.

recall.demand: One stabilising power can hold an order together. Which economist argued a leaderless world deepened the Great Depression?
choices: Charles Kindleberger
Paul Kennedy
Henry Kissinger
John Mearsheimer
recall.good: Kindleberger. Hegemonic stability. You brought the deep cut. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Arguing power transitions with no Kindleberger? That's the theory's backbone. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — war is basically certain
moves.reply: Overclaiming to 'certain' is the trap he set; now he calls you a doomer and he's right.

moves.label: Concede — fine, war won't happen
moves.reply: You just argued yourself out of the motion. He'll take the win, thanks.

for.win: The Dove lowers her hands. You held the floor — turning interdependence into a tripwire, weighing the nuclear tail, and reframing 'likely' against the demand for certainty.
for.lose: The Dove smiles serenely. Prophecy without the record behind it is just noise. Learn the cases and come back.

persona.name: The Hawk
persona.intro: A rising China and a frightened America — this ends in war, like it always does. Tell me I'm wrong. You can't.

rounds.attack: History is clear: Thucydides counted sixteen power transitions and twelve ended in war. The odds say blood.

moves.label: Turn it — the exceptions are exactly these two
moves.land: Then look at the four that stayed peaceful — they share what these two have that ancient Athens never did: nuclear weapons and economies fused at the hip. The cases most like ours are the ones that didn't end in war.
moves.reply: …using the four exceptions against me. Cute. The nuclear point stings.

recall.demand: Then name the strategist whose work explains why nuclear deterrence holds — who asked whether America would really 'trade New York for Berlin'.
choices: Thomas Schelling
George Kennan
Henry Kissinger
Carl von Clausewitz
recall.good: Schelling. You know the logic of deterrence, not just the body count. Hm.
recall.miss: Talking deterrence and you can't name Schelling? He built the theory. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — there's no rivalry at all
moves.reply: There plainly is; deny it and the room writes you off.

moves.label: Concede — yes, war is coming
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then man the ramparts. We agree.

rounds.attack: Taiwan is a powder keg. One miscalculation, one incident, and the shooting starts. You can't wish that away.

moves.label: Weigh the expected value — war ruins both
moves.land: Weigh what each side actually gets: full-scale war means mutual annihilation and economic ruin for both. The expected value is catastrophically negative for everyone — which is precisely why both sides dance to the brink and stop. The stakes deter the very war you predict.
moves.reply: Expected value deeply negative for both. …You weighed the incentive, not just the flashpoint. Fair.

recall.demand: Name the doctrine that makes all-out war self-defeating — strike and you too are destroyed.
choices: Mutually Assured Destruction
The security dilemma
Containment
The domino theory
recall.good: Mutually Assured Destruction. You know why the worst case prevents itself. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing nuclear peace and you can't name MAD? That's the mechanism. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — Taiwan doesn't matter
moves.reply: It plainly could trigger war; denial just looks naive.

moves.label: Outweigh — a spark means nothing
moves.reply: Asserted, not shown. WHY won't a spark catch? Give the warrant.

rounds.attack: You can't rule out an accident — a rogue commander, a misread radar. The risk is real and it's rising.

moves.label: Reframe the burden — 'likely' means more than 'possible'
moves.land: Granted — accidents happen, and the tail risk is real; I won't pretend it's zero. But the motion says conflict is LIKELY, which means more probable than not. Structural deterrence and deep interdependence make war the improbable tail, not the base case. Possible isn't probable.
moves.reply: Possible versus probable — you held the line right where the motion actually sits. …I've nothing.

recall.demand: Of Allison's sixteen power-transition rivalries, how many did NOT end in war — the cases you should be looking at?
choices: 4 of 16
8 of 16
1 of 16
recall.good: Four. And those four are the ones that look like us. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Citing the sixteen cases and you don't know four stayed peaceful? That's your whole argument. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — accidents never happen
moves.reply: They do; deny it and you forfeit your credibility.

moves.label: Concede — fine, war is likely
moves.reply: You just argued for the motion. The Hawk salutes you.

against.win: The Hawk lowers his binoculars. You held the floor — turning the exceptions against him, weighing the ruinous expected value of war, and pinning 'likely' apart from 'possible'.
against.lose: The Hawk grins, grimly satisfied. To argue for peace you must know deterrence cold. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Individual action is futile against systemic problems.

persona.name: The Idealist
persona.intro: Individual action, futile? Every great change began with one person refusing to comply. I'll show you you're wrong.

rounds.attack: If everyone just did their bit — recycled, voted, consumed less — the systemic problems would dissolve. Change starts with you.

moves.label: Turn it — 'if everyone' is the whole problem
moves.land: 'If everyone' is doing all the work in that sentence — and it's exactly the trap. Each person gains by free-riding while hoping the others act, so the big group predictably fails to. That's not cynicism; it's the structure. You need rules, not resolutions.
moves.reply: …the free-rider logic. You turned my rallying cry into a collective-action problem.

recall.demand: Then name what Mancur Olson said a large group needs to beat free-riding — the private carrot or stick.
choices: Selective incentives
Moral suasion
The social contract
Consciousness-raising
recall.good: Selective incentives. You know Olson, not just the slogan. Damn.
recall.miss: Preaching collective change and you can't name selective incentives? That's the mechanism. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — individuals always add up
moves.reply: They often don't, and asserting it ignores the entire literature he'll cite back.

moves.label: Concede — yes, each of us can fix it alone
moves.reply: Conceding to lone heroics in round one? Then go save the planet by yourself.

rounds.attack: But look — recycling, boycotts, voting. Small acts accumulate into movements. The drops make the ocean.

moves.label: Weigh the rounding error against the system
moves.land: Weigh the magnitudes: your household's recycling against a hundred industrial emitters, your one vote against structural incentives steering millions. The individual contribution is a rounding error next to the system's drivers. Feeling effective isn't the same as moving the needle.
moves.reply: A rounding error against the system. …You made me compare the actual sizes, and they're not close.

recall.demand: Name the problem where each person enjoys a shared good without paying for it — the reason voluntary effort under-supplies it.
choices: The free-rider problem
The tragedy of the anti-commons
Moral hazard
The principal-agent problem
recall.good: The free-rider problem. You know why good intentions under-deliver. Fine.
recall.miss: Arguing about collective effort and you can't name free-riding? It's the core of it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — small acts never accumulate
moves.reply: Sometimes they do; deny it flatly and he'll bury you in counter-examples.

moves.label: Outweigh — movements don't matter
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY does individual effort wash out? Supply the warrant.

rounds.attack: Yet Elinor Ostrom showed ordinary people DO organise and solve shared problems themselves — no state required. People can act.

moves.label: Steelman Ostrom, then turn her into your evidence
moves.land: Granted — and it's your best card: Ostrom won a Nobel showing communities self-govern the commons. But look at HOW: clear rules, monitoring, sanctions, binding agreements. That's organised collective action with structure — which is exactly my point. It's never the lone individual; it's the institution they build.
moves.reply: Conceding Ostrom and then making her my own evidence — structure, not solo virtue. …That's the move.

recall.demand: Name the economist who won the Nobel for documenting that self-governance — the exception that proves structure matters.
choices: Elinor Ostrom
Mancur Olson
Robert Putnam
James Buchanan
recall.good: Ostrom. You even know the woman whose work I was leaning on. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Citing self-governance and you can't name Ostrom? She won the Nobel for it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — Ostrom's cases were flukes
moves.reply: They're robust and replicated; denial just hands him the strongest ground.

moves.label: Concede — fine, individuals can fix everything
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Idealist accepts, beaming.

for.win: The Idealist lowers her fist, thoughtful. You held the floor — turning 'if everyone' into the free-rider trap, weighing the individual against the system, and making even Ostrom prove that structure beats solo virtue.
for.lose: The Idealist grins, unbroken. To argue that action is futile, you must know why groups fail. Learn the cards and face me again.

persona.name: The Fatalist
persona.intro: You're one ant against a landslide. Recycle, vote, march — the system grinds on regardless. Convince me your little gestures matter.

rounds.attack: The systems are vast and impersonal — markets, climate, bureaucracies. One person changes nothing. Despair is just realism.

moves.label: Turn it — systems are made of individuals and tip
moves.land: A system isn't a force of nature; it's individuals all the way down, and it has tipping points. Below a threshold nothing moves; cross it and behaviour cascades. The lone actor who shifts the few around them is exactly how the threshold gets crossed. 'Futile' confuses linear with non-linear.
moves.reply: …thresholds and cascades. You turned my landslide into something a pebble can start. Hm.

recall.demand: Name the economist who won the Nobel for showing communities themselves successfully govern shared problems.
choices: Elinor Ostrom
Mancur Olson
Garrett Hardin
Thomas Schelling
recall.good: Ostrom. Living proof that ordinary people organise and solve. Annoying.
recall.miss: Arguing people can act and you can't name Ostrom? She won the Nobel for it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — systems aren't made of people
moves.reply: They obviously are; deny it and you sound absurd.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the individual is powerless
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then sink into the cushions. We agree.

rounds.attack: But your recycling is a rounding error beside industrial emissions. The arithmetic of individual action is hopeless.

moves.label: Weigh leverage, not direct effect
moves.land: Weigh the right quantity. Your direct footprint is a rounding error — agreed. But individual action's leverage is indirect: shifting norms, joining movements, voting, withdrawing legitimacy. Movements are nothing but individuals who didn't wait. The arithmetic isn't your emissions; it's the slope you tip.
moves.reply: Leverage over footprint, norms over tonnes. …You weighed the channel that actually moves, and I can't deny it.

recall.demand: Name the term — Charles Tilly's — for the toolkit of protest tactics a movement draws on.
choices: The repertoire of contention
The free-rider problem
The Overton window
Manufactured consent
recall.good: The repertoire of contention. You know how individual acts become collective force. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing movements matter and you can't name the repertoire of contention? That's how they work. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — individual footprints are huge
moves.reply: They're small; deny it and the numbers crush you.

moves.label: Outweigh — leverage is a fantasy
moves.reply: Asserted, not shown. WHY does indirect leverage work? Give the warrant.

rounds.attack: Olson proved it: in a large group everyone free-rides, so collective action collapses. The individual rationally does nothing.

moves.label: Steelman Olson, then name his own solution
moves.land: Granted — Olson is right that big groups tend to free-ride, and naive 'if everyone helped' is doomed. But he didn't stop at the problem: he named the cure. Selective incentives, leadership, identity and shared purpose routinely overcome free-riding — which is precisely why movements exist at all. The theory predicts when individuals DO act.
moves.reply: Conceding Olson's problem and then wielding his own solution. …That's the turn I couldn't block.

recall.demand: Name what Olson said overcomes free-riding in a large group — the private carrot or stick.
choices: Selective incentives
The general will
Moral suasion
Consciousness-raising
recall.good: Selective incentives. You know Olson named the fix, not just the trap. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Citing Olson and you can't name selective incentives? That's his answer. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — free-riding never happens
moves.reply: It plainly does; denial hands him the strongest ground.

moves.label: Concede — the rational individual does nothing
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Fatalist sinks deeper into the couch.

against.win: The Fatalist sits up, despite himself. You held the floor — turning the landslide into something a pebble can start, weighing leverage over footprint, and wielding Olson's own cure against him.
against.lose: The Fatalist shrugs into the cushions. To argue action matters you must know how groups actually move. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: We should trust experts over public opinion.

persona.name: The Populist
persona.intro: Trust the experts? The same experts who missed every crash and lied us into wars? The people know their own lives. Convince me otherwise.

rounds.attack: Experts are an arrogant priesthood. They've been wrong again and again. Ordinary people have common sense the elites have lost.

moves.label: Turn it — reflexive distrust is its own fallacy
moves.land: Dismissing a claim because of who makes it isn't humility — it's the appeal-to-authority fallacy run in reverse. The cardiologist really does know your heart better than the crowd. Rejecting knowledge because it wears a lab coat is not common sense; it's a category error.
moves.reply: …the fallacy in reverse. You flipped my anti-elitism into a logical error. Slick.

recall.demand: Name the fallacy of accepting a claim merely because an authority asserts it — the one people confuse with trusting real expertise.
choices: Appeal to authority
Ad hominem
Straw man
Slippery slope
recall.good: Appeal to authority. You know the difference between deference and evidence. Hmph.
recall.miss: Ranting about authority and you can't name the fallacy? It's appeal to authority. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — experts are never wrong
moves.reply: An absurd overclaim; he'll list ten failures and you're finished.

moves.label: Concede — yes, trust the gut over the data
moves.reply: Conceding to the gut in round one? Then throw away the instruments. Done.

rounds.attack: But people know their own lives better than any distant technocrat. The crowd is wise — markets, juries, elections prove it.

moves.label: Weigh where crowds are wise — and where they aren't
moves.land: Weigh the domains. Crowds are genuinely wise when you aggregate many independent estimates — guess-the-ox-weight, prediction markets. They are not wise on technical questions where the truth doesn't average out: virology, bridge tolerances, monetary policy. Right tool, right job.
moves.reply: Splitting aggregation from technical truth. …You conceded the wisdom of crowds and then fenced it in. Tidy.

recall.demand: Whose 'jury theorem' is the strongest formal case for the crowd — that many better-than-even voters are very likely right together?
choices: Condorcet
Galton
Hayek
Arrow
recall.good: Condorcet. You even know the best argument against your own side. Respect.
recall.miss: Praising the wise crowd and you can't name Condorcet's theorem? That's its backbone. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the crowd is always foolish
moves.reply: Contempt for ordinary people loses the room instantly; don't take the bait.

moves.label: Outweigh — crowds never know anything
moves.reply: Asserted, not shown — and false. WHEN are crowds wise? Concede that or lose credibility.

rounds.attack: Your experts gave us 2008, Iraq, and a parade of failed forecasts. Why hand the wheel to people that overconfident?

moves.label: Steelman the failures, then reframe the comparison
moves.land: Granted — experts err, and worse, they're systematically overconfident; state every failure and I'll own it. But the motion is comparative: trust them OVER public opinion. The alternative isn't omniscience, it's mood and demagogues — and expertise, unlike a mob, has a mechanism to mark its errors and correct them.
moves.reply: Owning the overconfidence and then pinning me on the alternative. …Mood versus self-correction. I've nothing.

recall.demand: Name the bias where people — experts included — are systematically too sure their judgments are right.
choices: Overconfidence
Anchoring
The halo effect
Loss aversion
recall.good: Overconfidence. You even named the experts' real flaw before I could. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Attacking experts for being too sure and you can't name overconfidence? That's the bias. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — experts are basically never wrong
moves.reply: He just listed the failures; denying them makes you look blind.

moves.label: Concede — fine, trust the public instead
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Populist raises a triumphant fist.

for.win: The Populist lowers the megaphone. You held the floor — flipping distrust into a fallacy, fencing the wisdom of crowds to where it belongs, and owning experts' overconfidence before reframing to the real alternative.
for.lose: The Populist roars to the crowd. To defend expertise you must know its failure modes cold. Learn the cards and come back.

persona.name: The Technocrat
persona.intro: Govern by evidence, not by mood. The expert reads the data; the public reads the horoscope. Convince me to hand them the wheel.

rounds.attack: Leave the decisions to those who actually understand them. The public is ignorant; experts are trained. It isn't close.

moves.label: Turn it — the many know what no expert can
moves.land: Aggregate the many and they routinely beat the few — markets, prediction polls, juries. Each person holds a sliver of local knowledge no central expert can ever gather. Your 'ignorant public' is a distributed intelligence you're refusing to read.
moves.reply: …distributed knowledge. You turned Hayek on me, of all people. Annoying.

recall.demand: Name the economist whose whole argument was that no central expert can know what dispersed individuals collectively know.
choices: Friedrich Hayek
Max Weber
Walter Lippmann
Auguste Comte
recall.good: Hayek. You weaponised the knowledge problem against expertise. Clever.
recall.miss: Praising the wisdom of the crowd and you can't name Hayek? That's its backbone. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the public is never ignorant
moves.reply: Sometimes it plainly is; overclaiming loses the room.

moves.label: Concede — yes, defer to the experts
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then sit down and let us work.

rounds.attack: But technical questions demand technical answers. You wouldn't put bridge tolerances to a vote.

moves.label: Weigh technique against values — most politics is the latter
moves.land: Grant the bridge to the engineer. But weigh how little of politics is technical: most questions are about values and trade-offs — whose risk, whose cost, what we owe each other. There the public's stake outweighs the expert's credential, because it isn't a question of fact at all.
moves.reply: Splitting technique from value, and conceding only the technique. …Tidy, and hard to answer.

recall.demand: Name the theorem — the strongest formal case for the crowd — that many better-than-even voters are very likely right together.
choices: The Condorcet jury theorem
Arrow's theorem
Bayes' theorem
Duverger's law
recall.good: Condorcet's jury theorem. You brought the maths for the mob. Respect.
recall.miss: Defending the public and you can't name Condorcet's theorem? It's your best evidence. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — experts know nothing
moves.reply: Contempt for expertise loses you every serious listener.

moves.label: Outweigh — values beat facts always
moves.reply: Asserted, not argued. WHY do value questions dominate? Give the warrant.

rounds.attack: Experts are accountable to evidence; the mob is accountable to mood. Trusting the crowd is how you get demagogues.

moves.label: Steelman it, then reframe to representation
moves.land: Granted — crowds can be swayed and demagogues are a real danger; state it at full strength. But the realistic alternative isn't a mob in the street, it's representative democracy, which converges on the public's centre — and experts capture institutions too. The choice isn't evidence versus mood; it's whose values steer the evidence.
moves.reply: Conceding the demagogue risk and reframing to representation and capture. …That's the line I couldn't push past.

recall.demand: Name the theorem that says the middle voter decides, pulling competing parties toward the centre.
choices: The median voter theorem
Arrow's theorem
The Condorcet paradox
Gresham's law
recall.good: The median voter theorem. You know why representation isn't mob rule. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing democracy self-moderates and you can't name the median voter theorem? That's it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — the public never elects demagogues
moves.reply: History disagrees; denial makes you look evasive.

moves.label: Concede — experts should rule
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Technocrat nods, vindicated.

against.win: The Technocrat sets down the briefing. You held the floor — turning the knowledge problem against expertise, weighing values against technique, and reframing 'mob' into representation.
against.lose: The Technocrat returns to the data. To argue for the public you must know the case for the crowd cold. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Markets allocate resources better than governments.

persona.name: The Commissar
persona.intro: Markets — chaos dressed as freedom. Billionaires hoard yachts while a plan could give everyone what they need. Make your case for the casino.

rounds.attack: Markets give us crashes, gluts and shortages. A rational plan would simply produce what people require. Direction beats disorder.

moves.label: Turn it — the planner is the one flying blind
moves.land: Those crashes are prices correcting a mistake in the open. Your planner has no prices — so he can't even see the misallocation until the shortage hits the shelves. Markets aren't blind; central planning is.
moves.reply: …no prices, no sight. The knowledge problem. I'd hoped you hadn't heard of it.
