recall.demand: Then name him. Which economist's whole case was that no planner can know what dispersed prices already know?
choices: Friedrich Hayek
John Maynard Keynes
Milton Friedman
Karl Marx
recall.good: Hayek. The use of knowledge in society. You've done the reading, comrade.
recall.miss: You wield the argument but can't name Hayek? Then it isn't yours. Go and learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — markets don't really have crashes
moves.reply: 2008 says otherwise. Deny the cycle and the room stops believing a word.

moves.label: Concede — yes, planning is more rational
moves.reply: Conceding to the plan already? Then hand me the clipboard and sit down.

rounds.attack: Yet planning built Soviet heavy industry and put the first man in space. Coordinated will beats your scramble.

moves.label: Weigh the whole record, not the showpieces
moves.land: Weigh all of it, not two trophies: chronic shortages, a famine that killed millions, queues for bread, and a system that finally collapsed. High variance, catastrophic downside, and no price signal to self-correct on the way down.
moves.reply: The graveyard against the showpieces. …Yes. The variance is the part we never advertised.

recall.demand: There was a famous debate over whether planners could just fake prices. Name the economist who argued they COULD — and lost to Hayek.
choices: Oskar Lange
Leon Trotsky
Paul Samuelson
Rosa Luxemburg
recall.good: Lange. The socialist calculation debate. You know the history, not just the slogan.
recall.miss: Don't know who argued the other side? Then you don't really know the debate. It was Oskar Lange.

moves.label: Deny it — those achievements were faked
moves.reply: They were real enough; denying them makes you the one ignoring evidence.

moves.label: Outweigh — space flight proves nothing
moves.reply: Too cheap. Say WHY a prestige project doesn't redeem the system, or it stands.

rounds.attack: But markets fail — pollution, monopolies, the 2008 crash. Admit the state must run the show.

moves.label: Steelman the failures, then reframe to 'comparative'
moves.land: Granted — markets fail on externalities and monopoly; put your strongest case and I'll concede each one. But 'allocate better' is comparative: governments fail too, and worse, because they lack the very price signal that would tell them they're failing. Best isn't flawless — it's self-correcting.
moves.reply: Steelmanning my own examples, then pinning me on 'comparative'. …That's the move I had no answer to.

recall.demand: Even shared resources — the commons — aren't only saved by the state. Who won a Nobel showing communities govern them themselves?
choices: Elinor Ostrom
Milton Friedman
Karl Polanyi
Amartya Sen
recall.good: Ostrom. Neither plan nor pure market. You even took my fallback. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Lecturing me on the commons and you can't name Ostrom? She won the Nobel for it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — markets never fail
moves.reply: Even Hayek admitted failures. Deny them and you've lost your own credibility.

moves.label: Concede — the state should run it all
moves.reply: From 'markets fail sometimes' to 'nationalise everything'? You leapt off the cliff yourself.

for.win: The Commissar sets down the clipboard. You held the floor — exposing the planner's blindness, weighing the whole record, and steelmanning market failure before reframing to the comparative.
for.lose: The Commissar permits himself a thin smile. Slogans without the names behind them are just noise. Learn the cards and report back.

persona.name: The Free-Marketeer
persona.intro: The market is the greatest information machine ever built. Government is the boot that breaks it. Defend the planners — I'll wait.

rounds.attack: Leave it to the market. Prices coordinate millions of strangers with no central command. Nothing allocates better.

moves.label: Turn it — prices lie when costs land on others
moves.land: Prices coordinate beautifully — until the cost lands on a third party. Then the market price is simply wrong, and it over-produces the harm precisely because the polluter never pays. The 'information machine' goes blind exactly where it matters most.
moves.reply: …externalities break the price signal. You turned my machine against itself. Tch.

recall.demand: Name the economist who showed external costs make the market price wrong — and that bargaining could, in principle, fix it.
choices: Ronald Coase
Milton Friedman
Adam Smith
Friedrich Hayek
recall.good: Coase. You know your market failures from the inside. Fine.
recall.miss: Arguing market failure and you can't name Coase? He won a Nobel for it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — prices are always right
moves.reply: Externalities are textbook; deny them and you lose every economist listening.

moves.label: Concede — yes, markets always allocate best
moves.reply: Conceding in round one? Then deregulate everything and goodbye.

rounds.attack: Markets are efficient; the state is waste and queues. Whatever government touches, it bungles.

moves.label: Weigh the things markets simply won't supply
moves.land: Weigh the whole basket. Some goods the market won't provide at all — basic research, public health, a justice system — because no one can charge for them. Set bureaucratic waste against the entire categories of value markets leave on the floor, and 'allocate better' starts to wobble.
moves.reply: Public goods the market won't touch. …You weighed what's missing, not just what's wasteful. Hm.

recall.demand: Name the problem where everyone benefits from a good without paying, so the market under-supplies it.
choices: The free-rider problem
Moral hazard
Adverse selection
The principal-agent problem
recall.good: The free-rider problem. You know exactly where markets fall silent. Good.
recall.miss: Arguing for public provision and you can't name free-riding? That's the reason. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — markets supply everything
moves.reply: They don't supply pure public goods; denial sinks you.

moves.label: Outweigh — government waste is the only issue
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY does waste outweigh market failure? Warrant, please.

rounds.attack: But governments fail too — capture, corruption, the Soviet collapse. Public choice exposed the myth of the benevolent planner.

moves.label: Steelman government failure, then hold the comparison
moves.land: Granted — government failure is real, and public choice is right that planners aren't angels; I'll concede every case. But the motion is comparative: markets allocate BETTER. For the whole class of public goods and externalities, they allocate worse — so the blanket claim fails even if the state is flawed too.
moves.reply: Conceding government failure and still holding the comparison on public goods. …That's the move I couldn't break.

recall.demand: Name the corrective tax that prices an external harm so the market price finally tells the truth.
choices: A Pigouvian tax
A tariff
A poll tax
Quantitative easing
recall.good: The Pigouvian tax. You even know the fix, not just the failure. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing markets misprice harm and you can't name the Pigouvian tax? That's the remedy. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — governments never fail
moves.reply: A silly overclaim; he'll bury you in examples.

moves.label: Concede — markets win, end of story
moves.reply: You let public choice stampede you into conceding the motion.

against.win: The Free-Marketeer pockets his Hayek. You held the floor — turning prices against themselves on externalities, weighing the goods markets won't supply, and conceding government failure without losing the comparison.
against.lose: The Free-Marketeer smiles thinly. To argue for the state you must know market failure cold. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Marx's critique of capitalism is still relevant today.

persona.name: The Economist
persona.intro: Marx? A 19th-century relic whose value theory was demolished and whose predictions all failed. Tell me why we still read him.

rounds.attack: Marx's labour theory of value was refuted by the marginalists over a century ago. The whole edifice rests on a broken foundation.

moves.label: Turn it — the LTV isn't what's still relevant
moves.land: Granted, the labour theory of value lost to marginalism — but that was never the living part of Marx. What endures is the critique: alienation, commodification, the tendency of capital to concentrate and to lurch through crises. You're knocking down the one wall everyone already abandoned.
moves.reply: …conceding the value theory to save the critique. You ceded the ground I expected to fight on.

recall.demand: Name Marx's concept for workers estranged from their labour, its product, and themselves.
choices: Alienation
Surplus value
False consciousness
Commodity fetishism
recall.good: Alienation. You know which Marx is still alive. Fine.
recall.miss: Defending Marx's relevance and you can't name alienation? It's his most cited idea. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — the labour theory of value still holds
moves.reply: Almost no economist agrees; die on that hill and you lose the whole debate.

moves.label: Concede — yes, Marx is obsolete
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then close the book. We're agreed.

rounds.attack: And his great prophecy failed: capitalism didn't immiserate the workers, it enriched billions. He got the future flatly wrong.

moves.label: Weigh what he got right against what he got wrong
moves.land: Weigh both columns. Wrong: immiseration, the inevitable collapse. Right, and strikingly: the relentless concentration of capital, recurring crises, the global commodification of everything. Relevance isn't infallibility — a diagnosis can be sharp even where the prognosis missed.
moves.reply: Separating diagnosis from prophecy, and scoring the diagnosis. …That's a fairer ledger than I wanted to keep.

recall.demand: Which modern economist's finding — that the return on capital outpaces growth, r > g — revived Marx's worry about capital concentrating?
choices: Thomas Piketty
Milton Friedman
Paul Krugman
Joseph Schumpeter
recall.good: Piketty. r greater than g — Marx's concern in modern data. You came armed.
recall.miss: Arguing capital still concentrates and you can't name Piketty? r > g is the headline. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — workers were immiserated after all
moves.reply: Living standards rose enormously; deny it and you're the one ignoring data.

moves.label: Outweigh — predictions don't matter
moves.reply: Too glib. Say WHY a failed forecast doesn't sink the theory, or it sinks.

rounds.attack: And Marxism in power gave us the gulag, the famine, the wall. The whole project is morally bankrupt. Case closed.

moves.label: Steelman the horrors, then split critique from regime
moves.land: Granted — and at full force: Marxist states produced mass murder on a historic scale; I won't soften it. But the motion is about Marx's CRITIQUE of capitalism, not the regimes that flew his flag. A diagnosis of capitalism's pathologies can be acute even if every prescription drawn from it failed catastrophically.
moves.reply: Owning the body count, then severing the critique from the regime. …That distinction is the one I couldn't collapse.

recall.demand: Name the superseded doctrine — that a good's value comes from the labour embodied in it — that Marx inherited from Ricardo.
choices: The labour theory of value
Surplus value
Dialectical materialism
The falling rate of profit
recall.good: The labour theory of value. You know precisely which part to abandon and which to keep. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Debating Marx's economics and you can't name the labour theory of value? That's the crux. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the communist regimes weren't that bad
moves.reply: A grotesque denial; you lose every listener and deserve to.

moves.label: Concede — Marx is discredited by the gulag
moves.reply: You let him fuse the critique with the regime — and conceded the motion.

for.win: The Economist closes her notebook. You held the floor — conceding the value theory to save the critique, scoring the diagnosis against the failed prophecy, and severing Marx's analysis from the regimes that abused it.
for.lose: The Economist permits a dry smile. To defend Marx you must know exactly which Marx to defend. Learn the cards and return.

persona.name: The Marxist
persona.intro: Alienation, exploitation, capital devouring everything — Marx described the world you live in. He is more relevant than ever. Tell me he's a relic.

rounds.attack: Marx's core insights — alienation, exploitation, class power — describe modern capitalism perfectly. The man saw our world coming.

moves.label: Turn it — the vague parts fit anything; the testable parts failed
moves.land: The parts that 'fit perfectly' — alienation, exploitation — are elastic enough to fit any era; that's not predictive power, it's a horoscope. The parts that were testable — the labour theory of value, ever-deepening misery, inevitable revolution — were refuted. What survives is the unfalsifiable; what was falsifiable, fell.
moves.reply: …separating the unfalsifiable from the refuted. You turned 'always relevant' into 'never testable'. Tch.

recall.demand: Name an economist of the 1870s marginal revolution that replaced Marx's labour theory of value with marginal utility.
choices: Jevons
Engels
Keynes
Veblen
recall.good: Jevons — the marginalists. You know what buried the value theory. Hm.
recall.miss: Arguing the value theory was refuted and you can't name the marginalists? Jevons led them. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — every Marxist prediction came true
moves.reply: Most plainly didn't; overclaiming loses the room.

moves.label: Concede — yes, Marx is fully relevant
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then workers of the world, unite. We agree.

rounds.attack: And Piketty proved Marx right — capital concentrates, r exceeds g, the rich pull away exactly as he foretold.

moves.label: Weigh what survived against what collapsed
moves.land: Weigh both columns honestly. Survived: some concentration of capital, recurring crises. Collapsed: immiseration (living standards soared), the revolutionary proletariat (the middle class grew), the value theory. And Piketty is a liberal reformer, not Marx — borrowing one worry from a thinker doesn't resurrect his system.
moves.reply: Piketty isn't Marx, and the ledger is mostly red for the prophet. …A fairer accounting than I wanted.

recall.demand: Name the discredited doctrine — that a good's value comes from the labour embodied in it — at the centre of Marx's economics.
choices: The labour theory of value
Marginal utility
Comparative advantage
Surplus value
recall.good: The labour theory of value. You know which load-bearing wall fell. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing Marx's economics failed and you can't name the labour theory of value? That's the crux. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — capital doesn't concentrate
moves.reply: Piketty's data says it can; flat denial sinks you.

moves.label: Outweigh — predictions don't matter for relevance
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY do the failed predictions not count? Warrant it.

rounds.attack: His critique of capitalism's crises still bites — 2008, inequality, precarity. The diagnosis is alive even if the cure failed.

moves.label: Steelman the diagnosis, then show capitalism adapted
moves.land: Granted — capitalism does lurch through crises, and Marx saw that clearly; I'll concede the diagnosis has teeth. But his deeper claim was that the system COULDN'T reform its way out — and the welfare state, central banks and regulation are exactly the self-correction he said was impossible. The diagnosis survives; the prognosis that made him Marx does not.
moves.reply: Conceding the diagnosis and then turning the self-correction against the prognosis. …That's the split I couldn't hold.

recall.demand: Name the economist whose r > g finding is often misread as vindicating Marx — though he's a liberal reformer, not a Marxist.
choices: Thomas Piketty
Friedrich Engels
Rosa Luxemburg
Antonio Gramsci
recall.good: Piketty — claimed by Marxists, no Marxist himself. You know the difference. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Leaning on capital concentration and you can't name Piketty? r > g is the modern hook. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — capitalism never has crises
moves.reply: 2008 says otherwise; denial discredits you.

moves.label: Concede — the diagnosis makes Marx relevant
moves.reply: You let the diagnosis carry the prognosis — and conceded the motion.

against.win: The Marxist lowers the banner. You held the floor — separating the unfalsifiable from the refuted, weighing what survived against what collapsed, and turning capitalism's self-correction against the prognosis.
against.lose: The Marxist raises a fist, vindicated. To argue Marx is obsolete you must know exactly which Marx fell. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Inequality, not poverty, is the central economic problem of our time.

persona.name: The Growthist
persona.intro: Inequality? Who cares if the rich get richer, so long as the poor get less poor. Envy isn't an economic problem. Prove me wrong.

rounds.attack: Poverty is what matters — absolute deprivation. The gap between rich and poor is just envy dressed up as policy.

moves.label: Turn it — concentrated wealth rigs the rules
moves.land: It isn't envy — it's power. Concentrated wealth buys politics, media and the rules themselves, then writes them to entrench its position and pull the ladder up. Inequality isn't downstream of poverty; it's one of the engines that manufactures and perpetuates it.
moves.reply: …wealth as political power, not just envy. You moved it from feelings to mechanisms. Annoying.

recall.demand: Name the economist whose finding — the return on capital outruns growth, r > g — showed wealth concentrating over two centuries.
choices: Thomas Piketty
Milton Friedman
Simon Kuznets
Friedrich Hayek
recall.good: Piketty. r > g. You brought the data, not just the grievance. Fine.
recall.miss: Arguing wealth concentrates and you can't name Piketty? r > g is the whole case. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — inequality has no real effects
moves.reply: It plainly shapes power and opportunity; deny it and you look naive.

moves.label: Concede — yes, only poverty matters
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then we agree. Off you go.

rounds.attack: A rising tide lifts all boats. Grow the pie and everyone's slice grows — chasing the gap just shrinks the pie.

moves.label: Weigh the level against the distribution
moves.land: Weigh both, not just the level. When the gains pool at the very top, the tide lifts the yachts and leaves the rowboats aground — median wages can stagnate for decades while GDP climbs. Growth without distribution is a number that stops describing most people's lives.
moves.reply: Median stagnation under rising GDP. …You weighed distribution against the headline, and the headline lost.

recall.demand: Name the standard measure of inequality — 0 means everyone equal, 1 means one person holds it all.
choices: The Gini coefficient
The Lorenz ratio
The Theil paradox
The Phillips curve
recall.good: The Gini coefficient. You can actually measure what you're arguing about. Good.
recall.miss: Debating inequality and you can't name the Gini coefficient? It's how we measure it. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — growth always reaches everyone
moves.reply: Decades of flat median wages say otherwise; denial sinks you.

moves.label: Outweigh — distribution is irrelevant
moves.reply: Asserted, not argued. WHY does the split not matter? Give the warrant or fold.

rounds.attack: Frankfurt had it right: what matters morally is that everyone has enough, not that some have more. Sufficiency, not equality.

moves.label: Steelman sufficiency, then show inequality is upstream
moves.land: Granted — and at full strength: if everyone had genuinely enough, the gap might be a moral footnote. But 'enough' isn't fixed. Relative position determines political voice, housing, schooling, the rules of the game — so inequality sits upstream of who can ever reach 'enough' at all. The gap manufactures the deprivation.
moves.reply: Granting sufficiency and then placing inequality upstream of it. …That ordering is the thing I couldn't reverse.

recall.demand: Whose 'veil of ignorance' argues inequalities are just only if they benefit the worst-off?
choices: John Rawls
Robert Nozick
Harry Frankfurt
Amartya Sen
recall.good: Rawls. The difference principle. You know the philosophy under the economics. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing about fair distribution and you can't name Rawls? The veil of ignorance is the canon. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — having 'enough' doesn't matter
moves.reply: Dismissing sufficiency outright concedes his strongest, most humane point.

moves.label: Concede — sufficiency is all that matters
moves.reply: You let him win the framing — and conceded the motion with it.

for.win: The Growthist pockets his calculator. You held the floor — recasting the gap as power not envy, weighing distribution against the headline, and steelmanning sufficiency before placing inequality upstream of it.
for.lose: The Growthist shrugs, satisfied. To argue inequality is central you must measure and name it. Learn the cards and come back.

persona.name: The Egalitarian
persona.intro: The gap is the wound — the rich pulling ever further from the rest. Tell me poverty alone matters and watch me take you apart.

rounds.attack: The widening gap is the central problem. When the top pulls away, society fractures and the rich rewrite the rules.

moves.label: Turn it — a widening gap can mean the poor are rising
moves.land: A gap can widen precisely because the poor are getting richer fast and the rich faster still — that's a side-effect of progress, not the disease. Fixate on the gap and you may smash the very growth that's lifting the floor. The wound to watch is deprivation, not distance.
moves.reply: …the gap as a by-product of a rising floor. You turned my wound into a growing pain. Tch.

recall.demand: Which country's reforms lifted nearly 800 million from poverty — in millions — even as inequality inside it soared?
choices: About 800 million
About 80 million
About 8 million
About 300 million
recall.good: Eight hundred million — while its Gini rocketed. Rising floor, widening gap, both at once. Hm.
recall.miss: Arguing about poverty and inequality and you don't know China lifted ~800 million? That's the case. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — inequality has no effects at all
moves.reply: It plainly shapes power; deny it and you look naive.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the gap is what matters most
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then we agree. Off you go.

rounds.attack: But inequality buys political power — the rich capture the rules and rig the game against everyone below.

moves.label: Weigh capture against absolute deprivation
moves.land: Weigh the two harms. Capture is real — but set it against absolute deprivation: a poor family's life is transformed by clean water, a clinic, a school, none of which depends on whether a billionaire exists. The first duty is the floor; the gap is the second-order worry.
moves.reply: The floor before the gap. …You weighed deprivation against distance, and deprivation wins on urgency. Fair.

recall.demand: Name the economist whose 'elephant curve' showed the global poor were among globalisation's biggest winners.
choices: Branko Milanovic
Karl Marx
Joseph Stiglitz
Gabriel Zucman
recall.good: Milanovic. You know who actually gained at the bottom. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing the global poor rose and you can't name Milanovic's elephant curve? That's the evidence. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — money never buys power
moves.reply: It plainly can; flat denial loses the room.

moves.label: Outweigh — capture is irrelevant
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY does deprivation outrank capture? Warrant it.

rounds.attack: Rawls settled this: justice means improving the lot of the worst-off, and runaway inequality betrays them.

moves.label: Steelman Rawls, then turn the difference principle
moves.land: Granted, and at full strength: Rawls is right that we judge a society by its worst-off. But his difference principle PERMITS inequality exactly when it lifts the worst-off — which growth-driven inequality often does. By his own test, the target is the floor, not the gap. You've cited my best witness.
moves.reply: Turning the difference principle on its author. Floor not gap, by Rawls's own rule. …I yield.

recall.demand: Whose 'veil of ignorance' argues an inequality is just only if it benefits the worst-off?
choices: John Rawls
Robert Nozick
Harry Frankfurt
Amartya Sen
recall.good: Rawls. You know the philosophy well enough to flip it. The floor is yours.
recall.miss: Leaning on fairness and you can't name Rawls? The veil of ignorance is the canon. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the worst-off don't matter
moves.reply: A monstrous concession of the moral high ground; you lose.

moves.label: Concede — the gap is the true injustice
moves.reply: You let Rawls stampede you into conceding the motion.

against.win: The Egalitarian lowers the scales. You held the floor — recasting the gap as a by-product of a rising floor, weighing deprivation against capture, and turning Rawls's own principle toward the floor.
against.lose: The Egalitarian rebalances the scales, satisfied. To argue poverty over inequality you must know the numbers and the philosophy. Learn the cards and come back.

motions.text: Endless economic growth is the wrong goal for a rich society.

persona.name: The Cornucopian
persona.intro: Endless growth, the wrong goal? Growth IS the goal — more wealth, more options, more solved problems. Tell me why a rich society should stop.

rounds.attack: Growth cures everything: pensions, healthcare, the climate transition itself. More GDP means more of every good thing. Why on earth stop?

moves.label: Turn it — past a point, growth stops buying wellbeing
moves.land: For a poor country, yes — growth is liberation. But for an already-rich one, each extra point of GDP buys less and less actual wellbeing while the ecological bill keeps rising. The goal should shift from 'more' to 'better': distribution, time, sustainability.
moves.reply: …diminishing returns to wellbeing in a rich society. You turned 'more' into 'enough'. Hm.

recall.demand: Name the paradox: above a certain income, more money barely lifts reported happiness.
choices: The Easterlin paradox
The Lucas critique
Baumol's disease
The Veblen effect
recall.good: The Easterlin paradox. You know the evidence that money stops buying happiness. Fine.
recall.miss: Arguing rich societies should stop growing and you can't name the Easterlin paradox? That's the keystone. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — growth always raises wellbeing
moves.reply: Above a point it barely does; deny the evidence and you lose the room.

moves.label: Concede — yes, growth should be the goal forever
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then to the moon. Goodbye.

rounds.attack: But growth funds the green transition itself — the R&D, the solar, the carbon capture. Stop growing and you can't afford to go green.

moves.label: Weigh the ecological ceiling against the funding story
moves.land: Weigh it against the ceiling: infinite material growth on a finite planet eventually outruns any efficiency gain. The real question is whether GDP can keep rising while resource use falls in absolute terms — and where it can't, more growth just funds a faster overshoot.
moves.reply: The finite-planet ceiling against my funding story. …You weighed the constraint I keep waving away.

recall.demand: Name the term for GDP rising while resource use and emissions fall in absolute terms — the test green growth must pass.
choices: Absolute decoupling
The rebound effect
Degrowth
Creative destruction
recall.good: Absolute decoupling. You know the exact thing that has to be true. Good.
recall.miss: Arguing green growth and you can't name absolute decoupling? That's the whole bet. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — there are no ecological limits
moves.reply: Physics disagrees; deny limits and you forfeit every serious listener.

moves.label: Outweigh — growth funds everything, end of story
moves.reply: Stated, not shown. WHY does funding beat the ceiling? Supply the warrant.

rounds.attack: Degrowth is a fantasy that would freeze the poor in poverty and crash living standards. You'd halt progress in the name of vibes.

moves.label: Steelman it, then narrow the motion to rich societies
moves.land: Granted — and at full strength: for the developing world, growth is non-negotiable, and crude degrowth would be cruel. But the motion is about a RICH society. For them the goal can shift from raw GDP to what GDP was always a proxy for: health, leisure, a livable planet, fair distribution. Not no growth everywhere — a better goal where there's already plenty.
moves.reply: Conceding the poor world and narrowing to the rich one. …That's the line I couldn't push you off.

recall.demand: Name the broader index — adjusting for health and education, not just output — often proposed to dethrone GDP.
choices: The Human Development Index
The Gini coefficient
Gross National Product
The CPI
recall.good: The Human Development Index. You know what a better goal would even look like. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing GDP is the wrong goal and you can't name what replaces it? The HDI is the headline. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — degrowth would hurt no one
moves.reply: It would hurt the poor; deny that and you concede his most humane point.

moves.label: Concede — growth must stay the goal
moves.reply: You let him keep the goalposts — and conceded the motion.

for.win: The Cornucopian throttles back. You held the floor — turning 'more' into 'enough', weighing the finite ceiling against the funding story, and narrowing the motion to the rich societies it was always about.
for.lose: The Cornucopian grins and guns the engine. To argue against endless growth you must know the evidence cold. Learn the cards and come back.

persona.name: The Degrowther
persona.intro: A rich society chasing more GDP is a fat man ordering another course. Enough is enough. Tell me why the rich world should keep growing.

rounds.attack: Endless growth on a finite planet is a delusion. A wealthy society should stop the treadmill and simply live.

moves.label: Turn it — growth isn't more stuff, it's better stuff
moves.land: You picture growth as more landfill. But long-run growth isn't piling up matter — it's productivity and technology: doing more with less. That's precisely what funds shorter hours, cleaner energy and longer, freer lives. Stopping it freezes the very tools that would lighten the load.
moves.reply: …growth as productivity, not tonnage. You turned the treadmill into a ladder. Hm.

recall.demand: In the Solow model, sustained growth in income per person comes mainly from which term — the 'A' in the equation?
choices: Total factor productivity
Capital accumulation
Population growth
Trade surplus
recall.good: Total factor productivity. You know growth is ideas, not stuff. Fine.
recall.miss: Arguing about growth and you can't name total factor productivity? It's the engine. Learn the card.

moves.label: Deny it — the planet isn't finite
moves.reply: It plainly has limits; deny them and you lose the room.

moves.label: Concede — yes, the rich should stop growing
moves.reply: Conceding the motion in round one? Then welcome to the steady state. Goodbye.

rounds.attack: But every extra point of GDP burns more of the world. Growth and a livable planet cannot coexist.

moves.label: Weigh the assumption — growth can split from resource use
moves.land: Weigh the buried premise: that GDP and material throughput are welded together. They aren't — economies already grow while cutting emissions in absolute terms. And halting growth locks in today's debts, pensions and an unfunded climate transition, with no slack left to fix anything.
moves.reply: Decoupling, plus the slack growth buys to fix things. …You weighed the constraint I keep assuming away. Fair.

recall.demand: Name the term for GDP rising while resource use and emissions fall in absolute terms.
choices: Absolute decoupling
The rebound effect
The Jevons paradox
Degrowth
recall.good: Absolute decoupling. You know the thing that has to be true — and increasingly is. Respect.
recall.miss: Arguing green growth and you can't name absolute decoupling? That's the whole bet. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — emissions can't ever fall with growth
moves.reply: Several economies already prove otherwise; denial sinks you.

moves.label: Outweigh — the planet always loses
moves.reply: Asserted, not argued. WHY must growth wreck the planet? Warrant, please.

rounds.attack: A rich country already has enough. Chasing more is greed dressed as prudence — the marginal gains are trivial.

moves.label: Steelman 'enough', then point at the unfinished world
moves.land: Granted — for the already-rich, the marginal point of GDP buys little extra happiness; I'll concede the diminishing returns at home. But 'enough' is static and the world isn't: growth funds the innovation that lifts the still-poor and pays for the energy transition. Even a sated society needs it to finance the future.
moves.reply: Conceding the diminishing returns and then pointing past the border. …That's the move I couldn't counter.

recall.demand: Which country's reforms lifted nearly 800 million people out of poverty — in millions, the proof of what growth delivers?
choices: About 800 million
About 80 million
About 8 million
About 200 million
recall.good: Eight hundred million. One country, one generation, the gift of growth. Floor's yours.
recall.miss: Arguing growth still matters and you don't know China lifted ~800 million? That's the headline. Learn it.

moves.label: Deny it — the marginal gains are huge at home
moves.reply: Above a point they're small; deny the evidence and you lose.

moves.label: Concede — the rich world has enough, stop
moves.reply: You conceded the motion. The Degrowther plants a tree in triumph.

against.win: The Degrowther sets down the seedling. You held the floor — turning growth into productivity, weighing decoupling against the finite-planet premise, and pointing the unfinished world past a sated society's border.
against.lose: The Degrowther smiles, unmoved. To argue for growth you must know what it actually is. Learn the cards and come back.
